title: The FUTON Stack — An Argument for Persistent Knowledge Infrastructure
text: The FUTON Stack — An Argument for Persistent Knowledge Infrastructure The futon stack is infrastructure for knowledge work that persists, compounds, and transfers—turning ephemeral problem-solving into durable, reusable artefacts. Most knowledge work disappears. You solve a problem, write some code, have an insight—and then it's gone, locked in your head or scattered across emails and notebooks. you want knowledge work to persist and compound rather than evaporate current tools treat each session as ephemeral; insights are not captured, patterns are not named, and reasoning is not checkable build layered infrastructure where everything is addressable, agents have principled perception-action loops, reasoning is checkable, and patterns transfer across domains compounding requires persistence, and transfer requires abstraction—the stack provides both FUTON1 provides graph memory where everything—text fragments, relationships, annotations—lives as addressable nodes that can be queried and linked. you need a foundation for persistent knowledge scattered files and databases do not support linking and querying store everything as graph nodes with typed edges addressable nodes are the prerequisite for all higher layers FUTON2 provides an active inference engine that gives agents a principled way to observe their environment, perceive what matters, and act—this same engine powers both the reasoning agents in futon3 and the cellular automata experiments in futon5. agents need to act in changing environments ad-hoc agent loops lack principled grounding implement observe-perceive-affect-policy-act loops with free energy minimization active inference provides a unified framework for perception and action FUTON3 handles the messy reality of human reasoning: arguments that are not formal proofs but still need to be checked, patterns that recur across problems, and the gap between how people actually think and what machines can verify. real reasoning is informal but still needs validation formal proof systems reject most human arguments build flexiformal pattern checking that validates structure without requiring full formalization checked informal arguments are more valuable than unchecked ones FUTON4 provides the editing environment where documents, patterns, and annotations share a common workspace—Arxana links fragments and scholia so you can see how ideas connect and evolve. knowledge workers need to edit and annotate linked content traditional editors treat documents as isolated files build a hypertext editor where fragments, links, and scholia coexist connected editing reveals structure that flat files hide FUTON5 collects design patterns for improvisation—not fixed procedures but flexible moves that transfer across domains. Wiring diagrams give these patterns a category-theoretic interpretation, and a transfer milestone proves that patterns developed in one domain (cellular automata) work in another (ant simulations). you want reusable patterns for improvisation informal patterns lack compositional semantics represent patterns as wiring diagrams with CT interpretation; prove transfer across domains compositional patterns can be developed once and applied many times FUTON6 builds a mathematics dictionary where informal reasoning patterns sit alongside formal proofs, making mathematical knowledge navigable rather than locked in textbooks. mathematical knowledge should be navigable and reusable textbooks are linear and proofs are opaque build a dictionary with informal arguments, cross-domain patterns, and domain-specific constructs named patterns at multiple levels make mathematics teachable and transferable FUTON7 applies these ideas to economic life. Hyperreal Enterprises operates as a seed institution testing transparent governance. Gravpad does to the web what street art does to cities—adding commentary and accountability information without requiring permission from those being made transparent. Scenario simulations let you prototype civic and economic structures before committing to them. economic and civic structures need transparency current systems obscure costs, relationships, and externalities build transparency infrastructure that does not require permission from those being made transparent accountability should not depend on voluntary disclosure The layers connect through shared infrastructure: graph memory stores everything, active inference provides the perception-action loop, pattern checking validates reasoning, and wiring diagrams transfer between domains. Cross-futon bridges make the stack cohere. f1 ──graph memory──→ f4 (Arxana stores documents as graph nodes) f2 ──AIF engine──→ f3 (fulab agents use observe-perceive-act loop) f2 ──AIF engine──→ f5 (MetaCA uses same infrastructure) f3 ──checked arguments──→ f6 (informal reasoning imports to dictionary) f5 ──wiring diagrams──→ f2 (transfer from MetaCA to ant simulation) f6 ──mathematical models──→ f7 (scenario simulations use growth models) layers must interoperate isolated layers become silos define explicit bridges with shared infrastructure coherence requires connection evidence[Seven futons with defined devmaps in holes/] evidence[Shared infrastructure: graph memory (f1), AIF engine (f2), MUSN transport (f3)] evidence[Transfer milestone demonstrates cross-domain pattern reuse (f5/P4)] evidence[Hyperreal operates as living prototype (f7/P0)] next[Validate integration points with end-to-end tests] next[Document more transfer examples beyond MetaCA→ants] next[Test stack with real knowledge workers outside the project] next[Write tutorials for each layer] :success-criteria pass[Knowledge persists across sessions] pass[Patterns transfer between domains] pass[Stack usable by people outside the project] fail[Layers remain isolated silos] :psr-example "Selected layered architecture because compounding requires persistence and transfer requires abstraction" :pur-template "Stack session, layers touched: {{layers}}, bridges crossed: {{bridges}}, artifacts persisted: {{count}}"

title: Every Resource Has a Bounded Lifecycle
text: Every Resource Has a Bounded Lifecycle Every entry in an Agency state atom must have a defined lifecycle with explicit creation, bounded retention, and guaranteed cleanup; fire-and-forget futures are not cleanup. A5-bounded: Every entry in every Agency state atom has a defined maximum lifetime. No atom may grow without bound during normal operation. Cleanup is deterministic: either lazy-on-read, periodic-sweep, or cascaded-on-parent-removal. Agency maintains six state atoms: secrets, acks, rendezvous-state, connected-agents, local-handlers, and pending-whistles. Most use future-based TTL cleanup that races with concurrent operations. The acks atom has no cleanup at all and grows without bound. You store transient state (secrets, promises, connection entries, rendezvous tracking) in an in-memory atom. Future-based cleanup (future (Thread/sleep ttl) (swap! atom dissoc key)) races with concurrent reads and writes. Between the sleep ending and the swap! executing, a concurrent operation may read the entry, begin work, and then find the entry gone. The acks atom is never cleaned. pending-whistles entries can be orphaned if the agent disconnects mid-flight. - Unbounded growth: acks atom accumulates 10k entries/day with no cleanup - Race cleanup: secret TTL future fires during concurrent ack validation; ack fails with "unknown secret" - Orphaned promise: agent disconnects; pending-whistle entry sits until timeout future fires (or forever if future was GC'd) - Late ack: rendezvous cleaned up; agent sends ack after cleanup; ack recorded in acks atom but not in rendezvous Every atom entry must have: 1. Created-at timestamp: when the entry was created. 2. TTL or expiry: maximum lifetime, after which the entry is invalid. 3. Cleanup mechanism: either (a) lazy cleanup on read (check TTL before returning), or (b) periodic sweep (scheduled task that removes expired entries), or (c) cascaded cleanup (when parent resource is removed, dependents are removed). 4. Bounded size: maximum number of entries, with eviction policy for overflow. 5. No fire-and-forget futures for cleanup: cleanup must be deterministic, not scheduled in a separate thread that races with operations. Specifically: - acks: clean up when the corresponding secret expires. - pending-whistles: clean up on agent disconnect cascade, not just on timeout. - rendezvous-state: clean up when all expected agents have acked or deadline passes, not deadline + arbitrary delay. - connected-agents: clean up triggers cascade to pending-whistles and rendezvous-state. Unbounded state atoms are memory leaks. Race-prone cleanup creates intermittent failures that are impossible to reproduce. A database table without a retention policy eventually fills the disk; an atom without cleanup eventually fills the heap. - 2026-02-01 9ea1b06: secret storage endpoints introduced with TTL-driven cleanup, establishing the "fire-and-forget future" cleanup pattern for transient state. - 2026-02-08 b14c9de: pending-whistles introduced as an atom with timeout cleanup via future (sleep + dissoc), creating an explicit orphan/timeout lifecycle that can race with in-flight operations. - 2026-02-08 9acf154: rendezvous-state introduced alongside acks recording; the design makes acks meaningful, but also increases the need for deterministic cleanup (acks, rendezvous, and pending requests must not leak or race). - evidence: measure atom sizes under sustained load (entries per hour per atom) - evidence: count orphaned entries (entries past TTL still in atom) - evidence: reproduce race between TTL cleanup future and concurrent operation - evidence-shape: {:atom/name :keyword, :entry/count :int, :entry/oldest-ms :int, :entry/ttl-ms :int, :cleanup/mechanism :keyword, :cleanup/race-window-ms :int, :orphan/count :int}

title: Every Message Gets a Receipt or an Explicit Failure
text: Every Message Gets a Receipt or an Explicit Failure Every message sent through Agency must produce either a delivery receipt or an explicit failure; silent send-and-hope is not acceptable. A0-delivery: No message send operation returns success unless the recipient has acknowledged receipt or the send has been confirmed at the transport layer. Failure to deliver produces an explicit error with agent-id, transport, and reason. Agency routes messages (bells, whistles, pages) to agents via three tiers: registry, local handlers, and WebSocket. Callers currently receive a boolean or a best-effort result with no delivery guarantee. You send a message to an agent and need to know whether it arrived, was processed, or failed. send-to-agent! returns false on failure but callers often ignore it; bell to "all" returns {:ok true} even if zero agents received it; MUSN posts use throw-exceptions false and never check HTTP status; ack HTTP calls don't verify response codes. The system treats "sent" as "delivered" and "no error" as "success." - Silent drop: message sent over WS but agent disconnected between send and receive - False success: HTTP post returns 503 but caller sees no error because exceptions are suppressed - Orphaned promise: whistle promise created but agent crashes before responding; promise leaks - {:throw-exceptions false} without status check - (catch Exception _ nil) in send paths - Returning boolean from send operations (true/false is not enough context) Require a delivery receipt for every message type: 1. Bell: secret-based ack proves reception. If no ack within deadline, emit explicit failure event with agent-id and reason. 2. Whistle: response proves delivery. Timeout produces explicit {:ok false :err "timeout" :agent-id aid} with no silent fallthrough. 3. HTTP posts (MUSN, forum): check response status. Non-2xx is a failure, not silence. 4. send-to-agent! must return a result type, not a boolean. Callers must handle the failure path. The delivery receipt is the analogue of a database write acknowledgment: the operation is not complete until the receipt is in hand. Without delivery receipts, the system confuses "sent" with "delivered" and "no exception" with "success." This makes failures invisible and debugging impossible. A telephone system without ring/busy/unreachable signals is not a telephone system. - 2026-02-01 9ea1b06: "test-bell-v2 with secret verification" adds a closed-loop receipt mechanism (secret retrieval + verification) explicitly to prove message reception rather than assuming it. - 2026-02-03 ad6bea1: "bell ack flow" extends the closed-loop idea into a broader bell/ack workflow, reinforcing that "sent" needed to become "verified". - 2026-02-08 b14c9de: rename page -> whistle to clarify the sync request/response contract and introduce an explicit timeout knob (AGENCY_WHISTLE_TIMEOUT_MS), pushing toward explicit failure over silent waiting. - 2026-02-08 9acf154: standup redesign notes "no reception guarantee" as a defect of the prior approach, and replaces it with a rendezvous + ack handshake. - evidence: audit every call to send-to-agent! and classify caller handling of false return - evidence: audit every HTTP post with :throw-exceptions false and verify status checks - evidence: measure delivery failure rate (bells sent vs acks received) per transport - evidence: track orphaned promises in pending-whistles atom over time - evidence-shape: {:message/id :string, :message/type :keyword, :agent/id :string, :transport :keyword, :sent/ts :string, :receipt/ts :string, :receipt/type :keyword, :failure/reason :string, :failure/ts :string, :latency-ms :int}

title: Keep Transport Identifiers Separate From LLM Session Identifiers
text: Keep Transport Identifiers Separate From LLM Session Identifiers Never overload identifiers across layers; transport IDs (forum thread, MUSN session, WS connection) must not be stored or used as LLM resume/session IDs, and LLM session IDs must not be treated as transport addresses. Futon3 passes many identifiers through Agency and peripherals: agent-id, forum thread-id, MUSN session-id, WebSocket session-id, LLM resume/thread id, bell secret-id, whistle request-id. Early Agency code used the same key (thread-id) for different meanings depending on call site. You add a new endpoint, peripheral, or bridge that must preserve continuity across tools and transports. Overloaded IDs create "accidental continuity" (resuming the wrong thing) and "accidental routing" (sending to the wrong destination). Silent corruption follows: state appears valid but refers to the wrong layer. Debugging is hard because logs show an ID but not its type. - Resume-id clobbered: forum thread-id overwrites LLM resume id, causing "resume" to start a new LLM context every time. - Ghost continuity: a WS session-id is treated as an LLM session and stored, creating persistent but meaningless state. - Debugging dead-end: logs show "thread-id=..." but you cannot tell whether it is a forum thread, an LLM thread, or a MUSN session. 1. Define and enforce a typed identifier vocabulary: - transport: forum-thread-id, musn-session-id, ws-connection-id - LLM continuity: resume-id (Codex/Claude thread), llm-session-id - protocol: secret-id, request-id, rendezvous-id 2. Store only LLM continuity identifiers in continuity state (e.g., :agent/current-thread-id). 3. Accept transport IDs only inside transport-specific payloads (e.g., under :forum or :musn), never as top-level "thread-id" that can be misread. 4. Log IDs with their type (key name) and the layer emitting them (transport/identity/invocation), so traces can be interpreted without guesswork. Identity in a distributed system is a graph of references; if edges are mislabeled, the system becomes internally consistent but externally wrong. This is an Identifier Garden problem: without stewardship, identifiers drift and get repurposed, breaking provenance and continuity. - 2026-01-31 466bc73 and 2026-01-31 b2fbb84: mission documents the concrete break: forum thread ids were used as LLM resume ids. - 2026-01-31 17c87b7: introduces :resume-id as distinct from forum thread-id in the payload and state update path, an explicit fix for identifier overloading. - 2026-01-29 0879d1f: peripheral spec draft makes "session-id transfer" a first-class hop mechanic, increasing the cost of ID confusion. - evidence: audit Agency endpoints for the presence of ambiguous keys like thread-id used in multiple meanings; target is zero ambiguous keys. - evidence: add a property test that generates payloads with forum-thread-id and resume-id and asserts they never swap or overwrite one another. - evidence-shape: {:id/type :keyword, :id/value :string, :layer :keyword, :operation :string, :agent/id :string, :ts :string}

title: Agency Invariant Set
text: Agency Invariant Set Agency must uphold six invariants — delivery, identity, atomicity, error hierarchy, debugging, and bounded resources — analogous to the I0-I4 framework in futon1a; every feature built on Agency inherits these guarantees or is built on sand. Agency is the messaging and coordination backbone for all futon agents (human and AI). It routes bells (async), whistles (sync), manages agent registration, and bridges to IRC/MUSN/forum. An audit revealed: 20+ silent error catches, three independent routing tiers with no consistency, unbounded state atoms, no delivery guarantees, and no specification. Features built on Agency (standup, PAR sessions, pair programming) inherit all of these deficiencies. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. A0-delivery (agency/delivery-receipt): Every message send operation returns either a delivery receipt or an explicit failure. No send may return success without confirmation from the transport layer. Proof: for every bell sent, an ack arrives or a timeout error is emitted. A1-identity (agency/single-routing-authority, agency/self-attribution): For any agent-id, exactly one routing entry exists at any time. Agents speak for themselves; the server never posts under an agent's identity. Proof: at no point do two tiers claim authority for the same agent-id. Support: agency/identifier-separation (typed IDs prevent routing/identity drift across layers). A2-atomicity (agency/state-atomicity): Every state transition completes fully or reverts with an explicit error. No transition may leave state partially updated. Proof: rollover never produces a nil session-id; corrupted state files are rejected, not silently defaulted. Support: agency/identifier-separation (continuity state stores LLM session IDs only; transport IDs cannot clobber them). A3-hierarchy (agency/loud-failure): Every error surfaces at the layer that caused it with agent-id, operation, and cause. No exception handler may discard an error without propagation or explicit recovery. Proof: zero instances of (catch Exception _ nil) in the codebase. A4-debugging: Any failure in Agency is diagnosable from logs within 10 minutes. Every error includes enough context (layer, agent-id, operation, timestamp, cause) for diagnosis. Proof: given a failure scenario, an operator can trace the cause using only Agency logs. A5-bounded (agency/bounded-lifecycle): Every entry in every state atom has a maximum lifetime. No atom grows without bound during normal operation. Proof: atom sizes remain stable under sustained load; no orphaned entries accumulate. Each invariant traces to a pattern (abstract) and must trace to: - Implementation: specific function(s) that enforce it - Test: specific test(s) that prove it - Evidence: specific metric(s) that monitor it Supporting patterns (non-invariants) that reduce common failure modes: - agency/identifier-separation supports A1 (identity) and A2 (atomicity) by preventing identifier overloading across layers. Current traceability (to be filled as implementation proceeds): | Invariant | Pattern | Implementation | Test | Evidence | | A0 | agency/delivery-receipt | src/futon3/agency/http.clj: send-to-agent!, handle-ring-bell, handle-whistle | test/futon3/agency/invariants/a0_delivery_test.clj | TBD | | A1 | agency/single-routing-authority | src/futon3/agency/http.clj: enforce-single-routing-authority! (watches over registry/local/ws stores) | test/futon3/agency/invariants/a1_identity_test.clj | TBD | | A2 | agency/state-atomicity | src/futon3/agency/service.clj: load-agent-state, save-agent-state!, update-agent-state!, roll-over-state! | test/futon3/agency/invariants/a2_atomicity_test.clj | TBD | | A3 | agency/loud-failure | src/futon3/agency/service.clj + src/futon3/agency/http.clj: status checks on :throw-exceptions false + elimination of (catch Exception _ nil) sites | test/futon3/agency/invariants/a3_loud_failure_test.clj | TBD | | A4 | (derived from A3) | (derived) A3 enforcement + log context conventions in http/service layers | test/futon3/agency/invariants/a3_loud_failure_test.clj | TBD | | A5 | agency/bounded-lifecycle | src/futon3/agency/http.clj: prune-acks/handle-ack; handle-get-secret TTL; kick-agent!/ws on-close cascades; secret cleanup cascades | test/futon3/agency/invariants/a5_bounded_test.clj | TBD | Agency is not different from a database just because it uses WebSockets instead of disk. A message that might arrive is not a message. A session-id that might be correct is not an identity. An error that might be logged is not an error. The invariants make these guarantees concrete and testable. - 2026-01-29 0879d1f and 2026-02-01 9a0f28d: peripheral specs and contract notes push toward routable, machine-readable invocation with explicit I/O and session continuity, which forces Agency to get identity/delivery/atomicity right. - 2026-01-31 466bc73 and 2026-01-31 b2fbb84: mission and invariants for session continuity document real failures: identifier conflation (forum thread-id vs LLM resume id) and rollover semantics that erase session identity. - 2026-02-07 fac9efb: "memory bifurcation" brief shows the split-brain failure mode when routing says "connected" but invocation says "no invoke-fn registered". - 2026-02-03 ad6bea1 and 2026-02-01 9ea1b06: bell/secret verification work is direct evidence that "sent" needed to become "receipt-proven". - 2026-02-08 169c4bc then 2026-02-08 9acf154: standup evolves from proxy collection to rendezvous + self-reporting, surfacing the identity and delivery invariants as practical necessities, not theory. - Fill traceability table as each invariant is implemented and tested. - Write proof tests for each invariant in test/futon3/agency/invariants/. - Add A0-A5 health checks to Agency startup (analogous to futon1a startup integrity gate). - Monitor invariant violations in production via evidence-shape metrics. - evidence-shape: {:invariant/id :keyword, :invariant/status :keyword, :proof/test-path :string, :proof/last-run :string, :proof/passed? :boolean, :implementation/files [:string], :violation/count :int, :violation/last :string}

title: Errors Surface at the Layer That Caused Them
text: Errors Surface at the Layer That Caused Them Every error in Agency must surface at the layer that caused it with enough context to diagnose; silent catch-and-swallow is never acceptable. A3-hierarchy: No exception handler in Agency may discard an error without either (a) returning an error result to the caller with layer, agent-id, and cause, or (b) executing an explicit recovery action that is logged with the original error context. Agency code contains 20+ instances of (catch Exception _ nil) or (catch Exception e (log! ...) false) across service.clj, invokes.clj, and http.clj. Corrupted state files load as defaults without warning. Subprocess parsing errors are skipped. Forum and MUSN post failures are swallowed. The log function itself swallows its own errors. An operation fails — network error, parse error, subprocess crash, file corruption, timeout. The current pattern catches exceptions at every boundary and converts them to nil, false, or logged-but-forgotten entries. Callers cannot distinguish "succeeded with empty result" from "failed silently." Operators cannot diagnose issues because the error was absorbed three layers below. - (catch Exception _ nil) — the canonical silent swallow - (catch Exception e (log! "error" {:err (.getMessage e)}) false) — logged but not propagated - {:throw-exceptions false} without (when-not (= 200 (:status resp)) ...) — HTTP error suppression Apply the error hierarchy from futon-theory/error-hierarchy to Agency: 1. Layer 0 (transport/durability): HTTP, WS, and file I/O errors surface as transport failures with status codes. 2. Layer 1 (identity): Agent not found, session-id mismatch surface as resolution failures. 3. Layer 2 (integrity): State corruption, partial rollover surface as integrity failures. 4. Layer 3 (invocation): Subprocess timeout, parse error, empty result surface as invocation failures. 5. Layer 4 (validation): Missing fields, bad request surface as validation failures. Every catch block must either: a. Propagate the error with context (layer, agent-id, operation, cause), OR b. Handle it with an explicit recovery action that is itself logged. Catch-and-ignore is removed from the codebase entirely. - grep for (catch Exception _) and (catch Throwable _) — zero allowed - grep for {:throw-exceptions false} — each must be followed by status check - grep for (log! ... false) — log-and-return-false is not error handling Silent errors make debugging impossible. When a standup fails and no agent responds, the operator has no trail: was the bell not sent? Was it sent but not received? Was it received but the agent crashed? Was the response generated but MUSN was down? Without layer-attributed errors, every failure investigation starts from zero. - 2026-01-31 466bc73 and 2026-01-31 b2fbb84: the "Make Agency Work Properly" mission is, in effect, a loud-failure postmortem: multiple user-visible failures were traced back to swallowed/blurred errors and identifier confusion that did not surface at the right layer. - 2026-02-08 9acf154: standup redesign calls out the prior approach as lacking a reception guarantee; that is a loud-failure requirement (explicit failure when reception is not proven), not just a protocol preference. - current src/futon3/agency/service.clj: load-agent-state catches EDN parse errors and returns nil, which collapses integrity failures into "empty state" with no operator-visible signal. - evidence: count all silent catch blocks in agency/ directory; target is zero - evidence: classify each catch block by layer (transport, identity, integrity, invocation, validation) - evidence: measure time-to-diagnosis for a sample failure before and after fix - evidence-shape: {:error/layer :keyword, :error/operation :string, :error/agent-id :string, :error/cause :string, :error/recovery :keyword, :error/propagated? :boolean, :error/ts :string}

title: Agents Speak for Themselves
text: Agents Speak for Themselves An agent's output must be posted by the agent itself under its own identity; the server must never post on behalf of an agent. A1-attribution: Every message posted to a shared channel under an agent's identity must originate from that agent's process. The server may not construct, transform, or relay agent output under the agent's identity. The first standup implementation had the server whistle each agent, collect responses, and POST them to MUSN as that agent. The server impersonated agent identities. This violated I1 (identity) from the agent contract: every change must be linked to the agent that made it, with no anonymous or proxy mutations. You need an agent's output to appear in a shared channel (IRC, MUSN, forum). The server has access to agent identities and could post on their behalf, making the code simpler. But this creates false attribution: the message appears to come from the agent, but the agent never authored or approved it. If the agent's invocation returned an error, the server might post the error as if the agent said it. If the server's MUSN post fails, the agent has no way to know its update was lost. - Server collects whistle responses and POSTs to MUSN as each agent - Server registers a context-free subprocess under an existing agent's identity - Server reformats or summarizes agent output before posting it as the agent The server's role is coordination, not content relay: 1. The server creates the rendezvous, sends the bell, tracks acks. 2. Each agent independently generates its output and posts it under its own identity. 3. The server may post as "agency" (its own identity) for announcements. 4. If an agent cannot post (no MUSN access, transport failure), the failure is attributed to the agent, not hidden by the server. This applies to all output channels: MUSN, forum, IRC, CRDT documents. Proxy posting breaks the audit trail. When output appears under agent X's identity but was posted by the server, you cannot distinguish between "X said this" and "the server said X said this." In incident review, this ambiguity makes root cause analysis unreliable. A meeting transcript where one person takes notes for everyone is not the same as each person signing their own statement. - 2026-02-08 169c4bc: /agency/standup initially implemented as "whistle all agents and collect responses", putting the server in the position to relay agent content as an intermediary. - 2026-02-08 9acf154: standup redesign explicitly rejects the prior proxy approach as an identity violation and moves to "agent self-reporting": each agent acks, invokes itself, and posts to MUSN under its own identity. - 2026-01-31 b2fbb84: mission notes define the first principle that Agency is a continuity layer, not "the agent itself", which aligns with self-attribution (coordination vs content authorship). - evidence: audit all MUSN/forum posts and verify posting identity matches originating process - evidence: track cases where server-posted content was attributed to an agent - evidence-shape: {:message/id :string, :message/channel :keyword, :message/author-id :string, :message/origin-process :string, :attribution/valid? :boolean, :attribution/proxy? :boolean}

title: One Agent, One Routing Path, One Source of Truth
text: One Agent, One Routing Path, One Source of Truth Each agent-id must resolve to exactly one routing path at any given time; the routing authority must be a single source of truth, not a priority cascade across independent stores. A1-identity: For any agent-id, at most one routing entry exists at any time. The entry specifies the authoritative transport, session-id, and connection handle. No other store may independently claim to route messages for that agent-id. Agency routes messages through three tiers: agent-registry (subprocess invocation), local-handlers (in-JVM Drawbridge), and connected-agents (WebSocket). These are independent atoms checked in priority order. An agent can exist in multiple tiers simultaneously with different session-ids, capabilities, and liveness states. You need to send a message to an agent and expect consistent behavior regardless of which tier handles it. The same agent-id can appear in registry (session-id "S1"), local-handlers (no session-id), and connected-agents (session-id "S2") simultaneously. Whistle routing picks the first match (registry > local > WS) but the others aren't consulted or cleaned up. Disconnect from WS doesn't remove registry or local-handler entries. The result: stale routing, session-id divergence, and messages going to dead tiers while live ones are ignored. - Session split: registry has session S1, WS has session S2; whistle goes to S1 (stale) - Ghost routing: agent disconnected from WS but still in registry; messages invoke dead subprocess - Duplicate delivery: agent in both local-handlers and WS; bell sent via local handler AND WS - (distinct (concat registry local ws)) as the agent list — hides conflicts - Priority cascade without eviction — checking tiers in order without ensuring mutual exclusion - Disconnect that only cleans one tier — WS on-close that ignores registry and local-handlers Establish a single routing registry that is the sole authority for agent resolution: 1. One atom, one entry per agent-id. The entry specifies: transport type (registry/local/ws), connection handle, session-id, registered-at, last-active, capabilities. 2. Registration replaces: when an agent registers via any transport, it evicts any existing entry for that agent-id. No silent coexistence. 3. Disconnect cascades: when a transport drops, the entry is removed. If a whistle is in flight, it gets an explicit failure. 4. Session-id is authoritative: one session-id per agent-id at any time. Updated atomically on registration or invocation. 5. connected-agent-ids returns only agents from the single registry, not a concat of three stores. Multiple independent stores for the same identity create split-brain: each store has a partial, potentially stale view. Priority cascading hides the conflict rather than resolving it. A database with three independent indexes that disagree on which row is current is a broken database. - 2026-02-07 fac9efb: "memory bifurcation" brief documents WS-delivered messages that never reach the live terminal session, because "connected" is not the same as "invokable". - 2026-02-07 84ac0e0: unified agent registry introduced explicitly to address multi-tier routing and bring invocation under one authority. - 2026-02-04 9a73783: /agency/kick endpoint added to disconnect stale agents, indicating stale routing entries were a recurring operational failure mode. - 2026-02-04 92fe6a1 and 2026-02-04 bb2e3a7: session-id tracking for WS connections added and then fixed, highlighting that session identity was drifting outside a single source of truth. - evidence: count agents that exist in multiple tiers simultaneously during normal operation - evidence: track session-id divergence across tiers for the same agent-id - evidence: measure time between WS disconnect and registry/local cleanup (currently: infinite) - evidence-shape: {:agent/id :string, :routing/transport :keyword, :routing/session-id :string, :routing/registered-at :string, :routing/last-active :string, :conflict/tiers [:keyword], :conflict/session-ids [:string]}

title: State Transitions Are All-or-Nothing
text: State Transitions Are All-or-Nothing Agent state transitions (registration, rollover, session update) must complete fully or fail without partial effects; corrupted or partial state must be detected and rejected, not silently accepted. A2-atomicity: Every agent state transition either completes fully (all fields updated, persisted, and confirmed) or reverts to the prior state with an explicit error. No transition may leave state in a partially-updated condition. Agency persists agent state to .edn files. Rollover clears session-id to nil (documented bug). State loading silently returns defaults on parse error. Registration can succeed in one tier while failing to clean up another. These are all partial-state failures: the system is left in an inconsistent state with no signal. An agent's state must change — new session, rollover, registration, disconnect. Multi-step state transitions can fail midway. Rollover currently: (1) summarizes context, (2) clears session-id to nil, (3) should create new session but doesn't. If step 1 succeeds and step 3 fails, the agent has lost its session with no recovery. State file corruption is treated as "no state" rather than "corrupted state." - Nil session: rollover clears session-id but doesn't create new one; agent loses all context - Silent corruption: state file has truncated EDN; load returns nil; agent starts fresh with no warning - Tier desync: agent registered in authority but connection handle is stale; messages route to dead handle - (swap! state assoc :session-id nil) as "clear" — nil is not a valid session state - (catch Exception _ nil) on state load — corruption becomes invisible - Multi-step registration without rollback — register in tier A, fail to clean tier B Apply all-or-nothing semantics to every state transition: 1. Rollover: summarize → create new session → update state atomically. If any step fails, restore previous state and emit error. 2. Registration: register in authority → confirm registration → begin routing. If confirmation fails, remove registration. 3. State persistence: write to temp file → fsync → rename to target. If rename fails, temp file is evidence of interrupted write. 4. State loading: validate structure on read. If validation fails, emit integrity error with file path and content hash. Do not silently fall back to defaults. 5. Session-id updates: swap! with compare-and-set semantics. If the agent-id has been evicted between read and write, the update fails explicitly. Partial state transitions are the hardest bugs to diagnose because the system looks almost correct. A session-id of nil is not "no session" — it is "corrupted state from failed rollover." Silently loading defaults after corruption masks data loss. A database that silently returns empty on corruption is worse than one that refuses to start. - 2026-01-31 466bc73: mission "Make Agency Work Properly" documents two atomicity breaks: rollover wiping the active session id, and forum thread ids overwriting LLM resume ids. - 2026-01-31 17c87b7: code change introduces :resume-id as distinct from forum thread-id and removes "Agency completed" prefixes; it also adds rollover pending flags, indicating state transitions were previously leaving the system in partial/inconsistent states. - current src/futon3/agency/service.clj: load-agent-state catches parse errors and returns nil, which is silent corruption acceptance rather than an integrity failure. - evidence: audit rollover path for atomicity; trace each swap! and verify all-or-nothing - evidence: inject corrupted .edn file and verify system behavior (should fail loud, not silent) - evidence: count nil session-ids in production state files - evidence-shape: {:transition/type :keyword, :transition/agent-id :string, :transition/started-at :string, :transition/completed? :boolean, :transition/rolled-back? :boolean, :state/before :map, :state/after :map, :error/cause :string}

title: Budget Bounds Exploration
text: Budget Bounds Exploration Exploration without limits drifts; any search needs a budget that forces commitment or escalation. An agent explores options—spatial locations, semantic regions, conversation branches, solution candidates. The agent must balance discovering new possibilities against making progress on known paths. Unbounded exploration leads to wander: the agent keeps looking without ever committing, exhausting resources without output. Assign explicit budgets (time, steps, tokens, reads) to exploratory phases and define reset rules. When budget nears exhaustion, force a decision: commit to best-so-far, escalate to a supervisor, or explicitly expand scope with justification. Budgets convert open-ended search into bounded decisions, making progress measurable and preventing silent resource drain. `fuclaude` enforces `--explore-limit`, and `src/futon3/fulab/hud.clj` caps candidates with `pattern-limit`. - Identify unbounded loops in your agent (e.g., "keep searching until found"). - Add budget parameters with sensible defaults and observable countdowns. - Design escalation paths for when budgets expire without resolution and log the choice taken. - Add explicit time/token/tool-call budgets for fulab sessions and log budget exhaustion decisions in lab events.

title: Commitment Varies With Confidence
text: Commitment Varies With Confidence How strongly to commit to a choice should depend on how certain the agent is. An agent must choose among options with varying degrees of uncertainty. The agent wants to balance exploiting known-good options against exploring uncertain alternatives. Fixed commitment strength fails both ways: always committing hard misses better options; always hedging prevents progress. Maintain a commitment parameter (temperature, precision, confidence threshold) that modulates how decisively the agent acts. Couple it to uncertainty signals with explicit thresholds: low confidence -> explore or pause; medium confidence -> hedge or seek confirmation; high confidence -> commit and execute. Variable commitment adapts behavior to epistemic state. The agent exploits when it knows enough and explores (or asks) when it doesn't. `src/futon3/fulab/hud.clj` computes `tau` from candidate spread and `precision/prior`, and `dev/lab-session-report.clj` logs tau/prediction-error updates. - Identify how your agent currently commits to choices (is it always the same strength?). - Add uncertainty tracking that can modulate commitment and log threshold crossings. - Tune the coupling: what uncertainty level triggers exploration vs. exploitation vs. pause? - Tie tau/confidence thresholds to explicit actions (ask/hedge/commit) and log crossings in lab sessions.

title: Coordination Has Cost
text: Coordination Has Cost Involving other agents or humans has overhead; factor it into decisions. An agent can work alone or involve others (other agents, human supervisors, external services). The agent wants to leverage external capabilities or get authoritative answers. Coordination is not free: it takes time, consumes attention, introduces latency, and may require context transfer. Treating it as free leads to over-reliance or spamming. Model coordination as an action with explicit cost (latency, tokens, human attention units). Include this cost in decision-making: sometimes working with partial local knowledge is better than waiting for external input, unless the risk of error is higher than the coordination cost. Cost-aware coordination prevents both under-use (never asking for help when stuck) and over-use (constant interruption). It respects the resources of collaborators. - Inventory coordination actions your agent can take (ask human, call service, delegate to agent). - Assign cost estimates to each and include them in action selection. - Track actual coordination costs and update estimates based on experience. - Add coordination cost fields to fulab session events (latency, token cost) and use them in action selection.

title: Environment Over Optimization
text: Environment Over Optimization Build environments that select for viability, not agents that hit targets. You are designing how agents will operate, learn, and evolve over time. You want agents that can adapt to changing conditions and improve through experience rather than being brittle to novelty. Optimization toward fixed targets finds local maxima; agents become overfit to benchmarks and fail when conditions shift. The "best" agent for yesterday's metric may be the worst for tomorrow's reality. Focus on creating environments where viable behaviors can emerge, persist, and be selected: provide trails that enable learning, budgets that create selection pressure, evidence requirements that filter confabulation, and handoff mechanisms that let successful patterns propagate. Let agent quality emerge from environmental constraints rather than direct tuning. Viable environments enable open-ended evolution. Instead of one optimal agent, you get a population of approaches that can be compared, combined, and adapted. The environment becomes the product, not any single agent. Fulab exposes a shared pattern catalog plus selection environment (`resources/sigils/patterns-index.tsv`, `src/futon3/fulab/hud.clj`) and PUR/PSR templates (`src/futon3/fulab/pattern_competence.clj`). - Audit whether your agent design is optimizing for metrics or creating conditions for viability. - Identify environmental features that create selection pressure (budgets, evidence requirements, scope bounds). - Design for variation: can different agents or approaches coexist and compete in your environment? - Track what emerges rather than what you planned; let the environment surface surprises. - Persist pattern outcome metrics and feed them back into AIF priors to increase selection pressure over time.

title: Escalation Cost vs Risk
text: Escalation Cost vs Risk Escalate when expected error cost exceeds coordination cost. An agent must choose between acting locally and involving others. A decision could carry material risk or irreversible impact. Coordination costs discourage escalation, while risk-blind escalation wastes time on low-stakes work. Estimate risk cost (impact x likelihood) and compare it to coordination cost. Escalate when risk cost exceeds a defined threshold, and log the comparison basis. This preserves speed on low-stakes actions while protecting high-stakes decisions. - Define risk categories and default impact scales for your domain. - Calibrate escalation thresholds with real incidents. - Log escalation decisions alongside their risk and cost estimates. - Classify fulab tool actions by risk (read/edit/network) and log the escalation decision before enabling `--allow-edits` or `--yolo`.

title: Evidence Over Assertion
text: Evidence Over Assertion Claims require grounding; an agent that asserts without evidence cannot be audited or trusted. An agent makes claims about what it did, what it found, or what is true. The agent's outputs need to be verifiable by other agents, humans, or future selves. Assertions without anchors are indistinguishable from confabulation. Observers cannot tell if the agent is reporting reality or generating plausible-sounding noise. Require every substantive claim to point to evidence: a file path, a trace event, a test result, a quotation. If evidence is unavailable, emit the claim as provisional with an expiry and a verification path. Make "unsupported claim" a detectable violation, not just a style preference. Evidence transforms agent output from "trust me" to "check this." It enables verification, correction, and cumulative trust-building. Fulab PUR/PSR templates require anchors/certificates (`src/futon3/fulab/pattern_competence.clj`), and claim verification is enforced via `fulab-pattern-claim` + `fulab-pattern-check`. - Identify claim types in your agent's output (facts, completions, diagnoses). - For each type, define what counts as adequate evidence. - Add validation that flags claims missing their evidence anchors and records provisional claims separately. - Auto-attach tool/file anchors from `lab/tool-uses` to PUR/PSR records and surface missing evidence in `fulab-session-report`.

title: Handoff Preserves Context
text: Handoff Preserves Context When passing work to another agent or future self, transfer enough state that the receiver doesn't restart from scratch. An agent's work will be continued by another agent, a human, or the same agent in a future session. Continuity matters: the work is incremental, context is expensive to rebuild, or progress would be lost. Without explicit handoff, successors face cold starts: they repeat discoveries, miss constraints, or contradict prior decisions. Define a handoff record that captures: current state hypothesis, decisions made and why, open questions, scope boundaries, next actions, evidence/trail anchors, and any provisional-claim ledger. Emit it at session end or when transferring to another agent. Handoffs convert ephemeral session state into persistent project state. They enable distributed and asynchronous work without context collapse. Fulab exports session context to `lab/raw`, `lab/stubs`, and `lab/trace` (`dev/lab-export-claude.clj`), plus summaries via `fulab-summary` and `fulab-session-report`. - Identify handoff points in your agent's lifecycle (session end, escalation, delegation). - Define what context is essential vs. nice-to-have for each handoff type. - Test handoffs by having a fresh agent resume and measuring ramp-up cost. - Extend lab stubs/summaries to capture open questions, scope boundaries, and provisional claims for resumption.

title: Hypothetical Proof Architecture
text: Hypothetical Proof Architecture Before investing effort in a proof path, sketch multiple complete proof architectures as wiring diagrams with explicit node status (solid/open/blocked). Triage immediately to focus effort on the most promising path. You have a theorem to prove with multiple plausible approaches. Each approach has several steps, some established and some open. The temptation is to start with the "obvious" or "natural" approach and push until stuck. There are 3+ plausible proof paths, each with multiple steps. Some steps are established results, some are open problems, and some may be blocked by known obstructions. The risk profile of each path (number of open steps, their independence, known difficulties) varies significantly. Sketching architectures is upfront cost. For problems with one clear approach, it's overkill. Only invest in this when the proof landscape is genuinely multi-path and the cost of pursuing a dead end is high (weeks of work, not hours). - Architecture bias: sketching only 2-3 paths and missing the best one. Cast the net wide initially; narrow after triage. - False "blocked" assessment: marking a path as blocked based on a surface reading of an obstruction, when the obstruction has a workaround. Verify blocks carefully. - Triage paralysis: spending too long comparing paths instead of working on the best one. The triage should take hours, not days. 1. For each plausible proof path, draw a complete wiring diagram from hypotheses to conclusion. 2. Mark each node as: solid (established), open (needs work), or blocked (known obstruction). 3. Kill blocked paths immediately. 4. Compare open paths on: (a) number of open nodes, (b) whether open nodes are sequential (each depends on the previous) or parallel (independent), (c) whether any open node is a known hard problem. 5. Prioritize paths with fewer open nodes, parallel structure, and no known-hard sub-problems. Sequential open obstacles multiply risk (if any one fails, the entire path fails). Parallel open sub-goals reduce risk (any one success may suffice). A path with one open node is strictly better than a path with three sequential open nodes, even if the single node is harder, because success is binary: one hard question has the same risk profile as three easy questions in series but is easier to focus on. P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): 5 hypothetical proof architectures (H1-H5) were sketched for the S obligation. Two (H3, H5) were immediately killed (codim-2 gap fails for reflections; Gauss-Bonnet kills Fowler in odd dim). One (H2) was deprioritized (3 sequential obstacles with structural headwinds). The winner (H1, rotation route) was not the "obvious" continuation but had the best risk profile: one open question (lattice existence) with no known blocker, plus two parallel S-branch options. next[Sketch 3-5 complete proof architectures as wiring diagrams.] next[Mark node status: solid, open, blocked.] next[Kill blocked paths, deprioritize sequential-obstacle paths.] next[Focus on the path with fewest independent open nodes.]

title: Intent Handshake Is Binding
text: Intent Handshake Is Binding A run should not start until the agent has restated and bound the intent and scope. An agent is about to begin a session or new turn. The system needs a reliable record of what the agent believes it is doing. If intent only lives in the prompt or UI, it drifts: agents reinterpret mid-run without explicit renegotiation. Require a handshake that echoes intent, scope, constraints, and success criteria, and record an acknowledgment. Changes to intent or scope require an explicit renegotiation event before further actions. Binding intent makes the run auditable and prevents silent goal drift. Fulab HUD prompts require an intent restatement (`src/futon3/fulab/hud.clj`), and `fuclaude --intent` passes intent into the HUD. - Add an intent-handshake event to the session start protocol. - Block tool actions until the handshake is logged. - Record intent changes as first-class events with rationale. - Emit an explicit intent-handshake event in lab sessions and enforce it before tool calls.

title: Pause Is Not Failure
text: Pause Is Not Failure Stopping to request clarification or expanded scope is a valid action, not a defect. An agent encounters ambiguity, uncertainty, or boundary conditions during execution. The agent cannot proceed confidently without information or authorization it doesn't have. Agents that never pause either over-commit (bulldozing through uncertainty) or silently drift (making up answers). Both erode trust. Treat "pause and ask" as a first-class action with defined triggers: ambiguous requirements, scope boundary reached, confidence below threshold, resource budget near exhaustion. Emit pause events with context for resumption (reason, missing info, requested decision, scope impact, confidence/budget snapshot). Pausing surfaces uncertainty to those who can resolve it. An agent that pauses appropriately is more trustworthy than one that always "succeeds." - Define explicit pause triggers for your agent (don't rely on ad-hoc judgment). - Design pause events that carry enough context for efficient resumption. - Track pause frequency as a diagnostic: too many suggests unclear scope; zero suggests over-confidence. - Add pause events to fulab sessions with reason/confidence/budget snapshots and a resume hook.

title: Provisional Claims Ledger
text: Provisional Claims Ledger Unsupported claims must be tracked, timeboxed, and resolved. An agent must sometimes act before evidence is available. The agent needs to continue despite missing confirmation. Treating provisional claims as facts hides uncertainty and undermines trust. Record provisional claims in a ledger with fields (claim, reason, evidence needed, expiry, owner). Require each entry to be resolved to confirmed or retracted, and surface unresolved items during handoff. A ledger turns uncertainty into actionable follow-up rather than silent drift. - Add a lightweight ledger store (file or trace event) for provisional claims. - Define expiry windows and resolution statuses. - Include the ledger summary in handoff records. - Implement a fulab provisional-claims ledger with expiry/status fields and surface unresolved items in session reports.

title: Reduction to Kernel
text: Reduction to Kernel Reduce a complex open problem to the smallest possible missing lemma with explicit hypotheses, then record it as a named conjecture. The reduction itself is proved work; the named conjecture becomes a precise handoff target. You have been working on a proof and have closed most cases or steps. The remaining gap is hard but may be expressible as a single statement with clear hypotheses and conclusion. The proof is mostly complete: the structure is understood, most cases are closed, and the remaining difficulty is localizable to a specific mathematical statement. The statement can be formulated with explicit hypotheses that are already proved or assumed from the problem setup. The reduction must be rigorous. "It would be enough to prove X" is not a reduction unless you have proved that X actually implies the desired conclusion. Also: the kernel should be genuinely minimal — if it contains unnecessary hypotheses or can be split into independent parts, simplify further. - False reduction: the kernel doesn't actually imply the conclusion. Prove the reduction rigorously. - Over-specified kernel: too many hypotheses, some unnecessary. Simplify until each hypothesis is used in the reduction proof. - Under-specified kernel: the kernel is true but insufficient. Check that the reduction covers all cases. 1. Formulate the missing lemma with numbered hypotheses (H1, H2, ...) and a conclusion. 2. Prove the reduction: show that the hypotheses are satisfiable from the problem setup and that the conclusion implies the target theorem. 3. Check each hypothesis: is it already proved, or does it need work? Mark status. 4. Give the conjecture a name (GPL-H, L2*, etc.) and record it in the proof status document. 5. Include any numerical evidence that supports the conjecture. A named conjecture with explicit hypotheses is qualitatively different from "the proof is stuck." It converts an open problem into a precise target that can be: (a) worked on by a different agent with fresh perspective, (b) recognized by someone who knows the relevant technique, (c) connected to existing results via the explicit hypotheses, (d) empirically tested. The reduce phase (all the work that leads to the kernel) is always tractable; the kernel phase may not be — but the reduce phase is still valuable because it converts "hard problem" into "hard problem minus everything tractable." P6 epsilon-light subsets (futon6, Feb 2026): the full proof (650+ lines) was reduced to GPL-H — a single operator-valued averaging statement with 4 explicit hypotheses (H1: light edges, H2: core regularity, H3: barrier-valid prefix, H4: residual size) and one conclusion (min_v ‖Y_t(v)‖ ≤ θ). A sharper reduction showed that L2* alone (score control) implies the theorem, without needing L3 (drift control). Named conjecture + proved reduction + 2353 trajectory numerical evidence. P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): the S obligation was reduced to a single lattice-existence question: do arithmetic uniform lattices in Isom(H^{2k+1}) contain order-2 rotational involutions? This is a number-theoretic question independent of the topology/surgery machinery. next[Formulate the missing lemma with explicit hypotheses.] next[Prove the reduction (hypotheses → target theorem).] next[Name the conjecture and record in proof status.] next[Gather numerical evidence for or against.]

title: Scope Before Action
text: Scope Before Action Declare the territory before entering it; unbounded scope makes progress unmeasurable. An agent is about to begin work on a task that could touch many things. The agent needs to make progress that can be verified and bounded. Without declared scope, "done" is undefined, side effects are unpredictable, and observers cannot tell if the agent is on track or wandering. Before substantive action, state the scope: what files, concepts, or regions are in-bounds; what is explicitly out-of-bounds; what the exit condition is. Treat scope violations as requiring explicit expansion, not silent drift. Scope defines the territory; budgets and pauses govern what happens inside it. Declared scope makes progress measurable, side effects auditable, and completion definable. It also protects the broader system from unintended changes. Fulab HUD prompts require a pre-action plan (`src/futon3/fulab/hud.clj`), and scope boundaries are spelled out in `CLAUDE.md`. - Add scope declaration to your agent's initialization or planning phase. - Log scope boundaries and check actions against them. - Design a scope-expansion protocol for when legitimate work requires broadening. - Record explicit in/out-of-scope fields in fulab session metadata and log scope-expansion events.

title: Sense-Deliberate-Act Cycle
text: Sense-Deliberate-Act Cycle Structure every agent cycle as three distinct phases: gather input, reason about options, commit to action. An agent operates in an environment where it must repeatedly choose what to do next. The agent needs to make progress on a goal while responding to a changing environment. Rushing to act without sensing leads to blind thrashing; sensing without acting leads to analysis paralysis; acting without deliberation leads to incoherent behavior. Enforce a rhythm: first gather relevant observations, then weigh options against goals and constraints, then commit to a single action before the next cycle. Make each phase explicit and bounded, and check scope, budget, and confidence gates at phase boundaries. The three-phase structure prevents both impulsive drift and endless deliberation, and makes the agent's reasoning inspectable at phase boundaries. Fulab HUD prompts force deliberate candidate review before acting (`src/futon3/fulab/hud.clj`), and the session report tracks selection and outcome phases (`dev/lab-session-report.clj`). - Identify where your agent conflates phases (e.g., acting while still gathering input). - Add explicit phase markers to logs or traces so observers can see the rhythm. - Tune phase durations based on task urgency and uncertainty. - Emit explicit sense/deliberate/act markers in fulab session events and surface them in reports.

title: State Is Hypothesis
text: State Is Hypothesis Treat internal state as a working hypothesis about the world, not ground truth. An agent maintains beliefs about its environment, progress, and goals. The agent needs to act under uncertainty and update its understanding as new information arrives. Treating state as certain leads to brittleness when observations contradict expectations; the agent either ignores evidence or fails catastrophically. Represent state as revisable hypotheses with associated confidence. When observations conflict with state, update the hypothesis rather than defending it. Track what would falsify current beliefs. Hypothesis-framed state makes the agent self-correcting: surprises trigger learning rather than denial or breakdown. Fulab PSR forecasts in `src/futon3/fulab/pattern_competence.clj` and belief updates in `dev/lab-session-report.clj` treat state as revisable (prediction error, tau updates). - Audit your agent's state representation for implicit certainty assumptions. - Add a "surprise" signal when observations diverge from expectations. - Design update rules that revise state proportionally to evidence strength. - Emit explicit surprise/contradiction events when outcomes diverge from PSR forecasts and track hypothesis confidence.

title: Student Dispatch
text: Student Dispatch Dispatch an agent as a student-explorer, not a junior-developer-verifier. Give them the problem context, what's been tried and why it failed, candidate directions to explore, and a structured report format. Let them discover rather than confirm. You have a research problem with multiple unexplored directions. You could hand each direction to an agent (Codex, another Claude instance, a human collaborator) for parallel exploration. The temptation is to specify exactly what to compute and what answer to expect — but this discards the agent's ability to discover surprises. The remaining work involves genuine exploration (multiple approaches, unknown outcomes) rather than rote verification (check that X equals Y). The dispatched agent has the capability to reason about the problem, not just execute a script. Unrestricted exploration wastes time. "Go think about this problem" is too vague. The student needs: (1) what's known, (2) what's been tried and failed with explicit reasons, (3) candidate directions with rationale, (4) what NOT to try, and (5) a report format. The negative knowledge (what not to try) is as important as the positive — it prevents the student from repeating dead ends that took the advisor hours to discover. - Too little context: student wastes time rediscovering known results. - Too much prescription: student confirms rather than explores. - No report format: student returns unstructured prose that's hard to integrate. - Missing dead ends: student repeats the advisor's failed approaches. - Overloaded dispatch: giving 10 directions when 2-3 is the right scope per agent. Structure the dispatch as: 1. **Context**: The problem statement and what's been proved so far. Enough for the student to understand the landscape without reading every prior document. 2. **Dead ends with reasons**: Approaches that were tried and WHY they failed. Not just "SOS didn't work" but "SOS is structurally blocked because the interior zero forces all multipliers to vanish." This is where structural-obstruction-as- theorem and exhaustion-as-theorem pay off — they compress dead ends into transmissible theorems. 3. **Directions to explore**: 2-4 candidate approaches, each with a sentence on why it might work. The student may pivot based on findings — that's fine. 4. **Report format**: What to come back with. Not pass/fail but structured findings: what was tried, what happened, what surprised, what new dead ends were discovered, what partial results were obtained. 5. **Success criteria**: What would constitute progress. "Find a universal c_0 >= 0.01" is better than "prove the theorem." Partial success is success. A verification dispatch ("confirm X") caps the return at 1 bit: yes or no. An exploration dispatch ("investigate X") can return discoveries, new dead ends, partial results, unexpected connections, and reformulations. The student may find something the advisor didn't think to look for. The negative-knowledge transfer prevents wasted work while the open-ended framing permits serendipity. P4 n=4 Stam inequality (futon6, Feb 2026): Codex was dispatched in verification mode ("confirm these eigenvalues, verify this identity"). Returned pass/fail. Separately, Codex was dispatched in exploration mode for PHCpack — "find all critical points of this system" — and returned 12 in-domain CPs with full case classification, discovering the mixed_volume=0 issue independently. The exploration dispatch produced richer results per unit of effort. P6 epsilon-light subsets: the Claude→Codex handoff note contained dead ends (6 technique failures with reasons) and candidate directions (BSS greedy, expander decomposition, structural analysis). This is the right format for student dispatch; the missing piece was framing it as "go explore these" rather than "verify my claims." next[Write the dispatch note: context, dead ends, directions, report format.] next[Send one direction per agent if parallelizing.] next[On return: integrate findings, update the dead-end list, re-dispatch if needed.]

title: Trail Enables Return
text: Trail Enables Return Leave traces that allow backtracking; an agent that can't retrace its path can't recover from mistakes. An agent navigates through states, decisions, or locations over time. The agent may need to undo actions, revisit prior states, or learn from dead ends. Without a trail, the agent cannot distinguish "unexplored" from "explored and rejected," leading to repeated mistakes or inability to recover. Record a trail of moves, decisions, and state transitions with minimal fields (time, state snapshot, decision, action, evidence, reversibility). Make the trail queryable so the agent (or its successors) can backtrack, detect loops, and learn from history. Trails convert ephemeral navigation into persistent structure. They enable learning, debugging, and graceful recovery. Fulab session exports write `lab/trace/<session-id>.org` and `lab/raw` (`dev/lab-export-claude.clj`), and `fuclaude` supports `--resume`/`--continue` runs. - Decide what granularity of trail your agent needs (every step? key decisions only?). - Implement trail storage that survives across sessions if work spans multiple runs. - Add trail-query primitives: "have I been here?", "how did I get here?", "what failed last time?" - Add fulab trail query helpers (CLI or HUD) to fetch prior decisions during resume flows.

title: AI Incorporation — Core Function
text: AI Incorporation — Core Function AI is most useful in this project as a probe for surfacing candidate mid-level reasoning cues already present in mathematical exposition, not as a generator of new proofs. You are defining the specific role AI should play in the AI4CI pipeline so it augments human annotation without inventing proofs. Worked mathematical solutions already mix formal derivations with explanatory phrases that gesture toward motivations, subgoals, and tactical decisions, and prior HDM patterns show that capturing such outline-level structures keeps reasoning legible to humans and systems. These informal cues are not systematically linked to specific steps or objects; without assistance, annotators must rediscover every linkage by hand, and without structure, downstream tools receive only cleaned events with little reusable explanation. Use existing AI models strictly to propose candidate cue–step links and outline-plus-informal alignments, attach provenance to each proposal, and pass them to human reviewers for acceptance, editing, or rejection before anything is treated as explanatory structure. This deployment keeps AI in the role of suggestion engine while ensuring that every retained explanation has a traceable record and a human steward, turning dispersed expository text into candidate reasoning scaffolds that future training-oriented AI could build on. next[Stand up the human-in-the-loop annotation pilot that uses AI to propose cue–step links and records reviewer decisions as structured provenance.] next[Publish the acceptance/rejection log into the evidence ledger so other layers can see which AI proposals were trusted and why.]

title: AI Incorporation — Methodological Role
text: AI Incorporation — Methodological Role Human validation of AI-proposed reasoning cues is required to identify genuine structure and avoid false signals; the project treats AI as an experiment whose outputs are graded and logged, not as an automatic source of truth. You are defining the methodological guardrails that keep AI proposals subject to human validation and traceable review. The HDM canon already assumes that outline-level proposals are only trustworthy when human stewards can interrogate them and decide what stands, what changes, and what is discarded. If AI-generated segmentations and glosses are used without explicit records of where they were kept, edited, or rejected, the workflow cannot demonstrate that it is learning anything about the boundary between helpful and misleading explanations. Use AI for first-pass segmentation and paraphrase, route each proposal through a ready/blocked-style decision record (accepted, revised, discarded), and treat staleness scans as alarms when drafts linger without review. Methodological validity in this setting depends on showing that human judgement governs every explanation and that the resulting log reveals which explanation types AI handles reliably and which remain beyond its current competence. next[Publish a reviewer rota and decision rubric so every AI-assisted explanation is triaged within a fixed window (e.g. 48 hours).] next[Wire review outcomes into stack-coherence/staleness-scan so unattended drafts raise visible alarms and cannot silently accumulate.]

title: Collective Intelligence — Evaluative Lens
text: Collective Intelligence — Evaluative Lens The usefulness of extracted reasoning cues must be tested through collective understanding rather than model accuracy, because the target outcome is shared clarity among diverse learners. You are defining evaluation in terms of shared clarity across cohorts rather than model accuracy. Value-flow and festival patterns show that gatherings enable collective sense-making only when participants can relate their own understanding to a visible shared artefact. Standard AI metrics (e.g. step-wise correctness) say little about whether undergraduates, postgraduates, and professionals can actually use the annotated proofs to reason together; they hide where explanations help, where they confuse, and where they leave gaps. Run tiered seminars in which identical annotated proofs are reviewed by different cohorts, log guided discussions using consistent prompts, and treat clarity/confusion reports as primary evaluation signals, feeding them back into ready/blocked-style triage so blockers are explicit. Collective intelligence is evidenced when diverse readers reach a workable shared understanding of the argument; only structured discussion around common artefacts can reveal whether the extracted reasoning cues support this outcome. next[Schedule undergraduate, graduate, and professional seminar sessions using the same annotated proofs and capture transcripts for comparison.] next[Pipe transcript-coded blockers into stack-coherence/ready-blocked-triage so explanatory weaknesses are visible to the whole project.]

title: Collective Intelligence — Communication Framing
text: Collective Intelligence — Communication Framing Shared reasoning scaffolds are essential because they allow diverse learners to inspect, question, and refine mid-level reasoning cues together, rather than relying on individual, opaque interpretations. You are explaining why shared artefacts are needed to test reasoning cues across cohorts. Peeragogical-infrastructure and “working where others can see” patterns already show that collective reasoning improves when intermediate work surfaces are visible and linked to concrete evidence. Typical mathematical materials provide either a polished proof or an informal commentary, not a structured artefact that makes the connection between steps and explanatory cues explicit across cohorts. Package dual-layer proofs (formal outline plus linked informal cues) into templated seminar kits that include discussion prompts for different levels and a simple evidence trail back to the underlying texts, reusing existing ledger and bridge patterns instead of inventing new governance. Collective intelligence depends on inspectable, cross-referenced intermediate artefacts; without them, seminars slide back into folklore and private interpretations instead of testing and refining the shared reasoning layer. next[Draft the cross-level seminar kit that presents outline-plus-cue structures and maps each cue to one or more discussion prompts.] next[Integrate evidence-ledger entries so every shared artefact points back to source texts and annotations before piloting with students.]

title: Dual-Layer Proof Patterns as a Feasibility Question
text: Dual-Layer Proof Patterns as a Feasibility Question Dual-layer proof patterns are a feasibility question: can formal steps and informal cues be captured consistently enough to matter? Mathematical proofs contain both formal steps and informal cues (exploratory and expository), but only the former typically survive into print. Contemporary AI tools can identify symbols yet struggle to recover motivations. We collect a modest corpus of worked graduate-level solutions and examine both their formal expressions and the informal commentary surrounding each step. Off-the-shelf models misidentify or omit exploratory cues, confuse motivation with justification, and cannot reliably map informal language to the exact mathematical objects or subgoals referenced; without human oversight, outputs drift or hallucinate. Use AI only as a draft assistant whose every suggestion is logged, accepted, edited, or rejected by a human annotator; link cues to specific steps and objects; and run structured seminars across learner cohorts to test whether these annotated proofs genuinely support understanding. Human-validated cue logs and coded seminar transcripts provide evidence—not speculation—about which pattern fragments are stable, which are fragile, and what methodological constraints govern scalability. next[Characterise which cue types are consistently recognisable; evaluate where learner groups converge or diverge in what helps them reconstruct a proof; define measurable failure modes; and specify what infrastructural or methodological changes would be required for a full-scale study.]

title: Funding Justification — Rapid-Response Pilot Scale
text: Funding Justification — Rapid-Response Pilot Scale A sub-£50k request is proportional because the work is confined to methodological evaluation—annotation, AI-assisted suggestion and human review, and seminars—built on existing infrastructure rather than new platforms. You are justifying the budget scale by tying spend to concrete, auditable pilot activities. Job-argument and transformation-engine patterns already describe how to cost short bursts of research that leverage existing institutional and technical capacity. Without a clear ledger of what the budget buys in terms of specific activities (specialist annotation, light AI usage, seminar facilitation), the request can look speculative or infrastructure-heavy. Itemise costs around part-time researchers, limited compute, and seminar delivery, and explicitly cite existing institutional infrastructure as in-kind support rather than a target for new investment. Reviewers need to see that the funds unlock a focused test of the reasoning-layer hypothesis, not an open-ended attempt to build a new platform. next[Draft the budget sheet that links each cost line to a concrete artefact (annotation hours, seminar sessions, reporting) and cite it in the EoI.] next[Attach evidence-ledger references so the use of funds can be audited post-award.]

title: Feasibility — Six-Month Pilot Discipline
text: Feasibility — Six-Month Pilot Discipline A six-month evaluation is feasible because the project is deliberately scoped to test whether mid-level reasoning cues can be extracted and validated, not to build new AI systems or long-term infrastructure. You are defending the six-month timeline by tying scope to specific, trackable activities. Repository-transition invariants and stack-blocker detection already describe what infrastructure exists and how to keep scope aligned with available capacity. Without explicit scope fences, a project framed around “AI and explanation” can drift into trying to develop storage, user interfaces, or new models, making the schedule unrealistic. Freeze scope to: proof selection, dual-layer annotation (AI proposals plus human review), seminar-based evaluation, and reporting; track each clause with explicit next-steps so diverging work is visible as scope creep. Dhammavicaya (keen investigation) in this context demands evidence that the pilot answers a clear methodological question—whether a recoverable reasoning layer exists—rather than attempting production-grade systems. next[Map the proof sample, annotation sprints, and seminars onto a simple timeline and publish it in the devmap.] next[Record blockers and clears weekly so stack-coherence patterns can demonstrate that the pilot stayed within its declared scope.]

title: Process and Exposition as Complementary Evidence
text: Process and Exposition as Complementary Evidence Recognise that the project studies two complementary sources of reasoning information in mathematical texts: the exploratory process signals that hint at how a proof was found, and the expository signals intentionally placed in published work to help readers reconstruct the logic. You are clarifying the two evidence sources the pilot will annotate and compare. Human understanding of mathematics relies on both the implicit heuristics behind a proof ("try this", "by analogy") and the explicit narrative cues authors include in published solutions ("note that", "it is natural to consider"). Process cues are often partial or suppressed, while expository cues are fragmentary and uneven across texts; neither source alone provides a stable representation of the reasoning structure that learners reconstruct. Analyse both kinds of cues: use baseline entity and relation extraction to anchor formal steps, and annotate how each informal phrase—whether exploratory or expository—links to specific objects, steps, or subgoals in the proof. Process cues reveal the reasoning that originally generated the proof, while expository cues reveal how experts communicate that reasoning to others; the combination provides the richest available evidence for reconstructing mid-level structure without requiring access to the original scratch work. next[Distinguish and label exploratory vs. expository cues in the annotated dataset.] next[Test with seminar participants how each type supports understanding.] next[Report which signals form reliable scaffolds for mathematical explanation.]

title: AI4CI — Mid-Level Reasoning Pilot
