text: AI4CI — Mid-Level Reasoning Pilot The project’s core contribution is to test, in a tightly scoped pilot, whether the informal, mid-level reasoning moves inside mathematical solutions can be made explicit, validated, and shown to help different cohorts understand proofs. You are summarizing the pilot’s core claim and the minimum evidence needed to validate it. AI systems currently train on polished proofs and expositions that omit much of the exploratory reasoning and heuristic guidance that human mathematicians rely on when solving graduate-level problems. The remaining informal layers live in the textual wraparound of worked solutions and in oral explanations; extracting their structure requires a disciplined workflow, not just more model capacity—AI proposals, human validation, and collective evaluation must be combined so that evidence about the reasoning layer is explicit. Deliver a focused pilot that (a) selects a small set of graduate-level worked problems; (b) uses existing tools to propose links between informal phrases and formal steps; (c) has annotators accept, edit, or reject each proposal; and (d) tests the resulting dual-layer proofs in seminars with undergraduates, postgraduates, and professionals to see which cues genuinely support understanding. Once we know whether a stable mid-level reasoning layer can be captured from exposition—and where it breaks down—we can state clearly what kind of process-level data will be needed for future AI that aims to train humans, and what cannot be obtained from textual traces alone. next[Assemble a cleared mini-corpus of graduate-level exam solutions with both symbolic steps and expository text, coordinating with data stewards for release notes.] next[Specify the annotation protocol (including AI proposal settings and review rubric) and register it in the evidence ledger before piloting.] next[Design the seminar prompts and coding scheme so clarity/confusion signals can be fed back into future iterations.]

title: Proof Patterns as a Hypothesised Mid-Level Hierarchy
text: Proof Patterns as a Hypothesised Mid-Level Hierarchy Recognise that the project treats proof patterns as a hypothesised mid-level hierarchy, analogous to the hierarchy of mathematical concepts, and uses a small, controlled study to see whether local fragments of this hierarchy can be made visible. You are framing proof patterns as a mid-level hierarchy the pilot can sample in a controlled way. Mathematicians rely on recurring tactics—"reduce to a simpler case", "apply a standard theorem", "argue by symmetry"—that function like proof patterns: reusable structures sitting between informal heuristics and fully formal derivations. This implicit hierarchy of proof patterns has never been systematically mapped, and a six-month pilot cannot construct it in full. Existing texts only show traces of these patterns, mixed with both exploratory and expository language. Use a gain-of-function style approach: focus on a small, curated set of worked proofs, amplify the strongest informal and expository cues, and see whether any stable, recognisable pattern fragments can be annotated consistently across examples. If such fragments can be identified and linked to specific objects and steps, they provide the first empirical foothold on an underlying proof- pattern hierarchy, even if only at a local scale. If they cannot, this reveals real limits on what present methods can recover. next[Treat recurring tactic descriptors that survive annotation as candidate proof-pattern atoms.] next[Report how often they appear, where they fail, and what cues were discarded.] next[Use findings to guide future, larger-scale work on proof-pattern structure.]

title: Distinguishing This Project from Current Mathematical AI SOTA
text: Distinguishing This Project from Current Mathematical AI SOTA Understand that the project addresses a gap untouched by current mathematical AI systems: not solving problems, but exposing the reasoning cues—both exploratory and expository—that humans rely on to understand mathematical work. You are distinguishing AI4CI from current SOTA by focusing on explanatory cues rather than solution accuracy. State-of-the-art models such as ChatGPT or AlphaGeometry can often produce plausible solutions to textbook or competition-style problems, showing strong pattern-matching and symbolic fluency on polished inputs. These systems do not reliably check their own work, cannot explain their reasoning at the level needed for teaching, and fail to produce stable links between informal phrases and the specific steps or objects they reference. Their outputs also lack insight into how humans reconstruct proofs from published exposition. Treat problem-solving capability as separate from explanatory capability, and focus the project on analysing how existing proofs communicate reasoning: what exploratory traces remain, what expository cues guide the reader, and whether these signals can be structurally annotated. Explanation and understanding depend on reconstructing intermediate motivations and relationships, not on producing correct final answers. Current SOTA models offer limited guidance here, leaving a gap that this pilot is uniquely positioned to explore. next[Use AI only as a draft annotator for linking informal cues to symbolic steps.] next[Contrast human vs. model judgement on explanation quality.] next[Report where explanatory capability breaks down despite strong problem-solving.]

title: Technical Grounding — From NER/RE to Informal Structure
text: Technical Grounding — From NER/RE to Informal Structure Existing math-aware NLP tools can anchor the extraction of reasoning cues by identifying objects and relations, but they cannot determine which informal phrases convey tactic or motivation without human judgement. You are grounding the pipeline in existing NER/RE outputs while clarifying what still requires human review. Baseline tools can already parse mathematical text, tag entities and relations, and suggest step boundaries that point to where explanations might attach. These tools only indicate where symbols occur and how they relate; they do not by themselves distinguish between phrases that encode genuine reasoning moves and those that merely narrate, summarise, or smooth the exposition. Treat NER/RE outputs and step boundaries as anchors, cluster recurring informal phrases around them, and subject resulting “reasoning cue” hypotheses to human review rather than accepting model guesses as structure. This isolates the real research question—whether human-recognisable reasoning structure can be recovered from exposition—from the underlying engineering, avoiding overclaim about what current NLP can deliver on its own. next[Prototype the anchor-plus-cue method on a small proof sample and record success/failure for each hypothesised reasoning cue.] next[Document how rejected cues were generated and reviewed so future work can refine both the NLP components and the human protocol without changing the underlying infrastructure.]

title: AI4CI — Human-Centred Future of AI
text: AI4CI — Human-Centred Future of AI Future AI can and should be built that can train humans in cognitively intense skills, which requires an explicit, structured account of the mid-level reasoning cues humans already use to understand complex work. You are framing the long-term AI4CI vision around explicit reasoning cues that support human learning. Contemporary AI systems can solve many formal problems in domains like mathematics, but they typically learn from polished outcomes rather than from the reasoning processes that human learners depend on. These processes do not appear as full interaction logs; they survive mainly in the expository layer as informal hints, motivations, and tactic-describing phrases. We do not yet know whether these traces can be systematically identified, linked to precise steps, and represented as a stable structure that generalises across problems and cohorts. Treat expository traces as candidates for an underlying reasoning layer and design a principled way to surface, examine, and test them, combining AI proposals, human validation, and collective evaluation. Only by making this tacit reasoning layer explicit can we both deepen our scientific understanding of how humans communicate complex thinking and provide the process-level structures that future AI will need in order to help people build expertise rather than merely reproduce correct answers. next[Develop and test a constrained workflow in mathematics that extracts, validates, and evaluates mid-level reasoning cues, and use the results to state clearly whether a recoverable “reasoning layer” exists that AI could train on.]

title: Admissibility as Recursion-Safety — Gate the Action CLASS Before You Rank
text: Admissibility as Recursion-Safety — Gate the Action CLASS Before You Rank In a self-modifying inference loop, gate each action CLASS with a per-class admissibility predicate (`can-propose?` / `action-admissible?`) checked BEFORE ranking. That predicate — not an ad-hoc loop guard — is the cycle-stopper that keeps self-modification recursion-safe. An AIF agent that can propose actions which modify its own action space, inventory, or goal (self-reference): extend the typed-edge inventory, deform the goal-structure, pursue a capability not on its pre-registered ascent. The agent's action space includes self-modifying moves — actions that re-author the agent rather than act within its fixed niche. Without a principled gate, self-modifying actions compose into runaway recursion: the agent expands its own powers, which expands what it can propose, unboundedly ("ants starting parliaments"). The reflex fix — bolting per-situation loop guards onto the ranker — is fragile, un-auditable, and multiplies with every new action class. Define a per-class admissibility predicate and apply it BEFORE expected-free-energy ranking. Un-registered `:pursue`, goal-extending `:decompose`, and unagreed operator-exit advances are **inadmissible** — refused (or NAG'd), never scored. Only admissible classes reach the ranker. The per-class predicate IS the recursion-safety; no separate runaway guard is needed, because the unsafe classes never enter the policy at all. "Water doesn't flow uphill; ants don't start parliaments." The EFE goal is bound to the pre-registered ascent; off-goal and self-extending moves are BHK arrows that do not compose into that ascent (task-as-arrow), and the inherited I4 exogeneity (the fast loop cannot force the glacial — structural-tension-as-observation) is what makes the binding hold. Gating at the **pursuit** boundary, not the discovery boundary, is the right cut: discovering an off-ascent capability is fine (it becomes a NAG), pursuing one needs consent. One structural property replaces a scatter of per-action guards. - Order matters: admissibility runs BEFORE ranking; an inadmissible action must never appear in `rank-actions`/`rank-star-map-actions` output. - Pairs with pattern-warranted-choice-point: an admissibility refusal NAGs with the admissibility warrant (which class, why inadmissible, what registration would make it admissible). - Pairs with niche-construction: admissibility is the boundary the endogenous-extension (aif2) direction is permitted to move — and exactly where it must be re-mechanised if it does. - evidence: inadmissible-refusal count by class; any admissibility breach (an inadmissible action that got ranked) is a bug, not a tradeoff. - evidence-shape: {:admissible/refusals {:keyword :int}, :admissibility/breaches :int, :registration-events :int} Inference loops with a FIXED action space and no self-modifying classes (there is nothing for admissibility to gate — ordinary EFE ranking suffices). Discovery/observation (never gate discovery; gate only pursuit). - M-capability-star-map INV-G: the `:cap/pentagon` pursuit is machine-refuted; un-registered `:pursue` + goal-extending `:decompose` are refused before ranking (`futon3c/.../logic/capability_star_map_invariants.clj`; `futon2/.../aif/efe.clj action-admissible?` → `rank-star-map-actions`). "Water doesn't flow uphill" enforced in code, not just argued.

title: Risk Term as Squared Deviation Plus Predictive Variance
text: Risk Term as Squared Deviation Plus Predictive Variance Compose the pragmatic (risk) EFE term as bias² (squared deviation of predicted mean from preference prior) + variance (predictive uncertainty contribution). Both terms in the same units; both pulling the agent toward predictable closeness to preference. The pragmatic value term in Expected Free Energy is supposed to penalise candidates whose predicted outcomes are far from the agent's preferences. A naïve implementation reads only the predicted mean — but AIF is Bayesian, so the *uncertainty* about whether the predicted mean is right also matters. You want the risk term to penalise both: - **bias**: predicted state is far from preferred state (the candidate is unlikely to land near preference) - **variance**: high predictive uncertainty about where the state will land (even if the predicted mean is at preference, the agent isn't confident it'll get there) A candidate with low bias and low variance is preferred over a candidate with low bias and high variance, all else equal. A risk term that uses only `(mean - prior)²` ignores predictive uncertainty. Two candidates with identical means but different variances rank equal under bias-only risk — which is wrong: the high-variance candidate carries higher operational risk of missing preference even though it has the same expected outcome. Compute the risk term per institution (or per state-instance) as: `risk[i] = (mean-D[i] - prior-D)² + (mean-A[i] - prior-A)² + var-D[i] + var-A[i]` Both the squared-deviation (bias²) and the predictive variance contribute additively to the per-instance risk. Average over instances in the band for the band-level risk-term. Configurable priors per opts. Under a Gaussian observation likelihood, the expected squared deviation from preference is `bias² + variance` (the variance-bias decomposition). Including both terms makes the risk match the canonical pragmatic value in AIF. Including only bias is a common implementation shortcut that produces a non-Bayesian agent. - Confirm your forward model returns predicted variance, not just predicted mean. If only mean is available, you can only compute the bias half — and the agent is not properly belief-aware in its risk scoring. - Read predicted (mean, variance) per state-instance from the forward-model output; compose the per-instance risk as `Σ ((mean_k - prior_k)² + var_k)` over coordinates k. - Average over instances in the relevant scope (band, cohort, agent's responsibility area). Comparable across candidates if the scope is fixed. - Document the priors: which coordinate has which preference value, why, where it lives in config. Priors should be configurable per opts, not hardcoded. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-05, 2026-05-14): risk-term-v3 implemented at notebooks/ukrn_v3_efe.clj:42-58. Uses both (D, A) coordinates; reads predicted variance from HO-04's forward model; PRIOR-D = PRIOR-A = 0.85 with opts override. Test risk-term-v3-has-prior-and-variance-properties verifies the variance contribution is additive. Closes the materially-incomplete-policy-score finding from codex-6's review of the UKRN scoping note. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-05.md. - Practice: ensure the prior is reachable. A prior of (1.0, 1.0) on a coordinate that asymptotes below 1.0 produces a permanent positive bias contribution that nothing can drive to zero — that's interpretable but should be deliberate. Calibrate the prior to a reachable preference, not an aspirational ceiling, unless you specifically want the agent to be perpetually striving.

title: Belief State as Operational Hypotheses
text: Belief State as Operational Hypotheses Maintain a compact belief map of operational hypotheses that is updated each step. The agent needs an internal state about what it is doing and why, beyond the raw trace. You want decisions to depend on tractable hypotheses (progress, blockers, pattern fit, uncertainty) rather than raw conversation history. If the belief state is just the conversation, the agent cannot cleanly update, compare, or falsify its own assumptions. Represent (mu) as a belief map of operational hypotheses (for example: :goal, :subgoals, :current-hypothesis, :blockers, :pattern-fit, :expected-next-observation, :uncertainty), updated at each step using observation and outcomes. A compact belief state makes predict -> observe -> update implementable and testable. - Define :aif/belief-state schema in tatami_schema.clj with keys [:goal :subgoals :current-hypothesis :blockers :pattern-fit :expected-next-observation :uncertainty]. - Extend aif_bridge/aif-step->event to validate mu against the schema before emitting :aif/tick events. - Add (mu-diff prev-mu next-mu) helper and log diffs as :aif/belief-delta events in pattern_competence.clj. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-01, 2026-05-14): per-institution BeliefState schema with mean+variance per coordinate, named handle (not inlined), centralised initialisation via initial-belief-state. Evidence: notebooks/ukrn_v2_contracts.clj:22-30; notebooks/ukrn_v2_substrate.clj:286-298. Validation: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-01.md. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-01): trajectory-CSV emission of belief means and variances per tick, enabling visible belief evolution in the output stream. Evidence: notebooks/ukrn_v2_runner.clj:110-140. - Practice refinement: prefer a *named schema handle* (e.g. BeliefState) over inlining belief shape inside agent/instance schemas — keeps the schema stable across update-rule changes and reusable by predictive-forward-model code. Surfaced 2026-05-14 in HO-01 review. - Practice refinement: centralise initialisation in a single helper (e.g. initial-belief-state) rather than duplicating tick-0 values across constructors. Surfaced 2026-05-14 in HO-01 review.

title: Candidate Pattern Action Space
text: Candidate Pattern Action Space Treat action selection as choosing from a bounded candidate set of pattern IDs. Action selection in fulab often means selecting (and committing to) a pattern to apply next. You want pattern choice to be legible and comparable, and you want to avoid collapse into one habitual pattern. If the action space is any pattern at any time, evaluation becomes unstructured and selection becomes arbitrary or dominated by recency. Define (a) as a constructed candidate set of pattern IDs produced by retrieval plus gating rules, with bounded size and explicit reasons for inclusion and exclusion. Constraining the action space makes downstream scoring meaningful rather than performative. - Add :aif/candidate-entry and :aif/candidate-chosen event types to tatami_schema.clj. - In learn_or_act/expand-hints, emit :aif/candidate-entry for each pattern in :search/candidates. - In learn_or_act/decide success path, emit :aif/candidate-chosen with pattern-id and runner stats. - Create aif_coverage.clj with (coverage-report session-id) that computes entered-vs-chosen ratios per pattern.

title: Decomposed Prediction Noise as Named Variance Contributions
text: Decomposed Prediction Noise as Named Variance Contributions Compose predictive-noise variance from named, domain-meaningful contributing sources, not from a single opaque σ². Each source maps to a structural feature of the candidate action. The Gaussian noise wrapper around a deterministic forward-model kernel needs to assign variance to its predictions. A single hardcoded σ² is operationally inflexible and analytically opaque — there's no way to ask *why* this candidate has high predictive uncertainty. You want predictive noise to be tunable (each source has a calibration constant), auditable (per-candidate variance decomposition emitted in the trace), and operationally meaningful (the agent's uncertainty about a candidate reflects identifiable structural features of that candidate). A single σ² hardcoded into the noise wrap conflates multiple sources of uncertainty into one knob. Tuning becomes guesswork (which knob should I turn?); diagnostics become impossible (was the high G ambiguity from missing capabilities, off-target facet emphasis, or mode-boundary proximity?). Decompose the predictive noise σ² into named additive contributions, each driven by a structural feature of the candidate: - Coverage uncertainty: σ² += k_coverage × (1 − fraction-of-capability-portfolio-online). Less of the agent's capability stack is firing → more uncertainty about how the candidate's effects propagate. - Specificity uncertainty: σ² += k_specificity × (1 − facet-emphasis-coverage). The candidate emphasises a narrow vs broad facet of the observation space → off-facet effects less predictable when the emphasis is narrow. - Boundary uncertainty: σ² += k_boundary × 𝟙[predicted-state near classification-mode-boundary]. Near a regime-change threshold, small noise produces large mode-class differences → predictive uncertainty about *what cell the agent ends up in* is high even when uncertainty about (state-coordinates) is low. Each k_* is a configurable constant. Initial values are calibrated against intuitive cases; validation harness can refine via sensitivity sweeps. Named contributions give every variance increment a domain-meaningful story. Auditing a high-G candidate becomes "this candidate's variance is dominated by coverage uncertainty, because most of the capability portfolio is offline"; tuning becomes "the coverage term is over-weighted, drop k_coverage from 0.01 to 0.005". A single opaque σ² admits neither. - Identify the 2–4 structural features of your candidate action space that should contribute to predictive uncertainty. - Define a configuration map of k_* constants; thread through the forward model's opts argument. - Emit the variance decomposition (per-source contributions) in the predictive trace alongside the total variance. The decomposition is what diagnostic UIs and validation harnesses consume. - Calibrate: pick initial k_* values that produce intuitive orderings on a handful of test cases. Sweep in validation if outputs aren't behaving. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-04, 2026-05-14): three-source decomposition implemented in notebooks/ukrn_v3_forward.clj prediction-noise-variance (lines 91-120). Sources: capability portfolio fraction, facet emphasis coverage, mode-threshold proximity. Constants: DEFAULT-K-CAP=0.01, DEFAULT-K-FACET=0.005, DEFAULT-K-THRESHOLD=0.02, DEFAULT-THRESHOLD-EPSILON=0.05. Smoke output shows the threshold-proximity term operationally meaningful: SYN2 with predicted D=0.519 (within 0.05 of threshold 0.5) gets variance 0.029, producing a bimodal mode-probability distribution (50.8% absorbed + 42.4% mismatch) that correctly reflects regime-change ambiguity. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-04.md. - Practice: emit the decomposition keys alongside the total variance in the trace record. Consumers (validation harness, UI panels, EFE term computations) can read whichever component they need.

title: Evidence Precision Registry
text: Evidence Precision Registry Make evidence weighting explicit by logging a precision registry per observation channel. The agent must treat some inputs as more reliable than others (tests vs narrative claims, trace anchors vs inferred intent). You want the agent to discount low-trust evidence without discarding it, and to become stricter when outcomes are volatile. Without an explicit precision layer, evidence weighting becomes implicit prompt rhetoric and cannot be audited. Represent (Pi_o) as a per-channel precision registry keyed to observation features (and/or evidence sources), and apply it wherever prediction error, scoring, or gating occurs. Making precision explicit turns trust into a tunable control surface rather than an undocumented bias. - Define :aif/precision-registry schema in tatami_schema.clj with channel keys [:tests :typecheck :static-analysis :tool-output :user-constraints :model-inference]. - Add default-precision-registry to pattern_competence.clj with initial weights (e.g., :tests 0.9, :model-inference 0.5). - Emit :aif/precision-adjusted events when check-pur or check-psr modifies channel weights based on anchor resolution failures. - Expose (precision-for channel session) helper for G-term computation in aif_bridge.clj.

title: Expected Free Energy as Multi-Term Scorecard
text: Expected Free Energy as Multi-Term Scorecard Compute expected free energy as named terms with persisted breakdowns, not a single opaque scalar. The agent needs a single scalar (G) per candidate pattern, derived from separable considerations. You want pattern selection to balance delivery risk, ambiguity, information value, and cost in a way you can tune and audit. A single opaque score encourages post-hoc rationalization and makes tuning indistinguishable from storytelling. Compute G(a) as a weighted sum of named terms (risk, ambiguity, information gain, constraint violation, cost, coordination pressure), and store the term breakdown for each candidate. A decomposed G makes disagreements concrete (which term dominated) and enables targeted adjustment. - Define :aif/g-breakdown schema in tatami_schema.clj with term keys [:risk :ambiguity :info-gain :constraint-violation :cost :coordination-pressure]. - Extend aif_bridge/extract-evidence to decompose G into named terms instead of scalar g-mean. - DONE: Add :aif/g-terms key to psr-template in pattern_competence.clj. Evidence: src/futon3/fulab/pattern_competence.clj - Store term breakdowns in PSR :forecast section. - Add (flip-analysis psr) that computes which term delta would have changed the chosen pattern. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-05, 2026-05-14): four-term scorecard scaffold at notebooks/ukrn_v3_efe.clj score-candidate-belief-aware (lines 102-135). Terms: risk-term-v3, ambiguity-term-v3, pattern-efe (placeholder until HO-06), priority-alignment. Smoke output shows {risk 0.167, ambiguity −4.32, pattern-efe −0.1, priority-alignment 0.030, G −4.28}. Term breakdown emitted as a map, not just a scalar. See companion patterns aif/belief-aware-risk-term and aif/predictive-entropy-as-ambiguity for the term-form specifications. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-05.md. - Practice refinement (HO-05): when terms have very different natural scales (e.g. linear-space risk ~0.1 vs log-space ambiguity ~−4), the λ weights in `G = λ_p · risk + λ_e · ambiguity + ...` must be calibrated to balance magnitudes. Surface the scale-asymmetry as a calibration concern, not as a bug.

title: Experimental Comparison of EFE Term Variants
text: Experimental Comparison of EFE Term Variants When an EFE term admits multiple theoretically defensible formulations, build them all as alternative implementations and let the validation harness select between them empirically. Do not pre-commit to one variant on a priori grounds. Some EFE terms (notably pattern-EFE-style terms, info-gain composites, multi-source ambiguity terms) have multiple plausible operationalisations. Each variant is defensible in theory; differences may be small in some operational regimes and large in others. Picking one a priori risks choosing wrong; picking by argument risks rationalising rather than measuring. You want the agent's term implementation to be the one that *demonstrably* discriminates candidates well, recovers known operational outcomes well, and produces traceable comparisons. You want the choice between variants to be a finding, not a stance. A common failure mode is to implement one variant, get plausible outputs, and ship — never knowing whether a different variant would have produced sharper discrimination or better operational fidelity. Another failure mode is to argue for one variant in committee, ship, and discover months later that an unselected variant would have been substantively different. Build the competing variants as alternative implementations: - Pure functions with matching signatures: `(variant-A candidate state opts)`, `(variant-B candidate state opts)`, etc. - Selectable via opt: e.g. `:term-variant :a` / `:b` / `:c` in the EFE scorer. - Default variant is whichever is closest to the prior baseline (e.g., the v2 pre-rewrite term form) — preserving backward compat under regression testing. Then run the validation harness against each variant under matched configurations. Named validation properties (recovery-rate, headline-outcome, discrimination-score, computational-cost) constitute the comparison metrics. Pick the winner empirically. Building both is cheap relative to the operational risk of picking wrong. Building both also forces the architectural seam (dispatch on opt; matching signatures) which is itself a valuable clean-up. And the *delta* between variants — measured per-run, per-config — is a finding worth reporting even after one variant wins. - Identify the variants. Name them explicitly (R-1, R-2, R-3 in the literature-style; or by characterising principle, e.g. capability-gated vs probabilistic-compound). - Implement each as a pure function with the same signature shape. Add a dispatcher at the EFE scorer (single `:term-variant` opt). - Define comparison metrics in the validation harness: - Recovery-rate against known classifications. - Headline-outcome stability (does the variant change a paper's quantitative claims?). - Candidate discrimination (G-spread across top-K; higher spread = more discriminating). - Trajectory-class behaviour (do simulated trajectories show qualitative patterns correctly under each variant?). - Computational cost (per-EFE-evaluation latency). - Run the harness; pick the winner on the merits. - **Term-set parity**: when comparing variants of one term within a larger EFE that has *other* terms (or other patterns the term aggregates over), preserve the larger term set across variants. If variant-A applies to 5 patterns and variant-B applies to 3 of those 5, the comparison is confounded by term-set drift, not just by variant semantics. Either both variants cover the full term set (extending the smaller variant to handle the missing terms gracefully, e.g. as a no-(D, A)-constraint case) or neither does. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-06, 2026-05-14): R-1 (capability-gated) and R-3 (compound capability-gate ∩ (D, A)-region) of pattern-EFE implemented at notebooks/ukrn_v3_efe.clj:117-127, 129-151. Dispatched via `:pattern-efe-variant` opt. Smoke comparison on a single high-band candidate: R-1 G = −4.28, R-3 G = −4.28 — meaningful 5% difference in the pattern-EFE component, small G-level difference. Term-set parity preserved: codex extended Joe's 5-pattern mapping to all 8 v2 patterns to keep comparison clean. HO-11 will run the empirical comparison across full headline + lesion configs. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-06.md. - Practice: small per-tick differences in a single EFE term can compound across many ticks into large differences in trajectory outcomes — or they can wash out. Empirical comparison settles this; intuition doesn't.

title: Variational Free Energy as a Per-Tick Scalar
text: Variational Free Energy as a Per-Tick Scalar Compute and emit variational free energy F = 0.5 × mean(Π · ε²) per tick as a canonical scalar that summarises agent surprise. AIF computes two distinct quantities. **G** (Expected Free Energy) is per-candidate-action, drives policy. **F** (Variational Free Energy) is per-tick, summarises how surprised the agent currently is by its observations. They are different objects; conflating them is a common documentation hazard. You want a single, comparable-across-time scalar that says "how badly is the agent's current belief explaining what it just observed?" — useful for validation (F should decrease on average as the agent learns), diagnostics (F-spikes flag surprise events worth investigating), and operational triggers (F-above-threshold can signal hyperparameter adjustment). Without an explicit F-per-tick, the agent's belief evolution becomes opaque — there's no scalar to plot, no acceptance criterion to test, no operational alarm to trigger. And G-per-candidate is not a substitute: G is about the future; F is about the present. Implement F as a pure function (mu, observation, precision-opts) → non-negative scalar, applying the formula F = 0.5 × mean(Π_k · ε_k²) over all observation channels k. Emit it as part of the per-tick trace alongside μ and ε. When μ matches observation exactly, F should be zero by construction. F is the quantity AIF agents are minimising (variationally); making it observable per tick gives a clean validation target (V3: F decreases on average) and a clean operational signal (sudden F-jumps merit attention). Keeping F distinct from G in vocabulary, file location, and trace schema prevents the cross-stack confusion where one is mistaken for the other. - Implement free-energy as a pure function in the same namespace as the belief update (canonical pairing: same module owns both rules). Pure function, takes precision options as inputs. - Trace F per tick alongside μ and ε; include in CSV/evidence emissions. - Acceptance: F = 0 when belief matches observation; F ≥ 0 always; F decreases over a run on average. The third property is V3 in the AIF completeness validation harness. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-02, 2026-05-14): free-energy implemented as pure function in notebooks/ukrn_v3_belief.clj:42-51. Hand-computed test cases pass. Available for the V3 validation property in the planned validation harness. - Practice: when documenting an AIF surface, refer to F as "free energy" or "variational free energy" and G as "expected free energy" or "EFE-per-candidate". Cross-stack vocabulary discipline reduces handoff ambiguity.

title: Hierarchical Budget-Aware Action Selection
text: Hierarchical Budget-Aware Action Selection When multiple agents operating over shared state can independently choose actions that share consumable resources, resolve conflicts at multiple budget hierarchy levels: aggregate setup-budget conservation across all agents per tick; per-instance forward projection of each action's downstream resource consumption to detect instances that would predictively exhaust. A multi-agent (or multi-band, or hierarchical) AIF setup gives each agent or sub-agent local autonomy: each scores candidate actions and selects via softmax. But the candidates often consume shared resources — setup budget for capability activation, engagement-budget for per-instance participation, attention budget across the agent's responsibility area. A naive *union* of independent selections will violate resource constraints whenever multiple agents simultaneously prefer expensive candidates. You want collective action selection that respects budget constraints at every hierarchy level. You want the agent (a) to never recommend allocations that exceed available aggregate budget per tick, and (b) to factor in *downstream* consequences of each candidate on per-instance budgets so the agent doesn't recommend "great-looking now" candidates that cause instances to exhaust their budgets in the next K ticks. A naive union-of-selections leaves the budget invariant unenforced — over-subscription happens silently. A naive single-coordinator approach throws away the value of the local-agent factoring, requiring all candidates to compete in one big softmax. Neither is right. Implement conflict resolution at *each* hierarchy level explicitly: - **Aggregate level**: a coordinator function `resolve-conflicts` that takes per-agent selections, applies them in priority order (e.g. importance band, deadline order, severity rank), debiting shared budget per applied action. Actions that exceed remaining budget are dropped to a no-op baseline or downgraded; trace records which were dropped and why. - **Per-instance level**: a `feasibility-penalty` EFE subterm. For each candidate, project per-instance resource consumption forward over K ticks using a cheap approximation (constant status; only the budget decays). Count instances predicted to fall below their minimum-viable budget threshold. The penalty scales linearly with that count, multiplied by a tunable λ weight. Both layers produce trace fields. The trace fields land in the per-tick record (R8) so the agent's reasoning about resource constraints is auditable. Conservation at the aggregate level is a *hard* constraint (you literally can't spend more than the budget; violating it makes the simulation incoherent). Forward-projecting per-instance consumption is a *soft* constraint (the agent might be willing to risk some instances exhausting if the candidate's other terms are sufficiently good). Hard constraints belong in the action selector; soft constraints belong in the EFE term. Implementing both gives the agent the right kind of attention to budget at every level. - Identify the budget hierarchy in your domain: aggregate (per-tick setup or attention budget shared across agents) and per-instance (resource each instance consumes to participate, with a threshold below which the instance disengages). - Implement `resolve-conflicts`: priority-ordered application; per-agent fallback to no-op baseline; trace records. - Implement `feasibility-penalty`: K-tick forward projection; cheap approximation by default (constant non-budget status; only budget decays). Avoid full kernel-replay over K ticks unless the cheap approximation gives wrong answers. - Calibrate the aggregate budget against the actual action-cost distribution: pick a value that admits one expensive action or two cheap actions per tick; tighter than "everything fits", looser than "always blocks". - Calibrate λ_feasibility: should produce a penalty large enough to deter clearly-truncating candidates but not so large that no candidate ever passes it. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-07, 2026-05-14): `resolve-band-conflicts` at notebooks/ukrn_v3_kernel.clj:30-79 implements aggregate setup-budget conservation in band priority order (high → middle → thin). `budget-feasibility-penalty` at notebooks/ukrn_v3_efe.clj:205-211 implements per-institution K=4 tick projection; λ=0.5 per predicted truncation. Smoke output: a candidate against population with 6 high-band institutions at budget=20 produces feasibility-penalty=3.0 (6 at-risk × 0.5), shifting G from −4.28 to −1.28 (+70% deterrent). Closes V9 (setup-budget conservation) and V11 (per-institution budget feasibility). Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-07.md. - Practice: duplicate same-tick proposals (two agents proposing the same action) should typically pay the aggregate cost once, not twice — debit on first-occurrence-of-action-id, not per-agent. Mirrors set-semantics of resource activation. - Practice: K-tick forward projection complexity should match operational stakes. Full kernel-replay K times per candidate is expensive; the cheap approximation (status held constant; budget decays linearly) is usually sufficient because the agent's decision is *should I avoid candidates that drain budgets* not *what exactly will happen K ticks from now*. The approximation is fit for purpose.

title: Niche Construction as the Bootstrap Loop of an Inference Agent
text: Niche Construction as the Bootstrap Loop of an Inference Agent An inference agent whose generative model depends on an externally-authored substrate cannot, *as currently architected*, construct its own niche; the agents operating its peripherals do, and the agent's false-floor readings are how those agents know what to construct. (Scope matters: this is a property of the current niche-authoring arrangement, not a theorem about active inference — see HOWEVER-endogenous below.) An active-inference agent (e.g. the futon War Machine) reads a substrate of typed vertices and edges, computes T / ∇T / ΔT or analogues, and ranks actions. Its inference is bounded by the typed-edge inventory of the substrate it can see. The substrate is itself authored by other agents and operators. You are designing an AIF agent whose generative model depends on a structured substrate (hypergraph, knowledge graph, typed event log) that is authored by parties other than the agent itself. The agent cannot extend its own substrate's typed-edge inventory — it has operations on values within the niche but not on the meta-level structure of the niche. When action classes surface that the inventory doesn't cover, the agent reads ΔT = 0 (false floor), not error. It looks confident-and-wrong; it is in fact correctly-uninformed, and the substrate is incomplete. Treat false-floor readings as **niche-construction signals**, not bugs. Each false-floor names a typed-edge family the substrate is missing relative to the action classes agents actually take. The operators-and-agents who use the inference agent do the niche construction: they add the missing typed-edge families, ingest the missing vertex types, derive the missing relations. On the next tick the agent sees a richer niche and ranks more accurately. Niche construction (Lewontin 1983; Odling-Smee / Laland / Feldman 2003; Friston in active-inference terms) is the loop by which an organism modifies its environment so its inference becomes tractable. The futon agent is in the same loop; only the niche is symbolic (a typed graph) rather than physical. Confident false-floors masquerading as signal is the worst outcome — the agent makes apparently-warranted-but-actually-uninformed choices. Visible false-floors that operators can read as "edges missing here" is the right outcome — the agent's blindness becomes the input to its own niche's improvement. The "cannot" above is scoped to the current architecture, where the substrate is authored by parties other than the agent. It is NOT a theorem about active inference. Two strands show the boundary can be redrawn so niche-construction becomes endogenous: (a) hierarchical AIF learns high-level priors that re-weight uncertainty-tolerance — Kiverstein & Miller (2023) on playfulness: a learned high-level prior expands the phenotypic bound on tolerated surprise, sending the agent to the competence edge where new structure is found; (b) the variational free-energy principle has been applied to niche construction directly (Constant / Ramstead / Veissière / Friston, "A variational approach to niche construction"), redrawing the Markov blanket to include the constructed niche so inventory-edits become variational moves over an extended boundary rather than an external handoff. The futon realisation is the **aif2** direction: a boundary-tier set of criteria (mechanising AIF+ I1 boundary-integrity + I3 timescale-separation) over whether and how the WM may re-author its own typed-edge support — distinct from the inference-tier R1-R12. The false-floor / zero-anamnesis lull, under a learned playfulness prior, reads not as "hand off" but as "forage at the edge" — the niche-construction trigger from the inside. See M-aif2. - Surface false-floor readings as such — don't silently zero-out a signal; report "ΔT = 0 (no incident edges of supported family)" so absence is legible to operators. - When new action classes are added to a ranking surface, audit which typed-edge families would feed ΔT (or analogue) for that class, and which are present-vs-missing in the substrate. - For the futon stack as of 2026-05-27: the WM's ΔT over `code/v05/related-mission` works for sorry-actions but gives ΔT = 0 false-floor for anchor-reframe / file-edit / excursion-step actions. Construction backlog: (a) feed `code/v05/mission-cross-ref` (already in substrate from M-weird-modernism Task 8 single-parser consolidation) into the Laplacian; (b) derive `code/v05/file → mission` from `:mission/code-paths`; (c) ingest E-prefix excursion docs as a typed vertex family (currently not ingested). - Connection to aliveness synthesis (M-action-cost-modelling §3.8): anamnesis = un-discharged tension drives niche construction; niche construction discharges anamnesis into mana. The three terms form a single loop, with niche construction as the operative mechanism by which agent-substrate aliveness shifts. - Sibling-pattern dependency: when authoring missions that ship new action classes, the mission's INSTANTIATE phase should explicitly enumerate the niche-construction-audit per class (which edges feed the Laplacian, which are absent). Treat per-class niche-construction state as first-class mission metadata, not implicit. - aif2 / endogenous niche-construction (2026-05-31): treat the action-class inventory itself as hidden state to be inferred (an extension of R12, or candidate R13), and mechanise the AIF+ I1 (boundary integrity) + I3 (timescale) invariants for the case where the boundary is *permitted to move*. The meta-model is `futon2.aif.*` modelled as its own AIF+ `.aif.edn` lifeform. See M-aif2 (IDENTIFY).

title: Policy Precision as Commitment Temperature
text: Policy Precision as Commitment Temperature Maintain a commitment temperature that modulates how strongly the policy commits to low-G choices. Even with identical scores, the agent sometimes should explore alternatives and other times should commit. You want exploration versus exploitation to depend on operational pressure (deadlines, repeated failures, user impatience, instability), not on randomness alone. Without an explicit (tau), the agent either thrashes or tunnels with no controllable dial. Maintain (tau) as a commitment temperature that modulates softmax over (-G/tau), coupled to diagnostic signals (recent regressions, uncertainty in (mu), contradiction rate, time pressure, repeated test failures). A single commitment dial allows systematic control of stochasticity without changing the scoring model. - Add :aif/tau-adjustment event type to tatami_schema.clj with keys [:prev-tau :next-tau :trigger :diagnostic-signals]. - Implement tau-coupling rules in aif_bridge.clj: increase tau on :test-failure or :uncertainty > 0.7; decrease on :tests-passing streak. - Persist tau history in lab/aif/tau-cache.edn keyed by pattern-id; load on session start. - Add (policy-entropy session) metric to aif_coverage.clj; correlate with outcome stability in session summaries. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-05, 2026-05-14): abstain? rule implemented at notebooks/ukrn_v3_efe.clj:75-92. Computes G-spread across top-K candidates, divides by τ, abstains if the resulting discriminability is ≤ floor (default 0.5, configurable). Edge case: < 2 candidates returns true (degenerate). Test abstain-fires-only-under-low-discriminability covers well-separated, weakly-separated, threshold, and just-over-threshold regimes. Closes R6 abstain criterion for UKRN v3-runner. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-05.md. - Practice (HO-05): abstain semantics are part of R6 in the AIF completeness criteria. An implementation that has softmax without abstain is operationally incomplete — it always picks something, even when statistically indistinguishable candidates would warrant inaction. Make abstain explicit; make the threshold configurable.

title: Predictive-Coding Belief Update with Variance Evolution
text: Predictive-Coding Belief Update with Variance Evolution Update beliefs via predictive-coding (μ ← μ + α·Π·ε) and evolve variance with a sensor-variance floor so uncertainty stays meaningful. The agent receives an observation each tick and must integrate it into its belief state. The integration rule determines both mean trajectory and uncertainty trajectory. You want belief updates to be principled (Bayesian-shaped under Gaussian approximation), tunable (single learning rate; per-channel precision), and operationally robust (variance doesn't collapse to zero; doesn't blow up). Without an explicit update rule the agent either slams beliefs to each observation (over-trusts) or never moves them (over-anchors). Variance with no sensor-variance floor decays toward zero under any informative-observation history, killing the predictive-entropy term in EFE for later ticks. Implement two coupled updates per tick: - Mean: μ ← μ + α · Π · ε, where ε = observation − μ, Π is per-channel precision, α is learning rate. - Variance: var ← (1−α)·var + α·(observation − new-μ)² + σ²_sensor, where σ²_sensor is the sensor's intrinsic variance floor. The residual against the *new* mean (not the old mean) is what informs the variance update — this matches the moment-matched EWMA approximation of Bayesian update under Gaussian likelihood. The mean rule realises predictive coding (Friston et al.); the variance rule keeps belief uncertainty in a meaningful regime where ambiguity terms in EFE stay informative. σ²_sensor as a *configurable* parameter supports noiseless-mode sanity checks and sensitivity sweeps without recompilation. - Implement update-mu as a pure function: (mu, observed-state, opts) → BeliefState. Take α, Π, σ²_sensor from opts with named defaults. - Use observation − new-mean (post-update residual) in the variance term, not observation − old-mean. The shorthand can confuse handoff specs; cite the acceptance-criterion hand-calculation as source of truth. - Floor variance at 0 explicitly via (max 0 (...)); under σ²_sensor > 0 the floor is rarely tested in practice but the explicit floor protects against pathological inputs. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-02, 2026-05-14): update-mu and free-energy implemented at notebooks/ukrn_v3_belief.clj:1-51. α=0.4, Π=1.0, σ²_sensor=0.02 defaults configurable via thresholds map. Verified across 8 hand-computed test cases. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-02.md. - Validation: variance should shrink under low-prediction-error observations (test A4: var goes from 0.04 to 0.024 under perfect prediction and σ²=0); grow under surprise (test A3: var goes from 0.04 to 0.080 under ε=0.5 and σ²=0.02). Both tests should be in the validation harness for any new AIF implementation following this pattern.

title: Ambiguity Term as Predictive Entropy of the Observation Distribution
text: Ambiguity Term as Predictive Entropy of the Observation Distribution Compute the epistemic (ambiguity) EFE term as the entropy of the predictive observation distribution under each candidate. For a diagonal-covariance Gaussian, this simplifies to `0.5 × log(σ²_D × σ²_A)` (dropping additive constants that don't affect candidate ranking). The epistemic value term in Expected Free Energy is supposed to favour information-gaining actions — candidates that produce *less ambiguous* observations, so the agent can refine its beliefs efficiently. A naïve implementation uses heuristic proxies (capability-portfolio breadth, count of available action branches, action-class diversity). These approximate but don't actually compute the AIF quantity. You want the ambiguity term to be the *true predictive entropy* of the observation distribution under each candidate. Candidates that produce sharper predictions (lower predictive variance) get lower ambiguity; candidates that produce diffuse predictions (high predictive variance, near-threshold predictions, etc.) get higher ambiguity. The agent prefers ambiguity-reducing candidates because they're information-gaining. Substituting a heuristic for the actual entropy makes the agent's "epistemic" preferences correlated-with-but-not-equal-to information theory. The agent may prefer actions that have many sub-options but produce nothing informative; or avoid actions that look unambiguous in heuristic terms but produce truly precise observations. Heuristic-based epistemic terms are common but not AIF-canonical. For a candidate action producing predicted observation distribution `o ∼ N(μ, Σ)`, the differential entropy of `o` is: `H[o] = 0.5 × log((2πe)^k × det(Σ))` where k is the dimension of the observation vector. For diagonal-covariance (independent channels), `det(Σ) = Π_k σ²_k`. For comparing across candidates, the additive constants (`0.5 × k × log(2πe)`) drop out, leaving: `ambiguity-comparable(candidate) = 0.5 × log(Π_k σ²_k)` In two dimensions (D, A): `ambiguity-comparable = 0.5 × log(σ²_D × σ²_A)`. Predictive entropy is the AIF-canonical epistemic quantity. The diagonal-Gaussian simplification is tractable and matches the diagonal-covariance assumption that downstream code (mode-quadrant integration; visualisation) already uses. Dropping constants preserves comparability across candidates while avoiding spurious absolute-entropy precision — a value of `−4.3` in dropped-constants form is comparable to `−4.4` for a different candidate but doesn't claim to be "−4.3 bits". - Verify your forward model returns predicted variance per observation channel. If not, the entropy isn't computable. - Floor the variance per channel (`max(variance-epsilon, var_k)`) before passing to log, to avoid `log(0)` under near-deterministic candidates. variance-epsilon = 1e-12 or similar. - Decide whether to keep or drop the Gaussian constants. Drop them for comparable-across-candidates output; keep them for absolute-entropy interpretation. Document the choice in the function docstring. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-05, 2026-05-14): ambiguity-term-v3 implemented at notebooks/ukrn_v3_efe.clj:60-73. Diagonal-Gaussian factorisation; constants dropped; variance-epsilon floor. Smoke output shows value ≈ −4.3 for a representative high-band candidate. Test ambiguity-term-v3-is-monotonic-and-finite verifies monotonicity and finite behaviour under near-zero variance. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-05.md. - Practice: when comparing this term against pragmatic and other EFE terms in the final G composition, note the scale difference — the entropy form is in log-space (typically yielding values in the range [-10, 0] for variance in [1e-4, 1]), while pragmatic risk² is in linear coordinate-square space (typically [0, 2] for unit-bounded coordinates). The λ_e weight in `G = λ_p · risk + λ_e · ambiguity + ...` must be calibrated to balance the magnitudes.

title: Shared Kernel for the Predictive Forward Model
text: Shared Kernel for the Predictive Forward Model Extract the deterministic dynamics core into a pure shared kernel; have both the live step and the predictive forward model call into it. One implementation, two callers. An AIF agent that scores candidate actions via Expected Free Energy needs a predictive forward model — a function that takes a candidate action and returns the predicted next-state distribution. The naive implementation maintains a separate "shadow" dynamics for the predictive call, which inevitably drifts from the live dynamics as the code evolves. You want the predictive forward model's outputs to be principled (the agent's beliefs about candidate actions match what the live dynamics would actually do under those actions), maintainable (one set of dynamics rules to update), and verifiable (a single regression-test surface that catches accidental divergence). Two implementations of the same dynamics is two implementations to maintain, two places for bugs to hide, two surfaces where the forward model's predictions can disagree with what the live step actually does. The cost of maintaining bit-equivalent shadows grows quadratically with the dynamics complexity. Factor the live step into (a) a *pure deterministic kernel* taking explicit (state, action, seed, opts) and returning a next state, and (b) a *thin orchestration wrapper* that threads defaults and calls the kernel. The wrapper preserves the live API; the kernel becomes callable by: - The wrapper, in live operation. - The predictive forward model, for candidate scoring — typically via a second arity that admits supplied candidate actions and skips the live action-selection step. The predictive forward model then becomes a thin probabilistic wrapper around the same kernel: call kernel with candidate, add Gaussian noise (or other principled uncertainty representation), produce next-state distribution. One implementation of the deterministic dynamics is the only place where the rules live. The kernel is what the live step does *and* what the forward model predicts. Any update to one is automatically reflected in the other. The bit-equivalence test (live-path output unchanged under refactor) is the cheapest catchnet for accidental drift. - Audit the live step for impurities: I/O calls, atom mutations, time-of-day reads, side-effect emissions. The kernel must be pure; impurities belong in the wrapper. - Define the kernel signature with explicit (state, action, seed, opts) — no implicit context, no defaults inside the kernel itself. - Add a second arity for the forward-model seam: `(kernel state ext seed opts candidate-actions)` — supplied actions skip live action selection. - Document the RNG-consumption divergence: when candidate actions are supplied, the kernel doesn't consume action-selection RNG. The forward model's Gaussian noise wrap is the source of predictive uncertainty, not kernel RNG draws. This must be in the kernel docstring. - Capture a pre-refactor regression baseline. Commit it (e.g. as a CSV fixture). Automated test compares post-refactor output to baseline byte-for-byte. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-03, 2026-05-14): step-kernel extracted to notebooks/ukrn_v3_kernel.clj:159-193; engagement-step reduced to 8-line wrapper at notebooks/ukrn_v2_engagement.clj:51-58; bit-equivalence regression fixture at test/fixtures/ho03_v11_headline_trajectory_baseline.csv. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-03.md. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-04, 2026-05-14): predict-engagement-step at notebooks/ukrn_v3_forward.clj:122-149 wraps step-kernel 5-arity with Gaussian noise propagation; smoke output shows threshold-proximity behaviour discriminates candidates correctly. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-04.md. - Practice: keep the kernel and the forward model in separate namespaces. The kernel is the deterministic shared core; the forward model is the probabilistic wrapper. Separation makes the call surface for downstream EFE consumers clear.

title: Status-Gated Belief Update for Multi-Instance Agents
text: Status-Gated Belief Update for Multi-Instance Agents Update beliefs only for instances the agent is actually observing this tick. Paused, truncated, dropped, or otherwise out-of-loop instances retain their prior belief unchanged. When an AIF agent operates over multiple instances (institutions, sessions, processes, conversation threads), each instance has an engagement status that determines whether the agent receives meaningful observations from it. The naive update-everything-every-tick policy is operationally wrong when some instances are not contributing fresh information. You want the belief evolution to faithfully reflect what the agent actually saw — not what it would have seen under unconditional observation. You want paused or truncated instances to retain their last-known belief as a marker for "the agent stopped observing here at this prior", rather than drifting under noise or stale dynamics. A blanket "update every instance every tick" policy will: - Mistake rollback dynamics (e.g. paused-status state rollback) for genuine observations, eroding the agent's stored belief about non-observed instances. - Cause truncated instances' beliefs to drift toward their frozen-but-decaying state, producing post-truncation noise in trace records. - Make it hard to read trace records, because every instance moves every tick regardless of whether it should. Gate the belief update on instance status, distinguishing *engagement status* (does the agent act on the instance this tick) from *observation availability* (does the agent see the instance's state this tick): - For status :active — agent is engaging *and* observing. Apply update-mu using the post-step state. - For status :paused — agent is *not engaging* but *is still observing* (the dynamics still computes the instance's (D, A) state; only the engagement-side effects are rolled back). Apply update-mu using the post-step (D, A) as observation. - For status :truncated — the agent's relationship with the instance has ended; no further observations are meaningful for the simulation's purpose. Retain pre-step :mu unchanged. The trace record emits :mu for all instances every tick. The agent's belief about a :paused instance evolves under observation noise (variance grows by sensor-variance per tick) and tracks the post-step (D, A) coordinates; only a :truncated instance shows a frozen belief. Belief is a record of what the agent learned from observation. Updating it when no observation was made introduces a fiction; preserving it when no observation was made preserves the operational meaning. Status-gating makes the gating decision explicit and auditable. - Identify the canonical status states in your domain (e.g. :active / :paused / :truncated for engagement-style agents; :running / :blocked / :complete for session-style agents). Document which are observation-bearing. - Implement the gate as a case-dispatch in the per-tick post-processing step, *not* inside update-mu itself. update-mu stays a pure function over (μ, observation, opts); the gate decides whether to call it. - Test: run a population with an instance in non-active status; verify the instance's belief is unchanged across the tick. Run another with the same instance returning to active; verify belief updates resume. - DONE (UKRN v3 HO-02, 2026-05-14): status-gated update first implemented in notebooks/ukrn_v2_engagement.clj. Active gets update-mu; paused and truncated retain pre-step :mu. Test paused-and-truncated-institutions-keep-their-beliefs verified that initial implementation. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-02.md. - REFINED (UKRN v3 HO-08b, 2026-05-15): the original "only :active updates beliefs" semantic was over-conservative. Under the v3 integration where most institutions go :paused early (abstain cascade until capabilities come online), the over-conservative gate caused beliefs to never evolve over the run — surfaced as four cascading test failures (belief-movement; noiseless-variance-decay; both lesion-contrasts). The corrected semantic distinguishes engagement (the agent's action) from observation (the agent's perception): :active and :paused both update; only :truncated freezes. Implementation in notebooks/ukrn_v3_kernel.clj postprocess-institution. Test renamed to truncated-institutions-keep-beliefs-paused-institutions-update. Evidence: handoffs/v3_runner/validation_HO-08b.md. - Practice: the gate is a *post-step* decision, applied after the dynamics step has run. The dynamics may still update other state (NPT factors, capabilities) for non-active instances via rollback logic; that's about action, not perception. The agent's belief tracks what the agent observes, which can continue under :paused even when engagement is paused. - Lesson: when defining "the agent isn't observing this instance" for a status-gated update, ask explicitly whether the post-step state still carries the instance's coordinates. If yes (e.g., dynamics computes (D, A) for paused instances and the simulation reports them), then *observation is still happening* and beliefs should update. Reserving the freeze for genuinely-no-more-observations cases (truncated, dropped, deleted) keeps belief evolution coherent across the run.

title: Structured Observation Vector
text: Structured Observation Vector Treat each step as a typed observation vector so scoring and learning can be compared across time. A pattern-guided agent must decide based on tool output, trace events, and user feedback. You want the agent's observation to be comparable across steps so scoring and learning do not collapse into prose interpretation. Tool output and user feedback arrive as heterogeneous artifacts (json, logs, diffs, snippets, natural language) that are hard to compare or weight consistently. Maintain an explicit (o) as a typed, normalized feature map derived from session state (for example: test status, compile status, diff size, failing spec count, user-stated constraints, time since last anchor, contradiction flags). A stable observation vector is the prerequisite for meaningful precision control and policy scoring. - Define :aif/observation-vector schema in tatami_schema.clj with keys [:test-status :compile-status :diff-size :failing-spec-count :user-constraints :time-since-anchor :contradiction-flags]. - Add (extract-observation-vector session-state) to aif_bridge.clj that normalizes tool output into the typed map. - Include observation vector in :aif/tick events; require it for PSR context/anchors validation. - Add (observation-delta o1 o2) and log deltas alongside policy changes in learn_or_act/decide.

title: Term-to-Channel Traceability
text: Term-to-Channel Traceability Require each score term to declare the observation channels and precision settings it consumed. A pattern-guided agent evaluates candidates with a multi-term expected free energy score built from heterogeneous evidence. You want tuning decisions and failures to be diagnosable at the level of which evidence actually drove each score term. Without explicit traceability, terms like risk or ambiguity silently absorb whatever signals are available, making post-hoc explanations indistinguishable from rationalization. Require every G term contribution to declare the observation keys it consumed, the precision channels applied, and the intermediate values used to compute that term, and persist this mapping alongside the score. Explicit term-to-channel linkage prevents semantic drift in scoring terms and makes policy behavior mechanically inspectable. - DONE: Validate PSR :aif/g-terms provenance keys (term-id, observation-keys, precision-channels, intermediate-values, final-contribution) in check-psr. Evidence: src/futon3/hx/logic.clj - DONE: Add (dominant-channels psr) analysis that flags when a single channel accounts for >60% of a term's value. Evidence: src/futon3/hx/logic.clj - DONE: Add term provenance + dominant channel summaries to fulab pattern reports. Evidence: src/futon3/fulab/pattern_competence.clj, dev/lab-pattern-report.clj - DONE: Emit :aif summaries in MUSN turn start/select/use responses and log them in musn_stream. Evidence: src/futon3/musn/service.clj, dev/musn_stream.clj, src/futon3/musn/schema.clj - BLOCKED: Define :aif/term-provenance schema in tatami_schema.clj with keys [:term-id :observation-keys :precision-channels :intermediate-values :final-contribution]. blocked-by[tatami-schema] - BLOCKED: Include term provenance in fulab-pattern-check CLI output for top-3 candidates. blocked-by[term-provenance-schema, fulab-pattern-check]

title: Baseline Cyber-AIF Ant
text: Baseline Cyber-AIF Ant Treat the baseline cyber-ant as a narratable instance of the Futon2 AIF loop: its observation ABI, predictive-cycle trace, hunger dynamics, and policy harness are all frozen so Futon5 can lift the behaviour into an operator. You are turning the Futon2 AIF loop into a portable pattern asset for Futon5. You want a generated agent to behave exactly like today’s handcrafted AIF ants, including mode hysteresis, hunger/tau coupling, and softmax tilts. The implementation currently lives as code and tests inside Futon2; none of those behaviours are catalogued as pattern data Futon5 can compile. Canonically describe the loop from `g-observe` → `perceive/perceive` → `affect/update-tau` → `policy/choose-action`, referencing the single-tick trace (`doc/trace/single_tick.*`) and policy harness goldens so Futon5 has deterministic source material. Once the narrative and fixtures exist as pattern assets, Futon5 can attach a `:cyber/baseline` operator that emits an AIF config identical to Futon2’s defaults, making cyber-ants “pattern flashed” twins of the current species. next[Bind this description to a Futon5 operator signature that exports the `:aif` config delta plus textual explanation for cyber-ant flashing.]

title: Cargo Return Discipline Pattern
text: Cargo Return Discipline Pattern When an AIF agent carries significant cargo yet keeps returning without depositing, clamp tau, penalise reuse of :return, and prioritise deposit completion. The pattern generalises to any delivery/return loop. You are preventing cargo return thrash in cyber-ant policy. The agent has cargo ≥ 0.05, repeatedly chooses :return while `:dep` = 0, or stalls near the nest. Without explicit clamps the agent “thrashes”: it walks home, refuses to deposit, and never re-enters outbound mode, starving the colony or the task. Detect cargo-stall streaks, apply negative G adjustments to :return until a deposit event fires, slightly boost :hold when resting on the nest, and cap tau around 0.65 so the agent exploits the completion action. Emit telemetry for stalled runs so analyzers can intervene. The same logic applies to graph walkers (deliver package, reward commit) or any pattern that alternates gather/deliver phases. next[Bind this pattern to Futon5’s uplift so cyber-ants (and future courier agents) inherit the stall detector and tau clamp.]

title: Hunger ↔ Precision Coupling Pattern
text: Hunger ↔ Precision Coupling Pattern Hunger drives precision: cyber-ants honour Futon2’s goldens so that `tick-hunger` + `update-hunger` + `hunger->tau` feed into `modulate-precisions` and `update-tau`, including reserve pressure and depot/risk contributions. You are exporting hunger-to-tau coupling so Futon5 can flash faithful agents. The affect layer reports hunger trends (`dhdt`), ingest shortfalls, and colony reserves matching the six golden scenarios (normal, starvation, overstimulation, heavy-cargo, high-risk, high-ingest). Without explicit coupling rules the Futon5 operator cannot guarantee that a flashed agent reproduces the tau annealing Futon2 already verifies. Reference the hunger/tau goldens and declare the response curve: hungrier ants lower tau, home safety lifts tau, deficit reserves subtract from tau, and clamp logic cuts exploitation during high-risk cargo returns. Futon5 needs those declarative mappings to export a faithful cyber-ant affect config; otherwise the new agents would drift away from the proven hunger dynamics. next[Expose this coupling as metadata in the cyber-ant operator so Futon2 can attach the generated config per species.]

title: Adaptive Trail Tuner Pattern
text: Adaptive Trail Tuner Pattern Regulate pheromone laying by coupling trail gradients to hunger, novelty, and reserve pressure so trails serve as communicative signals rather than noise. You are tuning pheromone output so trails carry useful signal. The local pheromone signal is weak, novelty high, or reserves deficit, while the agent is outbound or maintaining a corridor. Without adaptive scaling, ants either flood the board with trails (entropy) or fail to leave breadcrumbs when scouts discover food deserts. Bias :pheromone G downward when novelty is high and cargo low, but penalise it near the nest or during reserve crises; anneal tau upward to encourage exploration pulses. Use the Futon2 analyzer’s `:pher` metrics to adjust the laying rate. The same principle applies to graph walkers emitting hints or proofs: you want signaling to adapt to novelty and resource pressure. next[Expose the trail-tuner knobs via Futon5 so cyber-ants (and future graph agents) can publish adjustable signal intensity.]

title: White-Space Scout Pattern
text: White-Space Scout Pattern Cyber-ants inherit the “white space” doctrine: when food + pheromones slump below the epsilon bands and novelty is high, anneal tau upward, penalise foraging, and gently bias toward pheromone laying or scouting returns. You are declaring the white-space heuristic so cyber-ants can mirror Futon2 behavior. Observations satisfy the Futon2 `white?` detector — food trace, pheromone trace, and recent gather are all low, and the ant is off-nest. Without this guard the agents burn ticks circling barren cells, starving the colony even when hunger pressure says “exploit elsewhere.” Encode the heuristics currently embedded in `policy/choose-action` as a pattern operator: raise G-adjustments for :forage, lower them for :return and :pheromone, and stretch tau when the scout sits on empty nest tiles. Futon5 needs the declarative rule (“white space implies scout stance”) so it can flash cyber-ants or future agents with the same homing instinct. next[Link this pattern to the cyber-ant operator so Futon5 emits the matching `:white-space` action deltas and tau clamps.]

title: Mana-Gated Work: action selection bounded by available budget
text: Mana-Gated Work: action selection bounded by available budget Action selection should be constrained by available budget or license, not by priority alone. A proposed action is *gated* — permitted to run — only when the operator's session-level mana balance can sustain its expected cost. Block-closure at hinges awards mana; allostatic-load drains it; the gate is the live intersection of "what does this action cost" and "what does the session have to spend." Without the gate, priority sorting alone recommends everything that is locally desirable, regardless of whether the substrate can sustain its execution. With the gate, the system selects within a budget the operator's metabolic state can actually afford. The candidate invariant `mana-gated-work` was named in the futon5a stack-stereolithography queue (`run-064`, `F-budgeted-action-selection`) with the summary: "Action selection should be constrained by available budget or license, not by priority alone. Some proposed work should be selectable only when enough budget is available, but this remains weakly implemented." The mission `M-bounded-in-flight-state` formalises the *balance dynamic* (`structure/mana-allostasis`) the gate operates on; this pattern names the gate itself. Production precedent: `futon5/scripts/nonstarter_mana.clj`'s `sospeso` command computes `(1-p)*C` to pool as pure *dana* (Buddhist generosity) when an action of cost C is committed at confidence p. The pool IS the session-level budget; the confidence-weighted cost IS the gating signal. The system is selecting which proposed action to run from a queue (the priority queue, the mission queue, the agent backpack, etc.), and the actions vary in cost. Pure priority-sorted selection has no metabolic awareness: - High-priority but high-cost actions can be selected even when the session's mana balance is depleted, accelerating substrate corruption. - Low-priority but low-cost actions that would maintain balance never get a turn because higher-priority items always exist. - The operator's felt fatigue has no path into the action- selection loop. - **Priority-only selection** (no gate): the default broken state this pattern names. - **Hard-cap-only selection** (no priority): everything below a threshold runs in arbitrary order; misses important work. - **Per-agent budgets** (precursor): see `p4ng/agent-as-mana-unit-was-the-wrong-unit`. - **Counterfeit gate-pass**: action declares its cost as lower than it actually is to slip through. Mitigated by cost-confidence weighting (sospeso) and post-hoc reconciliation against actual block-closure cost. Gate the selector: a candidate action runs if and only if the session's current mana balance can afford its expected cost. Define cost in terms of the channels of `mana-allostasis`: working-tree pressure increment, mission-proliferation increment, session-sprawl increment, untriaged-evidence increment. Define *afford* in terms of the session's running balance + a small safety margin. Reject (with `:reason :insufficient-budget`) rather than execute when the gate fails. Selection becomes a two-step process: 1. Priority sort the candidate set. 2. Walk the sorted list; for each candidate, ask the gate "can the session afford this?" Take the first that passes; defer the rest with explicit reason. - Selector consistently rejects high-priority items: budget is depleted at session level. Operator should close blocks (any drain channel) before continuing. - Selector consistently accepts everything: gate may not be wired, or budget thresholds may be too generous. Recheck cost-quantum estimates. - Selector accepts one action then immediately rejects the next at apparently equal cost: stochastic gate behaviour points at miscalibrated confidence in the cost estimator. The `nonstarter_mana.clj` precursor's *sospeso → dana* pattern is operationally sound. An action committed at confidence p with cost C *gives* `(1-p)*C` to the pool — confidence- discounted cost is the right cost-quantum because low-confidence actions burn budget proportionally more even when they succeed. Dana (generosity) is the right metaphor: an action's cost is given to the future operator who will close the eventual block. The session that takes on cost is the session that owes the closure. Action-selection budgets attach to sessions, not to agents. See `p4ng/agent-as-mana-unit-was-the-wrong-unit` for the precursor reasoning. An agent has no metabolism beyond its turn; the session is the temporal frame in which budgets integrate. A multi-agent session pools its mana economy at the session level, not partitioned per-agent. - structure/mana-allostasis — the balance dynamic the gate consults. - structure/block-as-futonic-revolution — the unit whose closure replenishes the budget. - invariant-coherence/drain-channel-shape — the per-channel cost estimators feed the gate. - p4ng/agent-as-mana-unit-was-the-wrong-unit — the precursor unit-error this pattern corrects. - futon5a/holes/stack-stereolithography-runs/run-064-budgeted-action-selection--mana-gated-work.md — the candidate invariant in the queue this pattern formalises. - futon5/scripts/nonstarter_mana.clj — the production-code precursor. Priority captures what matters in the abstract; budget captures what the system can actually sustain right now. Both readings are needed. A priority-only selector is a recipe for substrate corruption (the operator runs out of capacity to close blocks faster than load accumulates). A budget-only selector is a recipe for stagnation (high-priority work never gets selected because something cheaper always squeezes in). The gate composes them.

title: The Campaign Is a Temporary Autonomous Institution
text: The Campaign Is a Temporary Autonomous Institution When several Missions depend on one shared knowledge structure that no single Mission can own, run them through a **Campaign** — a Temporary Autonomous Institution one tier above Mission that charters a joint goal, delivers and verifies the shared standard, and then **dissolves**, leaving the constituent Missions as the durable residue. Some work decomposes into a cluster of Missions that all build towards the *same* standard (a metric, schema, contract, substrate). The cluster has coordination needs — ordering, a shared deliverable, a joint completion criterion — that sit above any one Mission. You have multi-Mission work whose members share one dependency, and the joint goal is real but owned by no single Mission. Mission-shape mis-fits this two ways (see [[campaign-coherence/shared-standard-has-no-single-owner]]): a Mission that grows to hold the cluster loses Mission discipline; a tangle of Missions with no organising frame lets each look successful while the joint goal slips. And a *standing* institution over-fits: it persists past its purpose, accreting coordination overhead with no end. Charter a **Temporary Autonomous Institution** with the 7-phase Campaign spine: CHARTER (joint goal, often from a War Bulletin) → CONSTITUTION (survey dependents + governance) → ESCROW (register held dependencies) → STANDARD-ARGUE → STANDARD-VERIFY (the shared standard, fit for all) → RUN/DELIVER (keystone ships it) → DISSOLUTION. Constituent Missions run their **own** lifecycles; the Campaign coordinates, never re-runs their phases. Built to end: when the joint completion criterion fires, the Campaign dissolves and the Missions remain. Temporariness is the point.
