The cluster needs an institution *for a while* — to own the shared standard's cross-mission adequacy and the escrow that holds dependent work — but a permanent one would outlive its goal and become overhead. Autonomy (self-governance for the duration) + temporariness (dissolution on joint-criterion) is exactly what a bounded cross-mission effort wants. The War Room persists and narrates; the Campaign ends and delivers. - Distinguish keystone Mission (builds the standard) from paired/dependent Missions (consumers) in CHARTER membership. - Make the joint completion criterion genuinely *cross-mission* ("standard verified AND ≥1 dependent requirement released-and-consumed"), never "all members done." - At DISSOLUTION, hand any unsatisfied escrow entries back as ordinary dependencies / follow-on missions — named, never dropped. - First instance: `Campaign-substrate-completion` (keystone M-substrate-metric; paired M-aif2 + M-differentiable-code).

title: Cross-Mission Escrow — Hold Dependent Work in Two Release Steps
text: Cross-Mission Escrow — Hold Dependent Work in Two Release Steps Register each cross-Mission dependency on a shared standard as a **held requirement** that releases in two steps — `held → contract-released` (on STANDARD-VERIFY) `→ satisfied` (on delivery) — so dependent work is *named but not built on sand*, and the requirement neither blocks the cluster nor silently disappears. In a Campaign, paired (dependent) Missions need things from the shared standard the keystone Mission delivers. They must not build the dependent slices before the standard exists — but those requirements must not be forgotten either. A Mission has work that depends on a shared standard another Mission (or the Campaign) is still establishing. Two naive options both fail. Build the dependent slice now → you build on sand (the standard may change or mis-fit). Drop the requirement until "later" → it goes silent and the dependent Mission quietly diverges or the joint goal slips. And a single release point ("wait until the standard ships") blocks the dependent Mission longer than necessary — it could be *designing to the spec* well before the live delivery exists. Put every dependency in an **escrow ledger** entry: `{:from-mission, :on <standard|keystone>, :requirement, :status}`. Mark the dependent slice `:held` (named, not built). Release in **two steps**: STANDARD-VERIFY freezes the contract → flip to `:contract-released` (the Mission may now build *to the verified spec*, unblocked but not on sand); RUN/DELIVER ships the live standard → flip to `:satisfied` (the Mission consumes it). At DISSOLUTION, any entry not `:satisfied` becomes an ordinary dependency / follow-on mission — named, never dropped. The two-step release separates *contract certainty* from *delivery*: a verified contract is enough to build against (decoupling the dependent Mission's progress from the keystone's delivery latency), while live delivery is what completes consumption. Naming the requirement in a ledger makes "we're holding off building this" a first-class, auditable state rather than an implicit gap. This is HEAD-as-escrow (a mission HEAD that crystallises intent without committing to schema) lifted to the cross-mission case: the requirement is escrowed *across* the Campaign's membership. - One ledger entry per dependency; status is one of `:held | :contract-released | :satisfied`. - Name what triggers each release: STANDARD-VERIFY → contract-released; RUN/DELIVER → satisfied. - Treat `:held` count + oldest-held age as Campaign-health telemetry (a long-held requirement is a stall signal). - First ledger: Campaign-substrate-completion — `M-aif2` holds "curvature as tension-signal", `M-differentiable-code` holds "continuous embedding for code-graph gradients", both `:on M-substrate-metric`.

title: A Shared Standard Has No Single-Mission Owner — That's Why the Campaign Exists
text: A Shared Standard Has No Single-Mission Owner — That's Why the Campaign Exists A shared standard that several Missions must build towards needs an ARGUE + VERIFY of its **cross-mission adequacy** that no constituent Mission can own; that ownerless adequacy-check is precisely why Campaign-shape exists, and it is the Campaign's load-bearing phase (STANDARD-VERIFY). Several Missions depend on one shared knowledge structure (a metric, schema, contract, substrate). Each Mission knows what *it* needs from the standard; none can see whether the standard fits *all* of them. A standard must be the same across multiple Missions, and "is this standard adequate for everyone who depends on it?" is a question with an answer. No single Mission can answer it. Absorb the standard into one Mission and it gets built to that Mission's needs — the others inherit a mis-fit and each *looks* successful while the joint goal silently slips (proxy-problem substitution). Leave it implicit and each Mission builds its own version — it **forks** into per-Mission shadows that don't compose. Make the standard's **cross-mission adequacy** a first-class deliverable owned by a Campaign. STANDARD-ARGUE argues *why this standard, fit for all consumers*; STANDARD-VERIFY verifies it **as a design, before any Mission builds to it** (logic-model-before-code at Campaign tier: conforming witness ⇒ 0 violations; one adversarial trace per consumer-requirement ⇒ caught). A requirement the standard can't meet is a Campaign blocker, not a Mission's problem. On VERIFY-pass the contract freezes — *that* is "the shared standard to build towards." The adequacy check is structurally ownerless: it ranges over requirements that live in *different* Missions, so it can only be performed one tier up. This is the `structure/what-problem-is-this-actually-solving` answer to "why not just a Mission?" — without the Campaign, the shared standard is either captured (mis-fit for the others) or forked (no shared standard at all). Verifying it before anyone commits is what stops the Missions building toward a moving or mis-fit target. - In STANDARD-ARGUE, show per-consumer that the standard satisfies each escrowed requirement; surface any it can't (revise the standard or re-scope the member). - In STANDARD-VERIFY, plant one adversarial trace per consumer-requirement; the coverage contract is per-requirement, not sampled. - Keep this distinct from the keystone Mission's *own* VERIFY: the Campaign verifies "fit for all consumers" (the contract); the Mission verifies "this build is sound" (the implementation). - Worked failure to cite: war-bulletin-10 WR-21's three-way fork of the thin scalar field — the evidence that a single Mission could not have owned the substrate-2 metric.

title: Free Solo and the Rope (the autonomy/tail-risk career tension)
text: Free Solo and the Rope (the autonomy/tail-risk career tension) A career-mode tension that does NOT resolve by picking a side. The mode with the most autonomy and the highest upside — **C** (consulting / "free solo") — is also the mode with **unbounded downside**: a single failure can be terminal ("sudden death"). Both naive resolutions fail. Pure-C free-solos an un-roped route and bets the operator on never falling. Pure-**A** (industry) caps the downside but surrenders the autonomy and optionality that were *the actual objective* — the rope becomes a cage. The resolved form is **the rope**: hold a **basket** (B academic + C consulting) in which **B backstops C's tail**, and treat any A-commitment as a **bounded experiment that preserves optionality** — sample the arm, observe, retain the option, do not dilute. The Anthropic Fellowship's 4-month-bounded-with-retention shape is exactly this: a Thompson-sampling move on A-mode that keeps the rest of the basket live. *Before you free-solo El Capitan, climb it roped a bunch of times.* The same operator-thinking-with-metaphor surfaces independently across the corpus, which is what makes it a pattern and not an essay-local mood: - **Anthropic Fellows Q7 / §6** — the B+C basket; B as "the rope that prevents C-mode failures from leading to sudden death"; the Fellowship as temp-A retaining optionality; "applying ≠ taking"; not equity-dilutive. - **Glasgow Q6** — "Before you climb El Capitan without a rope, you should do it with a rope a bunch of times" (the academic role as the rope for learning the route). - **COGITO §6** — the free-solo-vs-funding-pursuit contradiction; the "job as customer" reframe. The interest-mining reduce flagged free-solo/rope as a cross-EOI *merge candidate* (shared backbone). This pattern IS that shared identity: a constellation node that points HERE is a peer in the topology without claiming to be an interest-star. The tension is a genuine conflict of forces; the pattern holds them, it does not dissolve them (see substructure). - **Autonomy / upside** pulls toward C (the work Joe actually wants to do is C-shaped: research-entrepreneur, missing-customer, Hyperreal). - **Tail-risk / ruin** pulls toward A's floor (C-mode failures compound; one can be terminal). - **The goal is the optionality itself** — so a resolution that eliminates optionality (pure-A) has defeated its own purpose, even though it "wins" on downside. - **A bounded experiment is not a commitment** — applying ≠ taking; a retention-option is information-with-the-arm-kept, not a trap. - **Free-soloing without a rope.** Choosing C with no B backstop: one failure is terminal. This is the failure the rope exists to prevent. - **Abandoning C for A's safety.** Caps the downside but surrenders the autonomy that was the objective. The rope becomes the cage; the operator is safe and not doing the work they wanted. - **Reading "rope" as "never solo".** The rope is for *learning the route*, not for never climbing it. A permanent rope is a never-realised C. - **Collapsing a bounded experiment into a commitment.** Treating the Fellowship (or any temp-A) as terminal — reading the fine print as a trap, or taking it as if permanent — discards the info-gain-with-retained-option that made the arm worth sampling. - **Modelling the modes as statically fungible.** Reputation, skill, and customer-relationships accumulate in one mode and translate (with friction) into another; a resolution that ignores the exchange-matrix M_{ij} mis-prices every basket.

title: Dead Code Hygiene
text: Dead Code Hygiene Keep MUSN behaviour legible by pruning experiments, deprecated flows, and orphaned namespaces before they are mistaken for supported features. You are aligning the codebase with the devmap so only supported paths remain visible. Repository-transition diagnostics already insist on tracking code paths to explicit obligations. RID-era handlers and paused experiments still live in the tree with no devmap references, confusing refactors and reviewers. Schedule periodic dead-code sweeps: identify unreferenced namespaces, obsolete protocol handlers, and one-off experiments; delete or archive them; and ensure devmaps point only at active code paths. Dhammavicaya requires that “what the system does” and “what the devmap claims” match; dead code collapses that link. next[Run `clojure -M:test` with namespace coverage and flag modules unused outside tests.] next[Archive RID protocol handlers once MUSN adapters replace them, citing commits in the evidence ledger.]

title: Stay Coupled to the Surrounding Field
text: Stay Coupled to the Surrounding Field Collaborative work needs deliberate, recurring coupling to its surrounding field — adjacent projects, external readers, prior art — or it accretes its own private vocabulary, repeats solved problems, and rejects useful inputs as foreign. The pattern is to schedule and structure the coupling, not to hope it happens; the surface form to detect ("Not Invented Here," fenced field, blinkered horse) is named in Guattari's transversality framing as the absence of a coefficient that has to be set. Distributed peer-learning projects and small teams default to inward attention. In-group vocabulary tightens; in-group references stack; the project becomes legible to itself faster than it becomes legible to anyone else. Without counter-pressure, the same dynamics that produce focus produce isolation. Adjacent projects solve overlapping problems independently and never compose. External readers find no entry path. The "transversality coefficient" — the rate of permitted exposure — has to be set deliberately or it sets itself to zero. The pattern operates on the axis: focus ↔ exposure. Irreducible: a project cannot simultaneously be at maximum inward attention and maximum outward porosity. Each unit of coupling work costs focus; each unit of unbroken focus costs coupling. Real costs: deep focus is what lets a small group make progress on hard problems. Sustained focus without exposure is what makes that progress invisible to (and unusable by) anyone outside it. Both effects are continuous; the question is whether the coupling rate is named. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a deadline tightens, when a project encounters its first internal vocabulary that wasn't there before, and when a newcomer arrives and finds the entry-cost prohibitive. - Not-invented-here build: the group writes a custom version of a tool / framework / vocabulary that already exists, without recording why the existing artefact was rejected. - Vocabulary drift: in-group terms calcify with no equivalent in adjacent fields; the project becomes harder to explain over time, not easier. - Newcomer rejection: arrivals consistently bounce off; the group attributes it to the newcomer rather than reading it as exposure-surface failure. - Cross-project blindness: another project solves the same problem in parallel and the group doesn't notice for months or years. - Defensive overfocus: criticism from outside is reflexively rejected as "they don't understand the context"; the rejection is the symptom, not the response. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Scheduled exposure: name a recurring slot — monthly external review, periodic prior-art audit, regular cross-project show-and-tell — where the project deliberately steps outside its own frame. Cadence matters more than depth. (2) Adjacent-project mapping: maintain a list of projects working on overlapping problems, with current state and one-line interface. The list is a wrapper artefact; the maintenance is the coupling. (3) NIH-detection: when the group reaches for a custom build, ask explicitly what existing artefact was considered and rejected. Make reuse the default branch; force "make" to justify itself. (4) Newcomer-as-probe: treat each newcomer's stuck moment as evidence that the coupling rate is too low — the entry path measures the project's exposure surface. (5) Friendly external readers: maintain at least one named external reader who isn't a contributor but knows the project well enough to flag in-group drift. Engaged when: the project's vocabulary, references, and design choices are recognisably composed with its surrounding field, and at least one structured exposure surface is current. Failing when: project vocabulary has diverged from any neighbouring usage, contributors cannot name the closest adjacent project, or the project's own reuse-vs-make decisions never include explicit reuse-search.

title: Expect Process Cost; Name the Friction
text: Expect Process Cost; Name the Friction Problem-solving in collaborative work always takes time, attention, and friction; expecting tools, platforms, or processes to come pre-built (or to "just work" once installed) is the failure mode that strips a project of its own learning. The pattern is to name the magical assumption explicitly, estimate its friction cost, and budget for the work the project will actually have to do — preserving the friction-as-learning property the project depends on. Voluntary peer-learning projects routinely reach for the next tool / framework / process under the implicit hope that adoption will dissolve the underlying problem. Sometimes adoption helps; often it just relocates the problem (now we have the same coordination issue, plus a new tool to learn). The deeper failure is that "magical thinking" robs the project of the *process* — the working-through that constitutes much of what a peer-learning project is meant to produce. If the tooling were truly that good, the handbook wouldn't need to exist. The pattern operates on the axis: faith in tooling ↔ attention to process cost. Irreducible: a project cannot simultaneously be working on the underlying problem and waiting for tooling to make the underlying problem disappear. At any moment one or the other is happening. Real costs: tooling really does matter — a good substrate halves the work. But the marginal value of tooling is bounded above by the project's actual problem; past that bound, tooling investment is displacement. Both effects are continuous; the question is whether the project knows which side of the bound it is on. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever the project hits a frustration that has a "if only we had X" response, whenever a new tool appears in the discourse, and whenever a contributor proposes adoption rather than configuration of an existing tool. - Pre-built fantasy: "the ideal platform would come with X already solved" — said without engagement with whether such a platform exists or could exist. - Adoption cascade: a new tool is adopted, brings a problem, which is solved by adopting another tool, and so on; each round defers rather than discharges the underlying issue. - Friction-blindness: contributors propose adoption without naming the onboarding or maintenance cost; the cost is paid silently by whoever ends up doing it. - Process-stripping: a frustration that was teaching the project something gets dissolved by tooling, and the project later realises the learning is gone with it. - Stress-driven habit shift: under pressure the project falls back on already-trained tools rather than reaching for the most appropriate one (echoing the Science Magazine quote in the source — habit displaces goal-directed choice under stress). Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Name the magical assumption: when the next tool / process / framework is proposed, write down what specifically is expected to become easier, by how much, and on what timescale. The act of writing usually changes the proposal. (2) Friction budget: maintain an explicit estimate of the project's available attention. New adoptions get a friction line item — onboarding, configuration, ongoing maintenance, integration with existing tooling. When the budget overruns, something gets dropped. (3) Adopt-after-use: try to solve the underlying problem with existing tooling first. If the existing tooling visibly fails, the diagnostic information is what justifies adoption. Without that diagnostic, adoption is speculation. (4) Preserve process learning: when a frustration is dissolved by tooling, ask what the project was *learning* from that frustration. If the answer is something useful, recover it deliberately (e.g. document the now-tooling-handled problem so contributors who need to understand it still can). (5) Magical-thinking audit: periodically review which assumptions about tooling have actually paid off and which have not. Pattern revision based on evidence beats the next adoption proposal. Engaged when: every tooling adoption decision has a recorded prior expectation and a recorded post-hoc audit. Failing when: tools accumulate without commensurate progress on the underlying problem, or the project repeatedly proposes the same kind of tooling solution with no acknowledgement of why prior versions didn't deliver.

title: Design for the Participation Gradient
text: Design for the Participation Gradient Voluntary collaborative learning produces a continuous gradient of participation — from full completion through partial engagement to silent observation — and that gradient is structural, not pathological. The pattern is to design for the gradient: separate metrics per participation tier, low-cost partial-participation paths, low-cost re-entry, and explicit acceptance that "lurker" and "non-completer" are valid project states rather than failures to be eliminated. Online peer-learning groups (MOOCs the canonical case, but the dynamic is general) attract orders of magnitude more lurkers than completers. Stanford's MOOC AI class started with 100,000+ and finished with 12%; that ratio is structural to voluntary, low-entry-cost, asynchronous learning. The failure mode named "messy with lurkers" is not the participation gradient itself but the *misreading* of it as broken — applying completion-rate metrics borrowed from compulsory education, designing as if the gradient should be flat, or treating lurkers as a defect to be filtered. The mess is real; the misreading is the antipattern. The pattern operates on the axis: completion-rate metrics ↔ participation-gradient design. Irreducible: a single metric cannot simultaneously honour the value of completion and the value of partial participation — they answer different questions. The choice is which question the project's design optimises. Real costs: completion is a real outcome and metric. Designing only for completion truncates the project's reach to the small minority that completes. Designing for the gradient accepts attrition as a feature and instruments accordingly. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever the project reports its statistics, whenever onboarding is redesigned, and whenever a funder asks about completion rates. - Completion-only metric: project reports its success as completion percentage, treating attrition as universal failure. - Hidden gradient: partial participation has no recognised value, so partial participants leave invisibly and the project is surprised by the resulting headcount. - High-cost re-entry: someone who lurked for a month finds the cost of joining mid-stream prohibitive; the lurking phase that should produce participants instead produces departures. - Lurker-shaming: project communications treat lurkers as a problem to be solved rather than a tier to be designed for. - Cohort-only thinking: the project assumes a fixed cohort, then reads the gradient (which is what voluntary participation actually is) as cohort failure. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Multi-tier metrics: separately track completion, partial completion (named milestones), active engagement (visible contribution), and reach (lurker count, content access). Each tier has its own success criterion. (2) Low-cost partial paths: explicit value at each gradient level — a lurker who never contributes still gets something; a partial-participant who quits at week three has done something useful; the completer is the highest tier but not the only tier. (3) Low-cost re-entry: attrition is reversible. Someone who dropped at week three can rejoin at week eight without restarting. The infrastructure for re-entry (tagged checkpoints, durable artefacts, async-friendly content) is the design move. (4) Acknowledge dissipation: name the participation gradient explicitly in the project's self-description. This converts attrition from embarrassment to design feature. (5) Pair with carrying-capacity: the same participants who lurk in one phase may contribute in another; the same group's carrying capacity is bounded; treating lurkers as inactive contributors-in-waiting respects both. Engaged when: project reports separately track lurkers, partial participants, and completers; design decisions visibly accommodate all three. Failing when: a single completion-rate number is the headline metric, or onboarding makes partial participation unavailable.

title: Respect the Long Tail; Design Against the Bargain You Strike With It
text: Respect the Long Tail; Design Against the Bargain You Strike With It Participation in voluntary online collaboration follows a power law (90/9/1, Zipf, long-tail) as a structural property of networks, not as a defect of any particular community. The pattern is to acknowledge this explicitly, design with the power-law shape in mind, and resist provisionist responses ("if we just change the system, participation will be equal") that mistake an emergent network property for a fixable bug. Within the power-law shape, real moves still exist (lower-the-floor, raise-the-ceiling, rotate-who-is-in-the-1%) — they just aren't moves toward flatness. Asynchronous online groups invariably show steeply unequal participation: a few power contributors, a layer of occasional ones, a long tail of lurkers. The same shape governs city sizes, word frequency, energy use, and most network phenomena. Communities repeatedly attempt to flatten it ("wouldn't it be great if everyone participated equally?") and repeatedly fail in the same way. The antipattern is not the power law itself but the misreading: treating its persistence as evidence the community has chosen the wrong system, the wrong tools, or the wrong norms. The persistence is structural; the system, tools, and norms have other failure modes worth fixing, but the power-law shape isn't one of them. The pattern operates on the axis: equality aspiration ↔ structural reality. Irreducible: a community cannot simultaneously be voluntary, low-entry-cost, asynchronous AND have flat participation distribution. The first three conditions produce the fourth (long tail) by themselves. Real costs: equality of voice is a legitimate aspiration; the project's claim to be peer-driven depends on it. But power-law dynamics are an emergent property of the network, not a policy choice. Both forces operate continuously; flattening one (per design) does not eliminate the other (per network structure). Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever participation statistics are reported, whenever a moderator considers a new "engagement intervention," and whenever a community accepts a proposal that promises to "fix" engagement asymmetry. - Provisionist proposal: "if we change the system / tooling / norms / onboarding, participation will be more equal" — without engagement with why prior interventions of this shape failed. - Equality-as-failure-state: any deviation from flat participation is read as evidence of dysfunction, prompting interventions that don't change the distribution. - Power-law denial: project reports omit the long tail entirely, focusing on the 1% / 9% as if they were the whole community. - Symbolic-violence blindness: the project treats whose framings dominate as a neutral fact, missing that the power-law shape produces asymmetric influence over shared meaning. - Conflation of voice and frequency: a quiet participant raises a concern; the response is "well, you haven't been very engaged" — substituting frequency-of-prior-contribution for legitimacy-of-current-contribution. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Acknowledge structurally: name the power-law shape in the project's self-description. Move from "we hope everyone participates equally" to "we expect 90/9/1 and design for it." (2) Lower the floor: make low-cost participation valuable on its own terms (see collaboration-coherence/messy-with-lurkers). Power-law-aware design extracts more value from the long tail rather than trying to shorten it. (3) Raise the ceiling: make high-engagement participation more rewarding without requiring it. The 1% is real; supporting them is legitimate. The error is conflating "support the 1%" with "make everyone the 1%." (4) Rotate the 1%: deliberately pass the most-active role across participants over time so no single person gets stuck at the top of the distribution (which is a carrying-capacity issue, not a participation-equality one). (5) Distinguish equality-of-voice from equality-of-frequency: equal voice is about whose contributions are taken seriously when they occur, not about contribution counts. The former is achievable; the latter is structurally unattainable in voluntary networks. (6) Symbolic-violence check: per the source's Sapir-Whorf / Bourdieu reference, the most-frequent participants shape the language and norms of the group. Power-law-aware moderation includes deliberate counter-pressure on whose framings dominate. Engaged when: the project's design and metrics treat the long tail as a feature; engagement asymmetry is accepted at the structural level while specific failure modes (silenced voices, single-person bottlenecks) are addressed individually. Failing when: project leadership pursues "equal participation" as the goal, or the failure of equality-engineering interventions is treated as a community pathology rather than as evidence the goal was misframed.

title: Close the Feedback Loop with an Action; Avoid the Bateson Double-Bind
text: Close the Feedback Loop with an Action; Avoid the Bateson Double-Bind Reflection and feedback have value only when there is a mechanism for acting on them; the failure mode is feedback channels that absorb critique without consequence — the Bateson double-bind in which the receiver invites criticism while making any effective criticism unwelcome. The pattern is to close every feedback loop with a named action surface: where critiques go, who decides, what gets changed, what doesn't, and why. Criticism without an action surface is noise; the *art of paragogical praxis* is to make something useful out of what would otherwise be noise. Peer-learning projects, like most reflective communities, accumulate feedback channels (forums, retrospectives, action reviews, comment threads, evaluation surveys). The failure mode is not too much reflection — it is reflection without a connected action surface. Contributors offer critique; the critique is heard; the project does not change in response. Over time, contributors stop bothering, or the most useful critics leave. The Bateson double-bind makes this concrete: "go ahead, criticise me — but all effective criticism will be unwelcome." When the implicit reception of criticism is hostile or null, the explicit invitation is destructive. The pattern operates on the axis: reflection ↔ action. Irreducible: a feedback channel cannot simultaneously be a free-flowing reflective space AND a tightly bounded action queue. The project must decide which channel is which, and how each transitions to the other. Real costs: reflection without action is hollow; action without reflection is reactive. Both pure modes fail; the question is how the project structures the interface between them. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every retrospective, every survey, every "tell us how we're doing" prompt — and especially when feedback arrives that the project would prefer not to act on. - Open invitation, closed reception: "we welcome criticism!" followed by reflexive defensiveness when criticism actually arrives. The double-bind in its purest form. - Reflection without closure: retrospectives become weekly lament with no commitments; over time they stop being attended. - Anonymous absorption: feedback arrives via survey or comment box, gets summarised, and the summary disappears. No one can say what changed. - Critic-as-problem: when criticism is uncomfortable, the focus shifts to "how the critique was delivered" rather than what it said. The deflection is the symptom. - Echo-chamber retrospectives: the same group reviews its own work without external eyes; critique that would be useful is structurally absent. See also collaboration-coherence/isolation. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Action-surface naming: every feedback channel has a recipient (named role or person), a decision cadence (when proposals get adjudicated), and an output convention (how the project records what changed and why). No channel exists without these three. (2) Triage discipline: incoming feedback is sorted into act / defer / decline / out-of-scope, with the rationale recorded. Decline is a legitimate outcome; absence-of-decision is not. (3) Time-boxed reflection: retrospectives have a closing action — at least one named change to be tried before the next retrospective. Otherwise, the retrospective converts to lament. (4) Visible track record: maintain a public log of "changes made in response to feedback" so contributors can see whether their critique landed. This is the wrapper pattern applied to the feedback loop. (5) Name the double-bind: when the project notices itself implicitly punishing useful criticism (defensiveness, no-action, reframing the critic as the problem) — name the dynamic explicitly. The double-bind dissolves when both parties can see it. Engaged when: contributors can point to recent changes the project made in response to recent feedback, and contributors who offered feedback know whether it landed or not. Failing when: critique flows in but nothing flows out; or contributors quietly stop offering useful feedback because the previous round was absorbed without effect.

title: Find the Moving Dimension; Don't Confuse a Stuck Axis with a Stuck Project
text: Find the Moving Dimension; Don't Confuse a Stuck Axis with a Stuck Project Apparent stasis in a multi-dimensional project is almost always a single dimension having stopped while others remain available; the failure mode is identifying with the stuck dimension and concluding the whole project is stuck. The pattern is to identify which dimensions are actually moving, work deliberately on those, and accept the stuck dimension as out-of-reach for now (rather than spending energy on the dimension where progress is most expensive). This is "find the moving dimension," not "force the stuck one." Voluntary, distributed projects routinely encounter dimensions on which progress slows to zero — a maintainer who can't find time, a tool that won't ship, a funder who won't decide, a contributor who has stepped back. When a project's identity has crystallised around the stuck dimension (e.g. "we're the project that's waiting for X"), the felt experience is total stasis even though most of the project is still movable. Living systems, the source notes, are never really in stasis; what is happening is that one or more dimensions of life are moving very slowly. The grilled-cheese-sandwich metaphor catches it: even a balanced diet has individual foods that aren't on the menu today. The pattern operates on the axis: pursuing the stuck dimension ↔ rotating to a moving one. Irreducible: a project cannot simultaneously be patient with a stuck dimension and treat its stuckness as the project's defining state. Patience requires the project to keep moving on other dimensions. Real costs: the stuck dimension might be load-bearing — abandoning it forfeits something the project needs. Pursuing it might be the only path forward. Equally, pursuing it past the point of diminishing returns starves dimensions where progress is cheaper. Both forces operate continuously. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a contributor looks at the project and sees the stuck-thing first; when frustration converts to identity ("we are the people waiting for X"); when fresh energy shows up and gets routed to the stuck dimension instead of a moving one. - Stuck-dimension identification: the project's self-description leads with what it's waiting for ("we're stuck on X") rather than what it's doing now. - Misallocated energy: fresh contributor energy is repeatedly routed to the stuck dimension where it bounces; the moving dimensions have no one assigned to them. - Felt-total-stasis: the perceived stuckness is total even though external observers can name multiple moving dimensions. The discrepancy is itself diagnostic. - Carrying-capacity exhaustion masquerading as stasis: a single contributor's bandwidth limit reads to the project as the project being stuck. See peeragogy/carrying-capacity for the disambiguation. - Premature pivot: under stasis felt as total, the project pivots — abandoning the moving dimensions along with the stuck one. The opposite failure mode of stuck-dimension identification, but produced by the same misreading. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Dimension inventory: enumerate the project's current dimensions (technical, social, content, infrastructure, external relations) and rate each for current movement. The act of enumeration usually surfaces moving dimensions the contributor had stopped seeing. (2) Deliberate rotation: choose one moving dimension to focus on for a defined period; deliberately don't pursue the stuck one. The constraint is the discipline. (3) Stuck-dimension monitor: maintain a low-cost watch on the stuck dimension (per-quarter check-in, named monitor) so the project notices when it becomes movable again, without letting it dominate attention while it remains stuck. (4) Identity decoupling: state explicitly that the project is not defined by its stuck dimension. This is harder than it sounds — the stuck dimension is often the most-discussed thing precisely because it isn't moving. (5) Carrying-capacity respect: stasis on one dimension is often a carrying-capacity symptom on a contributor (they're maxed out on something else, including life). Pair with peeragogy/carrying-capacity rather than treating stasis as project failure. Engaged when: the project can name at least one dimension it's currently making progress on, and the stuck dimension is monitored without dominating attention. Failing when: every internal conversation returns to the stuck dimension, or the project's identity has merged with what it's waiting for.

title: Be Honest About Tie Strength; Match Asks to Tie Type
text: Be Honest About Tie Strength; Match Asks to Tie Type Weak ties and strong ties serve different functions; both are useful, neither is "better." The failure mode is self-deception about which kind of tie a relationship actually is — calling a weak-tie audience "peers," calling a strong-tie team "the network," or asking weak-tie services from strong-tie relationships and vice-versa. The pattern is to name the actual ties honestly, match asks to tie type, and convert ties deliberately when the project needs the conversion. Peer-learning projects often blur the distinction. Participants share a forum, watch each other's video calls, read each other's posts — and conclude they are "peers" in a strong sense. In practice, most such ties are weak: useful for diverse information, weak for instrumental support. Strong ties are reciprocal, demand-bearing, sustained by repeated context-rich interaction. Weak ties bring more diverse knowledge but cannot be asked for the favours strong ties can. The handbook's source note catches it: "I'm failing to be a good peeragogue... should be responsible not only for your own learning but for your peers' learning"; if no one is taking responsibility for anyone else's learning, the relationship is a weak-tie audience, not a peer-tie team. Self-deception about which kind of tie is in play converts to disappointment when the wrong kind of ask is made. The pattern operates on the axis: aspirational tie-strength ↔ actual tie-strength. Irreducible: a tie cannot simultaneously be cheaply joinable (audience-shaped) and reciprocally demand-bearing (team-shaped). Each tie is one or the other at any moment, and the conversion between them is deliberate work. Real costs: aspirations to peer-like reciprocity are part of what brings a community together. Naming actual tie-strength can feel like puncturing the aspiration. But asks calibrated to aspiration rather than reality reliably fail and corrode trust. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever someone introduces "the community" or "the network" without distinguishing layers, whenever a request flies through a forum that is structured as audience but treated as team, and whenever a member feels betrayed because the implicit ask wasn't met. - Peer-illusion: the project calls everyone a "peer" while actual ties are mostly audience-shaped; instrumental asks fail and the project reads the failure as participation pathology. - Co-consumer claim: members report being "co-learners" when the actual relationship is co-watching the same content (a 4th-wall audience, in the source's framing). - Forum-as-team: an audience forum is treated as a team channel; significant decisions are posted to it and the random uptake is read as community endorsement. - Strong-tie ghosting: someone asks a strong-tie favour through a weak-tie surface, gets no response, and concludes the community has failed them — when the actual issue is the wrong surface. - Conversion-by-osmosis fantasy: the project assumes weak ties will become strong through proximity alone, without the deliberate context-rich interaction that conversion actually requires. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Honest naming: in the project's self-description, distinguish layers: audience (read-only, weak ties), participants (occasional, weak-to-medium), contributors (engaged, medium-to-strong), team (committed, strong, reciprocal). Use the names consistently. (2) Match ask to tie: information and weak-signal asks (recommendations, tool suggestions, perspective) belong on weak-tie surfaces; instrumental asks (review my draft, debug with me, cover my workload) belong on strong-tie surfaces. Posting strong-tie asks to weak-tie audiences gets random uptake at best. (3) Deliberate conversion: weak ties become strong through *repeated context-rich interaction* — pair work, named co-facilitation, sustained back-and-forth. Project design that makes conversion easy (named pairings, mentorship pairs, working groups) extends the strong-tie layer over time. (4) Don't grandfather aspiration: when the project's self-description outpaces the actual tie strength, revise the self-description rather than scolding the participants. The community is the data; the labels should match. (5) Pair with carrying-capacity: strong ties cost more per relationship than weak ties; respecting the carrying capacity of strong-tie holders is part of honest tie-management. Engaged when: project self-description distinguishes audience / participants / team layers; asks are routed by tie-type; named transitions exist between layers. Failing when: "peers" is the only label, asks are made indiscriminately, or members feel betrayed because the implicit relationship was stronger than the actual one.
