text: Git Churn as Behavioral Signal Ingest raw git commit counts per file as a behavioral complement to structural complexity, keeping them separate so they compose freely. Tornhill's "Code as a Crime Scene" showed that files which change frequently AND are complex are "hotspots" — likely sources of bugs. Files that always change together have "temporal coupling" — hidden dependencies. Giugliano demonstrated this at multi-million-line scale from Emacs. We want to identify hotspots (high risk), temporal coupling (hidden deps), and knowledge concentration ("who knows this file?"). Git history is noisy — formatting commits, mass renames, and merge commits inflate change counts without indicating real complexity growth. Ingest raw commit counts as code/file-churn hyperedges (commits-all-time, commits-last-90d, last-touch). Store behavioral and structural signals separately so downstream analysis can compose them (churn x complexity = hotspot) or filter noise (exclude merge commits) without re-ingesting. Behavioral signals (what DID change) complement structural signals (what IS complex). A file with high complexity but zero churn is stable. A file with low complexity but high churn is volatile. Neither signal alone identifies the hotspot — only their composition does. - evidence: hotspot ranking (top 10 files by churn x complexity) - evidence: temporal coupling pairs (files that change together > 5 times) - falsifying-observation: if top hotspots are all test files or configs, the metric is capturing noise not signal — recalibrate.

title: Extend, Don't Rewrite
text: Extend, Don't Rewrite When 80% of the required functionality already exists in a tested script, add to it rather than writing a replacement. Layer 0 of M-futon-enrichment requires namespace topology, git churn, and indentation complexity ingested as hyperedges. The existing ingest-three-columns.py already handles namespace/var/requires ingestion with tested HTTP helpers and error handling. The existing ingestion script handles the hard infrastructure (HTTP POST, error handling, count verification, EDN parsing) and 80% of the data. It lacks git churn and indentation complexity functions. Add a --layer0 flag and two new functions (~65 lines) to the existing script rather than writing a new enrichment-specific script. I-4 (Read Before You Write) — the existing code embeds design decisions about endpoint format, penholder auth, error recovery, and verification that would need to be re-discovered in a new script. Extension preserves these decisions; rewriting discards them. - evidence: diff of ingest-three-columns.py before/after Layer 0 addition - evidence: --layer0 --count output showing new hyperedge types

title: Indentation as Universal Complexity Proxy
text: Indentation as Universal Complexity Proxy Use mean/max indentation depth as a cheap, language-agnostic complexity bootstrap; refine with language-specific analysis in later layers. The reflection API provides rich structural metadata for Clojure (arglists, protocols, dispatch). But .el, .py, .edn, and .js files have no reflection endpoint. A universal complexity signal is needed for the cross-repo hotspot analysis in Layer 0. We need a complexity metric that works for .clj, .el, .py, .js, and .edn files — all languages in the futon stack. Indentation depth correlates with nesting but misses semantic complexity (a deeply-nested but simple cond vs. a flat but algorithmically dense function). It's crude. Ingest mean-depth, max-depth, and line-count per file as code/indentation-complexity hyperedges. Treat this as a bootstrap signal — good enough to identify outliers ("why is this file nested 12 levels deep?"), refined in later layers with AST analysis or treesit. A crude universal metric that exists NOW is more useful than a precise language-specific metric that doesn't exist yet. Giugliano validated this at multi-million-line scale: "Indentation is good enough to apply in general. Even Lisp gets formatted in a standard way." The key is using it to FIND weird things, not to MEASURE exact complexity. - evidence: outlier report — files with max-depth > 10 or mean-depth > 5 - evidence: comparison with reflection-based complexity for Clojure files (do indentation outliers match protocol/multimethod complexity?) - falsifying-observation: if top-indentation files are all auto-generated or data files, the metric is noise — exclude those file patterns.

title: Each Layer Is an Evidence Entry
text: Each Layer Is an Evidence Entry Each enrichment layer run produces a meta/enrichment-layer hyperedge that records what was ingested, when, and what was surprising — making the enrichment process itself auditable evidence. Enrichment layers produce hyperedges about the codebase. Without layer metadata, we cannot distinguish "layer 0 ingested at 10:00" from "layer 0 re-run at 14:00 after fixing a bug." The enrichment history becomes opaque — exactly the opacity enrichment is meant to resolve. Each layer produces hyperedges (namespace topology, churn, complexity). Without a record of the layer itself, the enrichment has no provenance. Was this the first run? A correction? What changed since last time? Each layer run POSTs a meta/enrichment-layer hyperedge containing: layer number, ISO-8601 timestamp, hyperedge counts (before/after by type), anomaly list (unexpected findings), and a human-readable summary. Layers are idempotent — re-running updates edges, not duplicates them. XTDB bitemporality preserves ALL runs regardless. The layer record IS evidence in the evidence-over-assertion [示] sense. It answers "what did we know as of layer N?" with a precise, timestamped, verifiable answer. The evidence-ledger [本] pattern demands that claims cite reproducible proofs — the layer metadata is the proof that the enrichment actually happened and produced specific, countable artifacts. - evidence: meta/enrichment-layer hyperedge for Layer 0 with actual counts - evidence: diff between two runs of the same layer (idempotency check) - evidence-shape: {:layer :int, :timestamp :string, :before {:type :count}, :after {:type :count}, :anomalies [:string], :summary :string}

title: Layered Ingestion Architecture
text: Layered Ingestion Architecture Structure enrichment as six layers (L0-L5) where each layer addresses one enrichment concern and depends on the previous layer being verified. The code browser needs six kinds of enrichment data: docs (existing), mission provenance, pattern provenance, evidence binding, tension surface, and cross-futon dependencies. Ingesting all six at once would be fragile (errors in topology corrupt provenance) and unverifiable (too many moving parts to check). Six enrichment concerns need to be ingested into the hyperedge store, each with different data sources and validation criteria. Later layers depend on earlier layers being correct (mission provenance references namespaces from L0; evidence binding references missions from L1). Ingesting them simultaneously means errors cascade silently. Six layers, each verified before the next: L0: Namespace topology + complexity + churn (structural ground truth) L1: Mission provenance (var → mission, from mission docs + git blame) L2: Pattern provenance (var → pattern, from PSR/PUR evidence) L3: Evidence binding (var → evidence entries) L4: Tension surface (var → invariant violations) L5: Cross-futon dependencies (var → var across repos) The reflect-in-layers [节] pattern says layered reflection builds shared understanding. Each layer is a checkpoint: verify L0 topology before attempting L1 provenance. Hexagram-53 [引] says durable change is built incrementally. The dependency chain (L0→L1→...→L5) makes each step small enough to review and correct independently. - evidence: Layer 0 verified (namespace count matches reflection API) - evidence: Layer 1 verified (every var→mission edge traceable to a mission doc or git blame commit) - evidence: replay query showing L0→L1 growth in XTDB

title: Rational Reconstruction Over Bulk Import
text: Rational Reconstruction Over Bulk Import Build the codebase's self-representation through layered rational reconstruction — replaying enrichment as if discipline had been maintained all along — rather than a one-shot static analysis dump. The futon stack has 5+ years of development history across 8+ repos. A bulk static analysis could produce a comprehensive snapshot, but it would have no provenance (when was this edge discovered?), no correction trail (which early assumptions were wrong?), and no transferable methodology (how would someone else do this for their codebase?). We want enrichment that is replayable, correctable, and transferable to other codebases. Rational reconstruction is slower than bulk import — each layer must be verified before the next begins, and corrections between layers require additional ingestion runs. Structure enrichment as numbered layers (L0-L5), each a timestamped batch of hyperedges with its own evidence entry. XTDB bitemporality makes each layer queryable as-of its ingestion time. Corrections in later layers supersede but don't erase earlier layers. The growth of understanding is itself navigable. Three advantages compound: (1) REPLAYABILITY — "what did we know about futon3c.peripheral as of layer 3?" is answerable via bitemporal query. This is impossible with a one-shot dump. (2) INCREMENTAL CORRECTION — early layers WILL have errors (orphan namespaces that are actually entry points, churn spikes from mass renames). Later layers fix them. The correction history shows where the codebase's self-image was wrong — itself valuable knowledge. (3) METHODOLOGY TRANSFER — the discipline of "enrich incrementally, record what you find, correct as you go" is the discipline we'd want any team to adopt. Building it on our own code first validates the process. The learn-as-you-go [日] pattern ensures each layer captures not just findings but surprises and learnings. - evidence: Layer 0 run with meta/enrichment-layer record - evidence: Layer 1 run that corrects at least one Layer 0 anomaly - evidence: bitemporal query showing enrichment growth between layers - falsifying-observation: if Layer 0→L1 correction rate is < 5%, the rational reconstruction overhead may not justify itself over bulk import — reassess at that point.

title: EoI Tension Prompt — Non-Conventional CV Shape Honesty
text: EoI Tension Prompt — Non-Conventional CV Shape Honesty When an outward EoI is being authored for a role whose knowledge/experience clauses are calibrated to a particular career-arc shape (e.g. "7+ years in technical policy research / think-tank / applied research"), and the author's CV substantially exceeds the floor but in a non-conventional shape (e.g. distributed volunteer work, parallel research positions, dual roles), the EoI must name the unconventional shape rather than pretend conventionality. The pattern is similar to the foreclosure-honesty pattern: name what is true rather than what is expected. Applies during `address-now` tagging of an EoI Tension on experience-floor / CV-shape clauses. The prompt asks: what relevant experience do you have, and what is the shape it takes that differs from the role's apparent expectation? The role's posting specifies an experience floor or a CV shape, AND the author's experience meets or exceeds the floor but in a shape the posting did not explicitly name. The underrepresented-groups paragraph in many postings does legitimate work — the EoI's response to a CV-shape clause should take that paragraph literally when present. Naming non-conventional shape is not the same as apology for it; the discipline is description, not deferral. Author drafts a short CV-shape-honesty paragraph that names the substantive relevant experience (counted concretely where possible) in its actual shape, without forcing it into the conventional shape the posting implied. Per writing-coherence/name-what-you-drop and structure/whose-question-is-this: forcing one's CV into a shape the recipient expected is consultant-voice and risks under-counting relevant experience. Naming the actual shape is operator-voice and lets the recipient calibrate their reading accurately. Author drafts the CV-shape paragraph in their own register; eoi-engine assembly inserts it; reviewer checks that the relevant experience is named in its actual shape, with concrete duration or scope figures where available. Minted 2026-05-11 as part of the Arxana Essays annotation flow for the Anthropic Institute first-draft, alongside tension-foreclosure and tension-free-solo-rule. Surfaced from the strawman's diagnostic 6 for that case ("7+ years experience clause reads as a floor for a particular shape of CV ... Joe has substantially more than 7 years but in a non-conventional shape").

title: EoI Tension Prompt — Foreclosure Honesty
text: EoI Tension Prompt — Foreclosure Honesty When an outward EoI's acceptance would foreclose other active basins (other employment, freelance work, ongoing relationships, geographic continuity, IP-scoped self-directed work), the EoI must name what is being let go rather than pretending the decision is foreclosure-free. Pretending "no foreclosure" is the failure mode the strawman discipline names; the EoI's Right Speech requires the drop list to be co-located with the inheritance list. Applies during `address-now` tagging of an EoI Tension. The prompt asks the author: which of your other active basins would this engagement foreclose? Name the foreclosures explicitly in the EoI; do not let them remain implicit. The role's terms (salary, geography, time commitment, IP) would materially alter or end other active relationships, projects, or obligations the author is carrying. Naming foreclosures inside an outward EoI must be calibrated. Excessive foreclosure-listing reads as ambivalence rather than honesty. The pattern is: name the substantive foreclosures succinctly; do not pretend they do not exist; do not catalogue every minor adjustment. Author writes a short foreclosure-honesty paragraph naming the substantive losses an acceptance would entail. Length: one paragraph or less. Per writing-coherence/name-what-you-drop: silent inheritance of scope is the failure mode. Per structure/unresolved-tensions-at-closure: tensions that should be preserved-and-named must not be forced into resolution by omission. The foreclosure-honesty paragraph is the EoI's sorry-preservation move at the institutional-scope level. Author drafts the foreclosure paragraph in their own register; eoi-engine assembly inserts it; reviewer checks that the paragraph names the substantive foreclosures rather than catalogue-listing. Minted 2026-05-11 as part of the Arxana Essays annotation flow for the Anthropic Institute first-draft. Three tension-prompt flexiargs were created (foreclosure / free-solo-rule / cv-shape) as annotation sources because the existing eoi-engine VERIFY pass surfaced three `address-now`-tagged tensions whose content Joe had not yet supplied.

title: EoI Tension Prompt — August-2026 Free-Solo Rule Honesty
text: EoI Tension Prompt — August-2026 Free-Solo Rule Honesty When an outward EoI is being authored while the author holds a publicly-stated rule against applying (e.g. Joe's August-2026 free-solo policy: no grants, no VC, no job applications), the EoI must address the rule honestly: either (a) state that the application is the considered output of a phase-space MAP, not application-as-relief-from-uncertainty, or (b) state that the rule is being re-examined in light of a specific surfaced alternative, or (c) name that the rule applies and this is the exception and why. What the EoI must not do: pretend the rule does not exist. Applies during `address-now` tagging of an EoI Tension on outward applications written under a no-apply stance. The prompt asks: do you flag the rule to the recipient, or do you not? If yes, in what framing? If no, what makes this exception coherent under the rule's spirit? The author's public stance (or stance known to plausible recipients) includes a no-application rule, AND the artefact being authored is an application. The rule's framing inside the EoI itself is calibrated by who the recipient is and what they already know. If the rule is not publicly visible to this recipient, raising it pre-emptively may look performative; if it is publicly visible, omitting it looks evasive. Author chooses one of routes (a) / (b) / (c) and writes a short rule-honesty paragraph in their own register. Per structure/whose-question-is-this: the EoI is the author's speech-act, in inhabited mode. Pretending the rule does not exist is consultant-voice; naming it honestly is operator-voice. The Right Speech discipline requires the latter. Author drafts the rule-honesty paragraph; eoi-engine assembly inserts or omits it per the author's chosen route; reviewer checks that the framing matches the recipient's actual visibility. Minted 2026-05-11 as part of the Arxana Essays annotation flow for the Anthropic Institute first-draft, alongside tension-foreclosure and tension-cv-shape. Surfaced from the strawman's diagnostic 3 for that case (Mama-Claude's a/b/c options for the August-2026 free-solo rule).

title: Argument for the Equity Pattern Domain
text: Argument for the Equity Pattern Domain == PART I: The Equity Loop == E1. [Evidence: equity.tex, theoretical synthesis] Three inputs — Sen's capability approach, Ostrom's commons governance, and Alexander's pattern-language method — reduce to a single design criterion: does this system close the loop between contribution, governance, and capability? E2. [Evidence: equity.tex, five diagnostic questions] The criterion decomposes into five questions: 1. Contribution: What kinds of labour keep the system alive? 2. Recognition: How does doing that work create legitimate stake? 3. Governance: What rights do contributors have to shape the system? 4. Capability: How does participation enlarge real opportunity to act? 5. Feedback: What mechanisms show whether the loop is working? E3. [Evidence: equity.tex, failure modes table] Six ways the loop breaks: contribution without governance (extraction), governance without capability expansion (performative), capability without shared stake (training for exit), governance without contribution (managerial), contribution without feedback (motivation decay), local adaptation without shared stewardship (fragmentation). == PART II: The Five Patterns == P1. [Pattern: equity/confident-adaptation] Adaptation without clarity is guesswork. Equity loop joint: contribution→stake. Coordination: Low (1 actor). P2. [Pattern: equity/protected-interaction] Delivery without provisioning produces overload. Equity loop joint: governance→capability. Coordination: Medium (2 actors). P3. [Pattern: equity/shared-maintenance] Local adaptation without stewardship fragments the commons. Equity loop joint: capability→contribution. Coordination: Medium-high (community). P4. [Pattern: equity/contribution-pathways] Recipients without voice remain recipients. Equity loop joint: contribution→stake→governance. Coordination: High (infrastructure). P5. [Pattern: equity/visible-impact] A programme that cannot see its own effects cannot learn. Equity loop joint: feedback (whole loop). Coordination: Very high (6+ actor chain). == PART III: The Coordination Gradient == The five patterns are not independent recommendations. They form a gradient: each requires more actors, in longer chains, to resolve. A programme that addresses patterns 1-3 will improve its training input. A programme that also addresses patterns 4-5 will build the institutional architecture needed for that input to persist as collective practice. The gradient explains why partial success is common: an institution that resolves conditions 1-3 but not 4-5 will see good delivery but fragile sustainability. This is not a failure of effort; it is a predictable consequence of incomplete institutional architecture. == PART IV: Relevance to FUTON == CONCERN: FUTON's own coordination layers face the same equity questions. Do contributors to the pattern library gain recognised scope to shape the stack? Does participation in missions enlarge real capability? Does the glacial loop close the feedback chain? Every FUTON layer should be testable against the five diagnostic questions from equity.tex. If the equity loop does not close, the layer is extractive regardless of its stated intentions. The university case (futon7/holes/M-another-university.md) demonstrates what happens when a well-funded programme coordinates activities without coordinating the architecture that makes those activities productive. FUTON exists partly because that failure is not specific to universities — it is the general form of the problem. == THESIS == The five equity patterns specify, in conditional form, what must hold for a distributed collective production system to close the equity loop. They were derived from one empirical case but the loop they inspect is domain-independent. The coordination gradient they form is a structural prediction: systems that resolve the lower-complexity conditions but not the higher-complexity ones will produce partial, fragile outcomes — not because participants lack motivation, but because the institutional architecture is incomplete.

title: Confident Adaptation (as published in paper v2.3)
text: Confident Adaptation (as published in paper v2.3) Trainers cannot adapt confidently without knowing what must be retained and what can be changed. The programme should publish an expectation scaffold — a clearly enunciated stance on what is fixed (core topics, minimum delivery format, evaluation expectation) and what is flexible (local sequencing, depth, audience, delivery mode) — ideally produced by the training community rather than issued to them, so that trainers' confusion is converted into acts of governance rather than private compensation. The programme publishes a current expectation scaffold stating what is fixed and what is flexible. The scaffold is produced with trainer input and revised in light of their experience. This is NPT Coherence — specifically 1.2 Communal Specification: a shared understanding of what is being done and why. It is an intervention-tier pattern with low coordination: a central agency (the Training Project) can resolve it by producing and maintaining the scaffold. The paper describes this as the most tractable of the five patterns. Its absence is cited as a direct contributor to architectural mismatch mode; its presence is a precondition for multiplied input. A central programme trains intermediaries who deliver in varied local settings. Trainers bring motivation and partial competence but enter without a shared understanding of what the programme actually requires — which elements are non-negotiable, which admit local variation, and what "ready to deliver" looks like. The training's own community-and-research dimensions may be unknown to trainers who registered for the course alone. The programme has not published the fixed/flexible distinction. Trainers report uncertainty about what was fundamental, how many sessions were required, and whether the courses were part of a research project (FG2A.15, FG2B.1; T2A: "It wasn't very clear to us how many sessions we needed to have attended, which ones were fundamental"; T2B: "I didn't realise when I first signed up for it that these courses were part of this research project"). Where the expectation was explicit, the programme became an "effective entry point" (FG3.4; T3: "It was useful to have a template of what was expected"). The gap is informational, not a skill gap — an absence of communal specification rather than an absence of capability. - Missing scaffold: trainers guess what is essential and deliver fragmented versions - Scaffold-as-decree: scaffold exists but is issued without trainer input and becomes a compliance instrument - Frozen scaffold: produced once, never revised; drifts from practice - Scope invisibility: trainers unaware of the programme's research or community dimensions beyond the training itself The Training Project produces a central expectation scaffold that enunciates what is fixed and what is flexible. Production is reconnoitred with trainers rather than issued to them: the scaffold converts their confusion into acts of governance and becomes revisable by the community that uses it. The scaffold is not a compliance checklist; it is a minimum specification that makes local adaptation a formative act rather than guesswork. NPT Coherence: 1.2 Communal Specification is the shared understanding that makes collective action possible. Trainers reported high COM-B self-efficacy ("I understand what this requires of me" M=4.90) individually, but communal specification was absent at the programme level — which is what produces fragmented delivery even where individual capability is high. Tier and coordination: This is an intervention-tier failure that can be resolved at low coordination. A single central actor (the programme team) is sufficient. The paper is most prescriptive here because the pattern is most tractable. Governance framing: The scaffold is an act of governance rather than a directive. The trainers' role in its production matters: a scaffold issued top-down converts into compliance; a scaffold reconnoitred with the community converts confusion into shared authorship of the programme's definition. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Coherence 1.2 Communal Specification as stated in the companion journal article. Tier: Intervention. Coordination: Low (central agency). Implementation-mode link: absence contributes directly to architectural mismatch; presence is a precondition for multiplied input. The paper is most prescriptive here — the pattern is most tractable of the five. - Publish the expectation scaffold before the next cohort - Produce it with trainers, not for them - Make the fixed/flexible distinction the scaffold's central content, not an annex - Design the scaffold as revisable so it remains a governance instrument rather than a decree - Test by asking a new trainer to explain what is expected after reading the scaffold alone

title: Confident Adaptation: Scaffolded Becoming
text: Confident Adaptation: Scaffolded Becoming Participants in a distributed programme can adapt confidently only when the programme publishes a current expectation scaffold that distinguishes what is fixed from what is flexible. The scaffold is not a compliance checklist. It is a form-giving governance instrument, produced with trainers and revised from their experience, that converts access to materials into real capability for local adaptation. No participant enters the programme without access to a current expectation scaffold that distinguishes fixed from flexible elements, defines sufficient participation, and is revised in light of trainer experience. A centrally designed programme distributes materials and training into varied local settings. The programme depends on local adaptation, but adaptation is a formative process rather than a private act of compensation. In NPT terms this is Coherence 1.2 Communal Specification: a shared understanding of what is being done and why. In capability terms, the conversion at stake is informational: the participant needs enough structure to become a competent local adapter rather than a recipient guessing at hidden rules. In the paper's tier language this is an intervention-tier, low-coordination pattern: a central programme can initiate it, but it only remains live if trainers help revise it. A central programme trains intermediaries who deliver in varied local settings. Trainers bring motivation, partial competence, and local knowledge, but they enter without a shared understanding of which elements are non-negotiable, which admit local variation, what counts as ready to deliver, or whether the programme includes research and community dimensions beyond the course itself. The agent is in a condition of becoming: local judgement can develop, but only if the rules of the game are legible enough for productive learning to begin. The fixed/flexible distinction is not published. Trainers report uncertainty about what was fundamental, how many sessions were required, and whether the courses were part of a research project (FG2A.15, FG2B.1; T2A: "It wasn't very clear to us how many sessions we needed to have attended"; T2B: "I didn't realise when I first signed up for it that these courses were part of this research project"). Where an expectation was explicit, the programme became an effective entry point (FG3.4; T3: "It was useful to have a template of what was expected"). The gap is informational, not a simple skill gap: individual self-efficacy can be high while communal specification remains absent. Without form-giving information, trainers cannot calibrate adaptation, assess adequacy, or distinguish creative variation from accidental deviation. - Missing scaffold: trainers guess what is essential and deliver fragmented versions - Arrested formation: the agent cannot begin productive learning because the rules are opaque - Guesswork adaptation: local changes happen without knowing what must be retained - Scope invisibility: participants are unaware of research or community dimensions beyond training - Scaffold-as-decree: the scaffold exists but is issued without trainer input and becomes compliance - Frozen specification: the scaffold is published once and never revised The programme publishes an expectation scaffold before the next cohort. It states the fixed elements (core topics, minimum delivery format, evaluation expectation, sufficient participation) and the flexible elements (local sequencing, depth, audience, delivery mode). It is produced with trainers, not merely issued to them: confusion becomes input to governance, and the scaffold remains revisable from the start. The scaffold says what the programme is, what it is not, and where the trainer's judgement is expected to operate. NPT: Communal Specification is the shared understanding that makes collective action possible. Trainers may individually understand what they think is required, but fragmented delivery follows when the programme-level specification is missing. Sen: The offer of materials and training remains nominal unless participants can convert it into practical capability. The scaffold is a conversion factor: it turns access into the possibility of competent local adaptation. Sloman/Lovelace and whole-board play: Information here is form-giving, not mere signal transmission. The scaffold is not a Jacquard card that makes the trainer perform; it shapes the conditions under which the trainer's own developing competence can take productive form. Without the rules of the game, not even productive failure is possible. Governance: A scaffold issued once and frozen becomes a decree. A scaffold produced with trainers and revised by their experience is the first instance of rules-in-use being made legible to the agents they govern. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Coherence 1.2 Communal Specification via the UKRN T3 analysis and companion paper. Tier: Intervention. Coordination: Low (central agency initiates; trainer participation keeps it live). Implementation-mode link: absence contributes to architectural mismatch; presence is a precondition for multiplied input. Canonical deepening: informational conversion and form-giving scaffold. Paper-specific mechanism: expectation scaffold produced with trainers and revised as governance. - Publish the expectation scaffold before the next cohort - Make the fixed/flexible distinction the scaffold's central content - Produce it with trainers, not for them - Design the scaffold as revisable from the start - Test: can a new trainer explain what is expected after reading the scaffold alone? - Treat this as the lowest-coordination condition and resolve it before higher-coordination patterns depend on it

title: Adaptation Without Clarity Is Guesswork
text: Adaptation Without Clarity Is Guesswork Participants in a distributed programme can adapt confidently only when they know what is fixed and what is flexible. Without that scaffold, adaptation becomes guesswork and the agent's becoming is arrested before it can begin. No participant enters the programme without access to a published expectation scaffold that distinguishes fixed from flexible elements and defines sufficient participation. The scaffold is designed to be revisable in light of participant experience. A centrally designed programme distributes materials and training to local settings that differ in resources, culture, and existing infrastructure. The programme depends on local adaptation — but adaptation is a formative process, not a compliance task. Each participant enters in a condition of becoming: they have motivation, partial competence, and a local setting, but they do not yet know what kind of agent this programme needs them to be. In NPT terms this is Coherence (1.2 Communal Specification): a shared understanding of what is being done and why. An agent enters a distributed programme in a condition of becoming. The programme depends on their local adaptation — their capacity to develop, through interaction with materials, setting, and experience, the practical judgment that constitutes competent local delivery. This is analogous to the opening phase of whole-board play: the agent needs to know the rules of the game before productive learning can begin. The programme does not publish the distinction between what is fixed and what is flexible. The agent cannot internalise the programme's structure as their own operating structure because that structure is opaque. Without knowing what counts, the agent cannot calibrate their adaptation, assess their own adequacy, or distinguish creative local variation from accidental deviation. The result is not merely confusion but arrested formation: the agent remains a recipient of materials rather than becoming a competent local adapter. This is like asking someone to play Go without telling them the rules — not even bad play is possible, only flailing. - Arrested formation: agent cannot begin productive learning because the game's rules are opaque - Guesswork adaptation: trainer modifies content without knowing what is essential - Fragmented delivery: different institutions deliver incompatible versions - Invisible scope: participants unaware of programme dimensions beyond training (e.g. research, community) - Frozen specification: scaffold published but never revised, becoming a decree rather than a governance instrument The programme publishes a scaffold that distinguishes fixed from flexible elements — not as a compliance checklist but as the minimal specification that makes local adaptation a formative process rather than guesswork. The scaffold gives form to the agent's becoming: it says what the programme is, what it is not, and where the agent's own judgment is expected to operate. This is informational conversion in the Sloman/Lovelace sense (Sloman, 2010; Lovelace, 1843): information as form-giving, not signal transmission. The scaffold does not programme the trainer. It provides the conditions under which the trainer's own learning process can generate the right internal structure — the local perceptual filters that enable competent adaptation without seeing the whole board. Sen: The conversion at stake is informational — but "informational" here means the conditions under which the agent can convert a nominal offer into a real capability to adapt, deliver, and develop. Without form-giving information, the offer remains nominal: the agent has materials but not the conditions for becoming a competent user of those materials. The scaffold is a conversion factor: it converts access into the possibility of productive learning. Sloman/Lovelace: Early information-based machines (e.g. Jacquard looms) used information to control physical actions. But as Lovelace foresaw, computing machinery acts on information and on abstract mechanisms for acting on information (Sloman, 2010). The scaffold is not a Jacquard card that makes the trainer perform an action. It is a specification that shapes the abstract conditions under which the trainer's own developing competence — a virtual machine in Sloman's sense — can take productive form. The competent local adapter is not a state that can be transmitted; it is an internal structure that emerges from a learning process, like AlphaZero's local filters that emerge from whole-board play. Ostrom: The scaffold is the first instance of rules-in-use being made legible to the agents they govern. But legibility is the beginning of co-evolution, not the end. As the agent develops through interaction with their local setting, they will encounter situations where the fixed/flexible boundary itself needs revision. If the scaffold is genuinely a governance instrument rather than a decree, it must be revisable by the agents it shapes. At this pattern's coordination level (one actor), the co-evolution is embryonic — but its absence here forecloses it at every subsequent level. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Coherence (1.2 Communal Specification) via the UKRN T3 analysis. Mapped to the equity loop at contribution→stake: contribution without clarity creates no recognised stake. Deepened via Sloman/Lovelace: informational conversion is form-giving, not signal transmission. The scaffold is analogous to the rules of Go: without them, not even productive failure is possible. Coordination requirement: Low (1 actor). - Publish the scaffold before cohort 1, not after problems emerge - Test: can a new participant explain what is expected of them after reading the scaffold alone? - Design the scaffold as revisable from the start — not a frozen decree but a living specification - This is the lowest-coordination condition (1 actor: the central programme team) and should be resolved first

title: Contribution Pathways (as published in paper v2.3)
text: Contribution Pathways (as published in paper v2.3) Without explicit and well-maintained pathways for sustained contribution, trainers remain recipients or at best conduits rather than co-producers; delivery becomes fragile and goodwill-dependent. The programme requires local delivery labour; it should also ensure that those doing the delivery gain governance rights over how that delivery happens, with sustained contribution leading to recognised standing. This is Ostrom's collective-choice principle applied to training governance. Every participant who sustains engagement beyond initial training has at least one visible route to contribute to programme development or governance. Sustained contribution creates recognised standing. The coordinator role is resourced and trained. This is NPT Cognitive Participation — specifically 2.4 Activation: how procedures and actions that sustain delivery are collectively defined. It is the first architecture-tier pattern and requires high coordination (governed infrastructure). The paper names this pattern as the one that separates absorbed input from multiplied input: where co-ownership emerged, engagement sustained; where it did not, engagement remained precarious and vulnerable to the trainer leaving. A programme has trained intermediaries who have developed local competence and may be contributing adaptations back to the shared materials (Pattern 3 resolved). Sustaining engagement beyond initial training depends on whether those trainers are receivers of a centrally-defined programme or co-producers with recognised scope to shape it. The programme's long-term viability rests on the latter. There are no explicit pathways for contribution beyond delivery. No peer cohorts, no shared adaptation reviews, no mentoring structure. The Community of Practice exists but most trainers are unaware of it (T1: "I don't think I was aware of the Community of Practice"). Peer channels exist but go unused (T2B: "in theory, there's a teams channel, but I've never seen anyone use it"). The ORCA coordinator role — which should serve as the backbone of community infrastructure — is undertrained and under-supported (T3: "the ORCAs really didn't get any training"; FG3: "reactive rather than helpful"; "potentially undertrained relative to their level of responsibility"). Where co-ownership emerged (FG1.19, FG1.25), sustained motivation followed: T1 — "That ownership felt really important to me; and so then going on and sharing it and integrating it into my own practice"; T1 — "I wouldn't have delivered that training if I hadn't had this framework." Where it did not, engagement was precarious (FG3.11). Trainers articulate the knowledge-exit risk directly (T3: "At some point I potentially leave with that knowledge and it doesn't get used as much as it could have"). COM-B: "I see the value" M=5.37 vs. "I feel positive" M=4.21 — a gap between value recognition and positive activation. - Goodwill-dependent delivery: practice survives only as long as the individual persists - Invisible community: CoP exists formally but trainers are unaware - Dead channels: peer exchange channels created but unstewarded and unused - Undertrained coordinators: ORCA role exists but "reactive rather than helpful" - Knowledge exit: trainers leave with knowledge that the programme fails to retain - Extractive structure: system benefits from trainer labour without granting governance voice - Value/activation gap: COM-B shows value is seen (5.37) but positive activation is weak (4.21) The programme builds governed infrastructure: a steering group drawn from active contributors, a contribution log that makes otherwise-invisible labour visible in career-relevant terms, peer exchange channels that are actively stewarded rather than merely created, mentoring structures, and a properly resourced and trained coordinator role. Sustained contribution leads to recognised standing in the programme's governance structure. Governance standing logically follows from meaningful contribution, not the other way around. Shared investment in community infrastructure presupposes capability return — participants invest because the investment enlarges their real capability to contribute and benefit. NPT Cognitive Participation: 2.4 Activation names the work of collectively defining procedures that sustain a practice. Without contribution pathways, no one but the central programme team has the standing to define — so activation stays private, and practice survives only as long as individuals do. Ostrom's collective-choice principle (explicitly cited by the paper): those who sustain the commons earn recognised rights to shape it. The principle operationalises the equity loop's governance joint. A programme that benefits from trainer labour without granting governance voice is extractive by structure, regardless of its stated intentions. Architecture tier: This is the first pattern that requires governed infrastructure rather than organisational decision or community norm. The steering group, contribution log, mentoring structure, and coordinator role are infrastructure — they exist across cohorts and enable sustained contribution at scale. High coordination follows: multiple roles must orchestrate, and the orchestration itself must be governed. Convergence with Pattern 5: contribution pathways (P4) and visible impact (P5) share architecture: trainers who contribute to the design via P4 also need to see their effects via P5 to remain contributors. Both failures appear together in absorbed-mode institutions. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Cognitive Participation 2.4 Activation as stated in the companion journal article. Tier: Architecture. Coordination: High (governed infrastructure). Implementation-mode link: this pattern separates absorbed input from multiplied input. The paper names the structural principle (collective-choice, governance-follows-contribution) and operationalises it via steering group, contribution log, and stewarded coordinator role. - Establish a steering group drawn from active contributors - Build a contribution log that makes invisible labour visible in career-relevant terms - Resource and train the coordinator role before expecting community to emerge - Actively steward peer channels: facilitation, not just creation - Design the governance so that sustained contribution creates recognised standing - Test: does a motivated trainer have a visible route into co-ownership within the first year?

title: Contribution Pathways: Governance Follows Contribution
text: Contribution Pathways: Governance Follows Contribution Engagement sustains when trainers become co-producers with recognised scope to shape the programme, not merely recipients or conduits for a central offer. Sustained contribution should create governance standing. Without explicit contribution pathways, delivery becomes goodwill-dependent and the programme benefits from trainer labour without granting voice over the conditions of that labour. Every participant who sustains engagement beyond initial training has at least one visible route to contribute to programme development, governance, or community support. Sustained contribution creates recognised standing. The coordinator role is resourced and trained. A programme needs trainers to sustain engagement beyond the first delivery wave. In NPT terms this is Cognitive Participation 2.4 Activation: how procedures and actions that sustain delivery are collectively defined. In Ostrom terms this is the collective-choice problem: can affected participants modify, extend, and help govern the programme, or only consume it? In the paper's tier language this is the first architecture-tier pattern and requires high coordination. In capability terms it is the transition from being shaped by a system to shaping it. Trainers have developed local competence through iterative delivery and their adaptations are flowing into the shared commons. The system is learning from variation. But the trainers' relationship to the system may still be one of consumption: they receive the programme, adapt it locally, and upstream improvements, without recognised scope to influence direction, priorities, or structure. Long-term viability rests on moving from receiver to co-producer. There are no explicit pathways for contribution beyond delivery. No peer cohorts, shared adaptation reviews, mentoring structure, steering group, or contribution log exists. The Community of Practice exists but most trainers are unaware of it (T1: "I don't think I was aware of the Community of Practice"). Peer channels exist but go unused (T2B: "in theory, there's a teams channel, but I've never seen anyone use it"). The ORCA coordinator role is undertrained and under-supported (T3: "the ORCAs really didn't get any training"; FG3: "reactive rather than helpful"). Where co-ownership emerged, sustained motivation followed (FG1.19, FG1.25; T1: "That ownership felt really important to me"). Where it did not, engagement remained precarious and vulnerable to the trainer leaving (FG3.11; T3: "At some point I potentially leave with that knowledge and it doesn't get used as much as it could have"). COM-B shows a value/activation gap: "I see the value" M=5.37 vs. "I feel positive" M=4.21. - Capped becoming: agent develops local competence but cannot reshape the system - Goodwill-dependent delivery: practice survives only as long as the individual persists - Invisible community: CoP exists formally but trainers are unaware - Dead channels: peer exchange channels are created but unstewarded and unused - Undertrained coordinators: ORCA role exists but is reactive rather than helpful - Knowledge exit: trainers leave with knowledge the programme fails to retain - Extractive structure: system benefits from trainer labour without granting governance voice - Value/activation gap: value is recognised but positive activation remains weak The programme builds governed community infrastructure: a steering group drawn from active contributors, a contribution log that makes otherwise-invisible labour visible in career-relevant terms, actively stewarded peer channels, mentoring structures, adaptation reviews, and a properly resourced coordinator role. Sustained contribution creates recognised standing in programme governance. Governance standing follows meaningful contribution, not the other way around. Shared investment in community infrastructure presupposes capability return: participants invest because the investment enlarges their real ability to contribute and benefit. NPT: Activation is the collective definition of the actions and procedures that sustain a practice. Without contribution pathways, only the central programme has standing to define; activation stays private. Sen: Capability expands when participants move from receipt to co-ownership. The deepest capability expansion is not skill acquisition, but the freedom to revise the conditions under which action takes place. Whole-board play: This is the transition from playing within a fixed architecture to modifying the architecture itself. A distribution list delivers content; a community of practice co-evolves content, delivery, and governance. Ostrom: Collective-choice arrangements give those who sustain the commons recognised rights to shape it. A programme that benefits from trainer labour without granting governance voice is extractive by structure, regardless of stated intentions. Convergence with visible impact: contribution pathways and visible impact share architecture. Trainers who contribute to design also need to see their effects to remain contributors. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Cognitive Participation 2.4 Activation. Tier: Architecture. Coordination: High (governed infrastructure). Implementation-mode link: this pattern separates absorbed input from multiplied input. Canonical deepening: capability as the freedom to revise programme conditions. Paper-specific mechanism: steering group, contribution log, and governance-follows-contribution. - Establish a steering group drawn from active contributors - Build a contribution log that makes invisible labour visible in career-relevant terms - Resource and train the coordinator role before expecting community to emerge - Actively steward peer channels: facilitation, not just creation - Define explicit contribution pathways: adaptation review, mentoring, programme governance - Design governance so sustained contribution creates recognised standing - Test: does a motivated trainer have a visible route into co-ownership within the first year?

title: Recipients Without Voice Remain Recipients
text: Recipients Without Voice Remain Recipients Engagement sustains when participants become co-producers with recognised scope to shape the programme — not just consumers of a centrally defined offer. Without contribution pathways, the agent's becoming is capped: they can develop local competence but not reshape the system that shapes them. Every participant who sustains engagement beyond initial training has at least one visible route to contribute to programme development, governance, or community support. Sustained contribution creates recognised standing in the programme's governance structure. A programme needs trainers to sustain engagement beyond the initial training wave. In NPT terms this is Cognitive Participation (2.4 Activation): how procedures and actions that can sustain delivery are collectively defined. In Ostrom's terms this is the collective-choice problem: can affected participants modify, extend, and help govern the programme, or only consume it? In the whole-board-play analogy, Patterns 1-3 gave the agent the rules, the conditions to play, and a way for local learning to propagate backward. This pattern asks whether the agent can modify the rules themselves. Trainers have developed local competence through iterative delivery (Pattern 2) and their adaptations are flowing into the shared commons (Pattern 3). The system is learning from its own variation. But the trainers' relationship to the system is still one of consumption: they receive the programme, they adapt it locally, they upstream improvements — but they do not govern how the programme evolves. Their learning improves the materials but does not give them a voice in the programme's direction, priorities, or structure. There are no explicit pathways for contribution beyond delivery and materials upstream. No peer cohorts, no shared adaptation reviews, no mentoring structure. The Community of Practice exists on paper but most trainers are unaware of it. Peer channels have been created but go unused. The ORCA coordinator role — which should serve as the backbone of community infrastructure — is undertrained and under-supported. The agent's becoming is capped: they can develop as a deliverer but not as a co-governor. This is like an AlphaZero that can play and learn within the game but cannot modify the game's parameters, training regime, or architecture. It remains a creature of its original design, however skilled it becomes within those constraints. In human systems, this cap on becoming is felt as: "At some point I potentially leave with that knowledge and it doesn't get used as much as it could have." - Capped becoming: agent develops local competence but cannot reshape the system - Goodwill dependency: practice survives only as long as the individual persists - Invisible community: CoP exists formally but trainers are unaware of it - Dead channels: peer exchange channels created but unstewarded and unused - Undertrained coordinators: ORCA role exists but "reactive rather than helpful" - Knowledge exit: "at some point I potentially leave with that knowledge and it doesn't get used" - Extraction: system benefits from trainer labour without granting governance voice The programme builds community infrastructure from the start: peer exchange channels that are actually stewarded (not just created), mentoring structures, and a coordinator role that is properly resourced and trained. Visible routes to share, mentor, or adapt turn private motivation into repeated participation. Crucially, these are not just communication channels — they are governance instruments. Through them, the trainers who do the hardest lifting gain recognised scope to shape what the programme becomes. The shift from recipient to co-producer is not just a change in role but a change in the kind of agent the person is: from a local adapter operating within fixed constraints to a co-governor whose experience reshapes the constraints themselves. Sen: Capability expands when participants can move from receipt to co-ownership and contribution. But the deepest capability expansion is not skill development — it is the transition from being shaped by a system to shaping it. This is the becoming that equity requires: not just the freedom to act within given conditions, but the freedom to revise the conditions under which action takes place. Whole-board play: In the AlphaZero analogy, this is the transition from playing within a fixed architecture to modifying the architecture itself — changing the learning rate, the network structure, the reward signal. In human systems, this transition is what distinguishes a community of practice from a distribution list. A distribution list delivers content. A community of practice co-evolves the content, the delivery, and the governance of both. The trainers who sustain engagement are not just good players — they are people whose experience should reshape how the game is set up for future players. Ostrom: This is the collective-choice arrangement: positions and recognised scope determine whether participants can organise and contribute. Community infrastructure that is created but not stewarded is indistinguishable from no infrastructure. Without contribution pathways, motivation remains individual and exits with the person. This is where the equity loop either closes or breaks: contribution that creates recognised stake, stake that gives governance rights, governance that improves the conditions for future contribution. If this joint breaks, the system is extractive — it benefits from the trainer's labour without giving them a voice. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Cognitive Participation (2.4 Activation) via the UKRN T3 analysis. Mapped to the equity loop at contribution→stake→governance: contribution without recognised scope is extraction. Deepened via whole-board play: the transition from playing within fixed constraints to modifying the constraints is the transition from recipient to co-governor. Ostrom: positions and collective-choice arrangements determine whether participants can organise and contribute. Coordination requirement: High (infrastructure). - Resource and train the coordinator role before expecting community to emerge - Steward peer channels actively — facilitated, not just created - Define explicit contribution pathways: adaptation review, mentoring, programme governance - Design governance so that sustained contribution creates recognised standing - Test: does a motivated trainer have a visible route into co-ownership within their first year? - This requires governed infrastructure (high coordination) and should be resolved after conditions 1-3

title: Protected Interaction (as published in paper v2.3)
text: Protected Interaction (as published in paper v2.3) The breadth of open-research topics exceeds what any single trainer can confidently cover. The resolution is to let each trainer declare a delivery profile — the modules they will own — and for the programme to treat institutional coverage as a network property across its trainers rather than a requirement of each individual. Each institution commits an explicit profile of its coverage aims and resourcing. Each trainer has a declared delivery profile. Each participating institution has a committed coverage profile with named resourcing. The programme maintains a current view of coverage as a network property. This is NPT Collective Action — specifically 3.3 Skill Set Workability and 3.4 Contextual Integration. It is an intervention-tier pattern with medium coordination, requiring two formal actors: the Training Project and the Institutional Lead (or other local representative). Where weak coordination leaves the trainer absorbing the gap alone, the pattern produces absorbed input; where team-working is supported, trainers grow in competence and the pattern contributes to multiplied input. A programme trains intermediaries who deliver open-research topics spanning a wide territory (statistics, data management, software, publication practices, ethics, reproducibility, etc.). Delivery depends on the trainer's capacity to cover the territory competently — but the territory is broader than any single trainer's primary expertise, and many trainers are professional staff delivering outside their primary discipline. The breadth produces a breadth-versus-depth tension compounded by impostor syndrome. Trainers report feeling inadequately prepared (FG1.15, FG2A.13; FG3.13, FG2A.4). Sessions attempt to cover too much and lose interaction depth (T1: "give it more time than you expect"; T2B.17: delivers only a fraction of material learned; T2A: "I didn't feel prepared to talk about all the areas"; T3: "There's a little bit of impostor syndrome, because it's still new to me and no one's taught me it!"). COM-B "I am psychologically able" M=4.85, high individually, but the breadth gap is structural: trainers silently absorb a coordination problem that extends beyond their remit. - Breadth overload: trainers silently cover topics outside their primary expertise without team support - Impostor-driven delivery: trainer reaches a session under-prepared because declaration was not possible - Un-profiled institutions: institution participates without naming what it covers or what it resources - Invisible coordination: coverage problem extends beyond the trainer's remit but is absorbed by the trainer alone - Per-trainer coverage requirement: the network's coverage is treated as an expectation of each individual rather than a distributed property Each trainer declares a delivery profile — the modules they will own. The programme treats institutional coverage as a network property across its trainers, not a requirement of each individual. Each participating institution commits an explicit profile of its coverage aims and the resourcing (time, scope, team support) that matches. Coverage becomes a visible distribution across the network rather than an invisible overload on each trainer. NPT Collective Action: 3.3 Skill Set Workability is the fit between what the work demands and what the trainer can reasonably do; 3.4 Contextual Integration is the fit between the work and its institutional context. Breadth overload breaks both. Named profiles restore the fit at both levels. Two-actor coordination: The pattern cannot be resolved by the Training Project alone — the institution must name a coverage profile and resource it. Coordination rises from Low (Pattern 1) to Medium. The Institutional Lead (or Local Network Lead in the post-ORP setting) is the second formal actor. Network-property framing: Treating coverage as a network property is a structural move, not an operational one. It reframes what the programme is asking of any single trainer — not "cover everything" but "own a declared subset, with coverage guaranteed across the network." This is what prevents trainers from silently absorbing the coordination problem. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Collective Action 3.3 Skill Set Workability and 3.4 Contextual Integration as stated in the companion journal article. Tier: Intervention. Coordination: Medium (programme + Institutional Lead). Implementation-mode link: weak coordination → absorbed input; supported team-working → contributes to multiplied input. The paper names a specific mechanism (delivery profile, institutional coverage as network property) that the canonical equity pattern renders more abstractly. - Ask each trainer to declare the modules they will own - Ask each institution to commit an explicit coverage profile with resourcing - Publish the aggregate coverage across the network so gaps are visible to the programme, not only to individual trainers - Audit breadth-vs-depth in sessions: where a trainer is covering outside their declared profile, surface that to the Institutional Lead - Test: can every trainer point to the modules they own and know which modules a colleague owns?

title: Protected Interaction: Profiled Provisioning
text: Protected Interaction: Profiled Provisioning Training delivery succeeds only when a trainer's declared delivery profile is matched by institutional provisioning. The breadth of open-research topics should be treated as a network coverage property, not as a demand on every individual. Without protected time, administrative backing, manageable scope, and team support, the trainer absorbs a structural coordination problem as personal overload. Each trainer has a declared delivery profile. Each participating institution has a committed coverage profile with protected time, administrative backing, and manageable scope. The programme maintains a current view of coverage as a network property. A programme trains intermediaries who are expected to deliver locally across a broad open-research territory. Delivery depends on trainer competence, but also on institutional conditions: rooms, protected time, administrative support, clear role mandate, and manageable scope. In NPT terms this combines Collective Action 3.3 Skill Set Workability and 3.4 Contextual Integration. In Ostrom terms this is the provisioning problem: resources must be supplied rather than assumed. In the paper's tier language this is an intervention-tier, medium-coordination pattern requiring at least the programme and an Institutional Lead or local representative. A trained intermediary has internalised the programme scaffold and is ready to develop local competence through delivery. They need to deliver, iterate, fail, adjust, and develop practical judgement in their setting. The topic landscape is wider than any single trainer's primary expertise, and many trainers are professional staff delivering outside their main discipline. The institution provides no protected conditions for iteration, and the programme has no declared delivery profiles. Sessions try to cover everything, crowding out interaction and depth. Trainers report inadequate preparation and impostor syndrome (FG1.15, FG2A.13; FG3.13, FG2A.4; T2A: "I didn't feel prepared to talk about all the areas"; T3: "There's a little bit of impostor syndrome"). They absorb four to six roles that the programme design distributes across actors: trainer, materials adapter, marketer, evaluator, local coordinator. The breadth gap is structural even when individual psychological ability is high (COM-B "I am psychologically able" M=4.85). - Breadth overload: trainers cover topics outside their expertise without support - Impostor-driven delivery: trainer reaches the room under-prepared because profile declaration was impossible - No iteration: trainer delivers once and never develops local competence - Role overload: trainer absorbs roles designed for distinct actors - Un-profiled institutions: institution participates without naming coverage aims or resourcing - Per-trainer coverage requirement: network coverage is treated as an individual requirement - Goodwill-dependent delivery: practice survives only while the individual persists Each trainer declares a delivery profile: the modules they will own and the limits of that ownership. Each participating institution commits an explicit coverage profile with named resourcing: protected time, rooms, IT/admin support, team coverage, and a manageable delivery scope. The programme publishes aggregate coverage across the network so gaps are visible to the programme, not only to individual trainers. Coverage becomes a distributed property of the network rather than an invisible expectation placed on each person. NPT: Skill Set Workability is the fit between work demands and what the trainer can reasonably do; Contextual Integration is the fit between the work and the institution's resources. Breadth overload breaks both. Sen: The conversion at stake is temporal and organisational. Informational clarity from Pattern 1 does not become competence unless the trainer has the time and conditions to iterate. Whole-board play: AlphaZero could not learn by reading about Go; it needed games. The trainer has far fewer games, so each delivery event must be protected enough to be formative. Rushed, overpacked, undersupported, or one-off sessions do not let local competence develop. Ostrom: The action situation works only when the relevant resources are provisioned. Where the institutional resource is absent, the individual fills a structural gap and practice survives only as long as they do. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Collective Action 3.3 Skill Set Workability and 3.4 Contextual Integration. Tier: Intervention. Coordination: Medium (programme + institutional representative). Implementation-mode link: weak coordination produces absorbed input; supported team-working contributes to multiplied input. Canonical deepening: protected iteration as the condition for competence development. Paper-specific mechanism: declared delivery profiles and institutional coverage as a network property. - Ask each trainer to declare the modules they will own - Ask each institution to commit a coverage profile with named resourcing - Define the minimum support package: time, space, admin, team support, scope - Publish aggregate coverage across the network so gaps are visible - Audit breadth-vs-depth where trainers cover outside their declared profile - Test: can every trainer deliver without absorbing roles that should be distributed?

title: Delivery Without Provisioning Produces Overload
text: Delivery Without Provisioning Produces Overload Training delivery succeeds only when the institution provides protected conditions — time, space, administrative support — not just a trained person. Without provisioning, the agent cannot iterate, and without iteration, no local competence structure can develop. No institution participates in the programme without providing named delivery support that includes protected time, administrative backing, and a manageable delivery scope. The support is designed to enable iterative development, not just one-off delivery. A programme trains intermediaries who are then expected to deliver locally. Delivery depends not only on the trainer's competence but on institutional conditions: rooms, protected time, administrative support, manageable scope. In NPT terms this is Collective Action (3.3 Skill Set Workability, 3.4 Contextual Integration). In Ostrom's terms this is the local provisioning problem: the action situation works only if resources are supplied rather than assumed. In the whole-board-play analogy, Pattern 1 gave the agent the rules of the game; this pattern asks whether they can actually play. A trained intermediary has internalised the programme scaffold (Pattern 1) and is ready to develop local competence through delivery. Like AlphaZero after learning the rules, the agent now needs to play — to deliver, iterate, fail, adjust, and develop the local perceptual structure that constitutes practical judgment in their specific setting. Each delivery is a game: a structured interaction from which the agent learns. The institution provides no protected conditions for iteration. The trainer has no dedicated time, no administrative support, and no clear role mandate. Sessions try to cover everything, crowding out the interaction that makes them formative. The trainer absorbs four to six roles (trainer, materials adapter, marketer, evaluator, local coordinator) that the programme design distributes across distinct actors. Without protected conditions, there are no games to learn from — the trainer reads the materials but never develops the internal structure that comes from doing. Impostor syndrome and overload are symptoms of an agent who has the rules but cannot play. - No iteration: trainer delivers once and never develops local competence - Role overload: trainer absorbs 4-6 roles designed for distinct actors - Impostor syndrome: professional staff delivering outside primary expertise without support or repetition - Breadth pressure: sessions cover everything, interaction disappears, no learning from the encounter - Goodwill-dependent delivery: practice survives only as long as the individual persists Participating institutions provide named delivery support: protected time in workload models, rooms, IT and administrative backing, and a manageable subset of topics. The programme requires institutional co-investment as a condition of participation, not as an optional extra. The point is not just to enable one delivery event but to create the conditions for iterative development: each session builds on the last, each local adaptation deepens practical judgment, each interaction with participants generates the local filters that no central specification could have provided. Sen: The conversion at stake is temporal and organisational. The agent has informational clarity (Pattern 1) but cannot convert it into competence without the time and conditions to iterate. Capability is not a state to be transmitted but a structure that develops through protected interaction with the environment. Without iteration, the nominal capability granted by training attendance remains nominal. Whole-board play: AlphaZero could not learn Go by reading about Go. It needed to play — millions of games, each one refining internal structure through feedback. The trainer's situation is analogous but with a crucial difference: the trainer gets far fewer games. Each delivery session is a precious iteration. If sessions are rushed, overpacked, undersupported, or unrepeatable, the trainer cannot develop local competence any more than AlphaZero could learn from three games with a broken clock. Ostrom: Protected delivery is the first pattern that requires two actors (programme + institution) to coordinate. The programme provides the scaffold and materials; the institution provides the conditions for iteration. Where both act, delivery succeeds and competence develops. Where the institutional resource is absent — "the amount of rooms we can book is a big issue"; "I'm more or less a single person" — the trainer absorbs the gap alone. The individual fills a structural gap, and the practice survives only as long as they do. This is the provisioning problem: resources must be actively supplied, not assumed to exist. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Collective Action (3.3, 3.4) via the UKRN T3 analysis. Mapped to the equity loop at governance→capability: governance that does not provision capability is performative. Deepened via whole-board play: competence develops through iteration, not transmission. Without protected conditions for iteration, the agent has the rules but cannot play. Ostrom: local resource provision structures the immediate action situation for delivery. Coordination requirement: Medium (2 actors). - Require institutional co-investment as a condition of participation - Define the minimum institutional support package (time, space, admin, scope) - Design for iteration, not one-off delivery: the first session is the beginning of learning, not the end - Test: can the trainer deliver without personally absorbing roles that should be distributed? - This requires 2 actors (programme + institution) and should be resolved after condition 1

title: Shared Maintenance (as published in paper v2.3)
text: Shared Maintenance (as published in paper v2.3) Trainers praise the materials as a gold standard but content ages, requires local adaptation, and cannot easily be upstreamed. The result is ad hoc rework as invisible labour. The missing norm is a coordination rule: every adaptation used more than once is shared, with the adapter credited as author, and a light-touch review cycle makes distributed stewardship the norm rather than the exception. Local adaptations can flow back into the shared materials through a defined light-touch review cycle. Adapters are credited as authors. The upstream pathway is no harder than the downstream consumption pathway. This is NPT Collective Action — specifically 3.2 Relational Integration and 3.4 Contextual Integration. It is an intervention-tier pattern with medium coordination, but the coordination takes the form of a community norm rather than an organisational decision — a developing knowledge commons that requires distributed stewardship across a contributor community. Where materials are reworked locally without upstreaming, the pattern's absence is the defining signature of absorbed input mode. A programme distributes high-quality training materials that trainers use and praise. Trainers encounter materials that age, that need adaptation to local settings, and that could be improved by the rework each trainer does privately. Contributing back to the shared resource would improve it for future trainers and reduce aggregate maintenance work. No upstream channel exists. Each trainer reworks materials independently; adaptations stay local; the "gold standard" reputation erodes as content drifts from practice. Maintenance falls to whoever notices a problem — ad hoc, unrecognised, on top of already constrained time. Workload and capacity concerns are the most prevalent theme in the corpus (34 of 134 turns, 25%). COM-B "policies, procedures, and resource allocation are appropriate" M=3.78 (below midpoint — the only pattern-relevant COM-B item to score below 4). Trainers: T1 calls the Carpentries lessons a "gold standard"; T1: "every time I've done it, I haven't given enough time"; FG1.9 praises the materials. Open licensing was planned but the stewardship infrastructure was not built. - No upstream channel: local learning never propagates; the commons degrades - Licensing without stewardship: open licence exists but no one curates or reviews - Invisible rework: maintenance is unrecognised work that compounds overload - Ad hoc sharing: "a couple of colleagues have uploaded their slides" — unsystematic - Drifting gold standard: reputation maintained while practice diverges The programme establishes a coordination rule: every adaptation used more than once is shared, with the adapter credited as author. A light-touch review cycle makes distributed stewardship the community norm. The contribution pathway is no harder to use than the consumption pathway. This is the commons governance move — Ostrom's "rules matched to local conditions" applied to a developing knowledge commons. NPT Collective Action: 3.2 Relational Integration is the work of maintaining trust and cooperation between actors whose efforts the practice depends on; 3.4 Contextual Integration is the fit between the practice and its institutional-organisational context. Invisible rework breaks both — the trainer carries unreciprocated maintenance labour, and the materials drift from the practice they were meant to support. Community-norm framing: Unlike Patterns 1 and 2, this pattern cannot be resolved by an organisational decision. A central scaffold or a declared profile can be issued top-down; a stewardship norm cannot. Coordination takes the form of a community rule of shared authorship, which the programme can seed but the community must sustain. This is what the paper means by "distributed stewardship." Commons framing (Ostrom 1990): A knowledge commons requires rules matched to local conditions. "Every adaptation used more than once is shared, credited as author" is one such rule — lightweight, low-cost, and aligned with how trainers already create value. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Collective Action 3.2 Relational Integration and 3.4 Contextual Integration as stated in the companion journal article. Tier: Intervention. Coordination: Medium, but community-norm rather than organisational-decision. Implementation-mode link: unshared rework is the defining signature of absorbed input. The paper names a specific coordination rule (every adaptation used more than once is shared, credited as author) and cites Ostrom 1990 directly. - Establish open licensing with an active upstream channel (not licensing alone) - Adopt the coordination rule: every adaptation used more than once is shared, adapter credited as author - Implement a light-touch review cycle with named reviewers - Make contributing as frictionless as consuming (the friction gradient should favour upstream flow) - Surface the aggregate labour: count contributions, count reviews, show the commons at work - Test: can a local adaptation reach the shared repository within one cycle?

title: Shared Maintenance: Stewarded Commons
text: Shared Maintenance: Stewarded Commons Materials stay current and trusted only when local adaptation flows back into a stewarded commons. Open licensing is not enough. The programme needs an upstream channel, author credit for adapters, and a light-touch review rule - every adaptation used more than once is shared - so local learning becomes shared infrastructure rather than invisible private labour. Local adaptations can flow back into the shared materials through a defined light-touch review cycle. Adapters are credited as authors. The upstream pathway is no harder than the downstream consumption pathway, and the materials commons has active stewardship beyond the original author.
