A programme provides high-quality training materials that trainers praise, adapt, and maintain informally. Materials age, local settings differ, and each adaptation is a learning event. In NPT terms this is Collective Action 3.2 Relational Integration and 3.4 Contextual Integration: maintaining connections between materials, trainers, and programme. In Ostrom terms this is a knowledge-commons stewardship problem. In whole-board-play terms, Patterns 1 and 2 gave the agent the rules and conditions to play; this pattern asks whether what is learned from play can update the shared structure. Trainers are developing local competence through iterative delivery. Each local adaptation discovers something about what works in a setting, what fails, and what should be added, removed, or resequenced. If those adaptations can flow back, future trainers inherit a better resource and aggregate maintenance work falls. No upstream channel exists. Trainers rework materials independently; adaptations stay local; the "gold standard" reputation erodes as content drifts from practice. Maintenance falls to whoever notices a problem: ad hoc, unrecognised work on top of constrained time. Open licensing was planned but stewardship infrastructure was not built. Workload and capacity concerns are the most prevalent corpus theme (34 of 134 turns, 25%), and the COM-B item "policies, procedures, and resource allocation are appropriate" is below midpoint (M=3.78). This is like a learning system that plays games but never updates its weights. - No backward propagation: local learning stays local and shared weights never update - No upstream channel: local adaptations cannot reach the commons - Licensing without stewardship: open licence exists but no one curates or reviews - Invisible rework: maintenance is unrecognised work that compounds overload - Ad hoc sharing: slides appear informally without a reliable curation path - Drifting gold standard: reputation persists while practice diverges - Content drift: materials age without systematic review The programme establishes open licensing plus an active upstream channel, a light-touch review cycle, and a shared rule: every adaptation used more than once is shared, with the adapter credited as author. Contributing is made no harder than consuming. Local groups catalogue assets, a community of practice shares adaptations, and named reviewers steward the syllabus. The shift is from individual burden to community infrastructure. NPT: Relational Integration depends on trust in the people and materials the practice uses; Contextual Integration depends on fit with the institutional context. Invisible rework breaks both. Sen: Usable materials sustain capability beyond the initial event, but capability develops through use. If adaptations cannot flow back, the capability gain remains private and the commons degrades. Whole-board play: Backward propagation from local play into shared structure is what distinguishes a system that learns from a system that merely runs. The training programme's "weights" are its materials, syllabus, and practical knowledge. Ostrom: A knowledge commons requires rules matched to local conditions. "Every adaptation used more than once is shared, credited as author" is lightweight, low-cost, and aligned with the value trainers already create. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Collective Action 3.2 Relational Integration and 3.4 Contextual Integration. Tier: Intervention. Coordination: Medium, expressed as community norm rather than a single organisational decision. Implementation-mode link: unshared rework is a defining signature of absorbed input. Canonical deepening: backward propagation and co-evolution of resource and users. Paper-specific mechanism: light-touch review, author credit, and the "adaptation used more than once" rule. - Establish open licensing with an active upstream pathway - Adopt the rule: every adaptation used more than once is shared - Credit adapters as authors so invisible labour becomes visible contribution - Implement a light-touch review cycle with named reviewers - Make contributing as frictionless as consuming - Surface aggregate labour: count contributions, reviews, and accepted changes - Test: can a local adaptation reach the shared repository within one cycle?

title: Local Adaptation Without Stewardship Fragments the Commons
text: Local Adaptation Without Stewardship Fragments the Commons Materials stay current and trusted only when stewardship is distributed across a contributor community with open licensing, a shared repository, and a light-touch curation process. Without stewardship, local learning fragments and the whole system cannot learn from its own variation. Local adaptations can flow back into the shared resource through a defined curation process. The materials commons has at least one active steward beyond the original author. The upstream pathway is no harder to use than the downstream consumption pathway. A programme provides high-quality materials that are praised by trainers but that age, require local adaptation, and cannot easily be upstreamed. In NPT terms this is Collective Action (3.2 Relational Integration, 3.4 Contextual Integration): the work of maintaining connections between the materials, the trainers, and the programme. In Ostrom's terms this is knowledge-commons stewardship. In the whole-board-play analogy, Patterns 1-2 gave the agent the rules and the conditions to play; this pattern asks whether what the agent learns from playing can flow back into the system that shapes future play. Trainers are developing local competence through iterative delivery (Pattern 2). Each local adaptation is a learning event: the trainer discovers what works in their setting, what doesn't, what needs to be added or removed. These local adaptations are the system's equivalent of the internal representations that develop during whole-board play — local structure that responds to local conditions, discovered through interaction rather than specified centrally. There is no mechanism to upstream local improvements. Each trainer reworks materials independently. Adaptations stay local — the system's local learning never propagates. The "gold standard" reputation erodes as content drifts from practice. Maintenance falls to whoever happens to notice a problem — invisible labour on top of already constrained time. Open licensing was planned but the stewardship infrastructure was not built. This is like AlphaZero playing millions of games but never updating its weights: the games happen, local information is generated, but nothing flows backward into the shared structure. - No backward propagation: local learning stays local, the system's weights never update - Content drift: materials diverge from practice without systematic review - Invisible labour: maintenance is unrecognised work that compounds trainer overload - Ad hoc sharing: "a couple of colleagues have uploaded their slides" — unsystematic, fragile - Licensing without stewardship: open licence exists but no one curates, reviews, or upstreams The programme establishes open licensing and a shared repository with a light-touch curation process. Contributing an adaptation is made as easy as consuming a resource. Local groups catalogue assets, a community of practice shares adaptations, and training partners review and update the syllabus. The shift is from individual burden to community infrastructure. Crucially, the upstream pathway is not just for materials — it is the mechanism through which the programme learns from its own local variation. Each adaptation that reaches the shared repository refines the commons, making it a better conversion factor for future trainers. Sen: Usable materials are part of the ongoing conditions that sustain capability beyond the initial event. But capability is not static — it develops through use. When a trainer adapts materials, they are developing both their own competence and a local variant that may be better suited to a class of settings. If that variant cannot flow back, the capability gain is private and the commons degrades. Whole-board play: The backward propagation of local learning into shared structure is what makes the difference between a system that learns and a system that merely runs. AlphaZero's power comes not from any single game but from the fact that what is learned in each game updates the weights that shape future games. In the training programme, the "weights" are the shared materials, the syllabus, the accumulated practical knowledge of what works. Without an upstream pathway, local games are played but the system's weights never update. The resource and its users must develop together — that is the co-evolutionary logic. Ostrom: This is knowledge-commons stewardship: maintenance, adaptation, and reuse depend on shared rules and contributor roles. Open licensing enables sharing; it does not produce stewardship. The curation process and contributor roles must be designed alongside the repository. The shift from individual burden to community infrastructure marks the transition toward architecture-level coordination. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Collective Action (3.2, 3.4) via the UKRN T3 analysis. Mapped to the equity loop at capability→contribution: local capability that fragments instead of feeding back. Deepened via whole-board play: the backward propagation of local learning into shared structure is what makes a system that learns rather than a system that merely runs. Ostrom: knowledge-commons stewardship requires shared rules and contributor roles. Coordination requirement: Medium-high (community). - Establish open licensing with an explicit upstream pathway - Define the curation process: who reviews, who accepts, what the cadence is - Make contributing as easy as consuming — the friction gradient should favour upstream flow - Test: can a local adaptation reach the shared repository within one cycle? - This requires a contributor community (medium-high coordination) and should be resolved after conditions 1-2

title: Visible Impact (as published in paper v2.3)
text: Visible Impact (as published in paper v2.3) The programme needs evidence of downstream impact to improve, sustain trainer motivation, and justify institutional support, but current feedback mechanisms are thin. The resolution is to distribute monitoring across the actors it serves — cross-institutional peer evaluation where trainers interview each other's recipients using a lightweight instrument. This is Ostrom's monitoring problem: the current evaluation chain has too many links for the existing governance structure to sustain, so the governance structure itself must adapt via a reciprocal network. The programme maintains a complete evaluation chain from instrument design through cross-institutional analysis to feedback, with a named actor at each link and explicit resourcing for the cross-institutional analysis step. Feedback propagates to trainers and institutional leads. A cross-institutional peer evaluation mechanism is active. This is NPT Reflexive Monitoring — specifically 4.2 Communal Appraisal: shared mechanisms for evaluating what is working and what is not. It is an architecture-tier pattern with very high coordination — a multi-actor evaluation chain, the highest coordination requirement under the current design. The paper notes this is the *only* pattern where quantitative COM-B data and qualitative transcript analysis produce a convergent signal independently arriving at the same conclusion. Its failure is the central impediment to multiplied input at network scale; only fully resolved, it converts absorbed/mismatch dynamics into programme-level learning. A distributed training programme has resolved (or is resolving) Patterns 1-4: trainers have expectations, provisioning, stewarded materials, and pathways into governance. Local and community-level learning operate. But the programme cannot see its own aggregate effects across institutions, cohorts, and time. Its funders, its institutional leads, and its trainers all need evidence that the effort produces downstream impact — evidence the current feedback mechanisms cannot produce. Feedback mechanisms are thin. Trainers rely on optional post-session surveys that yield only positive responses or none at all (T2B: "I have no other ways of getting feedback short of people filling in the feedback form"; T2B: "As we get like a few answers and nobody says this was terrible, I generally think it's gone quite well"). Informal signals from colleagues are all that is available (FG2B.41, FG2B.36, FG2B.39). COM-B: "effects are being measured" M=3.35 — the lowest item across all survey waves, dropping to M=3.17 at 6-month follow-up. Cross-institutional analysis is absent. An evaluation workstream was funded but the evaluation chain — from instrument design through data collection to cross-institutional analysis to feedback back to trainers — was not built. This is the monitoring chain with too many links for the current governance structure to sustain. - Broken chain: instruments exist but no one analyses across institutions - Upward-only feedback: results reach funders but not trainers or institutional leads - Thin feedback: optional surveys yield only positive or absent responses - Workstream without chain: evaluation is funded on paper but the handoff chain is not built - Monitoring-chain overload: the chain has more links than the current governance can carry; the pattern fails because the structure was never adapted - Motivation erosion: trainers cannot see whether their effort matters beyond anecdote - Absent cross-institutional analysis: 4/4 ORP transcripts show this missing The programme develops and deploys cross-institutional peer evaluation: trainers interview each other's recipients using a lightweight instrument. Monitoring is distributed across the actors it serves — a reciprocal network. The evaluation chain is designed end-to-end before the next delivery event, with named roles at each link (instrument, collection, cross-institutional analysis, feedback). Feedback propagates back to trainers and institutional leads, not only upward to funders. The governance structure adapts to carry a monitoring chain the current structure cannot. NPT Reflexive Monitoring: 4.2 Communal Appraisal is the shared mechanism for judging whether a practice is working. Without it, improvements are private and the programme cannot learn at the level that matters — aggregate effect across institutions. The evaluation workstream is not an evaluation chain; building the workstream without building the chain is funded ambition without architecture. Ostrom's monitoring problem: Monitoring and information flows across action arenas determine whether the programme can learn and adjust. When the chain has more links than the current governance can span, two options exist — shorten the chain (reduce scope) or restructure the governance (add actors and redistribute responsibilities). Cross-institutional peer evaluation is a restructure: it distributes monitoring across the trainers themselves, converting them from producers of impression-based signals into a reciprocal evaluation network. Very-high coordination: This is the highest-coordination pattern (6+ actor chain). Resolving it requires trainers at multiple institutions + a lightweight instrument + consent and data-sharing governance + an analyst who can see across + a feedback loop back to trainers and leads. The paper is explicit that this is the hardest of the five. Convergent signal: This is the only pattern where COM-B quantitative data and qualitative transcript analysis produce the same conclusion independently — giving the claim more evidential weight than the other four. The design move (lightweight cross-institutional instrument) is correspondingly specific. Learning-loop completion: Patterns 3 and 4 propagate local learning into materials and governance respectively. Pattern 5 is the completion of the loop — aggregate outcomes propagating back into design, so the programme can judge whether the preceding four patterns are actually producing what they are meant to produce. Without Pattern 5, the evidence that the other four are working stays anecdotal. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Reflexive Monitoring 4.2 Communal Appraisal as stated in the companion journal article. Tier: Architecture. Coordination: Very high (multi-actor evaluation chain, the highest of the five). Implementation-mode link: this pattern's failure bounds multiplied input at network scale; its resolution closes the learning loop. The paper is explicit that this is the *only* pattern with a convergent COM-B + qualitative signal, and is the most consistently absent under current governance. The paper's resolution (cross-institutional peer evaluation via lightweight instrument) corresponds exactly to the working paper's Step 3 in the bootstrap sequence. - Design the evaluation chain end-to-end before the next delivery cycle, not as a retrofit - Assign named roles at each link: instrument designer, collector, cross-institutional analyst, feedback reporter - Develop and deploy a lightweight cross-institutional peer evaluation instrument (trainers interview each other's recipients) - Establish the consent and data-sharing governance the peer-evaluation design requires - Resource cross-institutional analysis explicitly — the central link, and the most absent - Design feedback to propagate back to trainers and institutional leads, not only upward to funders - Test: can the programme produce one cross-institutional learning report within its first year?

title: Visible Impact: Evaluation Chain as Learning Loop
text: Visible Impact: Evaluation Chain as Learning Loop A programme that cannot see its downstream effects cannot learn, sustain motivation, or justify institutional support. The evaluation chain must run from instrument design through data collection, cross-institutional analysis, and feedback back to trainers and institutional leads. Where the current governance cannot carry that chain, the governance must adapt - for example through cross-institutional peer evaluation with a lightweight instrument. The programme maintains a complete evaluation chain from instrument design through cross-institutional analysis to feedback, with a named actor at each link and explicit resourcing for cross-institutional analysis. Feedback propagates to trainers and institutional leads. A cross-institutional peer-evaluation mechanism is active when governance permits it. A distributed programme needs evidence of downstream impact to improve its own design, sustain trainer motivation, and justify continued institutional support. In NPT terms this is Reflexive Monitoring 4.2 Communal Appraisal: shared mechanisms for evaluating what is working and what is not. In Ostrom terms this is the monitoring problem across action arenas. In whole-board-play terms, Patterns 1-4 gave the agent rules, provisioned play, material stewardship, and a route into governance; this pattern asks whether aggregate outcomes propagate back into programme architecture. In the paper's tier language this is an architecture-tier, very-high-coordination pattern: a multi-actor evaluation chain, the highest coordination requirement in the set. A distributed training programme has resolved or is resolving the preceding patterns. Trainers have expectations, provisioning, stewarded materials, and pathways into governance. Local and community-level learning operate. But the programme still needs evidence across institutions, cohorts, and time. Funders, institutional leads, trainers, and the programme itself need to know whether the effort produces downstream impact. Feedback mechanisms are thin. Trainers rely on optional post-session surveys that yield only positive responses or none at all (T2B: "I have no other ways of getting feedback short of people filling in the feedback form"; T2B: "As we get like a few answers and nobody says this was terrible, I generally think it's gone quite well"). Informal signals from colleagues substitute for evidence (FG2B.41, FG2B.36, FG2B.39). COM-B "effects are being measured" is the lowest item across survey waves (M=3.35, dropping to M=3.17 at 6-month follow-up). Cross-institutional analysis is absent; EV_analyse is absent across 4/4 ORP transcripts. An evaluation workstream was funded, but the chain from instrument to collection to cross-institutional analysis to feedback was not built. The chain has too many links for the current governance structure to sustain. - Blind system: the programme cannot see aggregate effects - Thin feedback: optional surveys yield only positive or absent responses - Informal-only evidence: trainers rely on impressions instead of shared analysis - Broken chain: instruments exist but no one collects, analyses, or reports cross-institutionally - Upward-only feedback: results reach funders but not practitioners - Workstream without chain: evaluation is funded on paper but handoff architecture is missing - Monitoring-chain overload: the chain has more links than governance can carry - Motivation erosion: trainers cannot see whether their effort matters beyond anecdote - Absent cross-institutional analysis: EV_analyse absent across 4/4 ORP transcripts The programme designs the evaluation chain before the next delivery cycle. Roles are named at each link: instrument designer, data collector, cross-institutional analyst, feedback reporter. Cross-institutional peer evaluation is developed and deployed: trainers interview each other's recipients using a lightweight instrument under consent and data-sharing governance. Monitoring is distributed across the actors it serves, forming a reciprocal network. Feedback propagates back to trainers and institutional leads, not only upward to funders. NPT: Communal Appraisal is the shared mechanism for judging whether a practice works. Without it, improvements remain private and the programme cannot learn at aggregate scale. Sen: Feedback is a conversion factor for persistence. Without visible consequences, capability decays into isolated effort; without evidence about whether conversion factors are working, the equity loop flies blind. Whole-board play: This is the outermost level of backward propagation. Pattern 3 updates shared materials; Pattern 4 updates governance; Pattern 5 updates the system's understanding of whether the whole learning process is producing the right effects. Ostrom: Monitoring and information flows across action arenas determine whether the programme can learn and adjust. When the monitoring chain has more links than the current governance can span, the options are to reduce scope or restructure governance. Cross-institutional peer evaluation is a restructuring move. Convergent signal: This is the only pattern where COM-B quantitative data and qualitative transcript analysis independently produce the same conclusion, giving the claim stronger evidential weight than the other four. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Reflexive Monitoring 4.2 Communal Appraisal. Tier: Architecture. Coordination: Very high (6+ actor evaluation chain). Implementation-mode link: this pattern's failure bounds multiplied input at network scale; its resolution closes the learning loop. Canonical deepening: aggregate feedback as outermost backward propagation/meta-learning. Paper-specific mechanism: cross-institutional peer evaluation through a lightweight instrument, matching the working paper's bootstrap Step 3. - Design the evaluation chain end-to-end before the next delivery cycle - Assign named roles at each link: instrument, collection, cross-institutional analysis, feedback - Develop and deploy a lightweight cross-institutional peer-evaluation instrument - Establish consent and data-sharing governance for peer evaluation - Resource cross-institutional analysis explicitly - Design feedback to propagate back to trainers and institutional leads, not only to funders - Test: can the programme produce one cross-institutional learning report within its first year?

title: A Programme That Cannot See Its Own Effects Cannot Learn
text: A Programme That Cannot See Its Own Effects Cannot Learn A programme learns and sustains motivation only when feedback is structured, visible, and shared across institutions. Without cross-institutional monitoring, the backward propagation that makes the whole system a learning system does not reach the outermost level — and the equity loop does not close. The programme has a complete evaluation chain from instrument design through cross-institutional analysis to feedback, with a named actor at each link and explicit resourcing for the cross-institutional analysis step. Feedback propagates to trainers and institutional leads, not only to funders. A distributed programme needs evidence of its downstream impact to improve its own design, sustain trainer motivation, and justify continued institutional support. In NPT terms this is Reflexive Monitoring (4.2 Communal Appraisal): shared mechanisms for evaluating what is working and what is not. In the whole-board-play analogy, Patterns 1-4 gave the agent the rules, the conditions to play, a way for local learning to propagate into shared materials, and a route into co-governance. This final pattern asks whether the whole system can see its own effects and adjust — whether backward propagation reaches all the way from outcomes to architecture. The programme has resolved the preceding conditions: expectations are clear (Pattern 1), delivery is protected (Pattern 2), materials are stewarded (Pattern 3), and trainers have contribution pathways into co-governance (Pattern 4). Local learning propagates into materials and governance. But the system's learning operates only at the level of individual adaptations and community conversation. It does not yet have a way to see its own aggregate effects — across institutions, across cohorts, across time. Feedback mechanisms are thin. Trainers rely on optional post-session surveys that yield only positive or absent responses. Cross-institutional sharing is limited: formal channels exist but go largely unused. No one performs cross-institutional analysis. The programme cannot demonstrate impact to the institutions it depends on for support. An entire evaluation workstream was funded but the evaluation chain — from instrument design through data collection to cross-institutional analysis to feedback — was not built. This is the deepest failure of backward propagation: the system plays, the system learns locally, but the aggregate signal — what is actually working across the whole landscape — never reaches the actors who could adjust the system's architecture. Without this signal, the agents within the system cannot know whether their becoming is on track. Feedback is not just a management tool; it is what makes the whole system reflexive rather than blind. - Blind system: the programme cannot see its own aggregate effects - Thin feedback: optional surveys yield only positive or absent responses - Informal-only evidence: trainers rely on "you can kind of tell whether people are engaged" - Broken chain: instruments exist but no one collects, analyses, or reports cross-institutionally - Upward-only feedback: results reach funders but never propagate back to practitioners - Motivation erosion: trainers cannot see whether their effort matters beyond anecdote - Funded ambition without architecture: an entire evaluation workstream exists on paper but the handoff chain is not built The evaluation chain is designed before the first delivery event. Roles are assigned explicitly at each link: who designs instruments, who collects data, who analyses cross-institutional patterns, who reports back to trainers and institutional leads. Shared feedback converts isolated impressions into programme-level learning. The chain is resourced end-to-end, not just at the instrument-design end. The feedback does not stop at the funders' desk — it propagates back to trainers, to institutional leads, to the scaffold itself (Pattern 1), completing the circuit. This is the whole-board view: the system sees its own aggregate play and adjusts. Sen: Feedback is a conversion factor for persistence. Without visible consequences, capability decays into isolated effort. But more than that: feedback is what allows the system to assess whether its conversion factors are actually working — whether the scaffold (Pattern 1) is giving the right form, whether provisioning (Pattern 2) is sufficient, whether the commons (Pattern 3) is healthy, whether co-governance (Pattern 4) is real. Without this assessment, the equity loop is flying blind. Whole-board play: This is the final level of backward propagation. Pattern 3 propagates local learning into shared materials (updating the weights from individual games). Pattern 4 propagates trainer experience into programme governance (modifying the architecture). Pattern 5 propagates aggregate outcomes into the system's self-understanding (seeing the whole board). In AlphaZero, this is analogous to meta-learning: not just learning from games, but learning whether the learning process itself is producing the right kind of improvement. Without this level, the system can improve locally but cannot assess whether it is improving globally. It can play but cannot see its own play. Ostrom: This is the monitoring problem in its strongest form. Monitoring and information flows across action arenas determine whether the programme can learn and adjust. The learning chain crosses multiple actors and no single trainer can sustain it alone. An evaluation workstream is not an evaluation chain. The chain requires specific actors at each link — instrument designer, data collector, cross-institutional analyst, feedback reporter — and each link must be resourced. When any one is missing, the loop does not close. This is the most coordination-intensive condition and the most consistently absent — not because no one wanted to monitor, but because the monitoring chain has too many links for the current governance structure to sustain. Mechanic, in short: Derived from NPT Reflexive Monitoring (4.2 Communal Appraisal) via the UKRN T3 analysis. Mapped to the equity loop at the feedback joint: the mechanism that tells the system whether the loop is closing. Deepened via whole-board play: this is the outermost level of backward propagation — the system seeing its own aggregate play and adjusting. Without it, the system can improve locally but cannot assess whether it is improving globally. Ostrom: monitoring and information flows across action arenas determine whether the programme can learn. Coordination requirement: Very high (6+ actor chain). - Design the evaluation chain before the first delivery event, not as a retrofit - Assign named roles at each link of the chain - Resource cross-institutional analysis explicitly — it is the central link and the most absent - Design feedback to propagate back to practitioners, not just upward to funders - Test: can the programme produce one cross-institutional learning report within its first year? - This requires a multi-actor chain (very high coordination, 6+ actors) and is the final condition

title: Construction Discipline for Law Checking
text: Construction Discipline for Law Checking Use construction discipline (safe constructors) for runtime law checking; reserve property tests for offline verification; log test harness results as evaluation signals. Defining how to check CT laws (associativity, identity, functor preservation, naturality) in the exotic programming system. CT structures have laws that must hold, but checking laws at every operation is expensive. No checking allows invalid structures to propagate; full runtime checking is slow; pure property tests miss runtime violations. Use construction discipline: smart constructors that validate laws on creation, preventing invalid structures from existing. Reserve property-based testing (e.g., test.check) for offline verification of constructor correctness. Log test harness outcomes as additional evaluation signals for regime quality. Construction discipline provides runtime safety without per-operation overhead (validate once, trust thereafter). Property tests provide confidence in the constructors themselves. Test logs contribute to exotic scoring (regimes that pass more tests are healthier). exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, Law-checking strategy entry. - Implement smart constructors for Category, Functor, NatTrans. - Write property tests for law preservation. - Add test pass/fail rate to regime evaluation signals.

title: Dual-Track Generated Patterns
text: Dual-Track Generated Patterns Generated patterns are dual-tracked: drafts carry `:status :draft` in meaningful namespaces, then promote to stable IDs on acceptance with review evidence. Defining how patterns generated by the exotic system are managed before becoming canonical. The system may generate new patterns (via meta-exotic programming or pattern extraction), but not all generated patterns are worth keeping. Treating generated patterns as immediately canonical pollutes the library; discarding them loses learning; mixing drafts with stable patterns creates confusion. Use dual-track: drafts live in namespaced IDs (e.g., `gen/<domain>/<slug>`) with `:status :draft`. Review process checks evidence and fit. Promotion moves pattern to stable namespace with `:status :stable` and records review outcome. Rejected drafts are archived, not deleted. This creates a clear path from generation to canonization while preserving the audit trail. Draft namespaces prevent accidental use of unreviewed patterns. Archive preserves learning even from rejected ideas. exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, Generated-pattern policy entry. - Define draft namespace convention. - Implement promotion workflow with evidence requirement. - Add archive storage for rejected drafts.

title: Dual Windowing
text: Dual Windowing Use two window types: primary (fixed evaluations) for quick ratchet tests, secondary (mission-completion) for interpretable checks once mapping stabilizes. Defining what constitutes a "window" for ratchet memory and delta-scoring. The ratchet mechanism needs to detect improvement over time, but "time" could mean evaluations, generations, wall-clock, or mission completions. Fixed evaluation windows enable rapid testing but lose mission-semantic meaning; mission-completion windows are interpretable but require stable mission mapping before they work. Implement both. Primary windows use fixed evaluation counts (e.g., 100 evals) for early ratchet testing. Secondary windows use mission completions once the VISION-to-EXECUTION mapping is stable. The primary window dominates ratchet decisions until mission windows stabilize. This allows iterative development (test the ratchet quickly with primary windows) while building toward the interpretable goal (mission-aligned windows for exotic scoring). exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, Window definition entry. - Implement primary window counter in exoevolve. - Define mission-completion detection logic. - Add window-type field to ratchet state.

title: Full Lift Registry with Lisp Templates
text: Full Lift Registry with Lisp Templates Lift registry uses full Lisp-style expressions for CT templates and lift rules, with evidence/version metadata per entry for provenance and automation. Defining the schema for the exotype-xenotype lift registry that bridges patterns to CT structures. The lift registry must map sigil patterns to CT templates in a way that supports provenance tracking and eventual automation. Simple key-value mappings lose the structure needed for composition; opaque blobs prevent inspection; metadata-free entries can't track where templates came from. Use Lisp-style expressions for `:ct-template` (composable, inspectable) and `:lift-rules` (transformations from pattern to template). Include `:evidence` (what supports this mapping), `:version` (which futon1 version), and `:source` metadata per entry. Lisp expressions are homoiconic (code as data), making templates manipulable by the same system that uses them. Evidence metadata supports the contemplative layer. Version tracking enables live sync from futon1 as source of truth. exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, Lift registry schema entry; resources/exotype-xenotype-lift.edn structure. - Define CT template s-expression grammar. - Implement lift rule interpreter. - Add evidence/version fields to registry entries. - Prototype the pattern REPL handshake: pattern-id -> ct-template -> vision skeleton -> plan functor stub -> run -> evidence bundle -> lift proposal.

title: Graded Naturality with Curriculum Tightening
text: Graded Naturality with Curriculum Tightening Naturality checking is graded (not boolean) and curriculum-tightened; commutativity residuals are logged for analysis, not hard-failed before M14. Defining how strictly to enforce the naturality condition on ADAPT transformations. The naturality square (PLAN changes must commute with mission execution) is the core coherence check for adaptations. Boolean pass/fail is too strict early on (everything fails) and hides information; pure permissiveness loses the signal entirely. Use graded metrics: mission-path edit distance as primary, evidence-vector distance as soft penalty/bonus. Log commutativity residuals (difference between PLAN(f;g) and PLAN(f);PLAN(g)) without hard-failing. Tighten tolerance as the curriculum advances; post-M14, naturality violations may become blocking. Graded checking provides signal during development (how close to commutative?) while logging builds the evidence base for later decisions. Curriculum tightening means early exploration isn't penalized but mature systems are held to standards. exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, Naturality strictness entry; Basecamp invariants section. - Implement mission-path edit distance metric. - Add residual logging to adapt.clj. - Define curriculum schedule for tolerance tightening.

title: Hybrid Execution Semantics
text: Hybrid Execution Semantics EXECUTION category objects are milestones with MMCA traces as evidence, preserving both CT interpretability and simulation grounding. Defining what "objects" and "morphisms" mean in the EXECUTION category of exotic programming. The CT layer must be interpretable (auditable reasoning) while remaining grounded in actual simulation behavior. Pure milestone semantics lose the richness of how execution actually proceeded; pure trace semantics drown in detail without categorical structure. Use milestones as the categorical objects and morphisms (discrete, auditable checkpoints), but attach MMCA traces as evidence artifacts. The traces support the milestone claims without replacing the categorical structure. This keeps CT interpretability (you can ask "what missions were completed?") while grounding in simulation (you can inspect the actual execution path). It also aligns with nonstarter mechanics where clearing events are facts with supporting evidence. exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, EXECUTION semantics entry. - Define milestone schema (what constitutes a valid checkpoint). - Specify trace attachment format (which traces support which milestones). - Implement milestone extraction from MMCA runs.

title: Immutable Vision, Mutable Plan
text: Immutable Vision, Mutable Plan VISION is immutable once declared; PLAN may be revised but only with logged evidence linking to xenotype/exotype learning. Defining revision policy for the CT structures in exotic programming. Strategy adaptation (ADAPT natural transformation) requires plan changes, but unconstrained mutation destroys interpretability. Fully immutable plans cannot respond to evidence; fully mutable plans lose the distinction between coherent adaptation and goalpost-moving. Lock VISION (objects and morphisms) at declaration time. Allow PLAN functor revisions, but require each revision to cite evidence from EXECUTION. Failed plans receive weak positive scores for early failure that saves compute, rather than harsh penalties. This preserves the "what you said you would do" (VISION) as an auditable record while allowing "how you're going to do it" (PLAN) to evolve. The evidence requirement makes adaptations justified rather than arbitrary, supporting naturality checking. exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, Plan revision policy entry; exotic-programming-spec.md ADAPT naturality condition. - Implement VISION immutability check in category.clj. - Add evidence-citation field to plan revision records. - Define "early failure" scoring bonus.

title: Live Sync from Source of Truth
text: Live Sync from Source of Truth Treat futon1 as immutable/versioned source of truth for patterns; sync bidirectionally (drafts back via tri-store), logging pattern version IDs per run. Defining how the exotic programming system stays synchronized with the upstream pattern library. Patterns evolve in futon1; exotic programming depends on patterns; generated patterns may flow back upstream. One-time import drifts out of date; continuous sync without versioning loses reproducibility; one-way sync prevents learning from flowing back. Implement live sync: futon1 is the immutable, versioned source of truth for canonical patterns. Log which pattern version was used in each run. Sync is bidirectional: drafts generated by exotic programming flow back to futon1 via the tri-store (facts → memes → upstream proposal). Version logging enables reproducibility (you know exactly which patterns were active). Bidirectional flow closes the loop (exotic programming improves the pattern library that exotic programming uses). Immutable source of truth prevents accidental overwrites. exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, Import cadence entry; scripts/import_futon3a_patterns.clj. - Add pattern version ID to run logs. - Implement upstream proposal pathway for drafts. - Define version bump protocol for futon1.

title: Semi-Robust Baselines for Validation
text: Semi-Robust Baselines for Validation M16 baseline profile uses semi-robust batches: fixed pop/mutation/selection/budget, rotated seed sets across batches, multiple batches for A/B comparability. Defining the experimental profile for validating exotic xenotype against Mission 7/8 baselines. Validation requires A/B comparison between regimes, but MMCA has inherent stochasticity. Fully deterministic runs (single seed) overfit to that seed; fully random runs have high variance that obscures signal; single runs can't estimate variance. Fix structural parameters (population size, mutation operators, selection method, evaluation budget). Use fixed seed sets per batch, but rotate seeds across batches. Run multiple batches (e.g., 3 x 5k evaluations) to get variance estimates. Compare regimes within batches before comparing across. Semi-robust design balances reproducibility (same seeds within batch) with generalization (different seeds across batches) with statistical power (multiple batches). This is the minimal setup for detecting upward drift vs stationary distribution. exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, Baseline profile entry; README-mission8.md A/B design. - Lock parameter values in a config file. - Implement seed rotation across batches. - Define statistical test for "upward trend" detection.

title: Template-Driven VISION Initialization
text: Template-Driven VISION Initialization Initialize VISION from CT templates seeded from futon3a sigil patterns; fall back to degenerate vision when no pattern matches. Defining how a genotype acquires its initial VISION declaration. Exotic scoring requires a declared VISION, but genotypes don't naturally come with one. Requiring manual vision declaration doesn't scale; purely degenerate visions lose the interpretability benefit; random initialization produces noise. Seed CT templates from the futon3a pattern catalog (sigils + metadata), then lift to xenotype templates via the lift registry. When a genotype is created, match it to a template if possible; otherwise use degenerate vision (single object, identity morphism). Record template identity in lineage for provenance. Templates provide interpretable structure (the vision means something because it came from a pattern). The fallback ensures the system always works. Template provenance supports the contemplative layer's "how did you get here?" question. exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, VISION initialization entry; resources/exotype-xenotype-lift.edn. - Define template matching criteria (sigil similarity, hotword overlap). - Implement lift from pattern to CT template. - Add template-id field to vision records.

title: Tri-Store Lineage Model
text: Tri-Store Lineage Model Lineage uses a tri-store model: facts (append-only event log), memes (derived lineage graphs), notions (optional fuzzy index), consistent with nonstarter. Defining how to store and query lineage/provenance information for exotic scoring. The contemplative layer needs to answer "how did this genotype arrive here?" and "is this score earned or hacked?" A single flat log is hard to query for lineage; a derived graph alone loses auditability; a fuzzy index alone lacks grounding. Use three layers: (1) Facts = append-only event log as single source of truth (every mutation, every score, every adaptation). (2) Memes = derived lineage graph and summaries, rebuilt from facts. (3) Notions = optional fuzzy index for similarity queries. This matches the nonstarter tri-store architecture. Facts provide auditability (you can always replay). Memes provide queryability (you can ask about ancestors). Notions provide discoverability (you can find similar paths). The separation keeps each layer's guarantees clean. exotic-programming-curriculum.md Basecamp decision log, Lineage storage entry; nonstarter tri-store architecture. - Define fact event schema (mutation, scoring, adaptation events). - Implement meme derivation from facts. - Defer notions layer until provenance queries are clearer.

title: Bootstrap Loop
text: Bootstrap Loop Seed a term dictionary from a curated source, apply it to a messier corpus, absorb new terms from that corpus, and iterate. Each pass through the loop expands coverage and improves precision. You are building a mathematical NER kernel that must cover terminology from multiple sources with different levels of structure. PlanetMath provides curated, structured term definitions (pmdefines, pmsynonym, pmtitle) and Stack Exchange provides folksonomy tags and body-extracted terms from a much larger but noisier corpus. Starting from SE alone produces a noisy dictionary full of common English words. Starting from PlanetMath alone misses contemporary terminology and informal usage. Neither source alone provides adequate coverage. Bootstrap: PlanetMath seeds the kernel (high precision, limited recall) → apply to SE (discover gaps) → absorb SE tags and body-extracted terms (expand recall) → filter and merge → re-apply to SE (measure improvement) → iterate. Each cycle expands the kernel while maintaining the curated core's precision. The NNexus system (Ginev, 2014) demonstrated that PlanetMath terms alone provide useful auto-linking. The bootstrap loop extends NNexus's approach by using SE as both a test corpus and a term source. Evidence: 3 PlanetMath repos → 2,731 terms; all 63 repos → 19,236 terms; SE integration pending. next[Run full bootstrap after M-f6-ingest: absorb math.SE tags into kernel, re-run spotter, measure coverage delta.] next[Track precision/recall at each loop iteration to detect diminishing returns.] next[Apply same loop pattern to Arxiv in M-f6-arxiv: SE-expanded kernel → Arxiv → absorb Arxiv terms.]

title: Graph-Enhanced Evaluation
text: Graph-Enhanced Evaluation Two agents, same questions, one has the graph. The difference measures the value of structured mathematical knowledge representation. You are proving that the knowledge graph from M-f6-ingest makes mathematical question answering measurably better. Agent A (bare) receives only raw question text. Agent B (graph-enhanced) receives the question plus NER term annotations, pattern tags, scope records, cluster context, and related entities via graph queries. Graph context might be distracting on easy questions where the answer is obvious. The judge LLM's scores might not correlate with human judgement. Agent B might simply be longer-winded rather than more accurate. Stratify the evaluation by difficulty (easy/medium/hard). Use blind scoring (judge sees both answers in randomised order). Measure multiple dimensions: accuracy, completeness, coherence, depth. Spot-check judge scores against human ratings. Hypothesis: improvement is largest on hard questions where structure matters most. The AI4CI proposal designed this evaluation but never ran it. The thesis (§10.6) called for "actionable semantic domain and user models" — the graph IS the domain model. If structured representation doesn't measurably help, the decade-long thesis is wrong. If it does help, we know exactly what kind of structure matters and can scale to Arxiv. next[Build MathKnowledgeGraph query interface as specified in M-f6-eval.] next[Sample 200 questions stratified by difficulty from math.SE processed corpus.] next[Run paired evaluation and compute significance tests.]

title: Learning Event Detection
text: Learning Event Detection Detect learning events by tracking when new technical terms appear in a user's contributions, then measure the causal effect of social interactions (answers, comments, corrections) on these events using an impulse-damping model. You are measuring whether mathematical Q&A interactions cause learning, using the same method Corneli (2014, Chapter 6) applied to PlanetMath edit histories — now scaled to all of Stack Exchange using the 19,236-term NER kernel. Stack Exchange data dumps include full revision histories for every post, with timestamps. Each user has an observable vocabulary trajectory: the set of NER kernel terms they have used, growing over time. Social interactions (receiving an answer, a comment, an edit to one's question) are timestamped treatment events. A "learning event" is any post edit or new post in which a user introduces a technical term they have never used before. A new term in a user's output may be exposition (copying from a textbook) rather than genuine learning. The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model cannot distinguish these. High-frequency posters will show more "learning events" by volume alone. The method requires careful per-user normalization and distinguishing treatment from confound (did the user learn from the SE interaction, or from an external source between posts?). For each SE user with sufficient history (N posts > threshold): extract their term vocabulary trajectory using the NER kernel. Identify learning events (first use of each term). Identify treatment events (answers received, comments received, accepted answers on their questions). Fit the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck impulse-damping model: does a treatment event produce a detectable impulse in learning-event rate, and how quickly does it damp? Compare across difficulty strata and topic clusters. Corneli (2014) demonstrated this method on 445 PlanetMath users over 9 years (8,051 forum posts, 14,064 corrections, 3,867 learning-event edits). The method is classical — no GPU, no LLM — and scales linearly with corpus size. SE has orders of magnitude more data. If the same impulse-damping dynamics appear in SE that appeared in PlanetMath, it validates the thesis's model of peer-produced peer learning at scale. The fitted parameters then become a baseline for the Artificial Stack Exchange: do agent interactions produce the same learning dynamics as human interactions? next[Extract user edit histories from math.SE data dump (available after M-f6-ingest).] next[Run NER kernel term spotting per-user to build vocabulary trajectories.] next[Fit Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model to treatment→learning-event sequences; compare parameters with Corneli (2014) Table.] next[Use fitted human-learning parameters as a benchmark for M-f6-agents: do artificial agents exhibit similar impulse-damping dynamics?]

title: Negative Space Duality
text: Negative Space Duality What NER covers is formal scaffolding; what NER leaves behind is where informal reasoning patterns live. The two are complementary masks over the same text, not competing annotations. You are annotating mathematical text with both named entities (terms, definitions, symbols) and informal reasoning patterns (heuristics, strategies). NER term spotting identifies formal mathematical objects (named theorems, defined terms, variable bindings) and pattern tagging identifies informal reasoning moves (argue-by-contradiction, try-a-simpler-case, etc.). It is tempting to treat these as independent annotation layers applied to different documents or different classes of text. In fact, both systems fire on the same documents: high-term entities also have more patterns, not fewer. The duality is spatial within text, not across documents. Run both NER and pattern tagging on every document. Treat the NER-covered tokens as "formal figure" and the remaining tokens as "informal ground." Measure negative-space percentage (typically 87-99% of tokens). Use the ratio as a document-level feature: low negative-space means dense formal content; high negative-space means discursive reasoning. The Corneli (2014) thesis codes proofs as alternating formal steps (definition expansion, deduction) and informal moves (conjecture, heuristic selection). NER captures the former; the 25 math-informal patterns capture the latter. Together they give an agent structured understanding that flat text cannot. next[Validate duality on math.SE data after M-f6-ingest superpod run.] next[Use negative-space ratio as a feature in M-f6-eval stratified sampling.] next[Feed both layers to Agent B in M-f6-eval to test whether dual annotation outperforms either alone.]

title: Pattern as Strategy
text: Pattern as Strategy The 25 math-informal patterns are not just annotations — they are operational agent strategies. Each pattern tells an agent what to do next when reasoning about a mathematical problem. You are designing agents that use the math-informal pattern library as a repertoire of reasoning moves, following Pólya's tradition of heuristic problem solving. The 25 math-informal patterns each have a conclusion (what the pattern achieves), an IF/HOWEVER/THEN/BECAUSE structure (when and how to apply it), keywords (for recognition in text), and next-steps (what follows from applying it). Patterns as written describe human reasoning strategies. An LLM agent may apply them differently: it cannot truly "try a simpler case" the way a human does, but it can decompose a question and generate a simpler sub-question. The mapping from human heuristic to agent action is not always one-to-one. For each of the 25 patterns, define an agent-operational interpretation: what the Asker does with this pattern (generate a question), what the Answerer does (construct an answer step), what the Critic does (check a condition). Include the pattern's flexiarg keywords in the agent's prompt so it can name the pattern it is using. Track which patterns the agents actually use via PSR/PUR records. The Corneli (2014) thesis (§10.6) calls for agents that can "apply standard and social problem solving heuristics." The thesis Appendix B demonstrates that proofs can be coded as sequences of pattern applications. The 25 flexiarg patterns are the operational vocabulary for this coding. If agents can name and apply them, the thesis's computational vision is realized. next[Write agent-operational interpretation for at least 8 high-use patterns (the ones in M-f6-agents Table).] next[Include pattern keywords in Agent B prompt template for M-f6-eval.] next[After M-f6-agents Phase 1: measure which patterns agents cite most and whether citations are accurate.]

title: Proof as Social Process
text: Proof as Social Process A mathematical proof is a sequence of social-computational moves that can be coded along five dimensions: context, feedback, quality, structure, and heuristic. This coding bridges human reasoning and agent behavior. You are validating that the pattern tagger and agent system can analyse proofs in the same way the Corneli (2014) thesis Appendix B analyses them by hand. Appendix B of the thesis codes two proofs (Gowers & Ganesalingam, 2012) using a 5-category scheme: (1) context — expand definitions, scope the problem; (2) feedback — generate examples, try instances; (3) quality — form conjectures, build models; (4) structure — change descriptions, apply deductions; (5) heuristic — restrict to known, certify results. The thesis coding was done by hand on two proofs. Scaling to corpus-level requires automation. The 25 math-informal patterns partially cover the 5 categories but were not designed to partition cleanly into them. Some patterns span multiple categories; some categories lack dedicated patterns. Map each of the 25 math-informal patterns to one or more of the 5 thesis categories. Identify coverage gaps: categories where no pattern fires reliably. Use the Appendix B worked examples as test cases for the pattern tagger — do the automatically assigned patterns match the hand-coded categories? This is a unit test for the entire pattern-tagging enterprise. If the pattern tagger's output aligns with the hand-coded proof analysis, it validates both the tagger and the thesis's claim that proofs are structured social-computational processes. If it doesn't align, the gap tells us exactly which reasoning moves the tagger misses. next[Create a 25×5 mapping matrix: each pattern assigned to thesis categories (1)-(5).] next[Run pattern tagger on the two Appendix B proofs (if available in corpus) and compare with hand coding.] next[Identify thesis categories with thin pattern coverage; consider whether new patterns are needed.]

title: Q Turnstile A
text: Q Turnstile A A well-posed question constrains its answer. Agents that identify what they don't know and formulate the right question are doing mathematics, not retrieval. You are designing agents that interact through mathematical question-answering, following Kolmogorov's calculus of problems where Q⊢A means "question Q is resolved by answer A." In Kolmogorov's framework, a problem is solved by a construction; a compound problem (A ∧ B) is solved by solving both parts; a conditional problem (A → B) is solved by a method transforming any solution of A into a solution of B. Most Q&A systems treat questions as retrieval queries and answers as information dumps. This ignores the constructive content: a good question doesn't just ask for information, it specifies what kind of construction would count as adequate. An answer to the wrong question is not mathematics. Design the Asker agent to generate questions that constrain their answers: each question should specify what kind of construction (proof, example, counterexample, algorithm) would resolve it. The Critic evaluates not just whether the answer is correct, but whether it constitutes an adequate construction for the question posed. Stack Exchange voting is the social proof system; the Artificial Stack Exchange replaces social voting with agent-based evaluation. The Corneli (2014) thesis (§10.6) identifies problem posing as "the essence of pattern-making." The EPSRC LEAPQA proposal formalised this as Q⊢A. The SFI proposal framed it as the Artificial Stock Market applied to knowledge. All three point to the same insight: generating questions is harder and more valuable than generating answers. next[Implement question-type annotation in the Asker: proof-question, example-question, counterexample-question, algorithm-question.] next[Evaluate Critic against human judgement of answer adequacy, not just correctness.] next[Measure whether Asker-generated questions are more constraining (fewer adequate answers) than random SE questions.]

title: Scope Chain Tracking
text: Scope Chain Tracking Mathematical text introduces variables through scoped bindings (Let, Define, Assume) that create nested contexts. Tracking these scope chains gives agents awareness of what is "in play" at each point in a proof. You are building scope detection for mathematical NER, distinguishing global entities (named theorems, definitions) from local bindings (variables introduced for a specific proof or argument). Mathematical reasoning relies on Let-binding chains: "Let X be a topological space. Let f: X → Y be continuous. Assume X is compact." Each binding narrows the context and introduces variables that are meaningful only within that scope. Scope detection via regex (7 patterns for Let/Define/Assume/Consider/where/ for-any/set-notation openers) captures the syntactic signal but not the semantic nesting. A "Let" inside a proof inherits the scope of the theorem statement. Arxiv papers have scope chains crossing section boundaries. Implement in tiers. Tier 1 (classical, no GPU): regex scope-opener detection with position tracking — enough for M-f6-ingest. Tier 2 (small model): classify binding types (variable intro, function intro, assumption) and detect scope closure. Tier 3 (LLM): full dependency graphs across proof/theorem/section boundaries — needed for M-f6-arxiv. The Corneli (2014) thesis Appendix B notes that "variables can be introduced as examples, which can have either 'global' or 'local' significance" (p.197). The entity taxonomy (GlobalEntity vs LocalBinding) makes this distinction computational. Scope awareness is what separates a term spotter from a mathematical reasoner. next[Integrate Tier 1 scope detection into superpod-job.py as Stage 5 of M-f6-ingest.] next[Validate scope detection on physics.SE subset: expect >30% of answers contain Let/Define openers.] next[Design Tier 2 binding classifier for post-ingest enrichment.]

title: Self-Play Loop
text: Self-Play Loop Three agents — Asker, Answerer, Critic — form a self-play loop where each iteration improves the knowledge graph and the agents' own performance. You are building the Artificial Stack Exchange: agents that ask, answer, evaluate, and learn from mathematical questions using a shared knowledge graph. The Asker finds gaps in the knowledge graph (isolated nodes, missing inter-cluster links, ungrounded pattern annotations). The Answerer uses graph context to construct answers. The Critic evaluates QA pairs using the M-f6-eval scoring protocol. Self-play can degenerate: the Asker may generate trivial questions, the Answerer may ignore graph context, the Critic may be unreliable, and graph updates may introduce noise rather than signal. Without quality control, the loop amplifies errors rather than correcting them. Gate each iteration: Critic scores must exceed a threshold before graph updates are committed. Track evaluation scores over iterations — if scores plateau or decline, pause and diagnose. The Critic's evaluations should be periodically calibrated against human judgement (spot-checks from M-f6-eval). The Asker should be measured on question non-triviality, not just question volume. The Corneli (2014) thesis (§10.5) identified "simulation work with artificial agents" as the key missing piece. The SFI Complexity Postdoc proposal modelled this on the Artificial Stock Market: agents that trade create a market; agents that ask and answer create a knowledge commons. The loop works only if the commons improves — measurable via graph density, evaluation scores, and gap reduction. next[Implement Phase 1 of M-f6-agents: single-turn QA with graph context, baseline measurement.] next[Define quality gates: minimum Critic score for graph update, minimum question novelty for Asker.] next[Run 100-iteration pilot and measure graph growth (new relations, confidence scores, gap markers).]

title: Stratum Bridge
text: Stratum Bridge Stack Exchange is the learning stratum; Arxiv is the research stratum. Bridge concepts — terms, patterns, and clusters that appear in both — create Thurston's "channels for communication between the strata." You are connecting two corpora that represent different modes of mathematical activity: people helping each other understand (SE) and people creating new knowledge (Arxiv). The same mathematical concepts appear in both SE questions and Arxiv proofs, but in different registers: informal and pedagogical in SE, formal and terse in Arxiv. The NER kernel and pattern tagger provide a shared vocabulary for detecting these overlaps. Naive term matching will over-connect: "group" appears in both corpora but with different senses and scopes. Embedding similarity alone may conflate superficially similar but mathematically distinct concepts. The bridge must be precise enough to be useful and loose enough to discover non-obvious connections. Define bridge concepts as entities that appear in both corpora with (a) shared NER terms from the kernel, (b) shared pattern tags, AND (c) embedding similarity above a threshold. Rank bridges by information gain: a bridge that connects otherwise-disconnected clusters is more valuable than one that reinforces an existing connection. Feed high-value bridges to the Asker as question seeds. Thurston (1990) called for "the creation of channels for communication between the strata." The Corneli (2014) thesis (§10.3) cited this as a goal for PlanetMath. F6 realizes it computationally: the knowledge graph IS the channel, and bridge concepts are the points where learning and research illuminate each other. next[After M-f6-arxiv pilot: count bridge concepts between SE and Arxiv graphs.] next[Rank bridges by information gain and present top-20 to Asker for question generation.] next[Validate that bridge-seeded questions produce higher-quality QA pairs than gap-seeded questions.]

title: Blast Radius Control
text: Blast Radius Control Record blast radius explicitly for cross-futon changes so rollback scope and downstream risk stay inspectable. - Require blast-radius events for cross-futon changes; audit that the rollback scope matches actual artifacts.

title: Changelog-as-Trail
text: Changelog-as-Trail Use the changelog as a compact trail of clock-in, dependency, artifact, and clock-out events that can be rolled up into proof evidence. - Add a fixed template per entry (clock-in, deps, artifacts, clock-out) and schedule a periodic backfill into XTDB once proof events land. - Require every fulab pattern to include a :pattern-ref and validate that referenced devmap files/clauses exist. - Add a lightweight rollup that counts clock-out events per devmap prototype.

title: Agent Clock-In
text: Agent Clock-In Use explicit assumptions and trade-offs to improve decision quality and reduce churn. An agent is about to start a task that will change a codebase or knowledge base. An agent is working under pattern P1 and needs to invoke reasoning from pattern P2 to complete the current step. An agent finishes a unit of work and is ready to end the session with a checkable summary. An agent (or user) wants to commit changes produced during a clocked-in session to the codebase or knowledge base. During execution, an agent continuously exchanges prompts/responses with a model, and those exchanges trigger tool calls or file side effects. An agent needs to resume a prior conversation later to extend work or ask follow-ups within existing context. During work, an agent discovers a recurring reasoning structure that isn't captured by existing patterns. Before the full proof trail infrastructure exists, we need a way to simulate pattern-based work. FuLab patterns are implementation-level; devmap prototypes are design-level. A change or tool action could impact multiple subsystems or teams. A decision requires trading off speed, correctness, scope, or risk. You want the agent's work to be traceable, auditable, and explicitly linked to the design glossary. You want the proof path to capture compositional reasoning, not just a flat list of events. You want the session to end in a way that can be validated against the original intent, producing a sealable proof path. You want every commit to trace back to the design authorization and proof path that produced it. You want the experiment notebook to grow in real time rather than be reconstructed afterward. You want multi-turn conversations with traceable continuity. You want the pattern library to evolve based on lived practice, not just top-down design. You want to dogfood the pattern architecture while building it. You want to track how implementation work advances the higher-level devmap. You want failures to remain localized and diagnosable without full rollback. You want later reviewers to understand the decision without re-deriving it. Without an explicit declaration, the link between agent actions and design patterns stays implicit and hard to verify later. If dependencies live only in internal thought and are not recorded, you cannot reconstruct the structural rationale for why a step is valid. Without a clear ending, the path is often incomplete (missing status, artifacts, dependency summary), making audit and replay difficult. Standard commits record what changed, not why the change was permitted. If records are captured only after the session ends, you lose streaming stats, partial failure states, and mid-session intent shifts. If each call is treated as stateless, the agent cannot reliably carry forward constraints, evidence, and intent changes. Agents cannot unilaterally add patterns to the canonical library. XTDB persistence, MUSN enforcement, and check DSL aren't implemented yet. The connection between fulab patterns and devmap prototypes is implicit. Without a declared blast radius, incident response defaults to broad freezes or guesswork. Hidden trade-offs cause churn when requirements change or audits occur. Before substantive work starts, the agent emits a clock-in event that includes the primary pattern ID, intent description, and session context, declaring the design-authorization source for the session. [fulab/clock-in] @arg fulab/pattern-propose @title Agent Pattern Proposal @sigils [➰/了] [fulab/clock-in, fulab/clock-out, fulab/proof-commit] @arg fulab/devmap-xref @title Devmap Cross-Reference @sigils [➰/本] When an agent uses P2 reasoning in a P1 session, call the pattern-use API (record-pattern-use!) with a brief reason and optional parent-id; emit a :pattern/used event that declares the dependency edge. Before ending the session, the agent emits a clock-out event including the primary pattern, full dependency trail summary, completion status, and list of produced or modified artifacts. Record a proof-commit envelope (session-id, pattern trail, validation results) using the template and store it in the trail log until the commit gate is wired. Define a canonical notebook cell record (input/output, metadata, side effects) and use the template for manual capture until live streaming is wired. Maintain a runtime registry mapping futon session-id to the external fucodex CLI session identifier; resume requests use that identifier (e.g., `--resume`) to continue the conversation, and a new session-id references the ancestor session to preserve audit continuity. The agent records a pattern-proposal draft using the proposal template and claim event, with a draft IF/HOWEVER/THEN/BECAUSE structure and supporting trail evidence. Human stewards review proposals and promote to :accepted. Maintain a changelog file (e.g., fulab-changelog.org) where each entry explicitly records: clocked-in pattern, pattern dependencies used, artifacts produced, and clock-out summary. This serves as a human-readable proof trail. Record optional :pattern-ref metadata for fulab patterns and surface it in HUD summaries; treat missing refs as gaps until validation is enforced. Capture a blast-radius record before risky actions, naming affected surfaces, rollback scope, and detection signals; enforcement is pending. Capture a tradeoff record listing options considered, assumptions, chosen rationale, and reversal triggers; enforcement is pending. The clock-in event creates a non-optional anchor for the proof path, so later actions can be evaluated against the declared intent. - evidence: src/f2/claude.clj - clock-in-event records :clock-in/session-id for audit linkage. - Check that every side-effecting event traces back to a prior clock-in; treat any side effect without clock-in as a violation.

title: Agent Clock-Out
text: Agent Clock-Out Clock out by leaving a reconstructable trail from clock-in through dependencies and artifacts so the session can be audited and resumed without guesswork. - Verify that the clock-out pattern trail can be reconstructed from the session's clock-in + pattern-dep events; confirm artifacts match the actual change set.

title: Live Notebook Cell
text: Live Notebook Cell Treat each live notebook cell as a traceable proof event whose side effects can be compared against the actual session history. - Wire real-time cell capture into the session event pipeline. - Sample-compare cell side effects with actual system events (file changes, command logs); test whether cells can reconstruct a simplified proof path.

title: Pattern Dependency Declaration
text: Pattern Dependency Declaration Declare pattern dependencies explicitly so each session's proof path can be checked for cycles and justified against trace evidence. - Run DAG checks on dependency graphs per session (no cycles); sample dependency edges to confirm the reason is supported in cell/trace evidence. - Capture dependency reasons with channel tags (e.g., code/doc/test) so audits can map dependencies back to evidence inputs (align with aif/term-to-channel-traceability).

title: Proof-Conformant Commit
text: Proof-Conformant Commit Allow commits only when they conform to a verified proof path, so repository history reflects validated reasoning rather than ungrounded drift. - Implement the MUSN commit gate that rejects commits without a verified proof path. - Define a minimal validation rule set (existence, structure, correspondence); record failure types on each rejection to tune constraint strictness.

title: Session Resume
text: Session Resume Resume a session by extending the existing proof-path lineage rather than spawning a disconnected branch of work. - Define whether resume allows switching the primary pattern key; test that the proof path ancestor chain remains consistently reconstructable after multiple resumes. - Port the resume mapping to f2/claude for parity with fucodex. - Require proposals to cite at least one supporting trail event and record reviewer notes on accept/reject outcomes.

title: Trade-off Record
text: Trade-off Record Require an explicit trade-off record whenever scope or risk shifts so decisions remain auditable instead of dissolving into tacit judgment. - Require at least one tradeoff-record when a scope or risk change is accepted.

title: Agent Contract
text: Agent Contract Every agent operating in the FUTON stack must follow the agent contract: clock in, observe before acting, attribute all changes, respect invariants, and clock out with a proof trail. Agents (human or AI) interact with futon systems. The contract ensures that all agents produce auditable, attributable work that respects system invariants. Agents that violate the contract produce unverifiable changes. The applicability scope of the pattern (see substructure). - Human agents: Follow contract via tools (CLI, IDE integration) - AI agents: Follow contract via prompts and guardrails - Automated agents: Follow contract via code structure 1. CLOCK-IN/CLOCK-OUT: - Every session explicitly starts and ends - Session ID assigned at clock-in - Duration and outcome recorded at clock-out 2. OBSERVE-BEFORE-ACT: - Read state before proposing changes - Log observations as evidence - Never apply changes without observation phase 3. ATTRIBUTE-ALL-CHANGES: - Every change linked to agent identity - No anonymous mutations - Changes reference the observation that motivated them 4. RESPECT-INVARIANTS: - Check invariants before commit - On violation: stop-the-line, do not force through - Report invariant failures, do not hide them 5. PRODUCE-PROOF: - Every committed change has evidence chain - Proof path is replayable - Failed attempts also logged (for learning) The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - Anonymous change: Mutation without agent attribution - Blind change: Mutation without observation - Forced commit: Pushing through invariant violation - Ghost session: Changes without clock-in/clock-out Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. - Session middleware rejects unclocked changes - Commit hooks verify agent attribution - Invariant checks block non-compliant commits - Audit logs flag contract violations Unattributed changes are unauditable. Unobserved changes are reckless. Forced commits corrupt the system. The contract ensures that every agent, regardless of type, produces trustworthy work. next[Implement contract enforcement middleware] next[Add contract violation detection to PAR analysis]

title: All-or-Nothing Integrity (Invariant 2)
text: All-or-Nothing Integrity (Invariant 2) I2: Startup succeeds completely or fails loudly. Startup succeeds completely or fails loudly. Rehydration loads all entities or throws. No silent stubs, no partial loads. Failure reports exactly what failed and why. A system that boots with partial data is worse than one that refuses to boot. Partial state creates subtle bugs that surface hours later, far from their cause. Integrity means: whole and consistent, or not. The applicability scope of the pattern (see substructure). - Rehydration loads all entities or throws - No silent stubs, no placeholder values - No partial loads, no "best effort" recovery - Failure reports: what entity, what field, what was expected, what found - Relations verified to have valid endpoints The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). Corrupt entity -> 500 ENTITY_CORRUPT (details: entity-id, field, error) Dangling relation -> 500 DANGLING_REFERENCE (details: relation-id, missing-target) Schema mismatch -> 500 SCHEMA_MISMATCH (details: entity-id, expected, found) - Loading what we can, logging warnings for the rest - Creating stub entities for missing references - "Recovering" by skipping corrupt data - Async background rehydration that might fail silently Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. Layer 2 (core/rehydrate.clj) validates on load: - Every entity must deserialize completely - Every relation must reference existing entities - Missing references -> 500 INTEGRITY_VIOLATION with details - Startup blocked until all data validates Hydration needs similar invariants to ingest. You wouldn't rip a CD that didn't have proper 0's and 1's on it. The data must be whole to be trusted. Partial data creates partial truth, which is worse than no data. next[Implement blocking rehydration with validation in futon1a] next[Add relation endpoint verification on startup]

title: Baldwin Cycle
