If only one instance ever surfaces, record it as a special case explicitly — that absence of generalisation is itself a finding. IC-shape-first: For each candidate invariant entering MAP, the mission record contains either (a) a named protocol shape with ≥2 enumerated instances, or (b) an explicit `:special-case true` annotation with reasoning. Drift into MAP without one of these is itself a coherence violation. A candidate invariant arrives in the inventory as a single sentence ("Superseded autostashes do not remain in the live queue once equivalent commits have landed"). Implementing the literal sentence would yield a one-off check tied to a specific artifact-class. But many candidate invariants — especially in `archaeology-control`, `single-boundary`, `family-canary`-shaped families — are *instances of a more general protocol* that admits multiple implementations. Naming the protocol explicitly during IDENTIFY produces a sibling-namespace of invariants rather than a one-off; subsequent missions reuse the shape rather than rederiving it. A mission's IDENTIFY phase names a single candidate invariant and the team is about to move into MAP. Many invariants are not atomic — they are one slice of a protocol that recurs across artifact-classes. If the mission ships only the literal slice, the family stays narrow; the next agent reaching for "obsolescence-recognition for branches" rederives subsumption-test logic from scratch, possibly inconsistently. The pattern of "find the family, then exhibit instances" needs to be a methodological move, not an accidental discovery. - Implementing only the literal sentence of the candidate invariant when an obvious shape generalisation is at hand. Result: narrow, brittle, unreusable. - Inventing "subfamily" as a new structural element when namespace IDs (`shape/instance`) suffice. Result: inventory schema bloat for no semantic gain. - Forcing generalisation on a true special case. Result: phantom siblings that never get implemented and clutter the queue. During IDENTIFY, after naming the candidate invariant: 1. Ask: "what shape is this one instance of?" Write the protocol signature as a check-fn or predicate. 2. Enumerate at least 2-3 plausible instances of the shape. Each should be a named artifact-class with its own subsumption / verification / boundary test. 3. Only progress to MAP if a shape with multiple instances is visible. If only one instance can be named, record this explicitly as `:special-case true` in the mission doc — its absence of generalisation is a finding worth keeping. 4. Adopt namespace IDs (`<shape>/<artifact-class>`) for the sibling invariants. This avoids inventing "subfamily" as a structural element; the existing `family → invariants` shape supports namespace-discriminated siblings naturally. - `archaeology-control/obsolescence-recognition/{autostash,deferred-stub,pipeline-tracer,branch-merged,...}` — shape: subsumption-witness; instances: per-artifact-class. - `single-boundary/{evidence,bell-receipt,agent-registration,gate-traversal,mission-state-transition}` — shape: "all writes of class W traverse one boundary B"; instances: per-write-class. - `family-canary/{agency,tickle,portfolio,substrate-2-phase-1,war-machine-aif}` — shape: "every operational family has a recurrent live-fire signal"; instances: per-family check-fn. - `protocol-family-naming` — how to name the shape - `subsumption-witness` — one concrete shape (used by `archaeology-control/obsolescence-recognition/*`) - `library-coherence/family-as-protocol` — the structural read of inventory families Shape-first IDENTIFY is descriptive of what well-formed invariants look like in the futon stack already — `single-boundary` admits multiple write-class instances, `family-canary` admits multiple per-family check-fn registrations, `evidence-per-turn` admits per-write-source instances. Naming the move makes it repeatable and lets future agents stand on the shape rather than rederive it. It also surfaces special cases: when only one instance exists, that's a discovery worth recording, not a defect to paper over. - evidence: count missions whose IDENTIFY phase named a shape with ≥2 instances vs literal-only; trend over time. - evidence: count namespace-discriminated invariant IDs in `structural-law-inventory.sexp`; trend over time. - tooling: extend mission-lifecycle.md's IDENTIFY guidance with a one-paragraph pointer to this pattern.

title: Single-Locus: Uniqueness of Attribute per Identity
text: Single-Locus: Uniqueness of Attribute per Identity For an identity I and an attribute A, the system carries exactly one record `(I, A) → R`. The shape is uniqueness-of-mapping per (identity, attribute) pair: no two simultaneously-active records may exist for the same (I, A). Each artifact-class is a sibling invariant under the relevant family with namespace ID `single-locus/<artifact-class>`. IC-single-locus: For each registered `single-locus/<class>` sibling, no identity I exists in the live system for which the system carries simultaneous conflicting records `(I, A) → R1` and `(I, A) → R2` with R1 ≠ R2. Violations surface as `:family-fired :outcome :violation` evidence enumerating the offending identities. Many invariants in the futon stack are uniqueness claims: every agent-id resolves to ONE routing entry; every active work item has ONE home repo; every artifact has ONE live copy; every write-class has ONE boundary. These look distinct on the surface (different identities, different attributes, different value spaces) but share a structural shape: cardinality bound = 1 per (I, A) pair. Naming the shape produces a sibling family of invariants and lets check-fns share an enforcement vocabulary instead of being rederived per artifact-class. A class of artifacts has a uniquely-determined attribute (home, owner, canonical version, primary boundary) that the system depends on being unambiguous. Without explicit single-locus discipline, multiple records for the same (I, A) accumulate quietly: two open mission docs claiming to track the same work in different repos; two transport tiers both carrying the same agent-id; two `boundary/append!` aliases both writing to evidence; two branches each claiming to be the "live" branch for a feature. The collision is invisible until cross-record divergence produces downstream confusion. A simple per-attribute check ("does this artifact have a home?") is incomplete — it doesn't bound the OTHER direction (does the home appear ELSEWHERE too?). The shape needs both halves: every artifact has a record AND the record is unique. - **Implicit-only default with no explicit-override path.** An artifact whose home is only ever inferred from its filesystem position can't express deliberate cross-repo work. The `Home-repo:` annotation provides the override; missing it isn't the violation, contradiction is. - **Multiple-record warnings without identity scoping.** "Two records named X exist" is a meaningless message without naming the (I, A) pair the conflict applies to. - **Single-locus as enforcement of zero-cross-repo-references.** Cross-repo references are normal and useful. The invariant is about the AUTHORITATIVE record, not about whether other repos may reference it. - **Auto-fixing on violation.** Single-locus violations often involve substantive operator decisions (which copy is canonical?). Auto-deletion is destructive; surfacing + operator triage is the safe path. Build sibling invariants under the relevant family with namespace IDs of the form `single-locus/<artifact-class>`. Each sibling specifies four components: 1. **Enumerate-I**: produce the current set of identities of this class (e.g. `holes/missions/M-*.md`, `family-check-fns` registry, `git for-each-ref` output, agent-id set). 2. **Project-(I, A)**: for each I, extract A — its claim about the attribute. The projection may be implicit (the artifact's own location IS the answer) or explicit (an annotation in the artifact records it). 3. **Cardinality-test**: for each (I, A), assert |records| ≤ 1 in the system. Violations enumerate (I, A) pairs with multiple R values. 4. **Default-handling**: an artifact carrying no explicit annotation may use an implicit-default (e.g., a mission file's home-repo defaults to its own filesystem repo). Implicit defaults are part of the cardinality-1 set; an explicit annotation overrides without violating, so long as it's the only annotation. Wire each sibling as a probe check-fn through `futon3c.logic.probe/register-family-check!` returning the standard probe-result shape with `:detail {:identities-with-multiple-loci [{:identity :records [...]}]}` on violation. | Sibling | I (identity) | A (attribute) | R (record) | Default for missing record | |---|---|---|---|---| | `single-locus/mission-home` | active mission file path | home-repo | one repo path (annotated `Home-repo:` line OR implicit = mission file's repo) | implicit-home = mission file's own repo | | `single-locus/agent-routing` *(prior op exemplar via futon3/library/agency/single-routing-authority)* | agent-id | routing entry | `{:transport :session-id :handle :registered-at}` | (no default — agents either route or don't exist) | | `single-locus/artifact-live-copy` *(absorbs single-live-copy)* | artifact identity (e.g. tool / pattern / config file) | live copy location | one `<repo>:<path>` | implicit = canonical repo per pattern-library convention | | `single-locus/write-class-boundary` *(equivalent reframe of single-boundary)* | write-class | boundary-fn | one fn-var | (no default — every write-class must have an explicit boundary) | - `shape-first-identify` — the methodological move that produces this shape. - `subsumption-witness` — companion shape (binary witness vs uniqueness count). They coexist in the same family in some cases (e.g. `archaeology-control` carries both subsumption-witness siblings AND would carry single-locus siblings for the artifact-identity slice). - `bounded-disposition` — companion shape (per-artifact triage + bound vs uniqueness). Different obligations. - `protocol-family-naming` — naming convention. - `agency/single-routing-authority` (futon3) — the original-stock pattern that was a single-locus instance ahead of the shape's naming. Backwards-applied here. Single-locus is the right level of abstraction for the stack's many uniqueness claims. The shape is descriptive of patterns ALREADY operational (`agency/single-routing-authority`, `single-boundary` as a write-class single-locus) — naming it makes the move repeatable across new artifact-classes, with shared check-fn vocabulary. The cardinality test is universal; the per-class enumerator and projector are the actual work. - evidence-shape: `{:family-id :keyword :outcome :ok|:violation :detail {:scanned-identities int :violations [{:identity ... :records [...] :class kw}]}}`. - tooling: `Home-repo: <repo>` annotation convention for mission files (parse from front-matter; case-insensitive). - mission: `M-single-locus` (futon3c/holes/missions/) opens with mission-home slice as worked example, with agent-routing + artifact-live-copy as Codex handoffs. - back-application: tag `agency/single-routing-authority` as a prior single-locus exemplar in the futon3 library cross-reference table; no rename of the existing pattern needed, only a flexiarg note.

title: State-Snapshot-Witness: Periodic Point-in-Time Projection as Queryable Evidence
text: State-Snapshot-Witness: Periodic Point-in-Time Projection as Queryable Evidence For each long-lived runtime state container worth observing over time, the system periodically records a point-in-time projection of its full state as an evidence entry of shape `:event :state-snapshot` (or namespace-discriminated subtype). The snapshot is queryable after the fact, lets time-travel reconstruction work, and gives the apparatus a per-cycle witness of "what was true at boot N" without bespoke logging per inspectable subsystem. IC-state-snapshot-witness: For each registered `state-snapshot-witness/<container>` sibling, the durable evidence store carries at least one `:event :state-snapshot` (or namespaced subtype) entry per JVM boot, containing the full projection of the container's state at boot time. Reconstructing past state never requires evidence-aggregation gymnastics; one query returns one snapshot. The futon3c apparatus emits `:family-fired` evidence per family per probe sweep, carrying per-family `:detail`. Useful for "did family X fire just now?" but useless for "what was the operational-families inventory yesterday?" The Evidence Landscape stores per-event observations, not full-state snapshots. Reconstructing the inventory's state at a past moment requires walking every operational family's history and inferring; it isn't directly queryable. State-snapshot-witness fills that gap with one evidence entry per cycle that contains the full state projection. A long-lived state container's history is operationally meaningful (you'd want to ask "what was X at time T?" and have a direct answer). Existing per-event evidence (`:family-fired`, `:family-demoted`, `:pipeline-tracer-item`) records *deltas* and *individual checks*, not full-state. Reconstructing state at a past moment requires aggregating deltas, which loses precision when intermediate state isn't recorded. A snapshot evidence entry is direct: the entry's body contains the full state at the snapshot moment. A naive "log the state at every event" approach is wasteful (most events don't change state meaningfully). A naive "log the state never" approach is opaque. The right shape is periodic snapshots at construction time (boot) and on operator demand, with deltas in between. - **Snapshotting inside per-event evidence.** Wastes storage; confuses the deltas/state distinction. Snapshots are their own event type. - **Snapshotting volatile state without filtering.** A snapshot of a counter that increments per second is not a snapshot, it's noise. Project to semantically-meaningful state only. - **Per-tick snapshots without cadence discipline.** Hourly+boot+on-demand is enough for most containers; per-second wastes XTDB. - **Per-event computed snapshot.** Some apparatus emit a "snapshot" alongside every event-fire. Defeats the cycle-boundary purpose. Snapshots are timed, not event-coupled. Build sibling invariants under the relevant family with namespace IDs of the form `state-snapshot-witness/<container>`. Each sibling specifies four components: 1. **Container** — what long-lived state is being snapshotted (e.g. structural-law-inventory.sexp parsed; family-check-fns registry; git refs for ~/code/futon* repos; HUD widget last-render). 2. **Projection-fn** — `(fn [container]) → snapshot-data`. Produces a flat, EDN-serialisable map. Drops noisy fields; keeps semantically-meaningful state. 3. **Cadence** — at minimum boot-time (reachable-from-boot discipline) and on-demand. Optionally periodic via the canary apparatus. 4. **Emit-fn** — `(emit-snapshot! evidence-store snapshot-data)` writes one evidence entry through the boundary, tagged `[:invariant-queue :state-snapshot <container-id>]` with `:event :state-snapshot` (or namespaced subtype `:event :inventory-snapshot` etc.) carrying the full projection in `:body`. Wire each sibling at boot via `bootstrap.clj` (reachable-from-boot discipline — snapshot creation belongs in the construction path). Operator-on-demand variants live as `(snapshot-X-now! evidence-store)`. | Sibling | Container | Projection-fn | |---|---|---| | `state-snapshot-witness/inventory` | structural-law-inventory.sexp parsed | flatten families + scope-stack invariants to `[{:family-id :status :siblings [{:invariant-id :status :implemented-in}]}]` | | `state-snapshot-witness/registry` | `@futon3c.logic.probe/family-check-fns` | `(keys @registry)` plus per-family deferred?-flag | | `state-snapshot-witness/repo-refs` | `~/code/futon*/.git/HEAD` + active-branch | `[{:repo :branch :HEAD-sha :ahead-of-origin}]` | | `state-snapshot-witness/hud-render` | last HUD widget render | `{:widget-id :rendered-at :counts :motion-flag}` | - `shape-first-identify` — methodological move that produces this shape. - `reachable-from-boot` — companion shape: snapshot creation belongs in the construction path. The two compose: snapshots ARE the structural witness that boot-time-construction worked. - `family-canary` — adjacent: per-family-fire evidence is the delta; the snapshot is the cycle-boundary state. Together they reconstruct full history. State-snapshot-witness is the right shape for any state whose history matters. The shape complements the per-event evidence the apparatus already emits — together, snapshots-at-cycle-boundaries + deltas-between-cycles give reconstructible full history. The shape is also recursive: the apparatus's own state (families registered, probes active, tracers open) is exactly the kind of state worth snapshotting. The first sibling (inventory snapshot) ships this self-witness. - mission: `M-state-snapshot-witness` (futon3c/holes/missions/) opens with inventory-snapshot as worked example; remaining siblings handed to Codex. - tooling: snapshot evidence shape standardised — `:event :state-snapshot` body has `:container :state :emitted-at :probe-run-id?`. - integration: HUD widget extension — render last-snapshot timestamps as part of the canary fires section. - resolution: closes `track-4-2-snapshot-as-evidence` (tracer #4.2) — the original ask is satisfied by `:event :inventory-snapshot` and a worked first-sibling implementation.

title: Subsumption-Witness: A is Obsolete Relative to a Stronger Record P
text: Subsumption-Witness: A is Obsolete Relative to a Stronger Record P A latent artifact A is obsolete relative to a stronger record P when A's information content is subsumed by P, and A occupies a parallel/transient position while P is in the canonical/durable position. The subsumption test is per-artifact-class; the shape (A vs P, witnessed by a subsumption predicate) is universal. Each artifact-class is a sibling invariant under family `archaeology-control` with namespace ID `obsolescence-recognition/<artifact-class>`. IC-subsumption: For each registered `obsolescence-recognition/<class>` sibling, the live system carries no artifact of class `<class>` whose content is subsumed by a canonical record. Violations surface as `:family-fired :outcome :violation` evidence with the obsolete artifacts enumerated. The futon stack accumulates latent-work artifacts: git stashes after `pull --rebase --autostash`, deferred-stub probe registrations, open branches with cherry-picked commits, `.skip` markers on now-passing tests, `TODO: remove once X` comments where X has happened, pipeline-tracer items whose target work has landed but the close emit was never made. Each is invisible operational debt — present on disk, invisible in normal operation, occasionally rediscovered as confusion or duplicated work. Manual cleanup tools exist (e.g. `futon0/scripts/futon-sync.clj park`) but only run when an operator gets around to it. The invariant form converts "true when Joe gets around to cleaning up" into "the system continuously knows when it's not true." You need to bound the accumulation of a class of latent-work artifacts and the stronger-record exists in a canonical position you can compare against. The subsumption test is fundamentally per-artifact-class — there is no universal `is-obsolete?` predicate. Each artifact-class needs: - **A** — a way to enumerate latent artifacts of this class - **P** — what the canonical/durable record is - **subsumption test** — `is-A-subsumed-by-P?(artifact, record)` returning bool Trying to wrap them under one check-fn produces a god-function; trying to keep them separate without a shared shape produces inconsistent semantics across siblings. - Building a single `is-obsolete?` god-function. Each artifact-class needs its own subsumption test; pretending otherwise hides class-specific edge cases. - Conflating detection with cleanup. The probe is read-only; cleanup is destructive and stays operator-driven (`futon-sync.clj`, etc.). - Auto-running a destructive sweeper on detection. Race conditions; loss of operator judgement on edge cases. - Adding "subfamily" as a structural element. Namespace IDs (`shape/instance`) suffice. Build sibling invariants under family `archaeology-control` with namespace IDs of the form `obsolescence-recognition/<artifact-class>`. Each sibling implements three components: 1. **Enumerate-A**: produce the current set of latent artifacts of this class (e.g. `git stash list`, registry of deferred-stub families, set of open branches). 2. **Locate-P**: for each A, find the canonical record P that might subsume it (e.g. the commit graph reachable from HEAD; the live `family-check-fns` registry; the merged-PR list). 3. **Subsumption-test**: a predicate `(is-obsolete? A P)` that returns true when A's content is fully present in P. Wire each sibling as a probe check-fn through `futon3c.logic.probe/register-family-check!`, returning `:outcome :ok` (no obsolete artifacts) or `:outcome :violation :detail {:obsolete-artifacts [...]}`. The probe-canary apparatus (M-invariant-queue-unstuck) already surfaces these via `:family-fired` evidence, the HUD widget, and the operational-families view. Provide a strong-mode binding (pre-commit hook) for at least one sibling — the autostash slice is the natural one — to give a real computational guarantee: a commit that would leave obsolete artifacts behind is refused. | Sibling | A (artifact) | P (record) | Subsumption test | |---|---|---|---| | `obsolescence-recognition/autostash` | `git stash list` | reachable from HEAD | `git stash show -p N \| git apply --reverse --check` clean | | `obsolescence-recognition/deferred-stub` | `register-deferred-taps!` registrations | live `family-check-fns` | `(get @family-check-fns family-id)` returns non-deferred fn | | `obsolescence-recognition/pipeline-tracer` | open `:pipeline-tracer-item` | `:pipeline-tracer-closed` evidence | matching close-emit exists for `:track-id` | | `obsolescence-recognition/branch-merged` | `git for-each-ref refs/heads` | merged PRs / cherry-picked commits | `git cherry main <branch>` empty AND `gh pr list --state merged` includes branch | | `obsolescence-recognition/test-skip` | `.skip` markers in test files | passing-test set | run with skip removed; passes? | | `obsolescence-recognition/conditional-todo` | `TODO: remove once X` | grep / state of X | X-clause grep-checkable; X currently true? | | `obsolescence-recognition/dead-shim` | `// removed-X` aliases / shims | usage grep | zero usages outside the shim itself | - `shape-first-identify` — the methodological move that produces this shape - `code-coherence/dead-code-hygiene` — adjacent (cleanup of dead code) but operator-scheduled rather than continuously-bound - `library-coherence/family-as-protocol` — the structural read Subsumption-witness is the right level of abstraction for the entire `archaeology-control` family. It is a special case of `shape-first-identify`: the family name (`archaeology-control`, "Latent work should not accumulate as invisible operational debt") is the shape; the subsumption predicate is the protocol; each artifact-class is an implementation. Namespace-discriminated siblings give discovery, dogfood, and computational guarantee without inventing new structural elements in the inventory. - evidence: count of registered `obsolescence-recognition/*` siblings; trend. - evidence: per-sibling, count of obsolete artifacts detected per run; trend. - tooling: `M-archaeology-control` mission (futon3c/holes/missions/) scopes the first three siblings (autostash, deferred-stub, pipeline-tracer). - evidence-shape: `{:family-id :keyword, :outcome :ok|:violation, :detail {:obsolete-artifacts [{:class :keyword, :id :string, :superseded-by :string} ...]}}`.

title: Mundane Right Action: Refraining from Killing, Stealing, Sexual Misconduct
text: Mundane Right Action: Refraining from Killing, Stealing, Sexual Misconduct Refrain from killing living creatures, from taking what is not given, and from sexual misconduct — abstaining from the three forms of bodily misconduct. This operates in all situations involving bodily action — how we treat other living beings, how we relate to resources, how we engage in intimate relationships. - Refraining from killing: not intentionally harming living beings - Refraining from stealing: not taking what is not given - Refraining from sexual misconduct: not violating relational boundaries Less harm, more trust, cleaner relationships — but still within the world of actors and acted-upon, still attached to being one who refrains. Bodily actions create the most direct and often irreversible consequences. Harm done physically is harder to undo than harm done verbally or mentally. External compliance without inner transformation is fragile. And "being good" can become performance or suppression. The problem is not acting but acting from craving or aversion. Wrong action: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct Mundane right action: refraining from these three — AND awareness that the refraining itself can be grasped Practice the three refrainings: from killing (harming living beings), from stealing (taking what isn't freely given), from sexual misconduct (violating relational boundaries and trust). This is the content of mundane right action. Mundane right action creates conditions for safety, trust, and respect. But one can refrain from wrong action while still attached to being a "good person" or to the social status that moral conduct confers. This is better than wrong action but not yet liberation. - Notice the subtler forms: carelessness with beings, casual taking, boundary-blurring. - Track how bodily conduct shapes relationships and environments over time. - Ask: is this action reversible? does it preserve future options?

title: Mundane Right Concentration: The Four Jhanas
text: Mundane Right Concentration: The Four Jhanas Develop unified concentration through the four jhanas — progressively deeper states of absorption characterized by joy, ease, equanimity, and refined awareness. This operates in formal practice where attention becomes stable enough to rest without distraction. Concentration provides the platform for insight. - First jhana: seclusion from hindrances, joy and ease arise - Second jhana: thought subsides, concentration deepens - Third jhana: joy fades, equanimous ease remains - Fourth jhana: pure equanimity, refined mindfulness Deep peace, refined awareness, powerful platform for insight — but if disconnected from the other factors, leads only to refined rebirth, not liberation. The scattered mind cannot see clearly — too fragmented, too reactive, too caught up in proliferation. Some degree of stability is prerequisite for wisdom. Concentration states can become ends in themselves — blissful resting places that don't lead to liberation. And attachment to jhana can become subtle spiritual materialism. The problem is not concentration but concentration disconnected from wisdom. Wrong concentration: absorption that reinforces defilement or doesn't lead anywhere Mundane right concentration: four jhanas — AND awareness that the states can be grasped Develop the four jhanas: (1) first jhana with applied and sustained thought, joy and ease born of seclusion, (2) second jhana with joy and ease born of concentration, internal clarity, (3) third jhana with equanimous ease, mindful awareness, (4) fourth jhana with pure equanimity and mindfulness, neither pleasure nor pain. Mundane right concentration creates conditions for clear seeing — the stable, unified mind can investigate experience without being swept away. But one can attain jhana while still attached to the states themselves, to being a "jhana attainer," to the bliss and refinement. This is better than wrong concentration but not yet liberation — it leads to rebirth in Brahma realms, not to nibbana. - Establish the prerequisites: ethics, contentment, sense restraint, clear comprehension, mindfulness. - Learn to recognize and stabilize each jhana factor. - Use concentration as platform for investigation, not as final goal.

title: Mundane Right Effort: The Four Great Strivings
text: Mundane Right Effort: The Four Great Strivings Apply the four right efforts — preventing unarisen unwholesome states, abandoning arisen unwholesome states, cultivating unarisen wholesome states, maintaining arisen wholesome states. This operates in the ongoing work of mental cultivation. Progress requires sustained energy applied in the right directions — neither burning out nor stagnating. - Preventing: noticing conditions that give rise to unwholesome, not creating them - Abandoning: when unwholesome arises, not feeding it, letting it pass - Developing: creating conditions for wholesome to arise - Maintaining: when wholesome is present, sustaining the conditions Mental clarity, reduced reactivity, more capacity for concentration — but still within the world of practitioners and practice, still attached to progress. The mind tends toward habit-patterns. Without deliberate effort, unwholesome states proliferate and wholesome states decay. Change requires energy. Effort can become striving — tight, driven, exhausting. And effort toward "being good" can itself become attachment. The problem is not effort but misdirected or grasping effort. Wrong effort: effort toward sensuality, ill will, cruelty; or no effort at all Mundane right effort: four right efforts — AND awareness that the effort itself can be grasped Practice the four right efforts: (1) prevent unwholesome states not yet arisen, (2) abandon unwholesome states already arisen, (3) develop wholesome states not yet arisen, (4) maintain wholesome states already arisen. This is the content of mundane right effort. Mundane right effort creates conditions for mental transformation — without effort, change doesn't happen. But one can apply effort while still attached to progress, to being a "good practitioner," to achieving states. This is better than wrong effort but not yet liberation. - Notice which of the four is most needed now: preventing, abandoning, developing, maintaining? - Track when effort becomes striving or when relaxation becomes slackness. - Calibrate effort to conditions rather than to ambition.

title: Mundane Right Intention: Renunciation, Good Will, Harmlessness
text: Mundane Right Intention: Renunciation, Good Will, Harmlessness Cultivate thoughts of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness — replacing thoughts of sensuality, malice, and cruelty with their opposites. This operates in the stream of thought, where mental formations shape perception and action. The quality of intention determines the direction of the path. - Renunciation: letting go of what doesn't serve - Good will: wishing well for others, including difficult others - Harmlessness: refraining from cruelty even in thought Less conflict, less suffering caused, more capacity for generosity — but still within the world of intentions, still attached to being well-intentioned. The mind generates intentions constantly — some toward grasping, some toward ill will, some toward harm. These shape what we notice, how we interpret, what we do. Merely suppressing wrong intentions doesn't transform them. And "good" intentions can still involve subtle attachment — wanting to be seen as good, grasping at renunciation itself. Wrong intention: sensuality (grasping pleasure), malice (wishing harm), cruelty (enjoying others' suffering) Mundane right intention: renunciation, good will, harmlessness — AND awareness that these too can be grasped Cultivate the three right intentions: renunciation (releasing grasping, not acquiring more), good will (genuine wish for others' welfare), harmlessness (refraining from cruelty in thought). These are content-level intentions that redirect the stream. Mundane right intention is not wrong — it genuinely redirects mental activity away from harmful patterns. But it still involves identification with the intender and attachment to having good intentions. This is better than wrong intention but not yet liberation. - Notice the quality of current intentions: grasping or releasing? - When malice arises, cultivate good will for that being specifically. - Track how intention-quality affects subsequent perception and action.

title: Mundane Right Livelihood: Giving Up Wrong Livelihood
text: Mundane Right Livelihood: Giving Up Wrong Livelihood Give up wrong livelihood and earn a living by right livelihood — avoiding fawning, flattery, hinting, belittling, and using material things to chase after more. This operates at the level of sustained patterns of material support — how one maintains physical life over time. Livelihood shapes daily activity more than any single action. - Not trading in weapons, living creatures, meat, intoxicants, poison - Not using manipulation, flattery, or scheming to obtain support - Earning support through means that don't inherently involve harm Cleaner conscience, less complicity in harm, better material conditions for practice — but still within the world of earning and consuming, still attached to security. Everyone needs material support, but many ways of obtaining it involve harm: trading in weapons, living creatures, meat, intoxicants, poison; or subtler corruptions like flattery and manipulation. Livelihood is constrained by circumstances — not everyone has equal access to "pure" ways of living. And renouncing all livelihood is only possible within specific institutional structures. The problem is not having needs but meeting them through harm. Wrong livelihood: trades in harm, manipulates for gain Mundane right livelihood: avoids these — AND awareness that the ethical identity can become attachment Practice right livelihood by avoiding: trade in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants, in poison. For monastics: avoiding fawning, flattery, hinting, belittling, and using material things to chase material things. Earn support through skillful means. Mundane right livelihood creates conditions for ethical life — if your living depends on harm, every day deepens complicity. But one can practice right livelihood while still attached to the identity of being "ethical" or to the security that ethical reputation provides. This is better than wrong livelihood but not yet liberation. - Audit current livelihood: what harms does it depend on? - Notice when livelihood-anxieties drive compromises. - Explore whether livelihood can shift toward less-harmful forms.

title: Mundane Right Mindfulness: The Four Foundations
text: Mundane Right Mindfulness: The Four Foundations Establish mindfulness on the four foundations — body, feelings, mind, and phenomena — with clear comprehension, free from craving and aversion toward the world. This operates in the moment-to-moment awareness of experience. Mindfulness is the capacity to be present with what is happening without being swept away by it. - Body: sustained attention to bodily experience as it is - Feelings: recognizing the tone of experience (pleasant/unpleasant/neutral) - Mind: knowing the current state of the mind - Phenomena: recognizing patterns arising and passing Reduced reactivity, clearer seeing, more choice in response — but still within the world of meditators and meditation, still attached to states. Experience flows constantly but attention is usually captured by interpretation, reaction, or distraction. Without mindfulness, patterns run automatically. "Practicing mindfulness" can become another thing to do, another identity to construct, another way to feel good about oneself. The problem is not awareness but awareness that has become self-conscious project. Wrong mindfulness: attention captured by craving, directed toward harmful ends Mundane right mindfulness: four foundations — AND awareness that the practice itself can be grasped Practice the four foundations: (1) mindfulness of body (breathing, postures, activities, parts, elements, decay), (2) mindfulness of feelings (pleasant, unpleasant, neutral), (3) mindfulness of mind (contracted/expanded, concentrated/scattered, liberated/not), (4) mindfulness of phenomena (hindrances, aggregates, sense bases, awakening factors, truths). Mundane right mindfulness creates conditions for seeing clearly — without awareness of what's happening, wisdom has no material to work with. But one can practice mindfulness while still attached to "being mindful," to the calm that comes from attention, to progress in practice. This is better than wrong mindfulness but not yet liberation. - Establish regular practice of the foundations, beginning with body. - Notice when mindfulness becomes "trying to be mindful." - Let attention rest in experience without commentary.

title: Mundane Right Speech: Refraining from False, Divisive, Harsh, Idle Talk
text: Mundane Right Speech: Refraining from False, Divisive, Harsh, Idle Talk Refrain from lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter — abstaining from the four forms of verbal misconduct. This operates wherever speech shapes relationships and outcomes. Words are not neutral — they create connection or division, clarity or confusion, trust or suspicion. - Refraining from lying: not stating what is known to be false - Refraining from divisive speech: not speaking to create rifts - Refraining from harsh speech: not speaking to wound - Refraining from idle chatter: not wasting shared attention Better relationships, clearer communication, more trust — but still within the world of speakers and listeners, still attached to the outcomes of speech. Speech can harm directly (lies, harsh words) or indirectly (division, distraction). The habit-streams of verbal conduct run deep and often operate unconsciously. Mere silence avoids the issue. And "good speech" can become performance — saying the right things to be seen as righteous. The problem is not speaking but speaking unskillfully. Wrong speech: false, divisive, harsh, nonsensical Mundane right speech: refraining from these four — AND awareness that the refraining itself can be grasped Practice the four refrainings: from lying (what you know to be untrue), from divisive speech (setting people against each other), from harsh speech (words intended to wound), from idle chatter (pointless talk that wastes attention). This is the content of mundane right speech. Mundane right speech creates conditions for trust and clear communication. But one can refrain from wrong speech while still attached to being a "truthful person" or to the power that honest speech confers. This is better than wrong speech but not yet liberation. - Before speaking, check: is it true? is it unifying? is it kind? is it useful? - Notice when speech is driven by craving for approval or fear of conflict. - Track the effects of speech on relationships over time.

title: Mundane Right View: Provisional Explanatory Frames
text: Mundane Right View: Provisional Explanatory Frames Hold explanatory frames provisionally — believing in causation, consequences, and the meaningfulness of action while remaining open to correction. This operates in everyday situations requiring interpretation and decision. One needs working frames to act, but frames that calcify block learning. - Actions have consequences (karma operates) - Some things genuinely help, others harm - Learning from experience is possible - Feedback channels matter - Correction is possible and valuable Better decisions, better relationships, reduced harm — but still within the world of views, still attached to frames that work. Action requires some explanatory frame — you cannot act without some understanding of cause and consequence. Fixed frames block feedback. But abandoning all frames leads to paralysis or nihilism ("nothing matters anyway"). Wrong view: "Nothing matters, no consequences, no learning possible" Mundane right view: "Things matter, consequences real, learning possible — AND I hold this provisionally" Hold working frames: there IS meaning in action, there ARE consequences of conduct, there IS something to learn from feedback. But hold these as instruments, not as certainties that resist revision. Mundane right view is not wrong — it is incomplete. It partakes of good outcomes (better decisions, learning from feedback) but ripens in attachment (to being right, to the frame itself). This is better than wrong view but not yet liberation. - Notice when provisional holding tightens into certainty. - Use frames to act, then check outcomes against expectations. - Revise frames that consistently produce surprising outcomes.

title: Noble Right Action: The Abstaining Faculty Itself
text: Noble Right Action: The Abstaining Faculty Itself Not refraining-from but the desisting itself — the abstaining, abstinence, and refraining from bodily misconduct operating as factor of path in one intent on the undefiled. This operates in one developing the noble path. It is "the desisting, abstaining, abstinence, and refraining from the three kinds of bad bodily conduct" — the faculty of bodily restraint itself, functioning cleanly. Mundane: "I refrain from wrong action" (an I refraining) Noble: The abstaining faculty operating, intent on the undefiled - Not "I don't kill" but non-killing as expression of path - Action that neither grasps at outcomes nor avoids necessary intervention - Bodily conduct transparent to wisdom - Restraint that is not suppression but natural flow Even skilled refraining involves an actor — one who takes credit for not harming, who is proud of not taking. The restraint can become another form of self-construction. Bodily life continues — eating, moving, engaging. The question is whether action flows from identification or from the path functioning. "Right view, right effort, and right mindfulness keep running and circling around right action" — understanding wrong and right action (view), working to abandon wrong and cultivate right (effort), doing so mindfully. "For one of right action, wrong action is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong action are worn away." Noble right action is the abstaining faculty operating in context of the path — desisting, abstaining, abstinence, refraining — as the natural expression of one oriented toward liberation. Not "I don't harm" but non-harming as expression of path. The body acts constantly, but the quality of action differs when it flows from path rather than from craving. Noble right action is not a tighter grip on behavior but a transparency of bodily conduct to path-factors.

title: Noble Right Concentration: Immersion with Vital Conditions
text: Noble Right Concentration: Immersion with Vital Conditions "Unification of mind with these seven factors as prerequisites" — noble right immersion empowered by all path factors working together, leading to realization rather than refined rebirth. This is the culmination of the path — "noble right immersion with its vital conditions and its prerequisites." It is concentration that arises in context of all the other factors and leads to liberation. Mundane: jhana attained, refined states experienced, but disconnected from path-context Noble: "unification of mind with seven factors as prerequisites" — immersion that liberates - Not jhana in isolation but immersion supported by path - Concentration transparent to wisdom - Absorption that leads to insight, not to Brahma realms - The "ten factors" of the arahant: the eight plus right knowledge and right freedom Concentration alone, even deep jhana, does not liberate — it requires the support of all path factors. Without right view, right intention, right conduct, right effort, right mindfulness, immersion leads only to refined states, not to release. This is not a different technique — the four jhanas are the same. What differs is the context: the other seven factors functioning as vital conditions and prerequisites. "For one of right concentration, wrong concentration is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong concentration are worn away." Noble right concentration is "unification of mind with these seven factors as prerequisites" — immersion that is empowered by the whole path and leads to the two additional factors: right knowledge (the wisdom that ends defilements) and right freedom (liberation from rebirth). "Right immersion produces right knowledge. Right knowledge produces right freedom." The trainee has eight factors; the perfected one has ten. Twenty on the side of the skillful, twenty on the side of the unskillful — the ten factors plus the qualities they promote. "This exposition of the teaching on the Great Forty has been rolled forth. And it cannot be rolled back." "Right view comes first." From right view → right intention → right speech → right action → right livelihood → right effort → right mindfulness → right immersion → right knowledge → right freedom. The path is linear AND circular: each factor supports the others.

title: Noble Right Effort: The Striving Faculty Itself
text: Noble Right Effort: The Striving Faculty Itself Not striving-for but the striving faculty operating — energy arising and applying naturally in one intent on the undefiled, without a striver separate from the striving. This operates in one developing the noble path. Right effort functions "to give up wrong X and embrace right X" for each factor — the energetic commitment operating as path-factor. Mundane: "I apply the four efforts" (an I applying) Noble: The striving faculty operating, intent on the undefiled - Not "I am trying hard" but trying happening through one intent on the noble - Energy that neither exhausts through grasping nor dissipates through slackness - Effort transparent to path-factors - The four strivings operating without a striver Even skillful effort involves an efforter — one who takes credit for trying hard, who identifies with progress. Effort can become exhausting when there's someone getting tired. The path requires energy — things don't happen without some activation. The question is whether energy flows from identification or from the path functioning. Right effort is one of the three that run and circle around all the other factors: "Right view, right effort, and right mindfulness" — the effort to give up wrong and embrace right. "For one of right effort, wrong effort is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong effort are worn away." Noble right effort is the striving faculty operating in context of the path — "they make an effort to give up wrong and embrace right" — but the 'they' is transparent, not solid. Effort arising as expression of path, not as personal project. Right effort runs and circles around all the other factors — it is what makes the difference between understanding and doing, between knowing and practicing. Noble right effort is this energetic commitment functioning without an exhaustible efforter.

title: Noble Right Intention: The Thinking Faculty Itself
text: Noble Right Intention: The Thinking Faculty Itself Not particular intentions held but the thinking faculty operating — placing, directing, and embedding of mind in one intent on the undefiled. This operates in one developing the noble path. It is "the thinking, the placing of the mind, thought, planting, implanting, embedding of the mind, verbal process" — the directional faculty itself, not any particular direction. Mundane: "I cultivate renunciation, good will, harmlessness" (still an I cultivating) Noble: The thinking faculty placing and directing, intent on the undefiled - Not "I intend good things" but the placing-capacity operating cleanly - Not attached to outcomes of intention - The "verbal process" (feeds into speech) functioning in wholeness - Intention as factor of path, supporting immersion Even good intentions involve an intender. Renunciation can become grasping at letting go. Good will can become pride in being compassionate. Harmlessness can become aversion to harm. Abandoning all intention is not the answer — action requires direction. The problem is identification with the intender, not intention itself. "Right view, right effort, and right mindfulness keep running and circling around right intention" — understanding wrong and right intention (view), working to abandon wrong and cultivate right (effort), doing so mindfully. "For one of right intention, wrong intention is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong intention are worn away." Noble right intention is the thinking faculty functioning in the context of the path — the capacity to direct attention and shape action, operating free of attachment to any particular direction. "The placing of the mind" itself, not what it's placed upon. Vitakka (thinking, placing) is wider than discursive thought. In deep practice it becomes the directional quality of mind itself — where attention goes, how engagement unfolds. Noble right intention is this directional capacity undefiled.

title: Noble Right Livelihood: The Abstaining Faculty Itself
text: Noble Right Livelihood: The Abstaining Faculty Itself Not avoiding-wrong-livelihood but the desisting itself — the abstaining, abstinence, and refraining from wrong livelihood operating as factor of path in one intent on the undefiled. This operates in one developing the noble path. It is "the desisting, abstaining, abstinence, and refraining from wrong livelihood" — the faculty of livelihood-restraint itself, functioning cleanly. Mundane: "I earn by right livelihood" (an I earning) Noble: The abstaining faculty operating, intent on the undefiled - Not "I don't engage in wrong livelihood" but clean earning as path-expression - Material life that neither grasps at security nor avoids responsibility - Livelihood transparent to wisdom - Work that is offering rather than acquiring Even skillful livelihood involves an earner — one who takes credit for ethical earning, who is proud of avoiding harmful trades. The ethical livelihood can become another source of identity. Material life continues — the question is whether livelihood flows from identification with security or from the path functioning. "Right view, right effort, and right mindfulness keep running and circling around right livelihood" — understanding wrong and right livelihood (view), working to abandon wrong and cultivate right (effort), doing so mindfully. "For one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong livelihood are worn away." Noble right livelihood is the abstaining faculty operating in context of the path — the natural refraining from wrong livelihood that arises when one is oriented toward liberation rather than security. Not "I earn ethically" but ethical earning as expression of path. This is the last factor described as encompassed by right view, effort, and mindfulness. The final three (effort, mindfulness, concentration) are self-evidently involved. Livelihood is the most sustained form of action — it shapes daily life hour by hour. When this sustained pattern becomes transparent to path-factors, everyday activity becomes practice.

title: Noble Right Mindfulness: The Mindfulness Faculty Itself
text: Noble Right Mindfulness: The Mindfulness Faculty Itself Not practicing-mindfulness but the mindfulness faculty operating — "mindfully they give up wrong and take up right" in one intent on the undefiled. This operates in one developing the noble path. Mindfulness functions to monitor and guide the giving up of wrong and taking up of right — the awareness that allows course-correction. Mundane: "I practice the four foundations" (an I practicing) Noble: The mindfulness faculty operating, intent on the undefiled - Not "I am being mindful" but mindfulness happening through one intent on the noble - Awareness that neither grasps at clarity nor avoids confusion - Monitoring transparent to path-factors - The four foundations operating without a meditator Even skillful mindfulness involves a meditator — one who takes credit for attention, who is proud of presence. Mindfulness can become another identity-project. Awareness continues — the question is whether it flows from identification or from the path functioning. Right mindfulness is one of the three that run and circle around all the other factors: "Right view, right effort, and right mindfulness" — the mindful giving up of wrong and taking up of right. "For one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong mindfulness are worn away." Noble right mindfulness is the awareness faculty operating in context of the path — "mindfully they give up wrong and take up right" — but the 'they' is transparent. Awareness arising as expression of path, not as personal accomplishment. Right mindfulness runs and circles around all the other factors — it is what allows each factor to be practiced with clarity rather than blindly. Noble right mindfulness is this monitoring awareness functioning without a monitor separate from the awareness.

title: Noble Right Speech: The Abstaining Faculty Itself
text: Noble Right Speech: The Abstaining Faculty Itself Not refraining-from but the desisting itself — the abstaining, abstinence, and refraining operating as factor of path in one intent on the undefiled. This operates in one developing the noble path. It is "the desisting, abstaining, abstinence, and refraining from the four kinds of bad verbal conduct" — the faculty of verbal restraint itself, functioning cleanly. Mundane: "I refrain from wrong speech" (an I refraining) Noble: The abstaining faculty operating, intent on the undefiled - Not "I don't lie" but non-lying as expression of path - Speech that neither grasps at being heard nor avoids necessary communication - The verbal process transparent to path-factors - Abstaining that is not effortful but natural Even skilled refraining involves an abstainer — one who takes credit for not lying, who is proud of not being divisive. The refraining can become another form of self-construction. Speech continues — the question is whether it flows from identification or from the path functioning. What changes is not the content but the quality. "Right view, right effort, and right mindfulness keep running and circling around right speech" — understanding wrong and right speech (view), working to abandon wrong and cultivate right (effort), doing so mindfully. "For one of right speech, wrong speech is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong speech are worn away." Noble right speech is the abstaining faculty operating in context of the path — desisting, abstaining, abstinence, refraining — as the natural expression of one oriented toward liberation. Not "I refrain" but refraining happening through one intent on the noble. The synonyms pile up (ārati, virati, paṭivirati, veramaṇī) to indicate the faculty from multiple angles, not the act of any actor. This is the verbal-conduct-shaping capacity operating without defilement.

title: Noble Right View: The Wisdom Faculty Itself
text: Noble Right View: The Wisdom Faculty Itself Not a view held but the faculty of wisdom operating — the capacity to see clearly, undefiled by attachment to any particular explanation. This operates in one "intent on the noble, intent on the undefiled, who possesses the noble path and develops the noble path." It is not content but the quality of seeing itself. Mundane: "I hold good frames provisionally" (still an I holding) Noble: Wisdom faculty operating, intent on the undefiled - Not "I have the right view" but clear seeing operating - Not frame-holding but frame-releasing while still functioning - Not certainty about content but stability of the faculty - Wisdom functioning in context of the whole path All mundane views, even right ones, still involve clinging — subtle attachment to being correct, to the frame that works, to the comfort of explanation. Abandoning views is itself a view. The problem is not holding explanations but clinging to them. "Right view, right effort, and right mindfulness keep running and circling around right view" — the factors support each other. Noble right view is this mutual support functioning, not a position achieved. "For one of right view, wrong view is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong view are worn away. And because of right view, many skillful qualities are fully developed." Noble right view is not another (better) explanation but the wisdom faculty functioning free of defilement: the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the awakening factor of investigation of principles, right view as a factor of the path — operating in concert with all other factors. Content can always be grasped. What cannot be grasped is the seeing itself. Noble right view is the seeing, not the seen — the capacity to distinguish, not the distinction held.

title: Turn Library Arguments Into Pilots
text: Turn Library Arguments Into Pilots Convert a coherent library argument into a pilot that tests its main claims. You can read the library as a plausible argument but you do not yet trust its empirical validity. The argument sounds coherent, yet the claims have not been tested in practice. A persuasive narrative can hide weak assumptions or untested dependencies. Design a pilot that exercises the argument’s main claims end-to-end and capture evidence for each constituent pattern so the argument can be confirmed, revised, or narrowed. Empirical evidence trumps rhetorical flourish for pattern quality, and pilots expose which claims hold under real conditions. - evidence: a pilot plan that lists the argument’s claims and maps each to a measurable test. - evidence: a pilot report that flags at least one claim as confirmed, revised, or rejected. - evidence-shape: {:library :string, :argument :string, :claims [:string], :pilot-plan :string, :evidence [:string], :results {:confirm [:string] :revise [:string] :reject [:string]}}

title: Sigil Embedding Refresh Ritual
text: Sigil Embedding Refresh Ritual bake the refresh into the library workflow: every pattern PR that touches sigils must include regenerated matrices, we track the last refresh timestamp in `pattern_store.edn`, and CI fails when a pattern lacks embeddings; document the ritual in README + scripts You are keeping sigil embeddings in lockstep with the canon. the fake embedding couples every pattern/devmap clause via sigils, giving `check!` its nearest-neighbour hints when new patterns land (or sigils change) we often forget to rerun `clojure -M:sigils`, so `resources/sigils/{index,emoji-adjacency,hanzi-adjacency}` drift from the canon and hints become meaningless bake the refresh into the library workflow: every pattern PR that touches sigils must include regenerated matrices, we track the last refresh timestamp in `pattern_store.edn`, and CI fails when a pattern lacks embeddings; document the ritual in README + scripts similarity results only earn trust when the embedding reflects the latest canon—otherwise Prototype 2 devolves into hand-waving next[Record the last embedding refresh timestamp and enforce it in CI.]

title: Canon Evidence Ledger
text: Canon Evidence Ledger mirror the stack-coherence evidence-ledger practice inside the library: require each pattern entry to list concrete namespaces/docs/tests, add CI checks that fail when fields are blank, and update the ledger whenever new proofs land; store the citations next to the pattern IDs so the `check!` DSL can surface them You are ensuring every pattern claim has auditable, concrete evidence. the pattern store (`resources/pattern_store.edn`) declares which devmap clauses are blocked, in-progress, or done those records drift unless every clause cites verifiable evidence (README sections, namespaces, and tests) that anyone can inspect mirror the stack-coherence evidence-ledger practice inside the library: require each pattern entry to list concrete namespaces/docs/tests, add CI checks that fail when fields are blank, and update the ledger whenever new proofs land; store the citations next to the pattern IDs so the `check!` DSL can surface them a canon without an evidence ledger collapses into lore—dhammavicaya demands that every “ready” claim is backed by published artifacts next[Backfill missing evidence citations for the highest-priority patterns.]

title: Canon ↔ README Sync Ritual
text: Canon ↔ README Sync Ritual run the same sync ritual used on devmaps: diff the pattern store against README anchors, refuse to mark a pattern “ready” until the corresponding section exists (line references + timestamps), and capture the sync status inside the `library-coherence` ledger; when drift is detected, emit follow-up tasks and freeze the affected prototype until docs ship You are keeping README narratives aligned with the pattern canon. the README, devmaps, and pattern canon are supposed to tell the same story about what FUTON3 (and neighbours) actually ship README sections routinely lag behind the pattern store—new handlers or adapters show up in code/tests but never get cited as evidence, so prototypes appear “done” without a published description run the same sync ritual used on devmaps: diff the pattern store against README anchors, refuse to mark a pattern “ready” until the corresponding section exists (line references + timestamps), and capture the sync status inside the `library-coherence` ledger; when drift is detected, emit follow-up tasks and freeze the affected prototype until docs ship the canon exists to keep the public story honest—without README coverage, pattern maturity is impossible to audit next[Add a README-sync checklist entry for the next pattern marked ready.]

title: Canon Staleness Scan
text: Canon Staleness Scan schedule a staleness scan over every library source: compare file mtimes vs. last ledger update, diff sigils across devmaps, and record drift as `:status :drifting` until someone reruns `clojure -M:sigils` + the check DSL; surface the scan results in CI and refuse to publish embeddings when drift persists You are preventing stale sigils and proofs from silently drifting in the canon. flexiarg directories constantly evolve (devmap-coherence, stack-coherence, repository-transition, etc.) and feed the shared pattern store once a pattern lands in the canon we rarely revisit it; sigils, embeddings, and check fixtures go stale, so later runs cannot tell if a “blocked” clause is drifting or simply unmaintained schedule a staleness scan over every library source: compare file mtimes vs. last ledger update, diff sigils across devmaps, and record drift as `:status :drifting` until someone reruns `clojure -M:sigils` + the check DSL; surface the scan results in CI and refuse to publish embeddings when drift persists library coherence depends on time—not just content—staying aligned; a regular staleness scan keeps the canon trustworthy for downstream futons next[Define the staleness criteria and log the first scan run in the ledger.]

title: Canon Template Discipline
text: Canon Template Discipline enforce a canonical template across every `library/**.flexiarg`: lint for required metadata, forbid renaming the clause markers, and add CI that refuses commits lacking `@sigils`, `@references`, or the standard clause order; every pattern added to `resources/pattern_store.edn` must cite the lint status You are standardising flexiarg structure so tooling can ingest and validate the canon. devmaps and flexiarg libraries already follow a template (meta tags, IF/HOWEVER/THEN/BECAUSE, sigils) new patterns often copy-paste partial headers, omit `@sigils`, or rename clauses, so the store can’t ingest them uniformly enforce a canonical template across every `library/**.flexiarg`: lint for required metadata, forbid renaming the clause markers, and add CI that refuses commits lacking `@sigils`, `@references`, or the standard clause order; every pattern added to `resources/pattern_store.edn` must cite the lint status the canon only works when patterns stay machine-readable—template drift makes the check DSL brittle and the README evidence unverifiable next[Add a lint check that fails when required metadata or clause order is missing.]

title: Assemble Library Arguments via Summary Scan
text: Assemble Library Arguments via Summary Scan Use an LLM to assemble a coherent argument from pattern summaries when library ordering is unclear. You are reviewing a library where patterns should scaffold a coherent argument but the ordering is implicit or missing. The library’s argument exists in fragments across pattern summaries (!conclusion or devmap instantiated-by lines). Readers may not infer the argument without an explicit narrative flow. Use an LLM to scan the summary fields, cluster related claims, order them into a draft argument, and read it back for coherence and gaps. LLMs are strong at structuring and critiquing text, which helps surface missing links and redundancies. - evidence: a generated argument draft that cites the contributing pattern summaries. - evidence: a reviewer note listing at least one missing link or redundancy found by the LLM pass. - evidence-shape: {:library :string, :summaries [:string], :draft-argument :string, :gaps [:string], :redundancies [:string]}

title: Pattern Differentiation Alarms
text: Pattern Differentiation Alarms treat duplicated sigils as alarms: inspect the overlapping clauses, decide whether to merge them, split out a sharper pattern, or introduce a new check canon; document the decision and rerun the embedding cycle You are resolving sigil collisions so similarity checks stay meaningful. the same Tokipona/hanzi sigil pair keeps appearing across multiple devmaps or clauses repetition usually means we lack a specific pattern or haven’t articulated the distinctive obligation treat duplicated sigils as alarms: inspect the overlapping clauses, decide whether to merge them, split out a sharper pattern, or introduce a new check canon; document the decision and rerun the embedding cycle sigils are coordinates in the fake embedding—when they collapse, it signals our pattern library is too coarse for dhammavicaya to stay honest next[Log the next collision and document the merge or split decision.]

title: Integral Vanishes from A.E. Zero Integrand
text: Integral Vanishes from A.E. Zero Integrand Show ∫_A f = 0 when f = 0 a.e. on A via integral_eq_zero_of_ae + filter_upwards. Goal is an integral vanishing over a set where the integrand is a.e. zero. Need to bridge between set membership and ae filtering. Use integral_eq_zero_of_ae with ae_restrict_mem and filter_upwards for the witness. api[integral_eq_zero_of_ae] api[ae_restrict_mem] api[filter_upwards] tactic[exact integral_eq_zero_of_ae → filter_upwards [...] with x hx] The ae_restrict_mem bridge converts "f = 0 on A" to the filter statement Lean needs.

title: Coercion Bridge Between Type Universes
text: Coercion Bridge Between Type Universes When the mathematical proof lives in one type (ℝ) but the Mathlib API operates in another (ℝ≥0∞), wire through the directed coercion chain rather than trying to isomorphism-transport. You have proved a key lemma in ℝ (e.g., a limit, an inequality). The theorem you need to close operates on eLpNorm, which lives in ℝ≥0∞. There is a canonical coercion chain ℝ → ℝ≥0 → ℝ≥0∞ but it is NOT an isomorphism — it loses information at each step (negativity at ℝ→ℝ≥0, finiteness at ℝ≥0→ℝ≥0∞). The informal pattern (transport-across-isomorphism) says "prove in the easy setting and transport." But the coercion chain is not an isomorphism, so transport is not free. The tension: mathematical convenience (work in ℝ) vs API reality (goal is in ℝ≥0∞). The amelioration: make the bridge a named, reusable tactic sequence, not a per-proof ad-hoc construction. Your real-valued result needs to be used in an ENNReal/NNReal context, and the coercion chain applies (the quantities are nonneg and finite). Unlike transport-across-isomorphism, you cannot freely move results back and forth. The coercion is directed. ENNReal.toReal loses ⊤ → 0. NNReal.coe is injective but NNReal.mk requires a proof of nonnegativity. Each step requires an explicit compatibility hypothesis. (a) Prove the core mathematical content in ℝ where the API is richest. (b) Identify the coercion path: which coe/toReal/ofReal lemmas connect your ℝ result to the ℝ≥0∞ goal? (c) For each coercion step, discharge the compatibility side-condition (nonnegativity, finiteness, ne_top). (d) If the bridge is >5 steps, consider whether the lemma can be proved directly in ℝ≥0∞ instead. Sometimes the Mathlib API has a parallel version (e.g., ENNReal.rpow vs Real.rpow) that avoids the bridge. api[ENNReal.ofReal] api[ENNReal.toReal] api[NNReal.coe_le_coe] api[ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal] api[ENNReal.toReal_le_toReal] tactic[rw [ENNReal.ofReal...] → exact ... → simp [ne_top_of_lt]] Lean's type system enforces the distinction between ℝ, ℝ≥0, and ℝ≥0∞ that informal mathematics elides. The coercion bridge is the price of rigour. But the bridge is mechanical — once you know the path, each step is a named lemma (ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal, NNReal.coe_le_coe, ENNReal.toReal_le_toReal). The mathematical insight is in ℝ; the engineering is in the bridge. next[Identify which type the mathematical proof lives in.] next[Map the coercion path to the goal's type.] next[Discharge compatibility side-conditions at each step.] next[If bridge is long, check for a parallel API in the target type.]

title: Complex Polynomial Norm Estimates on Balls
text: Complex Polynomial Norm Estimates on Balls Bound polynomials or analytic functions on disks using Complex.norm_eq_abs + Metric.ball API. Goal involves bounding |f(z)| on a disk or circle in ℂ. Need to carefully distinguish open ball, closed ball, and frontier (sphere). Use Metric.ball/closedBall for the domain, Metric.frontier_ball for the boundary, Complex.norm_eq_abs for the norm. api[Complex.norm_eq_abs] api[Metric.ball] api[Metric.closedBall] api[Polynomial.eval] tactic[have → calc → mul_comm → classical] Mathlib's metric space API provides the topological scaffolding; the complex norm is just abs.

title: Connected Union via Common Point
text: Connected Union via Common Point When proving a union of connected sets sharing a common point is connected, argue by contradiction via open separations. You have a family of connected sets {C_α} and a common point x ∈ ∩ C_α, and you need to show ⋃ C_α is connected. The goal involves IsConnected or IsPreconnected applied to a union, and the hypothesis provides a common point in all components. "Union of connected sets is connected" is false in general — the common point hypothesis is essential. Without it, disjoint connected sets are a trivial counterexample. Use isPreconnected_sUnion from Mathlib. The key step: rewrite the indexed union as a set-indexed union via sUnion_range, then apply the combinator with the common point and individual connectedness. api[isPreconnected_sUnion] api[Set.range] api[Set.not_nonempty_iff] tactic[classical → by_cases → simpa [sUnion_range]] Mathlib's isPreconnected_sUnion handles the separation argument internally — you supply the common point and the per-component connectedness, and it composes the contradiction.

title: Construction Cost Asymmetry
text: Construction Cost Asymmetry When the mathematical insight is trivial but the Lean construction is ~50+ lines of engineering, use witness templates rather than building from scratch each time. The proof requires constructing an explicit mathematical object (a family of functions, a counterexample, a partition of unity). On paper, the construction is "obvious" — tent functions on disjoint intervals, bump functions with prescribed support, etc. In Lean, the construction requires defining the object, proving continuity, verifying bounds, checking support properties, etc. Informal math: "let f_n be tent functions with height 1/n" (1 line). Lean: define f_n, prove Continuous f_n, prove 0 ≤ f_n x, prove support ⊆ I_n, prove sup f_n = 1/n (50+ lines). The asymmetry is intrinsic — Lean demands proofs that paper elides. The amelioration is not to make Lean easier but to make the engineering reusable. The goal is existential (∃ f, P f) or requires producing an explicit mathematical object, and the object belongs to a common family (piecewise-linear, bump, indicator, characteristic function). The Lean engineering cost for common constructions is high because Mathlib provides the *pieces* (Continuous.piecewise, indicator, Set.Icc) but not the *assembled objects* (tent function family on disjoint intervals with prescribed heights). Each proof rebuilds the assembly from scratch. (a) Check if a witness template exists in ApmCanaries/Local/. (b) If not, build the construction once, prove its properties once, and add it to Local/ as a reusable module. (c) Future proofs that need the same construction import it rather than rebuilding. (d) The template becomes a formalization pattern entry — the construction IS the pattern. api[Continuous.piecewise] api[Set.indicator] api[MeasurableSet.indicator] tactic[refine ⟨fun n => ..., ?_, ?_, ?_⟩ → constructor → intro → simp] template[tent function family on disjoint intervals] template[bump function with prescribed support and integral] template[partition of unity subordinate to a cover] template[indicator function of a measurable set] template[piecewise-linear interpolation] The mathematical insight ("use tent functions") is the easy part. The Lean engineering ("define tent, prove continuous, prove nonneg, prove support disjoint, prove height") is the hard part. Amortizing the engineering across problems is the only way to make the 15-minute budget realistic for construction-heavy proofs. next[Identify which common family the witness belongs to.] next[Check ApmCanaries/Local/ for existing templates.] next[If missing, build once, prove once, add to Local/.] next[Future proofs import and instantiate.]

title: Continuous Linear Map Composition Properties
text: Continuous Linear Map Composition Properties Prove properties of composed bounded operators via ContinuousLinearMap API. Goal involves composition of bounded linear operators. Operator composition in Lean is Module.End.mul, not function composition. Use ContinuousLinearMap.comp_apply to unfold, then simp. api[ContinuousLinearMap.comp_apply] tactic[simp [ContinuousLinearMap.comp_apply]] The bundled operator API needs explicit unfolding before standard tactics work.

title: Field Simplification for Reciprocal Goals
text: Field Simplification for Reciprocal Goals Close reciprocal/division identities with field_simp + ne_of_gt for nonzero denominators. Goal involves x * (1/x) = 1 or similar reciprocal cancellation. Lean needs a proof that the denominator is nonzero. Supply ne_of_gt from a positivity hypothesis, then field_simp closes the algebra. api[ne_of_gt] tactic[field_simp → nlinarith] field_simp normalizes all division to a common denominator and cancels.

title: Finite Group Classification and Counterexamples
text: Finite Group Classification and Counterexamples Classify or produce counterexamples for finite groups using Fintype.card and ZMod.card. Goal involves group order, cyclicity, or commutativity of specific finite groups. Abstract group theory lemmas may not compute; need concrete Fintype instances. Use Fintype.card_perm, ZMod.card, IsCyclic.isCommutative, decide tactic. api[Fintype.card] api[ZMod.card] api[IsCyclic.isCommutative] api[Equiv.swap] tactic[decide → exact → classical] Lean's decide tactic closes concrete finite-group goals by computation.

title: Hilbert Space Orthogonal Projection Properties
text: Hilbert Space Orthogonal Projection Properties Prove projection properties (self-adjointness, idempotency, norm-one) via Submodule.starProjection API. Goal involves orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space. Abstract operator theory may be overkill; Mathlib has concrete projection API. Use Submodule.starProjection_apply_mem, starProjection_eq_self_iff, norm_starProjection. api[Submodule.starProjection_apply_mem] api[Submodule.norm_starProjection] tactic[constructor → intro → ext → simp] The starProjection API bundles self-adjointness and idempotency into the definition.

title: Lp Norm Comparison on Finite Measure Spaces
text: Lp Norm Comparison on Finite Measure Spaces Compare ‖f‖_p across exponents on finite measure via eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_mul_rpow_measure_univ. Goal is eLpNorm f p μ ≤ eLpNorm f q μ for p ≤ q on finite measure. The Mathlib lemma has a μ(univ)^{1/p - 1/q} factor that needs simplification. Apply eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_mul_rpow_measure_univ, then simplify μ(univ) (see measure-restrict-simplify). api[eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_mul_rpow_measure_univ] api[le_eLpNorm_of_bddBelow] tactic[have h := eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_mul_rpow_measure_univ → rw [...] → exact h] This is the standard Lp embedding on finite measure spaces.

title: Simplify Restricted Measure on [0,1]
text: Simplify Restricted Measure on [0,1] Collapse μ(univ) for volume.restrict (Icc 0 1) to 1, simplifying rpow and mul terms. Working with eLpNorm or integrals over volume.restrict (Icc 0 1). Lean doesn't auto-simplify μ(univ) = volume(Icc 0 1) = 1. Chain: Measure.restrict_apply → Real.volume_Icc → ofReal_one → one_rpow → mul_one. api[Measure.restrict_apply] api[Real.volume_Icc] api[ENNReal.ofReal_one] api[one_rpow] tactic[rw [...] → rw [...] → exact h] On probability-like spaces, μ(univ) = 1 collapses most comparison lemma outputs.

title: Cauchy Sequence Convergence in Metric Spaces
text: Cauchy Sequence Convergence in Metric Spaces Prove convergence by showing Cauchy via Metric.cauchySeq_iff + triangle inequality chains. Goal is Tendsto or convergence of a sequence in a metric/normed space. Direct epsilon-delta may require long calc chains. Use Metric.cauchySeq_iff to reduce to pairwise distance bounds, then calc + nlinarith. api[Metric.cauchySeq_iff] api[Metric.tendsto_atTop] api[Real.dist_eq] tactic[have → intro → calc → nlinarith → ring] Cauchy in a complete space gives convergence; the iff lemma handles the quantifiers.

title: Limit of t^{1/n} → 1 via Continuity
text: Limit of t^{1/n} → 1 via Continuity Prove t^{1/n} → 1 as n → ∞ by composing Real.continuousAt_const_rpow with 1/n → 0. Goal involves a limit of a^{f(n)} where f(n) → 0 and a > 0. ENNReal rpow continuity is incomplete in Mathlib; must work in ℝ. Use Real.continuousAt_const_rpow (a ≠ 0) composed with tendsto_const_div_atTop_nhds_zero_nat. api[Real.continuousAt_const_rpow] api[Real.rpow_zero] api[tendsto_const_div_atTop_nhds_zero_nat] tactic[have hcont := ... → have hlim := ... → exact hcont.tendsto.comp hlim] Continuity at 0 gives a^0 = 1 as the limit; the composition handles the filter.

title: Continuous Separation Function from Distance
text: Continuous Separation Function from Distance Separate disjoint closed sets by d(x,A)/(d(x,A)+d(x,B)) with empty-set guard. Goal is a continuous [0,1]-valued function separating closed sets. The naive formula has a zero-denominator risk when sets are empty. Guard the empty case (force distance=1), then use Metric.continuous_infDist_pt + Continuous.div. api[Metric.continuous_infDist_pt] api[Metric.infDist_nonneg] api[Continuous.div] tactic[have → exact → simp → ext → classical] Mathlib's infDist API handles the metric computation; you supply the nonvanishing denominator proof.

title: Tactic-Algebra Interference in Rewriting
