text: Tactic-Algebra Interference in Rewriting When an algebraic identity is correct but `rw` disrupts the goal's type structure (filter, Tendsto, Set.mem), use `convert` or `simp_rw` to rewrite within the structure rather than replacing the whole goal. You know the algebraic identity (e.g., ⟨h,h⟩ = ‖h‖²) and the goal is a Tendsto/Filter/Set statement that contains the LHS. Applying `rw` replaces the LHS but may change the goal shape in ways that break subsequent tactic application. Obligation A: rewrite the algebraic term (rw fires correctly). Obligation B: preserve the goal's filter/Tendsto structure for subsequent tactics. These conflict when `rw` changes the goal shape. The constraint-tension-resolution pattern says: name both obligations, find a tactic that satisfies both. `convert` and `simp_rw` are the alternative constructions that dissolve the tension. The goal has the form `Tendsto (fun n => f n) l (𝓝 target)` and you want to rewrite something inside `f n` or `target`, but `rw` at the top level changes the Tendsto structure. `rw` is greedy — it replaces ALL occurrences, including ones inside binders (fun n => ...) where the rewrite may not be valid or may change the function identity. `simp_rw` rewrites under binders safely. `convert` changes the goal and leaves the mismatch as a subgoal. `show` can manually restate the goal in the desired form. (a) If the rewrite is inside a binder (fun n => ...): use `simp_rw`. (b) If the rewrite is in the target (𝓝 value): use `convert` to replace the target and close the algebraic identity separately. (c) If the rewrite is structural (changing Tendsto to Filter.Tendsto or vice versa): use `show` to restate, then proceed. (d) Last resort: break the Tendsto into pieces using `have` lemmas for each convergent component, then reassemble with Tendsto arithmetic (Tendsto.add, Tendsto.sub, Tendsto.mul). api[real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq] api[real_inner_self_eq_norm_mul_norm] tactic[simp_rw [...] → convert ... using 1 → ring] tactic[have h1 := ... → have h2 := ... → exact h1.sub h2 |>.add ...] The tension is between algebraic truth (the identity holds) and tactic mechanics (the rewrite changes the goal shape). The informal mathematician doesn't see this tension because "substitute equals for equals" is seamless on paper. In Lean, the substitution must respect the term structure, and `rw` doesn't always do what the mathematician intends. next[Determine if the rewrite is inside a binder, in the target, or structural.] next[Choose simp_rw (binder), convert (target), or show (structural).] next[If all fail, decompose into have lemmas and use Tendsto arithmetic.]

title: Argue by Contradiction
text: Argue by Contradiction Assume the negation of what you want to prove and derive an absurdity. You want to prove a statement P and no direct construction or chain of implications is apparent. The conclusion P is existential ("there exists..."), uniqueness ("at most one..."), or impossibility ("no X satisfies..."), and direct proof routes are blocked. Proofs by contradiction can obscure the constructive content of a result, making it harder to extract algorithms or explicit witnesses. Some mathematical communities prefer direct proofs when available. Assume not-P. Use the assumed structure to build or derive objects, then show these objects violate a known fact. The contradiction forces P. Contradiction proofs gain traction by giving you an extra hypothesis (not-P) to work with. Many fundamental results (irrationality of sqrt(2), uncountability of the reals, infinitude of primes) were first proved this way. next[Write down the precise negation of P.] next[Identify what new objects or properties not-P gives you.] next[Find the known fact that these objects violate.]

title: Check the Extreme Cases
text: Check the Extreme Cases Test your conjecture at the boundaries: zero, infinity, the empty set, the trivial case. You have a general statement and want to know if it is plausible before investing in a proof. The statement involves a parameter, a set, or a structure that can take degenerate or extreme values. Extreme cases can be vacuously true or pathologically special, giving false confidence. Passing extreme-case checks is necessary but not sufficient. Instantiate the statement at every extreme: n=0, n=1, the empty set, the one-point space, the trivial group, infinite dimension, the identity morphism. Check whether the statement is true, vacuously true, or false. A failure at an extreme case is a cheap disproof. Extreme cases are the cheapest tests available. Many false conjectures die at n=0. Many correct theorems reveal their essential content at the boundary. next[List all parameters and identify their extreme values.] next[Evaluate the statement at each extreme.] next[Record which extremes are informative vs vacuous.]

title: Complexity Classification
text: Complexity Classification Place a decision problem (or a class of problems) in a specific complexity class — typically by exhibiting a reduction from a problem already in that class, or by proving membership constructively. A computational problem P has been defined, and its complexity is unknown or only roughly known. The paper's contribution is to classify P at a known level of the complexity hierarchy: P, NP-complete, PSPACE, decidable, undecidable, ETH-hard, and so on. You can construct a polynomial-time (or appropriate) reduction from a complexity-class-complete problem to P, or vice versa, establishing membership / hardness with a sharp boundary. Complexity-classification is *one specific subtype* of `characterization-result` — its analogue in non-computational settings is `classification-result` (e.g., classifying KMS states or AFD outer actions). The reasoning shape is "list-the-cases-and-show-exhaustion" but the deliverable is "the problem belongs to class C" rather than "the structure has these instances." Use this leaf only when the result is genuinely complexity-theoretic. 1. Construct the reduction (typically polynomial-time many-one or Turing) from a complexity-class-complete problem to P (for hardness) or from P to a problem already in C (for membership). 2. Verify the reduction is correct and within the resource bounds for the target class. 3. State the classification theorem: P is C-complete (or C-hard, or in C, as appropriate). Complexity classification is structurally a *one-shot characterization* that places a problem at a precise location in a known hierarchy. It depends on the existence of a complete problem for the target class (Cook-Levin, etc.); reductions are the workhorse construction. The family parent is characterization-result; this leaf is the complexity-theoretic specialisation. next[Identify the target complexity class and a complete / canonical problem in it.] next[Construct the reduction; verify resource bounds.] next[State the classification with the appropriate complete / hard / member language.]

title: Construct an Explicit Witness
text: Construct an Explicit Witness When you need to prove existence, build the object. You need to show that an object with certain properties exists. The existence statement is concrete enough that you can describe what the object would look like, and abstract existence arguments (Zorn's lemma, compactness, probabilistic method) either do not apply or would leave you without a usable object. Explicit constructions can be intricate and may obscure *why* the object exists. Sometimes a non-constructive proof reveals more about the landscape than a single explicit example. Build the object step by step. Define it concretely. Verify each required property. If the construction is complex, build intermediate objects and compose them. An explicit witness is the gold standard of existence proofs: it gives you something to compute with, to test, and to modify. Many of mathematics' most valued results are constructions (Cantor's diagonal, Weierstrass's nowhere-differentiable function, Vitali sets). next[List the properties the witness must satisfy.] next[Attempt to build an object satisfying them one at a time.] next[If stuck, relax a property and see what you can build.]

title: Construct an Auxiliary Object
text: Construct an Auxiliary Object Introduce a purpose-built object that mediates between what you have and what you need. You have a hypothesis and a conclusion, but no direct path between them. The gap between hypothesis and conclusion is structural: you need an intermediate object (a function, a sequence, a set, a morphism) that does not appear in the problem statement but whose existence would bridge the gap. Auxiliary objects can feel like magic when encountered for the first time. The skill is in recognising which construction is needed: truncation, mollification, partition of unity, Hahn-Banach extension, free object on generators, approximating sequence. Identify the gap. Ask: what kind of object would connect my hypothesis to my conclusion? Construct it explicitly. Verify it has the properties needed on both sides. Common auxiliary objects include: truncated random variables, bump functions, test morphisms, approximating sequences, and free resolutions. Many of the most important proofs in mathematics turn on a single clever auxiliary construction. The Radon-Nikodym derivative, the partition of unity, the resolvent operator — these are all auxiliary objects that became standard tools precisely because they bridge common structural gaps. next[Identify the structural gap between hypothesis and conclusion.] next[Survey known auxiliary constructions in your domain.] next[Build the object and verify it bridges the gap.]

title: Dualise the Problem
text: Dualise the Problem Reverse the arrows, take complements, or transpose — the dual problem may be easier. You have a problem stated in terms of maps, sets, or conditions, and direct approaches are stuck. The problem has a natural duality: a categorical opposite, a vector space dual, a Boolean complement, a Fourier transform, a Lagrangian dual, or simply the contrapositive of a logical statement. Not every problem dualises cleanly. Some dualities lose structure (the double dual may not be isomorphic to the original). You must verify that the dual problem actually helps. Reformulate the problem in the dual setting. Solve it there if easier. Translate the solution back. For logical statements, try the contrapositive before attempting direct proof. Duality is pervasive: Pontryagin duality, Stone duality, linear programming duality, Poincare duality, Serre duality. A problem that is opaque in one setting can become transparent in its dual. next[Identify which duality applies to your setting.] next[Reformulate the problem in the dual language.] next[Solve and translate back.]

title: Encode as Algebra
text: Encode as Algebra Translate a combinatorial, geometric, or analytic problem into algebraic language and solve it there. You have a problem in geometry, combinatorics, topology, or analysis that resists direct methods. The objects in your problem carry algebraic structure (composition, addition, multiplication) that direct methods are not exploiting, or there is a known algebraic invariant that captures the property you care about. The algebraic translation may lose geometric or combinatorial information. The algebra may be harder to compute with than the original objects. Not every problem benefits from algebraisation. Assign algebraic objects to your problem's ingredients: groups to symmetries, rings to coordinate systems, modules to representations, homology groups to topological spaces. Reformulate the problem as an algebraic question. Solve using algebraic tools (exact sequences, spectral sequences, Groebner bases, character theory). Algebraic encoding has been one of the most successful strategies in mathematics: Galois theory encodes field extensions as groups, algebraic topology encodes spaces as groups, algebraic geometry encodes varieties as rings. The algebra often reveals structure that was invisible in the original setting. next[Identify what algebraic structure your objects carry.] next[Choose the right algebraic invariant or encoding.] next[Translate the problem and solve algebraically.]

title: Estimate by Bounding
text: Estimate by Bounding Replace a complicated quantity with a simpler bound that is good enough. You need to control a quantity (an integral, a sum, a probability, a norm) but exact computation is infeasible or unnecessary. You need an upper bound (or lower bound) rather than an exact value, and standard inequalities (triangle, Cauchy-Schwarz, Jensen, Markov, Chebyshev, AM-GM) are available. Bounds lose information. A bound that is too loose is useless. The art is in choosing the tightest bound that remains tractable. Chaining too many inequalities can accumulate slack to the point of triviality. Identify which direction you need (upper or lower). Apply the most appropriate standard inequality. Check that the resulting bound is tight enough for your purposes. If not, try a different inequality or a more refined decomposition before bounding. Estimation is the engine of analysis and probability. Most theorems in these fields are proved by chains of inequalities, each replacing something complicated with something simpler. Knowing which inequality to reach for is a core skill. next[Determine whether you need an upper or lower bound.] next[Identify candidate inequalities from your toolbox.] next[Apply and check tightness — is the bound strong enough?]

title: Exhaustion as Theorem
text: Exhaustion as Theorem When multiple approaches to the same proof step all fail at the same quantitative barrier, prove that the barrier is fundamental to the technique class, not an artifact of any individual approach. You have tried several methods for a proof step (concentration inequalities, subsampling arguments, spectral bounds, etc.) and each gives a bound that is too weak by the same qualitative amount. The failure pattern is suspiciously consistent. Three or more techniques from the same family (e.g., "subsample and concentrate," "bound trace then convert to operator norm," "linearize the quadratic term") all fail at the same quantitative step, producing bounds with the same scaling deficiency. Consistent failure might be coincidence rather than structure. Before declaring the barrier fundamental, verify that the techniques genuinely span the family — not just three variants of the same idea. Also check whether a technique outside the family avoids the barrier entirely. - Premature exhaustion claim: the family is not actually exhausted. Check that new techniques outside the family avoid the barrier. - Overgeneralization: "no concentration argument can work" when the ceiling only applies to trace-based certification. Scope the barrier precisely. 1. Identify the common quantitative step where all techniques fail. 2. Formulate the barrier as a theorem: "any technique in class C that proceeds via step X produces a bound of at most f(n)" where f(n) is weaker than the target. 3. Prove the ceiling theorem (often by exhibiting a worst case for step X). 4. Record the ceiling as a lemma. It eliminates the technique class and redirects effort toward techniques outside the class. A proved ceiling theorem is qualitatively different from "we tried 6 things and they didn't work." It converts empirical failure into structural understanding: the barrier is not a failure of ingenuity but a consequence of the technique class's structure. This prevents future revisitation ("maybe if we try the 7th variant...") and focuses effort on genuinely different approaches. P6 epsilon-light subsets (futon6, Feb 2026): 6 subsample-and-concentrate techniques (trace/Markov, star domination, decoupling+MSS 1-shot, decoupling+MSS recursive, greedy/chromatic, rank spreading) all hit the quadratic-vs-linear scaling wall: spectral contribution scales as q² while set size scales as q. The trace-only ceiling was proved as a lemma (Step 1), eliminating the entire technique class and redirecting toward operator-norm-aware barrier greedy (a technique outside the class). next[List all techniques tried and their failure points.] next[Identify the common quantitative step.] next[Prove the ceiling theorem for the technique class.] next[Search for techniques outside the class that avoid the ceiling.]

title: Exploit Symmetry
text: Exploit Symmetry When a problem has symmetry, use it to reduce the work. You are working on a problem where some transformation preserves the relevant structure. The problem is invariant under a group action, permutation, rotation, translation, or relabelling, and you are doing redundant work on equivalent configurations. Not all apparent symmetries are real: a function may look symmetric but have hidden asymmetries. And exploiting symmetry requires proving the symmetry exists, which itself may be non-trivial. Identify the symmetry group. Use it to reduce to a canonical representative ("without loss of generality"). Count orbits instead of elements. Decompose representations into irreducibles. Apply fixed-point theorems when the action has no escape. Symmetry arguments can reduce exponential case analysis to a single case. The "WLOG" move is one of the most powerful sentence fragments in mathematics. next[Identify what transformations preserve the problem.] next[Choose a canonical representative for each orbit.] next[Reformulate the problem in terms of orbits or invariants.]

title: Failure-Mode Characterization
text: Failure-Mode Characterization Characterize the regime where a known result FAILS, rather than only characterizing where it holds. A theorem T is known under hypotheses H. It is natural to ask whether T extends to a broader class. Rather than producing yet another sufficient condition, the paper instead pins down the *boundary of applicability*: it identifies exactly the regime where T is no longer valid, often with quantitative or structural sharpness. You have a theorem T with hypotheses H and you want to articulate the *failure regime* — typically (a) examples that violate T outside H, (b) a structural reason the failure occurs, (c) a sharp boundary between holds-here and fails-here. Failure-mode characterization is structurally distinct from a *negative result* (T is false in this case). A negative result asserts something doesn't hold; failure-mode-characterization specifies the *regime* where it doesn't hold and the *structural reason* it doesn't. The latter is stronger — it tells the reader where the theorem still works, where it fails, and *why*. 1. Construct an explicit counterexample or family of counterexamples that lie just outside H. 2. Identify the structural feature of the counterexamples that makes T fail — the "failure mechanism." 3. State the boundary as a theorem: "T fails iff [structural condition]." 4. Optional: re-prove T with a refined hypothesis H' that excludes the failure regime. Failure-mode characterization is information-dense: it tells the community both where to apply T and where to stop. It also exposes the structural feature that drives validity, which often illuminates analogous theorems in adjacent settings. This pattern is closely related to `structural-obstruction-as-theorem` but distinct: that pattern is about a *method* failing on a problem, this pattern is about a *theorem* failing in a regime. next[Construct an explicit counterexample and verify it fails T.] next[Identify the structural feature that drives the failure.] next[State the boundary theorem precisely; check it is sharp.]

title: Find the Right Abstraction
text: Find the Right Abstraction When a proof is ugly or a pattern recurs, seek a higher-level framework where it becomes natural. You have a proof that works but feels ad hoc, or you see the same argument repeated in several settings. The proof involves case splits, coordinate choices, or auxiliary constructions that seem to serve no conceptual purpose, or the same lemma keeps reappearing in different guises across different domains. Premature abstraction obscures rather than clarifies: abstracting before you have enough examples risks building a framework that fits nothing well. The right abstraction is found, not prescribed. Identify the minimal structural assumptions your argument actually uses. Reformulate in terms of those assumptions alone. If a known framework (group, category, topological space, measure space) fits, use it; if not, you may have discovered a new one. The right abstraction turns a difficult proof into a trivial one. Much of 20th-century mathematics consisted of finding the right level of generality (e.g., Grothendieck's schemes, Eilenberg-Mac Lane's categories). next[List the properties your proof actually uses.] next[Search for existing frameworks that axiomatise those properties.] next[Reformulate and check whether the proof simplifies.]

title: Hybrid Certification
text: Hybrid Certification When a pure algebraic method is too slow and a pure numerical method isn't rigorous, combine them: use numerical computation to locate, exact arithmetic to certify. You need a rigorous result about a polynomial or algebraic system (root count, sign determination, bound verification) but the standard exact methods (Sturm sequences, Groebner bases, cylindrical algebraic decomposition) are computationally infeasible for the problem size, while purely numerical methods lack rigour. The exact method's bottleneck is a specific subroutine (polynomial GCD, resultant, matrix factorization) that scales badly with coefficient size or degree, but the qualitative structure of the answer (number of roots, sign pattern) can be determined cheaply by approximate computation. The hybrid method must be provably correct. The numerical step identifies candidates; the exact step certifies them. If the certification step fails (e.g., the approximate root is too far from the true root for sign determination), the method must detect this and fall back rather than produce a wrong answer. - Double roots: if two roots are very close, the numerical step may merge them and the sign-change count will be wrong. Mitigation: compare numerical root count with exact Sturm count on a COARSE interval first. - Coefficient explosion: the exact evaluation at a rational test point may involve very large integers. Mitigation: choose simple test points (small-denominator rationals). - False separation: numerical noise places a test point on the wrong side of a root. Mitigation: use exact arithmetic for the test point evaluation, not floating-point. 1. Use fast numerical computation (numpy, LAPACK, floating-point) to compute approximate answers: root locations, eigenvalues, sign patterns. 2. Design an exact verification step that checks the numerical answer: evaluate the polynomial at rational test points, verify sign conditions, count roots by IVT. 3. The exact step should be O(n) in the problem size (not O(n³) like the numerical step), since it's certifying known answers, not discovering them. 4. If the exact step disagrees with the numerical step, investigate rather than trust either. Exact symbolic computation has enormous constant factors (arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic, polynomial GCD over Z[x] with 100+ digit coefficients). Numerical computation is fast but approximate. The hybrid avoids the worst of both: fast location + cheap certification = rigorous result at numerical speed. P4 n=4 Case 2 (futon6, Feb 2026): Sturm's theorem on a degree-70 polynomial with 100+ digit integer coefficients ran for 4 hours without completing (polynomial GCD bottleneck). The hybrid method: numpy.roots for approximate root locations (O(n³), milliseconds), then exact sympy.Rational evaluation at midpoints between consecutive roots (O(n) evaluations, 0.2s total). Same rigour as Sturm. 72,000x speedup. next[Identify the bottleneck in the exact method.] next[Design a numerical locator + exact certifier pipeline.] next[Validate: compare hybrid result with exact method on a smaller instance.]

title: Induction and Well-Ordering
text: Induction and Well-Ordering When objects are indexed by a well-ordered set, prove the base case and the step. You want to prove a statement P(n) for all n in some well-ordered domain (natural numbers, ordinals, well-founded trees). The statement involves a natural number, a finite structure with a size parameter, or more generally any well-ordered or well-founded index. The inductive step can be harder than it looks — it requires proving P(n+1) from P(n) (or from all P(k) with k<n for strong induction). Choosing the wrong induction variable makes the step impossible even when the theorem is true. Choose the right quantity to induct on. Verify the base case. For the inductive step, assume P holds for smaller values and show it holds for the current value. Consider strong induction if simple induction is too weak. Induction is the fundamental proof method for discrete mathematics and much of algebra. Choosing the right induction variable is often the key creative step. next[Identify the right quantity to induct on.] next[Verify the base case.] next[Prove the inductive step, being explicit about where the hypothesis is used.]

title: Local-to-Global Argument
text: Local-to-Global Argument Prove something locally (on small pieces) and then assemble the local results into a global one. You want to establish a property of a large or complicated object. The object admits a decomposition into simpler pieces (open cover, partition, filtration, localisation at primes), and the property you want can be checked on pieces. Not every property is local. You must verify that local data can be patched: the pieces must be compatible on overlaps, and the patching procedure must not introduce new problems. Cover the object with pieces where the property is manageable. Prove it on each piece. Check compatibility on overlaps. Glue the local results into a global one, using partitions of unity, sheaf conditions, or patching lemmas as appropriate. Local-to-global is one of the deepest recurring themes in mathematics: sheaf theory, Mayer-Vietoris, local-global principles in number theory, partitions of unity in differential geometry. The power comes from reducing a hard global problem to many easy local ones. next[Decompose the object into local pieces.] next[Verify the property on each piece.] next[Check compatibility and assemble the global result.]

title: Monotone Approximation
text: Monotone Approximation Approximate a complicated object by a monotone sequence of simpler objects and pass to the limit. You want to prove a result for a general object (general measurable function, arbitrary open set, general measure) but your tools only work for simple ones. Your general object can be approximated from below (or above) by a monotone sequence of simpler objects, and the property you care about is preserved under monotone limits. Not all approximations are monotone, and not all properties survive limits. You must choose the right notion of approximation and verify that the limit argument is valid (monotone convergence theorem, continuity from below, directed completeness). Construct a monotone sequence of simple objects converging to your target. Prove the result for each element of the sequence. Apply a monotone convergence or limit theorem to conclude for the general object. This is the fundamental technique of measure theory and integration. Simple functions approximate measurable functions, compact sets approximate open sets, finite sums approximate series. The monotone convergence theorem makes the passage rigorous. next[Construct the monotone approximating sequence.] next[Prove the result for each element of the sequence.] next[Identify and apply the appropriate limit theorem.]

title: Numerical Scout
text: Numerical Scout Before attempting an algebraic or formal proof, map the problem landscape numerically to identify the structure that the proof must handle. You want to prove a statement about a continuous or polynomial function on a domain (e.g., positivity, uniqueness of extrema, critical point enumeration). The function has enough variables that the proof strategy is not obvious. The domain is bounded, the function is computable, and there are multiple plausible proof strategies (SOS, interval arithmetic, elimination, Groebner, etc.), but you don't know which will work. Numerical evidence does not constitute proof. Floating-point computation can miss critical points near boundaries, produce false precision, and confirm true conjectures whose proofs require entirely different techniques. The scout must inform the proof strategy, not replace it. - Scout finds zero violations → prover assumes the "obvious" approach works → but the proof technique fails for structural reasons unrelated to the landscape (e.g., SOS blocked by interior zeros). The scout informs WHAT to prove, not HOW. - Scout misses a critical point in a thin region → prover claims exhaustive enumeration → proof is incomplete. Mitigate: multiple independent searches, boundary-focused sampling, increase start count. 1. Grid evaluation: compute the function on a uniform grid over the domain. Record the minimum, maximum, and any near-zero values. 2. Critical point search: run multiple independent local optimization searches (L-BFGS, differential evolution) from random starting points. Use at least 3 independent searches with 1000+ starts each. 3. Domain boundary survey: evaluate on constraint boundaries (where disc=0, f=0, etc.). 4. Symmetry detection: check whether critical points cluster along symmetry subspaces. 5. Case structure identification: from the critical point map, identify natural subcases ordered by symmetry/difficulty. The scout reveals what the proof must handle: how many critical points, where they are, what the minimum margin is, which subspaces are trivial and which are hard. This guides the choice of proof technique. A proof strategy designed without scouting is guessing; one designed after scouting is engineering. P4 n=4 Stam inequality proof (futon6, Feb 2026): 4 numerical scripts with 11,000+ optimization starts mapped 12 critical points in 4D. This map identified the 5-case decomposition (Cases 1, 2, 3a, 3b, 3c by symmetry subspace) that led to algebraic proofs for Cases 1-3b. Without scouting, the case decomposition would have been unmotivated. next[Run grid evaluation + critical point search on the domain.] next[Identify symmetry subspaces from the critical point map.] next[Design the proof strategy based on the landscape, not the other way around.]

title: Optimise a Free Parameter
text: Optimise a Free Parameter When a bound depends on a free parameter, choose the parameter value that gives the best result. You have established a bound or inequality that contains a free parameter (epsilon, delta, t, lambda) and want the sharpest possible conclusion. The bound is valid for all (or a range of) parameter values, and different choices yield different strengths of conclusion. The optimisation may be analytically intractable. In that case, a sub-optimal but explicit choice (often guided by dimensional analysis or balancing terms) is better than an opaque optimal one. Differentiate (or otherwise optimise) with respect to the free parameter. If the optimum has a clean closed form, use it. If not, choose a value that balances the dominant terms — this typically gives the right order of magnitude. This pattern is the workhorse of concentration inequalities, moment methods, and approximation theory. The Chernoff bound, Bernstein inequalities, and Laplace method all follow by introducing an exponential parameter and optimising. next[Identify the free parameter and its valid range.] next[Optimise or balance terms.] next[Substitute back and simplify the resulting bound.]

title: Parametric Tension Dissolution
text: Parametric Tension Dissolution When two parts of a proof have conflicting requirements on a parameter, recognize the tension as a structural constraint and seek a construction that dissolves it by changing the underlying geometric or algebraic setup. Your proof has two logically independent obligations. Each constrains a shared parameter (dimension, degree, codimension, rank, etc.) in conflicting directions. The natural construction satisfies one obligation perfectly but creates headwinds for the other. Obligation A requires parameter p to have property X (e.g., n even), while obligation B benefits from property Y (e.g., n odd), and X and Y are incompatible. The conflict is not a matter of insufficient technique but of the parameter itself. Not every difficulty is a tension. If obligation B merely "prefers" Y but can be completed with X, the tension is aesthetic, not structural. Only apply this pattern when the conflict genuinely blocks or severely impedes completion. Also: the alternative construction that dissolves the tension must exist — don't assume it does without checking. - The alternative construction may not exist (the tension may be intrinsic to the problem, not just the approach). - The alternative may dissolve one tension but create another. Map all obligations before committing. 1. State the tension precisely: which obligations conflict on which parameter. 2. Ask: is there a different construction where both obligations want the same parameter value? This often means replacing the initial geometric or algebraic object (reflection → rotation, codim-1 → codim-2, etc.). 3. Check that the new construction still satisfies both obligations (it may make the previously-easy obligation slightly harder). 4. If the tension dissolves, record the resolution as a structural insight. Parametric tensions are theorems about the approach, not the problem. They reveal that the initial construction, however natural, is suboptimal for the full proof. Dissolving the tension often simplifies the entire proof architecture by removing structural headwinds that would otherwise require heavy machinery to overcome. P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): E2 obligation (place Γ in FH(Q)) requires even n (so fixed set has odd dimension and χ = 0 by topology). S obligation (upgrade to manifold) benefits from odd n (favorable L-theory parity, equivariant surgery available). Tension is structural for the reflection construction. Resolution: replace codimension-1 reflection with codimension-2 rotation in odd dimension. Both obligations then want odd n. The rotation route dissolves the tension and opens two parallel S-branch options (Wall surgery with favorable parity, or equivariant surgery with satisfied gap hypothesis). next[Identify which obligations conflict on which parameters.] next[Search for alternative constructions where the conflict dissolves.] next[Verify the alternative satisfies all obligations, even if less cleanly.]

title: Pass to a Subsequence or Subnet
text: Pass to a Subsequence or Subnet When a sequence does not converge, extract a convergent subsequence and argue from there. You need convergence or a limit, but the full sequence or net may not cooperate. You are working in a compact space (or a setting with a compactness hypothesis), and the sequence or net is bounded but not necessarily convergent. The subsequence may converge to something unwanted. You must verify that the limit has the properties you need, and that the argument does not depend on the specific subsequence chosen. Invoke compactness (Bolzano-Weierstrass, Alaoglu, Tychonoff, sequential compactness) to extract a convergent subsequence. Pass to it. Argue that the limit has the desired property. If necessary, show the limit is unique so the full sequence converges. Compactness arguments are the engine of analysis. "Pass to a subsequence" converts a possibly wild sequence into a tame one at the cost of losing control over indices — a trade-off that is almost always worth making. next[Verify the compactness hypothesis that justifies extraction.] next[Extract the convergent subsequence and identify the limit.] next[Check that the limit has the properties you need.]

title: Quotient by Irrelevance
text: Quotient by Irrelevance Identify what does not matter for your problem and collapse it away. You are working with objects that carry more structure than your problem needs. Different-looking objects behave identically for your purposes, and keeping track of the differences creates bookkeeping overhead or case splits. Quotienting loses information. You must verify that the operations and properties you care about are well-defined on equivalence classes, not just on representatives. Define an equivalence relation that identifies objects agreeing on what matters. Pass to the quotient. Verify well-definedness. Work in the quotient where the irrelevant distinctions are gone. Quotient constructions are one of the most universal moves in mathematics: integers from naturals, rationals from integers, homology from chains, projective space from vector space. Recognising when to quotient is recognising what the problem is really about. next[Identify which distinctions between your objects are irrelevant.] next[Define the equivalence relation precisely.] next[Check that your operations respect the equivalence.]

title: Reduce to a Known Result
text: Reduce to a Known Result Transform your problem until it matches the hypothesis of a known theorem, then invoke it. You want to prove a result and suspect it follows from something already established. The conclusion you need resembles the conclusion of a known theorem, but the hypotheses do not quite match your setup. Forcing a reduction to the wrong theorem produces fragile, unenlightening proofs. The reduction step must be natural, not a contortion. Identify the candidate theorem. Compare its hypotheses to your situation. Bridge the gap: verify missing hypotheses, apply a change of variables, restrict to a subcase, or reformulate to match. Then invoke the theorem. Mathematics is cumulative. The power of a proof is proportional to the depth of the results it can invoke. "By Theorem X" is the most efficient move in mathematics when X genuinely applies. next[Identify which known result has the conclusion you need.] next[Compare hypotheses: what is missing or different?] next[Bridge the gap or choose a different target theorem.]

title: Show Both Inequalities
text: Show Both Inequalities To prove equality, prove inequality in both directions. You want to show A = B (where A, B are numbers, sets, or objects in an ordered structure) and no direct computation yields both sides at once. Direct computation of A or B is infeasible, but you can bound A from above by B and from below by B (or equivalently, show A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A). The two directions may require completely different techniques. One direction is often trivial while the other requires the bulk of the work. Identifying which is which saves effort. Prove A <= B and B <= A separately (or A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A). Combine to conclude A = B. For the squeeze/sandwich variant: bound A from above and below by quantities that both converge to the same limit. This is one of the most common proof structures in analysis (sandwich theorem, integral bounds), set theory (Cantor-Bernstein), and algebra (showing ideals or subgroups are equal). It reduces equality to two often-simpler one-directional claims. next[Determine which direction is easier.] next[Prove the easy direction first to build intuition.] next[Prove the hard direction.]

title: Split into Cases
text: Split into Cases When a single argument cannot handle all situations, partition into cases and handle each one. You are trying to prove a statement that behaves differently depending on some condition or parameter value. The objects or hypotheses fall into a finite number of qualitatively different types, and the proof technique that works for one type fails for another. Too many cases make a proof unreadable and suggest you are missing a unifying idea. If you find yourself with more than 3-4 cases, consider whether a different approach (symmetry, abstraction, contradiction) would eliminate the case split entirely. Identify the exhaustive partition. Prove the result separately for each case. Verify the cases are exhaustive (no gaps) and handle any overlap. Common splits: positive/ negative/zero, finite/infinite, convergent/divergent, trivial/non-trivial. Case analysis is often the simplest proof strategy available, even if not the most elegant. Many results in combinatorics, number theory, and real analysis require it because the underlying structure genuinely behaves differently in different regimes. next[Identify the natural partition of your domain or hypothesis.] next[Verify the cases are exhaustive.] next[Prove each case, noting where the proof differs.]

title: Structural Characterization
text: Structural Characterization Give a complete intrinsic description of an object — what it is, in terms of simpler structures or invariants — rather than asserting properties about it. An object (an algebra, a representation, a measure, a group action, a category) has been defined or is the focus of attention. The paper's contribution is to *say what the object is* in a complete sense: as a quotient, as a fibration, as a tensor product, as a module over a smaller object, etc. — typically with a uniqueness or universality statement. You have an object X about which existing results give partial information (some properties, some bounds, some examples), and you can identify a description of X that is *complete*: another object Y plus a construction such that X is exactly built from Y by that construction. Structural characterization differs from `find-the-right-abstraction` in direction: that pattern abstracts from many examples to a unifying framework; this pattern starts with one object and resolves it into simpler components. It also differs from `exhaustion-as-theorem`: that lists all instances of a type, this describes one instance fully. Choose this leaf when the deliverable is *one* full description, not a list. 1. Identify the simpler components from which X can be built (Y plus a construction). 2. Establish the construction rigorously, with whatever uniqueness / universality clauses are appropriate. 3. Verify the structural identification by re-deriving known properties of X from the new description. A complete structural description of an object is the strongest possible characterization: it lets every property of X be derived from properties of Y plus the construction. When such a description exists, it is essentially always more useful than a list of properties, because it tells you why the properties hold. next[Identify the simpler structure Y and the construction that yields X.] next[State the structural identity precisely (with uniqueness / universal property).] next[Re-derive known properties of X from the identification.]

title: Structural Equivalence
text: Structural Equivalence Establish that two structures are structurally identical at the level of the relevant invariants — typically by exhibiting a bidirectional map (an isomorphism, an equivalence of categories, or a biduality) and verifying that the relevant operations transport across. Two structures X and Y are in view, often arising from different definitions or different settings (e.g., a cohomology constructed combinatorially and one constructed algebraically; a representation-theoretic invariant and a topological invariant). The paper's contribution is to show *they are the same thing*, in a structural sense. You can construct maps X → Y and Y → X and verify they are mutually inverse, *and* both maps preserve the operations / morphisms / metrics that the equivalence is supposed to preserve. Structural equivalence is symmetric. It differs from `transport-across-isomorphism`: that pattern *uses* a known isomorphism to transfer a result; this pattern *establishes* a new structural identity. It also differs from `structural-inclusion`: that is directional; this is bidirectional. Use this leaf when the paper's contribution is a new equivalence. 1. Construct both directions of the equivalence. 2. Verify they are mutually inverse (or mutually quasi-inverse, in the categorical case). 3. Verify preservation of the structural features of interest. 4. State the equivalence as a theorem; identify what consequences follow (since X and Y are structurally the same, anything proved about either is now available for both). A structural equivalence is the strongest possible relation between two objects: it says they are interchangeable for the purpose at hand. Proving such an equivalence often requires deep structural insight because the two sides typically arise from different traditions (combinatorial vs algebraic, topological vs representation-theoretic). The payoff is enormous: every result on either side is now available for both. next[Construct both directions of the equivalence map.] next[Verify mutual inverse / quasi-inverse status.] next[Verify preservation of the relevant structural operations.]

title: Structural Inclusion / Monotonicity
text: Structural Inclusion / Monotonicity Show that one structure contains, embeds into, or is dominated by another — with directional preservation of the relevant invariants. Strictly weaker than equivalence; strictly stronger than mere correlation. Two structures X and Y are in view, and the paper's contribution is to establish that X is contained in Y (in some structural sense), or that an invariant on X is dominated by the analogous invariant on Y, or that X embeds as a sub-object of Y. You can construct an order-preserving / structure-preserving map X → Y, or argue that the unit ball / minimal class / norm of X is contained in that of Y, with directional rather than symmetric content. Structural inclusion differs from `transport-across-isomorphism`: that pattern is symmetric (X ≅ Y); this pattern is directional (X ⊆ Y but not necessarily Y ⊆ X). Inclusion alone is weaker but often more useful in practice — many monotonicity results carry strict inclusion that no equivalence can replicate. Use this leaf when the relation is genuinely one-way. 1. Identify the inclusion / embedding / domination map and verify it preserves the structural feature of interest. 2. Verify that the inclusion is strict (or note explicitly when it is tight / non-strict). 3. Identify the consequence: what holds for X because it holds for Y, or what fails to hold because the reverse inclusion does not. Inclusion / monotonicity statements are the workhorses of comparison: they let one transfer results from a well-understood object to a less- understood one, or rule out behaviour by appeal to a containing structure. Cobordism, norm-domination, lattice-embedding, and sub-representation arguments all live here. next[Construct the structural map and verify directional preservation.] next[Determine whether the inclusion is strict or tight.] next[Identify the property of X that this inclusion gives access to.]

title: Structural Obstruction as Theorem
text: Structural Obstruction as Theorem When a proof method fails, characterize the failure as a theorem about the problem's structure rather than discarding the approach silently. You have tried a standard proof technique (SOS certificate, Groebner basis, spectral method, induction scheme, etc.) and it has failed — not due to insufficient computation, but apparently due to a structural feature of the problem. The failure is reproducible across multiple parameter settings (different degrees, different multiplier sets, different starting points) and the failure pattern suggests a structural reason rather than a computational limitation. Not every failure is structural. Computational failures (memory, time, numerical instability) look like structural failures when resources are insufficient. Before claiming a structural obstruction, verify that increasing resources (degree, precision, time) does not help, or identify the algebraic reason for the failure. - Premature declaration: calling a failure "structural" when it's actually computational. One failed SOS attempt doesn't prove structural infeasibility — but infeasibility at degrees 10, 12, AND 14 with multiple solver backends, plus an algebraic explanation, does. - Overgeneralization: concluding "no algebraic certificate exists" when only Putinar-type certificates are blocked. The obstruction is specific to the method, not to all methods. 1. State the obstruction precisely: what property of the problem blocks what method. 2. Prove the obstruction (even informally): show that the method CANNOT work, not just that it HASN'T worked. 3. Record the obstruction as a theorem or remark in the proof status document. 4. Use the obstruction to redirect: if method A is blocked, what does the obstruction tell you about which methods might succeed? A proved obstruction is as valuable as a successful certificate. It eliminates an entire proof strategy from consideration and often reveals structural information (interior zeros, indefiniteness, topological obstructions) that constrains the space of viable approaches. The alternative — silently trying the next method — wastes effort and loses information. P4 n=4 Stam inequality (futon6, Feb 2026): 7 SOS scripts at degrees 10, 12, 14 all infeasible. The obstruction: -N has an interior zero at x₀ where all constraint polynomials are strictly positive, forcing σ₀(x₀) = 0 in any Putinar decomposition. But σ₀ is SOS and vanishing at a point with positive constraints creates algebraic contradictions. This theorem immediately eliminated SOS as a strategy and redirected effort toward algebraic elimination, which succeeded. next[State the obstruction precisely.] next[Verify it's structural, not computational (try multiple settings).] next[Record it and use it to constrain the viable approach space.]

title: Technique Landscape Map
text: Technique Landscape Map When a problem sits at the intersection of multiple standard techniques, build a typed library of those techniques before attempting the proof. The library reveals the exact structural gap between existing methods and the target. You have a theorem to prove that resembles results in several papers, but no single paper's method directly applies. The temptation is to pick the "closest" method and adapt it. But without mapping the full landscape, you may miss that the gap is structural rather than parametric. Multiple published techniques (3+) partially address your problem — they prove related results with similar objects but different outputs, or the same output under stronger hypotheses. Building the library is upfront investment that may feel premature. Not every problem needs it — only problems where the mismatch between existing methods and the target is non-obvious. If one method clearly applies modulo a minor adaptation, just adapt it. - Over-investment: building an exhaustive library when the problem only needs one adaptation. Start with 3-4 methods; expand only if the gap remains unclear. - False bridge: classifying a method as "partial" when the gap is actually fundamental. Be honest about bridge status — partial means the core technique transfers; none means only the vocabulary transfers. 1. For each related method, construct a typed wiring diagram with nodes: Q (objective), D (decomposition), M (mechanism), C (certificate), O (output). 2. Add a bridge node B assessing the match to your target: direct, partial, or none. 3. For each B = partial, write down the exact structural mismatch. 4. Look for patterns across mismatches — they often share a common structural feature. 5. The common feature is the gap. Target it directly. The library converts vague intuition ("these papers are related") into a typed structural comparison. The bridge-status classification surfaces whether the gap is parametric (same structure, different bounds) or structural (different output type). Structural gaps require new ideas; parametric gaps require optimization. Knowing which you face changes the approach entirely. P6 epsilon-light subsets (futon6, Feb 2026): a library of 10 methods (D1-D10) was constructed with typed wiring diagrams. All 10 had bridge status partial or none. The common mismatch: all methods produce edge-weighted sparsifiers, not vertex-induced subsets. This structural gap — not visible from any single paper — directed the proof toward leverage-based vertex selection (a new technique) rather than adapting any existing method. next[Survey 3-5 related methods with typed wiring diagrams.] next[Classify bridge status for each: direct, partial, or none.] next[Identify the common structural mismatch across partial bridges.]

title: The Diagonal Argument
text: The Diagonal Argument Defeat any purported enumeration by constructing an object that differs from every item on the list. You want to show that a collection is too large to be listed, or that a certain map cannot be surjective. Someone claims a surjection or enumeration exists from a countable (or smaller) set onto a larger one, and the objects in the target can be defined pointwise. The diagonal construction requires the ability to "flip" or modify the diagonal entry. Not all settings admit this. The argument also only gives non-existence; it does not say how much larger the target is. Given the purported list f(1), f(2), ..., construct an object d that differs from f(n) at position n for every n. Since d differs from every listed item, d is not on the list, contradicting surjectivity. Cantor's diagonal argument is one of the most fertile ideas in mathematics, spawning Goedel's incompleteness theorems, Turing's halting problem, Russell's paradox, and the Lawvere fixed-point theorem. The same pattern recurs whenever self-reference meets totality. next[Identify the purported enumeration or surjection.] next[Construct the diagonal object.] next[Verify it genuinely differs from every listed item.]

title: Transport Across an Isomorphism
text: Transport Across an Isomorphism Prove something in one setting, then transport the result to an isomorphic setting for free. You need to prove a property of an object X, and there is an isomorphic object Y where the property is already known or easier to establish. X and Y are connected by an isomorphism (or equivalence) in the relevant category, and the property you care about is invariant under isomorphism. You must verify that the property is indeed isomorphism-invariant. Not all properties transfer: a specific element, an embedding into a particular ambient space, or a computational representation may not survive transport. Establish the isomorphism between X and Y. Prove the property for whichever side is easier. Invoke isomorphism-invariance to conclude for the other side. For structured settings, use the naturality of the isomorphism. "Isomorphic objects are the same for all mathematical purposes" is the fundamental principle of abstract mathematics. Transport lets you work in whichever representation is most convenient. next[Establish the isomorphism or equivalence.] next[Verify the property is invariant under it.] next[Prove in the easier setting and transport.]

title: Try a Simpler Case
text: Try a Simpler Case When a problem resists direct attack, try a simpler or smaller version first. You are stuck on a problem whose generality or size makes it hard to see what is going on. The problem involves parameters (dimension, cardinality, degree, number of variables) and no direct approach is working. Jumping to the simplest case can miss structure that only appears at intermediate complexity, and results for small cases do not always generalise. Reduce one or more parameters to the smallest non-trivial value. Solve that case. Examine what made it work and what would break if the parameter grew. Use the insight to guide the general argument. Simpler cases reveal the essential mechanism while hiding accidental complexity. Most successful general proofs were found by someone who first understood n=2 or dimension 1. next[Identify which parameter to reduce.] next[Solve the reduced case completely.] next[Articulate what generalises and what does not.]

title: Unfold the Definition
text: Unfold the Definition When stuck, go back to the definition and write out exactly what it says. You need to prove or use a property of an object, and the path forward is not clear. The statement involves a defined concept (compact, continuous, exact, measurable, adjoint) and you are treating it as a black box instead of engaging with its content. Definitions can unfold into multiple equivalent characterisations, and not all unfoldings are equally useful. Choosing the wrong characterisation can make the problem harder. Write out the definition of every technical term in the statement. Replace defined terms with their meanings. The proof obligation often becomes clear once the definitions are fully expanded. If multiple equivalent definitions exist, try each one. Most proofs at the textbook level consist of nothing more than carefully unfolding definitions. "I don't see how to start" almost always means "I haven't written out what the words mean." next[Identify which terms in the statement are defined concepts.] next[Write out each definition fully.] next[See which unfolding makes the proof obligation match your tools.]

title: The Probabilistic Method
text: The Probabilistic Method Prove existence by showing a random object has the desired property with positive probability. You want to show that an object with certain combinatorial properties exists, but explicit construction seems intractable. The desired property can be expressed as an event in a probability space on the set of candidate objects, and you can estimate the probability of failure. The probabilistic method typically does not produce an explicit object. It proves existence without construction. For applications requiring an actual witness, derandomisation techniques may be needed. Define a probability distribution on candidate objects. Show that the probability of having the desired property is positive (by union bound, expectation argument, Lovász local lemma, or second moment method). Conclude existence. Erdős's probabilistic method revolutionised combinatorics by proving the existence of objects (Ramsey graphs, codes, expanders) that no one could construct explicitly. The expected value alone often suffices: if the expected number of bad events is less than 1, a good object exists. next[Define the probability space on candidate objects.] next[Estimate the probability of failure.] next[Apply the appropriate probabilistic tool (union bound, expectation, LLL).]

title: Verify the Universal Property
text: Verify the Universal Property To show an object is "the right one", show it satisfies the relevant universal property. You want to prove that an explicit construction actually gives the correct categorical object (product, coproduct, limit, free algebra, tensor product, adjoint). The object you have constructed should be characterised by a universal mapping property: for every object of a certain kind, there exists a unique morphism through yours. Universal properties require checking both existence and uniqueness of the mediating morphism. Existence is usually the construction; uniqueness is often the harder part and is where most proof errors occur. State the universal property precisely. For existence: given an arbitrary test object and compatible data, construct the required morphism. For uniqueness: assume two morphisms work and show they are equal, typically by checking on generators or using a cancellation argument. Universal properties are the categorical way of saying "this is the canonical construction". Once verified, they give you all morphisms for free and make diagram-chasing arguments possible. They also guarantee that the construction is unique up to unique isomorphism. next[State the universal property precisely.] next[Construct the mediating morphism (existence).] next[Prove the mediating morphism is unique.]

title: Work Examples First
text: Work Examples First Build intuition from concrete examples before attempting a general proof. You have a conjecture or a definition and want to understand what it really says. The statement is abstract or involves multiple quantifiers, and you cannot yet see why it should be true (or false). Examples alone do not prove theorems, and poorly chosen examples can mislead by being too special or too symmetric. Compute several concrete instances. Choose examples that are generic (not too symmetric), that test boundary conditions, and that span different regimes of the parameters. Record what each example teaches you about the conjecture. Examples are the empirical base of mathematics. A conjecture you cannot verify on a single instance is a conjecture you do not understand. next[Pick 3-5 examples spanning different regimes.] next[Compute each one explicitly.] next[Record which features of the examples matter for the conjecture.]

title: Characterization-Result Family
text: Characterization-Result Family Your paper describes what some object or class of objects *is* — not whether one exists, not how it relates to another, but its intrinsic structure. An object or class has been singled out, and the question is "what does it look like?" — exhaustively (full structural description), partially (where it fails some property), in cases (classification), or in a sharp regime split (dichotomy). The paper's main contribution can be expressed as "we describe completely the structure of X", or "we classify all instances of X", or "we exhibit the regime where X fails property P", or "we show X belongs to one of two regimes". Characterization is the most populous family in mathematical literature (≈ 33 % of papers in our pilot — see `futon3/holes/excursions/E-math-prototype-pilot.md` Phase 2). Within it, the leaves diverge sharply: full-characterization is positive structural content; failure-mode is "where this fails"; classification lists cases; dichotomy is the special case of classification with two regimes. The analytic moves needed for each leaf are different. 1. Decide whether the paper aims at full description, partial / failure description, an enumeration of cases, or a binary regime split. 2. Pick the matching leaf member-pattern. 3. Identify the *witness* of the characterization: what theorem, equivalence, or list constitutes the description? exemplar[arxiv-2604.20815v1] # Zarankiewicz sharp dichotomy exemplar[arxiv-2604.20827v1] # Entropic OT failure-mode exemplar[arxiv-2604.20787v1] # Exchange-number complexity exemplar[arxiv-math/0603592v1] # KMS classification exemplar[arxiv-math/0603593v1] # AFD outer-actions classification member[math-informal/exhaustion-as-theorem] # full / classification member[math-informal/structural-obstruction-as-theorem] # failure-mode member[math-informal/split-into-cases] # dichotomy / classification member[math-informal/structural-characterization] # full description (new leaf) member[math-informal/failure-mode-characterization] # failure-regime (new leaf) member[math-informal/complexity-classification] # specific subtype (new leaf) Characterization papers do "describing-work" rather than "proving-X-exists" or "showing-X-relates-to-Y" work. The family parent serves as a coarse classifier; the leaves carry the analytic differences (e.g. dichotomy proofs almost always need a phase-transition argument; classification proofs need exhaustion). next[Decide whether the characterization is full, partial / failure-mode, classification, or dichotomy.] next[Identify the witness — list, theorem, equivalence — that constitutes the description.] next[Cross-check: does the paper *prove the characterization is exhaustive*, or only *exhibit examples*?]

title: Clarification (Meta-Tag, not a Pattern)
text: Clarification (Meta-Tag, not a Pattern) This is a meta-tag, not a strategic pattern. It marks papers (or pattern applications) where the `(context, tension, move)` triple cannot be meaningfully decomposed: either the paper is genuinely single-axis (its contribution is one observation), or the slot extraction failed. Pattern-classification has been attempted on a paper's reverse-morphogenesis output (see `futon3/holes/missions/M-pattern-application-diagnostic.md`); the three slots `situation_S`, `xiang_salience`, `arrow_constraint` are paraphrases of one description, with no substantive distinction. The three slots collapse into a single description; their pairwise semantic overlap is ≥ ~80 %. Collapsed triples are *informative*, not failures. Two distinct cases: (a) The paper is single-axis — clarifies one principle, extends an existing definition, surveys a body of work, or otherwise contributes a single observation rather than a multi-step move. This is fine. It must be *declared* as such, with the reason stated, rather than passing the slot-quality check silently. (b) The slot-extraction prompt failed — the LLM was unable to differentiate the slots. This is a producer bug, not a paper property. The classifier MUST distinguish (a) from (b). A clarification-meta tag with no reason is treated as a producer bug to fix; one with a stated reason is a valid mark of single-axis content. 1. If the paper is genuinely single-axis, attach a `:reason <enum>` field — e.g. `:single-axis-clarification`, `:survey`, `:definition-extension`. 2. If the slot-extraction failed, re-run the slot-extraction (per M-superpod-mark3 R-1 / slot-distinctness enforcement). 3. Do NOT lump (a) and (b) together as "clarification." exemplar[arxiv-2604.20820v1] # S-Prime principle (collapsed in pilot) exemplar[arxiv-2604.20788v1] # E-measure (collapsed in pilot) exemplar[arxiv-math/0603594v1] # Galois group rings (collapsed in pilot) # No member patterns; this is a meta-tag, not a family of strategic # moves. Papers tagged `clarification-meta:single-axis` are *not* # exemplars of a strategic pattern; they are exemplars of a paper-shape. # If a paper genuinely fits a leaf in another family, it should be # tagged there, not here. Per the IFR's "well-specified" property in `M-pattern-application-diagnostic.md`, distinct slots are required by construction. A collapsed triple either *reveals* that the paper is single-axis (a structural fact about the corpus) or *reveals* that the slot extractor failed (a structural fact about the pipeline). Treating both as the same hides both signals. next[Determine whether the collapse is single-axis (declare reason) or extraction failure (re-run).] next[If single-axis, do not lookup a strategic family — accept the meta-tag.] next[If extraction failure, route to slot-distinctness enforcement.]

title: Compose Independent Lemmas
text: Compose Independent Lemmas When a proof requires multiple independent pieces, establish each piece separately and then compose them in a final step that adds nothing new. Your main result follows from several sub-results that can be proved independently. The conclusion is a logical composition (conjunction, chain of implications, or substitution) of the pieces. The sub-results address different concerns (existence, uniqueness, nontriviality, notation compatibility, etc.) and no sub-result's proof depends on another sub-result being true. Independence must be genuine, not assumed. If lemma B uses lemma A as a hypothesis, they are not independent — B depends on A. The composition step must also be checked: it is tempting to wave hands at "combining" results when the combination itself requires a non-trivial argument (e.g., that two constructions refer to the same object, or that hypotheses of one result are satisfied by another). (a) Identify the independent pieces. Draw the dependency graph. (b) For each piece, verify it is self-contained: its proof uses only its own hypotheses and prior results, not sibling lemmas. (c) Write the composition step as a separate, explicit argument. It should be short — if it is long, one of the pieces is incomplete. (d) Check that the composition step does not silently introduce new claims. Every assertion in the composition must trace to a piece. Modular proofs are easier to review, easier to repair, and easier to generalize. When a reviewer finds a gap, modular structure localizes the damage: you know which piece is broken and which are unaffected. A monolithic proof hides dependencies and makes gaps contagious. next[List the pieces and draw the dependency graph.] next[Verify each piece is self-contained.] next[Write the composition step. Keep it short.] next[Trace every assertion in the composition to its source piece.]

title: Constraint Tension Resolution
text: Constraint Tension Resolution When two parts of a proof impose conflicting requirements on a shared parameter, recognize the conflict as a first-class structural constraint and search for a construction that satisfies both requirements simultaneously — typically by changing the underlying geometric or algebraic object rather than trying to force compatibility within the existing setup. Your proof decomposes into two or more obligations that share a parameter (dimension, codimension, degree, rank, characteristic, etc.). You have found a construction that cleanly discharges one obligation but discover that the parameter choice it forces creates genuine obstacles for the other. The obstacles are not failures of technique but consequences of the parameter value itself. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - The tension is intrinsic: every construction that satisfies A forces X. This is a structural impossibility result — record it. - The alternative construction dissolves the original tension but introduces a new one. Iterate: apply the pattern again to the new tension, or recognize that the problem may require a fundamentally different decomposition. - The alternative construction exists in principle but no concrete instance is known (e.g., "a lattice with an order-2 rotation in Isom(H^n)" exists if and only if a number-theoretic condition holds). The pattern has done its job — it has reduced the proof to a well-posed existence question — but the question remains open. 1. State the tension precisely: name both obligations, the shared parameter, and the conflicting requirements. Write it as a proposition: "For construction C, obligations A and B cannot both be satisfied because A needs p in X and B needs p in Y." 2. Determine whether the tension is intrinsic to the problem or specific to the construction. Ask: does every construction that satisfies A necessarily impose X on p? Or is X an artifact of this particular approach? 3. Search for an alternative construction C' where both obligations are compatible — where they both want the same parameter value, or where the parameter is no longer constrained. This typically means replacing the underlying geometric/algebraic object (e.g., reflection with rotation, codimension-1 with codimension-2). 4. Verify that C' actually satisfies both obligations. The new construction may make the previously-easy obligation harder (a legitimate trade-off) or may introduce new constraints. Map all obligations against C' before committing. 5. If the tension is intrinsic (no C' exists), record this as a structural impossibility result — it constrains the solution space and may redirect the entire proof strategy. Well-applied: - The tension is stated as a precise proposition with named obligations, named parameter, and named conflicting requirements. - The investigation distinguishes intrinsic tensions (problem-level) from approach-specific tensions (construction-level). - The alternative construction is verified against ALL obligations, not just the two that were in tension. - The resolution is recorded as a structural insight that informs future proof design. Badly-applied: - Declaring tension when the conflict is merely inconvenient, not blocking. If obligation B can still be completed with property X (just with more work), the tension is a preference, not a structural constraint. Do not pivot constructions for preferences. - Replacing the construction without checking that the new one actually satisfies the previously-easy obligation. The trade-off must be mapped. - Tunnel vision: finding an alternative construction that dissolves one tension but creates a worse one elsewhere. - Treating the tension as a dead end rather than information. Even if no resolution exists, the tension statement constrains the solution space and is worth recording. Obligation A requires parameter p to have property X (e.g., n even for Euler characteristic vanishing), while obligation B requires property Y (e.g., n odd for favorable L-theory parity or equivariant surgery availability), and X and Y are incompatible for the current construction. The conflict is not aesthetic preference but a genuine blockage: at least one obligation cannot be completed with the wrong parity/value. Parametric tensions are theorems about the approach, not the problem. When an initial construction discharges one obligation "too perfectly" by locking in a parameter value, the resulting structural headwinds for other obligations are predictable consequences, not bad luck. Recognizing the tension early — before investing in heavy machinery to overcome the headwinds — saves effort and often reveals a simpler proof architecture. The alternative construction that dissolves the tension frequently simplifies the entire proof by removing the need for workarounds. P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): The proof splits into two obligations — E2 (place Gamma in FH(Q) via a finite CW complex with rationally acyclic universal cover) and S (upgrade the finite CW complex to a closed manifold). The reflection construction in even dimension n discharges E2 perfectly: the codimension-1 fixed set has odd dimension, so its Euler characteristic vanishes (required by Fowler's criterion). But this forces n even, which creates three headwinds for S: (a) Equivariant surgery is BLOCKED (Costenoble-Waner gap hypothesis fails for codimension-1 fixed sets). (b) Wall surgery faces unfavorable even-dimensional L-theory parity. (c) No orbifold resolution technique is known. The tension statement: "For the reflection construction, E2 needs n even and S needs n odd; these are incompatible." Resolution: replace the codimension-1 reflection with a codimension-2 rotation in odd dimension n. The fixed set now has codimension 2 (so the equivariant surgery gap hypothesis is satisfied) and odd dimension (so L-theory parity is favorable). Both E2 and S want odd n. The tension dissolves entirely, and the problem reduces to a single lattice-existence question in number theory. next[State the tension as a precise proposition.] next[Determine if the tension is intrinsic or construction-specific.] next[Search for alternative constructions where conflicting requirements align.] next[Verify the alternative against all obligations before committing.]

title: Convention Bridge
text: Convention Bridge When two notational conventions refer to the same mathematical object (or differ by a known factor), make the identification explicit and prove it. Your argument needs to connect results stated in different notational conventions — e.g., starred vs unstarred polynomials, different normalization choices, author-specific definitions of the same concept. Two sources use different notation for what you believe is the same object, and your conclusion depends on equating them (or showing their ratio cancels). Convention differences are a common source of silent errors. What looks like "the same thing with different notation" may hide a genuine mathematical difference — a constant factor, a domain restriction, or an implicit specialization that does not always hold. Asserting equivalence without proof is precisely where reviewers find gaps. (a) State both conventions precisely, with citations. (b) Write the explicit relationship: A* = c · A, or A* = f(A), giving the transformation. (c) Prove the relationship holds in your parameter regime (e.g., q=1, x_i>0). (d) If the relationship is well-known, cite the specific proposition — do not write "it is well known that." (e) If only cancellation in a ratio matters, prove that the bridging factor is state-independent. Notation bridges that seem trivial to the author are the #1 source of reviewer objections in proofs that invoke external results. The five minutes spent making the bridge explicit saves weeks of back-and-forth. The bridge itself may reveal constraints you missed. next[Write both conventions side by side.] next[Identify the bridging factor or transformation.] next[Prove or cite the relationship in your parameter regime.] next[Check that the bridge holds at boundary cases (t→0, t→1, n=2).]

title: Existence-Result Family
text: Existence-Result Family Your paper shows that an object of a desired class exists. A class of objects has been defined or implied; whether the class is non-empty (or contains an instance with specified properties) is the salient question of the paper. The paper's main contribution can be expressed as "we show there is an X satisfying Y", or "we construct an X satisfying Y", or "for every precondition P there is an X with property Q". "Existence" admits many depths: pure-classical (object exists by an abstract argument), constructive (an explicit witness is exhibited), with-error-bounds (a witness is exhibited with quantitative tolerance), via-cross-domain-bridge (existence transferred from a different domain). The depth determines downstream usefulness — a theorem prover wants a constructive witness, an applied mathematician may need error bounds, a structuralist may accept abstract existence. Pick the leaf that matches the depth your paper actually reaches. 1. Identify the depth: pure-classical / constructive / with-error-bounds / via-bridge. 2. Locate the leaf member-pattern that matches the depth. 3. Identify the witness that the paper exhibits (or argues exists). 4. State explicitly what the witness shows and which preconditions determine it. exemplar[arxiv-2604.21888v1] # Kneser graph Hamilton cycle exists exemplar[arxiv-math/0603597v1] # Gevrey ultardistribution algebras (constructive) exemplar[arxiv-2604.20840v1] # Z/2-harmonic forms via 4-polytopes (constructive) member[math-informal/construct-an-explicit-witness] # constructive member[math-informal/construct-auxiliary-object] # constructive (indirect) member[math-informal/use-probabilistic-method] # pure-classical / non-constructive member[math-informal/numerical-scout] # with-error-bounds (hint of construction) Existence claims are the load-bearing skeleton of much of mathematical research, but they vary enormously in their constructive content. Putting the family parent above its members lets pattern-classification (manual or automated) recognise an existence-paper at family granularity even when the leaf depth is uncertain, then refine to the leaf when more detail is available. The family is the *useful coarse classifier*; the leaf is the *precise depth*. next[Determine the existence depth and pick the matching leaf.] next[Identify the witness explicitly (object + precondition for it).] next[Cross-check: does the paper *exhibit* the witness, or only *argue* one exists?]

title: Hypothesis Category Check
text: Hypothesis Category Check When invoking a theorem, verify that your objects live in the category (smooth, PL, topological, algebraic, measurable, ...) that the theorem is stated for. You want to apply a known result to objects in your proof, and the result's statement specifies regularity or categorical hypotheses on its inputs.
