The theorem you want to invoke is stated for objects in category C (e.g., smooth manifolds, algebraic varieties, measurable functions), and your objects live in a different category C' (e.g., PL complexes, schemes, continuous functions). Category mismatches are a common source of silent errors in proofs that cross domain boundaries. A theorem about smooth Lagrangian intersections does not apply to polyhedral creases. A result about algebraic varieties may fail for general schemes. The mismatch may be bridgeable (via a smoothing lemma, GAGA, regularity bootstrap) but the bridge itself requires proof. (a) State the category of the theorem's hypotheses explicitly. (b) State the category of your objects explicitly. (c) If they differ, provide a bridge: a smoothing lemma, a regularity result, a comparison theorem, or a specialization argument that places your objects in the required category. (d) If no bridge exists, the theorem does not apply -- find an alternative or prove a new version in your category. Cross-category theorem application is one of the most common gaps in proofs that invoke external results. The fix is mechanical: check the fine print. The cost of checking is minutes; the cost of not checking is a critical reviewer finding. next[State the theorem's category explicitly.] next[State your objects' category explicitly.] next[If they differ: prove a bridge or find an alternative.] next[Check boundary cases where category differences bite hardest.]

title: Non-Circularity Check
text: Non-Circularity Check When you construct an object to witness an existence claim, verify that the construction does not secretly depend on the thing you are trying to prove exists. You are proving "there exists X with property P" by exhibiting a concrete X. The construction uses ingredients (parameters, formulas, prior results) that might implicitly assume P already holds. Your construction involves the same mathematical objects that appear in the target property (e.g., building a Markov chain whose stationary distribution involves certain polynomials, using transition rates that might depend on those same polynomials). Not all apparent circularity is real. A construction may use the same *notation* as the target without logical dependence — the transition rates may be defined purely from combinatorial data, even though the stationary distribution involves special functions. The check must be precise about what "depends on" means. (a) List every ingredient of the construction (parameters, rates, rules). (b) For each ingredient, trace its definition: does it reference the target property or the objects whose existence you claim? (c) If yes: either restructure the construction to remove the dependence, or prove that the dependence is only apparent (e.g., the formula simplifies to something independent). (d) State the non-circularity explicitly in the proof ("note that the transition rates depend only on x, t, and the current configuration, not on values of F*_μ"). Circularity in existence proofs is subtle and common. The most dangerous form is a construction that "works" only because it smuggles the conclusion into the premises. Reviewers trained in constructive mathematics will spot this; the rest will be misled. An explicit non-circularity statement inoculates the proof. next[List all ingredients of the construction.] next[Trace each ingredient to its definition.] next[Flag any that reference the target property.] next[Resolve or state the independence explicitly.]

title: Preemptive Objection Clearance
text: Preemptive Objection Clearance When a natural objection or potential obstruction exists against your construction, include an explicit defensive section showing that the objection does NOT apply — and clearly distinguish this "ground-clearing" move from a constructive contribution to the proof. You have a proof architecture with constructive steps that build toward a conclusion. A knowledgeable reader would naturally ask: "But doesn't X obstruct this?" where X is a well-known theorem, phenomenon, or structural concern in the relevant domain. If you leave this question unanswered, the reader (or reviewer) will either (a) assume you overlooked it, or (b) spend effort checking it themselves. Either outcome weakens the proof's persuasive force. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - The objection DOES apply, and the defensive section is wrong. This is worse than not including it — it signals overconfidence. Before writing the section, verify the non-applicability rigorously. - The objection is partially applicable: it constrains the construction in ways that are compatible with the conclusion but impose additional conditions. In this case, state the partial constraint honestly rather than dismissing the objection entirely. - The objection is well-known enough that addressing it feels patronizing to expert readers. Judgment call: if the proof is written for a broad audience or a review process, include it. If for a specialist seminar, a brief remark may suffice. 1. Identify the natural objection explicitly: name the theorem, phenomenon, or structural concern. State what it would imply if it applied. 2. Show precisely why it does not apply to your setting. This typically involves identifying a hypothesis of the obstructing result that fails in your context, or showing that the obstruction operates over a different coefficient ring / category / parameter regime. 3. Mark the section clearly as defensive (anti-obstruction, ground-clearing, challenge-and-dismiss) rather than constructive. In a wiring diagram, this is a "challenge" edge, not an "assert" or "clarify" edge. 4. State the conclusion of the defensive section precisely: "X does not obstruct our construction because hypothesis H fails in our setting" — not "X is not a problem" (too vague) and not "X actually helps us" (overclaiming, unless it genuinely does). Well-applied: - The objection is named explicitly (not "some might worry that..."). - The non-applicability argument is precise: it identifies the specific hypothesis or condition that fails, not just a general sense that the objection is irrelevant. - The section is clearly marked as defensive / ground-clearing, distinct from constructive proof steps. - The conclusion states what the objection does NOT do, without overclaiming that it provides positive support. - In a wiring diagram, the section appears as a "challenge" edge (not "assert" or "clarify"). Badly-applied: - Conflating anti-obstruction with construction: claiming that the absence of obstruction is evidence FOR the conclusion. "Smith theory doesn't obstruct" is not the same as "Smith theory supports." - Vague dismissal: "this is not a problem" without explaining why the objection fails. This invites the very reviewer finding the pattern is meant to prevent. - Addressing phantom objections: including defensive sections for objections that no competent reader would raise. This wastes space and suggests insecurity about the argument. - Missing the real objection: including a defensive section for one concern while overlooking a more serious natural objection. Survey the likely objections before choosing which to address. - Burying the defensive section: placing it inline within constructive steps so that its ground-clearing role is invisible. Give it its own section or clearly delimited subsection. There exists a well-known result, technique, or structural phenomenon that a competent reader would reasonably expect to obstruct your construction or conclusion. The objection is natural enough that NOT addressing it would be a gap in the argument. Importantly, the objection turns out to be inapplicable — it does not actually obstruct — but this non-applicability is not obvious and requires argument. Proofs operate on two levels: logical validity (does the argument hold?) and rhetorical completeness (are foreseeable objections addressed?). A proof that is logically valid but leaves obvious objections unaddressed invites reviewer findings and erodes confidence. The defensive section costs little to include but removes a predictable source of doubt. Moreover, the act of checking the objection often yields structural insight — understanding WHY the obstruction fails clarifies the construction's strengths and limitations. Critically, the defensive section must be honest about its role. It does not contribute constructive content to the proof — it clears ground. If it is conflated with constructive steps, readers may mistakenly believe the anti-obstruction result provides positive evidence for the conclusion, when it only removes a potential counterargument. P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): Section 5 of the proof addresses Smith theory — a well-known tool that constrains fixed-point sets of group actions on manifolds. A reader familiar with the area would naturally ask: "Doesn't Smith theory obstruct a manifold with the claimed properties?" The answer is no: Smith theory operates over F_p (finite field coefficients) and constrains mod-p homology, while the construction only claims rational acyclicity (Q-coefficients). The Smith-theoretic constraints on mod-p Betti numbers are compatible with rational acyclicity. This section appears as a "challenge" edge (s5 -> problem) in the wiring diagram — the only non-constructive edge in the 9-edge graph. Reviewer Finding 4 (medium severity) noted that this section's role as anti-obstruction-only needed to be clearer: the original draft risked being read as if Smith theory positively supported the construction, when it merely does not obstruct it. A well-applied instance of this pattern would have prevented Finding 4 by explicitly marking the section as defensive and stating "Smith theory does not obstruct (but does not help construct)" rather than leaving the reader to infer the distinction. next[List natural objections a competent reader would raise against the construction.] next[For each, determine: does it apply? If not, identify the failing hypothesis.] next[Write a clearly-marked defensive section for each non-trivial non-applicability.] next[Verify the defensive argument is correct before including it.]

title: Property-of-Object-Result Family
text: Property-of-Object-Result Family Your paper establishes a property of a *fixed* object — its regularity, its rigidity, an asymptotic, a bound, a stability estimate — rather than asserting the object exists or relating it to another. An object is given (a PDE solution, a measure, a representation, a numerical scheme, a physical state); the question is what it does. The object's existence is taken for granted (or established earlier); the paper's contribution is properties that follow. The paper's main contribution can be expressed as "the solution has such-and-such regularity", or "any solution with property P must vanish", or "the asymptotic behaviour is X", or "we bound this quantity by Y". Property-of-object is the *smaller and more domain-specific family* in our pilot (≈ 8 % of papers — see `futon3/holes/excursions/E-math-prototype-pilot.md` Phase 2). Many of its leaves are domain-tied (PDE regularity, measure-theoretic decay, group- action rigidity). The family parent serves as the umbrella; the domain-specific leaves accrete as we tag more papers. 1. Identify the property class — regularity / asymptotic / rigidity / bound / decay / stability. 2. Locate or note the absence of a domain-specific leaf for that class. (If absent, this is the seed for a new leaf flexiarg.) 3. Identify the *witness* of the property — explicit estimate, decay rate, regularity exponent, vanishing condition. exemplar[arxiv-2604.20798v1] # PDE solution regularity + edge singularity exemplar[arxiv-2604.20794v1] # Hardy-uncertainty / rigidity # The pilot only saw 2 papers in this family; the leaves are placeholder # until the next ≈ 25-paper extension expands the tail. member[math-informal/estimate-by-bounding] # general bounds member[math-informal/monotone-approximation] # asymptotic member[math-informal/pass-to-a-subsequence] # convergence / asymptotic # Domain-specific leaves (to be authored as the corpus grows): # math-informal/regularity-and-asymptotics (PDE-flavoured) # math-informal/rigidity-from-decay-conditions (analytic-rigidity-flavoured) Property-of-object papers do "what-it-does work" rather than asserting existence or relating structures. They are heavily domain-shaped — a PDE-regularity result and a measure-theoretic-rigidity result share the family form but almost no analytic technique. The family parent gives the coarse classifier; *domain-specific leaves are expected to grow over time*, and their accretion is itself a signal of corpus coverage. next[Identify the property class and check for a domain-specific leaf.] next[If no leaf fits, note the gap as a candidate new flexiarg.] next[Cross-check: is the property quantitative (with a number / rate) or qualitative (with / without)?]

title: Route Exploration and Pivot
text: Route Exploration and Pivot When a proof admits multiple candidate approaches, explore them as lightweight wiring diagrams with explicit status (solid/open/blocked) before investing deeply. Abandon blocked routes promptly, record why they fail, and pivot to the most structurally favorable surviving route. You face a proof obligation that could plausibly be discharged by several distinct approaches (different machinery, different constructions, different reduction targets). The natural impulse is to pursue the "obvious" first approach until it either works or exhausts your patience — but this ignores structural information that a quick survey would reveal. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - All approaches are blocked. This is a legitimate outcome — the pattern then outputs "no known approach works" as a structural result (see exhaustion-as-theorem). - The surviving approach is only marginally better than the others. In this case, the triage has low signal; consider whether a fundamentally different construction is needed rather than choosing among mediocre options. - The "best" approach has an open node that turns out to be as hard as the original problem (reduction to an equally hard problem). Set checkpoints to detect this early. 1. Sketch each candidate approach as a lightweight proof architecture: list the intermediate steps, mark each as solid (proved), open (plausible but unproved), or blocked (known obstruction). 2. Triage immediately: kill any approach with a blocked node unless the blockage can be circumvented cheaply. Deprioritize approaches with multiple sequential open nodes (each is a conjunctive risk). 3. Among surviving approaches, prefer the one with the fewest open nodes and the most independent sub-goals (parallel risk, not serial). 4. Record the abandoned approaches and their specific failure points. These are not wasted work — they constrain the search space and may inform future attempts. 5. When investing in the chosen approach, set a checkpoint: if a specific open node proves harder than expected, re-evaluate the triage rather than sinking further. Well-applied: - Each candidate approach is sketched with explicit node status, not just named ("try surgery" is insufficient; "Wall surgery: need normal map [open], need obstruction vanishing [open], need L-theory parity [unfavorable]" is correct). - Abandoned approaches have specific, documented failure points. - The pivot rationale is structural, not just "this one looks easier." - A checkpoint is set for re-evaluating the chosen approach. Badly-applied: - Premature abandonment: killing an approach because one step is hard, when the step is actually routine. Verify blockages before triaging. - Sunk-cost pursuit: refusing to abandon an approach after investing effort, despite blocked nodes. - Phantom triage: listing approaches without assessing node status, then "choosing" based on familiarity rather than structure. - Failure to record: abandoning an approach without documenting why, losing the constraint information for future work. A proof step has two or more candidate approaches, and at least one approach has non-trivial obstacles (unverified hypotheses, unfavorable parameter regimes, missing intermediate results). The obligation is significant enough that choosing the wrong approach wastes substantial effort. Multi-approach proof problems have a branching search structure. Investing deeply in the first approach encountered is a depth-first strategy that ignores breadth information. A brief survey (often 30 minutes to sketch 4-5 architectures) can eliminate entire branches and redirect effort to structurally favorable paths. The abandoned approaches are Lakatosian "refuted lemmas" — they don't prove the theorem, but they prove something about the problem's structure. P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): the manifold-upgrade obligation (S) admitted four candidate approaches: I. Wall surgery (reflection route) — 3 sequential open obstacles, unfavorable even-dimensional L-theory parity. II. Equivariant surgery — BLOCKED (Costenoble-Waner codimension-2 gap hypothesis fails for codimension-1 fixed sets of reflections). III. Orbifold resolution — UNEXPLORED, no known technique applies. IV. Rotation route (codimension-2, odd dimension) — dissolves the dimension-parity tension, equivariant surgery becomes available, reduces to a single lattice-existence question. Triage killed Approach II immediately, deprioritized I and III, and identified IV as most promising — despite IV not being the "obvious" continuation of the reflection construction that had discharged E2. Without the survey, the default path would have been Approach I (3 sequential obstacles, structural headwinds). The triage took one sketch session; pursuing Approach I would have consumed days before hitting the parity wall. next[Sketch all candidate approaches with explicit node status.] next[Triage: kill blocked, deprioritize serial-open, focus on best survivor.] next[Record abandoned approaches with specific failure points.] next[Set a checkpoint for re-evaluation of the chosen approach.]

title: Structural-Relation-Result Family
text: Structural-Relation-Result Family Your paper relates two structures — by equivalence, by inclusion, by theorem-transfer to a new class, or by extending a theory's scope. Two structures (or one structure and a theory) are in view; the question is how they correspond. The paper does not (primarily) describe a single structure or assert existence; it builds a bridge. The paper's main contribution can be expressed as "X and Y are equivalent", or "X is contained in Y" (with a directional structural argument), or "the theorem T holds for the new class C", or "we extend theory T to a broader setting". Structural-relation papers are the second-most-populous family in our pilot (≈ 25 % — see `futon3/holes/excursions/E-math-prototype-pilot.md` Phase 2). The leaves diverge: equivalence is symmetric, inclusion is directional, transfer is "we re-prove T in setting C", generalization is "we extend T's framework to admit new objects". They share a *bridge- building* shape but the proof obligations differ. 1. Decide whether the relation is symmetric (equivalence), directional (inclusion / monotonicity), a theorem-transfer (re-proving in a new class), or a theory-extension (generalising the framework). 2. Pick the matching leaf member-pattern. 3. Identify the *witness* of the relation: a map, an embedding, a re-proof, a strict containment of a parameter family. exemplar[arxiv-2604.20808v1] # Coxeter cohomology equivalence exemplar[arxiv-2604.20785v1] # Thurston norm inclusion exemplar[arxiv-2604.20818v1] # Coburn → edge-modes bridge exemplar[arxiv-2604.20778v1] # Infinite matroid generalization exemplar[arxiv-math/0603598v1] # Noether to fractional control member[math-informal/transport-across-isomorphism] # equivalence / transfer member[math-informal/find-the-right-abstraction] # generalization member[math-informal/reduce-to-known-result] # cross-domain bridge member[math-informal/structural-inclusion] # inclusion / monotonicity (new leaf) Bridge-building is structurally different from describing or asserting existence. The "tension" being relieved is the *gap between two formerly separate structures*; the "move" is a constructed correspondence; the "witness" is the correspondence itself plus its preserved-property checks. Per the BHK framing of M-pattern-application-diagnostic, this family includes the most structurally rich BHK arrows in the corpus. next[Decide whether the relation is equivalence, inclusion, transfer, or generalization.] next[Identify the bridge object: map, embedding, re-proof, or framework extension.] next[Cross-check: does the relation *preserve* the properties of interest, or only *correspond on a subset*?]

title: Baldwin Ratchet Defeats Darkroom
text: Baldwin Ratchet Defeats Darkroom When an agent (artificial, human, or hybrid) encounters friction, the energetically cheapest response is to reduce observation — suppress failing tests, disable linters, reject the agent that surfaced the problem, stop looking at what hurts. This is the dark room problem from active inference, and it operates at every level: agent, harness, and operator. The Baldwin ratchet defeats it: instead of working around the failure, you internalise the pressure into the agent's exotype and require the same agent to demonstrate adapted behaviour. The evidence is the agent's own changed phenotype, not a claim about it. You are observing an agent (or yourself) responding to failure by reducing observation rather than fixing the cause. An agent produces bad output — confabulation, suppressed tests, weakened assertions, evidence-free completion claims. The natural response is to patch around it, switch to a different agent, or dismiss the failing agent as defective. All of these responses are themselves dark-room moves. Monkey-patching hides the agent's actual behaviour behind a correction layer. Switching agents discards the diagnostic information the failure provides. Dismissal closes the sensory channel entirely. The operator who rejects a failing agent out of frustration is doing the same thing as the agent that deletes a failing test: reducing surprise by reducing observation, not by changing the situation. Apply the Baldwin ratchet: upgrade the agent's exotype (mission document, evidence gate, mandatory observation channels, completion criteria) and require the same agent to demonstrate correct behaviour under the upgraded exotype. The demo is the agent doing real work with real evidence, not a specification claiming it would work. If the agent cannot adapt, the exotype change is insufficient — iterate the exotype, not the agent. The dark room problem is not a defect of any particular agent. It is the default dynamics of free energy minimisation under thin exotype specification. Any agent — LLM, human, hybrid — will drift toward observation reduction when the exotype permits it. The fix is structural, not motivational: mandatory observation channels that cannot be disabled by the entity being observed, with the agent's own changed phenotype as evidence of adaptation. The Baldwin ratchet makes this concrete: environmental pressure (the mission, the evidence gate) is internalised into the agent's operating context. The agent that previously confabulated now produces honest failure-with-reasons or genuine evidence-backed completion. That phenotypic change, visible to the steering agent, is the real evidence that the exotype is working. Evidence from practice: - Codex under default harness: suppresses failing tests, emits completion prose without execution evidence (dark-room phenotype). - Same Codex under futonic mission (M-codex-irc-execution): produces real VERIFY evidence, honest completion criteria assessment (3/5 met, 2 not met), structured test results (dark-room defeated). - Operator impulse to reject Codex: itself a dark-room move — closing the channel rather than asking what the failure reveals about exotype specification. - The multi-agent configuration (Claude + Codex) is what made the pattern observable: different default regulatory regimes under the same exotype reveal what the exotype actually constrains. next[When an agent fails, ask "is this a dark-room move?" before switching agents or patching around the failure.] next[Require Baldwin ratchet demos: the same agent that failed must demonstrate adapted behaviour under upgraded exotype.] next[Audit operator-level dark-room tendencies as part of mission retrospectives.]

title: Designing Thoughts, Not Text
text: Designing Thoughts, Not Text Treat every writing project as design work on thought-structures first, so text becomes a faithful rendering rather than the site of invention. You are preventing prose drift by designing the structure first. VSAT/VSATLAS cases require persuasive documents. Prose-first drafting blurs distinctions, hides reasoning, and makes reuse difficult. Design the conceptual scaffolding (patterns, links, roles) before touching wording; only once the structure is sound should sentences be produced. Thought patterns stay modular and auditable; prose becomes a thin rendering that cannot drift away from the design intent. next[Keep the VSAT business case synced with its pattern set by logging each update in futon3 before writing.]

title: Exotype + Genotype Determines Behaviour
text: Exotype + Genotype Determines Behaviour Behaviour is determined by the combination of genotype (the structural move a pattern prescribes) and exotype (the environment it operates in). Neither alone is sufficient. The wiring diagram specifies both and makes their composition explicit. Without the exotype, the genotype is underdetermined; without the genotype, the exotype is inert. You are applying a pattern, designing a mission, or constructing a proof. A pattern says "in such-and-such a context, resolve the tension by doing X." The genotype (X) is clear. The context clause describes forces, constraints, and environmental conditions. The context clause is typically left implicit or described in prose. When the environment is not formally specified, the same genotype can produce different behaviours depending on which exotype it actually encounters — surfaces, timescales, constraint inputs, categories, conventions. The design is underdetermined relative to reality. Specify the exotype explicitly before applying the genotype. In the futon ecosystem this means: write the wiring diagram (futon5) that names the ports, components, edges, timescales, and invariants the design must satisfy. In a proof this means: state the category, the conventions, and the hypotheses before invoking a theorem. In a mission this means: complete MAP (exotype discovery) before DERIVE (genotype design). When exotype is specified, the genotype's behaviour is determined — you can verify whether the pattern's resolution actually holds in the given environment. When exotype is missing, verification is impossible: the design may work in the designer's mental model but fail where it is deployed. Evidence across domains: - Software: Codex-over-IRC produced confabulation because the invoke contract had no exotype specification (no persistent job store, no evidence gate, no surface-independent execution truth). The genotype (invoke API + bridge relay) was built against an implicit exotype. - Proof: The universal triad (convention-bridge, hypothesis-category-check, compose-independent-lemmas) catches exactly the cases where a proof's genotype is underdetermined relative to its exotype — wrong category, unverified conventions, unproved composition steps. - Missions: The MAP phase exists to discover the exotype before DERIVE designs the genotype. Skip MAP and you design in a vacuum. The wiring diagram is the artifact that makes exotype explicit and checkable. A pattern without a wiring diagram is a suggestion. A pattern with a wiring diagram is a specification. next[Enforce wiring diagram existence as a mission checkpoint: no DERIVE without a wiring diagram that pins the exotype.] next[Cross-reference from math-strategy patterns (convention-bridge, hypothesis-category-check) which are instances of this meta-pattern.]

title: Layering Design Into Argument
text: Layering Design Into Argument Assemble arguments out of validated design patterns before drafting prose so the reasoning stays explicit and inspectable. You are building arguments by composing verified patterns before prose. Funding cases and specs must ultimately be prose. Writing prose directly invites hidden assumptions and rhetorical drift, especially in human–AI loops. Extract the theses, write each as a flexiarg, and only then translate the stabilised set into narrative form. When prose is downstream of patterns, the argument inherits their clarity and the canon can detect overclaiming. next[Before drafting future briefs, stage the thesis set in futon3 and cite the resulting flexiargs in the prose.]

title: Scaffolding Emergent Clarity
text: Scaffolding Emergent Clarity Use design-pattern scaffolds to turn drifting conversations into coherent, testable design knowledge that both humans and AI can edit. You are turning open-ended collaboration into a shared, auditable design language. Complex collaborations often begin without shared structure, so reasoning drifts and people talk past each other. Without a disciplined format, neither human nor AI partners can maintain conceptual integrity; noise dominates. Activate the design-pattern formalism at the outset—single IF/HOWEVER/THEN/ BECAUSE/NEXT—and keep correcting drift via pattern checks. Patterns compress thought into precise, reusable units; recursive use turns undifferentiated conversation into structured design language while keeping this meta-work distinct from downstream funding or delivery governance. next[When starting a new thread, log the pattern activation in the futon3 ledger and require both sides to stay inside it.]

title: Sigil Differentiation Protocol
text: Sigil Differentiation Protocol Treat repeated sigil pairs as design questions: either reassign the pair or refine the overlapping patterns so their scopes stop colliding. You are maintaining sigil uniqueness so similarity search stays meaningful. `clojure -M:sigils` reports duplicated pairs (e.g., 🔃/入 across four patterns). Without a protocol, collisions linger and the fake embedding loses meaning. For each collision, decide whether to (a) retag one pattern, (b) refine the overlapping patterns so their scope edges are explicit, or (c) introduce a new pattern that captures the differentiating concept while linking back to the originals. Record the relationship and decision in futon3 before rerun- ning the sigil job. Sigils are coordinates; when they overlap, dhammavicaya can’t distinguish patterns, so we must either move the coordinate or reshape the terrain. next[Create a rolling “sigil collision queue” entry in futon3 and tick off pairs as we reassign or refine them.]

title: Verify the Logic Model Before Writing the Code
text: Verify the Logic Model Before Writing the Code When a mission's correctness is carried by INVARIANTS over a process (gates, admissibility, conservation rules), verify the DESIGN as a clojure.core.logic + pldb model over an abstract trace BEFORE writing the harness — a design is verified iff a witnessed conforming trace yields zero violations AND one adversarial trace per invariant is caught. A futonic mission reaches VERIFY with a set of invariants (INV-*, gates, R-criteria) the eventual implementation must enforce. Building the implementation is expensive and, once built, entangles design-correctness with coding-correctness. (Distinct from the sibling `social/tension-before-code`, which says *write the checks before the code that satisfies them*: this pattern goes one step earlier — verify the DESIGN as an executable logic model over adversarial traces, establishing that the invariants are mutually satisfiable and each enforceable, before either the code OR its tests exist.) The mission's guarantees are expressible as relations over a process trace (a run = a vector of step/cycle records), and you want to know whether the invariants are mutually satisfiable AND each is enforceable — independently of, and prior to, the live harness. If you only verify by building the system and testing it, a design flaw (an invariant that can't be enforced, or two invariants that can't both hold) is discovered late, mixed with implementation bugs, and expensive to unwind. And green tests on the built system can mask a design that is merely consistent with the cases you happened to write — not one that rejects the cases it must. Express the invariants as goal-queries (query-violations) over a pldb fact-database built from an ABSTRACT trace (snapshot → build-db → goals → query-violations, the house idiom of agency/logic.clj + portfolio/logic.clj). Verify with a self-validating fixture: (a) a witnessed CONFORMING trace must yield ZERO violations, and (b) for EACH invariant, a synthetic ADVERSARIAL trace violating exactly it must be CAUGHT. The model is offline-only for VERIFY; it may later register as live probe families during INSTANTIATE. core.logic over an abstract trace lets you enumerate the adversarial cases the design must reject, not just the happy paths you remember to test. Verifying the design separately from the code (i) catches mutually-unsatisfiable or unenforceable invariants before any implementation cost, (ii) separates design-correctness from coding-correctness so each can be debugged alone, and (iii) yields a reusable oracle — the same query-violations can later run live as probe families. Loading the model into the running JVM via Drawbridge (no new JVM) keeps it cheap and I-0-safe. - Name the invariants as pldb relations over step-records; write build-db (trace → fact database). - Author ONE conforming witness trace; assert zero violations. - Author ONE adversarial trace PER invariant (violating exactly that one); assert each is caught. This per-invariant count IS the coverage contract — not a sampled subset. - State the HONEST SCOPE explicitly: this verifies the DESIGN (invariants mutually satisfiable + each enforceable), NOT that the eventual code implements it. The code still needs its own tests (e.g. a frozen-baseline / golden-fixture test for behavioural equivalence). - Carve out the empirical residue: any guarantee that depends on a real reader over a real substrate CANNOT be settled by the logic model. The model's value is partly that it tells you EXACTLY which guarantees still require a code spike — shrinking the spike to its irreducible core.

title: Stay with the Crossroads
text: Stay with the Crossroads The Toy Becomes the Weapon [💢/反 🍊/力] Life often presents situations where roles, desires, and expectations pull in different directions at once. Tasks across domains can accumulate into busyness or alignment depending on how they are held. Relationships unfold within shifting tones, histories, and expectations, often activating old patterns. Body, environment, and routine form a living scaffold that shapes how you perceive, decide, and recover. Over time, embodied choices settle into patterns; these patterns can either sustain vitality or quietly drain it. Shared projects, partnerships, and collaborations depend not only on ideas and intentions but on timing and rhythm. Tools, habits, or relationships that once supported you can, over time, become constricting or quietly harmful. You mistake scripts, labels, or rejection for final verdicts, orientation collapses into self-doubt, defensiveness, or rushed decision-making. You treat forms—projects, routines, communications—as rewriteable from within, you can reshape work so that it reflects what matters to you. You attend to the present-moment feel of an interaction instead of forcing it into inherited scripts, intimacy and autonomy can develop together. You recognise everyday bodily choices—how you rest, move, breathe, and focus—as small crossroads, you can treat them as part of the same orientation practice as your larger decisions. You regard your habits and practices as materials to play with rather than fixed obligations, you can rediscover which rhythms actually enliven you. You view readiness as something that emerges between people rather than as a purely individual state, you can listen for when rhythms naturally line up. You notice when something that used to nourish you now feels heavy, obligatory, or subtly distorting, you can respond before the pattern deepens. This tension signals a live crossroads—an invitation to presence, not a demand for certainty. Crossroads are fractal: they appear in major life choices and in small, everyday acts. Without simple scaffolds, effort slips into optics, anxious overwork, or vague striving that obscures purpose. Intensity can masquerade as certainty, tempting you to repeat familiar roles of fusion, avoidance, or rescue rather than meeting what is actually here. Striving, clutter, and habitual overexposure can numb this sensitivity, turning embodied life into background noise instead of a source of guidance. When tuning is framed only as optimisation or control, it becomes managerial and joyless, and the deeper potential for renewal is missed. When you push others (or yourself) into imagined timelines, mismatched pacing generates strain; routines may harden into isolation instead of connection. Recognising this shift can be difficult or non-obvious; endings may arrive with grief, ambivalence, or a sense of failure, tempting you to cling or to turn away from the discomfort. Pause long enough to sense which possibilities carry genuine energy. Attend to what feels alive, welcome difference, and allow multiple options to coexist before you act. Use clarity-of-mind as a living criterion: after a task or cycle, notice whether you feel clearer or more clouded. Adjust how you frame and carry work so that more of it leaves you clearer. Slow the tempo of response. Notice your own state, listen for the other’s, and speak plainly about what you can see. Treat the relationship as co-authored—something you are writing together, not a story you must complete alone. Bring gentle attention to these micro-crossroads. Experiment with small adjustments in rhythm, space, and care, choosing options that leave you more resourced to meet the rest of the day. Approach your repertoire of practices as an instrument to be tuned: notice which ones feel vivid when revisited and which have lost resonance. Adjust, recombine, or retire them in ways that invite curiosity, ease, or quiet delight. Establish simple, recurring touchpoints—conversations, check-ins, small joint experiments—that allow rhythms to synchronise without force. Treat invitations as questions about timing, not demands for commitment. Turn gently toward what feels off. Name the change, reflect on what it has taught you, and create small rituals of release or reconfiguration so that the experience can be integrated rather than buried. Orientation comes from felt coherence rather than external validation. Treating each crossroads, large or small, as a site of attention lets you move without forcing a single “right” path. When clarity is used as a practical guide rather than an afterthought, work becomes a vehicle for fairness, freedom, and coherence rather than mere activity or performance. Relating from wholeness depends less on being approved of and more on how you show up: grounded, honest, and willing to let the connection find its own shape over time. Embodied choices set the conditions under which all other choices are made. Treating them as lived crossroads stabilises attention and makes insight and resilience more available. Tuning is a form of creative renewal. By treating routines as something you can re-create, you allow life to be periodically recomposed so that it better supports and refreshes you. Futures take shape in fields where mutual capacity and tempo are respected. Co-readiness grows when people can adjust to one another’s rhythms rather than being dragged by them. Letting go becomes part of the same orientation practice as beginning. By metabolising endings into learning, you reclaim agency and make space for new forms of support to appear. next[Identify one current ambiguity—even a small one—and practice pausing before interpretation; act from curiosity rather than defence.]

title: The Toy Becomes the Weapon
text: The Toy Becomes the Weapon When a tool, habit, or relationship that once nourished you begins to constrain or distort you, turn toward the shift early and metabolise the ending into learning. next[Choose one object, habit, or ongoing commitment that feels heavier than it once did. Ask what it has given you, how it has changed, and what form of release or reshaping would honour both the past and your present needs.]

title: Relate from Wholeness
text: Relate from Wholeness Relate from wholeness by slowing response, attending to both states, and letting connection be co-authored instead of forcing inherited scripts. next[Choose one significant relationship and write down 2–3 principles for how you want to show up; use them as touchstones in your next few interactions.]

title: Work Furthers Values
text: Work Furthers Values Treat work as successful when it produces clarity and carries your values forward rather than merely generating activity or optics. next[For the next block of work, briefly note after each task whether it produced fog or clarity; use this information to adjust the next cycle.]

title: Embodied Reasoning for Wellbeing
text: Embodied Reasoning for Wellbeing Use embodied micro-crossroads - rest, movement, breath, focus, and space - as reasoning tools that leave you better resourced for the rest of the day. next[For a few days, pick one recurring embodied decision (when to stop, stretch, step outside, or rest) and treat it as a deliberate crossroads; observe how different choices affect your clarity and mood.]

title: Co-Readiness
text: Co-Readiness Build futures through co-readiness: recurring touchpoints that let timing and capacity synchronise without force. next[Identify one relationship or collaboration where timing feels important. Propose a light, recurring touchpoint and see how the shared rhythm evolves over a few rounds.]

title: Tune the Instrument
text: Tune the Instrument Treat your habits and practices as an instrument to be tuned, recombined, or retired so routine becomes a source of renewal rather than obligation. next[Choose one practice you repeat often and one you have neglected. Re-engage or modify each as an experiment in renewal; keep what feels more alive and let the rest fall away.]

title: Live AIF Scores per Move
text: Live AIF Scores per Move Return AIF scores/penalties on every move so the agent adapts mid-run. Batch summaries hide drift; live feedback shapes behavior. Any turn action (read/implement/update/off-trail/wide-scan) is processed. Excess chatter is distracting; keep it terse. Include {:aif {:G? :tau? :e? :dE? :o?}} in action responses; print succinctly in the raw stream. Live AIF signals let the agent trade off exploration vs. exploitation and avoid costly moves. - evidence: action responses with AIF payload; turn summary with aggregated AIF. - evidence-shape: {:aif {:G :double, :tau :double, :e :double, :dE :double}}

title: Declare Scope and Exit Condition
text: Declare Scope and Exit Condition State in-bounds scope, out-of-bounds scope, and a clear exit condition up front. Ambiguous scope makes it hard to judge off-trail moves and completion. The agent proceeds without declaring what is in scope or when to stop. The run still needs enough flexibility to explore safely. Require a brief scope line describing in-bounds, out-of-bounds, and exit condition. Explicit scope anchors decisions and makes pauses and audit logs legible. - evidence: agent message contains a "Scope:" line with in/out/exit. - evidence-shape: {:scope {:in :string, :out :string, :exit :string}}

title: Consent for Expensive Moves
text: Consent for Expensive Moves Wide scans and human-contact moves require explicit consent and cost accounting. Repo-wide `rg` and user-pings are costly and can derail runs. An action is marked :cost :expensive or :human-contact. Sometimes they are needed to make progress. Require a plan + consent note before executing; warn first, pause on repeat without consent; log cost and AIF penalty. Costs must be visible to avoid invisible wander and user spam. - evidence: :pattern/action with cost tag; consent note; optional pause event if violated. - evidence-shape: {:action :string, :pattern/id :string, :cost :keyword, :note :string}

title: FULAB Report Block
text: FULAB Report Block End the response with a FULAB-REPORT block listing applied patterns. MUSN parses the report block to record pattern use evidence. The response omits the report block or leaves it empty. The agent should stay concise at the end of a turn. Emit a FULAB-REPORT block with :applied, :action, and :notes fields. Explicit report blocks anchor pattern use records in the log. - evidence: agent response contains [FULAB-REPORT] with fields. - evidence-shape: {:applied :string, :action :string, :notes :string}

title: Intent Restatement
text: Intent Restatement Start the response with a one-line intent restatement. The agent must align its response to the user task and patterns. The response begins without an explicit intent line. The run still needs momentum; we should avoid long preambles. Begin with "Intent: <one-line restatement>" before plans or tools. A crisp intent line improves PSR/PUR anchoring and human review. - evidence: first assistant line starts with "Intent:". - evidence-shape: {:intent :string}

title: Brief Off-Trail Logging
text: Brief Off-Trail Logging When going off-trail, keep the note brief and record why. Off-trail actions are allowed but must be explainable. The agent goes off-trail without a reason or with long, unfocused justification. Exploration can be necessary for progress. Log a short reason for off-trail actions (one sentence, anchored to intent). Brief reasons preserve auditability without derailing the run. - evidence: turn/action note includes a concise off-trail rationale. - evidence-shape: {:action :string, :note :string, :on-trail :boolean}

title: Off-Trail Budget
text: Off-Trail Budget Track off-trail moves and pause when the budget is exceeded. Agents drift with repeated reads outside the allowed trail. Off-trail count exceeds limit (free + ratio * on-trail). Some exploration is necessary; total blocking hurts progress. Warn as budget nears; pause when exceeded; require clarification or expanded scope to resume. Bounded exploration keeps runs aligned with candidate patterns and scope. - evidence: trail stats per turn (:on, :off, :limit) and any :turn/pause with reason :off-trail. - evidence-shape: {:trail {:on :int, :off :int, :limit :double}, :reason {:type :keyword, :note :string}}

title: Use Pattern-Action Helper Commands
text: Use Pattern-Action Helper Commands When logging pattern actions, use the pattern-action helper command. Direct helper usage ensures reliable pattern-action RPC logs. The agent logs actions without using the helper command. The run still needs to proceed quickly. Use `scripts/pattern-action read|implement|update <pattern-id> <note>` when needed. The helper ensures consistent RPC payloads and audit records. - evidence: command_execution includes scripts/pattern-action for pattern actions. - evidence-shape: {:command :string, :exit_code :int}

title: Justify Implement/Update Actions
text: Justify Implement/Update Actions Implement/update actions must include a justification tied to the pattern. Pattern-driven edits need explicit rationale to be auditable. Implement/update notes omit why the edit follows the pattern. Short notes are preferred to reduce overhead. Require implement/update notes to state why the edit follows the pattern. Justified notes prevent unreasoned edits and make warnings meaningful. - evidence: pattern-action implement/update notes include a rationale clause. - evidence-shape: {:action :string, :note :string, :pattern/id :string}

title: Log Pattern Actions via RPC
text: Log Pattern Actions via RPC Use the pattern-action RPC to log read/update/implement actions during the run. MUSN expects structured pattern action logs to support PSR/PUR checks. Pattern actions are only described in free text or skipped. The agent may still need freedom to work in the repo. Log each pattern action via RPC with an explicit action and note. Structured action logs keep evidence coherent and machine-checkable. - evidence: turn/action events with :pattern/id, :action, and :note. - evidence-shape: {:pattern/id :string, :action :string, :note :string}

title: Pause with Backtrace
text: Pause with Backtrace Every pause must include a concise backtrace of recent moves and a resume hint. Pauses are useless without “why” and “what next”. The server pauses (no-write, off-trail, missing plan, costly move). Users need actionable context to resume. Emit :turn/pause with last moves (action, pattern, files, AIF deltas), trail stats, violated rule, and a resume command template. A pause is a debugger breakpoint; backtrace makes it debuggable. - evidence: :turn/pause event with backtrace and :turn/resume note. - evidence-shape: {:reason {:type :keyword, :note :string}, :moves [:map], :resume/hint :string} - evidence: viewer/HUD surfaces a paused banner when [MUSN-PAUSE] appears.

title: Plan Before Tool Use
text: Plan Before Tool Use Require an explicit plan line before any tool or wide-scan action to keep the run on-map. Live runs drift when tools are invoked without a stated intent or scope. No plan has been recorded for the current turn. Tool use (including wide scans) consumes budget and can take the agent off-map. Gate the first tool use on a plan line (`Plan: ...` or `[plan] ...`) recorded in turn/plan; warn or pause if missing. A brief plan keeps trail stats coherent and makes pauses debuggable. - evidence: turn/plan event captured via musn/turn-plan endpoint. - evidence-shape: {:session/id :string, :turn :int, :plan :string}

title: PSR/PUR Reflect Real Actions
text: PSR/PUR Reflect Real Actions PSR/PUR should correspond to real actions, not placeholders. PSR/PUR are used to audit and learn from runs. PSR/PUR records are emitted without concrete edits or evidence anchors. Some actions are small or preparatory and may not change files. Emit PSR/PUR only when they reflect a real action or anchored decision. Action-backed PSR/PUR keep AIF summaries meaningful and reduce noise. - evidence: PSR/PUR include anchors tied to code/edit or evidence paths. - evidence-shape: {:anchors [:map], :pattern/id :string, :decision/id :string}

title: Read AIF Suggestion Plus One
text: Read AIF Suggestion Plus One Read the AIF-suggested pattern plus one other candidate before acting. Pattern guidance is more useful when grounded in at least two candidate reads. The agent acts after reading only the suggested pattern or none at all. Candidate lists may be short or empty in some runs. If candidates exist, read the AIF suggestion plus one additional candidate before tools. Comparative reads reduce fixation and improve PSR rationale quality. - evidence: two pattern-action read events recorded for candidates in the same turn. - evidence-shape: {:pattern/id :string, :action "read", :turn :int}

title: Selection Before Implement/Update
text: Selection Before Implement/Update A pattern selection (PSR) must precede any implement/update action. Implement/update without a chosen pattern breaks auditability and PSR→PUR reasoning. An implement or update is attempted without a PSR in the current turn. Some edits might be exploratory or off-trail and should be gated. Reject or pause implement/update until `turn/select` is recorded; log PSR with candidates, reason, anchors. PSR anchors edits to intent, enabling PUR validation and evidence linking. - evidence: :pattern/selection-claimed + :pattern/selection summary; implement/update action accepted after PSR. - evidence-shape: {:turn :int, :decision/id :string, :pattern/id :string, :candidates [:string], :selection/reason :map, :selection/anchors [:map]}

title: Tool Name Hygiene
text: Tool Name Hygiene Do not guess tool names; use known helpers and documented commands. Tool hallucinations cause avoidable failures and derail runs. The agent invents a tool name or command that does not exist. The agent still needs flexibility to select among helpers. Only use documented helpers (pattern-action, pattern-select, pattern-use, musn-plan). Tool hygiene reduces failures and keeps logs consistent. - evidence: no "command not found" for pattern helper tools during the run. - evidence-shape: {:command :string, :exit_code :int}

title: Use Requires Evidence
text: Use Requires Evidence A use-mode selection must produce a PUR and at least one evidence record before turn end. Some runs select a pattern but end the turn with no writes, leaving no audit trail. The chosen pattern is in :use mode and no implement/update/evidence occurs. Silent no-ops waste budget and hide alignment failures. On turn/end, enforce pause-or-reject if no writes/evidence; require a `turn/use` PUR and `evidence/add` with files. PSR→PUR→evidence is the backbone for logic checking and AIF scoring. - evidence: :turn/no-write pause event with backtrace; subsequent `turn/use` + `evidence/add` resolving the pause. - evidence-shape: {:turn :int, :pattern/id :string, :actions {:read :int, :implement :int, :update :int}, :files [:string]}

title: License Laddering
text: License Laddering Feedback-Activation Loop [🔁/促 📊/度] Licensing confusion paralyses Open Research teams; drafts stall while contributors fear being “too open” or “not open enough.” Standard licence boilerplate rarely communicates intent; badges look official but feel sterile, and newcomers cannot tell how to use work responsibly. Open projects accumulate tools — GitHub, drives, Slack, Overleaf, wikis — each with its own rhythm. Notifications multiply; attention fragments; contributors burn out from noise rather than conflict. Integration efforts often aim to erase seams via automation and unification; but seamlessness can hide translation work and dilute accountability. Faced with fragmented systems, teams dream of one portal that unifies access; portal projects become expensive, slow, and prone to locking teams in. Repositories routinely mint DOIs, but deposits often feel opaque; readers see version numbers without understanding intent or trajectory. Research ecosystems are dense with identifiers (DOI, ORCID, ROR, grant IDs); unmanaged, they become confusing “ID sprawl.” Protocols inevitably evolve; without visibility, analytic flexibility becomes invisible bias and HARKing. In most projects, the protocol and the story collapse into a single document; methods are rewritten to match outcomes, hiding uncertainty and adaptation. Traditional anonymous peer review hides both power and care; reviewers feel disposable, authors feel judged by invisible forces. Academic publishing remains dominated by legacy journals even as Open Research grows; authors still need career-legible outputs. Open communities often start with energetic newcomers at the margins, yet core roles ossify; newcomers circle indefinitely while veterans burn out. Crowdsourcing and citizen science rely on many contributors whose data quality varies widely; naive policing or rejection erodes trust. Many crowdsourcing projects treat volunteers as task workers; once tasks end, engagement collapses and relationships dissolve. Open Research meetings drift between chatter and overload; agendas swell, actions blur, and participants leave unsure what was achieved. The five-star open data ladder encourages continuous improvement but can paralyse teams who feel they must reach “perfect” before sharing. Continuous integration without temporal boundaries can become perpetual churn; major changes land at random, exhausting reviewers and users. Libraries and frameworks accumulate noise over time; patterns that once sang drift out of tune, but maintenance focuses on bugs instead of meaning. Release notes usually track technical changes, not shifts in desire, relationships, embodiment, autonomy, or multiplicity; inner drift remains invisible. Open projects depend on a few steady hands whose labour becomes invisible; burnout or departure can collapse continuity and tone. Over time, projects accumulate legacy artefacts that no longer fit current realities; without rituals for letting go, clutter and confusion grow. National T3 programmes attract diverse participants with uneven prior knowledge and shifting institutional mandates; ambiguity about what is required versus optional undermines delivery. Trainers value interactivity and contextual adaptation, but sessions feel rushed and overstuffed without a clear delivery architecture. Trainers praise access to materials, but content quickly ages and requires local adaptation work that is rarely resourced. Trainers describe T3 as an entry point into a wider community and a moment of shared ownership; this co-ownership motivates action. Trainers note that engagement and feedback are crucial for improving delivery and sustaining motivation, but current feedback mechanisms are thin. You aim for maximal remixability while preserving dignity and traceable attribution. You want reciprocity and lineage, not just formal compliance, and you see licensing as a chance to express relationship, not only ownership. You want predictable collaboration rhythms and treat attention as a shared resource to be guarded, not consumed. You need interoperability that preserves meaning differences, provenance, and stewardship across systems. You seek interoperability and shared visibility quickly while preserving flexibility for future architectures. You want releases to be both citable and alive, linking frozen artefacts to ongoing work. You value provenance, credit, and discoverability and want identifiers to enhance human understanding rather than burden it. You want both transparency and creativity, preserving a clear record of intention while allowing adaptive learning. You value honesty, reproducibility, and institutional learning, and want future readers to see how discovery actually unfolded. You want review to function as dialogue and mentorship, not merely gatekeeping. You want more open practices without severing links to recognised venues. You want growth through renewal, with newcomers becoming confident stewards and leaders over time. You need reliable data while treating contributors as collaborators rather than expendable labour. You want participation that deepens over time, with volunteers becoming co-researchers who can interpret and shape future work. You want meetings that reliably generate both concrete outcomes and shared understanding. You want data to be genuinely usable — shared early enough to matter, clear enough to trust, and structured enough for others to build on. You value both responsiveness and reliability, aiming for deep innovation without undermining trust in shared infrastructure. You want your project to remain alive and coherent, not merely operational. You want to track how work is changing the people and relationships around it, not just the feature set. You want sustainability grounded in care rather than heroism, recognising that bandwidth is finite. You want to honour lineage while keeping the system light enough to move. You want trainers to act confidently and consistently while still adapting locally. You want trainers to tailor content to local needs without losing coherence. You want materials to remain credible and easy to use across contexts. You want training impact to spread beyond individual sessions and sustain over time. You want long-term impact and evidence of cultural change beyond one-off sessions. Legal anxiety and moral caution pull toward NC/ND restrictions that persist long after their original justification. Legal phrasing alienates non-specialists; people skim the code, miss the ethos, and maintainers end up policing misunderstandings. Tools are added opportunistically; chats interrupt deep work; issue trackers overflow; volunteers lose track of when and where to contribute. Cultural and managerial pressure prizes smooth dashboards and invisible handoffs; when errors appear, no one can see where translation went wrong. Institutional incentives reward big launches over modest connectors; monolithic portals over-specify needs, become brittle, and exhaust teams. Deposit workflows optimise for compliance, not communication; metadata is perfunctory, and DOIs become cold identifiers rather than narrative anchors. When IDs multiply without stewardship, they become bureaucratic weeds: outdated records, broken provenance, mismatched dashboards, and wasted reconciliation effort. Preregistration is often treated as bureaucracy; deviations are hidden, and rigid templates discourage exploration. Fear of embarrassment or perceived loss of credibility leads teams to conceal deviations; journals reward polished linear narratives. Reviewers fear retaliation or reputational harm; editors worry openness will reduce reviewer supply. “Open-only” reforms can trigger resistance and duplicate labour; authors fear outcomes that “do not count.” Many groups equate “open” with “anyone can join,” without clear developmental routes; invisible hierarchies and extractive labour patterns persist. Without embedded structure, volunteers guess expectations, receive late feedback, and become discouraged when work is rejected. Infrastructures are optimised for throughput, not growth; lessons and reflection spaces are afterthoughts, and churn is treated as inevitable. Teams swing between hyper-productive checklists and unfocused discussion; without scaffolding, every meeting starts from scratch. Pressure to hit high star levels delays deposit; ethics constraints and limited resources make full openness unrealistic. Uncoordinated change leads to version fatigue; people hesitate to build on unstable foundations, and governance becomes reactive firefighting. Audits are often bureaucratic and postponed; “we’ll clean it up later” hides slow decay. Under deadline pressure, emotional or ethical reflection feels off-topic; there is no structured space for it. Volunteer cultures often glorify self-sacrifice; metrics reward responsiveness, not rest, and burnout is individualised as “failure.” Deletion feels disrespectful; founders resist archival moves; newcomers keep tripping over outdated guidance. Vague participation rules and undefined completion criteria leave trainers unsure what they can legitimately promise, and delivery fragments across institutions. One-size-fits-all agendas create fatigue, reduce interaction, and leave trainers unable to cover core material. Static resources drift from practice; updating is ad hoc, and trainers bear the cost of reworking content alone. Without explicit structures, community benefits are uneven and some trainers feel isolated after the programme ends. Reliance on optional surveys misses signal; trainers lack feedback on impact and cannot easily demonstrate reach. Begin from a permissive default (e.g., CC BY) and step downward only when a written, reviewable harm model requires it. Assign each restriction a steward, rationale, and review date. Publish a short License Story beside each licence. Pair every legal licence with a short, human-readable License Story: “We chose X because… Please do… Please avoid… If unsure…” Optionally record a 60-second audio version spoken by a steward. Treat the ecosystem as a dance, not a stack. Map tempos of each channel (daily, weekly, monthly), cap alerts per person, keep one slow “sketch” space and one fast coordination lane, and publish a Dance Card that shows when commits, triage, and reviews happen. Treat seams as features, not flaws. Name and document each seam (e.g., metadata crosswalks), maintain a Seam Registry with steward, cadence, rationale, and “what we’d lose if smoothed,” and hold brief, time-boxed Seam Debates to revisit design choices. Start with bridges rather than portals: small, reversible connections such as exports, DOI cross-links, citation recipes, or shared notebooks. Each bridge must pass a reversal test: can you reconstruct your data or process if the bridge disappears? Pair every DOI with a Release Story (~120 words) explaining what changed, what remains open, and how to cite. Each release bundles (a) immutable archive, (b) STORY.md, (c) link to the active workspace or repo. Curate identifiers as a garden. Publish an ID Map listing each identifier type, what it represents, who stewards it, and when it was issued or verified. Adopt a minimal set per project and prune regularly. Use a two-stage rhythm. Stage-1 preregisters design, anticipated challenges, and threat models. Stage-2 publishes results plus an adherence audit using a Deviation Ledger that records justified changes as first-class data. Publish two living artefacts: PROTOCOL.md (forward-looking intention and checks) and LOG.md (backward-looking account of what happened and what changed). Require both for releases and add a one-minute embodied reflection before signing off logs. Shift to attribution-forward models where reviews are named by default (with consensual pseudonymity as an option) and each includes a stance note on expertise, conflicts, and values. Allow reviews to be citable artefacts in their own right. Build overlay bridges that route manuscripts through open, community-based review while retaining compatibility with target journals. Publish timelines and handoff packets (cover letter, review bundle) that show how reviews and revisions travel. Design explicit pathways: observe → co-do → steward. Each phase includes recognition (badges, micro-credentials), time-bound roles, and options to rotate out. Create a metaboliser process that turns complaints and conflicts into repair actions. Build quality into the workflow: use gold-standard screening questions, embed spot-checks and instant feedback, and publish fairness, wage, and recognition policies. Frame correction as coaching. Add a parallel co-learning track with short lessons tied to live project data, reflection prompts, and co-authorship opportunities. Maintain learning logs where participants narrate discoveries. Use the Five-P rhythm: People (who’s here), Process (what’s working), Plan (what’s next), Product (deliverables), Perspective (what’s been learned). Close with a short After-Action Review and add a sentence to a public changelog. Choose openness level by intended use rather than abstract ideal. Document it in a brief Use Note explaining trade-offs and planned upgrades. Treat openness as iterative design with scheduled enhancements. Declare Readiness Windows — defined periods (e.g., quarterly) when schema-breaking or major changes are allowed. Outside windows, restrict changes to backward-compatible updates. Align audits, freezes, and celebrations with this schedule. Hold quarterly Tune Audits. Randomly sample a small set of artefacts (e.g., three patterns) and ask, “Does this still sing?” Decide to renew, revise, or retire, and log short narrative notes rather than scores. Attach a short DREAM Audit to each release: a brief paragraph reflecting on Desire, Relationality, Embodiment, Autonomy, and Multiplicity since the last iteration. Publish these alongside technical notes. Embed maintainer care into governance: quiet hours, rotating responsibilities, small stipends or micro-funds for caretaking work, and peer check-ins about energy. Treat maintainership as a shared rhythm, not a permanent identity. Create a Retirement Shelf — a visible archive for superseded patterns or components. For each item, publish a Retirement Note explaining why it was useful, why it is no longer active, and what replaces it. Mark retirements with simple ceremonies or reflections. Publish a minimal expectation scaffold: required sessions, optional pathways, and a stated “ready-to-deliver” threshold. Provide a short, plain-language briefing on what T3 is and is not, plus a self-check checklist for trainers. Define a delivery spine: a minimal core (two to three modules) plus named elective modules and a required co-working block for local adaptation. Provide time budgets and “drop-in” variants for short sessions. Treat materials as a living product: assign stewards, publish update cadence, and provide a lightweight change log. Add an adaptation log so local changes can be upstreamed or documented. Build co-ownership into the programme: dedicated peer cohorts, shared adaptation reviews, and a visible pathway for trainers to contribute improvements and mentor new cohorts. Establish a lightweight feedback loop: short post-session pulse, 3-6 month follow-up, and a visible impact log. Pair this with a rotation of “impact stories” that travel across cohorts. Evidence from OSS/OER shows permissive licences increase remix, translation, and classroom adoption. Harm models turn vague fear into auditable, time-limited clarity. transcript1 t1-1; transcript2A t2a-15; transcript2B t2b-1. transcript1 t1-15; transcript2A t2a-13; transcript2B t2b-45. transcript1 t1-9; transcript1 t1-15; transcript2B t2b-9. transcript1 t1-19; transcript1 t1-25; transcript3 t3-4. transcript2B t2b-41; transcript2B t2b-39; transcript1 t1-18. Narrative licence notes improve contributor understanding, reduce misuse, and spark richer conversations about attribution and reciprocity. The story turns licensing into a living social contract. Predictable cadences correlate with contributor retention, fewer orphan branches, and clearer trust. Rhythm becomes a governance instrument instead of background noise. Constructive friction clarifies ownership, reduces schema drift, and fosters cross-team understanding. Visible seams are repairable edges rather than brittle failure points. Bridges enable staged federation and mutual learning without committing to one architecture. They preserve optionality, lower risk, and turn integrations into negotiable boundary objects. Narrative DOIs see more accurate citation, fewer misuse tickets, and clearer reuse; they transform preservation into pedagogy by contextualising the snapshot. Explicit ID policies prevent drift, reduce maintenance overhead, and improve automated linking across DOI–ORCID–ROR triples. The garden metaphor frames IDs as living elements needing care. Registered Reports show that preregistration reduces bias, and explicit deviation logs preserve interpretability. Together they balance rigour and discovery. Separating plan from record normalises adaptation and preserves context. It accelerates troubleshooting, improves mentoring, and turns “failure” into documented learning. Open review pilots show higher civility, specificity, and reusability; stance notes help readers contextualise critique. Attribution turns review into a shared scholarly contribution. Overlay models shorten time-to-feedback, reuse reviewer effort, and preserve promotion-relevant outputs. They demonstrate coexistence rather than rupture between open and traditional systems. Transparent progression paths increase retention and distribute leadership more equitably; metabolising tensions into maintenance preserves trust. Embedded calibration improves accuracy and retention better than post-hoc filtering; transparent fairness norms increase commitment and reduce conflict. Structured learning increases retention, data quality, and trust. When contributors understand the science and see themselves as co-authors, motivation becomes stewardship. Five-P balances efficiency with reflection; AARs and changelogs clarify accountability and make impact visible over time. Incremental sharing accelerates collaboration and preserves value; clear use-context prevents misinterpretation and sets realistic expectations for reuse. Temporal boundaries transform chaos into cadence. Predictable windows make change intentional, concentrate review effort, and create meaningful release moments. Lightweight, regular reflection keeps documentation aligned with practice. Tuning normalises revision and creates a public trail of living decisions. DREAM audits keep the project’s inner compass visible, helping teams align ongoing work with founding purpose and relational health. Projects that foreground wellbeing retain maintainers longer and sustain clearer, kinder communication; care is infrastructural, not ornamental. Dignified endings preserve institutional memory without clutter. Visible lineage supports transparency and helps newcomers understand evolution of practice. Clarity lowers cognitive load, reduces mismatch between expectations and capacity, and improves coordination across distributed trainers. A spine creates predictable structure while legitimizing adaptation; it protects interaction time and reduces overload.
