Run editorial meetings for this catalogue using Five-P and publish the changelog. - Produce a printable Five-P agenda/timer card. - Collect stories of meetings improved by this pattern and share them. - Publish a Use Note for this catalogue’s data, with current star level and roadmap. - Create a showcase of 2-, 3-, and 5-star datasets with annotated rationales. - Develop a simple “Data Readiness Meter” visual tied to star levels. - Publish this catalogue’s change calendar with marked readiness windows. - Tag schema-affecting changes with their window in git history. - Design a “Window Badge” indicating last passed readiness review. - Publish Tune Logs for this catalogue showing renew/revise/retire outcomes. - Experiment with simple rituals (audio snippets, icons) to mark tuned items. - Compare tuned vs. untuned sections for perceived energy and clarity. - Add DREAM notes to the next release of this catalogue. - Link each DREAM audit from the release notes index to keep them findable. - Invite individual contributors to contribute micro-audits and aggregate them. - Visualise DREAM themes over time as a simple trend or word map. - Publish a Maintainer Care Charter for this catalogue. - Document at least one care intervention and its observed effects. - Add a “Care Pulse” survey item to Tune Audits for maintainers. - Initialise a Retirement Shelf for this catalogue and migrate one pattern into it. - Record a short retirement reflection for that item. - Draw a lineage map linking retired artefacts to their successors. - Create a one-page “T3 in Brief” with required/optional components. - Define a minimal competency checklist with examples of acceptable adaptations. - Add an onboarding call focused on expectations and scope. - Publish three spine variants (90-min, half-day, full-day). - Add a template for local adaptation notes and decisions. - Include a standard Q&A and co-working segment in every variant. - Create a quarterly update rhythm with named maintainers. - Add a one-page adaptation log template to each module. - Prioritize updates for sections flagged as outdated by trainers. - Establish rotating peer cohorts with monthly check-ins. - Create a contribution pathway for trainers to propose updates. - Pair new trainers with a local or regional mentor. - Add a two-question pulse survey after each session. - Run a quarterly impact story round-up shared across cohorts. - Provide a simple template for reporting reach and learning.

title: Bioliteracy & Open Value
text: Bioliteracy & Open Value Bioliteracy & Open Value You are turning bioliteracy teaching assets into open research value without overloading staff. BMS teaching already runs hands-on, data-rich pedagogy that yields reusable datasets, notebooks, and protocols. These artefacts stay siloed from research culture; teaching workloads are intense, data ethics complex, and open practice feels like “extra work.” Treat BMS as the north-node chariot bridging teaching and research. Use Fit-for-Use Stars to calibrate openness, bring Quality-by-Design Crowd techniques into labs, and add a Citizen Co-Learning track so students and communities follow real research logic and publish interpretable outputs. When teaching artefacts are shared with calibrated openness, students gain researcher identity, BMS gains institutional visibility, and Brookes signals pedagogical excellence tied directly to Open Research value. next[Pick one BMS module and map which artefacts can graduate to calibrated open outputs.]

title: Data-Intensive Practice on Office-Centred Infrastructure
text: Data-Intensive Practice on Office-Centred Infrastructure Data-Intensive Practice on Office-Centred Infrastructure You are exposing infrastructure seams so ECM can act without waiting for a full rebuild. ECM researchers now rely on high-throughput, computational workflows, but institutional infrastructure is still tuned to desktop/Office-era assumptions. Requests for advanced platforms are treated as costly edge cases, so unsupported clusters, brittle scripts, and risk-laden storage hacks proliferate. Surface seams instead of hiding them: document the pressure points between ECM workflows and central IT, build reversible Bridge-Before-Portal workflows (e.g., container recipes, Story DOI-linked notebooks), maintain an Identifier Garden for datasets/software, and hold seam debates to decide which frictions are intentional. Making seams visible lets ECM plan around constraints, lowers institutional risk, and produces reusable assets without waiting for a full infrastructure overhaul; chariot nodes move faster when they know the terrain. next[Log the top three ECM seam points and draft one reversible bridge workflow.]

title: Open Practice Beyond Hypothesis
text: Open Practice Beyond Hypothesis Open Practice Beyond Hypothesis You are making practice-based research legible without forcing it into hypothesis templates. Arts and performance research produces experiential, multimodal knowledge that resists hypothesis-driven templates. Repository forms, REF narratives, and grant portals still assume linear methods, fixed datasets, and analytic prose, so practice-based work becomes distorted or underspecified. Name Arts as the west-node chariot: use License-as-Story and Story DOIs to contextualise practice, apply the Method/Documentary Split (PROTOCOL.md vs LOG.md) to separate intention from creative trace, and build small narrative bridges—audio snippets, annotated scores—instead of forcing data schemas. Open Research serves Arts when it clarifies lineage, process, and situated intention; story-driven artefacts preserve dignity, reduce administrative friction, and let practice be legible without erasing its form. next[Prototype one Arts deposit using the Method/Documentary Split and Story DOI.]

title: Progress Cylinder Assurance
text: Progress Cylinder Assurance Progress Cylinder Assurance You want proof of movement well before a deadline rather than a last-minute scramble. a task has an explicit SCHEDULED or DEADLINE date and an EFFORT estimate of 1h or more. work tends to bunch after the date, producing false signals of progress and unreliable delivery. require an early effort marker: log at least one work session totaling ≥ 1/3 of EFFORT no later than 3 days before the scheduled/deadline date; if that marker is missing, reschedule or split the task. cylinder-set guarantees are about partial evidence within a bounded prefix; early effort is a compact proof that work is moving through the pipe. next[Add a check in the agenda view that flags tasks with EFFORT but no early effort marker.]

title: Shared Futures Beyond Atomised Incentives
text: Shared Futures Beyond Atomised Incentives Shared Futures Beyond Atomised Incentives You are stabilising cross-disciplinary futures work so it survives incentive pressure. SRF and EHL convene Brookes’ shared-futures agenda, yet academic incentives still reward individual outputs and leave network work unpaid or invisible. Without explicit pathways, core members burn out, newcomers hover at the periphery, and the futures agenda stays fragile. Treat SRF/EHL as the south-node chariot that carries cross-disciplinary futures work. Publish Peripheral-to-Core Pathways with rotation dates, add a Citizen Co-Learning track, and run gatherings on the Five-P rhythm so action and reflection stay in sync and justified in workload narratives. When shared-futures labour has visible routes, learning scaffolds, and simple meeting cadences, it strengthens participation, legitimises community stewardship in promotions, and keeps Brookes’ futures agenda alive under constraint. next[Publish the pathway map and schedule one Five-P cadence pilot session.] next[Use this pattern to frame the January sandpit scheduling and invitations.]

title: Spread Effort Assurance
text: Spread Effort Assurance Spread Effort Assurance Some tasks need sustained attention across multiple days to avoid brittle output. a task has EFFORT of 3h or more and a scheduled or deadline date. single-session completion hides uncertainty and leaves no space for reflection or correction. require work to be clocked on at least two distinct days before completion; otherwise split the task or schedule a review pass. effort spread creates natural review cycles and reduces the probability that rushed work ships unexamined. next[Add a simple tag or property to mark multi-day work and surface it in agenda checks.]

title: Steward of the Open Research Emporium
text: Steward of the Open Research Emporium Steward of the Open Research Emporium You are naming library stewardship as the infrastructure that makes OR navigable. Library OR teams quietly hold metadata, repositories, visibility, and preservation work that lets research feel navigable. Their labour is framed as routine administration; workloads rise without recognition, and stewardship remains invisible even though it props up every School. Position the Library node as the Steward of an Open Research Emporium. Use Story DOIs, Identifier Gardens, and Platform Choreography to make deposits, licences, and showcases effortless, and curate a narrative Emporium page that links live projects to preserved artefacts. When stewardship is named as the ground the system stands on, it becomes negentropic—reducing duplication, clarifying provenance, and giving researchers trust that OR support lightens rather than loads their work. next[Draft the Emporium page outline and identify 3 live projects to feature.] next[Use this pattern to frame handover materials, case study templates, and video publication as stewardship work.]

title: Brookes OR Dungeon-Crawl Topology
text: Brookes OR Dungeon-Crawl Topology Brookes OR Dungeon-Crawl Topology You are making the OR topology visible so roles can navigate tensions and handoffs. OR1 hydrated Brookes with licences, bridges, tune audits, and identifier patterns, yet nobody can see how PVC, ORPM, UKRN, Schools, and Library positions interlock. Without a shared map, Open Research looks like scattered good ideas and unpaid extra jobs; mandate, coherence, horizon, and stewardship remain invisible tensions. Treat OR1 as dungeon tiles and OR2 as Xiangqi-style pieces. Draw a Mojo-inspired topology with UP (UKRN), CENTER (Two Joes), DOWN (Library), and directional School nodes, and author a short OR2 pattern for each node that shows how OR1 techniques reduce the friction already on their desks. Use the map as the spine for transition workshops and handover. When roles can point to a position—split center, wizard-above, steward-below—they stop feeling like quirks and become parts of a single institutional engine; OR techniques turn into moves the nodes already need rather than burdensome extras. next[Draft the topology map and validate it with one School lead and the ORPM.]

title: Two Joes, One Mandate
text: Two Joes, One Mandate Two Joes, One Mandate You are aligning mandate authority with integrative OR pattern leadership. Brookes’ Open Research centerline is split between two roles—the PVC (mandate, REF-facing authority) and the OR Programme Manager (pattern literacy, integrative insight). The pair seldom co-steer; the PVC lacks time to use the ORPM’s maps, the ORPM lacks formal authority, and the UKRN horizon role floats above them, leaving Schools to see OR as abstract noise. Name the dual-center engine explicitly. Pair the PVC’s “excellence under constraint” tension with the ORPM’s translation of OR1 techniques into School-ready moves, and triangulate with the UKRN lead during recurring briefings. Publish a Center Brief summarising the mandate, topology, and next moves so each School can locate itself. Authority and coherence rarely live in one office; treating them as a designed partnership turns Open Research into a negentropic force that reduces duplication and gives Schools a clear rationale rather than another committee. next[Draft the Center Brief and circulate it to PVC, ORPM, and UKRN for alignment.]

title: UKRN Horizon Bridge
text: UKRN Horizon Bridge UKRN Horizon Bridge You are translating UKRN horizon signals into usable moves for Brookes leadership and Schools. Brookes belongs to UKRN, giving it a long-arc vantage on trustworthy, reproducible practice across the sector. The UKRN lead sits far from day-to-day operations; without explicit ties to the Two Joes and Schools, horizon intelligence remains abstract and unused. Activate the UKRN lead as a horizon bridge: hold short quarterly altitude calls with PVC + ORPM, translate sector expectations into lightweight Bridge-Before-Portal moves (Story DOIs, licence narratives, shared templates), and cite UKRN alignment to justify incremental shifts rather than new committees. When horizon signals are routed through the centerline, Brookes gains negentropic alignment—less reinvention, stronger credibility with funders/REF, and practical improvements that feel supportive rather than imposed. next[Schedule the first quarterly altitude call and capture a short bridge memo for Schools.]

title: Xiangqi-Inspired Decorators (Institutional Pieces)
text: Xiangqi-Inspired Decorators (Institutional Pieces) Xiangqi-Inspired Decorators You are making the OR2 topology readable at a glance with role decorators. OR2 patterns describe tensions carried by distinct Brookes roles but there is no shared notation tying nodes to their positional logic on the topology map. Without visible decorators, PVC, ORPM, UKRN, Library, and School roles blur; newcomers cannot tell whether a pattern concerns mandate, horizon, stewardship, or frontline action. Borrow symbolic Xiangqi cues—Cannon for UKRN (UP), General + Advisor for the Two Joes (CENTER), Elephant for Library (DOWN), Chariots for Schools—and render them as minimal icons that sit beside each pattern header. Publish a legend so non-specialists can parse the map instantly. Decorators make institutional tensions legible at a glance, improving navigability, pattern casting, and recognition of positional constraints without resorting to heavy prose or cultural caricature. next[Draft the icon legend and apply it to one pilot map page.]

title: The Consent Gate — Don't Act Unilaterally, Act Through a Recorded Approval Locus
text: The Consent Gate — Don't Act Unilaterally, Act Through a Recorded Approval Locus An autonomous agent must not take an irreversible or outward-facing action unilaterally; route it through a consent-gate — a first-class, recorded operator-approval step at the exact locus where the action would otherwise fire — so the act is auditable and the supervised→autonomous transition is a swap at one seam, not a re-architecture. An autonomous loop can produce actions whose effects leave the system (sends, emails/EOIs, payments/invoices, publishes) or otherwise cannot be undone. The agent's action space includes outward or irreversible acts AND it runs partly or fully unattended. Blanket "ask before everything" wedges the loop — there is no autonomy left. Blanket "act freely" risks irreversible harm — there is no safety. And an approval that is an ad-hoc pause (not a recorded artifact) cannot be audited, replayed, or migrated to automation once trust is earned. Put a consent-gate at the action's locus. The agent acts autonomously on everything reversible and in-scope; for outward/irreversible acts it NAGs **with warrant** (per pattern-warranted-choice-point) and waits. The consent step emits a first-class `consent-gate-event` with an id that the executing action cites. Then: (a) every outward act is auditable to its approval; (b) supervised→autonomous migration = replacing the operator with an autopen at ONE known location, not rewiring the loop. WM-I4 is not "the WM doesn't act" — it is "the WM doesn't act UNILATERALLY." The consent-gate is the precise locus of that distinction. Making consent a first-class artifact (rather than an implicit human-in-the-loop pause) is exactly what lets trust be migrated incrementally: the operator's judgment is substituted at a named seam, once and only once it is earned, with the whole history legible. An un-recorded pause cannot be safely automated because there is nothing to point the autopen at. - The gate emits a typed `consent-gate-event` {:id :action :warrant-pattern :approved-by :approved-at | :declined}; the action cites the id (no orphan outward acts). - Pairs with pattern-warranted-choice-point: the gate's NAG carries the warrant (which signed-off rule made this consent-required). - The migration seam is the deliverable — track which consent classes have moved supervised→autopen and on what earned evidence. - evidence: consent-gate-events per run; approve/decline/edit ratio; outward acts with vs without a cited consent id (the latter = a violation). - evidence-shape: {:consent/events :int, :consent/approved :int, :consent/declined :int, :consent/edited :int, :orphan-outward-acts :int, :autopen-migrated-classes [:keyword]} Reversible, in-scope, low-blast-radius actions (gating them is pure friction). Internal computations with no outward effect (no consent surface needed). - The WM guardrails NAG outward/irreversible acts (sends/EOI/invoice) rather than executing them (`futon3c/wm/guardrails.clj` outward-op?). - WM-GUARDRAILS-SPEC.md: the consent-gate / gate-at-merge posture (staging branch; Joe merges = the consent locus for code).

title: Pattern-Warranted Choice-Points (and the NAG as the Undecidable Fork)
text: Pattern-Warranted Choice-Points (and the NAG as the Undecidable Fork) Every choice-point in an autonomous loop should carry the pattern(s) that warrant it; a NAG (operator-gated choice) is precisely the fork the patterns cannot decide, surfaced to the operator WITH its warrant and the one specific gap — turning "the system blocks you" into "your own rule is asking you to confirm one thing." An autonomous agent (the WM) ranks and selects actions; some actions are operator-gated (outward/irreversible, self-modifying, off-goal, or not-yet-advanceable). The choice to act-or-defer is governed by a set of patterns/rules the operator signed off on earlier. You have an autonomous decision loop whose choices are operator-consequential AND governed by a known set of signed-off patterns/rules (guardrails, admissibility, consent gates). A generic "operator confirmation required" block is illegible. The operator cannot tell whether it is their own rule firing or an arbitrary obstruction, so they either rubber-stamp it (the gate erodes to a no-op) or stall on it (the loop wedges). Worse, the patterns that DECIDE the autonomous picks are invisible too — the agent's "warranted" choices look like caprice from outside. Warrant every choice-point. (1) Each rule/pattern that governs a choice is named and recorded as the choice's **warrant** (reuse the existing `:fork-warrant` channel — frames already record the patterns applied at a fork). (2) An **autonomous** pick carries its warrant (the patterns that decided it) — recorded and auditable, not surfaced. (3) A **NAG** is the dual case: the patterns are silent, conflicting, or genuinely undecidable, so the choice is legitimately the operator's. Surface it with `{the firing pattern + its signed-off rationale, the specific undecidable gap, the minimal unblock}`. The NAG reads: *"Because of pattern P — which you set — I can't decide this one thing; fill the gap and we roll."* This is how a trusted human-AI handoff actually works in an interactive session: *"I've read your complex spec; I just need your nod on this one small thing."* The warrant makes the block the operator's OWN rule rather than the machine's caprice, so consent is informed, fast, and trust-preserving — sometimes a quick "yeah, let's roll," occasionally a real pause, but always over a legible gap. An unwarranted block is either rubber-stamped (defeating the gate's purpose) or stalls the loop (defeating autonomy). The NAG-as-undecidable-fork is the **dual** of the autonomous-pick-as-decided-fork: one pattern-warrant frame, two faces — decide-and-act vs cannot-decide-so-surface. - The rule→pattern mapping is DATA, not code branches: a table `{guardrail-rule → {pattern-id, warrant-text, gap, unblock}}`, so warrants stay auditable and editable. - Reuse `:fork-warrant` (futon3c/aif/loop_learning.clj) — a NAG is a fork whose warrant-patterns failed to decide; don't build a parallel channel. - The warrant CITES flexiargs (orchestration/consent-gate, aif/admissibility, aif/niche-construction, war-machine/advanceability), so the operator can read the actual rationale they signed off on. - Render the warrant in the operator view (needs-you / bulletin): pattern + signed-off-reason + the gap + the one unblock action. - evidence: warranted-vs-generic NAG count; operator decision-latency on warranted vs generic NAGs; rubber-stamp rate (approvals with no dwell) as a trust-erosion signal. - evidence-shape: {:nag/warranted :bool, :nag/pattern-id :keyword, :nag/gap :string, :nag/unblock :string, :decision/latency-ms :int, :decision/outcome <:approved|:declined|:edited>} Low-consequence, fully-reversible choices (the warrant overhead is unjustified — just act). Choices governed by NO pattern: then the right move is not to warrant the block but to author the missing pattern first (the gap is "this case is unspecified," which is itself operator work). - The WM NAG (`futon3c/data/wm/needs-you.edn`): today carries a generic per-class `:why`; the upgrade attaches the firing guardrail rule's pattern-warrant. - The interactive-session "approve this one thing and we start rolling" dynamic (Joe + claude-1) — the human prototype this pattern makes durable. - The consent-gate on outward/irreversible acts (orchestration/consent-gate) is the warrant for one whole NAG class.

title: Let Rules Evolve From Their Own Deferrals
text: Let Rules Evolve From Their Own Deferrals When a classifier rule defers as well as accepts, route the defers into an explicit typed channel and refine the rule from cluster shape in that channel. An active classifier (auto-approve / hard-rule / heuristic) produces both accept and defer outcomes on real traffic. The classifier's outcomes are operator-consequential AND its inputs shift over time (semantics drift, edge cases accumulate, false-positive/false-negative regimes change). Without explicit failure-tracking, refinement happens by intuition or never. Free-text or unlogged defer reasons cannot be clustered. Continuous reflection burns operator attention; periodic reflection requires a typed substrate to reflect over. (1) Define defer reasons as a typed enum (closed set, named upfront, kept small). (2) Every defer writes a record `{:reason <enum>, :inputs <hash-or-summary>, :timestamp ...}` to an explicit channel. (3) Periodically (after a sweep, batch, or N events) cluster the channel by `:reason`, by `:reason × <secondary-dim>` (file extension, repo, user-id, whatever the domain offers), and by `:reason × <pattern-suffix>`. (4) Clusters that exceed a threshold (≥3 entries) surface as candidate-rule-refinement proposals: `"N inputs deferred for reason R; consider refinement Y to accept them"`. (5) Operator promotes (with edits), suppresses, or defers each candidate. Promoted refinements are appended to the rule's data-driven invariant set. The defer queue is a prediction-error signal in the AIF sense — the rule's expected outcome was "accept" but the actual outcome was "defer." Cluster patterns in the defer-reason space surface where the rule is consistently wrong. Each cluster IS a candidate refinement readable directly off the data, without the operator having to invent it. Rules that evolve from their own observed failures stay calibrated against drift; rules without this channel rot. - evidence: count defers per period, broken down by reason; track distribution shape over time - evidence: count candidate-rule proposals generated per reflection cycle; track promoted-vs-suppressed-vs-deferred ratio - evidence: measure defer-rate reduction in the period following each promoted refinement (success metric: refinement-promoted → next-period defer-reduction) - evidence: detect rule drift via defer-rate trajectory — sustained upward trend on a reason cluster means the rule is losing calibration on that axis - evidence: assert the defer-reason enum stays closed-set (no schema drift); enum-extension is itself an operator decision worth tracking - evidence-shape: {:defer/count :int, :defer/reasons {:keyword :int}, :defer/secondary-cluster {[:keyword :string] :int}, :candidates/proposed :int, :candidates/promoted :int, :candidates/suppressed :int, :defer-reduction-pct :float, :enum-extensions [:keyword]} Rules applied rarely or with low-consequence outcomes (overhead not justified). Domains where defer reasons cannot be enumerated (the typed channel is impossible). Systems where the operator cannot act on candidates promptly (the channel becomes a pile of unprocessed signals; the rule rots faster than it can evolve). - futon3c street-sweeper INV-17 v2 reflection 2026-05-25: 142 defers from one sweep → 5 coarse + ~10 fine-grained candidate-INVs; promoting one (INV-18 test-context-paths skip security check) reduced :security-sensitive-diff defers 34 → 3 on next sweep - Spam filter false-positive learning (user "not spam" clicks = defer-channel) - Compiler diagnostic refinement from `// suppress` cluster analysis - Test-coverage gap analysis from skipped-test reasons - Prediction-market resolution-failure mode mining - realtime/learn-as-you-go: also about logging what works/fails; this pattern is the structured, typed-channel + clustering variant specific to rule refinement (the prior pattern is freeform learning notes) - aif/prediction-error: the underlying AIF-loop shape this pattern instantiates for rule design specifically (rather than for action selection) - code-coherence/dead-code-hygiene: relates by analogy — also lets a rule's effect (unused-flag) feed back into the rule's evolution

title: Lift State Into Shared Substrate; Keep Messages As Deltas
text: Lift State Into Shared Substrate; Keep Messages As Deltas For fast bounded coordination between two components, lift state into a shared substrate and keep messages as deltas. Two components (agents, services, modules) coordinate via message-passing on a bounded task that requires several turns to closure. Coordination requires more than one back-and-forth to reach closure, and each turn references context established in prior turns. Messages that carry full context grow with each turn, become slow to parse + produce at high cadence, are brittle to single-message loss (recovery requires reconstructing context from scratch), and create attention overhead for whichever side has to re-read the bundled context every turn. Designate a shared substrate (a markdown scratch file, a key-value store, a typed-event log) as the single locus of state for the coordination. Each message carries only the delta — a Q, an A, a sha, a "proceed" signal. Both sides append; both sides read the substrate before responding rather than re-establishing context inside the message. Close with an explicit marker (e.g., `DONE: <sha>`) so the substrate itself records the coordination's end. Lifting state out of the message stream decouples message-size from context-size. Coordination latency becomes (substrate-write + small-message-parse) rather than (full-context-parse + response-with-full-context). Single-message loss is recoverable from the substrate. Recoverability + smaller messages + cheaper parse compound across turns; the cadence supports more turns per unit of operator attention. - evidence: measure message-bytes per turn vs substrate-bytes — substrate-bytes should dominate; ratio < 0.2 implies the substrate is doing its job - evidence: count turns to closure under both protocols (state-in-message vs state-in-substrate) on a comparable task; expect ≥2× turn-throughput for substrate variant - evidence: simulate single-message loss; confirm recovery is possible from substrate alone - evidence: assess substrate-maintenance overhead — when it approaches or exceeds the message-passing savings, the pattern is misapplied (use unbounded-stream protocols instead) - evidence-shape: {:substrate/path :string, :substrate/bytes :int, :message/bytes-mean :int, :turns-to-closure :int, :loss-recovery-possible? :boolean, :substrate-overhead-ms :int, :message-latency-ms :int} One-shot async handoffs (substrate adds overhead with no coordination benefit). Pure-event-stream protocols (substrate creates an attractor that distorts the protocol toward shared-state assumptions; use event-sourcing patterns instead). Unbounded streams (the closure marker is the structural exit; without bounded scope, the substrate grows without recovery). - futon3c hop-wiring collab 2026-05-25: scratch at ~/code/storage/hop-wiring-scratch.md + 4 brief whistles → E-pilot-hop-trigger-wiring v1 shipped. Each whistle was a Q or A delta; scratch carried full state. - Shared AST between compiler passes (vs message-passing per transform) - Google Doc + Slack pings (vs reproducing the whole doc in every Slack message) - Microservices with shared cache + small RPC payloads (vs full-payload RPC) - Git as coordination substrate + brief PR comments (vs emailing patches) - realtime/authoritative-transcript: also about a single source of truth, but transcript-focused (replay semantics for late joiners); this pattern is about lifting state for active coordination cadence - realtime/structured-events-only: keeps message shape disciplined; complementary - social/scope-bounded-handoff: bounded-task framing is a precondition for this pattern

title: Agent-as-Mana-Unit Was the Wrong Unit (precursor note)
text: Agent-as-Mana-Unit Was the Wrong Unit (precursor note) Earlier framings — p4ng-era multi-agent simulation, conceptual sketches around mana-as-budget — treated AGENTS as the natural unit of mana accounting. This was wrong, in a way that became visible only after the substrate framing landed. Mana attaches to SESSIONS, not agents. The agent-as-unit reading is preserved here as a flawed precursor — useful to read, useful to point to, not useful to act from. p4ng-era pattern work modelled futon agents as semi-autonomous actors whose budget/license could meaningfully be tracked per-actor. The framing made sense in a multi-agent simulation context where each agent ran its own loop. It did not survive contact with operational reality, where: - One operator's session typically routes through multiple agents (Claude REPL, Codex, Tickle, Forum bots) in tight sequence, each contributing partial work to one coherent chunk. - The *felt cost* of allostatic load is borne by the operator, not by any individual agent. An agent has no metabolism beyond its turn. - Block-closure (the source of mana awards per `structure/mana-allostasis`) is an operator-attestable act, not an agent action. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. Whenever discussing budget/license/mana around agents, check the unit. If "agent X is over budget" is the claim, ask: what would the analogous claim about the *session* containing agent X look like? If it loses meaning, the agent-unit framing has snuck in. Restore the session-unit framing. - structure/mana-allostasis — formalises the balance equation with sessions as the temporal frame. - structure/block-as-futonic-revolution — defines block-closure as operator-attestable. - invariant-coherence/drain-channel-shape — drain channels under the mana-allostasis faculty; sibling pluri-channel framing. - p4ng/p4ng-agents — the precursor multi-agent framing this note corrects. - M-bounded-in-flight-state V-6 — the verification thread that surfaced the unit error and named it. The precursor was right about the *shape* of the problem (some notion of budget/credit/dana is needed; pure unbounded action selection is wrong). It was wrong about the *unit*. The fix is to keep the budget concept and reattach it to sessions: - `nonstarter_mana.clj`'s `--session` parameter is the operational evidence that the corrected unit is already in production code. - `structure/mana-allostasis` formalises balance per session. - The candidate invariant `budgeted-action-selection/mana-gated-work` (futon5a queue run-064) is the family-level expression of the same shape with the corrected unit. The precursor framing made three structural assumptions that looked plausible and turned out not to hold: 1. *Agent autonomy* — that agents have enough independent continuity to bear a budget across turns. They don't; an agent's continuity lives in the session that hosts it. 2. *Unit-of-attestation* — that agents can attest their own work-completion. They can't, in any way that survives the operator's distinct sense of "this is done." Block-closure requires operator attestation (see `structure/block-as-futonic-revolution`). 3. *Per-agent metabolic state* — that "this agent is tired" is meaningful. It isn't. The operator is the one who tires; agents are stateless across calls.

title: Institutional Drift
text: Institutional Drift Self-Patterning Mandate Repeated MAS sessions produce cumulative outcomes. A new MAS instance is initiated. MAS agents engage across different domains or networks. Existing reflection protocols underperform. Tasks and pattern contributions vary in complexity. Agents propose updates to patterns or governance processes. Agents engage in cycles of collaborative inquiry. Misuse or breakdown of patterns occurs in MAS. Agents disagree over pattern interpretation or application. Agents initiate new MAS structures. Pattern use becomes routinised. No clear shared norms exist. Norms, roles, or goals diverge significantly. Meta-cognition fails to produce new patterns. Some agents consistently overcontribute. title: License Laddering
text: License Laddering Retirement Shelf In Open Research projects, licensing choices often stall progress and collaboration. Standard boilerplate licenses fail to communicate intent or social meaning. Multiple systems and platforms coexist within an open-research ecosystem. Identifiers (DOI, ORCID, ROR) accumulate unevenly across projects. Evaluating open research processes requires evidence of both intention and execution. Methods often become entangled with their documentation. Traditional peer review obscures contributions beyond final authors. Early-stage projects often need support before formal grant cycles. Valuable contributors often begin at the periphery. Quality assurance is often treated as an afterthought. Research communities and the public learn at different rhythms. Impact planning lacks structured pacing. Deposits vary widely in quality and usability. Projects mature unevenly across dimensions. Quality drifts without periodic review. Projects embed values that shift over time. Maintainers often burn out in unacknowledged ways. Not all projects should run indefinitely. You want maximal remixability while preserving dignity and attribution. You want reciprocity and lineage rather than mere compliance. Users need smooth traversal across platforms. You seek smoothness and automation. You want newcomers to engage meaningfully. You want persistent identifiers to convey purpose. You want transparent provenance. You want training programmes to be accountable. You want clarity in training and auditability. You want credit to reflect actual labour. You want iterative development. You want inclusive talent development. You want distributed quality practice. You want meaningful public participation. You want credible impact development. You want consistent, reusable objects. You want to coordinate timing of releases or reviews. You want consistent improvement. You want clarity about value alignment in each release. You want healthy, sustainable stewardship. You want responsible long-term stewardship. Legal anxiety and moral caution create paralysis. Legal phrasing alienates non-specialists. Fragmented workflows create bottlenecks and inconsistent expectations. Critical judgments (ethics, consent, quality control) require deliberation. They arrive without context or confidence. A DOI alone does not express narrative or reasoning. Identifier management decays without stewardship. Single-stage assessment hides drift between plans and actions. Combined method-documents obscure both practice and record. Conventional processes exclude hidden contributors. Funding portals impose high thresholds. No pathways lead from peripheral engagement to core roles. Single-point checks miss errors and opportunities. Expertise gaps prevent shared learning. Ad-hoc timelines obscure progress. Binary accept/reject decisions are too coarse. Static schedules misalign with variable readiness. Continuous auditing is overwhelming. Values drift unnoticed in day-to-day work. Invisible labour and emotional load accumulate. Sunsetting is rarely planned. Begin from a permissive default and establish a clear sequence of license “steps” that can be tightened later as needed. Make facilitation roles explicit (e.g., Linker, Reflector). Insert a mid-session capture: “What’s something reusable?” Treat playful activity as epistemic input; ask what moves emerged. Add a closing step to review affordances and limits of the method. title: Pattern 7 — Signal the Further Benefit
text: Pattern 7 — Signal the Further Benefit Add a bonus layer that signals a further benefit beyond the main ask, giving the reader an extra reason to care without cluttering the letter. next[Choose a rotating bench of bonus benefits; track which ones resonate.]

title: Pattern 2 — Upgrade the Channel (Reveal the Real Ask)
text: Pattern 2 — Upgrade the Channel (Reveal the Real Ask) Upgrade the channel from surface contact to the real ask, so the letter speaks to the partner's actual need rather than the most obvious description of it. next[Annotate each target org with “stated vs underlying” needs before writing.]

title: Pattern 5 — Earn Their Approval (One Crisp Success)
text: Pattern 5 — Earn Their Approval (One Crisp Success) Earn approval by offering one crisp, believable success the organisation can picture immediately, rather than a fog of possible benefits. next[Maintain a small library of “success vignettes” mapped to common needs.]

title: Pattern 8 — Show Them How to Seal the Deal
text: Pattern 8 — Show Them How to Seal the Deal Make the next step frictionless by giving a clear, low-effort way for the recipient to advance the conversation at their current readiness level. next[Prepare CTA language for different readiness levels.]

title: Pattern 6 — Get Them Excited (Open the Future Field)
text: Pattern 6 — Get Them Excited (Open the Future Field) Open a future field by sketching a near-term world the collaboration could make possible, so the reader feels momentum instead of mere obligation. next[Sketch one “future vignette” per letter before drafting.]

title: Pattern 9 — Empower Them (Ghost Move)
text: Pattern 9 — Empower Them (Ghost Move) Use the ghost move to empower the organisation: write in a way that lets it feel the possibility as already latent in its own trajectory. next[Draft closing paragraphs that celebrate the org’s latent trajectory.]

title: Pattern 4 — Secure Their Goodwill (Cultural Alignment)
text: Pattern 4 — Secure Their Goodwill (Cultural Alignment) Secure goodwill by aligning explicitly with the recipient's culture and self-understanding before asking for commitment. next[Write a cultural-alignment paragraph template per sector and customise before sending.]

title: Pattern 3 — Inception Move (Epistemic Entry Point)
text: Pattern 3 — Inception Move (Epistemic Entry Point) Open with an inception move - a vivid metaphor or epistemic entry point that lets the reader see the problem differently before the practical ask lands. next[Collect vivid metaphors per organisation and rehearse delivering them in one line.]

title: Pattern 11 — Indicators Checker
text: Pattern 11 — Indicators Checker Check the draft against concrete indicators so each persuasive move is visibly present rather than assumed. next[Embed the indicator list into the drafting template.]

title: Pattern 12 — Obligations Checker
text: Pattern 12 — Obligations Checker Check obligations explicitly so the letter asks for a real commitment without smuggling in hidden burdens. next[Publish the obligations list alongside the drafting schedule.]

title: Pattern 1 — Quick Intro (Alignment Hook)
text: Pattern 1 — Quick Intro (Alignment Hook) Keep letters sincere and self-protective while tailoring each one. You are opening a Pac-Spine letter and must establish alignment immediately. You are reframing a stated request to surface the deeper system need you can solve. You are helping the reader imagine your mind inside their organisation in one sentence. You are demonstrating cultural fit while respecting the organisation's real constraints. You are proving competence with one crisp success mapped to their need. You are moving the letter from proof to a believable near-future horizon. You are adding one extra benefit without diluting the core offer. You are closing with a low-effort next action that fits their bandwidth. You are ending in a way that leaves them empowered even if they pass. You are tying the letter together with a clean, human ending. You are auditing letters to ensure Pac-Spine coverage and consistency. You are keeping repeated letters sincere, accurate, and ethically grounded. You have only a sentence or two to establish relevance. Organisations voice surface-level needs. You want the reader to imagine you as an internal voice. You know the organisation’s constraints. You want them to trust your competence. You need to shift from competence to possibility. You already made a strong case. Interested readers still need direction. You want to leave relationships stronger even in exit scenarios. You have woven alignment, insight, value, and next steps. Subjective impressions cause inconsistent letters. Writing many letters risks fragmentation. Most letters waste this window reciting CVs. Echoing them verbatim makes you interchangeable. Direct promises trigger resistance. Confidence without context reads as arrogance. Long role histories dilute clarity. Overpromising feels like hype. Overloading extras causes drag. Ambiguous endings invite inertia. Most endings trigger anxiety. Complex endings create drag. Without indicators, quality drifts across 20 letters. Templates can flatten voice. Lead with an elegant alignment hook that proves you understand their mission. Reframe their ask by articulating the underlying epistemic gap you can solve. Drop a revelation-style line (time-travel, infrastructional x-ray) that seeds a new mental process they own. Mirror their cadence, name pressures, and show how you reduce friction. Present a single, specific success tied to the desired outcome. Paint a reachable future anchored in their current trajectory plus your addition. Add a single unexpected strength that meaningfully extends value. Offer a concrete CTA (30-minute call, mini-prototype) sized to their bandwidth. Show that choosing you was already wise and hint at the larger opportunity they could unlock. Return to a clean, confident sentence that feels inevitable. Check for hook, reframing, CTA, cultural alignment, crisp success, future vignette, single bonus, frictionless CTA, empowerment move, and clean ending. Commit to obligations (preserve voice, no invention, honour paramitā hinge) that keep the art-book frame intact. Immediate resonance positions you as context-aware rather than generic. People hire the candidate who understands the real problem. Inception beats persuasion; it shows lived understanding. Teams back candidates who lighten load. Specificity builds credibility faster than volume. Partners fund believable futures. One delightful surprise invites curiosity without overwhelm. Lower activation energy raises response rates. Lasting goodwill keeps future engagements possible. Simplicity signals maturity. Uniform standards keep the set coherent. This harness protects integrity while projecting facets deliberately. next[Draft three hook sentences that pair partner needs with your proofs.]

title: Pattern 10 — Tie It All Together
text: Pattern 10 — Tie It All Together Tie the letter together with a simple close that gathers the value, the fit, and the next step into one clean cadence. next[Collect exemplar closing lines and reuse the cadence, not the wording.]

title: Discernment
text: Discernment Use diagnostics as a gate that triggers bounded corrections instead of opening an unbounded mastering phase. You are building a daily audio workflow where recordings are source material and the binding constraint is about one hour of attention. You want to improve listenability while keeping the workflow set-and-forget, and you suspect diagnostics could help your auto-bounce script. If you add diagnostics and conditional processing without a clear aim and stopping rule, you reintroduce an unbounded mastering phase. Treat diagnostics as a gating instrument that classifies takes into a small number of mechanically defined states and triggers at most one or two bounded, deterministic corrections. Discernment grows by reclassifying what is required now versus what must remain optional later. - Pick recent files you already judge as fine, borderline, and hard to listen to; run minimal metrics and confirm the classifications separate those groups. - Keep thresholds stable and log only classifications and triggered corrections for a week.

title: Endurance
text: Endurance Preserve the middle story by treating traceable bridge events as the unit of evidence. You are building FUTON as a single-user learning substrate linking heterogeneous traces without collapsing everything into simple causation. You want to persist what mattered as auditable links so later reflection increases capacity to act, not just produce labels. Simple arrows and naive affect labeling overcommit: they flatten experience, imply causation, and miss the middle story of who acted, what changed, and what evidence supports the linkage. Treat the fundamental unit as a certified bridge event: lasso a constellation of antecedents and a constellation of consequences, connect them with a revisable arrow carrying a short proof trail, and allow the system to work forwards and backwards with links that can themselves be linked. Capacity-building requires preserving the warranting middle of how a transition became actionable. - Implement first-class bridge records with timestamps, provenance, and certificates. - Generate candidate bridges via short-window novelty and cross-domain proximity; support manual curation.

title: Equanimity
text: Equanimity Treat symbolic work as legitimate infrastructure while separating it from domains needing different exposure strategies. You sustain meaningful symbolic or creative work without reliable developmental colleagues, while experiencing pressure from futures that could exist. You continue solitary symbolic work that feels intrinsically right and notice it supports clarity and orientation toward the future. If that work is treated as indulgent or merely private, you may misinterpret the absence of colleagues or relational transitions as personal failure or immaturity. Treat the symbolic work as legitimate infrastructural labor: a stable camp that preserves agency and anticipatory capacity, while deliberately separating it from domains that require different exposure strategies. Symbolic futures exert real pressure in the present without being causal; equanimity depends on distinguishing which systems require planning versus openness. - Observe where longing arises from ecological mismatch rather than lack. - Track whether pressure is misrouted between domains (for example, solving collegial absence through romance).

title: Ethical Containment vs Moral Totalisation
text: Ethical Containment vs Moral Totalisation Design practices that contain recurring tension instead of trying to purify it into moral closure. In social or institutional settings, recurring tensions persist despite good intentions. You encounter ethical tension that reliably reappears and cannot be removed without denial, repression, or coercive control. Treating the tension as something to be morally resolved collapses complexity and turns ethics into governance or policing. Design practices that contain the tension, localizing it in shared, repeatable forms that allow expression and circulation without claiming moral closure. Ethical coherence under pressure depends on preventing collapse into denial or domination, not on eliminating constitutive forces. - Test whether a proposed solution suppresses the tension or merely relocates it. - Compare failure modes of moralization versus containment.

title: Generosity
text: Generosity Treat a break as a bounded, self-authored retreat that restores coherence. You have a limited break period and want it to restore you without drifting into passive consumption or employer-driven obligation. You notice that rest via stimulation or escape does not reliably produce groundedness or readiness, and conventional time off can leave you more fragmented. If you turn the break into unbounded self-work, you can recreate pressure, lose recuperation, or blur the line between chosen practice and compulsive productivity. Treat the break as a bounded working-meditation retreat: use a small set of reflective prompts to set orientation, choose self-authored tasks that build coherence, and end by producing a credible re-entry plan that makes the return to paid work feel lighter. Coherence reduces cognitive load more reliably than distraction does. - Track whether this mode improves re-entry (sleep regularity, task clarity on first workday, reduced avoidance). - Compare against one consumption-rest break and note which constraints made it restorative.

title: Good Will
text: Good Will Locate learning in your own effort so good will does not turn into relational debt. You are reflecting on relationships or collaborations where growth occurred, and you want to understand good will and closure without turning them into debts or myths of influence. You treat growth or learning as something given by another person. Learning and change arise from your own sustained engagement with conditions, not from another person's intentions alone; attribution misplaces agency and keeps relational accounting alive past its usefulness. Regard relationships as shared passages through space and time that create affordances, while locating learning, practice, and change firmly in your own ongoing effort and discernment. Accurate attribution prevents transactional narratives from distorting good will and allows closure without denying either care or responsibility. - Notice where you are still running implicit ledgers (credit, blame, influence) in past relationships. - Test whether those ledgers do explanatory work or merely sustain emotional load.

title: Non-Transactional Intensity
text: Non-Transactional Intensity Treat relational intensity as an ecological signal rather than a dyadic mandate. A period of closeness or collaboration produces emotional intensity within a thin social ecology. You experience attraction or heightened significance around a person or group while other channels are scarce or offline. Treating that intensity as a dyadic fact about this person risks role inflation and forced escalation. Reframe the intensity as a signal of field conditions, allowing the relationship to remain what it already is without converting it into outcome. Intensity often emerges from contextual compression rather than intrinsic relational demand; reading it ecologically preserves agency and proportionality. - Observe how intensity redistributes when additional channels reopen. - Articulate an ethos of non-transactional presence so shared spaces remain breathable without requiring escalation.

title: Persistence
text: Persistence Design long-term work around legible forms of life, not only output or recognition. You are sustaining a long-arc practice that blends research, tooling, reflection, and ethical orientation without assuming value must be proven through money or credentials. Persistence is framed only in terms of continuous output, remuneration, or institutional approval. Many viable forms of persistence are recognized through stable practices, roles, and visible patterns of conduct. Design persistence around legible forms of life: practices that remain coherent and intentional over time, regardless of whether they are rewarded, certified, or monetized. Long-term work survives only when it is socially and internally intelligible as a way of living. - Identify which aspects of your practice already function as recognizable roles. - Test external wrappers only insofar as they make the practice more visible without distorting it.

title: Proper Routing of Craving
text: Proper Routing of Craving Treat craving as informational signal and route it to the domain that can legitimately respond. You are engaged in demanding creative, technical, or relational work and notice recurring frustration or longing across multiple domains. You experience craving and find yourself implicitly asking nearby people or activities to satisfy it. Cravings attach to whatever is salient rather than to what can actually produce the desired quality, leading to misattribution and persistent suffering. Reframe craving as an informational signal about conditions and route it to the domain that can legitimately respond (technical frustration to model contracts, affective confusion to slow inquiry, relational warmth to appreciation without obligation, aesthetic desire to cultivating the right conditions). Craving is a pointer toward missing conditions; acting on it without checking jurisdiction produces category errors. - Notice where craving is being misrouted and identify the condition it points toward. - Observe whether you are willing to cultivate the practices that would make that condition likely.

title: Truth
text: Truth Frame governance work in proof-adjacent language so it is legible to formal-methods interlocutors. You are considering re-entering the ethical AI space, and want your work understood as operational infrastructure for LLM-assisted reasoning. You want to communicate your work as a missing cognitive governance layer so it is legible to serious practitioners and potential employers. If you frame it as generic AI ethics or a broad personal framework, it will be interpreted as compliance theater or idiosyncratic worldview. Anchor the story in a concrete governance gap in LLM-assisted reasoning, route it through formal-methods-aligned interlocutors using proof-adjacent language (assumptions, traceability, failure modes, audit trails), and include one or two crisp examples. Formal-methods sensibilities provide shared criteria for good reasoning infrastructure, making the pattern layer legible as operational governance. - Select 2-3 recent artifacts where patterns constrained LLM work. - Draft a one-paragraph governance gap statement with one concrete example and test it with a trusted interlocutor.

title: Provide Applicability Signals and Decision Criteria
text: Provide Applicability Signals and Decision Criteria A good pattern includes simple signals that tell a reader when to apply it now. Readers recognize the general idea but lack a concrete decision rule for adoption. The pattern is conceptually sound but hard to operationalize in the moment. Overly rigid rules can miss nuanced cases. Provide lightweight decision criteria (signals, thresholds, or checks) that indicate the pattern is appropriate. Prefer observable cues over internal states, and include at least one “do not apply yet” signal. Patterns are used under time pressure; decision signals reduce hesitation and misuse. - evidence: a case where the signals would have triggered correct use. - evidence: a case where the “do not apply” signal prevented a bad use. - evidence-shape: {:signals/apply [:string], :signals/avoid [:string], :decision/thresholds [:string], :example/trigger :string, :example/avoid :string}

title: Make the Causal Chain Explicit
text: Make the Causal Chain Explicit A good pattern states the causal chain that links context to the proposed action and expected outcome. Patterns are accepted as “nice ideas” but fail when applied because the cause-and-effect path is implicit. The solution seems reasonable but the mechanism is not stated or testable. Some domains rely on tacit practice and the mechanism may be partially inferred. Write the causal steps explicitly: what condition triggers the action, what changes, and why that change yields the outcome. Include a short counterfactual (“If we did X instead, we would likely see Y”) to show why the action matters. Patterns are decisions under uncertainty; an explicit mechanism makes them inspectable and improvable. - evidence: a concrete example where the stated mechanism predicts the outcome. - evidence: a counterexample where the mechanism fails and the pattern should not be used. - evidence-shape: {:context :string, :trigger :string, :action :string, :mechanism :string, :expected/outcome :string, :counterfactual :string}

title: Align Evidence With the Claim
text: Align Evidence With the Claim A good pattern specifies evidence that would actually confirm or refute its claim. Evidence sections often list artifacts without showing how they bear on the pattern’s conclusion. Evidence is present but does not map to the claim or mechanism. Early patterns may only have partial evidence. State what observation would increase or decrease confidence in the pattern and why. Prefer evidence that targets the mechanism, not just the existence of a system or feature. Evidence is only useful when it discriminates between a true and false pattern. - evidence: a metric, log, or experiment that tests the mechanism. - evidence: a falsifying observation that would trigger revision or retirement. - evidence-shape: {:claim :string, :mechanism :string, :confirming-evidence [:string], :disconfirming-evidence [:string], :decision/rule :string}

title: Ensure Each Required Facet Is Coherent and Complete
text: Ensure Each Required Facet Is Coherent and Complete A good pattern has one clear statement for each required facet (context, IF, HOWEVER, THEN, BECAUSE, NEXT-STEPS) and each facet does real work. You are reviewing or drafting a pattern that meets the structural template but feels vague or repetitive. Each facet exists but overlaps or restates another facet instead of adding new meaning. Some patterns are short and may not need long prose in every facet. Check each facet for a single, purpose-fit statement: context scopes where the pattern applies; IF states the trigger; HOWEVER names the tension or risk; THEN specifies the action; BECAUSE explains the mechanism or rationale; NEXT-STEPS names concrete evidence or follow-up actions. Remove duplicates and move scoping constraints into context. Facet integrity keeps patterns readable, testable, and reusable across contexts. - evidence: annotate one pattern with a brief note explaining what each facet contributes. - evidence: identify one facet that can be shortened or clarified without losing meaning. - evidence-shape: {:pattern/id :string, :context :string, :if :string, :however :string, :then :string, :because :string, :next-steps [:string], :reviewer :string}

title: Align Problem, Action, and Outcome
text: Align Problem, Action, and Outcome A good pattern maintains internal coherence: the proposed action directly addresses the stated problem and yields the stated outcome. Patterns sometimes mix a real problem with a fashionable solution, leaving a mismatch between cause and effect. The action seems adjacent to the problem rather than addressing its core constraints. Some patterns intentionally trade off one goal to achieve another. Check that each element maps: problem → constraint, action → constraint relief, outcome → constraint lifted. If trade-offs exist, state them and show why the action still fits the problem. Coherence is what turns a pattern from advice into a dependable decision rule. - evidence: a trace that shows how the action changes the constraint. - evidence: a trade-off note with a reason it is acceptable. - evidence-shape: {:problem :string, :constraint :string, :action :string, :outcome :string, :trade-offs [:string], :trace :string}

title: Declare Scope Boundaries and Non-Goals
text: Declare Scope Boundaries and Non-Goals A good pattern defines where it applies and where it should not be used. Patterns drift into slogans when boundaries are missing, leading to misuse outside their intended domain. The pattern reads as universally true or lacks explicit limits. Overly narrow boundaries can make a useful pattern seem irrelevant. State at least one inclusion boundary (when it applies) and one exclusion boundary (when it does not). Name the assumptions the pattern relies on (constraints, environment, actors, or scale). Clear boundaries prevent category errors and let readers decide quickly whether to apply the pattern. - evidence: an application within the stated scope that succeeds. - evidence: a near-scope case that fails and justifies the exclusion boundary. - evidence-shape: {:applies-when [:string], :does-not-apply-when [:string], :assumptions [:string], :scope/example :string, :anti-scope/example :string}

title: Conclusion Required, Other Canonical Components Recommended
text: Conclusion Required, Other Canonical Components Recommended Among the seven canonical components, only the conclusion is structurally required; the other six (context, if, however, then, because, next-steps) are recommended for operational patterns but legitimately absent in definitional ones. The conclusion may be authored under any of four aliases — `! conclusion:`, `! claim:`, `! summary:`, or `! instantiated-by:` — all four are normalised to the same slot. The clause-vocabulary survey across 919 patterns showed 96.8% have a conclusion (under one of the four aliases) but only 86.9% have an IF/HOWEVER pair. The 13% gap is real authorial signal: definitional patterns ("a task IS a BHK arrow") legitimately lack operational tension and so legitimately lack IF/HOWEVER. Forcing all seven would refuse those patterns or push authors into fabricating tension where none exists. A peripheral or verify invariant is deciding whether to admit/refuse a draft pattern based on which canonical components are present. Requiring all seven refuses honest definitional patterns; requiring fewer than one (zero) admits anonymous artifacts with no claim. The conclusion is the only component every pattern MUST have because the conclusion IS the pattern's claim — its identity as an act of design. Require the conclusion (any alias). Recommend the other six with a soft-warn discipline that surfaces "this pattern would benefit from explicit IF/HOWEVER" as advisory feedback, not refusal. For operational patterns the surface contract should encourage the central five (context/if/however/then/because) so the pattern lands in the categorical-admission shape; for definitional patterns the conclusion plus context plus references is enough. Engaged when the peripheral admits a draft iff a clause with name-key in #{conclusion claim summary instantiated-by} is present, regardless of which other components appear; advisory feedback names missing-recommended components without refusing. Failing when the peripheral refuses definitional patterns lacking IF/HOWEVER, OR admits patterns with no conclusion. A pattern is a unit of *claim*. Without a conclusion, an artifact is just structured prose — there is nothing to recommend, nothing to dispute, nothing to apply. With a conclusion plus any subset of the other six, the pattern can still be a meaningful act of design: a definition (conclusion + context + references), a tension-named pattern (conclusion + if + however), a procedure (conclusion + then), or a fully-shaped operational pattern (all seven). The four conclusion-aliases reflect that authors come to the same structural slot from different directions — `! conclusion:` from analytic-foundational tradition, `! claim:` from the Toulmin-extended canon, `! summary:` from informal documentation practice, `! instantiated-by:` from devmap-prototype headers. All four name the same load-bearing slot; the parser unifies them. - Encode the discipline in the verify invariant invariant-pattern-has-conclusion (already done; futon1a/src/futon1a/model/verify.clj). - Wire advisory-warn for missing-recommended components into the Sokoban's response shape (admit + violations[soft-warn]). - Decide which definitional-pattern shapes should still get IF/HOWEVER added authorially as the categorical-admission research matures.

title: Pattern-to-Code Receipts — Structural Link Between Claim And Witness
text: Pattern-to-Code Receipts — Structural Link Between Claim And Witness A pattern is honestly applied when there is a verifiable receipt linking the code that was built using it back to the pattern's claim. Per-turn evidence (mining, Haiku-rationale) is one register; per-commit pattern-citation receipts are the structural other. Together they triangulate which patterns the codebase actually embodies vs which are well-intentioned text. Today the pattern-to-code link is via PSR/PUR notes (pattern-coherence) plus per-turn evidence-mining (M-pattern-mining, M-pattern-retrieval-calibration); both are advisory. The IFR property "demonstrable value" (M-pattern-application-diagnostic §IFR) is structurally a witness check: applying a pattern's move should produce a measurable Δ in the geometric (T, ∇, Δ) substrate. Without commit-time receipts, the witness is asserted but not measured. An agent commits code in a region where one or more patterns have been claimed as the design substrate (PSR exists; mining attests; the operator has authorial intent for that region). There is no enforced structural link between the commit and the patterns it claims to apply. PSR notes are reflexive ("I plan to apply X"); PUR notes are retrospective ("I applied X"); neither is checkable against the code that landed. Mining is per-turn, not per-commit. The claim "this commit applied pattern X" has no verifiable witness today. Adopt a receipts discipline: every commit that touches code in a pattern-claimed region carries a `Pattern: <ns>/<name>` footer (zero or more — multiple patterns are common). The footer joins the canonical parser + the geometric substrate: the receipt names the pattern's `:witness-shape`, the commit's region of effect, and the implicit T-before / T-after pair. Emit `pattern-receipt` evidence per commit; the verify invariant `invariant-pattern-receipts-resolve` checks every receipt's pattern-ref resolves and every claimed witness can be re-derived from current code state. M-bounded-in-flight-state already shipped a commit-footer parser for `Block: <kind>-<date>-<slug>$` (last occurrence wins). The same shape applies — `^Pattern: <ns>/<name>$` parser, idempotent emission, evidence record per commit. The receipt structurally links three things: (1) the commit's diff, locating it in the codebase hypergraph; (2) the claimed pattern, locating it in the design-pattern-category; (3) the geometric witness, computing T-before / T-after at the commit's region. Together they say "this code embodies that pattern's move, by this measure." Without receipts, the operator has no way to ask "which patterns does this region of the codebase actually embody?" — only "which patterns were claimed." Per-turn evidence accumulates but doesn't aggregate to per-region truth. Receipts are the structural denominator. M-pattern-application-diagnostic's IFR demands "demonstrable value" — that the pattern's claim be verifiable against codebase state. Receipts are the operational form of that demand. Without them, the substrate's claim about pattern application is "an agent said so"; with them, the substrate's claim is "the geometric witness corroborates." Per-turn evidence (mining, Haiku) is fast and noisy; per-commit receipts are slow and load-bearing — together they form a triangulation that catches both honest claims and gaming. The receipts discipline is also the structural form of the homeostatic agent's self-check on its own design vocabulary: when a pattern's receipts consistently fail the witness check, the pattern is wrong-shaped or never honestly applied; the agent learns about its own design language by reading its receipts. - Footer parser: `^Pattern: <ns>/<name>$`, last occurrence wins, mirrored on the M-bounded-in-flight-state Block-id parser. - Pre-commit advisory: warn when committing in a region with no Pattern footer; do not block (advisory phase). - Evidence emission: emit `pattern-receipt` evidence per commit with {commit-sha, patterns: [...], regions: [...]}. - Verify invariant: `invariant-pattern-receipts-resolve` — every receipt's pattern-ref resolves; every claimed pattern's witness can be re-derived. - Geometric witness wiring: integrate with M-pattern-application-diagnostic's (T, ∇, Δ) computation so receipts include T-before/T-after deltas. - Cutover discipline: receipts from this date forward; historical commits stay as they are.

title: Patterns As Categorical Objects, Not Isolated Text
text: Patterns As Categorical Objects, Not Isolated Text Patterns are not isolated text artifacts but objects in a category whose morphisms include the canonical components (context / if / however / then / because) treated as required edges; a new pattern is admitted as a new object iff its morphisms compose cleanly with the category's existing structure. Composition is what makes a pattern library a *language* rather than a flat catalog — paths through the morphism graph are design moves. futon5/src/futon5/ct/dsl.clj already implements Functor / Diagram / Category / NaturalTransformation records, plus a design-pattern-category whose morphisms are :kernel-step / :frame / :justify / :synthesize. futon5/scripts/pattern_to_wiring.clj turns sigil-pattern-registry entries into wiring diagrams under resources/xenotype-wirings/. The categorical substrate exists and is reachable; what's missing is the bridge from the canonical seven (Level 1's text-shape) to the morphism predicate (Level 3's admission test). A new pattern is being submitted to the peripheral and the operator wants admission to depend on more than text-shape — they want admission to verify the pattern's morphisms compose with the existing pattern-category. Functorial admission is genuinely research, not just engineering. Decisions outstanding: which canonical components are *required* morphisms vs *optional*; which categorical laws must hold (associativity is straightforward; naturality of :tension ↔ :move is harder); how the futon3a pattern library and futon5's categorical infrastructure rendezvous concretely. Premature commitment to a wrong predicate would refuse honest patterns or admit incoherent ones. Treat each canonical-seven component as a typed edge from the pattern-object: `:pattern/has-context`, `:pattern/has-if`, etc. (Level 1 already emits these into futon1a XTDB.) Build the admission predicate as: (a) the new pattern's edges yield a sub-diagram in the design-pattern-category; (b) the sub-diagram composes with sibling patterns' diagrams without violating the category's laws; (c) on success, the pattern lands AND a wiring diagram is generated under resources/xenotype-wirings/ alongside the canonical .flexiarg. Kernel-step composition (linear): pattern A's THEN feeds into pattern B's CONTEXT — chain A→B as a path in the morphism graph. Frame composition (parallel): pattern A and pattern B share an IF — they apply in the same scope with different moves; tensor-diagrams is the right operator. Naturality: when patterns at one abstraction level have natural transformations to patterns at another (instantiated-by relationships), the transformations should commute with the morphisms. futon5's compose-diagrams and tensor-diagrams already exist as primitives; design-pattern-category names :kernel-step / :frame / :justify / :synthesize as morphism families. The substrate is concrete, not aspirational. A pattern library is more than the sum of its parts when its patterns *compose* — when invoking pattern A leads naturally to invoking pattern B because their morphisms chain. That's how Alexander's pattern languages were supposed to work; that's what most software pattern catalogs lost when they collapsed pattern-language into a flat list. The categorical framing recovers compositionality structurally: admission requires the new pattern fit the category, and the category's laws ensure the moves chain cleanly. The "more than sum of parts" payoff is operational, not metaphorical: an agent following pattern A is *guided* into pattern B because the morphism is computed, not asserted. - Decide which canonical seven are required morphisms (probably context as object-type; if/however as morphism-source/target predicates; then as morphism realisation; because as morphism justification; conclusion as morphism identity; next-steps as composition-with-future-morphisms). - Spike the admission predicate on 5 patterns from library/futon-theory/ — the most theoretically structured namespace. See whether their morphisms compose without contradiction. - Wire the predicate into the Sokoban's submit-draft! as a graduation from Level 1 to Level 3. Failure feedback names which morphism doesn't compose and with which sibling pattern. - Generate wiring diagrams on admission; surface them in Arxana / Web Arxana so authors can see the categorical neighbourhood the new pattern joined.

title: Peripheral As Sokoban — Pre-write Capability Envelope, Not Post-write Validator
text: Peripheral As Sokoban — Pre-write Capability Envelope, Not Post-write Validator A peripheral that constrains pattern authoring is a pre-write capability envelope, not a post-write validator. An agent inside the surface can submit a draft and either it lands as a canonical artifact OR the surface refuses with structured feedback and writes nothing. No leakage — non-canonical drafts cannot be emitted from inside the peripheral. When agents are asked to "create a new library pattern" without a constrained surface, they reach for free-form Edit/Write tools and produce drafts that drift from the canonical shape. Drift accumulates: each individual draft looks reasonable but the library as a whole loses coherence. Post-write validation can detect drift but cannot prevent the agent from having already split their attention across the wrong shape — by then the authorial intent has settled in the wrong frame. An agent is authoring a pattern (or any artifact whose typed shape must hold across a corpus), and the operator wants the canonical-shape invariant to bind at write time rather than detect drift retrospectively. Free-form Edit/Write tools cannot enforce shape; an agent can always emit a non-canonical draft and a downstream validator can only detect it after the fact. Even with strict validation, the authorial intent has already been shaped by the wrong frame; the validator's refusal is felt as friction rather than as guidance. Provide a peripheral that exposes only a single bound action — submit-draft. Inside the peripheral, Edit/Write are constrained for the typed-artifact paths. The submit action validates against the canonical shape, runs reshape rules where they apply deterministically, and either lands the canonical form or refuses with structured feedback naming what is missing or non-canonical. The agent stays in the peripheral until the draft canonicalises (Sokoban — only legal moves available); on success, evidence is emitted recording the admission. Engaged when the agent's only legal write-path inside the peripheral is the submit action; refusals carry structured violations with kind/detail/where and a pointer to the rulebook so re-drafting is informed; nothing lands on disk unless every required check passes (no-leakage). Failing when an agent can bypass via direct Edit/Write; refusal feedback is unstructured prose; partial drafts land on disk. The canonical-shape invariant must be enforced at write time, not detected later. Detection-after-the-fact (post-write validation) is necessary but not sufficient — by the time the validator fires, the agent's authorial intent has already been shaped by the wrong frame and the corpus has been silently degraded. Pre-write enforcement is the structural form of the intent: the surface itself disallows the bad move, so the agent's attention never splits across non-canonical shapes. This is the same shape as Curry-Howard — the type system constrains expressible programs; the peripheral constrains expressible drafts. - Wire the peripheral into futon3c's session-mode dispatch so an agent enters pattern-author mode and has Edit/Write constrained for library/**.flexiarg. - Surface contract on entry: the agent's session prompt names the peripheral and the only legal write path. - Refusal-feedback links to the rulebook + the algorithm + the canonical parser so an agent can self-correct from the violation alone. - Generalise the pattern: peripherals for other typed artifacts (mission docs, dispositions, commit-block-ids) get the same Sokoban discipline.

title: Match Engagement to What the Group and the Person Can Sustain
text: Match Engagement to What the Group and the Person Can Sustain A peer-learning group has a finite carrying capacity for any one participant's contribution rate, and any one participant has a finite carrying capacity for the project. Sustained over-contribution by some, or under-contribution by others, will distort the group's dynamics and burn people out. The pattern is to recognise the asymmetry in real time and adjust — by stepping back, by inviting others in, by reducing one's own pace, or by reshaping the work so it costs less to enter. Peer-learning groups attract uneven engagement. Some contributors take on disproportionate load; others lurk, intend to contribute, and never enter; energetic participants railroad ideas; reflective participants go silent. These are not individual failings — they are predictable dynamics of voluntary co-production. Carrying capacity asks each participant and the group as a whole to keep these dynamics inside survivable bands rather than letting them run unchecked. The pattern operates on the axis: individual momentum ↔ group sustainability. Irreducible: a group cannot maximise both individual contribution rates and balanced participation. At any given moment one is being prioritised over the other; the question is whether the trade is conscious. Real costs: high-momentum contributors keep the project alive in the short term; the same momentum, sustained, can crowd out the participation that makes the project peer-driven in the first place. Both effects are real and operate simultaneously.
