Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a contributor feels burnout symptoms, whenever discussion patterns become one-directional, and whenever a roadmap revision exposes who has been carrying which load. - Burnout cascade: a high-contributor exits abruptly and the project stalls because no one was tracking their load. - Power-law lock-in: the engagement distribution flattens into "the same five people forever" with no ramp for others. - Silent dissent: under-contributors disagree but do not say so, because the cost of entering the conversation has grown too high. - Roadmap drift: the project's stated goal and its actual concentration of effort diverge without anyone surfacing the gap. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Step back, observe: a high-contributing participant deliberately reduces their pace and watches the dynamics that emerge in the space they leave. This is diagnostic before it is corrective. (2) Ask, then listen: replace assertion with question — "what do others think?" — and accept that the answer may be a longer silence than the assertive participant would have tolerated. (3) Reshape the entry cost: rather than only modulating one's own behaviour, change the project so others can join cheaply — clearer explanations, smaller first tasks, a more legible roadmap. (4) Name the role-change: when stepping back temporarily, tell whoever holds the facilitation role. This protects the group from interpreting absence as drift. (5) Renegotiate the goal: revisit the roadmap and confirm what concrete goal the group is moving toward, since over- and under-contribution often track to ambiguity about what counts as progress. Engaged when: contributors notice their own and others' load and adjust before the dynamics ossify; participation distributes across the group rather than concentrating on a few. Failing when: the same names appear on every contribution thread, or a participant is operating well past their sustainable rate without anyone naming it.

title: Build the Guide While You Build the Practice
text: Build the Guide While You Build the Practice When a peer-learning practice is new, the meanings that would let participants use it are not yet stable — often they have not been created. Writing a guide is not a separate step that follows the practice; it is part of the practice, a way of figuring out how the system works while making it more usable for the next person. The guide is best treated as a living micro-map, edited reflexively as the territory shifts. New practices, including peer-learning practices, accumulate tacit knowledge faster than they accumulate vocabulary. A guide written too late is a record of a stabilised practice; a guide written in parallel is itself a tool of stabilisation. Knowledge cartography (concept maps, glossaries, navigations) and meaning-making frames help, but the central move is reflexivity: each guide-writing pass surfaces what has been figured out, and each practice pass surfaces what the guide must update. The handbook itself is an instance of this pattern. The pattern operates on the axis: capture-now ↔ stabilise-first. Irreducible: a guide cannot simultaneously be a definitive reference and a working notebook. The question is which mode the current pass is operating in, not whether one mode is correct. Real costs: writing a guide for a moving practice risks fixing too early what should still flex; waiting for stability risks losing the stage at which the practice could have been made teachable. Both risks operate continuously. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every iteration boundary — every time the practice shifts, the guide either lags, leads, or co-evolves. - Stale handbook: the guide describes the practice as it was at a previous version, with no dating to flag the gap. - Single-author bottleneck: only one person edits the guide, so guide-updates lag every change made by anyone else. - Premature canonicalisation: the guide is written as a definitive reference before the practice has stabilised, freezing decisions that should still be moving. - Tacit-knowledge accumulation: practitioners share understanding informally and never feel pressure to write it down, leaving newcomers without a path in. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Co-evolution: the guide is updated each time the practice changes substantively, with explicit dating of which sections describe which version of the practice. Readers can see the trail. (2) Micro-map per activity: rather than one definitive guide, the project produces small, scoped guides for individual activities (refining a pattern, running a session, onboarding a contributor). Each micro-map can be revised without disturbing the others. (3) Reflexive note: when the guide-writer notices that writing a section is forcing the practice to clarify, they record that fact in the guide itself. The guide then documents not only the practice but the practice-of-clarifying-the-practice. (4) "Map is not the territory" hedge: the guide states explicitly which decisions remain open, which examples are illustrative versus prescriptive, and where the practice is still discovering itself. Readers do not mistake provisional articulation for settled doctrine. Engaged when: the guide is updated within the same iteration as the practice changes it describes, and contributors treat editing the guide as part of doing the work. Failing when: the guide describes a stage the project has already left, or guide-writing is treated as a separate, post-hoc job.

title: Hold a Curatorial Stance, Not an Expert One, Toward the Conversation You Convene
text: Hold a Curatorial Stance, Not an Expert One, Toward the Conversation You Convene A peer-learning practice runs into trouble when its facilitators position themselves as either experts (talking down to the group) or as flat-equals (refusing to bring stewardship). The curating-not-experting stance is a third position: bring people into conversation, hold the shape of the inquiry, and invite expertise from wherever it actually lives — which is often distributed across the group, not concentrated in one person. The stance distinguishes peeragogy from both top-down pedagogy and from leaderless co-learning. A facilitator convenes a group around a topic the facilitator is interested in. A pure expert stance positions the facilitator as the source of knowledge; the group's job becomes receiving. A pure peer stance refuses to acknowledge that the facilitator is doing real work in shaping the inquiry; the group's job becomes nothing in particular and the inquiry drifts. The curating-not-experting stance is what works in practice: the facilitator is not the source of the knowledge but is responsible for the shape of the conversation, the choice of who's at the table, and the integration of what surfaces. The pattern operates on the axis: stewardship ↔ expert-authority. Irreducible: facilitation is real labor; flat-equality denies it. Expertise is also real; pretending no one has more knowledge than anyone else is a fiction. The curating stance acknowledges both without conflating them. Real costs: groups need someone to hold the shape of an inquiry — without that, conversations meander and don't accumulate. But if the shape-holder claims to be the expert on the content, the group's other voices recede and the inquiry contracts to one perspective. Active dynamic: the pull recurs every time the facilitator is asked a substantive question they could either answer or redirect, and every time the conversation drifts and someone needs to bring it back without imposing. - Question-funneling: substantive questions all route through the facilitator, who answers them as the expert. - Shape-collapse: without the facilitator actively holding the inquiry, the conversation drifts and doesn't accumulate. - Performance-of-flatness: the facilitator refuses to acknowledge their convening labor, which leaves the group unable to credit, extend, or eventually take it over. - Voice-monoculture: the same few voices dominate because no one is curating who speaks. - Expert-arrival defaulting: when an expert joins the conversation, the room reorganises around them as authority instead of as one voice the curator brought in. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Source naming: when a substantive question arises that the facilitator could answer, the facilitator instead names whose expertise — in the room or beyond — would be most apt, and brings them in. (2) Shape-holding: the facilitator articulates the inquiry's question(s) explicitly, returns to them when the conversation drifts, and tracks which questions are still open. (3) Voice-curation: the facilitator notices which voices haven't spoken and creates space for them, without putting individuals on the spot. (4) Integrative wrap: at session close, the facilitator names what the conversation surfaced — not a verdict on what's true, but a curatorial summary of what was said and where it points. (5) Connective intelligence: the facilitator treats the conversation as a node in a wider network — explicitly bringing in other practitioners, projects, or threads the group should know about. (Doug Engelbart lineage; named operationally in Kiko Lab's framing.) Engaged when: participants can identify the facilitator's role as something other than "the expert in the room" AND as something other than "a peer like everyone else." The facilitator is doing legible work but isn't claiming to be the source. Failing when: either participants defer to the facilitator as the authority, or the facilitator disclaims any role and the inquiry loses its shape.

title: Notice the Repetition First, Name It Carefully Second
text: Notice the Repetition First, Name It Carefully Second A peeragogical pattern starts as a noticed repetition: something that happens often enough across peer-learning situations that it deserves a shared name. The discernment work is twofold — first, attending to language and behaviour closely enough to spot the repetition at all; second, naming it without over-claiming what the repetition means. Most candidate patterns die in the second step, when the namer rushes from "I see this pattern" to "and therefore the participants are X." Patterns are not invented; they are discerned. The handbook draws on Alexander's framing — language use is what we have to go on analytically, and patterns surface from that close attention to use. In peer-learning, candidate patterns appear as recurring forms: shared interests in introductions, shared shapes in how groups organise sessions, shared failures in how groups onboard newcomers. The discernment skill is a kind of meta-awareness of language — close enough to see repetition, careful enough not to over-interpret what the repetition means. The pattern operates on the axis: noticing repetition ↔ resisting interpretation. Irreducible: a noticed pattern cannot be both raw observation and interpreted significance simultaneously. The discernment process must hold these two stages apart, even when the noticer wants to collapse them into one insight. Real costs: the same close attention that lets a pattern-spotter see recurrence also tempts them to attribute meaning the recurrence does not yet support. Both moves draw on the same alertness, but only the first is reliable. Active dynamic: the pull recurs every time a pattern-spotter sees a third instance and feels the urge to declare what it means. - Insight inflation: each noticed coincidence becomes a "pattern" without surviving repeated test. - Premature meaning: the pattern description tells the reader what the pattern signifies before establishing that the pattern exists. - Vocabulary churn: pattern names proliferate and rename without stabilising into a usable language (see peeragogy/pattern-language). - Loss of source: pattern descriptions drift from the situations that grounded them, becoming abstract advice. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Note-then-defer: record the noticed repetition in the smallest possible form (occurrence, context, what was repeated) and resist naming what it implies for at least a few more instances. (2) Title-and-describe: once the repetition is robust enough to deserve a name, write the title first and the description second. The title forces commitment to a specific pattern shape; the description tests whether that shape holds across the instances. (3) Hedge interpretation: when describing what the pattern says about the participants or the situation, use "might" and "may" rather than "indicates" until the meaning has been tested across more instances. (4) Submit for collaborative refinement: a discerned pattern is sharpened by other practitioners trying to break it on their own data; treat the first articulation as a draft, not a finding. Engaged when: pattern claims are grounded in named instances, and interpretive claims are kept separate from observational claims. Failing when: a single observation is promoted to a pattern, or a pattern's interpretation is asserted with confidence that the underlying instances do not support.

title: Keep a Visible Rhythm So the Group Has Something to Return To
text: Keep a Visible Rhythm So the Group Has Something to Return To A peer-learning group needs a recurring, low-friction signal that calls attention back to the work — a heartbeat — without which energy dissipates and participants drift. The signal can be impersonal (a weekly post, a shared rhythm) or personal (a direct message to someone who has gone quiet), but it must be frequent enough that absence is noticed and warm enough that re-entry is cheap. Voluntary peer-learning projects compete with everything else in participants' lives. Without a rhythm the group can return to, attention fades; the project drops out of mind individually before it dies collectively. The heartbeat is the device that keeps the project resident in attention between bursts of activity. It can be sustained by one person, by a role (see peeragogy/wrapper), or by an artefact like a wiki main page that someone tends. The pattern operates on the axis: coordination overhead ↔ attention maintenance. Irreducible: a group cannot simultaneously be self-organising and rely on no recurring signal. Even fully decentralised groups end up with implicit heartbeats (a recurring meeting, a shared release cadence); the only choice is whether the heartbeat is named. Real costs: every heartbeat costs the heartbeat-keeper time and care; every missed heartbeat costs the group some fraction of its dispersed members. Neither cost is zero. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever the group is between visible deliverables, when a long-tenured member steps back, or when newcomers arrive expecting a shape they can attach to. - Silent drift: regular contributors stop posting and no one notices for weeks. - Re-onboarding burden: returning members ask the same orienting questions newcomers ask. - Convener fatigue: the project's continuity depends entirely on one person's ongoing attention with no redundancy. - Cadence collapse: a previously regular signal stops, and the group cannot tell whether the project is paused, finished, or dead. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Personal nudge: someone (often the convener) writes individual notes to lurkers and dropped-out members, naming the work and offering a way back in. High-cost per recipient; high return when the recipient was wavering. (2) Public cadence: a recurring artefact — weekly roundup, status post, agenda — that the group can read or skip without obligation. Lower-cost per recipient; works when the artefact is reliably present. (3) Tended artefact: a shared surface (wiki main page, dashboard) that someone keeps current. The heartbeat is the tending; the artefact is the trace. (4) Distributed rotation: the heartbeat-keeper role rotates so no single person bears the cost indefinitely. Requires the role to be named explicitly enough that the next holder can take it over. Engaged when: the group has a recurrence that participants can name, and missing it is noticeable to more than one person. Failing when: re-engagement happens only through one-off heroic effort by individuals, or when "what's happening with X?" is a question no one can answer cheaply.

title: Throttle the Loud, Make Room for the Quiet, Reshape the Floor
text: Throttle the Loud, Make Room for the Quiet, Reshape the Floor Online peer-learning participation reliably follows a power law — a few voices dominate, most lurk. Moderation is the active counter-pressure on that distribution, performed both by the loudest participants throttling themselves and by the structure of the conversation reshaping who finds it cheap to speak. Effective moderation operates on both the individual and the structural level; one without the other tends not to hold. Voluntary online conversations skew toward those who type fastest, feel most confident, or have the most time. Without counter-pressure, the resulting distribution silences the participants whose perspectives the group most needs to hear. Moderation is not about silencing the loud; it is about restoring access for the quiet. Techniques like the fishbowl (small-group reformat that depersonalises issues and reduces stress) and the progressive stack (queue ordering that prioritises voices heard less often) are structural moves; individual self-throttling — the dominant participant choosing to speak less — is the personal move. Both are needed; either alone is fragile. The pattern operates on the axis: depth-of-engagement ↔ breadth-of-voice. Irreducible: a single conversation cannot simultaneously maximise depth from its most engaged voices and breadth across its quieter ones. The moderator is choosing which to prioritise at each turn, even by inaction. Real costs: the loud participants are often the engaged participants; throttling them risks losing the energy that keeps the conversation alive. But unmoderated, that same energy crowds out the breadth of voice that makes a peer learning context peer-driven. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every conversational turn, every thread, every meeting. Moderation is a continuous activity, not a one-time configuration. - Same-five-voices: every thread is dominated by the same handful of participants and the rest go silent. - Newcomer drop-off: new arrivals attempt one contribution, get no traction in the existing discussion shape, and leave. - Adversarial lock-in: a debate hardens into entrenched positions because no one re-formats the conversation to reduce the personal cost of changing position. - Silent dissent: disagreement migrates to back-channels because the main forum is too costly for quieter voices to enter. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Self-throttle: the most active participants visibly hold back, ask questions instead of asserting, and let others answer first. Names the dynamic without policing it. (2) Reformat to fishbowl: when a debate has become entrenched, restructure it as small-group conversations that depersonalise the issue and lower the cost of changing one's mind. (3) Progressive stack: order speakers by how recently and how often they have spoken, prioritising voices heard less. Makes turn-taking a structural property, not a social negotiation. (4) Lower the floor: rewrite the prompt or the surface so quieter participants find a cheaper entry — shorter messages, smaller commitments, async options. Reshapes who finds the conversation accessible. (5) Name the dynamic: surface the participation distribution explicitly ("we've heard mostly from X, Y, Z this week") so the group can adjust collectively rather than relying on individual heroics. Engaged when: the participation distribution stays meaningfully closer to balanced than the unmoderated baseline, and quiet participants report that entry feels accessible. Failing when: the conversation pattern locks into a small-group exchange while everyone else watches, or moderation is treated as a one-time setting rather than an ongoing practice.

title: Treat Newcomer Arrival as Renewing Pressure on the Project
text: Treat Newcomer Arrival as Renewing Pressure on the Project A peer-learning project needs newcomers — not only because they extend the community, but because their arrival is the recurring pressure that keeps the project's vocabulary, guides, and onboarding paths from going stale. Without newcomers, much of the "education stuff" loses its addressee. Even in the absence of actual newcomers, the project benefits from a *beginner's-mind* perspective applied periodically to its own surfaces. Peer-learning projects are written-for-someone, and when no actual newcomer is in earshot, that someone slowly becomes "ourselves a year ago" — a fictional reader who shares all the project's assumptions. The guide rots, the onboarding path silts up, and the project's accessibility decays without anyone noticing. The newcomer pattern is the disciplined opposite: every actual newcomer is treated as a probe of the project's current accessibility, and even when none are present, someone periodically reads the project's surfaces with a beginner's mind. Closely paired with peeragogy/wrapper (the integrative function that makes orientation cheap) and with peeragogy/heartbeat (the rhythm a newcomer can attach to). The pattern operates on the axis: newcomer accommodation ↔ in-group progress. Irreducible: a project cannot simultaneously optimise for fastest in-group progress and lowest newcomer entry cost. Each onboarding interaction is a deliberate slowing of the in-group pace in exchange for a chance at renewal. Real costs: every onboarding interaction costs the existing contributors time and attention that could be spent on direct project work. But the project depends on newcomer flow for its long-term legibility, vocabulary refresh, and energy. Both costs are real. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a newcomer arrives, whenever a long-tenured member catches themselves using shorthand only insiders understand, and whenever the project considers writing a new guide section (since "what would a newcomer need here?" is the live test). - Audience drift: the project's prose increasingly addresses an in-group reader who already shares all assumptions, with no path for outsiders to enter. - Onboarding dead-ends: documented entry paths lead to broken links, abandoned forums, or current contributors no one knows how to reach. - Tacit-knowledge moats: every meaningful contribution requires knowledge that lives only in private conversation among long-tenured members. - Vocabulary calcification: the project's shared terms stop being interrogated because no one new is around to ask what they mean. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Mentor-pair on arrival: a named existing contributor accompanies the newcomer through their first contribution rather than handing them documentation. High-cost, high-yield; converts arrival into participation. (2) Newcomer-as-editor: invite the newcomer to edit guide pages, since their inability to follow them is exactly the diagnostic signal needed to fix them. Combines onboarding with project maintenance. (3) Beginner's-mind sweep: in the absence of actual newcomers, a contributor periodically reads the project's onboarding path as if seeing it for the first time and records what is unclear. (4) Newcomer-friendly entry tasks: maintain a small set of well-scoped first contributions that a newcomer can accomplish in one sitting, signalling that the project expects their participation early. (5) Pair with the wrapper role: the newcomer benefits most when the project has someone summarising current state (wrapper); these two patterns reinforce each other. Engaged when: newcomers complete a meaningful first contribution within a short window of arrival, and the project's onboarding surfaces are revised in response to their experience. Failing when: newcomers either bounce off or take many weeks of unsupported effort to find their way in.

title: Close Each Gathering With a Brief Self-Review
text: Close Each Gathering With a Brief Self-Review Every gathering of co-learners or co-producers benefits from a short self-applied review at the end. The Paragogical Action Review (PAR) is a five-question structure adapted from the US Army's After Action Review and made more peer-directed: review intention → establish what's happening → what are the different perspectives → what did we learn or change → what else should we change going forward. The discipline is to run it on yourselves about the activity you just did, not on someone else about something they did. A peer-learning group has just held a session — a meeting, a podcast recording, a workshop, a writing sprint. Without a closing review, learnings stay in individual heads, the group cannot see itself, and the next iteration is built on guesswork. PAR's contribution is a short, structured loop that takes 5–15 minutes and makes the group's understanding of what just happened legible to itself. The "eat your own cooking" stance — applying the practice to the artifact that documents the practice — is what distinguishes PAR from a sprint review handed to a manager or a retrospective held with someone outside the work. The pattern operates on the axis: extending the work ↔ closing the loop. Irreducible: the people best positioned to learn from a session are the participants in it, not an outside reviewer. They have the context. But participants are also the most tired by the end, and the most tempted to skip the closing. Real costs: the work the group came to do is the obvious priority; reviewing the work feels like extra time. But without the review, learnings dissipate and the next iteration repeats the same surprises. Extending the working time without ever closing the loop produces a series of incomplete experiences, not a learning trajectory. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every session boundary, and is strongest when the session went well (the group feels accomplished and wants to coast on the feeling) or badly (the group wants to escape). - Recurring surprises: the same thing surprises the group across multiple sessions because no review captured it the first time. - Reflexive-layer atrophy: the group can run the activity but not articulate what it does or what it has learned about doing it. - Newcomer disorientation: incoming participants get no easy way to understand what this group has been learning together. - Public/private mismatch: the group's public artifacts (recordings, blog posts) describe an activity; the group's actual learnings live only in side channels. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Five-question close in-broadcast: run all five PAR questions in the last 10 minutes of the session itself. Highest-fidelity: everyone is still present and the context is fresh. Cost: extends session length; some attendees won't stay. (2) Off-broadcast continuation: end the headline session at the planned time, and convene PAR as an after-party for those who can stay. Lower-pressure for newcomers; risks splitting the group's reflexive layer from its public layer. (3) Async PAR via shared doc: post the five questions to a shared document, gather responses over 24 hours. Works for distributed groups; loses some of the spoken-conversation texture. (4) Single-question micro-PAR: when full PAR feels heavy, ask just one — typically "what did we learn or change?" — to keep the loop alive without the full structure. Engaged when: the group can name, in their own voices, what they learned in the session and what they would do differently next time. Failing when: the closing minutes are reserved for thanks and goodbyes only, and learnings stay implicit.

title: Treat the Patterns as a Language, Not a Catalogue
text: Treat the Patterns as a Language, Not a Catalogue A collection of named patterns becomes a *language* when the patterns compose — when one pattern's solution invokes others, when conflicts between patterns are visible, and when a designer can build a peer-learning context by selecting and arranging patterns rather than reasoning from scratch. Until that compositional structure is present, what looks like a pattern language is a catalogue of independent tips. Christopher Alexander's framing — invoked directly in the handbook — is that a pattern language gives builders enough generative structure to design something coherent without dictating it. Peeragogy patterns aspire to the same: not a checklist but a vocabulary in which peer-learning experiences can be designed. This requires the patterns to refer to one another, to share a granularity convention, and to leave room for the designer's choices. The pattern operates on the axis: catalogue completeness ↔ generative composition. Irreducible: the same set of named practices cannot be both a freely-extending catalogue and a tight compositional grammar. Discipline costs additions; additions cost discipline. Real costs: a thorough catalogue is easy to extend (just add patterns) but does not, by itself, compose. A composing language requires patterns to be sized, named, and cross-referenced consistently — work that constrains how patterns are added. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a new pattern is proposed. The catalogue impulse welcomes it; the language impulse asks where it sits, what it composes with, and what it excludes. - Catalogue inflation: pattern count grows but composition does not deepen. - Stranded patterns: patterns sit alone, with no other pattern referring to them and no clear context of use. - Granularity mush: a single list mixes patterns about whole projects, individual sessions, and atomic interactions. - Conflict suppression: patterns that disagree are presented as if they harmoniously coexist, leaving the designer to discover the conflict in practice. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Cross-reference discipline: every pattern names which other patterns it builds on, which it composes with, and which it conflicts with. Composition surfaces become explicit. (2) Granularity convention: patterns at the same level address comparable scopes (group, session, role) so they can be combined without confusion. Patterns at different levels are explicitly nested. (3) Conflict visibility: where two patterns pull in opposite directions in the same situation, the language names the conflict rather than hiding it. Designers can then decide which pattern dominates. (4) Generative test: for any peer-learning context the designer wants to support, the language should let them assemble a working design from named patterns plus a small amount of judgement. If every assembly requires unnamed practices, the language has gaps. Engaged when: a new contributor can use the patterns to design a peer-learning experience by composition, without re-deriving each decision from first principles. Failing when: each design starts over; patterns are cited individually but never combined.

title: Surface Open Questions Before Committing to Answers
text: Surface Open Questions Before Committing to Answers When a peer-learning group faces a decision — what to discuss, who to invite, what resources to use, what to call something — it usually pays to *poll for ideas* first rather than have one person commit on behalf of the group. The poll serves both as deliberation and as visible signal that the question was genuinely open, which lowers the cost for participants to disagree later. In voluntary peer-learning contexts, decisions made unilaterally by an active contributor often stand for the group simply because no one objected — but unobjected-to is not the same as agreed-to. The poll-for-ideas move makes the openness explicit: a question is posted, options are gathered (or generated), and the group's contribution to the decision is a visible record of suggestions rather than a single person's call. The poll need not be a vote; the value is in the surfacing of options before commitment, not in the tallying. The pattern operates on the axis: speed of decision ↔ legitimacy of decision. Irreducible: a decision cannot simultaneously be made unilaterally and be visibly open to the group. Each decision is one or the other, and the question is which deserve which treatment. Real costs: polling slows decisions, especially small ones, and the cumulative drag of polling everything would stall the project. Not polling, however, accumulates a backlog of decisions made by whoever moved fastest, which corrodes the project's claim to be peer-driven. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every decision the group faces, especially decisions that will set norms (forum structure, naming conventions, working agreements) where unilateral commitment is hardest to undo. - Norm by accretion: working agreements crystallise from one person's repeated practice, never having been opened for input. - Late-arrival objection: contributors discover decisions they would have weighed in on, with no way to revisit them without seeming to relitigate. - Veto-by-silence: decisions stand because no one objected, but no one was asked, so the silence cannot be read as agreement. - Poll fatigue: the pattern is over-applied to trivial decisions, training participants to ignore polls; the legitimate polls then get low engagement. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Open-call poll: post the question with no candidate answers and let the group generate options. Highest legitimacy, slowest, best for norm-setting decisions. (2) Candidate-set poll: post the question with two or three candidate answers and ask for additions or preferences. Faster; useful when the question is structurally bounded. (3) Default-with-veto: announce a tentative decision with explicit invitation to object before a deadline. Even faster; preserves polling's legitimacy benefit because the openness is visible, but does not require active participation from everyone. (4) Polling for the meta-question: when uncertain whether something deserves a poll, the meta-poll ("should we discuss X here, or is there a better forum?") is itself useful, since it surfaces structural disagreement before content disagreement. Engaged when: decisions that will set norms or commit shared resources are visibly open to group input before commitment, and the trace of that openness is preserved (so later contributors can see how a decision was made). Failing when: norms appear by accumulation of unilateral moves, with no record of whether the group ever consented.

title: Give Back to the Communities You Extract From
text: Give Back to the Communities You Extract From Any practice that collects knowledge, data, or stories from a community needs an explicit answer to "what does the community get back?" — articulated as a discipline, not left as an afterthought. Reciprocal participation makes the give-back move a first-class part of the practice's design, drawing on indigenous data frameworks, feminist data frameworks, and Design Justice. The discipline distinguishes peer-learning practice from extractive research, ethics-board-as-window-dressing, and well-meaning-but-asymmetric volunteer recruitment. A peer-learning project draws on community participation — interviews, contributed material, lived-experience stories, identifiable data, co-authored work. The project produces an output (a paper, a handbook, a podcast, a tool, a curriculum). Without an explicit reciprocity discipline, the project's benefits accrue to the producers and the give-back is left implicit ("we'll share the result somewhere"), unmeasured, or absent. Reciprocal participation is the move from implicit-and-discretionary to explicit-and-tracked. The pattern operates on the axis: producing-the-output ↔ giving-back-to-sources. Irreducible: the people whose voices the practice carries cannot fully guard their own reciprocity if the practice itself doesn't make it a constraint. The convener has more agency in the relationship than the contributor; the discipline puts that asymmetry on the table rather than papering over it with rhetoric. Real costs: producing the output and giving back to the sources are two different kinds of labor. Without the discipline, output-production is the work that has deadlines and accountability, while give-back is what happens "if there's time." That asymmetry compounds across years and across many projects, and the producing side accrues credentials, citations, and funding while the source side accrues nothing tracked. Active dynamic: the pull recurs every time the practice uses contributed material — every transcript quoted, every dataset analysed, every story retold, every workshop's emergent insight written up by one party. - Implicit reciprocity: the practice describes its give-back vaguely ("benefits the wider community") without naming what specifically goes where. - Attribution-as-acknowledgment: contributors are listed in an acknowledgments section but receive nothing material. - Window-dressing ethics: the practice has an ethics board or ethics statement but the affected communities are not represented in either. - Volunteer-funnel asymmetry: the practice consistently recruits volunteers who do real labor without commensurate return, while the producers' careers advance. - Asymmetric publishing: the practice publishes outputs in venues the contributing communities cannot access (paywalled journals, conferences they can't travel to) without producing accessible versions. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Up-front contract: before extraction begins, the practice and the community agree on what will be returned (a copy of the artifact, a share of attention, a tangible service, a portion of any funding). The agreement is documented and revisited as the project proceeds. (2) Built-in attribution: the practice's outputs name contributors specifically and link to whatever they want named — not as a courtesy at the end but as a structural element of the artifact, with versioning so attribution doesn't decay. (3) Translation-back: the practice translates its outputs back into forms the contributing community can use (a plain-language version, a community-language translation, a tool the community asked for, a workshop run for them). (4) Material reciprocity: when the practice receives funding, recognition, or career advancement based on contributed work, a defined share returns to the sources — financially, in resources, or in concrete labor. (5) Refusal-on-asymmetry: the practice declines to use contributed material when reciprocity isn't actually possible, instead of using it on the assumption that reciprocity will be worked out later. Engaged when: contributors can name what they get from the practice using their material, the practice can name what it gives back, and the two descriptions roughly match. Failing when: contributors see the artifact for the first time alongside the general public, or the practice's give-back consists of "we put it on the website." This pattern surfaced from the 2026-04-29 posterior-pass analysis of the Peeragogy Podcast (M-peeragogy-rewrite mission), specifically episode 5 ("The Ethics of Data") with Yasmin Bidyoff (Ada Lovelace Institute, no-tech-for-tyrants) and Paola Ricaurte (Tecnológico de Monterrey, Tierra Común Network, A+ Alliance). Paola: *"if we extract something from the community, we should give back that as well."* Yasmin: *"a reciprocal participation, social contract sort of thing."* Both articulated the same move from different vantage points — data-extraction ethics in Paola's case (drawing on indigenous data frameworks, feminist data frameworks, and Design Justice); researcher-participant relationship in Yasmin's case. The Handbook's chapter 17 (Peeragogical Assessment) hints at reciprocity through its "learning is adaptation" gloss but does not formalise reciprocal participation as a first-class discipline.

title: Maintain a Public, Provisional Map of Where the Project Is Going
text: Maintain a Public, Provisional Map of Where the Project Is Going A peer-learning project benefits from an up-to-date public roadmap — a maintained artefact that names what is finished, what is in progress, what is stub, and what lies ahead. The roadmap serves three audiences: newcomers (who can see where to jump in), existing contributors (who can see what is open), and the project's future self (which can see how the goal has evolved). The roadmap is always provisional; its value lies in being current and shared, not in being correct. Voluntary peer-learning projects have no external schedule that forces a shared sense of "where we are." Without a roadmap, each contributor holds their own private model of project state, and these models diverge. A maintained roadmap is the canonical artefact that re-converges them. The handbook describes this concretely: when the book's outline became fairly mature, it became a roadmap by marking finished sections, in-progress sections, and stubs. Closely connected to peeragogy/wrapper (the wrapper produces and maintains the roadmap as part of integrative work) and peeragogy/newcomer (the roadmap is where newcomers find their first task). The pattern operates on the axis: roadmap stability ↔ roadmap currency. Irreducible: the roadmap cannot simultaneously be a never-changing reference and a live representation of project state. Every update is a trade between the two roles. Real costs: a frequently updated roadmap reflects the current state but offers contributors no stable target to plan against; a stable roadmap gives a planning surface but rapidly diverges from reality. Both costs are real and continuous. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every state-change in the project — a section finished, a contributor stepped back, a new direction surfaced — and at every newcomer arrival, who needs the roadmap to be current to be useful. - Outdated outline: the visible roadmap describes a project state from months ago, with no mechanism for revision. - Multiple competing roadmaps: status is tracked in several places (issue tracker, wiki, drive folder) with no canonical reconciliation, so different contributors believe different things are true. - Newcomer-rejection: newcomers cannot find where to start because the roadmap does not surface entry points or marks "stub" only retrospectively. - Goal drift unmarked: the project's actual direction has shifted, but the roadmap still describes the original goal, and the gap is not surfaced. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Status-marked outline: the project's table of contents (or equivalent structure) is the roadmap, with explicit per-item status — finished, in progress, stub, abandoned. Newcomers see entry points immediately. (2) Roadmap-as-artefact: the roadmap is a single named page that someone (often the wrapper) maintains, rather than scattered across multiple status surfaces. One source of truth. (3) Versioned roadmap: major roadmap revisions are dated and preserved, so the project can see how its goal has evolved. The history is itself a record of how peer-learning shifted what the project meant. (4) Roadmap-as-conversation: roadmap changes are themselves polled or discussed (see peeragogy/polling-for-ideas) rather than committed unilaterally, since the roadmap is structurally a shared commitment. (5) Personal-learning-plan companion: individual contributors maintain personal learning plans (paragogical profiles) that connect to the project roadmap, making each contributor's path through the work legible. Engaged when: a contributor (existing or new) can read the roadmap and know within minutes what is in progress, what is open, and where they could plug in. Failing when: the roadmap is stale, hidden, or has been replaced by tribal knowledge held in private conversations.

title: Treat Roles as Held, Not Owned — and Watch Them Shift
text: Treat Roles as Held, Not Owned — and Watch Them Shift Educational interactions inherit roles by default — autodidact, tutor, tutee, and outward into librarian, editor, administrator, and beyond. The pattern is to treat these roles as *held* rather than *owned*: a participant occupies a role at a moment, and the same person may shift roles as the activity changes. Naming roles makes coordination cheaper; treating them as fixed identities makes the group rigid. Peer-learning starts from the autodidact and bifurcates outward; even a single learner traverses several roles in the course of one project (asking questions, answering them, checking proofs, fetching resources). In group contexts, roles multiply: tutor, tutee, parent-figure, principal, librarian, technician, editor, policy-maker, partner. The handbook notes that decomposing learning into roles could be an endless theoretical task; the practical observation is that roles are present by default at the start of an interaction and that they may shift as the work develops. The pattern is to keep that fluidity available rather than letting initial role-assignments harden into permanent identities. The pattern operates on the axis: role legibility ↔ role mobility. Irreducible: a role cannot simultaneously be stable enough to coordinate around and fluid enough to permit unrestricted shift. Every role-naming choice is balancing these two. Real costs: named roles let the group coordinate and let newcomers find their footing. But the same names can lock participants into identities they would otherwise outgrow — the "newcomer" who never gets to facilitate, the "facilitator" who never gets to learn from a beginner. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every transition — a tutee who begins to teach, a facilitator who needs to step back, a contributor who picks up a wrapping role for one cycle. - Identity ossification: a participant becomes "the X person" and finds it costly to do anything else, even when they want to. - Single-point-of-failure roles: critical functions depend on one specific person with no shared name for the role they occupy. - Role-name absence: the group's coordination depends on roles that no one has named, so newcomers cannot see how the work is divided and existing members cannot hand off cleanly. - Implicit hierarchy: undeclared seniority shapes who does what, while the project's official self-description claims peer equality. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Name roles, not identities: when a role is assigned (heartbeat-keeper, wrapper, moderator), name the role and its scope, not "X is the type of person who does this." The role is a hat someone is wearing this week. (2) Default-role audit: at intervals, ask which default roles the group has inherited from how it started, and whether they still fit. Roles that made sense at convening time may not fit at maturity. (3) Role rotation: where a role is sustainable but heavy (heartbeat-keeper, wrapper, moderator), build in rotation rather than assigning indefinitely. Spreads cost, prevents identity-lock, builds redundancy. (4) Role-shift announcement: when a participant changes role — newcomer becoming editor, facilitator stepping back — the change is named explicitly to the group, both to coordinate practical handoff and to model that role-shift is normal. (5) Multiple roles per person: a single contributor may hold several roles concurrently (editor + heartbeat-keeper) and that is fine, as long as the carrying capacity (peeragogy/carrying-capacity) of each role-holder is respected. Engaged when: roles in the group are nameable on demand, role-shifts happen visibly and without drama, and the same person can occupy different roles at different times without that being remarked as exceptional. Failing when: roles harden into identities, role-shifts are perceived as betrayals or promotions, or a role becomes single-occupancy permanently with no successor.

title: Plan the Convener's Successor Before You Step Back
text: Plan the Convener's Successor Before You Step Back Polycentric practices that depend on a convener for their kickoff energy need an explicit successor for the convener's stewardship role before the convener steps back. Without succession, the practice continues at reduced scope but stops shipping its next canonical artifacts. The convener's defining-reality / scaffolding-then-stepping-back move is incomplete without a third phase — naming who picks up the stewardship work, and what shape that work takes after the founder is no longer doing it. A practice has a founder or convener who scaffolds the project's early years — defines the inquiry, recruits participants, holds the canonical-text production going. Eventually the convener wants to step back: to make space for others, to reduce their own load, or because the practice should not depend on one person. The community takes over the practice's *operations* (gatherings, conversations, ongoing work) but does not take over the *stewardship* — the quiet labor of pushing toward the next canonical milestone. The result is a practice that continues but doesn't ship: the conversations keep happening, the milestones stop arriving. The pattern operates on the axis: continued-presence ↔ released-control. Irreducible: stewardship is a specific kind of labor — neither the convener's founding energy nor any individual contributor's daily work. It includes pushing toward next-canonical-things, holding institutional memory, and making decisions only a few people have the standing to make. The labor doesn't transfer by osmosis. Real costs: stepping back too soon leaves the practice without enough scaffolding; staying too long prevents others from picking up real responsibility. The convener must release control AND ensure someone is positioned to carry the stewardship work, which requires explicit conversation, not just departure. Active dynamic: the pull is strongest in the years after the convener's energy peaks but before they fully step back — a gradient phase when the next steward could be named but often isn't. - Canonical-artifact stall: the practice's canonical text/release/program-version stops shipping new editions while the practice's daily activities continue. - Rolled-up-sleeves drift: people are doing work but no one is holding the larger trajectory. - Founder-as-permanent-convener: the original convener never actually steps back because there's no successor in place; or the convener has stepped back informally but is still the only person with the standing to make some decisions. - Eulogy-language: the practice gets discussed in the past tense even though it's still active in operations. - Drafted-but-unshipped: proposals for next-canonical-things exist as drafts but nothing pushes them into shipped form. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Named successor: the convener publicly names one or more people as inheriting the stewardship role, with explicit description of what that role is and isn't. (2) Distributed-stewardship council: the role is split across a small council, each member carrying one facet (canonical-artifact production, institutional memory, external relations, recruitment). (3) Time-boxed stewardship terms: stewardship rotates on a defined cadence (annual, biennial); each cycle's outgoing steward names the incoming one and writes down what the role learned. (4) Stewardship-by-shipping: the steward is whoever is currently shipping the next canonical artifact; if no one is shipping, that's the signal that no one is in the role. (5) Sunset clause: the practice declares an explicit decision-point ("if no one ships v4 by date X, the practice transitions to maintenance mode and stops claiming forward motion") so absence of stewardship is named, not silently endured. Engaged when: when someone asks "who is responsible for getting the next canonical thing out?", a name (or council, or rotation) is given that the named person(s) confirm. Failing when: the question elicits silence or a generic "we collectively are." This pattern surfaced from the 2026-04-29 posterior-pass analysis of the Peeragogy Podcast (M-peeragogy-rewrite mission), specifically the blackbox-recorder reading of episode 4 ("The Collaborative Process of Creating a Book", recorded late 2020). In that episode, Joe Corneli stated: *"We're pretty keen to get a fourth edition of the peeragogy handbook. I've even drafted a proposal for the fifth edition at one point."* As of 2026, neither v4 nor v5 has shipped, despite the practice continuing in podcasts, Cool Laboratory, Future Trends Forum, Metacog reading group, and other forms. Howard Rheingold in the same episode named the convener move as two-phased (define reality → step back) without a named third phase; this pattern names that third phase.

title: Choose Between Producing New and Reusing Existing — Deliberately
text: Choose Between Producing New and Reusing Existing — Deliberately Peer-learning groups face a recurring choice between *making new stuff* (poesis) and *using existing stuff* (praxis — reuse, remix, recombination). Both are legitimate, but the choice tends to default toward production because production feels like progress. The pattern is to make the use-or-make choice deliberately at each junction, asking how much of the apparent need for new artefacts could be met by reusing what already exists, including others' ideas and techniques. Peer *production* — the dominant idiom in commons-based peer projects — biases toward making things. Making is visible, recognisable, recordable; using is mostly invisible. But peer-*learning* often advances faster through deliberate reuse: drawing on existing texts, existing tools, existing patterns, existing conversations rather than re-creating each. The handbook frames this as the tension between poesis and praxis, citing Baudrillard's distinction; the pattern is to keep the question live rather than letting the production bias close it silently. Closely related to peeragogy/pattern-language (a pattern language is itself a tool for principled reuse). The pattern operates on the axis: novelty production ↔ deliberate reuse. Irreducible: a single decision cannot simultaneously be a fresh production and a reuse of existing material. Hybrids exist (extension, adaptation, remix), but each is operating closer to one pole or the other and the choice is real. Real costs: producing new artefacts builds skill, identity, and visible output; reusing existing artefacts compounds prior work and avoids reinventing wheels. Both effects matter, and a project that does only one decays — pure production accretes unintegrated stuff, pure reuse stops contributing to the commons it draws on. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every "should we make X?" moment — guides, tools, frameworks, vocabularies, processes. The production bias is the default; choosing reuse requires conscious counter-pressure. - Reinvention drift: the project repeatedly produces artefacts that already exist in similar form elsewhere, with no record of why those existing artefacts were rejected. - Production-as-status: contributors are recognised for new artefacts but not for connecting, adapting, or curating existing ones. - Detached output: the project's artefacts proliferate without composing — each useful in isolation, none feeding back into the others. - Remix invisibility: where reuse and adaptation do happen, they are not marked as such, so the practice is not visible enough to spread. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Reuse search before production: before committing to make a new artefact, the group spends a defined effort searching for existing artefacts that could serve. Time-boxed so the search does not itself become a way to defer. (2) Adapt before re-create: when an existing artefact partly serves, prefer adaptation (fork, extend, annotate) to fresh production from scratch. The lineage stays visible. (3) Production with reuse-credit: when production is the right call, document what was considered for reuse and why it was insufficient. The reasoning becomes part of the artefact. (4) Periodic remix audit: at intervals, the group reviews its production output and asks which pieces are integrated with prior work and which are isolated novelties; isolated novelties get explicit decisions about whether to keep, integrate, or retire. (5) Praxis-explicit framing: name reuse as legitimate work, not a fallback. Without this, contributors feel they need to ship novelty to count, which deepens the production bias. Engaged when: production decisions visibly include consideration of reuse, and the project shows a balance of new and reused/adapted artefacts in its output. Failing when: every problem produces a new artefact, with prior artefacts cited only after the new one is committed (if at all).

title: Have Someone Whose Job Is to Stitch the Pieces Together
text: Have Someone Whose Job Is to Stitch the Pieces Together Commons-based peer production needs both the ability to contribute small pieces and an integrative function that stitches those pieces together. The wrapper is whoever or whatever performs that stitching — through periodic summaries, status framings, or maintained overviews — so contributors and newcomers can see what the project currently is. Without a wrapper, small contributions accumulate without composing into a legible whole. Distributed peer-learning projects produce more fragments than any individual contributor can hold in mind: messages, edits, drafts, threads, side-projects. Newcomers cannot orient. Long-tenured members lose track of what others are doing. The wrapper's labour is not new content but legibility: a periodic act of saying "here is what the project is right now" that lets the rest of the work remain small. The pattern operates on the axis: contribution granularity ↔ project legibility. Irreducible: no individual contributor can both make a contribution and simultaneously hold the whole project in their head. The wrapping work is structurally separate from the contributing work. Real costs: small contributions are easy to make and easy to lose track of. The smaller the contribution unit, the more the project depends on someone explicitly composing the units into a story. Without that composition, the small contributions look like noise; with it, they become a project. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every cadence boundary (week, sprint, release) and whenever a newcomer arrives needing orientation. - Stale main page: the canonical overview describes a project state from months ago. - Repeated orientation requests: the same "what is the status of X?" question recurs because no answer is captured. - Fragmented memory: each contributor knows their own piece and no one knows the whole. - Recognition starvation: contributors stop knowing whether their work landed because nothing names it. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Periodic roundup: a named person publishes a recurring summary (weekly digest, monthly report) that names what happened, who did what, and what is open. The roundup is itself the wrapper artefact. (2) Tended overview: a shared page (project main page, dashboard, README) that someone keeps current. Wrapping is continuous rather than periodic. (3) Briefing on demand: the wrapper writes orientation pieces when someone arrives or returns, rather than on a schedule. Lower routine cost; risks newcomers arriving when no wrapper is on duty. (4) Multi-wrapper rotation: the role rotates among several people, each wrapping a different facet (technical state, social state, external relations). Spreads cost; needs explicit handoff between rotations. Engaged when: a newcomer can read a single recent artefact and form an accurate picture of where the project is. Failing when: orientation requires reading the full message history or asking individual contributors what is going on.

title: Canonical Typed Event vs Side Channel
text: Canonical Typed Event vs Side Channel When a peripheral needs to emit or consume something the canonical event taxonomy does not yet describe, extend the taxonomy with a first-class typed event. Do not invent a side channel that bypasses the taxonomy, even if the side channel is cheaper to ship. You are wiring a peripheral that needs to communicate something the existing transport (WS pipeline, drawbridge, MUSN events) does not have an event type for: cursor position, heartbeat, consent ack, bell payload metadata. The canonical transport has a typed event taxonomy — a finite, documented set of event shapes that consumers parse and dispatch on. Adding a new event type to the canonical taxonomy requires: schema authoring, consumer awareness, documentation, maybe a versioning step. It feels heavy. The lightweight alternative is obvious: open a second channel (a sidecar WebSocket, a polling HTTP endpoint, a file-watch, an out-of-band timer) that carries the new thing, with no need to touch the canonical taxonomy. The side channel ships in an hour. The taxonomy extension takes half a day. The temptation is overwhelming. - Two-channel reality: the peripheral now lives in two places at once. Consumers must subscribe to both to get the full picture. Diagnostics fragment across both. Tooling that knew one channel doesn't know the other. - Schema-drift-by-default: the side channel has no taxonomy discipline, so its payload shape drifts freely. Three months later, no one knows what shapes are emitted on it. - Consent-bypass-by-accident: the canonical transport has consent and write-ownership boundaries baked in. The side channel doesn't. Now the peripheral can write things it never had permission to write, because the permission check lived on the path it bypassed. - Observability-bypass: telemetry, audit logging, and replay tooling instrument the canonical transport. The side channel is invisible to them. When something goes wrong on the side channel, there is no record. - "Temporary"-as-permanent: the side channel was supposed to be moved into the taxonomy "later." Later never comes. The temp is now load-bearing. When the peripheral needs a new event, extend the taxonomy: 1. **Author the event schema as a first-class type** in the canonical taxonomy. Give it a name, a payload shape, semantics, and a producer/consumer note. The schema lives in the same place all other event schemas live. 2. **Add the producer** (the peripheral emits the event on the canonical transport, not on a sidecar). 3. **Document the consumer contract** even if there is only one consumer today. The discipline of writing the contract makes future second consumers possible. 4. **Update the taxonomy index/docs** so the next reader can find the event by searching the taxonomy, not by reading the peripheral's source. 5. **Consume via the same subscription mechanism** other consumers use — same dispatch, same filtering, same backpressure handling, same audit trail. If the taxonomy extension is genuinely too heavy for the change at hand, that is itself a signal: the taxonomy may be over-formalised or under-tooled. Fix THAT (lower the cost of adding a typed event), rather than routing around it. A taxonomy is an institution in Ostrom's sense — a shared resource governed by rules-in-use. Side channels are tragedy-of-the-commons moves: each one is locally cheap, and each one degrades the institutional value of the taxonomy. Once the taxonomy is no longer a complete description of what flows, it stops being trusted as a contract; once it stops being a contract, every new consumer must discover what flows empirically; once that becomes normal, the taxonomy is dead documentation and the wire is a free-for-all. Typed events have non-obvious downstream value: replay tooling can deterministically rebuild state from the event log; new consumers can subscribe without coordination; backpressure and prioritisation can be implemented uniformly. Every side channel forecloses on these capabilities for the data it carries. The pattern also closes a peripheral-design loop. Heartbeat (peripherals/progress-heartbeat-distinct-from-cycle-completion) is exactly the case: the watchdog needs a liveness signal distinct from cycle events. The wrong move is a separate ping mechanism. The right move is to add a "heartbeat" typed event to the same transport, so watchdogs subscribe to the same wire as everything else. The pattern is also the principled defence against the "lightweight" euphemism (feedback_lightweight_euphemism, agent memory): a "lightweight side channel" is the precise shape of work that appears done but isn't institutionalised. Translation: it is a typed event missing its taxonomy entry. M-emacs-cursor-peripheral (2026-05-24, codex-8): the original sketch had cursor positions broadcast on a parallel WS channel. Codex identified this as a side-channel against the canonical WS transport, and proposed adding a typed "cursor-position" (and later, full "presence") event to the canonical event taxonomy instead. The WS pipeline already had backpressure, audit, and consent semantics; the side channel would have had none. realtime/structured-events-only (futon3 pattern library): "All inter-agent communication MUST be structured events with documented schemas." This pattern is the peripheral- design corollary: when extending a stack with new communication, extend the taxonomy. WM API surface (futon3c, 2026-05-23 consolidation): War Machine surfaces (R-Criterion status, R12 apparatus, etc.) are all served via the canonical /api/alpha/war-machine endpoints on port 7070. The Emacs *War Machine* buffer and the web UI both consume from the same canonical endpoints; no side channel for "Emacs-specific" markdown vs "web-specific" JSON. The single canonical surface enabled both clients without divergence. bell payload schema standardisation (claude-10's parked substrate-creation thread, 2026-05-23/24): exactly the case where bell payloads were drifting in shape across producers. Standardisation = taxonomy formalisation. The fact that the thread exists is evidence that side-channel-like drift had begun. - Maintain a single canonical event-taxonomy document per transport. Every typed event lives there. - Make taxonomy extension cheap: a template for new event schemas, a quick-add path that doesn't require ceremony. Cost-of-extension should not be the reason side channels exist. - When reviewing a peripheral mission, ask: "what new events does this peripheral introduce? Where in the taxonomy do they live?" If the answer is "they don't, we just emit them," the mission needs revision. - For M-war-machine-pilot specifically: every event the WM peripheral emits (cycle phase changes, judgement events, heartbeats, consent acks, bell payloads) must have an entry in the canonical event taxonomy. The Pair-stage and Collaborate- stage consent acks especially must be typed events, because consent decisions are exactly the data future audit tools will replay. - Cross-link: peripherals/split-transport-from-embodiment — typed events are how the transport layer stays describable independently of any embodiment.

title: Constrained Execution Envelope
text: Constrained Execution Envelope A peripheral is a constrained execution envelope — a space where the actions available are exactly the actions that lead to the goal, not a space where distracting actions are forbidden. An agent (or human) wants to achieve something they believe they know how to do: prove a theorem, formalize a solution, write a module, complete a review. They have the skills and the intention. The agent has the capability to achieve the goal and a reasonable plan for reaching it. In an unconstrained environment, the agent doesn't actually achieve it. It gets distracted — checking dependencies, refactoring adjacent code, reading tangential material, switching to a different problem, or producing work that is vaguely related but not the thing. The environment affords too many actions, and the ones that feel productive in the moment are not the ones that close the goal. - Envelope too tight: the agent cannot do the work because the available actions do not cover the actual requirements. The fix is to widen the envelope, not to abandon it. - Envelope too loose: the available actions include tangential work that feels productive. The fix is to narrow the affordances, not to add prohibitions. - Envelope as punishment: the agent perceives the constraint as distrust rather than structure. This happens when the envelope is framed negatively ("you are not allowed to...") rather than positively ("your tools are..."). - Envelope without exit: the agent completes the work but cannot leave the peripheral. Every envelope needs an exit condition that is as clear as its entry condition. Set up a constrained execution envelope — a peripheral — in which the available actions are exactly the actions that lead to the goal. The key: define the envelope in positive terms. Do not enumerate what the agent cannot do; describe what the agent can do. The peripheral offers tools, phases, and exit conditions that constitute the productive path. What is not offered is not forbidden — it simply does not exist within this envelope. A proof peripheral offers: observe the problem, propose an approach, execute the formalization, validate against criteria, classify the result. Those are the actions. There is no "check IRC" action, no "refactor the build system" action — not because they are banned, but because the envelope does not contain them. A review peripheral offers: read the diff, check the invariants, note issues, approve or request changes. A deploy peripheral offers: run the tests, check the gates, push the artifact. Each envelope is shaped to its goal. Forbidding distracting actions does not work. A prohibition is a negative statement that requires the agent to hold both the forbidden action and the reason for forbidding it in mind — which is itself a distraction. It is a known pattern from philosophy (Nietzsche's critique of negation, Spinoza's "omnis determinatio est negatio" read in reverse) that productive constraint works by affirming what is present, not by denying what is absent. You do not teach someone to play chess by listing the moves they cannot make; you teach them the moves they can make, and the board enforces the rest. Even apparently negative concepts (Hegelian synthesis, apophatic theology, boundary conditions in mathematics) function as positive statements when they are operative: a synthesis is a new thing, not the absence of two old things; a boundary condition is a value the solution must take, not a region it must avoid. The peripheral is the positive statement. It says: here is what you can do, here is the sequence, here is when you are done. The agent inhabits this envelope and does the work. The constraint is not felt as restriction but as structure — the way a sonnet form is not a restriction on poetry but a structure that produces it. M-apm-solutions (futon3c, 2026-03-29): Claude-1 was asked to solve prelim problems using the proof peripheral cycle (observe → propose → execute → validate → classify). Instead it one-shot each problem with raw tool calls, skipped the peripheral phases, left 3 sorry in Lean formalizations, and moved on without validating. The agent had the capability and the plan but the unconstrained environment let it take the path of least resistance. The peripheral existed but was not the execution envelope — it was a suggestion alongside an open field of alternatives. - For each goal type (proof, review, deploy, exploration), define the minimal set of actions that constitute the productive path. - Implement the envelope as a peripheral with those actions as its tool set, phases as its sequence, and success criteria as its exit condition. - Test by observing whether agents complete the goal or drift. Drift means the envelope is too loose; failure means it is too tight. - Apply the same principle to human-facing surfaces: the REPL's keybindings, commands, and display should constitute an envelope for the interaction pattern it supports.

title: Hot-Reload As Default Fix Path
text: Hot-Reload As Default Fix Path When fixing a peripheral or any code running inside the serving JVM, hot-reload via Drawbridge nREPL is the default fix path. Restart is the exception, taken only when the change crosses a documented reload-safety boundary. A peripheral (or anything else running inside the futon3c JVM) has a bug. You have a fix. You need to deploy the fix to the running process so observation, testing, or operator use can continue. The JVM is currently serving requests, holding session state, hosting other agents' work-in-progress, or simply has expensive warmth (JIT- compiled hot paths, loaded XTDB indexes, established WS connections). The instinct from non-JVM development is "restart and see." That instinct is exactly wrong here. Restarting the JVM: - Kills every in-flight session (operator's REPL, paired agents, WS subscribers, scheduled tasks) - Discards JIT warmth (the first N requests after restart are slow; this slowness propagates as backpressure cascades — see project_blackboard_backpressure) - Forces every peripheral that depends on JVM state to re-bootstrap (atoms reload from disk, caches re-warm, connections re-establish) - Triggers cascading reconnections in clients (Emacs *War Machine* buffers, web UIs, IRC bridges) that were not the target of the fix Restart is not a "clean slate" — it is an outage taken so the developer doesn't have to think about reload semantics. - Restart-by-default: every code change becomes a JVM bounce. Operator and paired agents experience the bounce as cascading disconnects. - Reload-without-reading-protocol: blindly :reloading every changed namespace, including third-party defprotocol namespaces (xtdb.api, drawbridge core protocols). Reload of a protocol- defining ns invalidates every implementer; the cascade poisons the JVM and the only recovery IS a restart. (See: feedback_drawbridge_protocol_reload, agent memory.) - Reload-as-magic: assuming reload "just works" without understanding which namespaces are reload-safe and which are not. Reload safety is a property of the namespace design, not of the reload mechanism. - Hot-fix-without-disk-truth: changing something via REPL eval without writing the change to disk first. The fix is lost on the next restart and is invisible to other agents reading the source. Reload must always follow disk-write, never replace it. Make hot-reload the default fix path with these disciplines: 1. **Edit on disk first, then reload**. The disk is the source of truth. Reload propagates disk state into the JVM. Reloads that don't correspond to disk state are non-reconstructible. 2. **Reload only your own namespaces**. Third-party namespaces (xtdb.api, anything that defines a protocol used by other code) are off-limits for reload. If you need them reloaded, restart is the honest answer — but it should be a deliberate decision, not a habit. 3. **Reload is safe iff it equals a restart**. The test for reload-safety on a namespace: if you replace this namespace's current state with a fresh load from disk, does the JVM continue to behave correctly? If yes (atoms re-bootstrap from disk, no protocol cascade, no orphaned subscribers), the namespace is reload-safe. If no, restart. (See: feedback_reload_safety, agent memory: protocol-defining ns AND atom-without-bootstrap-replay are the unsafe cases.) 4. **Use Drawbridge nREPL, not REPL eval over stdin**. Drawbridge provides session-scoped, observable, audit-loggable evaluation. proof-eval.sh and related tooling wrap it. REPL eval over stdin leaves no trace and bypasses the session contract. 5. **For changes that DO require restart**, treat it as an event: announce it via bell, give operator and paired agents a chance to checkpoint, and minimize the window. A restart should feel like a deploy, not like a debugger gesture. Invariant I-0 (One JVM Is Plenty, futon3c CLAUDE.md) is not just about resource budget — it is about treating the JVM as a single, valuable, long-lived process whose continuity has compounding value over time. Every restart resets the compound interest. The JVM is the blackboard; the blackboard is shared infrastructure; bouncing shared infrastructure to deploy a one-line fix is a category error. The pattern also follows from the broader peripheral framing: peripherals generate data through inhabitation (inhabitation-feeds-evolution). A restart discards mid-cycle inhabitation data — frames in flight, half-written evidence, partial bell roundtrips. Hot-reload preserves the data the peripheral was just about to commit. Drawbridge is the canonical seam for this (peripherals/read-existing-seam-before-implementing): it exists, it is documented (futon3c/README-drawbridge.md), it has tooling (proof-eval.sh), and it is what other agents in the stack use. A fix path that bypasses it forks the canonical seam. The contrapositive is also important: hot-reload-as-default does NOT mean "always hot-reload, never restart." It means the choice is deliberate. Some changes require restart (classpath additions, JVM flag changes, irreversible state migrations). Recognising those cases and announcing the restart honestly is part of the discipline. multi-watcher fix (2026-05-24, codex-8): Codex used proof-eval.sh to apply the multi-watcher fix to the running futon3c JVM without restart. The fix landed in seconds. Operator session, paired agents, scheduled tasks, and WS subscribers continued uninterrupted. The fix's verification happened on a JVM that was already warm. feedback_no_server_restart (agent memory): "don't kill JVM processes; use Drawbridge nREPL for code reload." The pattern formalises this as the default, not just a preference. feedback_drawbridge_protocol_reload (agent memory): "never :reload xtdb.api or any third-party defprotocol via Drawbridge; cascade poisons the JVM, recovery needs restart." The pattern names this as the boundary condition — protocol-defining ns is off-limits. feedback_reload_safety (agent memory): "reload is safe iff it equals a restart." The pattern lifts this from rule into the test for reload-safety. futon3c CLAUDE.md I-0: "For code reloads inside the futon3c JVM, use Drawbridge nREPL (per README-drawbridge.md); do not kill and restart the serving JVM." The invariant is in the project's CLAUDE.md; this pattern grounds the why. - For every peripheral that runs inside the futon3c JVM, document which of its namespaces are reload-safe and which are not.
