The list belongs in the peripheral's own design doc. - When pairing on a fix, name the fix path explicitly: "hot-reload via Drawbridge" or "deliberate restart, here's why." Don't let the choice happen by reflex. - When designing a new peripheral, design for reload-safety from the start: atoms bootstrap from disk; no protocols defined in hot-edit paths; subscribers re-attach on reload rather than depending on JVM-process-identity. - For M-war-machine-pilot specifically: the WM peripheral's own namespaces should be reload-safe by design. The pilot's audit criteria should include "can be hot-reloaded via Drawbridge without disrupting the WM API surface or in-flight cycles."

title: Inhabitation Feeds Evolution
text: Inhabitation Feeds Evolution A peripheral is not just a constrained action space — it is a representational space that enables a learning loop. Inhabiting the peripheral generates the data that evolves the peripheral. If the peripheral is not inhabited, the loop is dead and the peripheral cannot improve. You have an interface — an action arena in Ostrom's sense — where agents (or humans) do work. The work produces outcomes. You want both the work and the interface to get better over time. The interface is more than a passive display: it is a space where actions happen, outcomes are observed, and the relationship between action and outcome can be recorded. Effective action is not just "doing things in a space." It requires a learning loop: the agent acts, observes the result, and the observation feeds back into future action. This is a transport problem — experience must move from the action space into a representation that can reshape future behavior. Without this transport, the agent acts but does not learn, and the interface affords but does not evolve. - Data-starved loop: the peripheral exists but nobody uses it, so no evidence accumulates and the designer has nothing to work with. This is the most common failure and the hardest to diagnose because the peripheral looks correct on paper. - Representation without transport: the peripheral captures data but the data never reaches the designer (or the glacial loop). Frames accumulate in SQLite but nobody queries them. Evidence is logged but never reviewed. - Evolution without inhabitation feedback: the designer changes the peripheral based on theory rather than usage data. The changes may be correct but are ungrounded — they solve imagined problems rather than observed ones. - Upsampling instability: the peripheral reshapes itself faster than the agent can adapt, creating a moving target. The learning loop needs damping, not just speed. Recognize that a peripheral is exactly the representational space where this transport happens. The peripheral is not merely a constrained execution envelope (though it is that too). It is a parallel space that mirrors the agent's actions in structured form — phases, events, frames, evidence — creating a representation that is legible to both the agent and the designer. This is the Baldwin effect operating on interfaces. In biology, the Baldwin effect describes how learned behaviors (phenotype) can guide the evolution of innate structure (genotype): organisms that can learn to exploit an environmental niche survive long enough for genetic changes that hardwire the adaptation. The learning happens fast; the structural change happens slow; but the learning is what makes the structural change possible. In the futon stack, the same dynamic operates at two timescales: - **Social loop (fast):** The agent inhabits the peripheral, acts within its phases, produces evidence, encounters friction or flow. This is the "learning" — the agent's experience within the representational space. - **Glacial loop (slow):** The peripheral designer reads the evidence, observes where agents drift or succeed, and reshapes the peripheral's phases, tools, and exit conditions. This is the "genetic change" — the structural evolution of the interface. The Baldwin insight: the fast loop generates the data that makes the slow loop possible. Without inhabitation, there is no data. Without data, there is no evolution. Without evolution, the peripheral stays misshapen. And a misshapen peripheral is not inhabited — completing the death spiral. The transport from futon2's AIF ants is the right analogy: cyberant programs represent ant foraging strategies in a parallel computational space. The ants act in the world; the programs represent those actions in a form that can be evaluated, compared, and evolved. The peripheral does the same thing for agent work: the agent acts in the problem domain; the peripheral represents those actions as phases, frames, and evidence entries in a form that can be inspected, compared, and used to reshape the envelope. The upsampling possibility: there is no fundamental reason the glacial loop must stay glacial. If the peripheral captures enough structured data in the social loop (rich frames, tool event sequences, outcome classifications), then the peripheral itself could be reshaped on the fly — adding phases, adjusting affordances, tightening or loosening the envelope — within the same session. This dissolves the boundary between learning and evolution. The agent's inhabitation of the peripheral generates the data that reshapes the peripheral that the agent is inhabiting. But — and this is the crux — none of this is possible if the agent does not enter the peripheral in the first place. The surface must earn inhabitation (see: peripherals/surface-earns-inhabitation) or the entire Baldwin loop is starved of data at the source. The symmetry between agents and humans reveals the pattern. When Claude bypasses the proof peripheral to one-shot tool calls, and when Joe bypasses the REPL to type in a terminal, they are both starving the same learning loop for the same reason: the primitive path has less friction. The consequence is the same in both cases: no structured data is generated, no evidence accumulates, no peripheral evolution is possible, and the gap between the primitive path and the infrastructure path never closes. The Baldwin effect is subtle because it requires seeing the peripheral as a representational space, not just a constraint. A constraint that is not inhabited is merely a rule. A representational space that is inhabited is a learning engine. The difference is whether the peripheral generates data that feeds back into its own design. This is why surface usability is not cosmetic. It is the entry condition for the Baldwin loop. A peripheral with perfect design but poor surface is like a genotype with perfect fitness in a niche that the organism never enters: theoretically optimal, actually inert. M-repl-wins-over-cli (futon3c, 2026-03-29): interrupt did not work, tool calls were opaque, streaming hijacked the cursor. Joe used the CLI instead. No evidence was logged, no frames were captured, no data was available to improve the REPL. Fixing the basics was not UI work — it was reopening the Baldwin loop by making inhabitation possible. M-apm-solutions (futon3c, 2026-03-29): Claude-1 was given the proof peripheral but one-shot every problem without entering the cycle. No phase transitions were recorded, no validation occurred, no evidence accumulated for improving the cycle. The peripheral existed but generated no data because it was not inhabited. futon2 AIF ants: cyberant programs evolved foraging strategies in a parallel representation space. The ants had to actually forage (inhabit the environment) for the programs to have data to evolve against. Ants that did not forage contributed nothing to the evolutionary loop. - Ensure every peripheral captures structured data (frames, events, evidence) as a side effect of inhabitation, not as an extra step. - Build review surfaces that make peripheral usage data visible to the designer (frame inspector, evidence queries, session replay). - Identify peripherals with low inhabitation rates and treat the surface friction as the primary diagnosis, not the peripheral design. - Experiment with social-loop peripheral adaptation: can the envelope tighten or loosen based on observed drift within a single session?

title: Pattern Becomes Peripheral
text: Pattern Becomes Peripheral A pattern that remains documentation has not yet become a peripheral. The transition from pattern to peripheral is the transition from describing what works to being the space in which the working happens — and that transition is what creates new capability, not merely new knowledge. You have a well-articulated pattern — or a library of them. The patterns accurately describe what works under what conditions. They have been grounded in evidence, stress-tested, cross-referenced. They are correct. But the situation they describe has not improved. The patterns are correct and the problem they address is real: there exists a productive way of working that is not being practiced. Correctness does not produce inhabitation. A pattern describes the right envelope but does not address whether anyone enters it or whether it evolves through use. The pattern sits in the library (or the programme design document, or the mission file) as a description of what would work — and the world continues not to work that way. This is not a failure of the pattern. It is a category gap. Pattern theory gives you the vocabulary for describing *what works under what conditions*. What it does not give you is the space in which the working happens, the surface that earns entry into that space, or the loop through which the space improves. Those are peripheral-theoretic concerns. The gap shows up identically across scales: - A developer has 800 patterns in a library but reaches for the CLI because the REPL (which instantiates the patterns as a working environment) has too much friction. - An AI agent has a proof peripheral defined with phases and exit conditions but one-shots every problem because entering the peripheral is harder than not entering it. - A national programme has five well-grounded design patterns but the institutional architecture that would instantiate them as lived practice is largely absent. In all three cases, the patterns are correct. In none of them is the pattern doing work. The pattern is a description; it has not yet become a space. - Pattern-as-commandment: "you must use the proof peripheral" produces compliance, not inhabitation. The agent enters the space under obligation and exits at the first opportunity. - Pattern-as-prohibition: "you must not use the CLI" blocks the alternative without making the peripheral attractive. Produces resentment and workarounds. - Absorbed input mistaken for success: the trainer delivered, the code was written, the problem was solved. But nothing was learned at the system level. Output without capability is the most common and least visible failure. - Blame allocated to inhabitants: "the trainers didn't embed the programme" / "the agent didn't use the peripheral" / "the developer didn't use the REPL." The diagnostic should be: the space didn't earn inhabitation, the surface had too much friction, or the Baldwin loop was starved. Recognise that pattern theory is necessary but not self-completing. The bridge from pattern to practice is *instantiation as peripheral*: the pattern must become a constrained execution envelope (what the space contains), with a surface that earns inhabitation (why anyone enters), feeding a Baldwin loop (how the space evolves from use). This bridge has a distinctive character that distinguishes it from both commandment and prohibition. The pattern-as-documentation says "here is what works" — a descriptive claim. A commandment ("thou shalt use the proof peripheral") tries to force entry through obligation. A prohibition ("thou shalt not use the CLI") tries to force entry by blocking alternatives. Neither works, for reasons the philosophical tradition has long understood: - Spinoza: joy (laetitia) is an increase in the power to act. A peripheral that earns inhabitation produces joy — the inhabitant finds their power to act increased by being inside it. A commandment produces obedience, which is not joy. A prohibition produces resentment or evasion, which is the opposite. - Nietzsche: affirmation is the only durable motivation. The peripheral must be affirmed — chosen because it is good, not endured because it is required. - Sen: capability is freedom, not functioning. The peripheral must create real freedom to act — conversion factors that turn nominal access into durable capability. A programme that provides access without conversion factors provides a pattern without a peripheral. The transition from pattern to peripheral is therefore not an implementation step ("now deploy the pattern"). It is a creative act: the construction of a space that is *worth inhabiting*, that increases the inhabitant's power to act, and that generates the data needed to evolve itself. Crucially, this means the moral weight falls on the *space*, not on the *inhabitant*. When a trainer doesn't embed the programme, or an agent doesn't use the peripheral, or a developer doesn't use the REPL, the diagnosis is not "the inhabitant is deficient" but "the space has not yet earned inhabitation." This is not moral grayness — it is a precise structural claim: the conditions for productive action have not been met, and the responsibility lies with whoever designs and maintains the conditions, not with whoever fails to thrive within inadequate ones. The absorbed-input mode reveals why this matters. In the absorbed case, an individual gains something — skills, experience, CV lines, working code — but the system gains nothing. The trainer leaves and takes the knowledge with them. The agent writes code but no institutional learning accumulates. The developer uses Stack Overflow and gets a working function but no understanding of why it works. What doesn't happen in the absorbed case is the creation of new institutions (Ostrom). The trainer doesn't create a community of practice at their institution. The agent doesn't produce evidence that improves the proof peripheral. The developer doesn't contribute a pattern back to the library. The individual transacts with the system but the system does not change. This is the "programming by Stack Exchange" failure mode applied universally. An interaction that produces output without producing capability is an interaction that has been *absorbed* rather than *institutionalised*. The output is real — the code works, the training was delivered, the problem was solved — but it is non-generative. Nothing was learned at the system level. No new institution was created. No peripheral evolved. The pattern-to-peripheral bridge is what converts absorbed input into institutional creation. When a pattern becomes a peripheral: 1. The envelope defines a positive action space (not a prohibition). 2. The surface earns entry (not commands it). 3. Inhabitation generates data (not just output). 4. The data feeds back into the peripheral's design (Baldwin loop). 5. The improved peripheral earns further inhabitation (virtuous cycle). At step 5, something new exists that didn't exist before: an institution in Ostrom's sense — a set of rules-in-use that govern a shared resource (the action space) and that evolve through the participation of their inhabitants. This is what the absorbed-input mode fails to produce, and it is what the pattern-to-peripheral transition is for. The Spinozan frame is the deepest one: the question is not "did the agent obey the pattern?" but "did the agent's power to act increase?" If it did, the pattern has become a peripheral. If it didn't — if the agent merely transacted and moved on — the pattern remains documentation, however correct it may be. M-repl-wins-over-cli (futon3c, 2026-03-29): the pattern library contained patterns for evidence logging, frame persistence, and coordination. None were operative until the REPL surface was made inhabitable. The patterns became peripherals only when the basics (interrupt, tool visibility, cursor stability) were fixed. M-apm-solutions (futon3c, 2026-03-29): the proof peripheral defined phases, criteria, and exit conditions. Claude-1 one-shot every problem. The pattern was correct; the peripheral was not inhabited. UKRN ORP T3 programme (paper_v2.4): five well-grounded design patterns, backed by NPT coding and transcript evidence. The patterns accurately described what would work. The institutional architecture that would instantiate them as lived practice was largely absent. Absorbed-input mode: trainers gained individual skills but no new institutions were created. - For each pattern in the library that is "known but not practiced," ask: has this pattern been instantiated as a peripheral? If not, the gap is not knowledge but infrastructure. - For each peripheral that exists but is underused, ask: does the surface earn inhabitation? If not, the gap is not design but UX. - For each peripheral that is inhabited but not improving, ask: is the Baldwin loop running? If not, the gap is not usage but feedback transport. - Treat the absorbed-input mode as a diagnostic, not a verdict. It tells you that individual transactions are happening but institutional creation is not. The fix is to build the bridge — envelope, surface, loop — not to blame the transactors.

title: Progress Heartbeat Distinct From Cycle Completion
text: Progress Heartbeat Distinct From Cycle Completion A peripheral's "is it alive?" signal must be a progress heartbeat distinct from its cycle completion event. Conflating the two produces watchdogs that fire on healthy long-running cycles (false positives) and watchdogs that fail to fire on wedged cycles still inside their nominal duration (false negatives). A peripheral has a cycle — a unit of work it opens, processes, and closes. A watchdog (or supervisor, or conductor, or operator) wants to know whether the peripheral is alive: making progress, or stuck. The peripheral's cycles can vary in legitimate duration (some take seconds, some take minutes), and the watchdog needs to distinguish "still working on it" from "wedged." The naive implementation uses cycle-open-duration as the liveness signal: if a cycle has been open longer than threshold T, the peripheral is "stuck." This conflates two different things: - **Cycle phase** (open / closed) — describes whether a unit of work is currently being processed. - **Progress liveness** — describes whether *anything* is happening inside the peripheral right now. A healthy peripheral can have a cycle open for 10 minutes while actively making progress every second. A wedged peripheral can silently freeze 5 seconds after opening a cycle and stay frozen until something kills it. Cycle-open-duration tells you neither. - False-positive watchdog: long but legitimate cycles trip the watchdog. The watchdog kills healthy work. Operators learn to widen T, which widens the blind spot for real wedges. - False-negative watchdog: a cycle wedges 5 seconds in and stays wedged for the remaining 9:55 of its nominal duration. The watchdog fires "on time" — too late to help. - Heartbeat-as-pulse-without-content: the peripheral emits "I'm alive" pings with no payload. The watchdog can't tell whether the peripheral is alive AND making progress, or alive AND in a tight retry loop, or alive AND deadlocked-on-IO-waking-up. - Conductor-as-watchdog: a conductor that steps the peripheral forward AND watches it for liveness conflates the regulator and the supervisor. When the conductor wedges, the watchdog wedges with it. Make the heartbeat first-class and distinct from the cycle: 1. **Emit progress heartbeats from inside the work**, not from cycle boundaries. The heartbeat is "I just did a meaningful unit of work" — a file processed, a frame written, an event handled. The heartbeat is keyed on `:last-progress-at` (or similar) and is updated by the work itself, not by the supervisor. 2. **Separate the heartbeat channel from the cycle channel**. Cycle start/end events carry "what work is this" semantics. Heartbeats carry "the work is moving" semantics. A watchdog subscribes to heartbeats; a UI subscribes to cycle events. (See: peripherals/split-transport-from-embodiment — heartbeats are a distinct transport concern.) 3. **Watchdog measures real silence**, not cycle-open-duration. The watchdog fires when (now - :last-progress-at) exceeds T, regardless of which cycle is open or how long it has been open. Cycles that legitimately take 10 minutes are fine as long as they emit a heartbeat every few seconds. 4. **Heartbeats carry a small payload** describing what just happened ("processed file X," "wrote frame N," "handled event type E"). This converts the heartbeat from a pulse into a diagnostic. When the watchdog fires, the last-heartbeat payload tells you what the peripheral was doing just before it wedged. 5. **The regulator (conductor / FM stepper / tickle) is separate from the watchdog**. The regulator paces work forward. The watchdog detects silence. The two should be implemented as distinct processes, ideally with the watchdog supervising the regulator. (See: project_war_machine_as_tm_on_manifold for the regulator-as-head-of-TM framing.) The problem is fundamentally one of clock alignment. Cycle phase runs on a work-bounded clock (this cycle takes as long as the work takes). Liveness needs to run on a wall-clock or a tick-clock (silence is measured in seconds since something happened). Trying to use one clock for both produces the FM-regulator-vs-watchdog confusion: the regulator wants long cycles for big work; the watchdog wants short cycles for fast detection; they cannot both win on the same axis. The fix — separate channels for separate clocks — is the same pattern as feedback_perceived_time_dual_clock (agent memory): two clocks must be bridged through an explicit convolution, not papered over by treating one as the other. Heartbeats and cycle events are two clocks; the convolution is the watchdog's silence calculation. The pattern has an institutional reading too: peripheral cycles are glacial-loop events (M-cycle, M-mission, M-cycle-of-cycles). Progress heartbeats are social-loop events (something just happened). The distinction is the same as inhabitation-feeds-evolution's fast/slow split, applied to the liveness question. multi-watcher fix (2026-05-24, codex-8): the watchdog was firing on healthy long-running cycles and failing to fire on cycles that wedged shortly after opening. Codex added an explicit `:last-progress-at` keyed on per-iteration work events; the watchdog was changed to measure real silence rather than cycle-open-duration. False positives dropped to zero; false negatives became detectable on the watchdog's own timescale. realtime/liveness-heartbeats (futon3 pattern library): the realtime patterns already articulate the distinction at the transport layer. This pattern lifts the distinction into the peripheral-design layer and makes it a design-time decision, not a runtime emergent. futon0 cron-jobs.edn (2026-05-23): the pattern-index-rebuild cron entry was added because the main work loop did not heartbeat its progress to a separate channel — the TSV file appeared "stale" because nothing was checking real silence on the index-rebuild work, only cycle-open-duration on the parent multi-watcher. M-war-machine-pilot (futon3c, DERIVE 2026-05-24): the mission selected "Tickle v2 mechanical FM regulator" over "Tickle v1 watchdog" precisely because v1 conflated regulator and watchdog. v2's mechanical FM regulator paces forward; the watchdog is then layered on top measuring heartbeat silence, not regulator cycle-open-duration. This pattern formalises the reasoning. - When designing any new peripheral with cycles, add a heartbeat schema to the transport layer at design time, not after the first watchdog false-positive incident. - Heartbeat payloads must be small but informative: at minimum timestamp + work-tag + counter. This is the same shape MUSN events use for tool-call telemetry. - Watchdog implementations must NEVER subscribe to cycle events for liveness. If a watchdog is found doing so, treat it as a latent incident regardless of current symptom status. - For M-war-machine-pilot specifically: the Tickle v2 conductor MUST be specified with a :last-progress-at heartbeat distinct from its cycle. The watchdog (whether bell-based, cron-based, or operator-pinged) subscribes to the heartbeat. This is the v0 observer-stage contract. - Cross-link: peripherals/canonical-typed-event-vs-side-channel — the heartbeat should be a first-class event in the transport taxonomy, not a parallel ping channel.

title: Read Existing Seam Before Implementing
text: Read Existing Seam Before Implementing When a mission proposes building a peripheral, the first move is not to design the peripheral — it is to locate the canonical seams in the existing stack the peripheral must thread through. If the mission as written would fork those seams, rewrite the mission before writing any code. A mission has been authored that calls for a new peripheral — a cursor peripheral, an editor peripheral, a notification peripheral. The mission specifies behaviour, surface, and (often) implementation sketch. The temptation is to read the mission and start building. The stack already has canonical infrastructure for one or more of the concerns the peripheral touches: transport (WS pipeline, drawbridge, agency dispatch), event schema (frame format, MUSN events), registration (peripheral registry, agent identity), or consent (gate pipeline, write-ownership boundaries). Missions are written from the problem side, not the infrastructure side. The author of the mission knows what the peripheral should DO; they may not know that the stack already has a WS event taxonomy that the new peripheral would either extend or fork. If the mission is implemented as written, the result is a peripheral that works but lives parallel to canonical infra — a second WS channel, a second event schema, a second registration mechanism. Each parallel path is a future migration cost and a present source of drift. - Mission-as-spec: treating the mission's implementation sketch as authoritative when it was authored before the canonical seam was located. The mission is a description of intent, not a design. - Read-but-not-located: searching for related files but not finding the actual seam the peripheral must thread through. Glob and grep are necessary but not sufficient; the seam may be in a transport contract document, a wiring claim, or a peripheral spec — not in a file whose name contains the peripheral's topic. - Forked-by-default: when the canonical seam is hard to find, the default action is to build parallel rather than extend. This is how the stack accumulates two of everything. - Mission-rewrite-skipped: locating the seam, recognising the mission would fork it, but proceeding anyway because "rewriting the mission feels like scope creep." This is exactly when the rewrite is cheapest — before any code commits the fork. Before writing any code for the peripheral, do a structured seam-read: 1. **Transport seam**: how do bytes get to and from the peripheral? Is there a canonical WS pipeline, drawbridge channel, or agency dispatch path the peripheral should use? If yes, extend it. If no, write down why no. 2. **Event seam**: what is the event taxonomy on that transport? Are there existing frame shapes that cover (or partially cover) what this peripheral emits/consumes? If yes, extend the taxonomy as first-class events, not as out-of-band messages. (See: peripherals/canonical-typed-event-vs-side-channel.) 3. **Registration seam**: how does the peripheral identify itself to the stack and to other agents/peripherals? Is there a registry? If yes, register; do not invent a parallel identity scheme. 4. **Consent seam**: where does this peripheral cross from "observing" to "writing"? Does the stack have a consent-gate or write-ownership boundary the peripheral must respect? (See: project_consent_gate in agent memory.) 5. **Prior-art seam**: has someone built a structurally-similar peripheral before, in this stack or in adjacent open-source projects (crdt.el for cursor presence; LSP for editor-side capability negotiation; ROS topics for typed transport)? Read it fully before designing. If any seam is missing in the mission as written, REWRITE THE MISSION before implementing. Rewriting a paragraph is an order of magnitude cheaper than rewriting committed code. The mission rewrite IS the design work the original mission elided. Invariant I-4 (Read Before You Write) is usually applied at the level of "before creating a new .clj file, search for existing files." This pattern is I-4 applied at the level of MISSIONS: before authoring code against a mission, locate the canonical seams the mission must thread. Missions are authored under time pressure, often by operators who know what they want the peripheral to do but not the full geography of the stack. The first agent to pick up the mission has the responsibility — not the option — to do the seam-read the operator could not do, and to push back into the mission if the seams require it. The cost of catching a fork at mission-rewrite time is one paragraph. The cost of catching it after one round of implementation is a refactor. The cost of catching it after a release is a deprecation cycle. M-emacs-cursor-peripheral (2026-05-24, codex-8): the mission was authored to propose a cursor peripheral. Codex began implementation, then stopped and identified that the mission as written would fork the canonical WS pipeline, invent a parallel event schema, and bypass the peripheral registry. Codex proposed rewriting the mission to use existing seams; Joe agreed. The rewrite happened before any cursor-peripheral code was committed. Forks avoided: one WS channel, one event taxonomy, one registration mechanism, one consent boundary. futon3c invariant I-4 (Read Before You Write): "Writing new code to solve an already-solved problem wastes time, introduces bugs, and ignores hard-won design decisions embedded in the existing implementation." This pattern extends I-4 from files to seams. M-war-machine-pilot (futon3c, in DERIVE 2026-05-24): the mission's DERIVE explicitly enumerates conductor candidates, transports, peripheral clone-from sources, and Playwright probes BEFORE choosing — the structure encodes the seam-read at the mission level. - For every new peripheral mission, the IDENTIFY phase must include a seam-read checklist (transport, event, registration, consent, prior-art). - When a mission is rewritten on seam-read grounds, record the rewrite as a checkpoint with the rationale — it is the highest- leverage design work in the mission. - Build a "canonical seams" index in the stack so that future seam-reads are bounded lookups rather than open-ended searches. - When pairing with another agent on a mission, the seam-read is a first-class deliverable, not a precondition assumed satisfied.

title: Read-Only First, Then Extend
text: Read-Only First, Then Extend A new peripheral's first instantiation should be read-only — observing, displaying, not writing. Write capability is added in a separate, later instantiation once observation has revealed what writes actually need to look like. You are about to instantiate a new peripheral. The mission describes both observation and action: see other agents' cursors AND move your own cursor visible to them; receive bells AND ring them; watch the War Machine state AND inject judgements. The peripheral, if fully implemented, would both read shared state and write to it — affecting other agents, other operators, or persistent substrate. Writing is irreversible in ways that observing is not. A misshapen observation produces a confusing display the operator can ignore. A misshapen write corrupts a substrate, surprises a collaborator, triggers downstream cascades, or — in the worst case — competes with another agent for write-ownership the peripheral did not know it was claiming. The full peripheral's blast radius is large; the read-only subset's blast radius is zero. - Write-before-shape-known: the peripheral writes events whose schema turns out to be wrong because nobody observed what the right schema would be. Now there is committed wire data to migrate. - Bidirectional from day one: the peripheral both reads and writes in v1, so any bug is in the bidirectional interaction surface, which is the hardest possible bug to debug. - Consent-elided: the peripheral's writes cross a consent boundary that nobody noticed because the design was focused on the round-trip experience, not on the per-direction implications. - Read-only as permanent: the converse failure — building the observer and never extending it, so the peripheral never closes its loop and never feeds the Baldwin cycle. Read-only is a first step, not a terminal state. Instantiate the peripheral in three escalating stages, each with its own checkpoint and consent step: 1. **Observer stage (read-only)** — the peripheral subscribes to the transport, renders presence/state in the embodiment surface, and writes nothing back. The operator/agent can see what the peripheral does and decide whether the observation is well-shaped. Blast radius: zero. Exit criterion: the observation is informative enough that "what writes should look like" becomes discoverable. 2. **Pair stage (consent-gated write)** — the peripheral can propose writes, but each write requires explicit consent (a confirmation step, a key press, a bell-ack roundtrip). Blast radius: bounded by per-write consent. Exit criterion: the writes have shown a stable schema and the consent prompts are no longer surprising. 3. **Collaborate stage (envelope-bounded write)** — the peripheral writes autonomously within a documented envelope (specific targets, specific event types, specific time windows). Consent is no longer per-write but per-envelope-grant. Blast radius: bounded by the envelope. Exit criterion: documented stable behaviour under autonomous operation. Each stage is a separate landing. You do not ship Pair without first landing Observer; you do not ship Collaborate without first landing Pair. Each stage produces its own evidence and its own Baldwin-loop data that informs the next stage's design. The escalation matches the natural epistemic order. To know what writes should look like, you need to observe what is being read and where the gaps are. To know what consent should feel like, you need to have made some writes and noticed the friction. To know what envelope is safe, you need to have made consent-gated writes long enough to see the failure modes. Skipping stages means designing later stages on speculation rather than observation. Speculative design is exactly what the peripheral framing is meant to displace. The pattern also matches the consent-gate-as-locus-of-WM-I4 principle: the consent step is a first-class artefact, and the migration from supervised to autonomous is the swap of operator- consent for autopen-consent at a single, documented location. That swap is only safe after the operator has spent enough time consenting to know what they are signing off on. The Pair stage is where that knowledge accumulates. Crucially, "read-only first" is not the same as "don't ship anything until you understand everything." Observer is a real shipped peripheral — it has inhabitation, it produces value (the display is used), it generates Baldwin-loop data. It is just a peripheral whose capability is exactly read, no more. M-emacs-cursor-peripheral (2026-05-24, codex-8): Codex proposed instantiating the cursor peripheral as read-only first (display other agents' cursors without broadcasting own position), then pair (broadcast own position with explicit opt-in), then collaborate (autonomous co-presence). Each stage maps to a separate landing with separate consent semantics. crdt.el (Emacs CRDT): the canonical workflow has "follow" mode (you observe another user's cursor) as a distinct capability from "share" mode (you broadcast your own state). Follow is strictly safer to enable; share requires more trust. M-war-machine-pilot (futon3c, DERIVE 2026-05-24): the mission's Pilot-I1 (consent-gated-substantive-action) and its envelope design (direct write within envelope; consent-gate at substantive granularity) implicitly assumes a path from observer to pair to collaborate. Making the stages explicit clarifies what "v0 audit by re-invoked claude-9" actually validates. futon3c blackboard backpressure (project_blackboard_backpressure, agent memory): hot paths synchronously block on emacsclient. A peripheral that wrote into those paths before observing the backpressure topology would cascade. Observer-first surfaces the backpressure topology BEFORE the peripheral takes a write-position in it. - For every new peripheral, define the three stages explicitly in the mission's IDENTIFY or MAP phase. Each stage gets its own success criteria and its own bell-ready landing. - When estimating timeline, treat the three stages as three missions' worth of work, not one. Observer alone can ship in hours; Pair takes days; Collaborate takes weeks or months. - For M-war-machine-pilot specifically: the v0 pilot should be the Observer-stage version of the WM peripheral. The audit by claude-9-re-invoked validates Observer shape. Pair and Collaborate stages are follow-on missions. - If an operator asks for "v1 with everything," push back with the stage breakdown. The conversation about which stage maps to which timeline is itself a Baldwin-loop event.

title: Split Transport From Embodiment
text: Split Transport From Embodiment A peripheral has two distinct concerns — how it moves bytes (transport) and how it manifests as presence (embodiment). Conflating them produces peripherals that cannot be re-transported, re-embodied, or composed. You are designing a peripheral that has a perceptible surface: cursor presence in an editor, a notification pop, a streaming display, a chat bubble. The peripheral both moves data and produces a felt presence in some surface. The peripheral has both an "over the wire" dimension (how messages arrive and depart) and an "in the world" dimension (how the agent or operator experiences the peripheral's effect). Mission authors and first-pass designers typically describe the peripheral as a single thing: "the cursor peripheral broadcasts cursor positions over WebSocket." Read carefully: this sentence fuses three concerns — transport (WebSocket), payload schema (cursor positions), and embodiment (a cursor showing up in someone else's editor). When implemented as a single thing, the peripheral cannot be swapped for a different transport (IRC, drawbridge), cannot be re-embodied (statusline indicator instead of cursor overlay), and cannot be composed with other peripherals that need the same transport but a different embodiment. - Tight-coupling of WS to overlay: changing the renderer requires touching the transport code; changing the transport requires touching the renderer. - Embodiment without transport contract: the peripheral shows up in the editor but there is no documented event schema another agent could implement against. The peripheral is a closed loop. - Transport without embodiment contract: bytes flow but no agent knows how to render them as presence. The transport is dead. - Embodiment-as-mission-name: naming the mission after the embodiment ("cursor peripheral") narrows the design space and masks the transport question entirely. Split the design explicitly into two layers and design each on its own terms: 1. **Transport layer** — answers: what events flow, in what schema, over what channel, with what reliability, with what backpressure, with what consent? The transport must be describable without reference to any specific UI surface. Other agents and other peripherals must be able to participate in the transport without sharing the embodiment. 2. **Embodiment layer** — answers: how does presence manifest in the surface where the operator/agent perceives it? Cursor overlay? Statusline glyph? Modeline indicator? Posframe? Each embodiment is a distinct rendering of the same transport. The embodiment must be describable as a function of transport events. Composition rule: the transport layer never imports from the embodiment layer. The embodiment layer subscribes to transport events. New embodiments are added by writing new subscribers; new transports are added by porting the event schema to a new channel. For missions about peripherals with both layers, the mission name should encode both. "Cursor peripheral" becomes "presence transport + cursor embodiment." The two halves can then have their own seam-reads, their own design questions, and their own delivery schedules. The stack already pays for this split implicitly everywhere it works: drawbridge separates message routing from agent representation; the War Machine separates the AIF engine from the markdown/web UI renderers; the REPL separates the chat protocol from the posframe surface. Where peripherals fail to be portable or composable, it is almost always because the split was elided at design time. The deeper reason is that transport and embodiment evolve at different timescales. Transport schemas are slow-changing institutional artefacts (changing them breaks every consumer). Embodiments are fast-changing UX artefacts (a posframe today, an overlay tomorrow). When the two are fused, the embodiment's fast-changing nature contaminates the transport — and the transport's institutional weight ossifies the embodiment. This split is also what makes peripherals composable. Two peripherals that share a transport layer can coordinate (cursor presence + selection presence both ride the same "editor presence" event stream). Two peripherals that share an embodiment surface can cooperate (a statusline that shows both build status and presence count). Without the split, every peripheral is a silo. M-emacs-cursor-peripheral (2026-05-24, codex-8): the original mission described "the cursor peripheral" as a single concept. Codex's seam-read identified that the mission was really proposing a presence transport plus a cursor-overlay embodiment; the rewrite separated them. The transport could then be reused for other presence concerns (selections, viewport ranges) and the embodiment could be swapped (overlay, statusline, posframe). futon3c War Machine: the AIF backend emits structured events; the markdown renderer (Emacs *War Machine* buffer) and web UI (hex layout) are two embodiments of the same transport. Adding the R-Criterion Status section to the markdown renderer did not require touching the web UI, and vice versa, precisely because the split was honoured. crdt.el (Emacs CRDT for collaborative editing): the transport is a CRDT-over-TCP protocol; the embodiment is the cursor/region overlays in the buffer. The two are cleanly separated; other embodiments (presence indicators in modeline) could be added without touching the CRDT layer. - In every peripheral mission, rename concepts so that transport and embodiment have distinct names. "Cursor peripheral" → "presence transport + cursor overlay." - For each layer, do an independent seam-read (see: peripherals/read-existing-seam-before-implementing). - When reviewing peripheral code, the test for split-cleanliness is: could a second embodiment be added without touching the transport module? Could the transport be ported to a different channel without touching the embodiment module? - For M-war-machine-pilot specifically: the WM peripheral's transport (bells, walkie-talkie, whistle, conductor steps) and its embodiment (Emacs *War Machine* buffer, web hex UI, future overlays on operator's editor) must be split-clean before INSTANTIATE.

title: Surface Earns Inhabitation
text: Surface Earns Inhabitation A productive interface that nobody uses is dead infrastructure; the surface must earn inhabitation by being less friction than the alternative. You have built a peripheral or surface with genuine capabilities — evidence logging, frame persistence, coordination, structured tool visibility — that the primitive alternative (a CLI, a one-shot API call, an ad hoc script) lacks. The surface offers real infrastructure advantages over the primitive path, and you want agents or humans to actually inhabit it rather than bypass it. The surface is cluttered, difficult to enter, or tedious to operate. Basic operations that work effortlessly in the primitive path (interrupt, inspect, navigate) are broken or awkward. The inhabitant spends their energy fighting the interface rather than doing the work the interface was built to support. So they don't use it. They reach for the primitive path because it has less friction, even though it has less capability. - Building capabilities before basics: the surface can do amazing things but can't be interrupted, so nobody trusts it with long-running work. - Treating UX as separate from architecture: "we'll polish the UI later" means the UI never gets polished because the architecture was designed without considering the inhabitant's experience. - Blocking the primitive path instead of earning preference: disabling the CLI doesn't make the REPL better; it just makes the user resentful. - Confusing feature count with inhabitability: adding more capabilities to an already-cluttered surface makes it worse, not better. Treat surface usability as load-bearing infrastructure, not cosmetic polish. Close every friction gap between the surface and the primitive alternative before adding new capabilities. The surface must be strictly better at the basics — responsiveness, interruptibility, visibility, stability — so that inhabitation is the natural choice, not a discipline exercise. Concretely: - Every operation the primitive path supports must work at least as well. - The surface's unique capabilities (evidence, frames, coordination) come free with inhabitation, not as extra steps. - If the inhabitant has to fight the surface, the surface is broken, not the inhabitant. Uninhabited infrastructure is dead infrastructure. The value of a peripheral is not what it *can* do but what it *does* do — and it does nothing if nobody is inside it. I-3 says peripherals are inhabited, not delegated. But inhabitation is not commanded; it is earned. The surface earns it by being the path of least resistance to productive work. This applies symmetrically to agents and humans. An agent that bypasses the proof peripheral to one-shot tool calls, and a human who bypasses the REPL to type in a terminal, are exhibiting the same behavior for the same reason: the primitive path has less friction. The fix is the same in both cases — not to block the primitive path, but to make the infrastructure path frictionless enough that it becomes the natural choice. M-repl-wins-over-cli (futon3c, 2026-03-29): the Claude REPL had evidence logging, frame persistence, agent coordination, and structured tool visibility — but interrupt didn't kill the server process, tool calls showed only opaque markers, streaming text hijacked the cursor, and port discovery was fragile. The CLI had none of the capabilities but all of the basics. Joe reached for Alacritty every time. Fixing the basics (interrupt, tool detail, cursor stability) was not UI polish — it was the work that made the infrastructure inhabitable. - Audit every surface for friction gaps against its primitive alternative. - Prioritize closing friction gaps over adding new capabilities. - Measure inhabitation (do agents/humans actually use the surface?) not capability (could they theoretically use it?). - Apply the same standard to agent-facing surfaces (peripherals) and human-facing surfaces (REPLs, dashboards, inspectors).

title: Turn a Null, a Dropout, or a Thin Cell into the Headline Finding
text: Turn a Null, a Dropout, or a Thin Cell into the Headline Finding When the data contain an apparent weakness — a cross-case null, a failed recruitment, a thin sub-sample — make that absence the affirmative finding rather than burying it in limitations. A null framed as "we found no difference across models" becomes the thesis "the service works in all models"; a recruitment failure becomes "the tool is not appropriate for this setting." Reframing absence as evidence pre-empts the reading that small n or missing data is underpowered failure. The multiple-case exemplar makes a cross-case null ("no differences in delivery across the three models") its headline claim — "primary care is primary care" — and borrows experimental replication logic so three cases read as a replication design, not a thin sample. The medication-safety exemplar turns its inability to recruit primary-care users into the central substantive result that the tool does not fit community settings. In both, the absence is mined, not excused. The pattern operates on the axis: absence-as-limitation <-> absence-as-finding. Irreducible: a null or a gap is information about the world; left in the limitations it reads as the study's failure, foregrounded as a result it reads as the study's contribution — the same datum, opposite valence. Real costs: reframing absence as evidence risks over-claiming from too little (a null from an underpowered study is not the same as a demonstrated equivalence). The discipline is to claim only what the absence licenses — a process/transferability claim, not a statistical equivalence — and to pair it with a design warrant (replication logic, maximum-variation sampling) so the null is interpretable rather than merely empty. Active dynamic: authors instinctively apologise for nulls and dropouts in the limitations. The stronger move is to ask what the absence demonstrates and lead with that. - Apology-burial: the null/dropout appears only as a limitation, forfeiting the finding. - Over-claimed-equivalence: a null from a small sample is presented as proven equivalence rather than as a bounded, process-level claim. - Naked-null: the absence is foregrounded with no design warrant, so it reads as underpowered rather than informative. Foreground the absence and warrant it. (1) Null-as-thesis. Schema: {:observed-absence <no difference / no effect> :reframed-claim <what the convergence means> :scope <process | transferability, not equivalence>} Effect: converts a null into a contribution without over-claiming. (2) Replication-logic warrant. Schema: {:cases <n> :logic "replication, not sampling" :what-replicates <finding across cases>} Effect: makes a small case count read as a design, not a thin sample. (3) Non-recruitment-as-finding. Schema: {:could-not-recruit <group/setting> :reframed "not appropriate for that setting" :evidence <why>} Effect: turns a recruitment gap into a substantive claim about fit. Engaged when an apparent weakness is presented as a result with an explicit warrant for the claim it supports. Failing when nulls or gaps appear only as apologies, or when absence is over-read as proven equivalence.

title: Put n, Setting, Method, and Frame in the Abstract
text: Put n, Setting, Method, and Frame in the Abstract A small-n PLOS ONE abstract should disclose the empirical shape before asking the reader to trust the interpretation: setting, participant/data count, qualitative or mixed-method design, analytic framework, and the kind of claim being made. The abstract does not need to apologize for n; it needs to show what kind of evidence n is, what it was used for, and how far the paper will carry it. The closest PLOS exemplars make their sample visible early: interviews, focus groups, observations, sites, cases, or workshops appear in the Methods paragraph before the Results paragraph moves to themes or implementation mechanisms. This presentation lets a reader calibrate the claim as feasibility, acceptability, process evaluation, implementation explanation, or thematic account rather than mistaking it for prevalence estimation. The pattern operates on the axis: evidence-shape disclosed early <-> interpretation-first abstract. Irreducible: when n is small, the reader must know what n denotes before judging the result. Participant count, site count, and data-source count are different warrants. Real costs: naming n, setting, framework, and design consumes abstract space that could otherwise hold findings. Overloading the abstract with methods can make it read defensively. The discipline is to put only the calibration facts needed for the reader to interpret the result. Active dynamic: authors often want to lead with the importance of the topic or with the strongest finding. PLOS qualitative abstracts read better when the evidence container is established first. - Result-before-design: the abstract states themes or implications before saying what data produced them. - Hidden-n: the full article eventually gives participant counts, but the abstract leaves the reader guessing whether n means interviews, sites, cases, or observations. - Framework-name-only: the abstract names NPT, reflexive thematic analysis, or mixed methods without saying how it shaped data collection or analysis. - Prevalence-leak: small-n qualitative findings are phrased like population frequencies rather than analytic findings. Make the abstract's Methods paragraph carry the calibration load. (1) Setting-count-design-frame. Schema: {:setting <where> :data-counts <participants/sites/sources> :design <qualitative | mixed-method | case-study> :analysis-frame <NPT | reflexive thematic analysis | framework synthesis>} Effect: the Results paragraph can then present analytic claims without defensive hedging. (2) Multi-source split count. Schema: {:interviews <n> :focus-groups <n> :observations <n> :documents <n> :sites <n>} Effect: useful when the small interview n is supported by additional data streams. (3) Claim-type tag. Schema: {:claim-type :feasibility | :acceptability | :implementation-process | :thematic-account | :framework-refinement} Effect: prevents qualitative n from being misread as prevalence n. Engaged when the abstract lets a skeptical reader answer, before the Results paragraph, "what data, from whom, where, analysed how, and for what kind of claim?" Failing when the abstract announces implications while hiding the empirical container until the Methods section.

title: Close Implementation Results With a Barrier-Enabler-Strategy Display
text: Close Implementation Results With a Barrier-Enabler-Strategy Display Implementation and open-science qualitative papers should convert themes into an action-facing display near the end: barriers, enablers, and strategies or recommendations aligned in one figure or table. This move lets PLOS readers see the practical yield without mistaking the paper for a checklist-only evaluation. The AMBER care bundle paper uses a figure for facilitators, barriers, and strategies for normalisation. Open-science exemplars use barrier tables, recommendation tables, or instrument frameworks. Training and BMC content cousins similarly end by translating qualitative findings into policy or practice implications. The pattern operates on the axis: thematic finding <-> implementable implication. Irreducible: a theme becomes useful for implementation only when the reader can see what blocks, enables, or changes practice. Real costs: an action-facing display can flatten analytic nuance and make recommendations look more certain than the data warrant. Keep the display tied to the preceding findings and label strategies as derived implications, not measured effects. Active dynamic: qualitative papers often save implications for prose Discussion. A compact display improves scanability and helps reviewers see contribution. - Theme-to-recommendation-leap: recommendations appear without a visible line from findings. - Barrier-list-only: barriers are named but not paired with enabling conditions or strategies. - Over-prescriptive-strategy: a small-n process evaluation states what should work generally rather than what the data suggest for similar contexts. - Duplicated-discussion: the table repeats the Discussion paragraph rather than reorganizing it. Add an aligned implementation display. (1) Barrier-enabler-strategy matrix. Columns: finding/theme, barrier, enabler, strategy, evidence source. Effect: makes the practical contribution inspectable. (2) Recommendation table. Columns: problem, recommendation, actor responsible, scope condition. Effect: useful for open-science and training papers. (3) Normalisation pathway figure. Nodes: coherence, participation, action, monitoring; overlays: barriers, facilitators, strategies. Effect: keeps NPT visible while making implementation advice concrete. Engaged when practical implications can be scanned without detaching from evidence. Failing when findings stay as themes only, or when recommendations arrive as unsupported Discussion rhetoric.

title: State the Coding Reliability Procedure
text: State the Coding Reliability Procedure A deductive, team-coded qualitative analysis should state its coding-reliability procedure explicitly: how many coders worked independently, how disagreements were adjudicated, and what role any third reviewer played. This is the procedural guardrail that distinguishes systematic analysis from "thematic vibes", and reviewers at a soundness venue expect to see it named, not assumed. Across the NPT exemplar set, methods sections state that coding was conducted independently by two or more researchers, with discrepancies resolved by adjudication or team discussion. The presence of an explicit reliability procedure is a rigour signal; its absence is a standard reviewer objection, regardless of how careful the actual analysis was. The pattern operates on the axis: reliability-procedure-named <-> reliability-assumed. Irreducible: the rigour of deductive coding is carried by how disagreements were handled, not by the coding scheme alone; an unstated procedure cannot be credited by a reviewer. Real costs: stating the procedure exposes its limits (e.g. no formal kappa, adjudication by discussion rather than statistic). Disclosing a lightweight procedure honestly is stronger than implying a heavier one; reviewers read silence as absence. Active dynamic: authors often describe the coding *framework* in detail while leaving the *reliability process* implicit. The two are different claims and both must be made. - Reliability-silent: the framework and codes are described, but who coded and how disagreements were resolved is never stated. - Single-coder-unmarked: one person coded everything and the text does not say so, leaving the reader to assume a team process that did not happen. - Adjudication-vague: "the team discussed discrepancies" without saying who decided or on what basis. Name the procedure as a discrete methods claim. (1) Independent-coders-plus-adjudicator. Schema: {:coders <n> :independence <fully | partial> :adjudicator <role> :basis <discussion | statistic>} Effect: makes the rigour procedure auditable. (2) Disagreement-handling. Schema: {:disagreement-rate <described?> :resolution <consensus | third-reviewer | re-coding>} Effect: shows that disagreements were surfaced and resolved, not papered over. Engaged when a reviewer can state how many people coded, independently or not, and how disagreements were resolved, from the Methods text alone. Failing when coding reliability must be assumed.

title: Let Coherence Do Early Results Work
text: Let Coherence Do Early Results Work In NPT papers, "coherence" should usually be more than the first construct in a list; it should establish the implementation problem the rest of the Results explain. If participants did not share what the intervention was for, how it differed from prior practice, or what counted as success, that sense-making work should become the opening empirical result. Several NPT exemplars begin the Results with coherence or sense-making before moving into commitment, workability, appraisal, or relationships between constructs. This ordering works because later implementation labour is easier to interpret once the reader understands what actors thought they were implementing. The pattern operates on the axis: sense-making as setup <-> sense-making as one equal bucket. Irreducible: implementation work depends on what actors understand the intervention to be. If coherence is unstable, later constructs inherit that instability. Real costs: leading with coherence can make the Results feel theory-led and may delay more concrete barriers. The solution is not to skip coherence, but to state it concretely: what was unclear, contested, persuasive, or newly understood. Active dynamic: NPT construct order can become rote. The pattern is engaged only when coherence actually structures the empirical story. - Rote-construct-order: coherence appears first only because NPT lists it first. - Abstract-sense-making: the section says participants "made sense" without naming the specific distinction, value, or purpose they made sense of. - Barrier-before-meaning: logistical barriers are presented before the reader knows what staff, patients, or trainees understood the intervention to be. - Coherence-without-consequence: the section does not show how sense-making shaped participation, work, or appraisal. Make coherence an explanatory entry point. (1) Difference-from-usual-care opener. Schema: {:old-practice <baseline> :new-practice <intervention> :actor-understanding <what changed>} Effect: grounds coherence in a concrete contrast. (2) Purpose-contestation opener. Schema: {:intended-purpose <design intent> :participant-reading <local interpretation> :implementation-effect <consequence>} Effect: turns coherence into a mechanism. (3) Coherence-to-next-construct bridge. Schema: {:coherence-finding <x> :downstream-construct <cognitive-participation | collective-action | reflexive-monitoring> :bridge <how x shaped y>} Effect: prevents construct sections from reading as parallel lists. Engaged when the coherence section tells the reader what the intervention meant locally and why that meaning shaped subsequent implementation. Failing when coherence is just a heading over generic approval or confusion quotes.

title: Adhere to a Named Qualitative Reporting Checklist (COREQ)
text: Adhere to a Named Qualitative Reporting Checklist (COREQ) A qualitative PLOS ONE paper should report against a named reporting standard — COREQ for interview/focus-group studies, or SRQR — cite it, and supply the completed checklist as supplementary information. This is cheap insurance against a "reporting standards" reviewer note and matches the venue's habit for qualitative work; it resolves a reporting-completeness force that generic methods prose does not. Reviewers and some editors of qualitative work expect adherence to an established reporting checklist, and several papers in the qualitative-health corpus report per COREQ and append the checklist. The checklist enumerates items (research team, reflexivity, study design, analysis, reporting) that a free-form methods section can silently omit. The pattern operates on the axis: reporting-against-a-named-standard <-> reporting-by-author-judgement. Irreducible: a named checklist makes completeness checkable item-by-item; without one, omissions are invisible until a reviewer notices them. Real costs: a checklist can encourage box-ticking and bloat the methods section. The discipline is to let the checklist surface genuine omissions (reflexivity, sampling rationale, saturation/stopping basis) while keeping the main-text methods readable and putting the full grid in supplementary information. Active dynamic: authors familiar with their own process underestimate which items a reader cannot reconstruct; the checklist is precisely the external view they lack. - Checklist-absent: no named reporting standard is cited, inviting a "which reporting guideline did you follow?" note. - Cited-not-supplied: COREQ is named but the completed checklist is not provided as SI. - Items-orphaned: the checklist is appended but several items it requires (e.g. reflexivity, stopping rule) are not actually addressed anywhere in the paper. Report against the standard and supply the grid. (1) Named-standard-statement. Schema: {:standard :COREQ | :SRQR :cited <yes> :si-checklist <attached>} Effect: pre-empts the reporting-standards reviewer note. (2) Item-coverage-pass. Schema: {:reflexivity <addressed?> :sampling-rationale <addressed?> :stopping-basis <addressed?>} Effect: uses the checklist to find and close real omissions before submission. Engaged when the paper names its reporting standard, cites it, supplies the completed checklist, and actually addresses each required item. Failing when reporting completeness rests on author judgement alone or the checklist is decorative.

title: Foreground Data Availability and Preregistration
text: Foreground Data Availability and Preregistration A PLOS ONE submission should foreground its data-availability statement and any preregistration prominently and in the venue-required form — not buried in a declarations block. Data availability is a non-negotiable publication gate at PLOS; preregistration is a soundness signal the venue actively rewards. These are compliance constraints checked at submission, distinct from anything that calibrates the reader's interpretation. PLOS requires a data-availability statement as a condition of publication, in a specified form, and treats it as a hard gate rather than a courtesy. Preregistration (e.g. an OSF registration link) is not required but is read as a positive soundness signal. The exemplars that clear the gate cleanly state both up front and in the expected format. The pattern operates on the axis: compliance-satisfied-in-required-form <-> compliance-implied-or-deferred. Irreducible: a hard submission gate is binary — the statement is either present in the required form or the submission stalls; no amount of analytic quality substitutes for it. Real costs: qualitative data raises genuine availability tensions (anonymised transcripts, ethics constraints on sharing). The resolution is to state the deposit plan and access conditions explicitly (e.g. repository, DMP reference, "available on reasonable request"), not to omit the statement. Active dynamic: authors often treat these as boilerplate to add at the very end. Because they gate the submission, drafting them early avoids a last-minute stall. - Statement-wrong-form: data availability is mentioned in prose but not in the PLOS-required statement form, so the submission system rejects it. - Availability-vague: "data available on request" with no repository, DMP, or access-condition detail. - Prereg-unlinked: a preregistration exists but no registration link is given, forfeiting the soundness signal. Treat the statements as gating artefacts, drafted in venue form. (1) Data-availability-statement. Schema: {:repository <name> :dmp-ref <link> :access-conditions <open | on-request | restricted-why> :form :plos-required} Effect: satisfies the hard gate in the expected format. (2) Preregistration-link. Schema: {:registry <OSF | other> :link <url> :scope <what was preregistered>} Effect: banks the soundness signal and lets reviewers check prereg against reported analysis. Engaged when the data-availability statement is present in the PLOS-required form and any preregistration is linked, before submission. Failing when either is implied, deferred, or in the wrong form.

title: Use the Second Data Stream to Disconfirm, Not Only to Corroborate
text: Use the Second Data Stream to Disconfirm, Not Only to Corroborate Where a study has more than one data stream or participant group, show that the additional stream was used to TEST and where necessary DISCONFIRM the first — and treat the divergence between sources as a finding in its own right. Asserting convergence is the weak use of triangulation; demonstrating that contradiction was sought, found, and interpreted is the credible one. The multi-source NPT exemplars do more than stack sources for breadth. The strongest cases explicitly sought non-confirmatory data, staged patient accounts against professional accounts on the same construct, or named intra-subject contradiction as an analytic object. This converts the perennial "you cherry-picked confirming quotes" objection into a demonstration that disconfirming evidence was handled. The pattern operates on the axis: triangulation-as-convergence-claim <-> triangulation-as-disconfirmation-test. Irreducible: convergence alone is consistent with cherry-picking; only the visible search for and treatment of disconfirming or divergent data shows the analysis could have been wrong and wasn't forced. Real costs: surfacing contradictions complicates a clean narrative and can read as an unresolved result. The discipline is to make the divergence itself the point (e.g. staff devalue X while patients value X), not to smooth it away. Active dynamic: authors reach for triangulation to claim robustness, and stop at "the sources agreed." The stronger move is to report where they disagreed and what that disagreement means. - Convergence-only: "data were triangulated" with no instance of contradiction reported, so robustness is asserted not shown. - Deviant-case-silent: no statement that non-confirmatory data were sought or weighed. - Divergence-smoothed: contradictory accounts are averaged into a bland consensus instead of being analysed as a finding. Stage the streams against each other and report the divergence. (1) Disconfirming-case clause. Schema: {:sought-nonconfirmatory true :resolution <how weighed> :claim-restraint "avoid unwarranted patterns"} Effect: shows the analysis was falsifiable in practice. (2) Counterpoint pairing. Schema: {:source-A <group> :source-B <group> :same-construct <X> :divergence <what differs> :as-finding true} Effect: turns A-vs-B disagreement into a substantive result, not noise. (3) Stream-as-validity-check. Schema: {:stream-1 "what actors thought happened" :stream-2 "what recipients experienced" :use "test stream-1"} Effect: positions the second stream as a check on self-report, not mere corroboration. Engaged when the paper reports at least one place where sources diverged and says what the divergence means. Failing when triangulation is invoked but every source is said to agree.

title: Use the Framework as Spine, Not as Substitute
text: Use the Framework as Spine, Not as Substitute A theory framework can organize the Results section, but each framework heading must carry an empirical rib: a local theme, concrete mechanism, or participant problem that makes the construct earn its place. "Coherence", "cognitive participation", "collective action", and "reflexive monitoring" work as section architecture only when the prose immediately names what those constructs looked like in this intervention, site, or professional group. The NPT exemplars repeatedly use constructs as visible results headings, often expanding them with local subtitles: making sense of ERAS, commitment and engagement with AMBER, professional values in stroke rehabilitation, or making primary care for transgender patients workable. The strongest register is not "we coded data to NPT"; it is "this NPT construct exposed this particular implementation work." The pattern operates on the axis: framework-as-navigation <-> framework-as-finding. Irreducible: a construct heading is not itself an empirical result. The result is the local work, tension, barrier, or enabling condition the construct makes visible. Real costs: adding local subtitles creates longer headings and sometimes uneven section lengths. Pure construct headings are cleaner. But clean construct headings can make the article look like a worked example of a theory rather than a study with findings. Active dynamic: theory-driven analysis pulls prose toward taxonomic display; PLOS register rewards taxonomic clarity only when joined to empirical specificity. - Construct-only-results: every result is just an NPT construct with quotes underneath. - Framework-overclaim: the discussion claims the framework explains implementation without showing which local observations carried the explanation. - Quote-as-rib: a participant extract is expected to supply empirical specificity that the surrounding prose never states. - Local-theme-erasure: inductive themes are flattened into framework buckets and lose the local story. Pair every framework section with a local claim. (1) Construct-colon-local-work. Heading schema: "<construct> - <local mechanism or work>" Effect: keeps framework navigation while foregrounding the empirical finding. (2) Framework table before results. Schema: {:construct <name> :definition <brief> :local-operationalization <what counts in this study>} Effect: frees the Results prose to discuss findings rather than define theory. (3) Relationship figure after construct sections. Schema: {:constructs <nodes> :local-tensions <edges> :variation <by site/group>} Effect: shows how the constructs interacted instead of leaving them as parallel bins. Engaged when each framework heading can be paraphrased as "in this setting, this construct meant X". Failing when removing the framework terminology would leave no clear empirical claim behind.

title: Sequence Inductive Coding Before the Deductive Framework, and Say So
text: Sequence Inductive Coding Before the Deductive Framework, and Say So When a named framework (NPT, COM-B, a conceptual model) is used to organise qualitative findings, state explicitly that the analysis coded inductively FIRST and mapped onto the framework SECOND — and that this ordering was chosen to keep interpretation data-driven. The sequence, made visible, is the warrant that answers the standard reviewer suspicion that a theory-led paper merely confirms its own theory. Across the NPT exemplars, the credible papers describe a two-stage analysis: an inductive/thematic first pass (often Braun & Clarke or constant comparison, in NVivo), then a deductive mapping of those themes onto the framework's constructs. The weaker move is to present the framework as if it generated the findings. Naming the order, and naming its purpose, converts a methodological choice into a rigour claim. The pattern operates on the axis: framework-as-confirmed-by-itself <-> framework-as-lens-applied-after-the-data-spoke. Irreducible: a deductive framework can always be accused of forcing data into its categories; only the visible inductive-first sequence rebuts that, because it shows the categories were tested against emergent themes rather than imposed. Real costs: the two-stage account takes Methods space and exposes that the framework was retrofitted rather than pre-registered as the analytic plan. Disclosing the retrofit honestly is stronger than implying the framework was primary; reviewers infer retrofitting anyway when results map too neatly. Active dynamic: authors who love their framework tend to lead with it. The discipline is to lead the Methods with the inductive pass and present the framework as the second, organising move. - Framework-first-silently: results are presented under construct headings with no account of how themes were derived, reading as circular. - Order-unstated: both passes happened but the text never says which came first, forfeiting the warrant. - Forcing-unaddressed: no sentence claims the sequence guarded against forcing, so the reader supplies the suspicion. Make the sequence and its purpose an explicit Methods claim. (1) Two-stage statement. Schema: {:stage-1 <inductive/thematic, tool> :stage-2 <deductive map onto framework> :order-stated true :purpose "avoid forcing"} Effect: the framework reads as a lens applied to data, not a mould. (2) Iterative-revisit clause. Schema: {:movement "back-and-forth between inductive and deductive" :revisits <n or "multiple">} Effect: shows the mapping was checked against the data, not one-directional. (3) Pre-committed construct question-battery (inverse form). Schema: {:construct->questions <table of operational questions per construct, established as the a-priori analytic frame in Methods>} Effect: when the framework IS primary, makes the deductive lens auditable instead of post-hoc. Engaged when a reader can state which analysis came first and why the order matters, from the Methods alone. Failing when findings appear under framework headings with no derivation account, or when the order is left for the reader to guess.

title: Turn Extra Data Streams Into a Triangulation Ladder
text: Turn Extra Data Streams Into a Triangulation Ladder When a small-n paper has interviews plus observations, case-note review, focus groups, systematic review, workshops, or documents, the Methods and Results should present those streams as a triangulation ladder: each stream has a distinct analytic job, and higher-level claims say which streams support them. Do not leave the extra data as an inventory. The PLOS exemplars often pair small interview counts with other evidence: observations in glaucoma pathway work, clinical notes and focus groups in AMBER, phased literature-review/interview/workshop design in open research data sharing, or focus groups plus patient interviews in stroke rehabilitation. The presentation becomes stronger when the paper explains how these streams corroborate, contextualize, prioritize, or challenge each other. The pattern operates on the axis: data-source inventory <-> data-source function. Irreducible: multiple data streams strengthen a claim only when the reader can see what each stream contributed. Counting more streams is not triangulation by itself. Real costs: explicitly assigning functions to streams may reveal unevenness: some sites have fewer observations, some workshops only validate rather than discover, some documents are contextual. That unevenness is useful if it bounds claims honestly. Active dynamic: Methods sections like to list data collection chronologically; Results sections like to synthesize. The ladder bridges chronology to synthesis. - Inventory-only-methods: data streams are listed, but no stream has an analytic role. - All-streams-all-claims: every finding is implied to be supported by all data, even when only interviews actually carry it. - Triangulation-as-buzzword: the word appears without showing convergence, complementarity, or disconfirmation. - Phase-confusion: a phased design has review, interviews, and workshop, but the Results do not separate discovery, prioritization, and generalizability. Assign and display the analytic job of each stream. (1) Data-stream function table. Columns: stream, count, source, analytic job, claims it can support, claims it cannot support. Effect: readers can calibrate synthesis claims. (2) Phased-results scaffold. Schema: {:phase-1 <mapping/discovery> :phase-2 <prioritization/depth> :phase-3 <validation/generalizability>} Effect: useful for open-science or mixed-methods articles. (3) Claim support tags. Schema: {:finding <x> :supported-by [interviews observations documents workshop] :role <convergent | contextual | discrepant>} Effect: keeps Results prose honest without overburdening every paragraph. Engaged when a reader can say which data stream did which analytic work for each major claim. Failing when interviews, observations, notes, and workshops appear as a Methods pile but vanish into undifferentiated Results.

title: Present Open-Science Studies as Practices, Barriers, Incentives, and Instruments
text: Present Open-Science Studies as Practices, Barriers, Incentives, and Instruments PLOS open-science papers should present findings in an operational register: practices, barriers, benefits, incentives, instruments, and recommendations.
