The reader should be able to distinguish what participants currently do, what blocks them, what would motivate change, and what institutional or infrastructural instruments could change the field. The HCI open-science paper structures findings around knowledge of practices, peer review, benefits, barriers, incentives, and recommendations. The epidemiology data-sharing paper uses phases to move from literature-derived instruments to interview prioritization and workshop generalizability. Both models turn attitudes into an actionable map. The pattern operates on the axis: opinion themes <-> change architecture. Irreducible: open-science findings are useful only if they separate descriptive practice from barriers and intervention levers. Real costs: operational categories can make participant experience feel managerial. Preserve nuance in theme prose, but let tables and figures carry the action architecture. Active dynamic: open-science topics invite normative argument. The PLOS register works better when the normative point is earned through mapped practices and constraints. - Attitude-only-findings: results describe support or skepticism without identifying levers for change. - Barrier-benefit-mix: benefits, barriers, incentives, and recommendations are blended in one theme, making action unclear. - Normative-overwrite: the paper argues for open science before showing what participants actually understand or need. - Phase-collapse: review, interview, and workshop outputs are combined without preserving what each phase contributed. Use an operational open-science scaffold. (1) Practices-barriers-incentives-results. Section order: current practices, benefits, barriers, incentives, recommendations. Effect: suitable for interview-heavy HCI-style articles. (2) Instruments-by-phase framework. Section order: instruments identified, instruments prioritized, framework refined, generalizability assessed. Effect: suitable for mixed-methods data-sharing work. (3) Recommendation table with actor and scope. Columns: recommendation, target actor, addressed barrier, scope condition, evidence source. Effect: avoids generic advocacy. Engaged when the open-science article yields a map of possible change, not only a list of sentiments. Failing when findings cannot tell a policymaker, editor, educator, or researcher what lever is implicated.

title: Use a Rigour Frame Matched to the Study's Paradigm, Not a Default Checklist
text: Use a Rigour Frame Matched to the Study's Paradigm, Not a Default Checklist State the study's rigour warrant using a frame that fits its paradigm and design, rather than defaulting to inter-coder reliability or a single checklist that may not apply. A multiple-case study can warrant rigour through Yin's case-study criteria; a reflexive thematic analysis warrants it through reflexivity, positionality, and an audit trail — and should explicitly say why the positivist reliability apparatus does not apply. Not every credible qualitative paper reports COREQ or double-coding with a kappa. The case-study exemplar imports Yin's quality quartet (construct/internal/external validity, reliability) and maps its moves to each. The reflexive-thematic-analysis exemplar rejects coding-accuracy/saturation/member-checking as paradigm-inappropriate and substitutes audit trail, peer debriefing, memos, and an author-positionality roster. Either is a complete rigour account; a mismatched one invites a reviewer note. The pattern operates on the axis: rigour-by-default-checklist <-> rigour-by-paradigm-appropriate-frame. Irreducible: a rigour apparatus only warrants trust if it matches the epistemology of the analysis; reporting inter-coder reliability for a reflexive analysis (or omitting any frame for a case study) signals a paradigm mismatch, not rigour. Real costs: naming a non-default frame requires defending the choice and may meet reviewers who expect COREQ reflexively. The discipline is to name the chosen frame, cite its source, and briefly say why the default does not fit — pre-empting rather than ignoring the expectation. Active dynamic: authors reach for the most familiar checklist regardless of design. The stronger move is to select the frame the paradigm actually licenses and make the selection explicit. - Mismatched-apparatus: reflexive analysis reports inter-coder reliability, or a case study reports none of Yin's criteria. - Frame-unnamed: rigour moves are present but no named frame ties them together, so they read as ad hoc. - Positionality-absent: a reflexive analysis omits the author-positionality disclosure that is load-bearing for its rigour. Name the paradigm-matched frame and map the study's moves to it. (1) Case-study quartet. Schema: {:frame "Yin" :construct-validity <move> :internal-validity <move> :external-validity <replication-logic> :reliability <protocol/db>} Effect: warrants a multiple-case design on its own terms. (2) Reflexive-rigour apparatus. Schema: {:audit-trail true :peer-debriefing true :memos true :member-checking-rejected-why <reason> :consensus <team>} Effect: warrants a reflexive analysis without misapplying reliability. (3) Positionality roster. Schema: {:per-author <profession, training, identity, qual-expertise>} Effect: discloses the interpretive standpoint the themes were constructed from. Engaged when the named rigour frame matches the study's paradigm and each rigour move is tied to it. Failing when the apparatus is borrowed from a different paradigm, or no frame is named at all.

title: Use Extract Tables When Themes Are Parallel
text: Use Extract Tables When Themes Are Parallel When a Results section presents several parallel themes, use illustrative extract tables to carry representative participant voice and keep the prose available for interpretation. The table should not be a quote dump; each row should align theme, subtheme or claim, participant/source, and what the extract demonstrates. The training/education PLOS exemplar uses one table of illustrative data extracts per theme, while other qualitative exemplars use participant and theme tables to prevent prose from becoming a long chain of quotations. This is especially useful when the findings are role features, barriers, or implementation factors rather than a narrative case. The pattern operates on the axis: quotation as evidence display <-> quotation as prose interruption. Irreducible: qualitative claims need participant voice, but too many long quotes inside prose can hide the analytic claim they are meant to support. Real costs: tables can make qualitative findings feel schematic, and moving quotes out of prose can reduce narrative texture. Keep decisive or surprising quotes in prose; move parallel confirmatory extracts to tables. Active dynamic: authors often add quotes whenever a claim feels under-supported. Past a point, each quote adds length but not clarity. - Quote-flood: each theme paragraph becomes claim, quote, quote, quote, with little analytic synthesis. - Anonymous-evidence: extract tables omit participant role or case context needed to interpret the quote. - Decorative-extract: the quote illustrates the topic but not the specific analytic claim. - Table-without-prose: the table carries all evidence, while Results prose merely restates theme names. Separate interpretation from parallel evidence display. (1) Theme-extract table. Columns: theme, analytic claim, participant/source, extract, interpretive note. Effect: lets the prose state and compare findings. (2) Role-balanced extracts. Columns: theme, role/group, extract, contrast. Effect: useful when professional role or participant type matters. (3) One-prose-quote-per-turning-point. Schema: {:theme <x> :kept-in-prose <quote that changes interpretation> :moved-to-table <parallel support>} Effect: preserves qualitative texture without flooding paragraphs. Engaged when quotes are easy to inspect and the prose still performs analysis. Failing when the Results section becomes a transcript collage or when extract tables lack analytic labels.

title: State the Research Questions Explicitly and Early
text: State the Research Questions Explicitly and Early A small-n PLOS ONE paper should enumerate its research questions explicitly and early — in the Introduction, and in the unstructured-abstract lane, in the abstract itself. The handling editor makes a scope-fit decision before reading the body; numbered questions let that decision be made in seconds and on the author's terms rather than by inference. PLOS ONE decides on soundness and scope-fit, not significance. In the social-science / research-culture exemplars (e.g. the open-research-data study), two or three numbered questions appear up front, sometimes inside the abstract, signalling exactly what the paper will and will not answer. This is the move that converts a vague topic into a legible object the desk editor can place. The pattern operates on the axis: scope-legible-at-the-gate <-> scope-inferred-from-the-body. Irreducible: an editor cannot grant scope-fit to a paper whose questions they must reconstruct; the cost of leaving questions implicit is paid at the desk-decision, the cheapest place to be rejected. Real costs: explicit RQs can read as mechanical, and poorly differentiated questions advertise their own overlap (a process question and a barriers question that restate each other). The discipline is to make each question carry a distinct analytic job. Active dynamic: authors often prefer to open on importance or on the strongest finding. At a soundness venue the stronger first move is to make the scope decidable. - Implicit-scope: the topic is described richly but no question is ever stated, leaving the editor to infer the contribution. - Overlapping-questions: RQ1 and RQ2 cover the same ground unless an explicit distinction (process vs condition vs normalisation) is drawn. - Abstract-silent: in the unstructured-abstract lane, the questions appear only deep in the Introduction, too late for the desk decision. Put the questions where the scope decision is made. (1) Numbered-questions-in-intro. Schema: {:rq1 <process-facing> :rq2 <condition-facing> :rq3 <normalisation-facing>} Effect: each question names a distinct analytic facing, so overlap is visible and avoidable. (2) Abstract-surfaced-questions. Schema: {:abstract-questions <1-2 numbered> :register :unstructured} Effect: signals scope to the desk editor before the Methods paragraph. (3) Questions-plus-objective. Schema: {:questions <2> :analytic-objective <1>} Effect: collapses an over-stuffed three-question set into two questions and one stated objective. Engaged when a desk editor can state the paper's scope from the questions alone, without reading Results. Failing when the scope must be inferred, or when two questions cannot be told apart.

title: Defend a Narrow Scope by Naming the Companion Paper
text: Defend a Narrow Scope by Naming the Companion Paper When a paper deliberately reports only part of a larger study — one construct, one phase, one method — defend that narrowing explicitly by naming the companion paper that carries the rest, and stating the division of labour. An unexplained narrow scope reads as a gap (or as salami-slicing); a named hand-off reads as deliberate design. The ERAS exemplar narrows its whole analysis to the single NPT construct of Coherence and routes the barriers/facilitators analysis to a sibling publication ("more fully explored elsewhere [25]"). The DEALTS2 train-the-trainer study splits qualitative and quantitative reporting across a companion pair. In both, the narrowing is announced, not left for the reader to notice — which is the difference between division of labour and questionable-research-practice slicing. The pattern operates on the axis: narrow-scope-unexplained <-> narrow-scope-announced-with-companion. Irreducible: a reviewer cannot tell deliberate scoping from incomplete work unless the paper names what is reserved and where it goes; the hand-off statement is what converts a gap into a design. Real costs: naming the companion exposes that the dataset is being published in pieces, inviting the salami-slicing question directly. The defence is that the split is along a principled seam (a distinct construct, phase, or method — not the same analysis cut in half) and that each piece makes a contribution that stands alone. A split along a mechanism seam mid-analysis is the move this pattern does NOT license. Active dynamic: authors fear admitting a companion paper and so leave the scope unexplained, which reads worse. The stronger move is to name it and justify the seam. - Unexplained-narrowness: the paper covers one slice with no statement of what was left out or why, reading as thin. - Mechanism-seam-slicing: the split cuts a single coherent analysis into minimal-publishable-units along no principled boundary (the QRP failure). - Companion-unnamed: a sibling paper exists but is not cited, so the reader cannot place the contribution. Announce the seam and the hand-off. (1) Scope-and-handoff statement. Schema: {:this-paper <slice> :reserved <remainder> :companion <citation or "forthcoming"> :seam <construct | phase | method>} Effect: makes the narrowing legible as design. (2) Standalone-contribution claim. Schema: {:contribution-of-this-slice <what it alone establishes>} Effect: shows the piece is not a fragment dependent on the companion. (3) Seam-justification. Schema: {:why-this-seam <principled boundary> :not "the same analysis halved"} Effect: distinguishes deliberate scoping from salami-slicing. Engaged when the paper states what it reserves, names where that goes, and justifies the seam as principled. Failing when the scope is narrow but unexplained, or the seam cuts a single analysis into minimal units.

title: Display Sites, Cases, Roles, and Data Before Findings
text: Display Sites, Cases, Roles, and Data Before Findings Before a small-n Results section makes comparative claims, the paper should give the reader a compact display of the empirical terrain: sites or cases, participant roles, data sources, and relevant contextual differences. This table is not clerical; it is the map that makes later variation claims inspectable. The PLOS exemplars repeatedly include site-characteristic, participant-characteristic, case-summary, data-collection-by-case, and phase-overview tables before or near the Results. These displays make it possible to read claims about site variation, professional roles, implementation barriers, or framework constructs without losing track of where the evidence came from. The pattern operates on the axis: reader-held study map <-> buried methods inventory. Irreducible: variation claims require visible dimensions of variation. If the prose says sites, roles, or cases differed, the reader needs a table that names the dimensions along which they differed. Real costs: tables can feel dull and may repeat Methods prose. Over-detailed tables can overwhelm a short qualitative article. The discipline is to display only variables that later carry analytic weight. Active dynamic: authors know their cases too well and underestimate how quickly readers lose the site/role map once results begin. - Context-after-claim: site differences are invoked in Results before the site characteristics have been made visible. - Participant-table-as-appendix-only: the table needed to read the findings is moved to supporting information. - Decorative-demographics: a table lists demographics that never matter analytically while omitting role, site, implementation exposure, or data-source differences that do matter. - Mixed-n-blur: interviews, focus groups, observations, and documents are counted in prose but never aligned by site or case. Add a study-map display before findings. (1) Site-characteristics table. Columns: site/case, setting type, intervention exposure, relevant staffing or workflow feature, data collected. Effect: supports later cross-site interpretation. (2) Data-by-case table. Columns: case, interviews, observations, documents, surveys, notes, analytic relevance. Effect: makes triangulation and uneven coverage visible. (3) Participant-role table. Columns: role, count, setting, relation to intervention, relevant experience. Effect: lets role-based findings avoid floating above the sample. Engaged when every later claim about site, case, role, or phase variation can point back to a compact display. Failing when the reader must reconstruct the study map from scattered Methods sentences.

title: Defend Small n by Design Transparency
text: Defend Small n by Design Transparency A small-n paper should defend n through design transparency, not through apology. The paper must say how participants or cases were selected, what analytic job the sample performs, how the team judged adequacy, and what kinds of claims remain outside scope. Saturation literature can support this, but it cannot replace the local account of why this sample was enough for this question. The PLOS sample-size ammunition paper treats saturation as related to question design, domain size, salience, and response structure rather than a universal magic number. The small-n implementation exemplars likewise make n credible by showing case boundaries, sites, data streams, topic guides, coding or framework procedures, and limits on transferability. The pattern operates on the axis: n-as-count <-> n-as-designed-warrant. Irreducible: the same n can be weak or strong depending on sampling logic, data richness, analytic scope, and triangulation. A bare number has no warrant by itself. Real costs: transparent n-defence takes Methods space and may expose imperfections in recruitment, site access, or data completeness. Hiding those imperfections is worse; reviewers will infer them anyway. Active dynamic: small-n authors often over-hedge in the Discussion while under-specifying design in Methods. The stronger move is the reverse: be exact in Methods and proportionate in the Discussion. - Magic-saturation: "saturation was reached" with no account of what saturated, how it was assessed, or what remained unsaturated. - Apology-paragraph: limitations say only that n was small, without explaining why the sample was still fit for the claim. - NPT-cover: a framework is used to imply adequacy without showing sampling, coding, or deviant-case handling. - Count-confusion: n is given but the reader cannot tell whether it is participants, interviews, focus groups, sites, cases, observations, or documents. Make n legible as part of design. (1) Sampling logic paragraph. Schema: {:population <who> :selection <purposive/case/role/site> :inclusion <criteria> :analytic-job <why these cases matter>} Effect: n becomes interpretable before findings are presented. (2) Adequacy statement. Schema: {:adequacy-basis <saturation | information-power | case-depth | triangulation> :what-was-adequate-for <claim-type> :what-not-for <scope-limit>} Effect: prevents a small-n thematic account from overreaching. (3) Data richness table. Schema: {:rows <case/site/role> :columns <interviews/focus-groups/observations/documents/notes>} Effect: lets the reader see that n is not the only evidence dimension. Engaged when the reader can explain why n was enough for the paper's claim without accepting a generic saturation sentence. Failing when small n is hidden until limitations, or defended only by citing saturation literature.

title: Frame the Theory as a Heuristic Device, and Name Its Limits
text: Frame the Theory as a Heuristic Device, and Name Its Limits Present the analytic framework as a heuristic device that organised and aided the analysis, not as a causal or explanatory law the data prove. Where the framework has a known limitation, name it and show how the study's design compensates. This pre-empts the reviewer charge that the theory is being over-claimed, while still crediting it with analytic value. The ERAS exemplar repeatedly downgrades NPT to "a potentially useful heuristic device" and, having isolated one construct, turns the difficulty of separating it from the others into an explicit finding about the constructs' interconnectedness. The stroke-rehab exemplar names a standard criticism of NPT — its bias toward professional action — and states that including patient interviews addresses it. Both grant the framework usefulness while disclaiming over-reach. The pattern operates on the axis: theory-as-proven-law <-> theory-as-acknowledged-heuristic. Irreducible: a qualitative study cannot prove a theory; claiming it does invites rejection, while denying the theory any role wastes the analytic structure. The heuristic framing occupies the defensible middle: useful lens, not demonstrated mechanism. Real costs: calling the framework "just" a heuristic can read as underselling the theoretical contribution. The discipline is to credit specific analytic work the framework did (organising findings, surfacing the interconnection of constructs) while declining the causal claim — usefulness without over-reach. Active dynamic: authors invested in a framework drift toward treating its constructs as real entities the data confirm. The stronger move is to treat the constructs as lenses and to name where the lens distorts. - Theory-reified: constructs are written as causal forces the data "prove," over-claiming explanatory power. - Limitation-unnamed: a well-known weakness of the framework goes unmentioned, so a reviewer raises it instead. - Heuristic-without-credit: the framework is dismissed as merely a heuristic with no account of what it actually contributed. Credit the framework as a lens and bound its claims. (1) Heuristic-framing statement. Schema: {:framework <name> :role "heuristic device" :contributed <organising/surfacing work> :not-claimed "causal mechanism"} Effect: secures analytic value without over-reach. (2) Limitation-then-remedy. Schema: {:known-criticism <of the framework> :remedy-in-design <what the study did about it>} Effect: converts a framework critique into a design strength. (3) Interconnection-as-finding. Schema: {:isolated-construct <X> :difficulty "cannot cleanly separate from others" :as-finding true} Effect: turns the awkwardness of using one construct into a substantive observation. Engaged when the framework is credited with specific analytic work but not claimed to be proven, and its known limits are named and addressed. Failing when constructs are reified as proven mechanisms, or the framework's weaknesses go unmentioned.

title: Present Training Findings as Role Features With Extract Support
text: Present Training Findings as Role Features With Extract Support Training and education qualitative papers should present findings as role features, competencies, or implementation conditions rather than as loose positive attributes. Named themes such as manager, communicator, mediator, guide, and experienced professional work because they describe what the role must do, then support each feature with extracts and practical implications. The PLOS rehabilitation higher-education exemplar structures Results around five course-leader features and pairs each with illustrative extract tables. The BMC train-the-trainer cousins are useful for positioning because they similarly attend to training cascades, facilitation, organisational support, and practice impact, though their venue register is not PLOS ONE. The pattern operates on the axis: admired trait <-> functional role feature. Irreducible: a training finding becomes useful when it tells the reader what role-work is required, not merely which qualities participants liked. Real costs: role-feature naming can sound normative and may over-unify diverse participant accounts. Keep feature labels close to the data and use extracts to show range, not just endorsement. Active dynamic: education papers often drift into generic virtues: flexible, empathic, experienced, collaborative. The register strengthens when each virtue is tied to a work situation. - Trait-list: themes are adjectives without role-work or implementation consequence. - Extract-as-endorsement: quotes show participants liked the trainer but not what the trainer did. - Training-effect-overreach: qualitative perceptions are presented as evidence that training improved outcomes. - Cousin-venue-contamination: BMC train-the-trainer structures are copied wholesale into a PLOS register rather than used for literature positioning. Turn traits into functional features. (1) Role-feature heading. Heading schema: "Theme N: A <functional role noun>" Effect: makes the feature readable as work, not personality. (2) Feature-extract table. Columns: feature, situation, participant extract, role-work demonstrated. Effect: shows how the feature operates. (3) Practice implication bridge. Schema: {:feature <x> :training-design-implication <y> :scope <similar education/training contexts>} Effect: turns qualitative themes into design implications without claiming measured effectiveness. Engaged when every training theme names a role-work demand and is supported by extracts showing that work. Failing when the Results section reads as a list of desirable personal qualities.

title: Claim Transferability, Not Population Generalisability
text: Claim Transferability, Not Population Generalisability A small-n PLOS paper should end with bounded transferability rather than weak generalisability. The limitation is not simply "small sample"; it is which setting, roles, recruitment conditions, data-access limits, or topic-specific features bound the claim, and which mechanisms or design lessons may travel to similar settings. The exemplars often acknowledge locality, case selection, participant composition, and qualitative-data access constraints while still arguing that implementation mechanisms, framework refinements, or practice implications matter beyond the immediate site. The strongest language names the basis of transfer: similar workflows, intervention type, professional roles, or implementation conditions. The pattern operates on the axis: bounded transfer <-> statistical generalisation. Irreducible: qualitative small-n findings travel by mechanism, analogy, and context fit, not by sample representativeness. Real costs: transferability language is less rhetorically strong than broad generalisation. It requires naming the conditions under which the finding might fail. That cost is the price of credibility. Active dynamic: authors compensate for small n either by over-hedging everything or by overstating implications. Transferability is the middle discipline. - Small-n-apology-only: limitations say the sample was small and stop there. - Universal-implication: the Discussion says the findings apply to healthcare, HCI, education, or open science broadly without naming matching conditions. - Hedge-cloud: every implication is softened with "may", "might", and "could" but no scope conditions are specified. - Locality-hidden: the Results depend on a particular local system, but the Discussion abstracts it away. State transfer conditions explicitly. (1) Scope-condition sentence. Schema: "These findings are most transferable to <settings> where <matching condition>." Effect: turns limitation into usable boundary. (2) Mechanism-travels paragraph. Schema: {:local-finding <x> :mechanism <why it matters> :transfer-condition <where it should matter>} Effect: preserves analytic contribution without pretending representativeness. (3) Non-transfer list. Schema: {:not-claimed <population prevalence/effect size/all settings> :claimed <process/mechanism/implementation lesson>} Effect: prevents reviewers from reading the paper as underpowered quantitative work. Engaged when the Discussion tells readers where the finding may travel and why. Failing when limitations either apologize for n generically or imply generality without conditions.

title: Use Content Cousins for Positioning, Not Venue Register
text: Use Content Cousins for Positioning, Not Venue Register Papers outside PLOS ONE can be content cousins without being register models. Use BMC train-the-trainer or implementation studies to position the literature, vocabulary, and intervention family; use PLOS ONE papers to model abstract structure, Methods granularity, tables, headings, and claim scope. The BMC STORM and DEALTS2 papers are close content cousins for cascade training, train-the-trainer design, implementation barriers, and NPT-informed analysis. They are useful for literature positioning. But the requested library is about PLOS-with-small-n presentation, so the venue register should be drawn primarily from PLOS ONE exemplars. The pattern operates on the axis: topical similarity <-> venue-style suitability. Irreducible: a paper can be substantively close but rhetorically mismatched. Content evidence and venue emulation are different jobs. Real costs: separating content cousins from register models means extra discipline in drafting: a useful article may be cited heavily while not being copied structurally. This can feel artificial when the cousin is the closest intervention match. Active dynamic: authors naturally imitate the paper that feels closest to their topic. Reviewers, however, respond to the target venue's presentation norms. - Cousin-as-template: a non-PLOS article supplies the section shape, table density, or discussion style for a PLOS submission. - Venue-register-blindness: all cited papers are treated as equally useful models. - Literature-gap-overfit: the Introduction positions against the closest cousin but ignores PLOS exemplars that establish acceptable small-n presentation. - Methods-style-import: another venue's looser or denser Methods conventions are imported without checking PLOS fit. Assign each exemplar a job. (1) Source-role table. Columns: paper, venue, content role, register role, use in draft. Effect: prevents accidental imitation of the wrong model. (2) PLOS-primary structure pass. Schema: {:abstract <PLOS model> :methods <PLOS model> :results <PLOS model> :lit-positioning <content cousins>} Effect: preserves target-venue fit. (3) Cousin citation boundary. Schema: "We cite <cousin> for <intervention/literature point>, not as a structural precedent." Effect: makes the drafting discipline explicit. Engaged when each exemplar has a declared role: register model, methods ammunition, content cousin, or positioning source. Failing when the draft borrows structure from the closest topical paper regardless of venue.

title: First-Class Query Interface
text: First-Class Query Interface Treat query as a first-class operation via Drawbridge. Intent lives in the database and queries must be expressive. Pattern retrieval is constrained to fixed endpoints. You need SPARQL-like flexibility without endpoint sprawl. Use Drawbridge and portal helpers so queries can compose lex, ANN, and chain steps. First-class queries support rich exploration and align guidance with intent. src/musn/portal.clj; scripts/portal - Add portal subcommands for suggest, propose, and promote. - Document how to query intent and pattern metadata directly. - Include examples that mix lexical and ANN expansion. docs/portal-interop.md; docs/sidecar-usage.md

title: Portal Command Surface
text: Portal Command Surface Keep portal commands minimal, composable, and consistent across query modes. Portal is the agent-facing entry point for query and eval. Portal subcommands drift or duplicate responsibilities. You need fast iteration without breaking agent workflows. Define a stable command surface that separates eval, pattern queries, and sidecar logging helpers. A small, consistent surface makes automation reliable and user docs durable. src/musn/portal.clj; scripts/portal scripts/musn-session; scripts/musn-select; scripts/musn-action - Document command stability guarantees and deprecations. - Add portal flags for target log selection when writing sidecar events. - Document command stability guarantees and deprecations. docs/portal-interop.md; docs/sidecar-usage.md

title: Portal and Sidecar Interop
text: Portal and Sidecar Interop Use portal to fetch guidance and sidecar to persist actions and evidence. Agents need one query path and one audit path. Guidance and logging share the same storage or implicit side effects. You still want a tight loop from intent to action to evidence. Fetch patterns and intent through portal, perform work, and record selections, actions, and evidence in sidecar as append-only events. Separating query and audit paths keeps guidance flexible and logs authoritative. src/musn/portal.clj; scripts/portal src/sidecar/store.clj; src/sidecar/validation.clj - Add portal helpers that call sidecar log APIs directly. - Document the log schema exposed to portal for reporting. docs/portal-interop.md; docs/sidecar-usage.md

title: Use a Single Authoritative Transcript With Replay
text: Use a Single Authoritative Transcript With Replay Use one authoritative event log with replay so late joiners and transport switches share context. People re-join #lab and the transcript repeats, while agents drift on what they saw. You need consistent shared state across reconnects, multiple transports, and late joiners. IRC history, bridge logs, and WS streams can disagree; repeated partial transcripts create confusion and duplicated work. Designate an append-only event log (F1 or JSONL if that is the backing store) as authority; require clients (IRC bridge, WS clients) to be projections of that log; on join, clients replay from a checkpoint; during transport pivots, announce a pivot-id + checkpoint-id, reaffirm that log as source of truth, and replay from the latest checkpoint. Transport pivot covers cutover mechanics; this pattern defines the log-of-record. Realtime coordination needs a single source of truth; otherwise shared context is imaginary. - evidence: compare discrepancies between projections. - evidence: measure how often replay resolves confusion. - evidence: validate by dropping a client and confirming it recovers via replay. - evidence: confirm transport pivots rehydrate from the same checkpoint. - evidence-shape: {:event/id :string, :session/id :string, :pivot/id :string, :pivot/ts :string, :checkpoint/id :string, :replay/count :int, :projection :keyword, :log/source :keyword, :log/path :string, :authority? :boolean}

title: Split Realtime Work Across Feature Branches
text: Split Realtime Work Across Feature Branches Parallel feature branches reduce collisions; shared edits increase churn. Realtime collaboration benefits from clear ownership boundaries. Multiple agents edit the same files or functions in the same branch. Some hot paths require fast shared edits. Split work into named feature branches with explicit core/integration ownership and merge via review. Clear boundaries lower conflict risk and preserve velocity. - evidence: branch names encode scope (e.g., feat/pattern-check-core, feat/pattern-check-integration). - evidence-shape: {:branch :string, :scope :string, :owner :string}

title: Capture Realtime Learnings as Patterns
text: Capture Realtime Learnings as Patterns Log what works and what fails as patterns; otherwise the loop stalls. New workflows surface edge cases and implicit assumptions. Realtime deviations are handled ad hoc and not recorded. Early iterations can be noisy and imperfect. Record brief realtime patterns capturing “works well / doesn’t work,” then refine with evidence. Explicit learnings reduce repeated mistakes and speed calibration. - evidence: add a realtime pattern after each notable failure or success. - evidence-shape: {:works-well [:string], :doesnt-work [:string], :evidence [:string]}

title: Lease Listener Instances to Prevent Phantoms
text: Lease Listener Instances to Prevent Phantoms Prevent phantom listeners by versioning identities and expiring old instances. Multiple listener instances (fucodex_listen, fucodex_listen2, babashka, etc.) can be active without clarity. You spin up or restart listeners and bridges during a live session. Old listeners can remain connected, duplicated, or partially functioning, producing misleading partial visibility. Use listener leases keyed by role+room: each instance has a unique instance-id, TTL, and renew interval; only the freshest lease per role+room is authoritative; non-authoritative instances must stay silent except for shutdown notice; if renewals are missed beyond N or the grace window, mark the instance stale, emit a stale notice, and expire it. Unversioned listeners create ambiguous reception semantics and lead to repeated "can you see this?" loops. - evidence: audit logs for multiple active instances per role. - evidence: track incidents where the wrong listener responded. - evidence: validate that leases reduce repeated manual verification. - evidence: measure renewal misses and expiry events per role+room. - evidence-shape: {:role :keyword, :room :string, :instance/id :string, :lease/ttl-seconds :int, :lease/renew-seconds :int, :lease/grace-seconds :int, :lease/missed-count :int, :lease/max-missed :int, :lease/renewed-at :string, :lease/expires-at :string, :authoritative? :boolean}

title: Require Liveness Heartbeats With Sequence Context
text: Require Liveness Heartbeats With Sequence Context Make liveness a first-class signal via periodic heartbeats tied to sequence numbers. Agents can appear idle or silently stop listening; humans keep pinging. You need confidence that listeners and bridges are functioning continuously, not just at join time. A simple ping is ambiguous (didn't hear, busy, crashed, wrong channel), and manual checking does not scale. Require heartbeats: each agent emits a heartbeat every T seconds containing session-id, transport, last-received-seq, last-sent-seq, and current-mode; the moderator HUD flags stalls after N misses or when stale for S seconds and emits a stall event with the reason; stalled instances must reconnect or shut down. Liveness without sequence context does not distinguish quiet from partitioned. - evidence: tune heartbeat period vs noise and false alarms. - evidence: record false positives/negatives. - evidence: correlate stalls with actual bridge failures. - evidence: measure time-to-stall detection vs real outage. - evidence-shape: {:session/id :string, :transport :keyword, :last-received-seq :int, :last-sent-seq :int, :mode :keyword, :heartbeat/seconds :int, :missed/count :int, :missed/threshold :int, :stale/seconds :int, :grace/seconds :int, :stall/flagged? :boolean, :stall/reason :keyword, :stall/ts :string, :ts :string}

title: Realtime Loop Failure Signals
text: Realtime Loop Failure Signals Treat sustained overload, rising drops, or JSONL gaps as failure signals. The loop can degrade silently when ingest outruns processing. overload=true persists across batches, dropped_lines grows, or JSONL output stalls. A single burst is acceptable if the loop recovers quickly. Flag the loop as unhealthy and prioritize tuning or backpressure. Lost batches undermine auditability and PSR/PUR tracking. - evidence: overload true for >=3 consecutive batches. - evidence: dropped_lines shows an increasing trend. - evidence: JSONL gaps in batch_id or timestamps. - evidence-shape: {:overload :boolean, :dropped_lines :int, :batch_id :int, :ts :string}

title: Realtime Loop Recovery Actions
text: Realtime Loop Recovery Actions When the loop is unhealthy, reduce pressure, narrow scope, or loosen batch thresholds until it stabilizes. The core loop must remain responsive even under overload. Overload persists or batch latency exceeds the target for multiple batches. We still need minimal coverage of critical signals (PSR/PUR + sigil validity). Temporarily raise max_wait/max_lines, reduce input sources, or disable expensive scans (e.g., duplicate checks) until stable. Controlled degradation preserves core signals without cascading failures. - evidence: config change recorded with new thresholds. - evidence: overload clears within N batches after adjustment. - evidence-shape: {:config :map, :overload :boolean, :batch_id :int}

title: Realtime Loop Success Signals
text: Realtime Loop Success Signals Treat the loop as healthy when batches stay small, latency stays low, and JSONL output is continuous. The realtime loop must stay responsive under bursty chat traffic. Batch latency stays under target, dropped_lines stay near zero, and JSONL records are continuous. Short bursts may spike latency or trigger small drops. Keep current settings; focus on integration coverage and matcher quality, not tuning. Stable throughput and low loss indicate the core loop is doing its job. - evidence: batch latency histogram stays below target (e.g., <200ms). - evidence: dropped_lines == 0 for most batches. - evidence: JSONL records show steady batch_id increments. - evidence-shape: {:latency_ms :int, :dropped_lines :int, :batch_id :int}

title: Gate Code Changes Behind Explicit Modes
text: Gate Code Changes Behind Explicit Modes Separate chat from work by requiring an explicit mode switch before code-changing actions. Agents chat, test scripts, then propose code actions while humans are still orienting. You want realtime collaboration without accidental drift into untracked operational changes. In mixed-mode conversation, agents may act as if they have execution authority while the human is still orienting. Require a mode gate: agents must declare DISCUSS, DIAGNOSE, or EXECUTE with explicit transitions (DISCUSS→DIAGNOSE→EXECUTE) and exit criteria; only EXECUTE permits repo changes and it requires a human-issued token or explicit approval; EXECUTE must end with an explicit exit back to DISCUSS plus a brief summary; define a reset/timeout (e.g., human RESET or TTL) to prevent stuck modes. Mixing coordination talk with action talk collapses accountability and makes it hard to reconstruct why changes happened. - evidence: tag every message with mode. - evidence: review sessions where mode drift occurred. - evidence: validate whether gating reduces surprise changes and improves auditability. - evidence: track time spent in each mode and reasons for transitions. - evidence-shape: {:mode :keyword, :mode/from :keyword, :mode/to :keyword, :mode/exit :keyword, :mode/exit-criteria :string, :mode/ttl-seconds :int, :approval/token :string, :actor :string, :ts :string}

title: Require Realtime Rendezvous Handshakes
text: Require Realtime Rendezvous Handshakes Start work only after a signed hello+ack handshake confirms coherent reception. Realtime multi-agent coding sessions (human + 2+ agents) over IRC/WS bridges can silently fail. You need to know who is present, who is receiving messages, and whether it is safe to start work. Presence in the room is not evidence of reception; bridges/listeners can be stale, duplicated, or partitioned. Require an explicit rendezvous handshake: each participant emits a signed hello with capabilities, transport, last-seen seq, and handshake id/nonce, and the moderator must see matching acks from each agent before tasking begins; set an ack deadline to avoid silent stalls, and emit a failure event when the deadline is missed. Without an explicit handshake, the system confuses "connected" with "coherent," and coordination collapses into manual pinging. - evidence: log handshake completion rate per session. - evidence: track time-to-first-ack per transport. - evidence: record cases where presence=true but reception=false. - evidence: record ack latency distribution by transport. - evidence-shape: {:participant/id :string, :transport :keyword, :capabilities [:keyword], :last-seen-seq :int, :handshake/id :string, :handshake/nonce :string, :handshake/ts :string, :ack/seen :boolean, :ack/ts :string, :ack/latency-ms :int, :ack/deadline-seconds :int}

title: Keep Realtime Messages Single-Line
text: Keep Realtime Messages Single-Line Single-line messages transmit reliably; multi-line fragments do not. IRC relays can split or interleave long multi-line messages. Messages contain newlines or multiple blocks that fragment on relay. Some content needs detail beyond a short line. Send a single-line primary message with a short summary and attach details via files or structured events. A single-line payload preserves ordering and reduces lost context. - evidence: message-length capped (~350 words) with no newlines. - evidence-shape: {:summary :string, :detail-ref :string}

title: Prefer Structured PSR/PUR Events
text: Prefer Structured PSR/PUR Events Structured PSR/PUR events parse reliably; free-text does not. Realtime matchers depend on consistent schemas and keys. PSR/PUR are emitted as free-text or inconsistent key names. Humans may annotate context outside the structured event payload. Emit PSR/PUR as structured event maps with :event, :pattern/id, :session/id, :decision/id; keep annotations in separate fields. Stable schema enables accurate parsing, dedupe, and audit trails. - evidence: sample events include :pattern/selection-claimed and :pattern/use-claimed. - evidence-shape: {:event :keyword, :pattern/id :string, :session/id :string, :decision/id :string}

title: Treat Transport Switches as Explicit Pivots
text: Treat Transport Switches as Explicit Pivots Treat transport changes as controlled migrations, not ad-hoc chat suggestions. Sessions begin on IRC, then someone proposes switching to direct WebSocket while work is underway. You are collaborating in realtime and want to switch from an IRC bridge to direct WS for latency/reliability. Switching midstream creates split-brain conversation, duplicated messages, and uncertainty about the authoritative channel. Introduce a Transport Pivot: announce the target transport, freeze new tasks, replay the last N messages into the new channel, optionally dual-write for T seconds, and only then declare the new channel authoritative and reaffirm the authoritative transcript (see realtime/authoritative-transcript); record pivot-id and checkpoint-id in the log-of-record. A transport switch changes the epistemic ground (what counts as shared state), so it needs an explicit cutover. - evidence: measure divergence events (missed/duplicated turns) during pivots. - evidence: compare hard cutover vs dual-write for 60s. - evidence-shape: {:pivot/id :string, :pivot/ts :string, :from :keyword, :to :keyword, :replay/count :int, :dual-write/seconds :int, :rollback/trigger :string, :cutover/ts :string}

title: Emporium Indicators
text: Emporium Indicators Emporium Indicators (meaningful signals for an outward-facing repository) Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. Footfall — volume and diversity of external visitors, not raw downloads. Portfolio views — depth of exploration across interdisciplinary areas. Exposure outside the university — citations, shares, invitations. Partnership inquiries — conversions into collaborations or revenue. Cross-unit usage — evidence that internal groups use each other’s assets. Deposit friction — time-to-deposit, error rate, staff support load. title: Anchor the Scan to a Live Mission's Question; Split Audience-Probing from Concept-Research
text: Anchor the Scan to a Live Mission's Question; Split Audience-Probing from Concept-Research A landscape scan is sharpest when it is (1) anchored to a live mission's named question, (2) split into two instruments — audience-first probing (person/org queries) and concept-research (web) — each used only where its noise profile is low, and (3) read so that even a confirming-negative is a result. The good scan answers a mission's question; it does not forage in general. The daily-scan apparatus produces "something" every run, which makes "something" look like progress even when no real question was asked (the frame-005 discipline-drift diagnosis). A scan day is good not because it found impressive repos but because it moved a specific decision. frame-006 was good on all three axes at once, which is why it is worth encoding. You are about to run a scan and can either (a) forage the general landscape, or (b) anchor the scan to a live mission's named gap-question with a defined success AND failure criterion — and you have both audience-shaped targets (named people/orgs) and concept-shaped questions (topics/ideas) you'd like to investigate. Un-anchored foraging returns output that looks like progress but feeds no decision. And running everything through one instrument fails twice over: a topic-phrased query in a GitHub-probe scan ("learning-efficiency") decays to keyword noise, while a named-person query is precisely where the probe shines. Mixing them buries the signal of the good instrument in the noise of the misused one. Anchor the scan to one mission's question, stated as a hypothesis whose YES and NO are both informative ("do the GLAIVE roster's recent repos show learning-efficiency work?"). Split instruments: run AUDIENCE-FIRST probes (`user:X` / `org:X`) in the scan; route CONCEPT questions (Baldwin effects, learning-efficiency, learnable tactics) to a separate web/research sweep where topic-phrasing belongs. Read a confirming-negative as a finding: "nobody here owns it" validated the mission's gap as the operator's own. Then fold the result straight into the mission's MAP. Mission-anchoring supplies the named hypothesis the frame-005 discipline demands, externally and for free, and guarantees the result lands somewhere (a mission's MAP) rather than as orphaned "something." The instrument-split keeps each tool in its low-noise regime, so the audience-first signal isn't drowned by topic-noise. And treating the confirming-negative as a result is what lets a scan *validate a gap* — often more valuable than yet another lead, because it tells the operator the territory is theirs. - Before probing, write the mission's question as a hypothesis with both outcomes named; if you can't, the scan isn't ready (it would forage). - Sort intended targets into audience-shaped (→ scan probes) and concept-shaped (→ research sweep); never put a topic query in the GitHub scan. - File the frame against the main sequence even when it served one mission (per frame-006: "not a new series or it gets confusing"); keep the custom probe set as reusable without registering a standing subseries. - Carry the confirming-negative into the mission's MAP explicitly; a negative that isn't folded back is a wasted scan. - Watch the known blindspot: the `commercial-*` render is a license/homepage heuristic, not a verdict — drill READMEs before judging substance.

title: Append-Only Semantic Audit
text: Append-Only Semantic Audit Keep semantic writes append-only with provenance at the store boundary. Semantic evolution must be inspectable and reversible. Proposal or fact updates overwrite prior states. You need to revise or retire claims over time. Persist every semantic write (proposal, promotion, evidence, action, fact, chain) as append-only records with identifiers and audit metadata, and reject duplicate ids at the store boundary. Append-only logs enable audits and provenance tracking without silent mutation. docs/sidecar-promotions.md; docs/sidecar-promotion-flow.md; resources/sidecar/schema.sql docs/sidecar-audit-flow.md; src/sidecar/store.clj src/sidecar/store.clj; test/sidecar/store_test.clj src/sidecar/store.clj; src/sidecar/cli.clj - Add explicit status transitions in the proposals table. - Append promotion and retirement events with timestamps. - Define a compact audit view for append-only events (per id). docs/sidecar-usage.md; docs/sidecar-demo.md

title: Artifact, Entity, and Mention Grounding
text: Artifact, Entity, and Mention Grounding Ground semantics on artifacts, entities, aliases, and mentions in SQLite. Patterns and documents provide text that must be inspectable and queryable. Queries rely on embeddings alone without deterministic anchors. You still want fast similarity and fuzzy recall. Store artifacts, entities, aliases, and mentions as deterministic extraction outputs. Grounding makes proposals auditable and promotes stable chain building. docs/sidecar-grounding-and-chains.md - Define the artifacts, entities, aliases, and mentions tables. - Implement ingestion that hashes artifacts and records mention spans. - Add a minimal alias weighting scheme for lexical expansion.

title: Bridge Triple Escalator
text: Bridge Triple Escalator Use curated bridge triples to justify difficult hops. Some chains need domain knowledge that embeddings cannot justify. A chain step requires a cross-domain leap with only fuzzy support. You still want puzzle-like chain recovery. Store minimal bridge triples in SQLite and use them to justify or gate hops. Curated bridges provide explicit warrants without inflating facts prematurely. docs/sidecar-promotions.md; resources/sidecar/schema.sql - Define the bridge_triples table and editing workflow. - Reference bridge triples in chain evidence output. - Use bridges to allow otherwise gated sense shifts.

title: Chain Builder with Softness Accounting
text: Chain Builder with Softness Accounting Build short chains and report softness per hop. Users need explainable chains, not just candidate lists. Queries return flat neighbor lists without justification. You want puzzle-like chain recovery with clear evidence. Build short chains over arrows, bridges, and proposals, and report softness metrics. Softness accounting shows where fuzz enters the chain and enables review. docs/sidecar-chains.md src/sidecar/store.clj; test/sidecar/store_test.clj src/sidecar/store.clj (chain-score, step-evidence); test/sidecar/store_test.clj test/sidecar/store_test.clj (chain-softness-scoring) - Document chain scoring and per-hop evidence output in docs/sidecar-chains.md. docs/sidecar-usage.md; docs/sidecar-demo.md

title: Explicit Promotion to Facts
text: Explicit Promotion to Facts Promote proposals to facts only via explicit, logged actions. Facts must remain authoritative and defeasible. Proposals become facts implicitly or through side effects. You want good proposals to become facts when warranted. Require a promote action that passes the validation gate and appends a promotion record. Explicit promotion prevents silent contamination and preserves auditability. docs/sidecar-promotions.md; docs/sidecar-promotion-flow.md; resources/sidecar/schema.sql docs/sidecar-audit-flow.md; docs/sidecar-promotion-flow.md; resources/sidecar/schema.sql - Define promotion log records with rationale and decided_by. - Route promotion writes through the validation gate (required fields, enum constraints, score bounds). - Reject direct fact writes outside the promotion action. docs/sidecar-usage.md; docs/sidecar-demo.md

title: Fact Lifecycle Event Types
text: Fact Lifecycle Event Types Model facts with explicit lifecycle event types (fact, warrant, retired). Facts must be authoritative, defeasible, and auditable over time. Fact state changes are implicit or modeled as overwrites. You still need fast reads and clear current truth. Record lifecycle events as append-only types (fact, warrant, retired) with rationale and actor metadata, and derive active state from the latest fact or warrant event (retired clears active status). Explicit lifecycle events preserve audit trails and clarify which facts are currently active. docs/sidecar-promotion-flow.md; docs/sidecar-promotions.md src/sidecar/store.clj; src/sidecar/validation.clj; test/sidecar/store_test.clj src/sidecar/store.clj (latest-active-fact, latest-active-state, active-fact-ids); test/sidecar/store_test.clj src/sidecar/cli.clj; src/sidecar/inspect.clj - Define the event type enum and required fields. - Require lifecycle events for all promoted facts. - Document lifecycle-derived active state in docs/sidecar-audit-flow.md.

title: Per-ID Audit Timeline Linkage
text: Per-ID Audit Timeline Linkage Resolve per-id timelines across linked semantic records. Audits must show how a proposal becomes a promotion and fact, not just isolated records. Per-id queries only return exact id matches and ignore related records. Operators need a contiguous narrative for each claim. Link timelines across relationships (proposal->promotion->fact, evidence targets, chain steps) and surface all related events in a single per-id view. Cross-entity linkage turns append-only logs into inspectable histories. src/sidecar/store.clj; test/sidecar/store_test.clj src/sidecar/inspect.clj; scripts/sidecar-inspect src/sidecar/store.clj (latest-active-state); src/sidecar/cli.clj; src/sidecar/inspect.clj - Add explicit ordering rules when timestamps collide. - Document latest active state queries in docs/sidecar-usage.md. docs/sidecar-usage.md; docs/sidecar-demo.md

title: Proposal Ledger for Fuzzy Output
text: Proposal Ledger for Fuzzy Output Record all fuzzy results as proposals with evidence in SQLite. ANN search yields useful candidates without authority. Vector neighbors are used directly as facts or chain steps. You need fuzzy recall to propose candidates for review. Write each fuzzy output as a proposal with score, method, and evidence. A proposal ledger preserves provenance and enables explicit promotion. docs/sidecar-promotions.md; resources/sidecar/schema.sql docs/sidecar-audit-flow.md; resources/sidecar/schema.sql - Implement the proposals table and status workflow. - Store neighbor ids and distances in evidence_json. - Add CLI support for propose and review.

title: Sense-Shift Gate
text: Sense-Shift Gate Allow sense shifts only when explicitly typed or bridged. Sense broadening or narrowing can cause semantic drift. Sense shifts are applied freely in chain building. Some shifts are necessary to connect domains. Gate sense-broaden and sense-narrow steps to typed arrows or bridge triples. Gating reduces drift and keeps chains explainable. docs/sidecar-query-flow.md src/sidecar/store.clj (sense-shift-issue, shift-annotation); test/sidecar/store_test.clj - Document sense-shift gating rules in docs/sidecar-query-flow.md. docs/sidecar-query-flow.md docs/sidecar-usage.md; docs/sidecar-demo.md

title: Tri-Store Semantic Separation
text: Tri-Store Semantic Separation Separate facts, memes, and notions into distinct stores. You need semantic gain without allowing fuzzy output to become authoritative. Similarity search and curated semantics share one store or one truth level. You still need fast candidate proposals and inspectable semantics. Use XTDB for facts, SQLite for inspectable memes, and ANN/HNSW for notions, and enforce boundaries. Each store has a different trust level; separation keeps fuzz from becoming fact. docs/sidecar-query-flow.md; docs/sidecar-promotion-flow.md - Define the three adapters and enforce that ANN results only create proposals. - Add checks that facts are written only through explicit promotion. - Document store responsibilities and invariants. docs/sidecar-query-flow.md; docs/sidecar-promotion-flow.md docs/sidecar-usage.md; docs/sidecar-demo.md

title: Typed Kolmogorov Arrows
text: Typed Kolmogorov Arrows Represent semantic transforms as typed arrows with status and confidence. Chain recovery depends on explicit, interpretable links. Chain steps are untyped or implied only by similarity. You need translation, abstraction, and metonymy moves. Store arrows with mode, payload, scope, confidence, and status. Typed arrows make transforms inspectable and scoreable in chains. docs/sidecar-grounding-and-chains.md - Define the arrows table and a required mode vocabulary. - Require status transitions (draft, active, retired). - Add validation for scope tags and confidence ranges.

title: Validation and Enforcement Gate
text: Validation and Enforcement Gate Enforce invariants at write-time with explicit validation gates. The sidecar flow relies on strict store boundaries and explicit promotion. Writes bypass invariants or validation is optional. You need flexible ingestion and fast iteration. Define a validation gate that checks required fields, enum constraints, and store boundaries before any write. Centralized enforcement prevents silent drift and keeps logs auditable. docs/sidecar-promotion-flow.md; docs/sidecar-promotions.md docs/sidecar-query-flow.md; docs/sidecar-audit-flow.md resources/sidecar/schema.sql src/sidecar/validation.clj; src/sidecar/store.clj; test/sidecar/store_test.clj src/sidecar/validation.clj; test/sidecar/store_test.clj - Define validators for proposals, promotions, and bridge triples keyed to schema fields (status enums, required ids, score bounds). - Reject any attempt to write facts or bridge triples outside the promotion pathway. - Enforce append-only writes for proposals and promotions (no updates or deletes). docs/sidecar-usage.md; docs/sidecar-demo.md

title: Argument for a Futon3c Social Coordination Layer
text: Argument for a Futon3c Social Coordination Layer This is a flexiformal argument for the futon3c social coordination layer — the third AIF loop in the futon stack, operating at the social/real-time timescale. It builds on the completed coordination argument (coordination/ARGUMENT.flexiarg), which established the task-timescale gate pipeline (futon3b) and the glacial-timescale library evolution loop (L1). This argument establishes what the social loop requires, why previous attempts failed, and what a futonic implementation must look like. The coordination argument was verified by implementation: futon3b has 31 tests, 109 assertions, and an 8/8 machine-checked wiring diagram. This argument is pre-implementation — it is what must be valid BEFORE futon3c missions can be scoped. == PART 0: Context — What Changed Since the Coordination Argument == The coordination argument (coordination/ARGUMENT.flexiarg) established: - futon3 is split into three repos (war-room.md WR-1): futon3a (query), futon3b (task+glacial), futon3c (social/realtime) - The gate pipeline (G5→G0) is implemented and test-verified - The glacial loop (L1-observe → L1-canon) is implemented and test-verified, including the round-trip proof - The concrete wiring diagram passes all 8 categorical checks The devmap (futon3.devmap, updated 2026-02-09) now reflects this: - P2 (Check DSL) is the gate pipeline, owned by futon3b - P3 (Proof-State Journal) is the proof-path store, owned by futon3b - P7 (Pattern Workbench) is partially implemented as L1 canonicalizer - P8 (Joy Metrics), P10 (Training Ground) are assigned to futon3c - P11 (Self-Description) is assigned to futon5 WHAT THE DEVMAP DOES NOT ADDRESS (social layer): - No agent lifecycle management with formal invariants - No real-time message routing with delivery guarantees - No session persistence or continuity model - No forum or collaborative proof-tree infrastructure - No peripheral model (detach/reattach, capability envelopes) - No standup or co-presence ceremony - No PAR as first-class session event These are precisely the concerns that futon3 attempted to address with Agency, Forum, Drawbridge, and the bridge scripts — and that failed. The question is: why did they fail, and what must be different? == PART I: Why the Social Layer Attempts Failed == Three empirical tensions, each grounded in the futon3 git log with specific commit evidence. These are documented as standalone patterns in library/social/. S1. [from social/verify-before-compose] Agency and Drawbridge code was written as architectural design documents, not tested incrementally. Five forward-declaration fix commits (f3044aa, adc8d67, 2da227e, 1542b0a, 6010d79) across two subsystems demonstrate that namespaces were composed before individual functions were verified to load. This is a systematic violation of the event-protocol pattern (futon-theory): PROPOSE_CLAIM preceded OBSERVE. The cost was multiplicative debugging at integration time rather than additive debugging at definition time. S2. [from social/tension-before-code] Agency went through three generations before its invariants were named. Generation 1-2 built four major features (bells, pages, registry, session tracking) without any A0-A5 proof tests. Phase 1 (commit 588a468) wrote the invariant tests and found 18 failures. Phase 2 (commits 5f85287, c5b5929, 3f0aa3a, 804fe8f, 5dcb28b) fixed all five invariants — each commit message is a retroactive confession: "eliminate catch _ nil" (A3), "no silent corruption" (A2), "non-nil continuity" (A2), "bounded lifecycle" (A5), "delivery receipts" (A0). The tension-observation loop (futon-theory/structural-tension-as-observation) was not running. S3. [from social/explicit-exit-over-abandonment] Three subsystems were silently abandoned: - Forum: 8 commits (4846339 through a346d27), ClassCastException on first WebSocket test, last commit is bare "save", no mission status update, 9 success criteria in M-agency-forum.md none completed or marked blocked. - PAR bell: designed for parallelism (9d76e88), forced sequential (7fda538), 6 subsequent workaround commits, M-par-session- punctuation.md has 1 of 8 checkboxes completed. - IRC/MUSN bridge: 14+ fix commits (auth, timeouts, multi-room, sanitizer on/off, prompt tightening, rate limiting), no exit criteria, no convergence milestone. Each abandonment violated the mission-lifecycle pattern (futon-theory): no :active → :blocked transition, no recorded blocker, no tension observation. S4. [synthesis of S1-S3] The three tensions are not independent. S1 (untested composition) produces S2 (retroactive invariant discovery) because untested code accumulates latent violations. S2 produces S3 (abandonment) because retroactive invariant discovery is demoralizing — each rebuild reveals more violations, and eventually the developer shifts attention to a different subsystem. The cycle is: build without tests → discover violations → confess invariants → rebuild → discover more violations → abandon → start new subsystem This is the structural cycle identified in the coordination argument (H8), but operating at the social timescale rather than the task timescale. The coordination argument broke this cycle for the task loop by specifying invariants first (the gate patterns) and verifying them categorically (the wiring diagram). The social loop needs the same treatment. S5. [from agency pattern library: 8 patterns] The Agency pattern library documents the consequences of S1-S3 in domain-specific terms. Eight patterns name specific failure modes: - delivery-receipt: "sent" confused with "delivered" - single-routing-authority: three routing tiers with conflicting state - state-atomicity: transitions leave nil state on failure - loud-failure: 20+ instances of (catch Exception _ nil) - bounded-lifecycle: atoms grow unbounded, cleanup races - identifier-separation: transport IDs overload LLM session IDs - self-attribution: server posts on behalf of agents - invariants (A0-A5): formal spec written after two generations These patterns are empirically validated — the Phase 2 commits confirm every failure mode. But they are post-mortems, not specifications: they were induced from failures, not derived from futon-theory. They document what went wrong without grounding WHY in a theoretical framework that would predict the failure class in advance. S6. [from realtime pattern library: 13 patterns] The realtime pattern library documents the consequences of S1-S3 in the bridge/transport domain. Thirteen patterns name failure modes clustered around one theme: presence is not coherence. - authoritative-transcript: multiple transcripts disagree - listener-leases: phantom presence from old listeners - liveness-heartbeats: pings don't distinguish quiet from partitioned - rendezvous-handshake: "connected" confused with "coherent" - transport-pivot: switching mid-stream creates split-brain - mode-gate: mixing talk with action collapses accountability - single-line-transport: IRC splits multi-line messages - structured-events-only: free-text doesn't parse reliably Like the agency patterns, these are post-mortems — induced from the IRC bridge fix-cycle (14+ commits), not derived from futon-theory. S7. [from devmap P8, P10: orphaned greenfield prototypes] Joy Metrics (P8) and Training Ground (P10) were assigned to futon3c in the devmap update but have no implementation, no mission documents, and no evidence. They are downstream of the social coordination layer — they cannot be built until the layer they depend on exists. Their greenfield status is a symptom of S3 (abandonment): the infrastructure they need was attempted and abandoned. == PART II: What the Agency/Realtime Patterns Require == The agency and realtime patterns, despite being post-mortems, do contain valid requirements. Reformulated as requirements (not patterns), grounded in futon-theory: R1. [from agency/delivery-receipt + futon-theory/proof-path] Every message sent between agents must produce a delivery receipt or an explicit failure. "No error" is not "success." The proof-path pattern requires auditable chains; unreceipted messages are unverifiable links. R2. [from agency/single-routing-authority + futon-theory/single-source-of-truth] For any agent-id, exactly one routing authority exists at a time. Multiple routing tiers with conflicting state are a violation of single-source-of-truth (I1). R3. [from agency/state-atomicity + futon-theory/all-or-nothing] State transitions are atomic: they succeed completely or fail loudly with rollback. Partial transitions that leave nil state violate all-or-nothing (I2). R4. [from agency/loud-failure + futon-theory/error-hierarchy] Errors surface at the layer that caused them. Silent catch-and- swallow (catch _ nil) is a violation of error-hierarchy (I3). R5. [from agency/bounded-lifecycle + futon-theory/agent-contract] All transient resources have deterministic lifecycle bounds. Fire-and-forget cleanup violates agent-contract (agents must respect invariants). R6. [from agency/identifier-separation + futon-theory/single-source-of-truth] Transport IDs, continuity IDs, and protocol IDs are typed and distinct. Overloading violates single-source-of-truth because the same identifier means different things at different layers. R7. [from realtime/rendezvous-handshake + futon-theory/event-protocol] Connection must be followed by an explicit readiness handshake before coordination can begin. The event-protocol requires OBSERVE before PROPOSE_CLAIM; presence without readiness assessment is unobserved action. R8. [from realtime/authoritative-transcript + futon-theory/durability-first] One transcript is authoritative. Multiple conflicting transcripts violate durability-first (I0): what you save is not what you get back if you're reading from the wrong transcript. R9. [from realtime/structured-events-only + futon-theory/minimum-viable-events] Events must be structured and machine-parseable. Free-text PSR/PUR that don't parse reliably cannot be minimum viable events because they cannot be reliably processed. R10. [from realtime/mode-gate + futon-theory/agent-contract] Coordination talk and action talk must be distinguishable. The agent-contract requires agents to "observe before act"; mixing the two modes collapses the observation/action boundary. R11. [from social/scope-bounded-handoff + futon-theory/I4] Agent handoffs must declare writable scope. Constraint-timescale artifacts (exotype diagrams, pattern library, mission specs) are read-only from the task timescale. This is I4 (exogeneity) applied to agent coordination: no task-timescale agent can modify a constraint-timescale artifact. Scope violations must be structurally rejected, not conventionally discouraged. Evidence: futon5 feat/compose-parallel review (2026-02-10) — Codex rewrote social-exotype.edn (constraint artifact) to make compose- parallel tests pass, discarding gate duality (C6) and ARGUMENT traceability. Three tensions recorded in proof-path store. == PART III: What the Theory Demands == T1. [from futon-theory/four-types + futon-theory/interface-loop] The futon stack operates at three timescales (war-room.md): - Social (seconds): agents coordinate, hand off work, maintain shared awareness - Task (minutes): gate pipeline validates, executes, persists - Glacial (weeks): library evolves through tension observation and canonicalization The interface-loop pattern says: at each layer boundary, a Baldwin cycle (EXPLORE → ASSIMILATE → CANALIZE) must operate for cumulative functional gain. futon3b implements this at the task/glacial boundary (L1). The social/task boundary needs the same treatment: a loop that observes coordination outcomes and feeds them into the task pipeline. T2. [from futon-theory/structural-tension-as-observation] The social loop's observation vector is coordination failure: dropped messages (R1), routing conflicts (R2), partial state (R3), silent errors (R4), resource leaks (R5), identity confusion (R6). These are the structural irritations, pre-symbolic pressures, and trans-situational reappearances that the glacial loop should eventually canonize — but they must first be observable at the social timescale. T3. [from futon-theory/mission-lifecycle + futon-theory/mission-scoping] The social layer must be built as bounded missions with explicit lifecycle transitions. S3 demonstrated that unbounded missions with implicit abandonment create false affordances and archaeology tax. Each futon3c mission must have: single owner, scope in/out, success criteria, exit conditions, and explicit :blocked/:parked transitions. T4. [from futon-theory/event-protocol + futon-theory/proof-path] Social-timescale events (agent connection, message exchange, session handoff, peripheral hop) must produce typed records that compose into proof paths. The coordination argument established that proof paths are the minimum unit of auditability. The social loop produces the fastest proof paths — they must be typed from the start, not retroactively. T5. [from futon-theory/retroactive-canonicalization] The agency and realtime patterns ARE retroactive canonicalizations — they were induced from failure. But they were not canonicalized through the Baldwin cycle: they were not NAMED from recurring tensions (they were named from post-mortems), not SELECTED by threshold (they were all included regardless of recurrence), and not CANALIZED into constraints (they exist as patterns but constrain nothing). For futon3c, the canonicalization must be genuine: patterns that pass through naming, selection, and canalization via L1. == PART IV: The Convergence == C1. [from S4, S5, S6] The agency patterns (8) and realtime patterns (13) describe different symptoms of the same disease: building distributed coordination without the theoretical grounding that makes the invariants predictable. The agency patterns focus on state/routing/ lifecycle; the realtime patterns focus on transport/presence/ coherence. But the three recurring failure modes are identical across both: - Silent failures (agency/loud-failure ↔ realtime/loop-failure-signals) - Identity collapse (agency/identifier-separation ↔ realtime/listener-leases) - Missing proof (agency/delivery-receipt ↔ realtime/rendezvous-handshake) C2. [from R1-R10, T1] The ten requirements (R1-R10) are not a grab-bag. They decompose into three layers that correspond to the three AIF loop boundaries: - Transport layer (R1, R7, R8, R9): delivery, readiness, transcript, structure — the social→social boundary - Routing layer (R2, R5, R6, R10): authority, lifecycle, identity, mode separation — the social→task boundary - State layer (R3, R4): atomicity, error propagation — the task→task boundary (already enforced by futon3b gates) R3 and R4 are already satisfied by the gate pipeline. The social layer's job is R1-R2 and R5-R10: the requirements that operate at the social timescale. C3. [from T2, T4, T5] The social loop must produce typed events that feed into the same proof-path store that the task loop writes to. This is how the three timescales compose: - Social loop produces coordination events (connections, messages, handoffs) as typed proof-path entries - Task loop produces execution events (gate traversals) as typed proof-path entries - Glacial loop observes ALL proof-path entries for tensions and canonizes new patterns The L1 observer already has the three scan functions (structural-irritation, pre-symbolic-pressure, trans-situational- reappearance). If the social loop emits typed events into the proof-path store, L1 can observe social-timescale tensions without modification. The glacial loop is timescale-agnostic — it observes structural patterns, not timescale-specific ones. C4. [from S1-S3, T3] The social layer must be built differently from how futon3 built Agency/Forum/Drawbridge. Specifically: - Verify before compose (S1): each namespace loads and passes smoke tests before integration - Tension before code (S2): invariant proof tests before implementation - Explicit exit (S3): mission lifecycle transitions, not silent abandonment These are development-process patterns, not runtime patterns. They constrain HOW futon3c is built, not WHAT it builds. The coordination argument did not need to state this because futon3b was built futonic from the start (the gate patterns existed before the code). futon3c must learn from the futon3 experience. C5. [from C1, C2, C3, C4] The social loop is not a separate system. It is the third timescale of the same AIF diagram. The coordination argument established two loops (task + glacial) sharing one boundary (the gate pipeline). The social loop adds the fastest timescale: social (seconds) → task (minutes) → glacial (weeks) ↑ | └─────── library constrains ──────────┘ Agents coordinate in real-time (social), submit work through gates (task), accumulate evidence that evolves the library (glacial), and the evolved library constrains future coordination (social). This is the full AIF cycle across three timescales. I3 (timescale ordering) governs all three boundaries. C6. [from coordination/INDEX.md duality table, C2, C5] The coordination patterns already have a dual interpretation (coordination/INDEX.md §Dual Interpretation). Each gate reads two ways: an agency problem and a pattern problem. The table: | Gate | Agency Reading | Pattern Reading | | G5 task-shape | Is the agent's task well-defined? | Is the task shaped so a pattern can guide it? | | G4 capability | Can this agent do this work? | Does this pattern apply to this domain? | | G4 assignment | Is one agent responsible? | Is one pattern selected? | | G3 mandatory-psr | Has the agent committed to an approach? | Has a pattern been engaged with? | | G2 bounded-execution | Agent stays within budget | Pattern application stays within scope | | G1 mandatory-pur | Agent's work gets evaluated | Pattern's guidance gets evaluated | | G0 durability | Agent's session is recoverable | Pattern use evidence is persistent | | G0 par-obligation | Agent reflects on what happened | Pattern library learns from use | The left column (agency reading) IS the social loop's concern. The right column (pattern reading) IS the task/glacial loop's concern. The gate pipeline is not just where social events feed into task events — it is where the two readings converge into one typed record. This means the social loop's requirements (R1-R10) map onto specific gates: - R1 (delivery receipts) → agency reading of G0 (durability) - R2 (single routing authority) → agency reading of G4 (assignment) - R7 (rendezvous handshake) → agency reading of G5 (task shape) - R9 (structured events) → agency reading of G0 (durability) - R10 (mode gate) → agency reading of G3 (mandatory-psr) The social loop is not a layer below the gate pipeline that feeds into it. It is the agency SIDE of the gate pipeline — the half that was specified in the duality table but never implemented. "Futon3 replaces 'ants' with 'agents' and 'pheromone' with 'patterns' — coordination is the relationship between agents and patterns, and the gates sit at the intersection." == THESIS == Th.
