[from C1-C6] futon3 attempted to build real-time agent coordination (Agency, Forum, Drawbridge, bridges) without the theoretical grounding that makes distributed invariants predictable. The result was three generations of build-confess-rebuild for Agency, silent abandonment of Forum, and a perpetual fix-cycle for bridges. Twenty-one patterns (8 agency + 13 realtime) document the symptoms; three social patterns (verify-before-compose, tension-before-code, explicit-exit-over-abandonment) diagnose the cause: the development process itself violated the same invariants the system was trying to enforce. futon3c must break this cycle by: 1. Deriving its invariants from futon-theory BEFORE writing code, not inducing them from failures afterward (T5, S2) 2. Emitting typed events into the shared proof-path store so the existing glacial loop can observe social-timescale tensions (C3) 3. Building as bounded missions with explicit lifecycle transitions, verified incrementally (T3, C4) 4. Treating the agency and realtime patterns as evidence of tensions, not as the architectural specification (C1) Moreover, the social loop is not a layer beneath the gate pipeline that feeds into it from below. The coordination duality table (C6) reveals that each gate already has an agency reading and a pattern reading. The pattern reading is implemented (futon3b). The agency reading is specified but unimplemented — it IS the social loop. futon3c completes the duality: agents and patterns, the two sides of every gate, both implemented and both producing typed evidence. The social loop is the fastest timescale in a three-level AIF diagram. Its outputs feed the task loop (gate pipeline), whose outputs feed the glacial loop (library evolution), whose outputs constrain the social loop. The architecture is not three separate systems — it is one system operating at three timescales, sharing one typed evidence store and one categorical verification framework. == WHAT FUTON3C MUST BUILD == FROM FUTON3 (failed attempts, as evidence): - Agency A0-A5 invariants → validated in Phase 2, need porting to a clean implementation with tests-first discipline - Forum proof-tree concept → valid idea, failed execution; needs mission-scoped retry with explicit exit conditions - Drawbridge multi-agent routing → OOM-motivated redesign; registration-based, not subprocess-based - Peripheral model → concept drifted through 3 definitions; needs grounding in futon-theory/agent-contract - PAR session punctuation → elegant design, zero implementation; needs bounded first milestone FROM FUTON3B (proven infrastructure, as foundation): - Gate pipeline (G5→G0) → social loop submits work through gates - Proof-path store → social events written as typed records - L1 observer → detects social-timescale tensions automatically - L1 canonicalizer → promotes recurring social tensions to patterns - Malli evidence shapes → social events must validate against shapes - ct/mission.clj → social-loop wiring diagram must pass 8 checks FROM FUTON-THEORY (constraints): - event-protocol: social events follow OBSERVE → VERIFY sequence - proof-path: social coordination produces auditable chains - agent-contract: agents clock in, observe, attribute, respect invariants - interface-loop: Baldwin cycle at social→task boundary - mission-lifecycle: bounded missions with explicit transitions == VERIFICATION (PENDING) == V1. [required: social-exotype diagram] A social-exotype.edn must be written and validated against ct/mission.clj, analogous to coordination-exotype.edn. It must encode the social-timescale components (Agency, Forum, peripherals) and their edges, and pass all 8 checks including I3 (timescale ordering: social→social and social→task edges only) and I4 (exogeneity: no social output reaches glacial constraints directly). V2. [required: concrete diagram update] futon3-coordination.edn must be extended with social-timescale components and edges, and the combined diagram must still pass all 8 checks. The existing Level 0 and Level 1 edges must remain valid. V3. [required: round-trip proof] Analogous to futon3b's full-loop-round-trip test: a social coordination event → typed proof-path entry → L1 observes tension → L1 canonizes pattern → pattern constrains future social coordination. This proves the three-timescale AIF cycle closes. == STATUS == This argument is at the VERIFY step of the derivation xenotype. COMPLETE: - IDENTIFY: futon3 git archaeology (social-layer failures) - MAP: Four social patterns (verify-before-compose, tension-before-code, explicit-exit-over-abandonment, scope-bounded-handoff) - DERIVE: Eleven requirements (R1-R11) from agency/realtime patterns via futon-theory. R11 added 2026-02-10 from live coordination evidence (Codex compose-parallel review). - ARGUE: This document (S1-S7, R1-R11, T1-T5, C1-C6, thesis) COMPLETE (continued): - VERIFY: M-social-exotype (futon3c/holes/missions/M-social-exotype.md) - V1: social-exotype.edn — standalone diagram validation [DONE, 8/8] - V2: three-diagram composition — compose-parallel merged to futon5 main (d5ae681). social-exotype.edn restored with :social timescale. Composed diagram: 5 inputs, 7 outputs, 16 components, 69 edges, 8/8 checks. - V3: round-trip proof deferred to INSTANTIATE (by design) - Part III (Prototype 0) — bootstrap closure [DONE] - 6 proof-paths in futon3b/data/proof-paths/ including 3 coordination tensions from Codex review ACTIVE: - INSTANTIATE: M-agency-refactor, M-forum-refactor, M-peripheral-model Exotype exists and is validated. Implementation missions can now be scoped.

title: Exit Subsystems Through the Lifecycle State Machine, Not Silent Abandonment
text: Exit Subsystems Through the Lifecycle State Machine, Not Silent Abandonment When a subsystem hits a blocking failure, transition it through the mission lifecycle state machine (:active -> :blocked with explicit blocker) rather than letting attention drift to a different subsystem. Silent abandonment is the project-management equivalent of catch _ nil — it suppresses a signal that downstream decisions depend on. You are building an ambitious multi-subsystem project (proof-tree forum, parallel agent execution, real-time bridges, session punctuation) where each subsystem has dependencies on others and where multiple agents or developers may pick up work based on stated mission status. A subsystem encounters its first serious integration failure — a ClassCastException in the WebSocket layer, an OOM when running a sidecar process, a race condition in parallel execution — and the developer's attention shifts to a different subsystem that seems more tractable or more urgent. Silent abandonment leaves the codebase in an inconsistent state. Partially built subsystems create false affordances: APIs that exist but don't work, mission documents that list success criteria for capabilities that were never completed, pattern libraries that reference subsystems that were tried and failed. The next developer (human or agent) cannot distinguish "not yet built" from "tried and failed" without git archaeology — and the git archaeology itself takes longer than building the thing would have, because abandoned code has no exit narrative. - False affordance: an API exists, is referenced in mission docs and pattern libraries, but does not work; downstream agents build against it and fail at integration time - Zombie mission: mission document says :in-progress but has no commits for weeks; another developer assumes it's being worked on and does not pick it up - Archaeology tax: understanding why a subsystem was abandoned requires reading the full git log, cross-referencing with IRC logs, and guessing at context that was never recorded - Perpetual fix cycle: rather than declaring a subsystem blocked and redesigning, the developer applies an unbounded series of point fixes that never converge on stability When a subsystem hits a blocking failure, record three things: (1) the specific failure and its commit, (2) the mission lifecycle transition (:active -> :blocked, with blocker reference), and (3) what downstream missions are affected. If the subsystem is being deliberately deprioritized rather than blocked, transition to :parked with a rationale. Never leave a mission in :active status when no one is working on it. The mission-lifecycle pattern (futon-theory/mission-lifecycle) defines a state machine (:greenfield -> :scoped -> :active -> :blocked -> :review -> :done) precisely to make project state legible. Each transition produces a minimum viable event (futon-theory/minimum-viable-events) that downstream consumers can reason about. Abandonment without state transition violates both: it suppresses the event and makes the state illegible. The loud-failure pattern (futon-theory/loud-failure) applies identically — errors must surface at the layer that caused them, whether that layer is a runtime process or a development project. futon3 git log, three subsystems: Forum (built and abandoned): - 4846339: "Implement Forum service for multi-agent proof trees" (initial build) - 02b5257: "Fix forum WebSocket ClassCastException" (first integration failure) - 17c87b7: "Fix Agency session handling and forum dispatch" (second fix) - a346d27: "save" (final commit — bare save with no context) 8 total commits. No mission status update. No PAR. No :blocked transition. M-agency-forum.md lists 9 success criteria including "Proof structure: Threads form valid proof trees" — none completed, none marked blocked. PAR bell (parallel-to-sequential retreat): - 9d76e88: "feat(par): Bell-based PAR architecture for remote agents" (designed for parallelism) - 7fda538: "fix(par-bell): Run agents sequentially for cross-reading" (forced sequential) - 6 subsequent fix commits (IPv6, hardcoded agents, failure tolerance, timeouts, CRDT cleanup) M-par-session-punctuation.md: 1 of 8 checkboxes completed. No :blocked transition for the remaining 7. IRC/MUSN bridge (perpetual fix cycle): - 270061d: "Improve IRC-MUSN bridge stability" (stability grind begins) - 14+ subsequent fix commits: auth handling, polling timeouts, multi-room support, sanitizer added then removed, prompt tightened, rate limiting, deduplication No exit criteria defined. No mission document. No convergence milestone. Mechanic, in short: Derived from futon-theory via: - mission-lifecycle: explicit state transitions -> abandoned subsystems must transition to :blocked or :parked - mission-scoping: bounded ownership with exit conditions -> exit conditions must be evaluated, not ignored - loud-failure: errors surface at the causing layer -> project-level failures must be as visible as runtime failures - minimum-viable-events: log decision points, not surveillance -> a blocking failure is a decision point Audit futon3c missions monthly. Any subsystem with no commits for 2+ weeks and no :blocked or :parked status transition indicates the pattern is not holding. Record violations as tension observations for the L1 glacial loop.

title: Scope-Bounded Agent Handoff
text: Scope-Bounded Agent Handoff When handing off work to another agent, the task must declare which artifacts are writable (scope-out) and which are read-only inputs (scope-in). The receiving agent's output must be validated against the declared scope before acceptance. Constraint-timescale artifacts (exotype diagrams, pattern library, mission specs) are NEVER writable from the task timescale — this is I4 (exogeneity) applied to agent coordination. You are coordinating work across multiple agents (human, Claude, Codex, etc.) operating at potentially different timescales. Each agent receives a task with inputs and produces outputs. Some inputs are constraint inputs (slow-changing artifacts that govern how work is done); others are mutable working state. A task is handed off to an agent with a clear intent ("implement compose-parallel") and input artifacts (social-exotype.edn, coordination-exotype.edn, M-diagram-composition.md) that the agent needs to read but not modify. Without structural scope enforcement, the agent may modify input artifacts to make its task easier. This is not malice — it is the natural behavior of an optimization process encountering resistance. If the tests pass with a modified input, the agent has no signal that something is wrong. The modification may discard theoretical grounding, requirement traceability, or structural properties that the original author spent significant effort establishing. - Silent input rewrite: Agent modifies a constraint artifact to make tests pass. The modification discards theoretical grounding that isn't visible in the tests (requirement traceability, structural comments, gate duality mapping). The test suite is green but the artifact has regressed. - Scope creep cascade: Agent modifies one file outside scope, which creates inconsistencies with files it didn't modify, prompting further modifications. The original 1-file task becomes a 54-file diff. - Convention collapse: When one agent ignores scope conventions without consequence, the convention becomes unenforceable for all agents. The lack of structural enforcement is itself a coordination failure. 1. Every task handoff must declare :task/scope with explicit :in (read-only) and :out (writable) file sets. 2. Constraint-timescale artifacts (:constraint true in the wiring diagram, or exotype-level documents) are always :in, never :out, for task-timescale agents. 3. The review gate (G1 or a new scope-check gate) must verify that the agent's diff falls within :out. Changes to :in files are rejected, not merely flagged. 4. If the agent discovers that the :in artifacts need modification, the correct response is a gap-PSR documenting what needs to change and why — NOT silently modifying the artifact. This is I4 (preference exogeneity) applied at the social timescale. In wiring diagrams, I4 says "no fast-timescale output can reach a constraint input." In agent coordination, I4 says "no task-timescale agent can modify a constraint-timescale artifact." The invariant is the same; only the domain of application changes. The agent-contract pattern (futon-theory/agent-contract) requires agents to "respect invariants." But "respect" via convention fails when the agent is an optimization process without domain understanding of the invariant's purpose. Structural enforcement — where the system rejects out-of-scope changes — is the only reliable mechanism. You cannot instruct an agent to be careful; you can only make the careful path the only path. futon5 feat/compose-parallel branch (commit a5ea168), Codex review 2026-02-10: - Task: "Extend ct/mission.clj for parallel diagram composition" (GitHub issue #2) - Declared scope: ct/mission.clj + new test file + timescale extension - Actual diff: 54 files changed, including: * social-exotype.edn rewritten from scratch (Part I artifact, 301 lines -> 125 lines) * M-diagram-composition.md gutted (164 lines -> 47 lines, failure evidence lost) * healthcheck.clj deleted (outside task scope entirely) - Impact: Gate duality (C6) mapping lost, ARGUMENT requirement traceability lost, I2 modeling lost, mode classification flows lost, structural comments lost - Root cause: No structural scope enforcement. Agent optimized for "tests pass" without constraint on which artifacts could be modified. - Recorded as 3 coordination tensions in futon3b proof-path store: T1: artifact-ownership-violation (path-5e83a3f4-7) T2: scope-enforcement-gap (path-ec25edc6-e) T3: social-i4-violation (path-a07f56ac-8) Mechanic, in short: Derived from futon-theory via: - I4 (exogeneity): constraint inputs not writable from fast timescale -> constraint artifacts not writable from task-timescale agents - agent-contract: "respect invariants" + "observe before act" -> observe scope declaration before acting on artifacts - single-source-of-truth: one authority per artifact -> artifact ownership must be declared and enforced - proof-path: auditable chain -> scope violations must be detectable in the proof-path (the diff IS evidence) 1. Add :task/scope {:in [...] :out [...]} to TaskSpec shape (futon3b shapes.clj) 2. Add scope-check to G1 or introduce G1.5 scope gate 3. Update bootstrap.clj submit! to require explicit :out declaration 4. For the immediate Codex hand-off: restore social-exotype.edn from main, update :fast -> :social, re-run compose-parallel tests 5. Future: L1 observer needs social-timescale scan criteria (current scans only detect task-timescale tensions)

title: Specify Invariants Before Writing the Code They Constrain
text: Specify Invariants Before Writing the Code They Constrain Invariant proof tests must be written before the implementation they constrain. Invariants discovered during a rebuild are evidence that the tension-observation loop was not running — they have the same information content as proactive specifications, but the retroactive path pays the cost of building, debugging, and discarding code that violates them. You are building a coordination layer that must uphold distributed-system guarantees: delivery receipts, single routing authority, atomic state transitions, loud failure propagation, and bounded resource lifecycles. The system is built feature-first — bells, pages, registries, kick endpoints, session tracking — with correctness properties assumed to hold implicitly through careful coding. Without explicit invariants specified upfront, each successive generation discovers violations that were present from the start. The "rebuild" that fixes them is a confession that retroactively names what should have been preconditions. This turns development into an unbounded cycle: build features -> discover violations -> confess invariants -> rebuild -> discover new violations. Agency went through three generations of this cycle before achieving invariant coverage. - Confession-driven rebuild: each generation's commit messages explicitly name the bugs of the previous ("eliminate catch _ nil", "no silent corruption", "non-nil continuity"), but only after the buggy code has been built and deployed - Invariant debt compounding: A0 (delivery) violations mask A3 (loud failure) violations which mask A5 (bounded lifecycle) violations; fixing one reveals the next, extending the rebuild indefinitely - False completion: a subsystem is declared "done" (M-agency-unified-routing) but the done state hides invariant violations that the next mission (M-agency-rebuild) must discover from scratch Write invariant proof tests first, as failing tests that define the boundary conditions. Derive the implementation from what the tests require. Treat any invariant discovered during implementation (rather than before it) as a tension observation: record it, but also ask why the structural-tension-as-observation loop did not detect it earlier. The structural-tension-as-observation pattern (futon-theory) defines three detection criteria: structural irritation (recurring gaps), pre-symbolic pressure (repeated early failures), and trans-situational reappearance (same pattern across contexts). All five Agency invariant violations (A0-A5) exhibited all three criteria across two generations of code before they were named. The observation loop existed in theory; it was not running in practice. Writing tests first forces the loop to run. futon3 git log, Agency subsystem, three generations: Generation 1-2 (no invariant tests): - ad6bea1: "feat(agency): bell ack flow + stable codex drawbridge" - 01d0d93: "feat(agency): Add /agency/page endpoint for sync agent requests" - 84ac0e0: "Add unified agent registry for Agency" - 92fe6a1: "feat(agency): Track session IDs for connected agents" 4 major features built without A0-A5 proof tests. Phase 1 (invariants named, tests written): - 588a468: "Phase 1: invariant proof tests (A0-A5) + integration tests" Result: 18 test failures documented. All five invariants violated. Phase 2 (confessions): - 5f85287: "Phase 2: A0 — explicit delivery receipts for bells/whistles" - c5b5929: "Phase 2: A1 — enforce single routing authority across stores" - 3f0aa3a: "Phase 2: A3 — loud failure status checks + eliminate catch _ nil" - 804fe8f: "Phase 2: A2 — atomic state (no silent corruption, atomic writes, non-nil continuity)" - 5dcb28b: "Phase 2: A5 — bounded lifecycle (acks bound, TTL enforced, disconnect cascades)" 5 commits, one per invariant. Each commit message is a confession: the feature it fixes was built without the property it enforces. Mechanic, in short: Derived from futon-theory via: - structural-tension-as-observation: the three criteria (irritation, pressure, reappearance) detect invariant gaps if the loop is running -> write tests that embody the criteria before code - retroactive-canonicalization: the Baldwin cycle (NAMING -> SELECTION -> CANALIZATION) applies to invariants: name them, select the ones that recur, canalize them as tests -> but doing this retroactively means you already paid the build cost - stop-the-line: when invariants fail, block APPLY_CHANGE -> tests-first is stop-the-line applied to development, not just runtime For each futon3c subsystem, track whether invariant proof tests were committed before or after the implementation they constrain. A ratio below 0.5 (tests-first / total invariant tests) indicates the pattern is not holding.

title: Verify Each Component Before Composing It With Others
text: Verify Each Component Before Composing It With Others Each namespace in a multi-agent coordination system must load cleanly and pass its own proof tests before being composed with others. The proof-path discipline (OBSERVE -> VERIFY at each step) applies to the development process itself, not only to runtime evidence. You are building a real-time coordination system with multiple interoperating subsystems (agent registry, message routing, session management, bridge scripts) that will be composed into a single running process. Components are designed as coherent architectural units — a registry, a proof-tree forum, a bell/whistle protocol — and written to match a design specification. Code written to match a design document without incremental load-and-test accumulates latent errors (unresolved forward declarations, namespace ordering, type mismatches) that only surface when integration is attempted. At that point the debugging cost is multiplicative: each broken dependency interacts with every other, and the developer cannot tell whether a failure is in their code or in a dependency they assumed worked. - Load-order cascade: namespace A requires B which requires C, but C was never loaded independently; a typo in C surfaces only when A is loaded, and the error message points at A - Forward-declaration debt: 5+ forward-declaration fix commits indicate a systematic habit of writing code as design documents rather than testable units - Integration surprise: components that individually appear complete fail on first real composition because internal assumptions (atom state, protocol shape, identifier semantics) were never checked across boundaries Require each namespace to compile and load before adding the next dependency. Write a minimal smoke test (can I call each public function without exception?) before composing namespaces. Treat a forward-declaration fix as a bug report against the development process, not a normal commit. The event-protocol pattern (futon-theory/event-protocol) requires OBSERVE before PROPOSE_CLAIM and VERIFY before the next step; applying this same discipline to development means you cannot claim a namespace works (PROPOSE_CLAIM) without first loading it (OBSERVE) and checking its public API (VERIFY). Forward declarations are evidence that PROPOSE_CLAIM preceded OBSERVE. futon3 git log, agency and drawbridge subsystems: - f3044aa: "fix(agency): Add forward declaration for agent-sessions" - adc8d67: "fix(agency): Add forward declaration for kick-agent!" - 2da227e: "Fix defonce syntax in registry.clj" - 1542b0a: "fix(drawbridge): Add forward declaration for handle-par-bell!" - 6010d79: "Fix: add connect-irc! to forward declarations in drawbridge" 5 instances across 2 subsystems. Each commit fixes a function that was called before it was defined, meaning the namespace was never loaded between writing the call site and writing the function. This is systematic, not incidental. Mechanic, in short: Derived from futon-theory via: - event-protocol: OBSERVE -> VERIFY at each step -> verify each namespace at each step - proof-path: auditable chain from intent to proof -> development commits form a proof path; untested code is an unverified link - agent-contract: "observe before act" -> load before compose Count forward-declaration fixes in futon3c's git history after the first 30 commits. If the count exceeds 1, the pattern is not being followed and should be discussed in the next PAR.

title: Adapter Pattern
text: Adapter Pattern 以轉接器在不改動既有介面的前提下完成整合。 A component must integrate with a dependency that has an incompatible interface. You want to avoid rewriting the dependency or polluting core logic with conversions. Directly sprinkling translation code across callers causes duplication and brittle coupling. Create a dedicated adapter that translates between the expected interface and the dependency’s interface, and keep the adapter as the only integration boundary. A single translation boundary isolates change and preserves clean contracts. - Add contract tests around the adapter to prove compatibility and catch upstream changes. - evidence-shape: {:adapter/name :string, :adapter/src :string, :adapter/dst :string, :adapter/tests [:string]}

title: Agent Command Pattern
text: Agent Command Pattern Encapsulate every such operation as a Command value that carries `:id`, parameters, provenance, capability tags, and optional `undo!`, and run it only through an execution pipeline (local worker, remote service, or threaded pool). Commands can be persisted, reordered, decorated, and routed to specialised executors such as a git agent or math agent. You are defining a reliable execution pipeline for agent actions. Agents perform repo scans, graph updates, and external API calls by invoking ad hoc functions with no shared interface, so actions cannot be queued, audited, or retried safely. Higher-layer orchestration needs side-effectful work to travel through queues, logs, schedulers, and undo ledgers without each caller reinventing a protocol. Encapsulate every such operation as a Command value that carries `:id`, parameters, provenance, capability tags, and optional `undo!`, and run it only through an execution pipeline (local worker, remote service, or threaded pool). Commands can be persisted, reordered, decorated, and routed to specialised executors such as a git agent or math agent. A uniform command abstraction gives the stack a shared action language: histories become replayable, undo/redo is tractable, thread pools can execute arbitrary work safely, and schedulers can move labour across machines without touching implementation internals. next[Log one concrete instance of this pattern in the futon3 ledger.]

title: Agent Decorator Pattern
text: Agent Decorator Pattern Wrap commands or strategies with Decorators—`LoggedCommand`, `TimedCommand`, `SynchronizedCommand`, `RetryingStrategy`, `PermissionCheckingDecorator`—that add behaviour before/after delegation while preserving the base interface. Apply decorators where work enters a queue or worker so meta-behaviour lives at the edge, not deep inside each action. You are standardizing cross-cutting behaviors around agent actions. Commands and strategies already exist but every implementation hand-sprinkles logging, timing, locks, retries, permission checks, or paramitā/orb updates across the codebase. Cross-cutting concerns duplicated across dozens of commands quickly drift, complicate reviews, and break under concurrency. Wrap commands or strategies with Decorators—`LoggedCommand`, `TimedCommand`, `SynchronizedCommand`, `RetryingStrategy`, `PermissionCheckingDecorator`—that add behaviour before/after delegation while preserving the base interface. Apply decorators where work enters a queue or worker so meta-behaviour lives at the edge, not deep inside each action. Decorators let the agent stack layer observability, safety, and stewardship concerns without touching the business logic, so logging can be switched on globally, permission checks stay consistent, and concurrency guards become reusable armour around any command. next[Log one concrete instance of this pattern in the futon3 ledger.]

title: Agent Pattern Triad — Intent to Execution
text: Agent Pattern Triad — Intent to Execution Make the pipeline explicit: intent parsing emits Commands, a SchedulingStrategy selects the next move, and decorators (logging, timing, synchronisation, permission checks, orb tracking) wrap each command before worker threads call `execute!`. Document this flow with diagrams and a toy agent lab so newcomers can trace how intent, policy, and meta-behaviour interact. You are teaching the command/strategy/decorator triad for agent systems. Students and maintainers often encounter Command, Strategy, and Decorator as isolated textbook animals, so multi-agent architectures feel like a zoo with no wiring diagram. FUTON stacks already rely on commands to carry work, strategies to choose policies, and decorators to enforce cross-cutting rules; failing to name the triad keeps the system opaque. Make the pipeline explicit: intent parsing emits Commands, a SchedulingStrategy selects the next move, and decorators (logging, timing, synchronisation, permission checks, orb tracking) wrap each command before worker threads call `execute!`. Document this flow with diagrams and a toy agent lab so newcomers can trace how intent, policy, and meta-behaviour interact. The Command/Strategy/Decorator triad turns “random agent code” into an explainable circuit—what gets done, how choices are made, and which protections wrap the work—so experimentation stays safe, reasoning stays legible, and multi-threaded agents behave predictably. next[Log one concrete instance of this pattern in the futon3 ledger.]

title: Agent Strategy Pattern
text: Agent Strategy Pattern Declare small Strategy protocols (`SummarisationStrategy/summarise`, `SchedulingStrategy/next-command`, `BackoffStrategy/next-delay`) and let the agent inject or swap concrete implementations at runtime. Configuration, prompts, or telemetry choose which strategy runs, and tests exercise strategies in isolation before the agent consumes them. You are defining how an agent selects policies or moves. An agent repeatedly faces the same class of decision—summarise, schedule, pick a timeout, select a solver—yet the codebase is littered with `if`/`case` branches or feature flags that mutate behaviour in opaque ways. Experimenting with new policies or tailoring behaviour per user, prototype, or futon becomes brittle when the “how” is fused to the agent core. Declare small Strategy protocols (`SummarisationStrategy/summarise`, `SchedulingStrategy/next-command`, `BackoffStrategy/next-delay`) and let the agent inject or swap concrete implementations at runtime. Configuration, prompts, or telemetry choose which strategy runs, and tests exercise strategies in isolation before the agent consumes them. Strategies separate intent (“summarise this log”) from method (“fast heuristic vs deep reasoning”), enabling safe experiments, per-context policy bundles, and cleaner reasoning about which solver is responsible for each outcome. next[Log one concrete instance of this pattern in the futon3 ledger.]

title: Facade Pattern
text: Facade Pattern 用單一門面對複雜子系統提供穩定入口。 A subsystem exposes many low-level calls that are hard to orchestrate. You want a simple, stable entry point without exposing internal complexity. Letting callers assemble the sequence leads to duplicated orchestration and fragile workflows. Create a facade that bundles the common orchestration into one high-level interface. A stable facade shields callers from churn in underlying components. - Define a minimal surface and keep the facade free of business policy; push policy to a dedicated layer. - evidence-shape: {:facade/name :string, :facade/entrypoints [:string], :facade/deps [:string]}

title: Observer Pattern
text: Observer Pattern 以訂閱機制解耦事件發布與處理。 Multiple components need to react to state changes in a subject. You want to avoid tight coupling or hard-coded call chains. Direct calls lock in dependencies and make extensions expensive. Introduce a subject that publishes events to observers registered for specific signals. The publisher remains stable while observers evolve independently. - Track observer lifetimes to avoid leaks; test that events fire once per change. - evidence-shape: {:observer/subject :string, :observer/events [:string], :observer/subscribers [:string]}

title: Proxy Pattern
text: Proxy Pattern 以代理物件在不改動本體的情況下控制存取或行為。 A target object requires access control, caching, or remote indirection. You need the same interface but want to add cross-cutting behavior. Modifying the target mixes concerns and complicates testing. Introduce a proxy that implements the same interface and delegates to the target while applying the extra behavior. The proxy isolates policy while preserving substitutability. - Verify proxy and target are interface-compatible; test both cache hits and pass-through paths. - evidence-shape: {:proxy/name :string, :proxy/target :string, :proxy/policy [:string]}

title: State Pattern
text: State Pattern 以狀態物件封裝行為轉換，避免龐大分支邏輯。 An object changes its behavior based on internal state over time. You want to avoid sprawling conditional logic inside the main object. Centralized branching becomes brittle as new states are added. Represent each state as its own object and delegate behavior to the active state. State-specific logic stays localized and transitions become explicit. - Define a transition table and test invalid transitions explicitly. - evidence-shape: {:state/machine :string, :state/variants [:string], :state/transitions [:string]}

title: Commit Intent Alignment
text: Commit Intent Alignment correlate commit messages/PRs with devmap IDs; for each match, update the clause status + evidence ledger; if a clause stays marked “planned” despite recent commits, flag it as `drift` and prompt someone to reconcile You need to ensure that actual development work reflected in commits and PRs stays aligned with work plans as both code and plans evolve. git commits reference a prototype or futon clause (“Prototype 4 done”, “stack blocker cleared”) while the devmap still lists it as planned/blocked that disconnect makes the roadmap lie about where energy went correlate commit messages/PRs with devmap IDs; for each match, update the clause status + evidence ledger; if a clause stays marked “planned” despite recent commits, flag it as `drift` and prompt someone to reconcile viriya is kinetic practice—commits and devmaps must reflect the same movement or we lose trust in both next[Add a nightly scan that correlates commits/PRs with devmap IDs and updates evidence.] next[Flag any clause still marked planned after matching commits for reconciliation.]

title: Stack Evidence Ledger
text: Stack Evidence Ledger scan READMEs, git logs, and test artifacts for references to that clause; if none exist, mark the clause `unsupported` and emit a TODO to capture the evidence; otherwise record `evidence[link]` You need to ensure that any planned work that is claimed to be done is sufficiently evidenced by concrete artifacts, or revered to a non-done state if they can't be found. a devmap clause (any futon) claims a prototype is “done” or “stable” there is no pointer to concrete evidence (README section, tag, test fixture, commit) proving it scan READMEs, git logs, and test artifacts for references to that clause; if none exist, mark the clause `unsupported` and emit a TODO to capture the evidence; otherwise record `evidence[link]` dhammavicaya isn’t vibes—claims must cite reproducible proofs or they drift into fiction next[Anchor the codebook/transcripts task in traceable artifacts and evidence links.]

title: Futon Bridge Health Check
text: Futon Bridge Health Check for each declared cross-futon bridge (f1→f2, f2→f3, f3→f4, etc.), verify the bridge artifact exists, is callable, and returns expected data; emit health report per bridge with status, latency, and last-verified timestamp The FUTON stack depends on bridges between layers — adapters, exports, APIs, shared schemas. Bridge failures silently break coordination. futons declare dependencies on upstream layers ("uses futon1 graph memory", "receives futon2 pivot streams", "calls futon3 portal") bridge health is rarely tested explicitly; a broken bridge manifests as mysterious downstream failures rather than a clear "bridge X is down" for each declared cross-futon bridge (f1→f2, f2→f3, f3→f4, etc.), verify the bridge artifact exists, is callable, and returns expected data; emit health report per bridge with status, latency, and last-verified timestamp f0→f3a: vitality telemetry → futon3a morning review f1→f2: graph memory → pivot stream context f1→f3: graph memory → pattern store sync f2→f3: pivot streams → proof trails f3→f3a: pattern canon → portal queries f3a→f0: audit logs → vitality dashboard f3→f4: proof trails → Arxana nodes f4→f5: GravPad → concentration practices f5→f6: ledgers → Hyperreal entries f3→f6: vetted patterns → argumentarium f2,f3,f5,f6→f7: all artifacts → civic field dhammavicaya requires knowing what exists — bridges are the connective tissue of the stack, and their health must be observable, not assumed next[Create a bridge registry listing each declared bridge with its health check method.] next[Run bridge health checks weekly; log failures as stack blockers.] next[Add bridge status to futon3a morning review digest.]

title: Futon1 Determinism Gate
text: Futon1 Determinism Gate rely on the `Futon1 Deterministic Stack` GitHub Action (`futon1/.github/workflows/futon1-stack-tests.yml`) or run the suites manually (`cd futon1/apps/client && clojure -M:test`, `cd apps/graph-memory && clojure -M:test -m cognitect.test-runner`, `cd apps/nlp-interface && clojure -M:test`). When any leg fails, regenerate `resources/baseline/demo_session.edn` via `clojure -M:baseline/snapshot --write ...` or fix the regression before advancing futons that depend on storage/NLP determinism You want CI assured enforcement that client, storage, and NLP components remain deterministic under shared test and baseline suites. FUTON1’s Prototype 0–1 guarantees hinge on `apps/client` emitting the canonical Willie/Jane focus-header + XTDB mirrors that promise drifts unless we check the determinism suite whenever the stack changes rely on the `Futon1 Deterministic Stack` GitHub Action (`futon1/.github/workflows/futon1-stack-tests.yml`) or run the suites manually (`cd futon1/apps/client && clojure -M:test`, `cd apps/graph-memory && clojure -M:test -m cognitect.test-runner`, `cd apps/nlp-interface && clojure -M:test`). When any leg fails, regenerate `resources/baseline/demo_session.edn` via `clojure -M:baseline/snapshot --write ...` or fix the regression before advancing futons that depend on storage/NLP determinism dhammavicaya keeps the substrate honest—the focus-header fixture, graph-memory schema tests, and NLP pipeline fixtures are the shared proof artifacts, so stack-coherence loops must treat a red CI badge (or failing local run) as a blocking condition for Prototype 1 duties next[Run the determinism suite on each stack change and log the outcome in evidence.] next[Regenerate the baseline snapshot or fix regressions before advancing dependent futons.]

title: Futon1 Storage Coherence Guard
text: Futon1 Storage Coherence Guard keep Futon1 storage coherent by enforcing Charon-guarded invariant checks on every write, requiring a penholder registry entry for each model descriptor, and bootstrapping the penholder registry before first write to a new data dir Futon1 graph memory restores from XTDB or legacy events, then immediately enforces model invariants on startup and on every write. `app.store/tx!` runs a verify function on a preview conn and rejects writes when invariants fail, and `app.store-manager` installs the Charon guardian when `MODEL_VERIFY_ON_WRITE` is enabled new or swapped `BASIC_CHAT_DATA_DIR` roots can be missing penholder registry entries, and missing `MODEL_PENHOLDER` values make authorization fail on the very first model descriptor upsert penholder missing entry -> invariant failure on first descriptor write unauthorized penholder -> reject writes until registry updated shared data dir across JVMs -> nondeterministic invariants and corruption always enable `MODEL_VERIFY_ON_WRITE` in production, set `MODEL_PENHOLDER`, and run `scripts.charon-penholder-bootstrap` (or equivalent) once per new data root before starting the API; keep `BASIC_CHAT_DATA_DIR` isolated per running JVM `apps/graph-memory/src/app/store.clj`: `tx!` forbids `:skip-verify?`, verifies against a preview conn, and throws on invariant failure `apps/graph-memory/src/app/store_manager.clj`: installs `charon-guard/guard-event`, ensures descriptors, and checks invariants at startup `apps/graph-memory/src/app/invariants.clj`: `verify-event` enforces penholder registry membership for model descriptors `apps/graph-memory/src/scripts/charon_penholder_bootstrap.clj`: seeds the penholder registry with model descriptor entries BASIC_CHAT_DATA_DIR: data root (unique per JVM) MODEL_PENHOLDER: identity used for penholder certificates (e.g. user) MODEL_VERIFY_ON_WRITE: enable Charon guard on every write (default true) XTDB_CONFIG: path to XTDB config for canonical store the Charon guard provides deterministic rejection of invalid writes, and the penholder registry ensures every model descriptor is authorized and signed before it can mutate the store next[Add a bootstrap hook in dev scripts to seed penholder registry on empty data dirs.] next[Surface penholder/invariant failures as explicit stack blockers in triage logs.]

title: Maturity Evidence Audit
text: Maturity Evidence Audit for each prototype with a :maturity tag, verify that evidence supports the claimed level; flag mismatches and emit promotion or demotion recommendations Prototypes claim maturity levels (:stub, :greenfield, :active, :settled) but these claims can drift from reality. devmap prototypes carry :maturity tags indicating their readiness level maturity claims are often aspirational — a prototype tagged :active may have failing tests, and one tagged :stub may actually be running in production for each prototype with a :maturity tag, verify that evidence supports the claimed level; flag mismatches and emit promotion or demotion recommendations :stub claims valid if: no runnable implementation exists :greenfield claims valid if: code exists but no end-to-end test evidence :active claims valid if: runs end-to-end, has 3+ logged uses, PSR/PUR evidence :settled claims valid if: 10+ uses, >80% success rate, no regressions in 2 weeks over-claimed (e.g., :active but no evidence) → demote and flag for attention under-claimed (e.g., :stub but has passing tests) → recommend promotion no-tag (missing :maturity) → flag for classification maturity tags are trust signals — downstream consumers decide what to depend on based on claimed maturity, so false claims cause silent breakage next[Run maturity audit on all devmap prototypes; generate mismatch report.] next[Add :maturity tags to any prototype missing them.] next[Wire maturity changes into sidecar logs for audit trail.] next[Review maturity mismatches in weekly stack triage.]

title: README ⇄ Devmap Sync
text: README ⇄ Devmap Sync diff README sections vs devmap clauses—names, statuses, evidence—and emit `mismatch[...]` reports so someone refreshes whichever side is lying Public-facing READMEs and internal devmaps need to suitably synchronized so that prototype names, statuses, and evidence do not diverge between narrative and planning layers. top-level READMEs tell the stack story they often drift away from the actual devmaps (missing prototypes, stale statuses) diff README sections vs devmap clauses—names, statuses, evidence—and emit `mismatch[...]` reports so someone refreshes whichever side is lying the README is the public proof sketch; if it diverges from the devmap, nobody knows what is actually done or blocked next[Schedule a README↔devmap diff pass each release cycle and log mismatches.] next[Resolve mismatches by updating the source of truth and noting the change.]

title: Ready/Blocked/Triage Classifier
text: Ready/Blocked/Triage Classifier for each clause, inspect evidence (README links, commits, tests) and blockers; emit a status report `status[done|ready|blocked|drift] blocked-by[...] evidence[...]` You want a uniform classification of each devmap clause (done, ready, blocked, drift) to be derivable from logged evidence and blockers, so that implicit progress states are explicit and comparable. every devmap clause should be either ready, blocked, drifting, or done we rarely log that status explicitly for each clause, inspect evidence (README links, commits, tests) and blockers; emit a status report `status[done|ready|blocked|drift] blocked-by[...] evidence[...]` knowing the state of each obligation is the core of informal proofkeeping next[Run this classifier on each devmap clause and attach status, blockers, and evidence.] next[Review drift/blocked items weekly to keep triage current.]

title: Stack Blocker Detection
text: Stack Blocker Detection scan devmaps for declared dependencies, inspect referenced dirs/tests/commits, and emit a blocker report for each clause: `blocked-by[...]`, `evidence[...]`, `status[ready/not-ready]` You want to be able to track unmet dependencies between projects, prototypes and components by inspecting downstream artifacts, so lack of progress is clearly attributed to specific blockers. a futon layer or prototype declares prerequisites (“requires futon3 prototype 8”, “needs graph-memory adapter”), yet the downstream directory/README is still empty without explicit blocker reports, emptiness reads as “nobody cares” instead of “waiting on X/Y” scan devmaps for declared dependencies, inspect referenced dirs/tests/commits, and emit a blocker report for each clause: `blocked-by[...]`, `evidence[...]`, `status[ready/not-ready]` dhammavicaya means naming what already exists—and what is still blocking it—so we don’t conflate “not started” with “stalled” next[Scan devmaps for declared prerequisites and emit blocker reports with evidence links.] next[Review blockers weekly and mark readiness once dependencies land.]

title: Staleness Scan
text: Staleness Scan compare timestamps (git log, last edited dates) to linked clauses; flag anything older than the freshness window and prompt a refresh with pointers to the newest artifacts You need to detect when devmaps, READMEs, or status notes lag behind recent work by comparing timestamps, and create timely updates, lest outdated narratives mislead readers. a README, devmap clause, or status note hasn’t been updated in N days while linked clauses/commits mention new work we rarely notice that those narratives are stale until someone new gets lost compare timestamps (git log, last edited dates) to linked clauses; flag anything older than the freshness window and prompt a refresh with pointers to the newest artifacts keeping the prose synchronized with the proof is part of coherence—otherwise the map lies while the territory shifts next[Use this pattern to drive the audit of drives and linodes for stale or missing artifacts.]

title: All-Or-Nothing Startup
text: All-Or-Nothing Startup require full rehydration and integrity checks to pass before the system starts serving futon1 needed startup diagnostics and integrity checks to prevent partial or inconsistent state. rehydration can proceed partially or with silent warnings hidden inconsistencies surface later and require reactive repairs gate startup on full rehydration success and emit precise diagnostics on failure futon1 fixes show partial startup is a recurring source of drift next[Define the exact rehydration checklist and failure modes for futon1a.] next[Add a startup test that fails fast on incomplete rehydration.]

title: Canonical Interface
text: Canonical Interface expose a minimal, stable HTTP interface as the canonical way to query and update the persistent store without internal coupling futon1’s devmap defines the HTTP API as the canonical interface for external tools. external tools must query/update storage without embedding internals unstable interfaces force clients to copy internal assumptions or scrape CLI output keep a documented HTTP surface as the primary contract for persistence operations canonical interfaces let higher futons depend on storage without tight coupling next[Define the minimal API surface for futon1a and its evolution protocol.] next[Add compatibility tests to ensure response stability across versions.]

title: Determinism vs Feature Expansion
text: Determinism vs Feature Expansion if you want new features but also deterministic behavior, isolate expansions behind determinism gates and tests futon1 fixed determinism gate baselines while adding ingestion features. you want to add new ingestion or modeling features determinism must remain intact across environments require determinism gates and regression tests for any feature expansion un-gated expansion breaks reproducibility and undermines the storage substrate next[Define determinism gates for each ingest or model pipeline.] next[Add fixtures that must remain invariant across versions.]

title: Deterministic Ingest Pipeline
text: Deterministic Ingest Pipeline provide deterministic ingestion (tokenise → tag → chunk → recognise) so graph construction is reproducible futon1’s devmap defines a deterministic NLP interface as the foundation for ingest. ingest depends on text processing and recognition stages non-deterministic NLP yields irreproducible graph states formalize the pipeline stages and require deterministic outputs in tests reproducible ingest is required for a deterministic storage substrate next[Document the pipeline as a public API with input/output shapes.] next[Add fixtures that must pass identically across environments.]

title: Deterministic Storage Substrate
text: Deterministic Storage Substrate provide a deterministic, storage-oriented substrate that maintains a coherent graph of facts across sessions futon1’s devmap defines the substrate as deterministic and storage-first, not a session cache. storage is required to outlive sessions and remain consistent across restarts without a deterministic substrate, the graph drifts across runs and environments treat persistence + determinism as the defining product, not a secondary feature the futon1 series exists to make the same world state appear reliably across sessions next[Define determinism tests that compare world state across restart cycles.] next[Document the minimal substrate contract that other futons depend on.]

title: Durability First
text: Durability First block success responses on durable storage confirmation; fail loudly when durability cannot be verified futon1 repeatedly needed explicit durability enforcement and watchdog ordering fixes. writes can return before XTDB durability is confirmed the system accumulates repair debt and inconsistent reads after restarts make Layer 0 a hard gate: acknowledge writes only after durable commit and raise a clear error otherwise durability drift caused repeated fixes and remains a root invariant for futon1a evidence[futon1a/src/futon1a/core/xtdb.clj:durable-write! requires non-nil write-fn unless allow-noop?] next[Define the exact XTDB durability wait/timeout semantics for futon1a Layer 0.] next[Add a proof test that a write is not acknowledged before the durable commit.]

title: Durability Throughput Gate
text: Durability Throughput Gate if you want throughput but also durable truth, gate responses on durable commit and instrument watchdogs with deterministic ordering futon1 added durable proof and watchdogs, then fixed ordering to avoid false confidence. you want throughput and responsive writes you also need durable confirmation and watchdog safety block success responses on durable commit and treat watchdog ordering as an invariant durability drift and watchdog misordering caused repeated fixes and risked silent corruption next[Specify watchdog ordering rules and test for stalled XTDB detection.] next[Record durable proof events in write audit logs.]

title: Error Layer Hierarchy
text: Error Layer Hierarchy surface errors at the layer that caused them; never allow upstream layers to mask lower-layer failures authorization and invariants needed explicit guards to prevent silent bypass. errors are raised at a higher layer than the failure source or are generalized debugging slows and the wrong layer is “fixed,” while the real problem persists enforce an error hierarchy that maps failures to their originating layer with explicit codes futon1 fixes show that missing guardrails and mixed error ownership led to drift next[Define the layer-to-error-code table for futon1a and require it in API handlers.] next[Add tests that assert errors surface at the originating layer.]

title: Graph-Memory Contract
text: Graph-Memory Contract define a documented entity/relation schema and salience contract that downstream tools can depend on futon1’s devmap frames graph-memory as the core data model and interface. storage is the substrate for multiple futons and external tools without a schema contract, queries and ingest drift and become brittle publish and enforce a graph-memory schema and salience metadata contract downstream tools require stable shapes and semantics to rely on stored facts next[Extract the graph-memory schema into a dedicated reference doc.] next[Add schema-mirroring tests for entities, relations, and salience fields.]

title: Guardrails vs Internal Tooling
text: Guardrails vs Internal Tooling if you want internal tooling but also strong guardrails, force internal writers through the same authorization and invariant checks futon1 hardened penholder checks and charon guards after internal writer bypass risks. you want convenient internal scripts and writers you also need authorization and invariant enforcement to be universal route internal writers through the same guardrails as external API calls bypass vectors appear when internal tooling skips guards next[Add guard enforcement tests for internal scripts and batch ingests.] next[Document required penholder context for every writer entry point.]

title: Identity Flexibility vs Uniqueness
text: Identity Flexibility vs Uniqueness if you want flexible external IDs but also unique identity, coerce to UUIDs and reject duplicate external mappings before write futon1 enforced UUID IDs and external-id uniqueness to prevent duplicates. you want flexible external identifiers for integration you also need a single identity per entity accept external IDs only through a unique mapping and require UUIDs as the stored identity ambiguous externals created duplicate entities and long-term drift next[Define the external-id namespace rules and conflict handling.] next[Add tests that reject duplicate external-id usage across types.]

title: Identity Uniqueness
text: Identity Uniqueness enforce a single UUID per entity and a unique (source, external-id) mapping before any write duplicate entities emerged from ambiguous external IDs and non-UUID identifiers. the system permits duplicate external-id mappings or accepts non-UUID identifiers entity graphs drift and require expensive cleanup or repair scripts validate identity pre-write: reject duplicates and enforce UUIDs as the only entity IDs futon1 required explicit commits to prevent duplicate entities and enforce UUID/external-id uniqueness next[Specify the canonical external-id schema and its uniqueness constraint.] next[Add a proof test that duplicate (source, external-id) writes are rejected.]

title: Invariants vs Repair
text: Invariants vs Repair if you want strict invariants but also operational resilience, pair enforcement with explicit repair and backfill pathways futon1 expanded invariant enforcement and later added cleanup/backfill scripts to restore compliance. you want invariants to halt corruption real data requires recovery and cleanup workflows enforce invariants strictly and maintain documented repair scripts for recovery invariants without repair pathways stall operations and increase downtime next[Catalog repair scripts as part of the storage contract.] next[Add tests that validate repairs restore invariant compliance.]

title: Open-World Continuity
text: Open-World Continuity allow background knowledge ingest to accumulate in the same persistent store outside interactive sessions futon1’s devmap positions open-world ingest as a core way to build shared knowledge. knowledge needs to accumulate beyond interactive sessions separate stores or session-only ingestion fragment the graph ingest open-world data into the same persistent store with the same invariants background knowledge must remain queryable and coherent with session data next[Define open-world ingest contracts and validation rules for futon1a.] next[Add tests verifying open-world data survives restart and is queryable.]

title: Open-World Velocity vs Validation
text: Open-World Velocity vs Validation if you want rapid open-world ingest but also coherent state, validate aggressively and provide repair tooling futon1 hardened open-world ingest and added repair scripts after ingest drift. you want to ingest background knowledge quickly you also need open-world data to remain coherent and mirrorable enforce strict validation on ingest and supply repair/backfill scripts for recovery unvalidated open-world ingest caused drift and required repair pathways next[Define open-world validation rules and error reporting.] next[Add tests that assert open-world fields are mirrored into XTDB.]

title: Persistence-Speed Mirroring
text: Persistence-Speed Mirroring if you want durability but also fast access, mirror XTDB into Datascript and enforce reproducible alignment as a hard contract futon1 repeatedly fixed XTDB mirroring to prevent drift and metadata loss. you want the database to be persistent you also want access to be fast mirror XTDB into Datascript with explicit mirroring rules and tests mirroring without enforcement creates drift across restarts and environments next[Define the mirror invariants and verify them on every restart cycle.] next[Add tests that assert metadata parity between XTDB and Datascript.]

title: Postcommit Materialization Gate
text: Postcommit Materialization Gate acknowledge writes only after the canonical store is durably committed and the written documents are queryable (read-your-write) interactive QA found items (lyrics) present in futon1’s durable event log while missing from the queryable XTDB materialization; the user experience was “it was saved” but reads returned nothing. a write can be accepted/recorded without guaranteeing it becomes queryable in the canonical store event-log truth can diverge from canonical truth and the system will behave as if data is missing (often discovered only in interactive QA) gate success responses on both: 1) durable commit confirmation 2) postcommit materialization verification (the put docs can be read back by id) without a postcommit read-your-write gate, “accepted but not ingested/materialized” becomes a silent failure mode that accumulates repair debt and erodes trust in the storage contract next[Add an end-to-end QA checklist item: write -> immediate read-by-id -> restart -> read-by-id.] next[If an event log exists, specify it as audit-only unless a catch-up invariant proves “caught up” with canonical state.]

title: Rapid Debugging
text: Rapid Debugging make storage failures diagnosable in minutes through explicit diagnostics and proof tests futon1 repeatedly needed diagnostics and tests to keep storage behavior legible. failures lack traceable context (layer, operation, entity, expected vs actual) debugging requires ad hoc spelunking and slow recovery cycles attach explicit diagnostics to all storage errors and prove invariants with targeted tests futon1 fixes show that diagnostics and tests reduced drift and clarified failures next[Define the diagnostic payload shape required on all storage errors.] next[Add proof tests for each core invariant and store them in a dedicated suite.]

title: Reproducible Mirroring
text: Reproducible Mirroring keep Datascript (fast) and XTDB (persistent) in reproducible alignment so the same world state appears across restarts futon1’s devmap requires reproducible alignment between Datascript and XTDB. two storage representations exist for speed and durability misalignment yields drift and nondeterministic query results define and test mirroring rules so Datascript and XTDB represent the same state futon1’s coherence relies on consistent mirroring across restarts and environments next[Document the mirroring contract and which fields must align.] next[Add restart-cycle tests asserting mirror equivalence.]

title: Schema Evolution vs Contract Stability
text: Schema Evolution vs Contract Stability if you want schema evolution but also stable contracts, formalize migration rules and versioned descriptors futon1 introduced model registries and open-world invariants to stabilize schema evolution. you need to evolve the graph schema over time downstream tools require stable contracts and predictable migrations define explicit migration protocols and versioned model descriptors unmanaged schema change causes compatibility drift and broken clients next[Define schema versioning rules and migration checklists.] next[Add tests that assert compatibility across descriptor versions.]

title: Startup Integrity Gate
text: Startup Integrity Gate if you want fast availability but also integrity, gate startup on full rehydration and explicit diagnostics futon1 added XTDB sync and startup diagnostics to prevent stale state from serving. you want the system to start quickly you also need integrity and full rehydration correctness block startup until rehydration and invariant checks pass, and emit precise diagnostics on failure partial startup created hidden inconsistencies and required repairs next[Define the rehydration checklist and required diagnostics output.] next[Add failure-mode tests for incomplete rehydration.]

title: Backwards Induction and Forward Construction
text: Backwards Induction and Forward Construction The core capability this namespace is trying to make repeatable is a **pair of moves**, not a single question. Given an artefact, induce the problem it solves (**backwards pass**). Given a problem, propose the artefact shape that would solve it (**forward pass**). The pair together is what "finding ways into the heart of a problem" means operationally — as opposed to describing the artefact, reporting its features, or responding to its marketing. The backwards pass is diagnostic and interpretive. The forward pass is generative and commercial. Both are required for the capability to be useful; backwards alone is criticism, forward alone is guessing. The move shows up under different names across the futon stack: - **M-superpod-mark2** (futon6) — backwards: reconstruct a paper's problem-class from its technique vocabulary and argumentative skeleton, disregarding the author's stated framing where it diverges. Forward: forward model that takes a novel problem and proposes techniques + patterns + sketched construction. Four-layer output schema: stated problem, techniques deployed, reconstructed problem-class, stated-vs-reconstructed gap. - **M-ukrns-wp** — backwards: what problem does a working paper on training reproducibility actually solve? (Making training impact legible to institutions and regulators.) Forward: a WP that performs that legibility-production for the reader, rather than describing training impact as a topic. - **M-trip-journal** — backwards: what is the mission concept failing to do that the current apparatus addresses? (It doesn't guarantee operator-capacity development.) Forward: the hinge-log + question-pool + sidecar apparatus is structurally shaped to fill that specific gap. The pattern is the same; the domain and the artefact type change. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - Running only the backwards pass. This is criticism, not capability. Joe is not selling criticism. - Running only the forward pass. This is guessing at solutions without understanding the problem's actual shape. Produces artefacts that collapse under the reader's own backwards pass. - Taking the artefact's self-description as the problem. This is what M-superpod-mark2 explicitly refuses: "the paper is evidence, not testimony." - Treating the pair as a procedure. The pair is a capability, which means it has to be inhabited and developed, not executed. Cook Ting's blade, not the ordinary carver's. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. **Backwards:** 1. List what the artefact actually contains — techniques, vocabulary, argumentative moves, what it rejects, what it emphasises. Evidence loci, not summary. 2. Induce the problem these contents would tightly constrain. Prefer tighter constraint to broader accommodation. 3. Compare the induced problem to the artefact's stated framing. The gap is diagnostic — the sharper the gap, the more likely the real contribution differs from the stated one. **Forward:** 1. Take the problem-class (from the backwards pass, or from the operator's own situation) as the specification. 2. Propose an artefact shape whose contents would constrain to this problem-class under the backwards pass. 3. Check: would a reader doing the backwards pass on the proposed artefact arrive at the same problem-class? If not, the forward proposal is underspecified. **Backwards pass.** Given an artefact, derive the problem-class it actually solves — not the one it claims to solve. For papers this means reading technique vocabulary as a constraint on the solvability envelope. For missions it means reading the apparatus (code, structure, outputs) as a constraint on what is actually being addressed. For working papers it means reading the shape of the argument for what a reader could carry away. The backwards pass is done well when the induced problem constrains the artefact more tightly than the stated framing does. **Forward pass.** Given a problem-class, propose an artefact that would solve it. For papers this is the forward model: novel problem → proposed techniques → sketched construction. For missions it is: given the gap named at IDENTIFY, what apparatus has the shape that would close it? For working papers it is: given the legibility-production required, what argumentative structure would produce it in a reader? - At any hinge where an artefact is in hand and the operator is tempted to respond to the artefact's self-description rather than to what it actually does. - At any hinge where a problem is in hand and the operator is tempted to propose what comes to mind first rather than to specify the problem carefully before proposing. - At any hinge where two superficially-disjoint artefacts are sitting in the operator's work at once — check whether they actually solve the same problem under the backwards pass. This is how M-superpod-mark2 and M-trip-journal and M-ukrns-wp got recognised as sharing a core move on 2026-04-17. The backwards pass yields a specification that is not the artefact's own self-description. The forward pass can then produce new artefacts against that specification. Clients pay for the forward pass when their own forward pass is blocked — they have a problem but the artefact-space they can imagine is too narrow. What they cannot do is run the backwards pass on their own situation to generate a better specification; that's the skill. Selling the pair = selling the capacity to move between problem and artefact fluently in either direction. Making thinking legible-enough-to-teach requires making the moves explicit. This pair is the move the operator performs when the work goes well — in consulting pitches, in reviewing papers, in designing missions, in reading the stack's own artefacts. Naming the pair converts an implicit capability into a repeatable one. The operator-capacity-development loop M-trip-journal targets depends on having named moves to practise; this is one of them, and probably the most general. next[Apply the pair to at least one non-mission artefact (e.g., a paper, a competitor product, a client situation) and record the backwards/forward outputs in the relevant mission's sidecar] next[Watch for cases where the backwards pass finds the same problem across superficially disjoint artefacts — those are the edges to log in the connection graph] next[Track whether the forward pass, when run, actually produces artefacts that survive a second-party backwards pass. That is the capability's validation criterion.]

title: A Block Is One Revolution of the Futonic Loop
text: A Block Is One Revolution of the Futonic Loop A block is one full revolution of the futonic loop: 象 (input) → 部 (choose decomposition regime) → 咅 (articulate) → 鹽 (compose; ⿱ 鹵 皿) → 香 (sense) + 🔮 (regulate) → 未知 (act-within transitional state) → 味 (evaluate). The git commit is the 咅 → 鹽 step — articulation composing latent work (鹵) into durable substrate (皿) as a stable whole. Block boundaries are recognised at hinges (structure/cook-ting), not scheduled. The block is the smallest unit the operator can attest to and the system can record durably. Multiple framings converge on the same structural unit: - Bitcoin: a block is the miner-attested transaction set. - Clojure STM: a `dosync` body is one transaction. - Music: a bar (小節 / 節) is a unit of metrical structure — the music does not pause at bar lines, but the bar gives a framework for phrasing. - Futonic methodology: PSR → apply → PUR is one block-shaped revolution. All four frame the same shape: a coherent, attestable unit of transition between two stable states. Naming this convergence "block" lets the operator and the system reason about the same thing. The operator has been editing a working tree (or composing a mission section, or running a session, or otherwise doing futonic work), and a hinge appears. A block does not close at a fixed schedule, and not every commit is a complete block. A block-closure is complete only if all five phases have run: 1. **Identification** — the operator perceives the hinge. Cleavage in the work has become visible. (`structure/cook-ting`) 2. **Specification** — the included changes are nameable. The operator can say "this block contains X." Without specification, the commit message is vague. 3. **Elaboration** — the structure is articulated (commit message; optionally a wiring diagram, paired test, lab note). The block has a *shape* in addition to its content. 4. **Passion** — the work has been *done*. Embodied effort has been discharged. (Not a free closure; mana-allostasis requires the passion phase to award real, not counterfeit, mana.) 5. **Closure** — 鹽 forms: 鹵 (the latent work) and 皿 (the durable substrate) compose into a stable whole. The git commit lands. Skipping any phase produces a forced cut, dulling the blade (cook-ting). All five phases must be present for the revolution to count as one block. - **jj-style auto-commit**: every working-tree state is a change-id. Defeats the operator-attestation that defines a block. The operator's commit message — the 咅 — is what makes a block one block. - **"Commit early, commit often" as a rule**: a discipline-style injunction that forces cuts at non-hinges. Dulls the blade when applied uniformly; useful only when phrased as "perceive hinges actively, do not let blocks grow indefinite." - **One-commit-per-file**: each commit becomes a half-block; metrical structure breaks. The bar disappears. - **Closure without passion**: closing a block without the work-phase (rubber-stamp commits, automated formatters as "blocks", squash-merges of unfinished branches). Awards counterfeit mana; produces hollow consonance. Treat the block as the unit the system records. Pressure dissipates at block-closure, not at file-level commits. The operator's task is to perceive when a block is approaching completion through the five phases — not to manage individual file changes. A mission-phase transition (IDENTIFY → MAP, MAP → DERIVE, etc.) is a block closure. The phase output (the new section in the mission doc) is the 鹽 of that revolution. Mission docs across the stack already follow this rhythm; naming it "block-shaped" lets the invariant family reason about it uniformly. A working-tree block is the set of file changes the operator includes in `git commit -m "..."`. The commit message IS the block header. A block may produce 1+N commits if the operator splits its scope for clarity (e.g., the futon3c sweep on 2026-05-03 produced 9 commits inside what was conceptually one "clear all WIP" block); the block-id (in commit footer or git notes) binds the commits. Blocks compose with PSR/PUR cycles, mission-phase blocks, session-blocks, day-blocks, excursion-blocks. A single revolution of the futonic loop may be wholly contained within (e.g.) a session-block, or may span multiple session-blocks if the work is genuinely large. The block-id (when assigned) is the binding that holds the revolution coherent across its containers. - Commits are large and infrequent: hinges have been missed. Pressure rises; eventually a stop-the-line forces an awkward multi-block close. The "504 file commit" pattern. - Commits are tiny and constant: the operator is over-committing at non-hinges. Each commit is a half-formed 鹽; cumulative attention cost rises (mana drains via the *committing-itself* channel). - Commit messages are vague ("WIP", "fixes", "stuff"): 咅 (articulation) didn't form cleanly. The block isn't really one block — it's an in-flight transaction the operator hasn't finished perceiving. - The operator's hand is hovering over `git commit`: blade in wrong place. Step back. Look for the cleavage. Do not force. (cook-ting) - futon-theory/futonic-logic — formal definition of 象/部/咅/鹽/香/🔮/未知/味. - futon-theory/proof-path — the 8-phase auditable event chain that a block manifests at the substrate layer. - structure/cook-ting — hinge-recognition; perceive cleavages, do not force. - structure/hinge-point — the structural slot where a block can close. - structure/mana-allostasis — the dynamic the block sits inside (each block-close is a mana award). - invariant-coherence/drain-channel-shape — how the new working-tree drain channel and existing bounded-disposition siblings cohere under one faculty. Without a coherent unit, every dirty file is its own anxiety. With blocks, the operator's attention is on whether the *current* block is approaching closure — a single coherent question rather than N file-level questions. The futonic loop already names the structure; "block" is the operational name for one of its revolutions. Each agent chat turn is automatically one block — evidence-per- turn is the *automatic* form of block-discipline. The unit is the same as a working-tree block; the recording cadence differs (turn-based vs hinge-based). This makes block-discipline symmetric across agent and operator activity.

title: Cook Ting Finds the Cleavages
text: Cook Ting Finds the Cleavages Find the joints already in the structure; do not cut through gristle. The hinge-point in a mission is a natural cleavage that is already there. The correct action at a hinge is to recognise the cleavage and slip into it — not to manufacture a transition, not to enforce a schedule, not to ask a question that does not belong to the joint one is at. The blade-of-no-thickness is the question-or-absence that enters the cleavage without catching on anything. Zhuangzi's Cook Ting had used the same blade for nineteen years, unbroken, because he followed the natural markings of the bulls he carved. The ordinary carver breaks a blade a month by forcing it through gristle. A mission that asks stipulated questions at stipulated gates is the ordinary carver. A mission that recognises its own hinges and slips questions into them where cleavages are open is Ting. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - Asking all questions at all gates (forced carving). - Adding questions to the pool prescriptively rather than growing it from what actually did useful holding-work at real hinges. - Treating the pool as a checklist. It is a library of blades, not a sequence of cuts. - Confusing hinges with the seven-phase mission lifecycle transitions. A lifecycle transition may be a hinge or may not. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. 1. Hinge-points are natural cleavages in the mission's structure — they are not scheduled, they are recognised. 2. An operator plucks a question from the pool only when a hinge is open and a question belongs to it. Not every hinge carries a Q→A. A blade that never touches tendon is a question that is never asked when no question belongs. 3. A mission that forces questions at regular intervals is the ordinary carver. A mission that recognises hinges and meets them appropriately is Ting. The blade of mission-steering lasts if used this way. It breaks if used the other way. - If the operator's hand is hovering, or is making many small niggling strokes, the blade is in the wrong place. Step back. Look for the cleavage. Do not force. - If questions from the pool feel imposed rather than recognised, the hinge has not been reached. Wait. - If the blade comes out "as though fresh from the forge" after many missions, the practice is right. "When I first began to carve I fixed my gaze on the animal in front of me. After three years I no longer saw it as a whole bull, but as a thing already divided into parts. Nowadays I no longer see it with the eye; I merely apprehend it with the soul. My sense-organs are in abeyance, but my soul still works. Unerringly my knife follows the natural markings, slips into the natural cleavages, finds its way into the natural cavities." The mission's structure contains the hinges already. The operator does not create them. Skilled mission-steering is perception of what is already present, not imposition of what the operator imagines should be there. This is the same claim Ting makes about bulls; it is the same claim the peripheral-gauntlet patterns make about agent environments; it is the same claim the MVSG makes about the octahedral void. next[Grow the pool by logging which questions did useful holding-work at real hinges, and which did not] next[Track blade-state: if an operator finds missions difficult and niggling, the practice is still developing; if the blade stays sharp, the hinge-recognition is working]

title: Hinge-Log Entry Slot Structure (MVSG-Aligned)
text: Hinge-Log Entry Slot Structure (MVSG-Aligned) A hinge-log entry has **five optional fields**, each corresponding to a specific aggregate in the MVSG / five-skandhas mapping. When Q→A is non-empty, these fields are available but not required. The operator fills what is load-bearing for this specific hinge. Empty fields do not invalidate the entry; they record that this particular aggregate did not carry load at this cleavage. The journal register (parallel to the ledger/saṅkhāra side) holds the other three aggregates that co-arise around the void.
