The slot structure is the minimum shape that lets those aggregates be addressed without collapsing them into each other or into saṅkhāra-style ledger content. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - Filling all five fields performatively → schema becomes checklist; drift toward life-logging. - Writing saṅkhāra-content (what was done, what was produced) into any slot → register collapse. - Paraphrasing first-person articulation into agent-voice → I-1 violation. - Summarising across entries → destruction of journal character. - Using the slots as a template for generating synthetic content where no phenomenology was actually present → fabricated phenomenology is worse than empty. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. 1. Pluck zero or more questions from the pool (`futon3/library/structure/`) if any belong to this hinge. 2. For each field where the operator has something load-bearing to say, write it in first person (I-1 applied to humans), lightly edited at most if agent-transcribed. 3. Leave fields empty where they do not carry load. Empty is structurally valid; performatively-filled is anti-pattern. 4. Record which learning-loop channels fired at this hinge (pattern library, operator vocabulary, connection graph, question pool). An earlier version of this pattern claimed "saṅkhāra is NOT among the slots — that's the ledger's territory." That framing was wrong in the way it conflated two distinct things: - **Content-saṅkhāra:** ledger-shaped records of what was done in the world (code shipped, mission executed, scan ran, PAR emitted). This belongs in the A→B saṅkhāra register via `reflect.clj` / PAR infrastructure. Smuggling it into the phenomenological slots DOES collapse registers — that anti-pattern stands. - **Operational-saṅkhāra:** the term-synthesis step that makes any entry exist at all. Writing a tension is fabrication. Naming a shift is fabrication. Constructing a learning-loop update is fabrication. The synthesis that inhabits the five-field type IS saṅkhāra. It is present in every hinge-log entry — in the shift slot explicitly (as phenomenological reconfiguration), and in the entry's bookkeeping (header, learning-loop-updates section, outcome) as the synthesis that holds the entry together. So: the five-field schema covers all five aggregates correctly — four content-aggregates (rūpa, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhāra) co-arising around the viññāṇa void. That is the MVSG structure applied as it should be. Saṅkhāra is inhabited, not excluded. The ledger/journal distinction remains: ledger-content is saṅkhāra-dense (verb-side records of what the system did); journal-content is rūpa/vedanā/saññā/saṅkhāra-co-arising-around-void (the phase's texture plus the synthesis that made the texture articulable). The journal is not aggregate-exclusive; it is register-distinct. **1. Entry state (rūpa — form).** The organisational/operational condition the phase arose in. What was the material-institutional state at the start? Examples: "mission doc drafted but untested", "three missions running in parallel", "operator came off a coach session and a coffee", "the scan cache was empty." **2. Dominant tension (saññā — perception/pattern-recognition).** What was pulling against what? Saññā is the pattern-matching aggregate; recognising a tension is saññā doing its work. Examples: "completeness vs speed", "ledger's formalism vs what I actually wanted to say", "agent's framing vs operator's voice", "three warm contacts pulling in different directions." **3. Shift (saṅkhāra — fabrication, active reconfiguration).** What was synthesised here that reconfigured the pattern? When saññā's pattern-match changes, saṅkhāra did the work — the shift slot holds the *phenomenological aspect* of that synthesis. Examples: "the mission's purpose snapped into operator-capacity-development frame", "what I thought was about reproducibility turned out to be about building AIQA", "saṅkhāra as register was wrong — saṅkhāra as synthesis step is right." **4. Residual unknowns (viññāṇa as preserved void — consciousness as space of co-arising).** What didn't settle, and shouldn't be forced to settle? This is the sorry-preservation field — the void that must remain open. Examples: "whether the hinge-log is training or just recording", "what the B→A model's shape will be once use-data arrives." **5. Energy signature (vedanā — feeling, hedonic tone).** The quality of mind in which the phase happened. Pressured, open, flat, locked-in, quietly flowing. Vedanā's gatekeeper work made legible. Not self-report about the operator's general state — specifically about the phase's texture. Examples: "profound but manageable", "crisp, satisfying, small-scale", "tired but the find carried energy." - **Fill** when the hinge is a natural cleavage (cf. `structure/cook-ting`) and at least one of the five fields has load-bearing content. - **Fill lightly** (one or two fields only) when the hinge is minor and most of the phase's phenomenology doesn't need articulation. The five-field schema is a maximum, not a quota. - **Skip entirely** (empty Q→A, empty fields, just record the crossing) when the hinge passed without any aggregate carrying load. This is the blade-of-no-thickness passing through the cleavage. The MVSG claim (TN-mvsg.md, TN-halliday-clines.md) is that the mission emerges as a qualitative object when the registers are held distinct without collapse. The five slots give addressable structure to the other-three-aggregates register without forcing content into it. Slot-filler is scaffolding for inhabited articulation, not a survey form. next[Record which slots get used most often across the first five missions that adopt the hinge-log format — low-use slots are candidates for simplification] next[Watch for slot-drift (e.g., "dominant tension" accidentally collecting saṅkhāra content) as a signal that slot definitions need sharpening] next[Applied-chaos-theory phase begins once the overt method has been used in ≥3 missions: perturbations (different hinge types, different question plucks, different agent participations) reveal the method's actual attractor basins, and the four-channel learning loop integrates the lessons]

title: Hinge-Point as Structural Slot
text: Hinge-Point as Structural Slot A hinge-point is a structural slot in a mission where direction can shift. The slot exists whether or not a question is asked and whether or not an answer is given. Empty Q→A at a hinge is structurally meaningful: it records that the hinge was encountered, no question fired, the mission proceeded. This is different from "no hinge existed." The slot holds the space. Missions tend toward state-machine shapes — transitions between phases, completion conditions, orchestrable ledger records. This shape is useful for coordination but it does not by itself produce the qualitative object the mission is ultimately for. The hinge is the mechanism by which a mission can be steered, not only progressed. Steering happens at hinges; progression happens between them. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - Predicting hinge count in advance ("this mission will have 3 hinges") - Stipulating which questions must fire at which hinge - Treating a routine phase transition as a hinge just because it's a named boundary - Answering hinge questions in third-person or in someone else's voice - Summarising hinge logs across missions ("Joe's most common residual unknowns are X") — this is exactly the database-move M-trip-journal is structurally protected against Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. Hinge-Q→As are consumed as mission-steering input. Once the mission closes, the log is preserved within the mission's directory but is NOT indexed across missions, NOT queried as personal-state history, NOT trended as operator data. If a pattern of entries across missions starts looking like a personal-state dashboard, that is drift — the hinge questions have leaked scope from mission-steering into life-logging. Agent-conversation turns (A(Joe)→B(agent)) carry a slot for pattern-tagging. Whether a pattern fires at a given turn is emergent; the slot is structural. Hinge-points are the mission-scale analogue: structural slots whose Q→A content is emergent, drawn from a pool, and may be empty. At a hinge, the operator may: a. Pluck one or more questions from the question-pool (library/structure/) b. Answer them in first person (I-1 applied to humans — delegation to an agent writing-as-the-operator is a category error) c. Or leave the hinge empty, recording only that it was reached The hinge-log entry preserves (a), (b), or (c) with equal dignity. An empty hinge is data about the mission; it is not an absence. 1. Routine phase transitions where the next step is mechanically determined (e.g., IDENTIFY exits when a human says "yes, proceed"). 2. Scheduled review points. Schedules produce ordinary carvers. 3. Any point where the operator is tempted to check in on themselves rather than the mission. That's life-logging drift. 1. A point at which the mission's direction is contingent on operator state, operator meaning-making, or external input that wasn't available at mission design time. 2. A point at which closing or proceeding without reflection would risk the sorry-preservation invariant — risk collapsing a typed void into a prematurely-settled answer. 3. A point at which the mission's phenomenological register (the operator's or agent's experience of being inside the mission) carries load-bearing information for the next segment. The qualitative object a mission produces depends on being steered at its hinges — held in the right tensions long enough for thinking to happen. A mission with no hinge-slots is a railroad. A mission with stipulated-gate cadence is an ordinary carver. A mission with hinge-slots and a pool of blades-of-no-thickness is Cook Ting's kitchen: the blade lasts, the bull is carved, and the king learns something about the conservation of vital forces. next[Log hinges as they fire in M-trip-journal's own recursive instance] next[Note which questions did useful holding-work — those prove themselves by being drawn from the pool repeatedly] next[If the pool grows beyond ~15 entries without use-frequency data, prune to what has actually held]

title: What state-transition is this checkpoint asserting against an interest-network entity?
text: What state-transition is this checkpoint asserting against an interest-network entity? Mission checkpoints update the interest-network not by mutating EoI entities directly but by emitting typed state-transition events that target them. This flexiarg declares the v1 vocabulary: eight event types (seven `state/*` events plus `link/asserted`) and a payload schema. The event log is append-only and provenance-bearing; the posterior projection derives entity standing by replay. The vocabulary is neutral — the same eight events apply to essay annotations, institution-objects, basins, and composite-arrow edges without entity-class-specific slang. The EoI corpus declares interests as a prior. Lived evidence from missions (M-interim-director during design 2026-05-14 → ~2026-05-28; downstream validation execution ~June–August 2026; EoI engine runs in any session) constitutes the likelihood. The interest-network surface renders the posterior. Without an explicit event vocabulary, mission outputs sit alongside the EoI corpus as parallel documents rather than as posterior updates; the network either ossifies (silent updates) or churns incoherently (overwrites without provenance). The vocabulary closes this gap by giving every state-transition a citable name. Three design choices the vocabulary makes, and why each beats its alternative. A free-form rationale field per checkpoint would be simpler but loses the structure that lets the projection compute coverage, detect inconsistencies, and render the network without re-parsing prose. Eight types is enough to discriminate (a) entity-lifecycle moves (spawned / refined / strengthened) from (b) closure moves (addressed / falsified / foreclosed / reopened) from (c) relational moves (link/asserted), while staying small enough that an operator can hold them in mind without consulting a sheet. Namespace is `state/*` — not `eoi/*`, `essay/*`, `basin/*` — so the same events apply to essay annotations, institution-objects, basins, and composite-arrow edges. Granularity is a separate field (`:target/granularity`), not part of the event-type. Cross-entity-class queries work naturally ("show me every entity that got addressed this week"); per-entity-class queries filter by granularity. `link/asserted` is its own event type, not a special case of `state/spawned`, because "new relation exists" and "new entity exists" have different downstream uses (relation surfaces as edge in the network view; entity surfaces as node). Overloading `state/spawned` would force the projection to discriminate by `:target/granularity` to know whether to render as node or edge — fine for the projection, opaque to the operator authoring the checkpoint. The eight event types, the payload schema, and the emission discipline. - `state/spawned` — Target entity is newly created. - `state/refined` — Target entity's framing has been sharpened (re-anchor, scoped). - `state/strengthened` — Target entity's standing has gained support from evidence. - `state/addressed` — Target entity (typically a tension) has been resolved by evidence; not falsified. - `state/falsified` — Target entity has been contradicted by evidence. - `state/foreclosed` — Target entity (typically a basin) has been deliberately closed off. - `state/reopened` — Target entity that was addressed/falsified/foreclosed has had its standing reset to `:live`. First-class so retraction isn't terminal. - `link/asserted` — A new cross-essay relation exists. Separate from `state/spawned` to avoid overloading "new target" with "new relation". Each event record carries these fields (EDN, keyword keys): - `:event/id` — unique within checkpoint - `:event/type` — keyword; one of the eight above - `:checkpoint/ref` — back-pointer to the checkpoint - `:target/entity-id` — the EoI entity this event targets - `:target/granularity` — keyword; one of `:essay`, `:section`, `:annotation`, `:institution-object`, `:basin`, `:composite-arrow` - `:prior-state` — keyword; standing before this event. Required for `state/*` events; optional/omitted for `link/asserted`. - `:posterior-state` — keyword; standing after this event. Required for `state/*` events; optional/omitted for `link/asserted`. - `:evidence/refs` — `[String]`; pointers to evidence artefacts (interview notes, go/nogo memos, plan drafts, EoI strawman sections, etc.) - `:operator/rationale` — `String`; the operator's plain-language reason. This is the load-bearing provenance field; the projection's posterior always traces back to an operator-asserted *because*. - `:link/src` — `String`; source entity. Only for `link/asserted` events. - `:link/dst` — `String`; destination entity. Only for `link/asserted` events. - APPEND-ONLY. Events are never edited or deleted. Mistakes are corrected by emitting a new event (typically `state/refined` or `state/reopened`) that updates the target's standing. The log is the authoritative source; the projection derives current state from log replay. - NO-OP DAYS EMIT NO CHECKPOINT. Daily cadence is fine when there's a real state delta — even a single `state/refined` on a single annotation counts. But synthetic checkpoints (an empty `:emitted-events` vector emitted just to satisfy a daily rhythm) are forbidden: they pollute the log with non-events and degrade the projection's signal-to-noise. - OPERATOR-ASSERTED BOUNDARY. Events are emitted at checkpoint boundaries by an operator, not inferred from prose by a processor. The event log is authored, not extracted. (Pre-checkpoint events — interview notes, go/nogo memos as they happen — are out of scope for v1.) - VALIDATION BLOCKS, NOT WARNS. Validation errors against this vocabulary block the checkpoint; the operator fixes the EDN and re-runs. Silent acceptance of malformed events would let drift land in the projection. Provenance is the load-bearing part of completeness-not-closure (the parent EoI mission's framing: the network becomes more complete under use because evidence accumulates, not because documents multiply). The projection's render answers "what is the standing of every EoI entity right now?", but the trail it carries answers "how did it get there?". Both are needed: without standing, the operator can't act on current state; without trail, the operator can't tell whether progress is real or a confabulation. The eight-event vocabulary fixes a discrimination-shape the projection can compute against; the append-only discipline preserves the trail; the explicit-emission rule keeps the authoring surface honest. The neutral `state/*` namespace makes the vocabulary reusable across entity classes — which is what lets substrate-2's sorry-typing, M-a-sorry-enterprise's mining-track, and `:sorry/r3d-per-entity-attribution` adopt the same vocabulary rather than re-inventing it per consumer. next[Step (b) commit: this flexiarg IS the deliverable. The vocabulary, payload, and emission discipline are committed here as the canonical design substrate. M-INC's INSTANTIATE step (b) is satisfied by this file's existence.] next[Step (c) projection: derive an EDN schema file from this flexiarg as needed by XTDB validators (`state/<spawned|refined|...>` as a keyword schema, the payload as a `clojure.spec`/`malli` schema, etc.). The flexiarg remains authoritative; EDN is procedural adaptation. War-machine vocabulary EDNs (`futon5a/data/war-machine-*-vocabulary.edn`) are structural references for the EDN form.] next[First emission: M-interim-director CP-1 (futon7) is the first concrete planned emitter, per M-INC §1 IDENTIFY. title: Mana Allostasis: Dissonance Is the Precursor to Resolution
text: Mana Allostasis: Dissonance Is the Precursor to Resolution The operator's metabolic state in the stack is the integral of (block-closures-at-hinges − allostatic-load-symptoms) over time. Block-closures award mana; allostatic-load symptoms drain it. The invariant is that net balance remains non-negative under sustained operation. Symptom channels are plural — working-tree dirt, mission-proliferation, session-sprawl, ahead-of-origin- without-disposition, untriaged-evidence — but they share a shape and an antidote: **perceive the hinge, close the block**. Allostasis is the cumulative cost of physiological adaptation to stressors. It is not a defect — it is the theoretical precursor to resolution. Dissonance in music is not noise; it is the structure that gives consonance its meaning. In a futon stack, allostatic load is the rising tension that makes block- closure satisfying and noticeable. Without load, closure is unmotivated; without closure, load becomes degradation. Complexity, similarly, is not a fault to be minimised. A working tree in flux is the right state to be in *while doing the work*. What the invariant guards is not the absence of complexity but the timely return to a state where the substrate's transactional discipline holds. The operator is operating a futon stack with pluri-channel work (working trees, missions, sessions, branches, evidence streams), and is at risk of either (a) accumulating load past the point of coherent resolution, or (b) discharging load prematurely into rubber-stamp closures. No single channel is the whole story. Working-tree dirtiness is one symptom-channel; mission-proliferation is another; session- sprawl is another. Each drains by its own dynamic. Aggregating them into a single "you're tired" signal preserves the felt sense; separating them allows targeted resolution. Both readings are needed. Equally: not every block can or should close immediately. Some load is the *passion* phase of a block in flight — the operator is doing the actual work that the block will record. Pressure is welcome there; the invariant is not "minimise pressure" but "perceive when pressure becomes overdue." - **Automation-of-closure**: forcing block-closure on a timer. Resolves dissonance without it being earned; produces hollow consonance. (jj-style; rubber-stamp commits.) - **Single-channel obsession**: tracking only working-tree pressure while letting mission-proliferation accumulate quietly. Drain is multi-channel; perception must be too. - **Mana-hoarding**: closing blocks for the award without the work. Each block-closure must rest on actual passion; otherwise the award is counterfeit, the system's metabolic sense miscalibrates, and real load goes unflagged. - **Dissonance-aversion**: forcing premature consonance. The operator commits to "feel done" rather than because the work is done. Music-theoretically: trite. - **Dissonance-luxuriance**: holding load indefinitely because "the work isn't ready." At some point dissonance becomes noise; the block must close even if imperfectly, then the next block can refine. Track the per-channel drain rate. Surface to the operator when a channel approaches hinge-cadence overdue. Award mana at block- closure-at-recognised-hinge (only with the passion phase completed). Visualise the balance trajectory so the operator can see whether the system is accumulating or recovering. Distinguish "open block in passion" from "open block past hinge-cadence." - Many open missions, many open sessions, dirty working trees: multi-channel drain. Operator likely feels tired; confirm via proprioceptive check. Targeted hinge-perception, channel by channel. - All channels low, blocks closing regularly: net mana positive; the system is in healthy oscillation. - One channel pinned high, others quiet: targeted resolution is called for — perceive the specific hinge that's overdue and slip the blade. - Mana awards landing without prior load: counterfeit. Closures are happening without real work. Investigate (the awards may be from the wrong phase — e.g., closing a block before the passion phase has run). - Operator reports tiredness but futon-sync looks clean: the drain may be coming from a channel not currently measured (untriaged-evidence, attention-on-too-many-PRs, etc.). Widen the drain-channel inventory. Consonance without prior dissonance is unmoving. A block-closure without prior accumulation is a non-event. The pressure function does not say "minimise load"; it says: when load approaches the natural resolution-point (a hinge), the operator should perceive it and act. The pleasure of the resolution scales with the load that preceded it. This is one reason cleanup blocks (after a long open passage) feel satisfying in a way that a hundred half-formed commits cannot. The five-phase block lifecycle (identification → specification → elaboration → passion → closure; structure/block-as-futonic- revolution) names *passion* explicitly. This is the embodied- effort phase — where adenosine actually accumulates, where work actually gets done. Without naming this phase, the model would suggest that closure happens through pure perception. Real work has cost; the cost is the precondition for real resolution. Working-tree dirt, mission-proliferation, session-sprawl, branch-bloat, untriaged-evidence — each a voice in a multi- voice composition. Harmolodics (Ornette Coleman) holds that harmony, melody, and rhythm are equally weighted; no single line dominates. The futonic invariant family has the same structure. Watching only one drain (e.g., working-tree dirtiness) while the others accumulate is monophonic listening. - structure/block-as-futonic-revolution — defines the unit that awards mana on close. - structure/cook-ting — the hinge-recognition that makes the close effortless. - structure/hinge-point — the structural slot where a hinge appears. - invariant-coherence/drain-channel-shape — how multiple bounded-disposition siblings share the drain-channel shape. - futon-theory/futonic-logic — the recognition loop the closure traverses. Sleep pressure is real. Music-theoretically, dissonance held too long without resolution becomes noise; resolved too early, music becomes trite. The same in stacks: allostatic load held too long without block-closure becomes substrate corruption (the M-live-geometric-stack manifold can't read it; agents and other operators see stale state). Resolved too early, blocks become hollow — work is "committed" without being done. The mana economy is the felt-sense interface to that physical reality.

title: What Tensions Would We Leave Unresolved If We Closed Here?
text: What Tensions Would We Leave Unresolved If We Closed Here? A hinge-pool question. Plucked when a mission is approaching closure. The question guards against premature closure — the failure mode where the mission is closed because its state machine is at its final node, not because the tensions it arose to hold have finished doing their work. Sorry-preservation applied to process: some tensions are supposed to stay unresolved, and the mission's job is to preserve them, not to force them. The mission lifecycle makes closure feel mandatory. A mission at DOCUMENT is supposed to DOCUMENT and finish. This is fine when the tensions that motivated the mission have actually been addressed. It is a category error when the tensions are still live and the mission is being closed because closing is the next state, not because the work is done. Closing a mission whose tensions are live is the same move as canonicalising a sorry into a proof before the sorry has been encountered as a sorry — it destroys the very object the mission was for. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - "No unresolved tensions" — almost always a sign the question has not been inhabited; go back to structure/whose-question-is-this - Listing every minor loose end equally — (a), (b), and (c) are structurally different and need different handling - Treating (c) as a failure of the mission rather than as its gift - Exporting everything as a sorry into a future mission that will never be run — the sorry is structural, not a TODO Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. 1. First person. What is still pulling against what that, if resolved, would force a claim I cannot support from inside this mission? 2. Distinguish three kinds of unresolved tension: a. SOLVABLE-BUT-NOT-YET: the mission could resolve this if it continued, and closing now would lose that chance. Do not close; extend. b. NOT-SOLVABLE-HERE: the tension is real but belongs to a different mission or scope. Name it, export it as a sorry, close this mission cleanly. c. STRUCTURALLY-VOID: the tension is the sorry the mission is supposed to preserve — collapsing it would destroy the mission's qualitative object. Name it, do not force resolution, close the mission with the void preserved in the journal register. 3. Each kind wants a different action at the hinge. Misclassifying (a) as (b) loses work; misclassifying (b) as (c) preserves voids that should have been solved; misclassifying (c) as (a) or (b) kills the Halliday object. - Schedule-driven closure ("we've been at this long enough") - Artifact-equals-mission conflation ("the WP is written, therefore the mission is done") - Loss of sorry-preservation: collapsing the typed gap into a prematurely-closed statement - "Success at the wrong exit" — mission passed its state machine's final node while producing no qualitative object - At any hinge within two hinges of planned closure - When the mission has produced its primary artifact and the temptation is to declare victory - When the operator notices relief at the prospect of closing, which is sometimes appropriate and sometimes a drift signal - When a reviewer or stakeholder is pressing for closure on a schedule external to the mission's actual progress The mission that closes correctly is the mission that stops when its work is done, where "work" includes tension-preservation as a legitimate terminal state. Cook Ting's blade does not force a final cut that the structure does not offer. A mission that has reached a joint where the tensions are (a) still resolvable in scope, (b) properly exported, or (c) structurally preserved — and acts according to which of these it is — carves the bull correctly. next[If (a): extend the mission, do not close] next[If (b): export the tensions as new-mission seeds, close cleanly] next[If (c): write the journal register's closure entry to name the preserved tension, close the ledger cleanly, preserve the void in the mission's permanent record]

title: What Problem Is This Actually Solving?
text: What Problem Is This Actually Solving? A hinge-pool question. Plucked when a mission is approaching a significant commitment of resources or closure on a phase whose framing may have drifted from the problem the mission originally arose to address. The question guards against proxy-problem substitution — the failure mode where the mission is progressing efficiently at the wrong goal. Missions naturally drift from their founding problem into problems that are better-defined, better-tooled, or more proximate to the operator's current competence. This drift is often productive — the original problem may not have been accurately described. But it is also the failure mode of "success at the wrong goal," which is indistinguishable from success internally while being worthless externally. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - Describing the artifact, not the problem ("We are producing a pattern library" — no, what problem does a pattern library solve?) - Citing the mission doc's original Motivation verbatim. If the mission has been running for any length of time, the Motivation section is frozen at IDENTIFY time; the actual problem has evolved (or should have). A verbatim citation is a drift signal. - Moral claims as problem statements ("We are doing this because it is important"). Importance is not a problem. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. 1. First person. I-1 applied to humans: you answer, not an agent writing as you. 2. One sentence if possible. If the answer takes a paragraph, either the problem has drifted or the answer is a list of several problems and the mission needs splitting. 3. Say what problem the mission is solving, not what it is doing. "We are building an X" is not an answer. "We are building an X because the problem of Y cannot be addressed without it" is. 4. If the honest answer is "I no longer know," that is a valid answer. The mission needs to stop at this hinge and re-identify before proceeding. - Drift from founding problem to tractable proxy - Mission-as-artefact-production rather than mission-as-problem-solution - DOCUMENT-phase writing that reads well but makes no claim about what changed because of the mission - The hermit-trap: missions that become self-sustaining practices rather than problem-solving vehicles - At IDENTIFY-exit: is the problem as-described in the mission doc the problem we are actually working on, or has the writing process already substituted a more tractable proxy? - At MAP-entry: the mapping exercise is about to consume real effort. Is the target of the map the actual problem? - At any hinge where the mission feels easy in a way the founding tension did not warrant. Ease at a hinge often signals that the hard problem has been silently replaced. - When presenting the mission to a reader (UKRN-S WP insight): the reader's first question will be "what problem is this actually solving?" If the mission can't answer in one sentence without hedging, the problem has drifted. The UKRN-S Working Paper reader's first question is always "what problem is this actually solving." Asking it inside the mission, repeatedly, at hinges, is the practice that makes the eventual Working Paper (or deliverable, or artifact) able to answer it when the reader arrives. The question is not a check on the mission; it is a shape of its competence. next[If this question has fired at three hinges with three different answers, the mission has drifted and should split or re-IDENTIFY] next[If this question has fired at three hinges with the same answer, the mission's problem-definition is stable and the question can retire until the next major phase transition]

title: Whose Question Is This?
text: Whose Question Is This? Before answering any hinge-pool question, pause and ask whose question it is. The question was drawn from a pool and is therefore structurally available to anyone. The answer must be inhabited — given in the operator's first person, about the mission the operator is in, at the hinge the operator is at. An answer given in anyone else's voice is a category error (I-1 applied to humans). An answer given as if from outside the mission is extractive mode. The question-pool is public. The answers are not. A pool question like "what problem is this actually solving" can be plucked at any hinge by any operator in any mission — but the answer is specific to this operator, this mission, this hinge. The failure mode: an operator plucks a question and produces a "correct-sounding" answer that would be defensible in a review meeting but does not come from inside the mission. That answer is extractive — it has used the question to produce a record rather than to let the question do its holding-work. The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure). - Generic best-practice answers ("the stakeholders are X, Y, Z...") - Answers that could have been given before the mission started - Answers written for a future reviewer rather than for the mission's current direction - Delegation: "let me ask the agent to draft this and I'll edit" — this is the I-1 violation and the hinge-log must not contain agent-drafted answers attributed to the operator Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. 1. Notice whose voice is composing the proposed answer. Yours? An imagined reader's? A previous consultant's? A template's? 2. If not yours: discard the proposed answer and sit with the question again. The question was plucked to hold you in a tension; if you have reached for someone else's voice, the tension has escaped and needs re-engaging. 3. The answer may be shorter, less articulate, less defensible than the voice-not-yours version. That is correct. Inhabited answers are often smaller. 4. "I don't know" in your own voice is a better answer than any articulate construction in someone else's. - Extractive-mode mission steering: producing records instead of thinking - Agent-impersonation at the journal register (the PAR/ledger side is agent-legible; the hinge-log side is not, by I-1) - The "consultant voice" failure: answers that would pass external review but do no holding-work inside the mission - Polishing over inhabitation: answers that are too finished to be human data (cf. "only an unfinished object is human data") - Before answering any other hinge-pool question that is drawn from the pool and feels "standard." - When an operator notices themselves composing an answer rather than finding one. - When an agent is present in the mission and there is a temptation to let the agent phrase the answer. (I-1 forbids. The agent can scaffold the question; it cannot inhabit the answer.) - When the answer, if read aloud, sounds like something a consultant would say rather than something the operator would say. The MVSG claim is that the mission emerges as a qualitative object when the registers are held distinct without collapse. The hinge-log is the journal register; answers in it must be inhabited. Without this question gating the others, "what problem is this solving" degrades into boilerplate and the journal register collapses into the ledger. With this question gating the others, the journal stays protected, and the mission has a chance of producing the qualitative object. next[If an operator finds this question firing at every hinge, the inhabitation posture may be unstable — consider whether the mission is being done in inhabited mode at all] next[If this question never fires, either inhabitation is habituated (good) or the pool is being filled with consultant-voice answers without notice (bad) — audit by reading a recent hinge-log entry aloud in your own voice and checking whether it sounds like you]

title: Argue Empirically, Not Persuasively
text: Argue Empirically, Not Persuasively At any stage where claims are first being put on the record — bootstrap stages of a system, ARGUE-phase missions, foundational sections of papers — claims must be derived from reasonable assumptions and present-tense observations, not speculated forward as downstream effects. "May foster X" is not a claim; it is a hope dressed as one. The discipline is: a claim belongs at the bootstrap if it follows from the bootstrap's own action under reasonable assumptions, not if it depends on a chain of effects the bootstrap has not yet produced. The remedy when such a claim is detected is to delete it (most often), demote it to an open question or future-work note (sometimes), or replace it with the what-must-follow restatement it was gesturing at (rarely — usually the speculation was masking the absence of any derivable claim). AI drafts and human first-drafts both tend to dress speculation as claim. The hedge "may", the modifier "potentially", the verb "foster" or "could lead to" — each does argumentative work without paying for it. In ARGUE-phase missions and in bootstrap-stage system descriptions, speculative claims pile up because the writer is working at the edge of what the system has done so far, and the speculation is filling space that empirical claim cannot yet fill. Distinct from `unearned-essentially` (about unsupported strength claims) and `hedged-lift` (about hedging that does the lifting): here the failure is *temporal* — the claim depends on stages the document has not yet brought into being. The pattern operates on the axis: claim ambition ↔ what the action under reasonable assumptions actually delivers. Irreducible: a claim either follows from the action under reasonable assumptions, or it depends on a chain the document has not yet built. No amount of hedging changes which of these is true. Real costs: a strong document may say less in early sections than the writer wants — empirically derivable claims at bootstrap are often modest and obvious. Restraining the claim to the empirical scope at hand can feel anticlimactic; permitting speculation feels generous, but creates load-bearing reliance on claims the document has not paid for. Active dynamic: the temptation grows whenever the writer wants the early section to feel weighty. The cure for the section feeling thin is not speculation; it is moving more empirically derivable content into the early section, or accepting that the section is short. - May-fostering: "may foster" / "could lead to" / "has the potential to" — each is the present participle of a verb the document has not earned. - Downstream borrowing: claims at stage N depend on stages N+1 or N+2 having occurred; when challenged, the writer points forward rather than at what the action has produced. - Hedge as warrant: a hedge ("perhaps", "in principle") is doing the work an argument would do — the reader is supposed to read the hedge as care rather than as the absence of derivation. - Persuasion-by-aspiration: the claim is rhetorically attractive and the writer treats this attractiveness as warrant. Delete or restrict the claim; replace with what must follow; or demote to open question. (1) Delete and stop: the simplest move. If the claim does not follow from what the action does, remove it. The remaining sentence is often short and sufficient. "This produces trainer-level visibility." is an entire claim. (2) Restate what must follow: replace "may foster X" with the empirical claim it was reaching for. If sharing evidence "may foster ground-up demand for community infrastructure", what *must* follow under reasonable assumptions is that trainers see findings; the demand-for-infrastructure claim depends on additional unbuilt machinery and should not be made here. (3) Demote to open question: if the speculation flags a genuine downstream variable the work needs to track, move it to a separate "open questions" or "what we will be watching" section. The demotion preserves the writer's intuition without letting the speculation pose as a derived claim. (4) Audit by must-follow test: read the claim and ask, "what would have to be the case for this to follow from the action just described, under reasonable assumptions?" If the answer requires additional steps the document has not specified, the claim is speculative. If the answer is "only the action just described, and nothing more", the claim is empirical and stays. Engaged when every claim in the section can be derived from the action just described, under reasonable assumptions, with no appeal to stages or machinery the document has not yet built. Failing when claims use "may", "could", "has the potential to", or "may foster" as warrant, or when the writer would, if challenged, defend the claim by pointing forward rather than by pointing at what the action makes inevitable.

title: Specify the Argument as a System, Not a Coverage Matrix
text: Specify the Argument as a System, Not a Coverage Matrix An argument that supports a decision must be specified as a system: a named outside (the reader and the decision the argument couples to), an inside (the claim+evidence structure), a boundary (what the argument settles versus what it hands off), and an active surface (what action the argument licenses once it has landed). The antipattern is to specify the argument as a coverage matrix — layered enumeration of open questions, findings, and closure-paths that all point inward at other items in the same enumeration. An argument with no outside has no decision to couple to; the paper drafted from such a spec inherits the same shape, becoming a section-per-item exercise in internal consistency rather than a coupled support for a live choice. An argument-spec is the upstream artifact from which a paper, memo, or recommendation gets drafted. If the spec is shaped as a layered enumeration — questions inside layers inside argument-layers, each item carrying a `:closure-path` to other items in the same spec — the drafting agent will faithfully reproduce that shape in prose. The result is the surface failures observed downstream in `plan-as-enumeration` (counted headings, calendar-paginated milestones, lists where the count is the perceptual unit) and `triad-inflation` (rule-of-three padding). Those are symptoms; the upstream cause is a spec that does not distinguish the regions of a coherent system from items in a checklist. The positive frame draws on the Active Inference wiring diagram (see `futon5/docs/chapter0-aif-as-wiring-diagram`): a system has five regions — environment, sensory surface, internal states, active surface, preferences — joined by typed interfaces, with timescale separations that prevent fast dynamics from corrupting slow structure. Applied to argumentation (the AIF-squared move: Active Inference Framework × Argumentation Interchange Framework): - Outside (environment): the reader-and-the-decision the argument is addressed to. - Sensory surface: what the reader brings in — prior beliefs, sector context, existing commitments. - Internal states: the claim+evidence structure; this is what coverage-checklist specs already capture. - Active surface: what operational move the argument licenses the reader to make. - Preferences/structure: the glacial commitments (audience identity, sector frame, funder identity) that shape what counts as a viable conclusion. A coverage-checklist spec captures only the third region and treats it as the whole. Specifying as a system means making the other four explicit. The pattern operates on the axis: internal coverage completeness <-/-> coupling to the external decision. Irreducible: either the argument's structure makes its boundary and active surface visible as named regions, or the structure consists of internal items with closure-paths pointing only inward, and the boundary becomes implicit. Real costs: specifying the boundary forces the writer to declare what the argument cannot settle — which feels like ceding ground before the argument even starts. Specifying the active surface forces the writer to name what action the reader should take, which exposes the recommendation to challenge before the warrant has been laid out. The coverage-checklist form preserves a comfortable ambiguity: every question is "in scope" and every closure-path lands internally, so the argument cannot be charged either with omission or with over-reach. Active dynamic: when the argument-spec is built collaboratively or evolved across drafts, items accumulate. Each new finding becomes a new layer entry; each new objection becomes a new question. Without an explicit boundary, there is no principled rule for excluding an item, so the spec keeps growing — and the paper drafted from it keeps growing in proportion. After-the-fact cut manifests (records of which items were dropped from the prose between drafts) are what an external boundary looks like once it has been imposed retroactively; a boundary specified at spec-time would have prevented most of those items from entering in the first place. - Layers all the way down: nested layers (questions inside layers inside argument-layers) with no rule for what stops the recursion. - Closure-paths point inward only: every `:closure-path` references other items in the same spec; nothing points at the reader's decision or at an external evidence source the reader could check independently. - Boundary by implicature: what's in scope is named, but what's out of scope is left implicit. The reader cannot tell what the argument refuses to settle. - Active surface conflated with internal layer: the recommended action is named as another layer item ("year-1 launch") rather than as the system's coupling-to-the-world. - Timescale flattening: fast-changing evidence (quarterly delivery counts) and glacial commitments (sector identity) are treated as co-equal layer items rather than as different-rate inputs to the system. - Coverage-as-warrant: the spec implies that having an item for every question means the argument is sound, when it only means the questions have been listed. - Spec form propagates downstream: when the spec is enumerative, the paper is enumerative; when the spec is system-shaped, the paper has a chance of being system-shaped. The reverse repair is harder — fixing prose after enumeration has set in is mostly cosmetic; fixing the spec changes what gets drafted from it. Specify the argument as a five-region wiring diagram before the layered content accumulates. (1) Name the outside first: who the argument is addressed to, what decision they face, what they will do with the argument once they have read it. This is the Markov-blanket cut between argument and world. (2) Name the active surface explicitly: declare what operational moves the argument licenses (e.g., "adopt the five-role design", "fund a three-year bridge", "stand the operation down at Year 2"). The active surface is not a layer item; it is the argument's coupling to the world, and should be named as its own region of the spec. (3) Declare the boundary: what does the argument settle, and what does it hand off to other arguments (companion papers, indicators work, future evidence waves)? An argument with no declared boundary is an argument that tries to cover everything, which is the spec-level source of Borgesian taxonomic accretion in prose. (4) Separate timescales: tag evidence-inputs by timescale (fast / medium / slow / glacial). When the argument depends on slow-moving structure (sector frame, funder identity), name that dependency rather than burying it in a layer alongside fast-moving evidence. (5) Let closure-paths point outward where appropriate: some closure-paths land internally (the design closes question Q2 via role configuration), but at least some must land externally (the recipient-level evaluation wave closes Q1 via empirical evidence the reader can independently check). An argument whose closure-paths point only inward is internally complete but externally suspended. (6) Apply downstream prose-side discipline second: once the spec is system-shaped, patterns like `plan-as-enumeration`, `triad-inflation`, and `name-the-decision-before-the-framework` become much easier to keep clean, because the prose now has a non-list shape to mirror. Prose-only de-AI-ification passes (see `algorithms/de-ai-ify.md`) cannot recover what the spec form did not provide. Engaged when the argument-spec's structure makes the outside, the boundary, and the active surface visible as named regions — not as layer items competing for attention with internal claim-evidence content. A reader inspecting the spec should be able to answer, without consulting the prose: who is this addressed to, what does it license them to do, what does it refuse to settle. Failing when the spec consists of layered enumeration with closure-paths pointing inward, and the boundary and active surface are recoverable only by reading the prose drafted from the spec. Diagnostic question: if a reader saw the argument-spec but not the paper, could they tell what the paper licenses the reader to do? If the only answer is "ratify the recommendation listed in the spec's `(recommendation-the-paper-supports)` slot", the argument has no active surface — the recommendation is a static label, not a coupling.

title: Bind Open Questions to Closure Mechanisms
text: Bind Open Questions to Closure Mechanisms An open question belongs in a decision-supporting document only if it is bound to a named closure mechanism. "This remains to be determined" is not enough. The document must say how the uncertainty closes: by a role, an evidence wave, a governance event, a threshold, or some other explicit mechanism. Otherwise the question is not being managed; it is being parked. Operational writing cannot eliminate uncertainty, but it can type it. The failure is not that a document contains unresolved questions; the failure is that the reader cannot tell whether those questions are expected to close through ordinary system operation or whether they are simply deferred indefinitely. Unbound uncertainty accumulates as ambient fog around the decision and makes the design look softer than it is. The pattern operates on the axis: acknowledged uncertainty <-/-> resolvable uncertainty. Irreducible: a question is either attached to a mechanism that can close it, or it is only being named as a gesture of conscientiousness. Real costs: binding a question to a closure mechanism forces the writer to expose ownership, timing, and evidence standards. This can reveal that the system does not yet know how it would learn what it claims it needs to know. Writers often prefer to preserve optionality by leaving the question open-ended. Active dynamic: every "we will need to learn", "future work", or "this depends on context" sentence is a likely site of slippage from typed uncertainty into unmanaged uncertainty. - Parked uncertainty: a live question is named but no actor or process is assigned to close it. - Future-work haze: the document says the issue will be examined later without saying by whom or through what event. - Governance vacuum: the need for a decision is acknowledged, but no forum or cadence exists in which the decision would actually be made. - Evidence without landing zone: the document calls for data collection but never says what decision that evidence would unlock or revise. Type the uncertainty and attach it to closure. (1) Name the closure mechanism: say "resolved by annual review", "closed by evaluator evidence wave", "owned by the bearer role", or equivalent. (2) Couple question to consequence: make explicit what becomes decidable once the question closes, so the reader sees why the uncertainty matters. (3) State the holding rule: if the question is unresolved now, say what the system does in the meantime rather than leaving action suspended. (4) Delete false openness: if no closure mechanism can be named, either redesign the system so one exists or stop presenting the issue as a managed open question. Engaged when every open question in the document is paired with a visible closure path and an interim operating rule. Failing when uncertainty is acknowledged rhetorically but not wired into any role, cadence, threshold, or decision path.

title: Correct Effect Claims with Relevant Denominators
text: Correct Effect Claims with Relevant Denominators Raw delivery counts do not warrant institutional-effect claims until they are corrected by denominators matched to the population that would need to be reached for the effect to be plausible. A numerator without a relevant denominator tells you activity, not reach; and reach, not activity alone, is the minimum precondition for institution-level change claims. Training reports, programme updates, and working papers often slide from "we delivered N sessions" or "N people attended" to implications about culture change, community uptake, or institutional effect. This is a scale error. The same numerator can mean saturation in one setting and trivial penetration in another. The denominator is not a statistical ornament; it is what gives the number argumentative meaning. The pattern operates on the axis: activity count <-/-> plausible reach. Irreducible: either the denominator is relevant to the affected population and the effect claim can be scaled accordingly, or the claim outruns what the count can support. Real costs: relevant denominators are often harder to gather, messier than the delivery count, and may reveal that a proud-looking numerator is organisationally thin. Writers therefore prefer counts because counts are clean and flattering. But effect claims built on flattering numerators are precisely what denominator discipline exists to stop. Active dynamic: the slippage appears whenever a programme wants to infer institutional consequence from centrally visible delivery metrics. - Numerator triumphalism: a large count is presented as self-interpreting. - Denominator mismatch: the denominator used is too broad, too narrow, or simply unrelated to the population whose change is being claimed. - Reach/effect collapse: modest exposure is narrated as if it already constituted institutional transformation. - Unique-person ambiguity: attendance or touch counts are used as if they were confirmed counts of distinct individuals reached. Re-express activity as proportionate reach before making effect claims. (1) Identify the affected population: academic staff, PGRs, the combined research community, or another population that matches the claim being made. (2) Compute the reach proportion on that denominator and state any uncertainty about uniqueness or completeness. (3) Use the corrected number to narrow the claim: low reach may still justify local learning claims, but not institution-shaping ones. (4) Preserve asymmetry: low reach can often falsify strong effect claims; high reach does not by itself prove effect, but it clears one necessary precondition. Engaged when delivery metrics are consistently paired with relevant denominators and the prose distinguishes activity from plausible reach. Failing when counts are left to imply significance on their own or when the denominator does not match the level of effect being claimed.

title: Facet Before Aggregating
text: Facet Before Aggregating When a measure aggregates across substantively different sub-categories — training topic, audience community, discipline, intervention type, recipient role — the aggregate measure conceals the actionable heterogeneity that the design recommendation actually depends on. Effect claims and design prescriptions should be made at the facet level where the underlying causal story holds, and aggregated only when the aggregation is interpretively defensible. Aggregating before faceting flatters the weaker case, ranks unlike entities as if they were comparable, and produces uniform recommendations across facets that need different interventions. Aggregate measures are easier to gather, easier to present, and easier to compare than facet-level ones. A single number per institution feels orderly; a vector of numbers per institution feels messy. But the orderliness is paid for in actionable lift: the design that follows from a flat per-institution number is necessarily blind to within-institution heterogeneity. Two institutions with the same headline reach can have entirely different facet structures (5% reach in one community with strong uptake vs 40% reach in another with weak uptake), and any recommendation that treats them alike is silently betting that the facet structure does not matter. When the rest of the document's evidence says it does, that bet is incoherent. The pattern operates on the axis: aggregate convenience <-/-> facet-level fidelity. Irreducible: either the measure is genuinely homogeneous within the aggregate, or the aggregate is concealing facet-level structure that the design recommendation depends on. Real costs: faceting requires more data structure, more interpretive care, and longer analysis cycles. It also exposes uncertainty that the aggregate hid. Writers and analysts often resist faceting because aggregate numbers look cleaner and are easier to put into a slide. But the cost of *not* faceting is paid downstream as recommendations that don't fit any actual sub-population. Active dynamic: the slippage appears whenever a programme's reporting infrastructure was set up before the design recommendation was sharpened. The reporting infrastructure produces aggregates because they were what the earlier purpose required. When the design recommendation later turns on facet-level questions, the aggregates are pressed into service anyway. - Aggregate-saturation conflation: a strong outcome in one facet plus a weak outcome in another are reported as a single average that flatters the weaker case and misrepresents the stronger. - Like-with-unlike comparison: institutions or interventions are ranked on aggregates without checking whether their underlying facet populations are comparable; the ranking misleads. - Facet-blind recommendation: the design's prescription is uniform across facets that need different interventions, because the aggregate cannot see them. - Reporting-infrastructure inertia: the team continues to report at the aggregate level because that is what the existing template captures, even after the design recommendation has shifted to a facet-level question. - Premature roll-up in dashboards: monitoring tooling collapses facet-level signals into a single index for display purposes, then that index becomes the operational measure. Facet the measure where the causal story differs; aggregate only after interpretive verification. (1) Identify the relevant facets: which sub-categories does the design recommendation actually distinguish between? Common candidates are intervention type, recipient population, discipline area, organisational sub-unit, or temporal phase. (2) Restructure measurement at the facet level: data capture, reporting templates, and analysis units should carry facet tags from the point of capture. Retrofitting aggregates after the fact is much harder than tagging at source. (3) Make recommendations at the facet level: when the design's claim is "this works for X but not Y", state that explicitly rather than as a population-level average. When the claim genuinely is population-level, defend why aggregation is interpretively warranted. (4) Test aggregation defensibility: before rolling facet-level signals up to a single number, ask whether a reader would draw the same operational conclusion from the aggregate as from the facet-level data. If not, the aggregate is hiding the actionable signal. (5) Compose with denominator-discipline: facet-level reach claims still need facet-level denominators (per audience, per discipline) to carry effect claims. Facet-before-aggregating and `correct-effect-claims-with-relevant-denominators` operate together: the first asks "what unit", the second asks "what scale". Engaged when measurement, reporting, and design recommendations operate at the facet level matching the causal story, and aggregation is reserved for cases where the homogeneity assumption can be defended. Failing when the document presents aggregate numbers (per-institution reach, programme-wide attendance, sector-level satisfaction) without checking whether the facets within those aggregates would point to different recommendations.

title: Match Region Weight to Argumentative Load
text: Match Region Weight to Argumentative Load Each region of an essay's AIF² wiring — outside (reader, decision), sensory (orienting context, evidence), internal (claim-and-evidence structure), active-surface (the operational move the argument licenses), preferences (glacial commitments and sector frame) — should occupy page-weight proportional to its argumentative load. The internal region (the design's claims and warrants) is typically the most load-bearing and should be the page-weight winner. When a low-load region — most often preferences (glacial context) or sensory (evidence summary) — runs longer than the internal region, the reader's perceptual unit becomes the heaviest thing on the page rather than the most load-bearing thing. Compress the over-developed region, shift the load to a sibling, mark it as a digression, or promote the region's status (if it's actually doing more work than the argument acknowledged). AIF² treats the essay as a typed open cover by regions, with each region playing a structural role analogous to a part of an Active Inference wiring diagram. In a well-balanced essay, the internal region (the system specification, claims, evidence-as-warrant) takes the most space because that's where the argument lives. Preferences (the glacial context that motivates the argument — sector frame, funder identity, audience) should be present but compact; the reader does not need a sector survey to be reminded that an institution is one of many actors. Sensory (orienting prose, evidence presentation) should scale with its support function — enough to ground the internal claims, not enough to dominate them. When these proportions invert — when, say, a section establishing "open research is one of many priorities" runs sixteen items of enumeration to land a one-sentence claim — the page-weight inversion confuses the reader about what the paper is actually arguing. The pattern operates on the axis: page-weight ↔ argumentative load. Irreducible: the reader's perceptual unit is what occupies the most page-weight; if the most page-weight is not the most load-bearing, the perceptual unit is misleading. Real costs: compressing an over-developed region risks losing detail that the argument actually needed. Shifting load to a footnote or annex moves the content out of the reader's primary scan path. Marking as digression weakens the section's relationship to the argument. Promoting a region requires admitting that the argument's scope was larger than declared. Each composition gives something up; the pattern's discipline is to choose explicitly rather than to leave the imbalance implicit and hope the reader gives the writer credit. Active dynamic: the pull toward over-development is strongest in evidence-citation work (a 2022 survey cited the eight themes; the writer reproduces all eight even though the claim only needs two), and in preferences-region work (the sector frame is invoked to motivate the argument, but the invocation grows into a survey of the frame rather than a brief gesture). The over-development feels like rigour at writing time; it reads as imbalance at reading time. - Preferences overrun: glacial context occupies more page-weight than the design region whose claims that context is supposed to motivate. - Sensory inflation: evidence-presentation dominates the claim it supports; the reader spends more time on the data than on what the data shows. - Exhaustive citation for incidental claim: a sub-claim that is genuinely supporting is given a 50-line evidence presentation as if it were load-bearing. - Enumeration without enumerative content: an N-item list is exhibited where the structural claim is that there exist many items, not that any specific item is doing work. This is `triad-inflation` scaled up — a sixteen-item list where two would suffice. - Meta-lede closing on overweight region: an over-developed region requires a "what this evidence tells us is..." summary at the end (because the reader's perceptual unit has drifted), which is itself a meta-lede failure on top of the imbalance. Match region weight to argumentative load. Pick one composition. (1) Compress in place. Augmentation schema: {:region <region-name> :compression-target <span-or-entity-id> :compression-ratio <approximate factor> :preserved-content <list>} Entity types produced: :compressed-region (the new tight version), optionally :source-reference-note (citing where the full content can be found if needed) Effect: the over-developed region shrinks to fit its argumentative load. Specific details that were over-presented are reduced to a sentence or a citation. Most appropriate when the over-developed content is incidental and the reader can take the structural claim without the enumerated specifics. (2) Shift load to a sibling region. Augmentation schema: {:from-region <overdeveloped-region> :to-region <footnote | annex | references> :shifted-content <list>} Entity types produced: :shifted-content-reference (the residual cross-reference in the original region) Effect: the heavy content moves to a footnote, annex, or references section; the original region retains only a brief gesture with a cross-reference. Most appropriate when the content has long-term value as reference material but does not belong in the argument's main scan path. (3) Mark as digression. Augmentation schema: {:digression-marker <prefix | sidebar | explicit-disclaimer> :return-point <span-or-entity-id>} Entity types produced: :digression-prefix, :return-marker Effect: the over-developed region is explicitly typed as a digression that the reader can skip without losing the argument. Weaker than (1) or (2) because the imbalance remains; appropriate when the content is genuinely interesting and the writer wants to keep it visible despite the imbalance. (4) Promote the region. Augmentation schema: {:promotion-target <region> :new-load-justification <claim that justifies the heavier weight>} Entity types produced: :promoted-region-claim (the new claim that makes the region's weight argumentatively load-bearing) Effect: the region's weight is retained, but its role in the argument is upgraded so the weight is justified. Appropriate when the over-development reveals that the writer was actually trying to make a heavier claim than the argument-spec captured. Engaged when each AIF² region's page-weight is proportional to its argumentative load, and when over-developed regions are either compressed, shifted, marked as digression, or promoted. A skeptical reader scrolling the section can tell from page-weight alone which region carries the most argumentative load. Failing when a preferences region (or any low-load region) is the heaviest unit on the page and the heaviest unit is not the load-bearing one.

title: Name the Decision Before the Framework
text: Name the Decision Before the Framework When a document exists to support an operational choice, it must name the choice before it unfolds the framework. The framework is there to warrant the decision, not to delay it. A reader who has to reconstruct the decision from pages of apparatus is being asked to do argumentative integration work the document should already have done. Writers often begin with models, taxonomies, and framing layers because those are easier to stabilise than a decision. The result is a document that feels thoughtful but leaves the live question implicit. This is not neutral ordering. It changes the reader's task from "evaluate this choice" to "infer what choice is even being proposed". In operational writing, that inversion is a coherence failure because the reader cannot tell what the framework is for. The pattern operates on the axis: framework-display <-/-> decision-clarity. Irreducible: either the document names the choice early enough for the reader to evaluate the rest as warrant, or it makes the reader infer the choice from surrounding machinery. Real costs: naming the decision early exposes it to challenge before all the nuances have been introduced. Writers resist this exposure by prefacing, layering, and framing. But a delayed decision makes every subsequent section harder to parse because the reader cannot tell which distinctions are load-bearing. Active dynamic: the temptation is strongest in papers that are partly analytical and partly programmatic. The writer fears sounding too blunt, so the bluntness is postponed until after the reader has already spent effort. - Framework-first drift: the document opens with layers, views, or distinctions while the operational choice remains unnamed. - Decision-by-implication: the recommendation is only recoverable from accumulations of evidence or from the conclusion. - Apparatus prestige: the framework is displayed as if its mere sophistication were itself a warrant. - Late thesis reveal: the section that finally states the choice reads like a surprise rather than like the point the paper has been prosecuting. Name the choice, then subordinate the framework to it. (1) State the decision in one sentence: say what should be built, adopted, rejected, or handed off. Do this before the explanatory framework expands. (2) Recast early sections as warrants: after the decision is named, let each framework component answer a visible question about why that choice follows. (3) Title for claim, not furniture: section headings should tell the reader what argumentative work is being done, not merely how many parts are coming. (4) Audit by inversion: ask whether a reader could delete the framework section and still say what choice the paper supports. If not, the decision has been hidden inside its warrant. Engaged when the reader can identify the operational choice in the opening movement and can read the rest of the document as support for that choice. Failing when the framework is intelligible but its bearing on a specific decision is still implicit until late in the paper.

title: Place Capabilities at the Scale of Their Absence
text: Place Capabilities at the Scale of Their Absence A capability should be placed at the scale where its absence is systematic and where its value can compound across cases. If the capability is locally absent in many institutions and only becomes economical, legible, or learnable when carried across cases, that is a warrant for network-scale provision rather than institution-by-institution expectation. Design arguments often slide from "institutions need X" to "therefore each institution should provide X". That step is not automatic. Many capabilities are precisely the ones local institutions are least able to sustain because they are thinly distributed, episodic, politically awkward, or only visible when evidence is aggregated across sites. The right question is not who needs the capability, but at what scale the capability can realistically exist and learn. The pattern operates on the axis: local ownership <-/-> viable bearing scale. Irreducible: either the capability can be expected to arise and persist locally, or the local absence is systematic enough that a higher-scale bearer is warranted. Real costs: moving a capability to network scale can look centralising, can increase coordination demands, and can obscure local variation if done crudely. But forcing a structurally absent capability back onto local actors does not preserve autonomy; it produces empty boxes in an organisational chart. Active dynamic: the pressure to localise comes from institutional norm and from the wish that every university should already be able to do the thing. The empirical test is whether they do. - Wishful localisation: the design assigns responsibility locally because local ownership sounds tidy, despite evidence of repeated absence. - Scale-blind diagnosis: the argument notes cross-case repetition of the same gap but still treats each case as an isolated deficit. - Economy denial: the capability requires comparison, aggregation, or specialist continuity that cannot be sustained in each site separately, but the document ignores this. - Bearer vagueness: the capability is said to matter, but no scale-specific bearer is named. Place the capability where it can exist, learn, and pay. (1) Diagnose the absence pattern: distinguish occasional local weakness from recurrent cross-site absence. (2) Ask what the capability needs to function: continuity, specialist expertise, comparative evidence, convening authority, or another property that may itself imply the right scale. (3) Name the bearer at that scale: if the answer is network-level, say so explicitly and defend why that bearer is better placed than each local institution. (4) Keep local interfaces explicit: higher-scale provision still needs local touchpoints, but those touchpoints are interfaces to the capability, not proof that the capability is locally borne. Engaged when the paper can show that capability placement follows from the pattern of absence and the conditions of viability, not from administrative preference. Failing when responsibilities are localised by default even though the argument's own evidence shows repeated local inability to carry them.

title: A Plan Is Not a List of Activities
text: A Plan Is Not a List of Activities A plan must name the commitments that are load-bearing, the decision points that branch the path, the observations that license the next step, and the conditions that would cause abandonment. A calendar-paginated bullet list ("Q0–Q4", "five-year roadmap", "monthly checkpoints") satisfies the form of a plan because succession-in-time already imposes ordering — but ordering is not planning, it is chronology. When the count of items becomes the perceptual unit, the decisions inside the plan are hidden in plain sight: five paragraphs of equal weight, of which perhaps two carry the actual branching. Plans accumulate calendar granularity because the calendar is the easiest scaffold. "Q0–Q4" satisfies the demand for a structured forward-look without forcing the writer to identify which moments are commitments and which are operational consequences of earlier commitments. The compulsion to enumerate every calendar slot reads as planning thoroughness, but it conceals which slots carry the real decisions. The reader cannot tell what would change if Q1 went badly versus if Q4 went badly — the items look symmetric on the page. Adjacent surface failure: when several sections in the same document carry counted headings ("Five operational roles", "Three things change each quarter", "Five quarterly milestones", "Five projects, five offer domains"), the rhetorical pattern itself becomes the perceptual unit; see `writing-coherence/triad-inflation` and `writing-coherence/structural-style-inconsistency` for the prose-side surface of the same compulsion. The pattern operates on the axis: activity-enumeration <-/-> decision-structure visibility. Irreducible: either the plan exposes its decision points and commitments as the primary structural units, or it presents activities in temporal order and asks the reader to infer where the decisions sit. Real costs: exposing the decision structure makes the plan look smaller than the bullet-count suggests. "Two decisions across a year, with operational consequences in between" reads less impressive than "five quarterly milestones", and stakeholders who expect a roadmap may read the smaller shape as under-planned. Naming decisions also exposes the gap between commitment and contingency — many "milestones" turn out to be operational consequences of earlier decisions rather than independent commitments — and that exposure is uncomfortable because it concentrates risk into a small number of identifiable moments rather than diffusing it across the calendar. Active dynamic: the pull toward enumeration recurs every time a plan must be presented to a stakeholder, funder, or board that expects a "roadmap"; the calendar grid is a ready-made format and asking "what are the decisions?" is harder than asking "what happens in each quarter?". The pull also recurs when the writer is themselves uncertain about the decision structure and the calendar offers a way to look planned without having to commit to which moments are the pivots. - Calendar-imposed granularity: the plan has N items because the year has N quarters or the programme has N months, not because there are N structural beats. The grid's count, not the design's, sets the item count. - Decision points disguised as milestones: a milestone like "first evaluation wave" hides the actual decision (which instrument; centralised vs distributed configuration; how findings get fed back) inside an activity label. - Activity-not-commitment confusion: each bullet describes what gets *done* in a period without saying what is being *committed to* by doing it, so the reader cannot tell what failing to do it would forfeit. - Symmetric-list flatness: every period gets a paragraph of equal weight, so the reader cannot tell which periods are pivots and which are operational. This is the form-side analogue of `triad-inflation`'s third-item freeloading, but at the section level. - Abandon-condition silence: no statement of "if X has not happened by Y, we [pause / re-plan / stand down]"; the plan reads as if every step is presumed to succeed. - To-do-list-as-plan: a flat list of items presented as a plan, with no internal structure beyond enumeration — common in "follow-on work", "what we would still need", "future directions" sections. Distinguishable from a genuine plan by the absence of any decision, observation, or abandon condition attached to any item. - Pre-announced count in heading: a section titled "Five quarterly milestones" or "Seven checks" or "Three walks" tells the reader that the count is what is being delivered, which is a tell that the items are not load-bearing in their own right. Subordinate the calendar to the decision structure. (1) Locate the decision points first: identify the moments where the plan branches (continue / vary / stand down; centralised / distributed; bridge / self-finance) and make those the primary structural units. The number of decision points sets the plan's shape, not the number of calendar slots. (2) Demote calendar to scaffold: keep dates where they constrain (deadlines, dependencies, evidence-readiness) but stop treating every calendar slot as a planning unit. Quarters without a decision or commitment can be summarised in a sentence rather than given a paragraph.
