(3) Distinguish commitments from activities: "we will hire a Training Manager by Q0" is a commitment; "the Training Manager schedules trainers" is an activity that follows from the commitment. Plans should foreground commitments; activities follow. (4) Couple decisions to closure mechanisms: each decision point names its evidence-input and its possible outcomes. This is `bind-open-questions-to-closure-mechanisms` operating inside the plan rather than around it. (5) State abandon conditions: each commitment that could plausibly fail names what would trigger reconsideration. A plan with no abandon conditions is a plan that has not been pressure-tested. (6) Title for the decision, not the count: section headings should name what argumentative or operational work the section does, not how many items follow. "Quarterly milestones through to the Year-2 decision" beats "Five quarterly milestones". Engaged when the plan's decision-and-commitment structure is recoverable in fewer items than the calendar-grid version would suggest, and when each decision point has a named evidence-input, possible outcomes, and an abandon condition. Failing when the count of bullets matches the count of calendar slots (or, more generally, when the item count is a property of the presentation format rather than of the underlying design). Diagnostic question: if a reader saw only the section's headings and item counts, could they tell which moments are pivots and which are operational consequences? If no, the plan is operating as an enumeration.

title: Present the Graph as Edges, Not Per-Node Adjacency Lists
text: Present the Graph as Edges, Not Per-Node Adjacency Lists When the load-bearing structural claim of a section is the *topology* of a small typed graph — the typed exchanges between five roles, the dependency couplings between seven capabilities, the message-passing contract between three layers — the section must exhibit the edges, not list the per-node outgoing-edge stacks. Per-node adjacency listings ("Node A hands to B; hands to C; hands to D. Node B hands to A; hands to D. ...") give the reader N paragraphs from which the graph's E edges must be reconstructed by inference. The page-weight scales with N (the number of nodes), not with E (the number of edges); the reader's perceptual unit becomes "list of role-paragraphs each ending in a hand-off stack" rather than "graph of typed contracts." The cure is to exhibit the edges directly — as a table, an explicit edge-list, or a topology paragraph — and let the role descriptions carry only their per-node identity work. AIF² and similar wiring-diagram framings treat systems as typed graphs. When a system has 4–8 nodes and 6–12 typed edges, the topology is genuinely the load-bearing structure: the design's contribution is *which edges exist between which nodes carrying what data*. Prose has two natural ways to present a small graph: (a) walk the nodes, listing each node's outgoing edges as the node is introduced; (b) introduce the nodes briefly and then exhibit the edge set as its own structural unit. Mode (a) is locally readable (each role-paragraph stands on its own) but globally illegible (the topology is only recoverable by mental aggregation). Mode (b) is structurally honest — the edges are visible as edges. The pattern recurs in role-design sections, layer-architecture sections, and message-passing-contract sections. The pattern operates on the axis: per-node locality ↔ topology visibility. Irreducible: a prose presentation either lists outgoing edges under each source node (and forces the reader to reconstruct the graph), or exhibits the edge set as a structural unit visible at a glance. The same edges, two presentation modes; the reader's perceptual unit differs. Real costs: per-node adjacency lists are easier to write — they preserve the natural narrative order ("Here is role A. Role A does X. Role A hands to B, C, D."). Exhibiting the edge set as a unit requires the writer to factor the topology out of the role descriptions, which can read as more abstract or as breaking the role-by-role flow. Some readers (those who think node-first) find adjacency listings easier to absorb; others (those who think edge-first) find topology exhibits clearer. The pattern's discipline is to match the presentation to the *claim's* load: if the claim is "the design's contribution is the contracts between roles," exhibit the contracts; if the claim is "each role has its own work," exhibit the roles. Active dynamic: the pull toward adjacency listing is strongest when the role descriptions and the hand-offs are mutually informative — the role's identity partly IS the hand-offs it owns. The writer reaches for "describe the role; then say what it does in the network" without realising that the topology has now been distributed across N paragraphs. - Adjacency stacks: each node-paragraph ends in a stack of "hands to X; hands to Y; hands to Z" clauses; the reader sees N stacks, must mentally union them into the edge set. - Page-weight scales with N, not E: if N=5 and E=8, the section has 5 role-paragraphs (page-weight ~5 × paragraph) instead of 5 short role-identities + 1 edge-list (page-weight ~5 × sentence + 1 × short-list). - Redundant edge mention: edge X→Y appears in node X's "outgoing" list, but the reader can't easily verify that Y's "incoming" obligation matches. Reciprocal edges (X→Y plus Y→X) get listed twice in two different paragraphs. - Topology only inferable, not visible: a skeptical reader cannot answer "how many edges does this design have?" without reading every node-paragraph and aggregating. This is the structural analogue of `plan-as-enumeration`'s "decision points disguised as milestones" failure. - Triad-on-every-node inflation: each role-paragraph ends in three or four hand-offs even when some roles only have one or two genuine outgoing edges — the writer pads to maintain stylistic parallelism, inflating the apparent edge count. Match the presentation to the load-bearing claim. Pick one composition. (1) Exhibit edges as a table. Augmentation schema: {:edge-columns <list of column names: From, To, Data-on-wire, etc.> :edge-rows <list of typed exchanges>} Entity types produced: :edge-table, :typed-exchange-row (one per edge) Effect: the topology is visible at a glance. Per-node descriptions become brief (one sentence each) since the hand-offs no longer live inside the role-paragraphs. Most appropriate when the edges have multiple typed properties worth showing (data shape, cadence, criticality). (2) Exhibit edges as a labelled list. Augmentation schema: {:edge-format (:source-arrow-target | :pair-symbol-data) :edge-items <list>} Entity types produced: :typed-exchange-item (one per edge) Effect: lighter touch than a table; reads as a focused prose-list rather than a structured display. Most appropriate when the edges are easy to describe in a phrase each and a table would feel heavy. (3) Exhibit topology in a paragraph. Augmentation schema: {:topology-style :flow-narrative | :coupling-summary :grouping-axis <by-cadence | by-criticality | by-direction>} Entity types produced: :topology-paragraph (one paragraph describing the graph as a whole) Effect: most prose-natural; loses some specificity but preserves narrative flow. Most appropriate when the edges are few enough to summarise in one paragraph and the writer wants to keep the reading-pace prose-y. Engaged when the section's edge set is visible as its own structural unit — a table, a labelled list, or a topology paragraph — and per-node descriptions carry only per-node identity work. A skeptical reader scrolling the section can answer "how many typed edges does this design have, and what does each edge carry?" without aggregating across multiple paragraphs. Failing when each node-paragraph ends in a hand-off-stack and the topology is only inferable by union.

title: Separate Configurable Choices from Load-Bearing Couplings
text: Separate Configurable Choices from Load-Bearing Couplings Robust system arguments distinguish between what may vary and what cannot be broken without changing the system's character. Configurable choices are not the same as load-bearing couplings. If the document treats both alike, it cannot tell adaptability from drift or experimentation from self-cancellation. Once a design is described, everything in it can look equally optional. That flattening is attractive because it makes the system seem flexible. But real flexibility depends on knowing which parts are safely adjustable and which relationships are carrying the design's causal load. Without that distinction, adaptation becomes indistinguishable from erosion. The pattern operates on the axis: permissible variation <-/-> constitutive coupling. Irreducible: some elements can vary without changing the system's identity, while others are load-bearing enough that breaking them yields a different system, not merely a local variant. Real costs: declaring couplings to be load-bearing narrows room for local tailoring and invites challenge about whether the system is over-specified. But failing to declare them shifts the cost into execution, where every local variation can claim legitimacy and no principled line exists between robust adaptation and silent abandonment. Active dynamic: the temptation is strongest when the writer wants the system to look portable across heterogeneous contexts. The pressure then is to describe everything as configurable. - Flat optionality: every component is presented as if locally selectable, leaving no visible system identity. - Hidden brittleness: a coupling is in fact essential, but the document only reveals that after failure. - Adaptation laundering: a change that removes a causal dependency is described as context-sensitive tailoring. - Scope mush: the paper blurs core architecture, local implementation choices, and cosmetic differences into one undifferentiated bundle. Mark the load-bearing couplings and fence the configuration space. (1) Name the couplings that make the system the system: these are the relationships whose removal would void the design's logic. (2) Separate them from tunable parameters: delivery cadence, staffing pattern, local framing, or tooling may be adjustable without touching the core coupling. (3) Use checks to police the boundary: if a local variation severs a load-bearing relation, classify it as system change rather than as mere adaptation. (4) Document the reason for each declared coupling: say what causal work it does, so the constraint is legible rather than arbitrary. Engaged when the paper clearly distinguishes adjustable design choices from constitutive relations and can explain why the latter matter. Failing when local variation is celebrated in the abstract but no principled boundary protects the system from dissolving into unrelated local practices.

title: Single-Seed Results Need Multi-Seed Validation
text: Single-Seed Results Need Multi-Seed Validation A stochastic simulation's output under a single random seed is not, by itself, a finding. Apparent contrasts between configurations may be sampling artefacts of the particular seed sequence rather than substantive differences in the dynamics. Reportable per-parameter contrasts must be averaged across multiple independent seeds, with cross-seed mean and variance disclosed; single-seed runs are reserved for development and clearly labelled if shown. This is true even when the simulation is deterministic given a seed — determinism establishes reproducibility, not generality. Stochastic simulations are common substrates for design-supporting claims, especially in active-inference, agent-based, and Monte-Carlo work. The simulation's output depends on a random-number-generator state. When configurations are compared without proper RNG isolation between them, apparent contrasts can arise from where in the seed-space the simulation happened to land rather than from the parameter difference being tested. Even with proper RNG resets, a single seed produces only one path through a distribution of possible trajectories; without sampling that distribution, the reader cannot tell whether an observed contrast is a real signal or an artefact of one fortunate or unfortunate trajectory. The discipline is harder than it looks: it requires explicit seed-reset infrastructure, multi-seed runners, cross-seed aggregation, and a reporting convention that disciplines the writer to disclose variance whenever they report contrast. The pattern operates on the axis: single-trajectory observation <-/-> distribution-grounded claim. Irreducible: a stochastic simulation either has its results characterised across enough seeds to estimate the distribution they came from, or its claimed contrasts may be artefacts of one trajectory's particular random walk. Real costs: multi-seed runs multiply simulation time by N, and cross-seed aggregation adds reporting overhead. Researchers under deadline often reach for single-seed runs, then write up their contrasts as if they were findings. Reviewers without simulation experience may not notice that variance is missing. The temptation is sharpest when a single-seed contrast looks compelling — exactly the situation where the contrast is most likely to be partially or wholly artefactual. Active dynamic: the failure recurs whenever the writer wants to claim a per-parameter difference (configuration A produces different outcome from configuration B) without first verifying that the difference survives across-seed averaging. - Sampling-artefact-as-finding: a contrast observed under one seed (or one seed sequence) is reported as a finding without checking whether it survives multi-seed averaging. - Seed-leakage: RNG state evolves across configurations during sequential testing, so apparent contrasts between configurations are partially driven by where in the seed-space each test happened to land. This is *worse* than single-seed-per-configuration because the contrasts can be generated by the shared evolving state rather than by the parameter difference. - Variance-blindness: only point estimates are reported across configurations; the reader cannot tell whether a 0.13 difference is meaningful or noise. - Premature publication of artefactual contrasts: a single-seed result becomes a quoted finding in subsequent work or in a paper, and only later (sometimes years later) is exposed as not surviving replication. - Replication-by-coincidence: a re-run of the same code with the same seed reproduces the result and is mistaken for replication; what is needed is reproduction across *different* seeds. - Determinism-as-warrant: deterministic-given-seed simulation behaviour is mistaken for generalisable claim; "we got the same number" is conflated with "this number is robust". - Audit absence: there is no record of how many seeds were run, what their CIs look like, or whether any contrast survives multi-seed averaging. Sample the distribution before claiming the contrast. (1) Reset RNG state explicitly between configurations. Inherit nothing from the prior run; seeds are not just initial conditions but full simulation state. Configurations should be testable in any order without the result depending on order. (2) Run each configuration under N independent seeds. Default thresholds: ≥20 seeds for sensitivity sweeps and parameter robustness checks, ≥50 seeds for headline findings that will appear in reports or papers. Document the seed range used. (3) Aggregate per-configuration: report cross-seed mean and confidence interval, not point estimate from a single seed. When the underlying distribution is non-Gaussian, prefer empirical CIs (quantile-based) over standard-error approximations. (4) For per-parameter contrasts: verify that confidence intervals do not overlap before claiming differentiation. If they overlap, the contrast is not robustly differentiated under the seed regime tested; either run more seeds or reduce the contrast claim's strength. (5) Distinguish statistical from illustrative runs. Single-seed runs used for development, debugging, or pedagogic figure generation should be explicitly labelled "illustrative" or "development run"; never reported as findings. (6) Compose with `aif/term-to-channel-traceability`. Each reportable claim discloses its seed range, configuration parameters, and the time window over which the score is integrated; this turns the seed discipline into an audit-trail discipline. (7) When the simulation is deterministic given seed, document this as reproducibility, not generality. Reproduction requires *different* seeds producing consistent ranges; same-seed reruns establish determinism only. Engaged when every per-parameter contrast in the simulation's reportable output appears with a cross-seed mean and CI, the seed range used is documented, and contrast claims are made only when CIs do not overlap. Failing when single-seed numbers appear in tables or text without variance disclosure, or when contrast claims are stated without checking whether the difference survives multi-seed averaging, or when the simulation's seed-reset discipline cannot be verified by reading the code.

title: Tag Evidence by Timescale When the Section Mixes Rates
text: Tag Evidence by Timescale When the Section Mixes Rates Evidence presented in prose has a timescale. Quarterly returns are fast (the value can move within months); focus-group findings are medium (slow to gather, stable over a year or two); sector surveys are slow (a one-time snapshot, expensive to refresh); institutional identities and funder structures are glacial. When a section synthesizes evidence from multiple timescales without distinguishing them, the reader cannot tell whether a verdict is fast-changing news that will look different next quarter or long-settled state that has been stable for years. Synthesis sentences in particular ("this evidence tells us X") are I3 failure sites because they fuse co-equal sentence-level claims across timescales the underlying evidence does not actually treat as co-equal. Working papers often draw on evidence from several timescales at once — quarterly delivery counts (fast), a one-time priorities survey (slow), a recent indicators pilot (medium), the sector's standing identity (glacial). Each is legitimate; together they form the evidence base. But the prose tends to flatten them, presenting each as one more sentence-level fact alongside the others. The flattening is most acute in the synthesis paragraph at the end of a section — where the writer needs to draw conclusions and reaches for "in short, this evidence tells us..." or similar, fusing facts that were measured on different timescales into one verdict the reader can't decompose. This is the section-scope analogue of `argument-as-coverage-checklist`'s timescale-flattening failure mode, but localised to a specific synthesis sentence rather than the argument-spec as a whole. The pattern operates on the axis: synthesis legibility ↔ timescale fidelity. Irreducible: either each evidence claim carries enough timescale context for the reader to know how fast its truth-value moves, or the synthesis fuses incompatible rates into a verdict that hides what it stands on. Real costs: adding timescale context to every evidence claim is wordy and pedagogical; the reader doesn't need "(fast, quarterly returns, 2024–26)" on every sentence. The cost is paid where the timescales actually matter — at synthesis points, at moments of cross-timescale comparison, and where a slow-changing fact and a fast-changing fact bear on the same conclusion. Active dynamic: the pull toward flattening is strongest in the synthesis paragraph. The writer wants to draw a single conclusion ("delivery happened at network scale but didn't settle practice change"); the underlying evidence supports multi-rate sub-conclusions ("delivery, measured fast, happened at scale; measurability of practice change, measured medium, is mixed; further evidence, on a longer horizon, is expected"). The fast verdict is honest about what the fast evidence shows; the synthesis fuses it with medium and longer-horizon notes and the reader can't tell which part is settled and which is still moving. - Timescale-flatten in synthesis: "this evidence tells us X" where the evidence is multi-rate. - Temporal ambiguity: a finding is named without saying when it was measured ("a final report reports a mixed verdict") so the reader can't tell if it's settled or fresh. - Historical-and-current coordinated by "and": a slow fact and a fast fact joined as if co-equal claims, when they actually belong to different epistemic categories. - Forward-looking promise without timescale: "various efforts are expected to contribute evidence" without saying on what horizon, by when, with what update cadence. - In short opener: "In short" announcing a synthesis without typing the synthesis's evidence — most common failure surface. Tag evidence by timescale at the points where the timescales matter. Pick one composition based on the section's structure. (1) Inline timescale tags. Augmentation schema: {:tag-locations <list of clauses to tag> :tag-format (:parenthetical | :prefix | :em-dash)} Entity types produced: :timescale-tagged-claim Effect: each relevant claim gains a small parenthetical or prefix tagging its timescale. Light-touch; preserves the existing structure. (2) Reorder by timescale. Augmentation schema: {:order :fast-first | :slow-first | :recent-first :grouping-style <by-paragraph | by-sentence>} Entity types produced: :timescale-grouped-section Effect: paragraphs (or sentences) reorder so all fast evidence groups together, then medium, then slow. Heavier rewrite; produces strong visual segregation of timescales. (3) Distinguish in synthesis. Augmentation schema: {:synthesis-target <span-or-entity-id> :timescale-types-distinguished <list of timescales>} Entity types produced: :timescale-tagged-synthesis-claim, optionally :forward-looking-evidence-note (separate sentence for forward-looking content) Effect: the synthesis sentence is rewritten to name each timescale's contribution separately rather than fusing them. Most appropriate when the body of the section is well-organised but the closing synthesis fuses what the body distinguished. Engaged when every synthesis sentence and every cross-evidence comparison names the timescales of the evidence it draws on; a skeptical reader can tell which part of the verdict will look different next quarter and which has been stable for years. Failing when "this evidence tells us X" or "in short, X" coordinates evidence from incompatible rates without distinguishing them.

title: Treat Content Refresh as Second-Order When Conditions Bind
text: Treat Content Refresh as Second-Order When Conditions Bind When the main constraints on outcomes are institutional conditions such as time, incentives, leadership support, workflow fit, and role ownership, redesigning training content is a second-order lever and should be argued as such. Content refresh may improve fit and uptake at the margin, but it should not be presented as the principal mechanism of change when the evidence says the binding constraints lie elsewhere. Content is the most visible and most controllable part of a training system, so it attracts disproportionate reform energy. This is understandable but often incoherent. If institutions are not giving staff time, reward, reinforcement, or practical routes to enact what training teaches, then even well-designed content will hit a ceiling set by those missing conditions. The causal story must follow the binding constraint, not the convenience of the intervention. The pattern operates on the axis: content optimisation <-/-> condition-setting leverage. Irreducible: if the limiting factor is mainly the surrounding institutional condition, then content redesign cannot honestly be described as the primary route to materially different outcomes. Real costs: saying content is second-order can feel anticlimactic, especially to teams whose main tool is curriculum design. It can also seem to under-value real improvements in relevance, disciplinary fit, or pedagogy. The point is not that content does not matter; it is that it matters within a larger causal envelope whose boundaries are set elsewhere. Active dynamic: the slippage recurs whenever demand signals about preferred topics or formats are treated as if they had already identified the dominant outcome lever. - Content solutionism: dissatisfaction with the current offer is treated as proof that a better offer would solve the larger problem. - Constraint displacement: evidence about incentives, recognition, or workflow barriers is acknowledged and then sidelined while the argument returns to curriculum. - Marginal-gain inflation: local improvements in fit are narrated as if they implied system-level change. - Instrument myopia: the intervention is defined by what the programme can easily change, rather than by what the evidence shows to be causally limiting. Argue content as a subordinate lever inside the binding conditions. (1) State the binding constraints first: name the institutional conditions that are doing the real limiting work. (2) Describe content refresh in its proper role: better fit, less alienation, improved uptake, or stronger local usefulness. (3) Link content gains to condition-setting mechanisms: show what additional structures would be required for better training to convert into changed practice. (4) Refuse overclaiming: if the surrounding conditions remain unchanged, say that content refresh alone is unlikely to produce materially different institutional outcomes. Engaged when the paper treats content redesign as one component of a wider system and explicitly subordinates it to the binding institutional conditions. Failing when the document's own evidence shows that incentives and support dominate, yet the recommendations still imply that curriculum revision is the main route to change.

title: Turn Design Into Checks
text: Turn Design Into Checks A design is not operational when it is merely describable. It becomes operational when it is accompanied by checks that can tell whether it is being upheld, drifting, or failing. Invariants, indicators, threshold rules, scenario tests, and handoff conditions are not optional implementation detail; they are part of the design's coherence. Writers often stop at architecture. They name roles, flows, and principles, and the design sounds complete because it can be narrated. But a narrated design without checks cannot distinguish faithful enactment from decorative adoption. The missing move is from "what the system is supposed to be" to "how we would know whether that remains true in operation". The pattern operates on the axis: described design <-/-> testable design. Irreducible: either the system includes ways to detect whether its critical properties hold, or those properties remain aspirational. Real costs: checks can feel reductive, can expose the weakness of concepts that sounded rich in prose, and can create obligations to gather evidence. But without them, the document has no disciplined way to tell robust configuration from ceremonial language. Active dynamic: principles are easier to write than thresholds; roles are easier to name than to validate; handoffs are easier to describe than to monitor. - Principle without witness: the document states an invariant but gives no observable sign by which it could be checked. - Threshold avoidance: action is said to depend on "sufficient" evidence, uptake, or readiness, but no threshold logic is named. - Scenario fragility: a design sounds coherent in the happy path but has not been pressure-tested against foreseeable failure cases. - Handoff opacity: transitions between phases or roles are described without entry or exit conditions. Express critical design claims as checks. (1) Extract invariants: identify which properties must remain true for the system still to count as itself. (2) Attach observables: for each invariant, specify what evidence, indicator, or event would count as a witness. (3) Define thresholds or triggers where possible: name the conditions under which the system changes phase, escalates, hands off, or revises. (4) Add at least one hostile scenario: show how the checks discriminate success from a plausible failure or mimic configuration. Engaged when the design's most important claims have corresponding observables, thresholds, or scenario tests. Failing when the reader can describe the system elegantly but still cannot tell what evidence would show that it is functioning as intended.

title: Verified Rewrite from Diagnostic Annotation
text: Verified Rewrite from Diagnostic Annotation Rewriting a diagnostic annotation into a verified improvement is a typed transformation f:(A, B) → C, not a textual edit. A is the typed diagnostic; B is the rewrite plan (composition-id chosen from the cited pattern's COMPOSITIONS menu, plus any augmentation for judgment calls); C is the post-rewrite tuple of new prose, updated annotation graph, and invariant-delta. The rewrite is *verified* iff no invariant in the post-state is weaker than in the pre-state AND the cited pattern's CHECK clause holds on the new span. Without verification, "fixing the diagnostic" is hope; with verification, the same typed problem cannot recur because the typed precondition that surfaced it no longer holds. When a diagnostic survey produces a list of structural problems and a rewriter sets out to address them, the typical move is "read the prose, fix what reads badly, move on." This works locally but accumulates failure modes: (1) the rewrite may close one diagnostic at the cost of opening another (a fix that compresses a region-balance issue may flatten timescale separation as a side effect); (2) the rewrite's *reason* is not recorded, so when the prose later drifts back toward the original failure, the prior rewrite cannot be cited or built on; (3) the rewriter's choices are not typed against the pattern that motivated the diagnostic, so "good prose" can drift away from the structural property the pattern was guarding. Typed rewriting solves all three by making the rewrite a function of (diagnostic, composition-choice) with verification against the invariant audit. The closure trace records the transformation so it can be inspected, reverted, or pattern-mined. The type signature, concretely: ``` A : a diagnostic annotation (:hx-type :annotation/comment) carrying {:endpoints [{:annotated <section, passage>} {:source :pattern-name <flexiarg-path> :passage <field-from-pattern>}] :severity <level> :status :open} B : a rewrite plan {:composition-id <id-from-pattern's-COMPOSITIONS-menu> :augmentation <judgment calls for ambiguity, optional>} C : a post-rewrite tuple — refined for entity-level discipline (the sheaf-of-rewrite reading; see below) {:prose <:after text — global section, redundant given operations + glue> :entities-before [{:id :eN :type <entity-type> :fate <keep|drop|replace|keep-with-glue-adjustment> :span "..."} ...] :operations [{:op <drop|keep|add|replace|move> :target :eN :rationale "..." :pattern-ref <optional flexiarg path> :with-entities <list of new entities for :replace and :add>} ...] :glue-adjustments [{:effect <effect-kind> :on :eN :caused-by [:op :target ...] :note "..."} ...] :annotations <new/updated annotations on the new prose> :invariant-delta {invariant [before-status after-status] ...} :verification {:check-clause-passes? <bool-or-quantified> :invariants-weakened [] :invariants-unchanged [...] :status :verified | :unverified}} ``` The entity-level decomposition treats the affected paragraph as a typed open cover, each entity carrying its type (`:meta-lede-transition`, `:question`, `:empirical-observation`, `:normative-claim`, `:hedged-closure-mechanism-gesture`, `:parking-closer`, `:closure-owner-reference`, etc.) and its fate under the rewrite. Each operation is a *local section* — a typed transformation on one entity. Glue-adjustments are the *compatibility conditions on overlaps* — derived effects on entities adjacent to a local operation (e.g., dropping a meta-lede forces the following clause to capitalize as sentence-initial; dropping a parenthetical hedge forces the preceding clause to grow its own terminal period). The sheaf-theoretic reading is not metaphor: local sections that satisfy compatibility on overlaps uniquely glue to the global section (the new prose). A rewrite is *verified* when (i) each operation is well-typed against its target entity's type, (ii) glue-adjustments are exhibited rather than left implicit, (iii) the invariant-delta has no [pass fail] entries, and (iv) the pattern's CHECK clause holds on the new entities at their declared types. The pattern operates on the axis: prose-correctness <-/-> structural-property-preservation. Irreducible: a rewrite either preserves the typed graph the diagnostic was annotating, or it changes the graph in a way that may invalidate other typed properties. There is no "neutral" textual rewrite — every change to the prose either updates the typed annotation graph or leaves the graph stale. Real costs: typed rewriting requires that the diagnostic be properly annotated (with a pattern citation, not a free-text complaint), that the cited pattern have explicit COMPOSITIONS, and that the post-state audit be computable. Each of these prerequisites is itself work. For one-off prose passes the overhead may exceed the value; the discipline pays off on artifacts that will be rewritten repeatedly, that have evolving structure, or that need to be auditable later. Active dynamic: the pull toward untyped rewriting is the temptation of "just fix it." Especially in writing work, the rewriter's skill is exactly the ability to fix prose without a spec — typed rewriting can feel like it's slowing the rewriter's strength. The right framing: typed rewriting doesn't replace the skill; it audits the skill's outputs so they accumulate rather than churn. - Closure without verification: a :before/:after record with no invariant-delta — looks like typed rewriting, isn't. Common in hand-rolled sweep logs. - Composition-id implicit: :scaffolding-used recorded too coarsely (e.g., the v6 sweep's `(:pattern :annotation)`) without naming which composition from the pattern's menu was applied. The choice is not auditable. - Invariant-delta absent: the rewrite changes the prose but the audit block isn't updated. No way to tell whether the rewrite strengthened the typed graph, weakened it, or left it unchanged. - Pattern-citation absent or wrong: a diagnostic without a `:source.pattern-name`, or one citing a pattern whose COMPOSITIONS don't actually fit the diagnostic, is not actionable by typed rewrite. The diagnostic is a complaint until a fitting pattern exists. - Verification by self-report: the rewriter declares the rewrite "clean" without an external check (machine-evaluated CHECK clause, or peer review of the invariant-delta). `:sweep-status :clean` is not by itself a verification result; it's an assertion. - Diagnostic deleted, not closed: the annotation is removed from the graph after the rewrite. Provenance lost; future drifts back toward the original failure cannot be detected because the typed precondition that surfaced it is no longer in the graph to be re-evaluated. - Blob-rewrite: the closure records a `:before` paragraph and an `:after` paragraph and treats the substitution as atomic, even when the rewrite plan internally names several structural moves. The typed plan ("drop the hedge, replace the parking-closer with a closure-mechanism reference, capitalize the following clause") is hidden inside a single string swap. This is the case the entity/operations/glue decomposition exists to refuse. A blob-rewrite is detectable by the absence of `:entities-before` / `:operations` / `:glue-adjustments` in the closure — even if the textual change is correct, the structural transformation is not exhibited and so cannot be inspected or composed. - Glue-adjustments left implicit: an operation has derived effects on adjacent entities (sentence-initial capitalization, missing terminal period, broken cross-reference) and the rewrite produces the textually-correct result without surfacing these as named adjustments. The reader cannot tell which textual changes are *operations* (load-bearing) and which are *forced compatibility moves* (consequential). Under the sheaf reading: the global section appears in the prose but the local sections that produced it are not visible. Structure each rewrite as f:(A, B) → C with explicit type signature. (1) Type the diagnostic at survey time: every `:annotation/comment` cites a pattern. If no pattern fits, either find one in the library, write a new flexiarg, or downgrade to a typeless complaint so it's clear the diagnostic isn't yet actionable. (2) Make composition-id explicit: the closure block names which item from the pattern's COMPOSITIONS list was applied. Compositions are stable per-pattern (their numbering survives flexiarg edits); the closure cites by composition number or canonical name. (3) Record the augmentation: any judgment call the composition required (which words to drop, which live misreadings to preserve, which cross-reference to bind to) is captured in :augmentation. The composition + augmentation together specify the rewrite uniquely. (4) Compute the invariant-delta: snapshot the audit before applying the rewrite, recompute after, record the delta as `{invariant [before-status after-status]}`. An empty delta means the rewrite was textual only (which may be fine, but should be visible). A non-empty delta is the rewrite's structural contribution. (5) Verify before closing: check the cited pattern's CHECK clause holds on the new span. Check no invariant weakened in the audit. Only then mark `:status :closed` and stamp `:verification :verified`. (6) Retain the diagnostic, don't delete it: closure preserves provenance. Future drifts back toward the original failure can be detected because the closed annotation is still in the graph, and the typed precondition can be re-evaluated against the (possibly drifted) prose. (7) Decompose the affected paragraph into typed entities before applying operations. Each entity carries an `:id`, a `:type` from a registered vocabulary (`:meta-lede-transition`, `:question`, `:empirical-observation`, `:normative-claim`, `:hedged-closure-mechanism-gesture`, `:parking-closer`, `:closure-owner-reference`, `:closure-support-reference`, `:closure-event-reference`, etc. — extensible per pattern domain), and a `:span` quoting its verbatim text. The entity vocabulary is the typed open cover of the paragraph. (8) Express the rewrite as a sequence of operations on entities, not as a blob substitution. Each operation names one of `{:drop :keep :add :replace :move}`, the target entity id, a rationale, and (for `:replace` and `:add`) the new entities being introduced — each itself typed and id'd. The augmentation fields from B map 1-to-1 to entity types in the `:with-entities` of `:replace`/`:add` operations (e.g., `:closure-owner` in augmentation produces a `:closure-owner-reference` entity). The operations list is the sequence of local sections; the global section (the new prose) is recoverable by applying the operations. (9) Surface glue-adjustments as explicit derived effects. When an operation forces compatibility moves on adjacent entities (capitalization, punctuation, cross-reference repair), record each as a `:glue-adjustment` with the effect kind, the affected entity, and the operation that caused it. This is the compatibility-on-overlaps condition made first-class; without it, the reader cannot distinguish operations (load-bearing) from glue (consequential), and rewrites cannot be composed cleanly. Engaged when every closed diagnostic has a complete f:(A, B) → C trace including composition-id, augmentation if any, invariant-delta, and verification status. A skeptical reader can inspect any closed annotation and reconstruct (i) what the original typed problem was, (ii) what rewrite plan was applied, (iii) what typed property the rewrite preserved or strengthened. Failing when closure records the textual change but not the structural transformation — i.e., when "fixed" cannot be distinguished from "fixed in a way that compensates for the cost it imposed elsewhere."

title: Protected Interaction
text: Protected Interaction Interaction time is protected when the delivery structure absorbs local variation. Where sessions try to cover everything uniformly, interaction shrinks, core concepts get diluted, and trainers feel unprepared to deliver outside their expertise. T3 sessions cover a broad range of open research topics; trainers have diverse disciplinary backgrounds and cannot realistically deliver all content with equal confidence. You want trainers to tailor content to local needs without losing coherence or confidence. A pilot with a single, fixed module and no need for local tailoring. Sessions vary in length and audience, and trainers need guidance on what to trim or expand. One-size-fits-all agendas create fatigue, reduce interaction, and leave trainers unable to cover core material; impostor syndrome compounds the problem for professional staff delivering outside their expertise. Trainers regularly overrun, report dropping content ad hoc, or describe impostor syndrome about breadth. Define a delivery spine: a minimal core (two to three modules) plus named elective modules and a required co-working block for local adaptation. Provide time budgets and "drop-in" variants for short sessions. A spine creates predictable structure while legitimising adaptation; it protects interaction time and reduces overload; trainers who focus on what they know deliver more confidently. "My top tips are to either give it more time than you expect" (T1); "I didn't feel prepared to talk about all the areas" (T2A); "There's a little bit of impostor syndrome, because it's still new to me and no one's taught me it!" (T3); "Probably 80% of the stuff I learned... I don't then replicate" (T2B). COM-B: "I am psychologically able" M=4.85. A fixed core preserves coherence while electives absorb local variance, keeping interaction time intact and reducing the breadth-versus-depth tension. If we deliver the full deck uniformly, interaction time shrinks, core concepts get diluted, and trainers feel unprepared. - Publish three spine variants (90-min, half-day, full-day). - Add a template for local adaptation notes and decisions. - Include a standard Q&A and co-working segment in every variant.

title: Architectural Pair
text: Architectural Pair Whether training inputs translate into sustained collective practice depends on the institutional architecture that receives them — specifically, whether structures exist to convert individual participation into shared stewardship and to generate evidence of impact that routes back to practitioners and decision-makers. These architectural conditions are both the most important determinants of normalisation and the least developed in the programme studied. The systematic weakness of NPT's Collective Action and Reflexive Monitoring domains in the T3 data points beyond input quality to the institutional structures that determine whether training normalises. You want training to produce collective, sustained practice change rather than individual, fragile goodwill. Institutions that already have functioning feedback and co-ownership structures for training programmes. The programme operates across institutions with no guaranteed local infrastructure for sustaining training outcomes. Architecture-level improvements require changes to the institutional environment — workload models, feedback systems, co-ownership pathways — that the programme can advocate for but cannot unilaterally enact. Trainers report isolation after the programme ends; formal sharing channels go unused; impact evidence is anecdotal or absent. Prioritise the architectural pair: design co-ownership structures that convert participation into shared stewardship, and feedback systems that generate visible evidence of impact. Recognise that these require institutional partnership, not just programme redesign. Without architecture, training inputs are absorbed by individual effort and decay when that effort is withdrawn; with architecture, the same inputs are multiplied into institutional capacity. Feedback-Activation Loop — COM-B item "effects are being measured" M=3.35 (lowest across all waves); Co-Ownership Engine — qualitative evidence of sustained engagement only where co-ownership was present (T1 t1-19, T1 t1-25, T3 t3-4). Co-ownership creates distributed maintenance of the practice; feedback creates the evidence base that justifies institutional investment in maintaining the architecture. If both patterns remain weak, even excellent training produces the "absorbed input" mode — individual goodwill carrying an unsupported practice. - Map current co-ownership and feedback infrastructure at participating institutions. - Identify minimal viable architectural interventions that do not depend on institutional mandate. - Test whether participatory evaluation designs (Corneli, 2023) can close the feedback loop using the programme's own open research practices.

title: Capability, Not Functioning
text: Capability, Not Functioning Training produces capabilities — real freedoms to act — only when conversion factors are institutional, not individual. Where the programme produces functionings (attended, delivered, felt motivated) without conversion factors (workload allocation, feedback infrastructure, contribution pathways), outcomes depend on individual goodwill and do not survive the individual's departure. Sen (1999) distinguishes functionings (achieved states) from capabilities (real freedoms to achieve those states sustainably), with conversion factors as the conditions that turn resources into capabilities. Open research training gives participants resources — knowledge, materials, motivation — but the question is whether those resources become durable capabilities or transient functionings. You want training outcomes that persist beyond the initial event and do not depend on individual goodwill to sustain them. A programme with direct control over all institutional conditions (e.g., a single-site pilot with dedicated staffing and mandated participation). A programme operates across institutions with heterogeneous infrastructure and cannot control local conditions. Most programme evaluation measures functionings — satisfaction scores, self-reported motivation, delivery counts — without asking whether the conditions exist for those functionings to persist as capabilities. A trainer who has motivation and knowledge but no workload allocation, no feedback system, and no contribution pathway has a functioning; they do not yet have a capability. The three implementation modes observed in this programme are distinguished precisely by their conversion-factor profiles: full (multiplied input), partial (absorbed input), absent (architectural mismatch). High motivation coupled with low institutional support; delivery that depends on individual champions; outcomes that vary by institution despite identical training inputs. Design programmes around conversion factors, not just training content. Evaluate whether the institutional architecture creates the conditions under which individual readiness becomes collective capability. Use the five patterns identified in this study as a conversion-factor checklist: Confident Adaptation (clarity), Protected Interaction (structure), Shared Maintenance (distributed stewardship), Contribution Pathways (co-production), Visible Impact (feedback). The practice gap in open research is a capability gap in Sen's sense — participants have the resources but lack the conversion factors. The intervention-level patterns (Confident Adaptation, Protected Interaction, Shared Maintenance) improve the resource; the architecture-level patterns (Contribution Pathways, Visible Impact) build the conversion factors. Without the latter, the former produce better-prepared individuals in unchanged institutions. COM-B survey — motivation M>5.3, institutional measurement M=3.35 (functioning without capability). Qualitative: "At some point I potentially leave with that knowledge and it doesn't get used as much as it could have" (T3) — a functioning that does not survive the individual. Multiplied-input mode shows what capability looks like: "I have integrated it into existing structures of content delivery" (T1) — the practice operates through structures, not individual holders. Conversion factors operate at the institutional level — they are not properties of the individual but of the environment. A trainer in a multiplied-input institution has the same knowledge as one in an architectural-mismatch institution; the difference is whether structures exist that convert individual readiness into collective practice. If we evaluate only functionings (did they attend? did they deliver? are they motivated?), we conclude the programme is working even where it is producing goodwill-dependent delivery that will not survive staff turnover. - Evaluate programmes using capability indicators (are conversion factors present?) not just functioning indicators (did participants report satisfaction?). - Map conversion-factor profiles across institutions before assuming uniform programme impact. - Design the operational signals from each pattern as embedded capability tracking (see t3/participatory-evaluation).

title: Contribution Pathways
text: Contribution Pathways Engagement sustains because participants become co-producers, not just recipients. Where contribution pathways are absent, delivery depends on individual goodwill and decays when that goodwill is exhausted or the individual moves on. T3 is designed as a cascade: national training produces local trainers. But cascade models risk treating trainers as delivery endpoints rather than co-owners of the practice. You want training impact to spread beyond individual sessions and sustain over time. A centrally delivered programme with no expectation of local trainer autonomy. Trainers want to share adaptations and sustain activity beyond their first session. Without explicit co-ownership structures — peer cohorts, contribution pathways, mentoring — community benefits are uneven and some trainers feel isolated after the programme ends. Trainers ask for peer support, express uncertainty about what happens after the course, or describe isolation. Build co-ownership into the programme: dedicated peer cohorts, shared adaptation reviews, and a visible pathway for trainers to contribute improvements and mentor new cohorts. Co-ownership turns individual participation into collective momentum and reduces drop-off after the initial training wave; it is the engine of normalisation. "That ownership felt really important to me; and so then going on and sharing it and integrating it into my own practice" (T1); "I wouldn't have delivered that training if I hadn't had this framework" (T1); "At some point I potentially leave with that knowledge and it doesn't get used as much as it could have" (T3). COM-B: "I see the value" M=5.37 (high), "I feel positive" M=4.21 (moderate — motivation present but not fully activated into ownership). Peer cohorts and contribution pathways convert one-off participation into ongoing shared stewardship, creating distributed maintenance of the practice. If contribution pathways are absent, engagement decays after initial delivery and the practice depends on individual goodwill. - Establish rotating peer cohorts with monthly check-ins. - Create a contribution pathway for trainers to propose updates. - Pair new trainers with a local or regional mentor.

title: COM-B Convergence
text: COM-B Convergence Quantitative COM-B survey data (T3 immediate n=52, T3 six-month follow-up n=7, T1 recipient baseline n=15) converge with the qualitative NPT findings: trainers report high motivation and perceived value (M>5.3) but consistently low institutional support for measuring effects (M=3.35), removing obstacles to uptake (M=3.38), and sustaining delivery (M=3.78). The bottleneck is not capability or motivation but opportunity — specifically, the institutional opportunity structures that would convert individual readiness into collective practice. Qualitative findings identified architectural deficits through focus group analysis; quantitative data from COM-B-aligned Likert surveys provide independent triangulation. You want to confirm that the qualitative patterns are not artefacts of sampling or interpretation. Purely qualitative studies or programmes without COM-B-aligned instruments. A programme has both qualitative and quantitative evaluation data and wants to integrate them. Survey response rates are low (especially n=7 for the six-month follow-up); quantitative findings are directional and triangulating, not inferential. Survey items on value and motivation score high; survey items on institutional support and measurement score low; the gap is persistent across survey waves. Use the COM-B profile diagnostically: motivation and capability are not the intervention targets; institutional opportunity is. Design programme improvements that target the weakest COM-B component rather than reinforcing what is already strong. When motivation is high and institutional infrastructure is low, adding more motivation-focused interventions (inspirational talks, value messaging) wastes resources; the leverage point is opportunity. T3 immediate (n=52): "I see the value" M=5.37, "effects are being measured" M=3.35; T3 follow-up (n=7): motivation items increase, institutional items static; T1 (n=15): same pattern — value high, effort distribution and measurement low. COM-B identifies the binding constraint; NPT explains the social processes through which that constraint operates. If we interpret high motivation as programme success and stop there, we miss the architectural deficit that prevents motivation from translating into practice. - Present the COM-B profile to programme stakeholders as a diagnostic, not a scorecard. - Target interventions at the weakest component (institutional opportunity), not the strongest (motivation). - Repeat the survey after architectural interventions to test whether the profile shifts.

title: Confident Adaptation
text: Confident Adaptation Trainers can adapt confidently because they know what is fixed and what is flexible. Where this clarity is absent, delivery fragments and trainers cannot coordinate their actions or assess whether they are doing enough. National T3 programmes attract diverse participants with uneven prior knowledge and shifting institutional mandates; ambiguity about what is required versus optional undermines delivery. You want trainers to act confidently and consistently while still adapting locally. A single local team with an agreed curriculum and direct supervision already has alignment. Multiple cohorts, diverse mandates, and distributed delivery teams need shared expectations. Vague participation rules and undefined completion criteria leave trainers unsure what they can legitimately promise, and delivery fragments across institutions. Repeated questions about "what counts" or inconsistent module selection across trainers. Publish a minimal expectation scaffold: required sessions, optional pathways, and a stated "ready-to-deliver" threshold. Provide a short, plain-language briefing on what T3 is and is not, plus a self-check checklist for trainers. Clarity lowers cognitive load, reduces mismatch between expectations and capacity, and improves coordination across distributed trainers. "It wasn't very clear to us how many sessions we needed to have attended, which ones were fundamental" (T2A); "I didn't realise when I first signed up for it that these courses were part of this research project" (T2B); "It was useful to have a template of what was expected" (T3). COM-B: "I understand what this requires of me" M=4.90. Clear requirements reduce ambiguity, which increases trainer confidence and yields more consistent delivery choices. If we only add more content or sessions without clarifying requirements, confusion persists and delivery remains fragmented. - Create a one-page "T3 in Brief" with required/optional components. - Define a minimal competency checklist with examples of acceptable adaptations. - Add an onboarding call focused on expectations and scope.

title: Visible Impact
text: Visible Impact The programme learns because feedback is structured, visible, and shared. Where feedback mechanisms are thin — optional surveys yielding only positive or absent responses, informal signals like reading the room — the programme lacks evidence of its downstream impact, cannot systematically improve, and cannot make the case for institutional support. Trainers note that engagement and feedback are crucial for improving delivery and sustaining motivation, but current mechanisms provide almost no usable signal; cross-institutional sharing channels exist but go unused. You want long-term impact and evidence of cultural change beyond one-off sessions. Programmes with robust, continuous evaluation already in place. Trainers report low survey response and lack of evidence about reach; institutional stakeholders ask for impact data. Reliance on optional surveys misses signal; trainers lack feedback on impact and cannot easily demonstrate reach; the absence of a feedback loop means the programme cannot learn or justify itself to institutional stakeholders. Trainers cannot point to concrete impact; rely on "nobody says this was terrible" as evidence; formal sharing channels unused. Establish a lightweight feedback loop: short post-session pulse, 3-6 month follow-up, and a visible impact log. Pair this with a rotation of "impact stories" that travel across cohorts. Regular feedback sustains motivation, reveals adaptation needs, supports accountability, and — crucially — generates the evidence base that justifies institutional investment in the architectural conditions the programme needs. "I have no other ways of getting feedback short of people filling in the feedback form" (T2B); "As we get like a few answers and nobody says this was terrible, I generally think it's gone quite well" (T2B); "Even if you don't get the feedback survey, you can kind of tell whether people are engaged" (T2B). COM-B: "effects are being measured" M=3.35 (lowest item across all waves); T3 follow-up M=3.17 (still lowest at 6 months). Frequent, low-friction feedback plus shared impact stories builds momentum and surfaces improvement needs early; visible impact evidence creates a case for institutional support. If feedback is limited to optional end-of-course surveys, impact remains invisible, motivation erodes, and the programme cannot argue for the workload allocation and institutional backing it needs. - Add a two-question pulse survey after each session. - Run a quarterly impact story round-up shared across cohorts. - Pilot participatory evaluation design (see t3/participatory-evaluation).

title: Implementation Modes
text: Implementation Modes Three implementation modes — multiplied input, absorbed input, and architectural mismatch — are distinguished not by training quality or trainer motivation but by the institutional architecture that receives the training. In multiplied-input mode, existing structures amplify the training into sustained collective practice. In absorbed-input mode, individual goodwill sustains delivery without institutional support, creating fragile dependence. In architectural-mismatch mode, motivated trainers face confusion and fragmentation because the institutional environment offers no receiving structure for what they have learned. Conventional programme evaluation treats success and failure as properties of the training; this pattern reframes them as properties of the institutional architecture. You want to explain why the same training produces divergent outcomes across institutions. A programme with direct control over institutional conditions at all delivery sites. A programme operates across institutions with varying infrastructure and observes divergent outcomes from similar inputs. The modes are not permanent features of institutions; they describe a relationship between input and architecture that can shift if architectural conditions change. Same training, different outcomes; motivation high but delivery fragile or absent; trainers describe institutional barriers rather than content gaps. Diagnose the implementation mode at each institution before attributing success or failure to the training itself. Invest in architectural conditions (workload models, managerial backing, feedback systems, co-ownership pathways) rather than solely in better inputs. When motivated, capable trainers fail to sustain delivery, the cause is almost never motivational or cognitive — it is architectural. Reframing the problem redirects intervention design from "better training" to "better receiving conditions." Qualitative implementation modes across four focus groups; COM-B motivation items consistently high (M>5.0) while institutional items consistently low (M<3.8); trainers in failure mode report "I struggled to fit everything together" (T2A) despite high engagement. Institutional architecture acts as a multiplier, absorber, or deflector of training inputs depending on the presence of workload allocation, feedback infrastructure, and co-ownership pathways. If we treat failure as a training problem and respond with better inputs into the same architecture, we repeat the cycle. - Classify participating institutions by implementation mode. - Design differentiated support: architectural investment for mismatch sites, maintenance support for absorbed sites, peer learning from multiplied sites. - Track mode transitions over time as architectural conditions change.

title: Intervention Triad
text: Intervention Triad Improving the training input — its clarity, structure, and maintenance — reduces confusion, overload, and rework at the point of delivery, but these intervention-level improvements are necessary, not sufficient, for normalisation; a well-designed input delivered into an unreceptive institutional environment still fails to embed. Programme evaluation typically focuses on improving the training input; these three patterns capture the intervention-level conditions that the programme can directly control. You want training inputs to be clear, usable, and maintainable across diverse institutional contexts. A single trainer with a fixed audience and stable, well-maintained content. Multiple trainers deliver across institutions with varying local conditions. Even well-designed inputs fail to normalise when the institutional architecture cannot receive them; intervention-level improvements are necessary but not sufficient. Trainers report confusion about requirements, overstuffed sessions, or outdated materials. Ensure the intervention triad is in place — clear expectations, adaptive structure, and maintained materials — while recognising that these address the input, not the transformation space. The triad reduces friction at the point of delivery; without it, trainers waste effort on ambiguity, overload, and content drift, leaving no capacity for the architectural work that sustains practice. Patterns 1-3 each supported by 3+ transcript sources across all four focus groups; COM-B items on psychological capability (M=4.85) and institutional resource appropriateness (M=3.78) corroborate. Clarity, modularity, and maintenance free trainer cognitive resources for the harder work of institutional embedding. If the intervention triad is absent, trainers exhaust themselves on input-level problems and never reach architectural engagement. - Audit the programme against each pattern in the triad. - Address intervention-level gaps before expecting architecture-level engagement. - Document which intervention-level improvements are within programme control versus requiring institutional action.

title: Shared Maintenance
text: Shared Maintenance Materials stay current because stewardship is distributed, not individual. Where maintenance falls to whoever happens to notice a problem, content drifts from practice, local rework multiplies, and trust in the programme's resources erodes. The Carpentries lessons are frequently cited as a "gold standard," but trainers rework content locally without a shared process for maintaining or contributing changes. You want materials to remain credible and easy to use across contexts. Content that is intentionally static or time-bound with no expected revisions. Trainers report outdated sections or make repeated local edits that are not shared. Static resources drift from practice; updating is ad hoc, and trainers bear the cost of reworking content alone, adding to the workload burden that is already the most prevalent theme (25% of annotated turns). Recurrent comments that modules are out of date, or multiple divergent local versions exist. Treat materials as a living product: assign stewards, publish update cadence, and provide a lightweight change log. Add an adaptation log so local changes can be upstreamed or documented. Named stewardship and cadence reduce drift and enable safe reuse, so trainers spend less time reinventing updates and more time delivering. "You'll see like a gold standard of how to run an intro to reproducible research session" (T1); "every time I've done it, I haven't given enough time" (T1); COM-B: "policies, procedures, and resource allocation are appropriate" M=3.78. Stewardship distributes maintenance work and creates a feedback channel between local adaptation and central content. If updates remain ad hoc, content trust declines, local rework multiplies, and the programme's "gold standard" erodes. - Create a quarterly update rhythm with named maintainers. - Add a one-page adaptation log template to each module. - Prioritise updates for sections flagged as outdated by trainers.

title: Participatory Evaluation as Architecture
text: Participatory Evaluation as Architecture The programme teaches open research practices — pre-registration, transparent documentation, peer review — yet its own evaluation infrastructure does not use them. A participatory evaluation design in which training events are treated as open research objects could close the Feedback-Activation Loop through the very practices the programme teaches, simultaneously generating evidence of impact and modelling the behaviour it advocates (Corneli, 2023). The Feedback-Activation Loop is the programme's weakest architecture-level pattern; conventional evaluation methods (optional surveys, informal signals) have failed to close it. You want to close the feedback gap without adding a separate evaluation burden. Programmes with functioning, well-resourced external evaluation; contexts where open documentation of training is prohibited. The programme already teaches documentation, pre-registration, and open sharing, and the feedback loop is demonstrably weak. Participatory evaluation adds complexity and depends on trainer willingness to document and share; institutional compliance requirements may constrain open publication. Feedback surveys produce low response and thin data; trainers cannot demonstrate impact; formal sharing channels go unused. Pilot a participatory evaluation design: trainers pre-register training rationale and expected outcomes, document delivery, and invite structured peer commentary using open infrastructure (e.g., Octopus.ac). Each training event becomes a small, documented experiment that generates impact evidence as a by-product of delivery. Embedding evaluation in the training activity itself, using the same open practices the programme promotes, addresses the feedback deficit, models the target behaviour, and generates reusable evidence — three functions for the cost of one. Present study findings — Feedback-Activation Loop is weakest pattern; COM-B "effects are being measured" M=3.35; cross-institutional sharing channels unused. Corneli (2023) proposed this design prior to the present evaluation; the present findings independently validate the need. Participatory evaluation converts the feedback loop from a separate administrative task into an integral part of the practice, reducing the additional burden and increasing alignment. If evaluation remains external to the training activity, it competes with delivery for scarce time and continues to produce thin, optional data. - Pilot with 2-3 willing trainers in the next cohort. - Use Octopus.ac or equivalent open platform for documentation. - Compare feedback quality and volume with conventional survey methods.

title: Transformation Space
text: Transformation Space Open research training operates within a transformation space — a set of institutional structures, incentive systems, workload models, and feedback mechanisms — that determines its outcomes regardless of input quality. The programme's primary constraint is not the quality of its training inputs but the institutional architecture through which those inputs are — or are not — translated into routine practice. A persistent practice gap separates attending open research training from routinely working differently; this is compounded by a research gap — the literature evaluates training content and satisfaction but not the implementation processes through which training does or does not translate into sustained practice change. Because we have not studied implementation, we lack the concepts and evidence needed to diagnose why the practice gap persists. You want to understand why well-designed training does not reliably produce practice change, and why studying training inputs alone cannot answer that question. A single-site pilot with full institutional backing and dedicated resources. A programme operates across multiple institutions with heterogeneous infrastructure and no direct control over local conditions. Most programme evaluation focuses on improving the training input (content, pedagogy, materials) without examining the institutional architecture that receives it; train-the-trainer models add further implementation challenges — translation, institutional support, workload, materials maintenance — each a potential point of failure. Motivated, capable trainers report inability to sustain delivery; the same training produces divergent outcomes across institutions. Analyse the transformation space: the institutional structures, incentive systems, workload models, and feedback mechanisms that determine whether any training input — however well-designed — produces lasting collective change. Use NPT to map social processes and COM-B to diagnose individual-level bottlenecks. Improving the input is necessary but not sufficient; without architectural capacity to receive, amplify, and sustain what training produces, impact depends on individual goodwill and decays when that goodwill is exhausted. T3 immediate survey — motivation items M>5.3, institutional measurement items M<3.4; qualitative implementation modes show architecture, not motivation, as differentiator. Institutional architecture multiplies or absorbs training inputs depending on the presence of receiving structures (workload allocation, feedback systems, co-ownership pathways). If we only improve training design without addressing architecture, we produce better-trained individuals in unchanged institutions, and normalisation fails. - Distinguish intervention-level from architecture-level findings in programme evaluation. - Map institutional receiving structures before designing training inputs. - Design evaluation frameworks that assess architectural capacity alongside training quality.

title: 2 Relationship to existing doctoral training
text: 2 Relationship to existing doctoral training talk4real augments existing doctoral training by embedding meta-learning infrastructure that lets scholars observe, model, and re-engineer the systems they inhabit. [🚢/氏] You are positioning talk4real as additive infrastructure rather than a competing DTP. Existing DTPs need cross-cohort learning without extra administrative load. Meta-learning often gets treated as optional or external. Embed the REPL method inside the programme so it scales across cohorts. Most doctoral programmes teach disciplinary technique but rarely teach how disciplines learn from one another. talk4real combines ethnography, computer science, and design so scholars can treat conversation, computation, and intervention as one method. The Supplement pilot treats conversation as data and prototype as publication, keeping every scholar inside a continuous REPL loop. The programme operates as a portable connective tissue for other DTPs, enabling cross-cohort self-correction without extra training burden. next[Map one concrete integration point with a partner DTP to illustrate fit.] next[Use this pattern to structure the research task on how doctoral training currently runs.]

title: Executive Summary
text: Executive Summary talk4real reimagines doctoral training as a shared experimental learning infrastructure that continually refines itself through reflexive, collective practice. [🏡/工] You are framing the executive summary as a compact, inspectable pattern. The proposal must persuade funders while staying aligned with the pattern canon. Narrative prose can obscure the reasoning and make claims drift. Anchor the summary in explicit pattern logic before drafting the final prose. Apply a REPL-style cycle—read, evaluate, print, loop—so ethnography, computational analysis, design, and collective reflection remain linked. Run coordinated doctoral projects that instantiate the same learning architecture in distinct domains. Treat each doctoral scholar as both a researcher and an agent of collective intelligence. Most doctoral programmes operate within disciplinary or thematic silos, limiting cross-boundary learning and system-level improvement. Collective-intelligence frameworks can capture feedback between researchers, institutions, and communities so research systems learn from their own activity. The model is structured by ethical reflexivity (co-authored representation), lightweight infrastructure (portable method), and polyphonic governance (synthesised voices). Related precedents include initiatives such as realtalk@MIT, PlanetMath.org, and Peeragogy. next[Refine the exemplars and verify each claim against the supporting pattern set.] next[Insert 1-2 current, funder-recognisable exemplars of collective-intelligence infrastructure.]

title: 5 Legacy and sustainability
text: 5 Legacy and sustainability talk4real leaves a durable legacy by coupling open, modular infrastructure with graduates who act as agents of collective intelligence. [🌱/友 ➰/互] You are explaining how the programme sustains itself beyond the funding window. Long-term impact requires both infrastructure and trained stewards. Single-host programmes often collapse when the grant ends. Build modular assets and graduate cohorts who can replicate the method elsewhere. The programme yields software components, data schemas, and design templates alongside researchers fluent in listening, analysis, and redesign. Each doctoral project produces a self-contained yet interoperable prototype, so sustainability never depends on a single host institution. The Supplement embodies this ethos as a collaboratively authored artefact that is simultaneously document, dataset, and performance. Graduates seed the method elsewhere while the open infrastructure supports new nodes linking universities, civic organisations, and cultural institutions into an evolving ecosystem. next[Add a concrete legacy pathway showing how a cohort would seed a new node.]

title: 1 Rationale for the choice of research subject area
text: 1 Rationale for the choice of research subject area talk4real is justified as an infrastructure for collective intelligence because it converts accumulative, non-reflective research systems into learning systems that can redesign themselves. [🚴/了] You are establishing the foundational justification for the programme. The research system lacks built-in reflexive learning loops. Existing audits emphasise compliance rather than adaptation. Introduce a REPL-style infrastructure that turns research into a learning system. Research policies, tools, and incentives currently pile up without coherent mechanisms for reflection. Institutions generate knowledge faster than they can interpret, while prevailing audits and surveys prioritise compliance over learning. The Supplement’s simulated dialogue, participatory annotation, and iterative synthesis show the research system studying itself in real time. Formalising a social-psychological REPL makes reflexive learning habitual from doctoral study to institutional governance. next[Align this rationale with current policy language used by target funders.]

title: Supplement workshop transcript
text: Supplement workshop transcript The Supplement operationalises talk4real’s REPL by staging a multi-agent workshop that prototypes listening infrastructure, governance, and design tensions in real time. [👄/口] You are using the Supplement as a concrete proof of the REPL method. Readers need evidence that the method works in practice. Abstract descriptions can feel speculative without a live prototype. Point to the workshop transcript as the operational demonstration. Facilitators run five segments mapped to Read, Evaluate, Print, Loop with defined roles—facilitator, recorder, reporter, persona agents—to interrogate the brief. Persona statements from researchers, doctoral scholars, developer-scholars, supervisors, administrators, and the talk4real team surface strengths, blind spots, and initial stances. Participants co-design minimal listening captures, consent protocols, tagging vocabularies, and assessment artefacts that treat stories as analyzable yet textured data. Live debate over anonymisation, governance boards, licensing, and preserving dissent keeps the Print phase accountable to what Read reveals, demonstrating the reflexive loop in action. next[Publish a short excerpted walkthrough highlighting the REPL phases.]

title: 6 Additional financial or other support resources
text: 6 Additional financial or other support resources talk4real can deliver scalable, ethical, self-renewing collective research development with modest resources by leveraging lightweight assets and distributed partnerships. [👫/女 🌞/工] You are justifying resource efficiency and partnership leverage in funding prose. Funders need to see that support costs stay proportionate to outcomes. Budget narratives can hide dependencies or inflate required resources. Ground the support case in concrete partner assets and shared infrastructure. The main assets are conversation, computation, and coordination already present in partner institutions, so core costs focus on stipends, workshops, and hosting. Partners such as the UK Reproducibility Network, PathOS, and the Oxford Schwartzman Centre plus allied studios and labs contribute mentoring and in-kind expertise. Open-source software, shared cloud infrastructure, and cross-university collaboration keep financial overhead minimal while maximising reach. Outputs remain freely available, ensuring continuing value beyond the funding window. next[Confirm partner commitments and update the support section with named in-kind contributions.]

title: 4 Supervision, training, and cohort-building activities
