text: 4 Supervision, training, and cohort-building activities talk4real’s supervisory and training model turns the cohort into a distributed research operating system that learns how learning itself can be designed. [👭/友] You are describing how supervision and training uphold the shared REPL method. The cohort needs a common protocol to keep projects aligned. Dispersed supervision can fragment practice and standards. Anchor training in shared rituals and artefacts that keep learning collective. Supervision is collaborative and polyphonic, pairing disciplinary mentors with methodological companions in ethnography, data science, and design. Training follows the shared REPL rhythm demonstrated in the Supplement, grounding every project in a common protocol. Cohort practices such as listening clinics and signal-boost workshops share data, analyse overlaps, and co-design interventions. Portfolio assessment with open datasets, code notebooks, design artefacts, and open peer review makes each scholar a co-investigator refining the collective infrastructure. next[Document the training cadence and attach a sample cohort calendar.]

title: 3 Added value to the field and the universities
text: 3 Added value to the field and the universities talk4real delivers added value by supplying replicable infrastructural DNA that universities and disciplines can use to build a federated commons for adaptive governance. [🌱/以] You are articulating the added value delivered to universities and the field. Stakeholders need to see concrete benefits beyond individual projects. Benefits can seem abstract without visible shared artefacts. Emphasise the commons outputs and the governance method they enable. Ten linked doctoral projects—talk4maths, talk4health, talk4policy, talk4arts, and others—test the same REPL architecture in different domains. Each project contributes stories, datasets, and tools to an evolving commons that lets institutions reflect collectively. The Supplement demonstrates cross-voice dialogue, thematic tagging, consent protocols, and reflective synthesis working as a live prototype. Universities gain a practical method for adaptive governance, and the wider field gains a way to study and iteratively improve epistemic systems. next[Name 2–3 exemplar domains and link their outputs to the shared commons.]

title: Separate FUTON0 Signals from FUTON4 Footholds
text: Separate FUTON0 Signals from FUTON4 Footholds Persistence Requires Infrastructure You are constructing a long-term working life oriented around exploration, sustainability, and alignment, rather than throughput or extraction. You are using a bounded high-agency interval to construct foundational tooling intended to support many distinct future lines of work over months and years. You are building foundational infrastructure (prototype 1A) intended to support long-term exploratory work rather than to directly achieve outcomes. FUTON0 is responsible for keeping you alive and oriented (health, energy, sleep, progress, oxygen levels), and FUTON4 is responsible for making movement possible (conceptual footholds, links, tools, affordances). The immediate goal is to enable sustained work on FUTON-5/6/7 rather than to directly produce their outputs. Persistence is interpreted as continuous effort or repeated pushing upward regardless of conditions. There is a temptation to blur these roles, which risks either false reassurance (instrumentation without traction) or unsafe exertion (traction without instrumentation). There is a persistent risk of mistaking the enabling infrastructure (base camp, workbench, prototype 1A) for either a finished product or a general-purpose appliance. In real terrain this behaviour is indistinguishable from foolhardiness and reliably prevents both safe summits and safe descents. Enforce the boundary: FUTON0 only tracks signals that answer "is continued ascent safe and worthwhile?", while FUTON4 only records structures that answer "what movements are possible from here?" Frame success as the existence and usability of a dedicated workbench: a tool explicitly designed to make later work tractable, modifiable, and repairable under real conditions. Treat prototype 1A as the construction of conditions under which persistence later becomes possible and sane. Safe exploration depends on separating situational awareness from action affordance; when those collapse, judgement degrades under fatigue and complexity. Long-arc productivity depends less on early outputs than on having a stable locus where work can reliably begin, pause, resume, and be re-tooled without re-inventing foundations. Validated persistence requires the capacity to stop, recover, resume, and change route without loss of viability, which cannot exist without prior infrastructure. next[For FUTON0, explicitly enumerate the questions you need answered to stay safe (energy, sleep debt, progress signal, recovery trend) and reject any data that does not clearly serve one of those questions.] next[For FUTON4, treat every hypergraph edge as a potential foothold, not a metric; its value is that it can be used later, not that it reflects current state.] next[Periodically check that FUTON0 never tells you how to climb and FUTON4 never tells you whether you should; if either starts doing the other’s job, you have found a fault line.]

title: Persistence Requires Infrastructure
text: Persistence Requires Infrastructure Persistence comes from infrastructure that makes ordinary start, pause, and resume possible; evaluate prototype work by enabling conditions, not by premature output. next[Evaluate prototype 1A only against enabling criteria (can future work start, pause, and resume safely?) rather than output metrics.] next[Treat any urge to push just a bit further on the infrastructure as a signal to stop and consolidate.] next[Assess persistence only after the workbench or base camp is used in ordinary conditions, not during its construction.]

title: Prototype 1A as Dedicated Workbench
text: Prototype 1A as Dedicated Workbench Treat Prototype 1A as a dedicated workbench for future FUTON work, not as a finished artifact or a place to accumulate unrelated furniture. next[Articulate in one place what the workbench is for and what it explicitly is not for (no furniture, no appliances, no finished artifacts).] next[Treat FUTON0 instrumentation as the safety system for using the workbench, not as part of the bench itself.] next[Let prototype 1B be evidence-driven: repairs, reinforcements, and extensions only in response to observed strain during real FUTON-5/6/7 work, not anticipated perfection.] next[Use this pattern to frame Release Prototype 1 as a workbench milestone, not a finished product.]

title: Anchor Case Maintenance — Stewarding the Worked-Contrast Pair (Implementation Pattern)
text: Anchor Case Maintenance — Stewarding the Worked-Contrast Pair (Implementation Pattern) The worked-contrast pair carries the multiplicativity claim concretely; it is load-bearing rhetoric, not illustration. But the pair ages: the cases chosen when the paper was written may no longer span the model's discriminative dimensions as the evidence base evolves. The service states which composition it is running on the axis between stable anchors (the current pair persists) and evolving anchors (cases replaced as the profile landscape shifts), and binds itself to the discipline that the current pair is named with a date and selection rationale, a succession plan exists, and each cycle reviews the pair's continued validity. This implementation pattern specifies the stewardship mechanic behind ukrns/worked-contrast. The meta-pattern makes a rhetorical claim about paired cases; this pattern addresses the operational question of how the pair is maintained as the programme evolves. Without a maintenance discipline, the paper's concrete cases drift into stale illustrations that contradict the current model. The worked-contrast pair (currently FG2A-P1 + FG3-A) is the concrete grounding of the multiplicativity claim that ukrns/diagnose-before-prescribing rests on; readers and institutions trained on it return to the paper expecting these anchors to remain legible across cycles AND the pair must continue to represent the model's discriminative extremes under the current evidence base. A single pair cannot simultaneously be maximally stable across cycles and maximally accurate under evolving evidence. Stable anchors cost accuracy — the pair may no longer reflect current evidence. Evolving anchors cost comparability — claims made with one pair are not directly comparable to claims made with another. The active pull shifts over time: early, when the paper's claims are newly established, stability is load-bearing; later, as evidence accrues and new extremes emerge, rotation becomes more honest. - Stale pair: current pair no longer represents the model's extremes but continues to be cited - Silent replacement: the pair changes without announcement; readers trained on the old pair are disoriented - Succession-plan-missing: no stated plan for when replacement happens or how - Rationale-missing: pair is named but the reason for the selection is not explicit - Case-drift: the scores for the named pair shift under evidence updates but the pair's role as representative is not reviewed The service operates an explicit composition on the axis between stable and evolving anchors, declares it, and stewards the pair against that declaration. (1) Fixed pair: FG2A-P1 + FG3-A remain canonical indefinitely; evolution of the profile landscape is described in annotations. Gives up accuracy over time. (2) Rotating pair: every cycle (or when a significantly better contrast emerges), the pair is updated. Gives up cross-cycle comparability; claims in different cycles rest on different cases. (3) Canonical + archive: the canonical pair is named with a date ("as of Cycle N, the canonical contrast is FG2A-P1 + FG3-A"); superseded pairs are archived with their cycle for historical comparability. Gives up simplicity. The paper currently operates at (1) — the pair is named but no stewardship discipline is declared. Engaged when: the current pair is named with a date and a selection rationale (why these two); a succession plan exists (when and how replacement happens); the pair's continued validity is reviewed each cycle. Failing when: the pair is used without review across cycles; the current pair no longer represents the model's extremes but has not been replaced; replacement happens silently without announcement. Multiplicativity claim is concrete: ukrns/diagnose-before-prescribing rests on the multiplicative D × A gate. The worked-contrast pair makes this claim inspectable — FG2A-P1 shows delivery-gating, FG3-A shows multi-constraint. If the pair no longer represents these extremes, the concrete grounding of the multiplicativity claim degrades. Rhetorical continuity vs empirical accuracy: readers returning to the paper across versions expect the same anchor cases; institutions that have built mental models around FG2A-P1 and FG3-A will not appreciate silent replacement. But the paper's empirical honesty depends on the cases being good contrasts. The composition choice names this tension. Succession planning: even under Composition (1), the pair will eventually become untenable. The pattern requires that a succession plan exist — when and how replacement happens — even if the current pair is fixed. Cross-pattern: the pair is downstream of ukrns/assumptions-commons (pair changes require provenance); upstream of ukrns/design-state-lineage (pair changes are versioned events). Mechanic, in short: this pattern stewards the worked-contrast pair across cycles; it serves worked-contrast's concrete-grounding claim by holding the axis between stable and evolving anchors explicit; without it, the paper's concrete cases eventually contradict its current claims. - Declare the current composition (most likely (1) for paper time, (3) for operational use) - For each cycle, review the current pair's validity against the current evidence base - If replacement is needed, announce it with the rationale (which new pair, why superseded) - Archive superseded pairs with their cycle identifier for historical comparison - Cross-reference with ukrns/assumptions-commons (pair changes are evidence events) and ukrns/design-state-lineage (changes are versioned)

title: Assumptions Commons — Governance of the Shared Evidence File (Implementation Pattern)
text: Assumptions Commons — Governance of the Shared Evidence File (Implementation Pattern) The file assumptions-v2.edn is not a configuration file; it is the declarative record of the programme's evidence state and the input to every computational claim the paper makes. Its governance is a commons-governance decision: who can change what, who reviews, how versions are tracked, and how contributors earn recognised standing. The service states which composition it is running on the axis between governed-commons and open-editable. Every value in assumptions-v2.edn has a traceable provenance (commit, rationale, reviewer if applicable). The current composition on the governance axis is declared publicly. Rollback is supported. This implementation pattern specifies the mechanics behind ukrns/self-application and ukrns/computation-as-exploration. Both meta-patterns require assumptions-v2.edn to be declarative, inspectable, and re-runnable; neither specifies who is allowed to change it. Without an assumptions-commons discipline, the meta-patterns are stances without operational reality. The pattern operates on the axis: governed-commons (formal change process with review) ↔ open-editable (low-friction contribution with post-hoc audit). Irreducible: a single file cannot be simultaneously maximally low-friction to contribute to AND maximally integrity-preserving. Real costs: governed costs contribution speed and lowers the friction-gradient that invites participation; open-editable costs integrity of the shared record and risks silent divergence. Active dynamic: early, when contributors are few and the evidence base is small, open-editable suffices; as the network grows and the file becomes consequential for operational decisions, governed-commons becomes more load-bearing. - Silent drift: values change without a rationale message; readers cannot reconstruct the change's purpose - Governance opacity: the current composition is not declared; contributors do not know what process applies - Rollback unavailable: changes are made via live-edit without version history; bad changes cannot be reverted - Commit-message theatre: every change has a message but the messages are uninformative - Contributor invisibility: contributors not credited; their standing in the commons not recognised Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Single maintainer + pull-request review: one named maintainer owns the file; contributors open PRs; maintainer reviews and merges. Gives up contributor autonomy; simplest to operate. (2) Working-group review: a small committee reviews all proposals; changes announced on merge. Gives up speed; distributes authority. (3) Open-editable with audit: anyone may edit; every change logged with contributor identity and rationale; rollback on challenge by any participant. Gives up veto; places trust in transparency + rollback. These compositions are not ranked; the paper currently operates as (1). Scaling to network operations may require (2) or (3). Engaged when: every value in assumptions-v2.edn traces to an identifiable proposal or log entry; contributors can see the change history; rollback is possible. Failing when: assumptions change with no traceable provenance; contributors cannot audit recent changes; the file drifts silently between publications. Ostrom collective-choice principle: those who sustain the commons earn recognised rights to shape it. Assumptions-v2.edn is a commons in Ostrom's sense — its maintenance benefits the whole network, its governance decides whose evidence counts. Per equity/contribution-pathways, governance standing follows contribution, not the reverse. Integrity of self-application: if the paper recomputes from assumptions-v2.edn, then uncaptured changes to the file produce argument changes that readers cannot trace. ukrns/self-application's claim depends on the file's integrity; the commons governance protects that claim. Projection into main patterns: ukrns/design-as-function-of-evidence requires that service changes trace to evidence updates. If the evidence file itself has no update trace, design-state changes cannot be explained. The commons governance is the precondition for that traceability. Mechanic, in short: Mechanic: who can change what in assumptions-v2.edn, under what process. Serves: ukrns/self-application, ukrns/computation-as-exploration, ukrns/design-as-function-of-evidence. Axis: governed-commons ↔ open-editable. Without this pattern: the meta-patterns' integrity claims are aspirational. - Declare the current composition (most likely (1) single maintainer + PR review) in the project README - Ensure every commit to assumptions-v2.edn carries a rationale message (not just a numeric diff) - Announce scale transitions: if the commons moves from (1) to (2) as the network grows, publish the change-of-governance - Cross-reference with equity/contribution-pathways: contributors to the assumptions file earn recognised standing

title: Calibrate Impact Promises to Current Indicator Capacity (Sketch)
text: Calibrate Impact Promises to Current Indicator Capacity (Sketch) A service should only promise demonstration where the measurement base exists to support the claim. Where indicator capacity is partial, the promise must narrow with it. The current paper's indicators track distinguishes between practices that can already be monitored at pilot scale and practices that still depend on immature standards, incomplete workflows, or manual checking. The pattern operates on the axis: broad impact promise ↔ currently demonstrable impact promise. Real costs: narrower promises can sound less ambitious, but broader promises outrun the measurement substrate and weaken trust. State which practices are currently demonstrable, which are still development work, and align service claims with that distinction.

title: Coding Provenance — Traceability of NPT Qualitative Coding (Implementation Pattern)
text: Coding Provenance — Traceability of NPT Qualitative Coding (Implementation Pattern) The numerical scores in assumptions-v2.edn did not arise spontaneously; they were derived from qualitative NPT coding of focus-group transcripts and then upgraded from textual judgements to [0, 1] values. Any computational claim in the paper rests on this upgrade. The service states which composition it is running on the axis between full claim-to-transcript traceability (every numerical claim walks back to specific transcript passages) and aggregate claim-to-score provenance (claims walk back to scored dimensions and coder identity, but not to individual passages). The coding protocol is documented. Coder identities are recorded. The qualitative-to-numerical upgrade is described at the declared granularity. The composition on the traceability axis is declared. The data cache is accessible under a declared policy. This implementation pattern specifies the empirical-provenance mechanic behind ukrns/computation-as-exploration. The meta-pattern claims the model makes conditional dependencies inspectable; this pattern addresses the upstream question — are the inputs themselves inspectable back to the qualitative evidence? Without a provenance discipline, the model's outputs are computable but the inputs are effectively oracle; the claim 'this is what the evidence shows' becomes 'this is what someone coded'. The pattern operates on the axis: full traceability (every NPT score walks back to specific transcript passages and coder judgements) ↔ aggregate provenance (scores walk back to scored dimensions and coder identity; specific passages not linked). Irreducible: provenance cannot be simultaneously maximally detailed AND maximally lightweight to maintain. Real costs: full traceability costs curation — passages must be cross-linked, coder notes preserved, access maintained; aggregate costs reverse-checkability — a reviewer asking 'how do you know this score is 0.40?' gets a general answer rather than a specific one. Active dynamic: early, when the scores are newly derived and claims are being actively contested, full traceability is load-bearing; later, when scores have stabilised and been cross-referenced, aggregate provenance may suffice for many readers. - Oracle scores: numerical values in assumptions-v2.edn with no traceable derivation - Lost coder identity: who scored what is not recorded - Undocumented protocol: the upgrade from qualitative code to [0, 1] value has no stated rubric - Cache inaccessibility: transcripts or coded passages exist somewhere but cannot be located - Review-request failure: a reviewer asking for provenance receives an unstructured answer - Granularity-confusion: the paper cites passages for some claims but not others with no declared principle Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Full claim-to-transcript traceability: every score in assumptions-v2.edn is linked to specific transcript passages with coder notes. Gives up lightweight maintenance. (2) Aggregate claim-to-score provenance: assumptions-v2.edn states the score, the coder(s), the date, and the scoring protocol; passages are archived but not linked per score. Gives up reverse-traceability at passage grain. (3) Differential granularity: indicator-level claims (the paper's specific quantitative points) trace to passages; general claims trace to scored dimensions. Gives up simplicity. The paper currently operates somewhere between (1) and (2) informally — transcript evidence is cited in prose but the assumptions-v2.edn entries do not carry explicit back-links. The proposed Annex C would make the operating composition explicit. Engaged when: any claim in the paper can be walked back to its empirical source at the declared granularity; coder identity and scoring protocol are recorded; the composition is declared. Failing when: a reviewer asks 'how do you know?' and the answer is unstructured; scores exist in assumptions-v2.edn with no linked provenance; the coding protocol is not documented; coder identity is lost. Qualitative-to-numerical is load-bearing: the upgrade from textual NPT codes to [0, 1] values is the single most important epistemic step in the paper's empirical chain. All downstream computation rests on it. Provenance is the audit trail for that step. Reviewer challenge defence: when a reviewer asks 'how do you know that FG2A-P1 has communal-specification 0.20?', the minimum adequate answer names the transcript passages, the coder, and the protocol. Without provenance, the answer is 'someone coded it' — which is not a defence. Coder-in-the-loop: provenance preserves coder identity and judgements. This serves two purposes: accountability (coders stand behind their work) and governance (future coders can trace how earlier judgements were made, which informs calibration). Commons-adjacent: the provenance record is itself a commons artefact. Its governance (who can add, who can audit, how retention works) mirrors ukrns/assumptions-commons. Projection into main patterns: without coding provenance, ukrns/diagnose-before-prescribing's profile signatures cannot be contested by institutions. A profile's classification depends on its NPT scores; an institution challenging its classification needs access to the provenance to mount a defence. Mechanic, in short: Mechanic: how the qualitative-to-numerical upgrade is traced. Serves: computation-as-exploration's inspectability claim at the upstream end. Axis: full traceability ↔ aggregate provenance. Without this pattern: the empirical base is oracle, the upgrade is private, and the paper's computational claims rest on unauditable judgements. - Produce Annex C (proposed in the writing plan) that documents the coding protocol, coder identities, and the qualitative-to-numerical upgrade - Declare the current composition on the traceability axis - Establish the data cache: where are the transcripts, the codebook, the coded passages, the upgrade mapping stored, and who has access - For composition (1) or (3): add back-links in assumptions-v2.edn (via a sidecar file or embedded metadata) pointing to passages - Cross-reference with ukrns/assumptions-commons (provenance is part of evidence governance)

title: Use Computation to Expose Dependencies
text: Use Computation to Expose Dependencies Use computation to expose what the design depends on, not to pretend certainty the evidence does not support. In the current paper, the model is doing four main jobs: showing how delivery and institutional architecture interact, checking what happens when key roles are removed, testing whether the design can plausibly pay for itself, and naming what would falsify its claims. That is a viability-checking use of computation, not a forecast. The discipline is to keep the model inspectable, to keep its assumptions separate from its conclusions, and to say plainly when a result is exploratory rather than predictive. The current working paper no longer uses computation as a general aura of rigour. It uses it where prose alone would be too loose. The simulation anchors delivery in measured training activity and architecture in qualitative evidence, then asks concrete questions: where do institutions sit under the design, what breaks if the Evaluator disappears, what changes if the Researcher-Advisor disappears, and does the unit economics look plausible inside the serviceable market. Those are design-checking questions. They help the paper move from argument into launch without claiming to know the future. The pattern operates on the axis: computation-as-exploration ↔ computation-as-prediction. Irreducible: a model that keeps its assumptions open and contestable is honest about uncertainty, but it cannot also speak with the false certainty of a forecast. A model that speaks as forecast usually hides more of its own construction. Real costs: exploratory computation is more honest and more inspectable, but it is rhetorically weaker than a clean prediction. Predictive computation can support sharper commitments, but if the evidence base is still thin it becomes overclaiming dressed as method. Active dynamic: the right position can change over time. Early in a service's life, exploration and stress-testing are the honest use. Later, after Year-1 evidence accumulates, some narrower predictive claims may become defensible. - Model-as-oracle: simulation output is cited as if it were observed fact - Decorative quantification: numbers are added for authority, not because they answer a specific design question - Hidden assumptions: the reader cannot tell what inputs or structural choices the result depends on - Unsupported precision: exact-looking outputs are narrated more confidently than the evidence warrants - Single-score collapse: a rich design question is flattened into one number that silently acts like a recommendation - Detached computation: the model produces outputs that are not tied to refutation conditions, launch checks, or operational decisions Use computation where it sharpens design judgement, and stop before it starts pretending to be more than that. (1) Design-checking only: use the model to expose dependencies, stress-test roles, and test viability claims, while keeping future predictions off the table. This is the current paper's position. (2) Design-checking plus bounded planning scenarios: keep the model exploratory, but also use it to compare a few explicit operating scenarios whose assumptions are published. Gives up some simplicity. (3) Predictive reporting: use the model to make forward claims on which commitments directly rest. Gives up much of the epistemic caution and should be reserved for a later evidence state. These compositions are not ranked in the abstract. The point is to say which one the service is using and why. Engaged when: each figure or result answers a specific design question; assumptions are inspectable; sensitivity or verification is reported where it matters; and any predictive language is clearly marked as such. Failing when: simulation output substitutes for evidence; the reader cannot see what the result depends on; or the computation produces no operational consequence beyond looking impressive. Some dependencies are hard to hold in prose alone: The design depends on interactions between delivery, institutional architecture, role placement, and timing. Computation helps make those interactions inspectable instead of leaving them implicit. Verification needs more than assertion: The role-removal asymmetry, the boundary-band result, and the economics crossover are all examples where the model is useful because it checks the design's logic against a formal structure rather than merely restating the author's belief. Falsifiability improves when the model is tied to explicit failure conditions: The strongest use of computation in the current paper is not that it produces numbers. It is that those numbers are linked to claims that could be shown false in Year 1. Exploration is not anti-rigour: A prior, a simulation, or a scenario walk can still be rigorous if the assumptions are clear, the question is well posed, and the result is not oversold. What matters is not avoiding computation, but keeping it proportionate to the evidence. Mechanic, in short: Derived from the paper's use of simulation to test viability, role dependence, and affordability without treating the model as a forecast engine. Describes one way the service can make design reasoning inspectable when the question is too interdependent for prose alone. Mapped to the learning loop between design and verification: the model helps check whether the proposed system hangs together before the service commits to instantiate it. Coordination requirement: Low to medium at paper time, higher if the service later turns the model into a live operational tool. - Keep assumptions and code paths inspectable enough that a reader can see what each result depends on - Tie every computational output to a concrete design question or refutation condition - Re-run the model after substantive Year-1 evidence arrives, and publish what changed in the service-facing interpretation - Keep operational reporting plainer than the underlying harness: the code can be detailed while the service story stays decision-facing - Avoid making predictive claims until the evidence base is strong enough to justify them explicitly

title: Cycle Position Publication — Declaring the Current Pareto Composition (Implementation Pattern)
text: Cycle Position Publication — Declaring the Current Pareto Composition (Implementation Pattern) The service's current composition on the openness/governance Pareto is not a retrospective characterisation; it is a stated position the service can point to before events run and institutions can contest. The service states which composition it is running on the axis between cycle-level declaration (one statement per annual cycle, events read through it) and event-level declaration (every service event carries its two-axis costing at the point of commitment). The current cycle's Pareto composition is publicly declared. Each event within the cycle carries its two-axis costing. Institutions have a declared contestation channel. This implementation pattern specifies the publication mechanic behind ukrns/open-the-triangle. The main pattern's invariant requires every service event to be explicitly costed on two axes and a stopping point stated. Without a publication discipline, costing happens internally and the stopping point is a post-hoc reading of what the service happened to do. The pattern operates on the axis: cycle-level declaration (one position published per cycle, events run under it) ↔ event-level declaration (each event carries its own two-axis costing at the point of commitment). Irreducible: cannot be simultaneously maximally event-flexible and maximally cycle-coherent. Real costs: cycle-level costs event-specific flexibility — events within the cycle are constrained by the declared stopping point; event-level costs coherence — the cycle's overall shape is only reconstructible post hoc. Active dynamic: early in a programme, events are few and cycle-level suffices; as events multiply and become heterogeneous, event-level becomes more accurate. - Post-hoc characterisation: the composition is reported as what happened rather than declared as what will happen - Silent events: service events run without costing - Cycle-declared, event-divergent: events within the cycle violate the declared position without announcement - No contestation channel: institutions cannot engage the composition choice before events run - Declaration-as-boilerplate: the declaration is published but carries no specific reasoning Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Per-cycle declaration: at the start of each annual (or other) cycle, the service publishes its current Pareto composition — which of the three compositions from ukrns/open-the-triangle it is running (low-governance loop / governance-first / subset pilot). Events run under the declared position. Gives up within-cycle flexibility. (2) Per-event declaration: every service event (T1 wave, peer-evaluation pilot, scaffold publication) carries its openness gain and governance cost at the point of commitment; the cycle's overall position is the aggregate. Gives up cycle-level coherence. (3) Both cycle-level + event-level: the cycle declares the stopping position; events reconfirm or flag divergence. Gives up simplicity. The paper currently describes the pattern and includes a Pareto table (§4) but does not declare an operational composition. Engaged when: the current composition is statable and reference-able at any time; institutions know which composition applies to a given event; contestation is possible before events run. Failing when: composition is a post-hoc characterisation; institutions discover what happened after the fact; events run under no declared position; the paper describes the axis but operational practice ignores it. Contestability before the fact: the purpose of declaration is to allow institutions to engage the composition choice before events run — so network input can shape the position rather than merely observe it. A post-hoc characterisation cannot be contested. Governance-cost as commons good: the governance costs listed in the Pareto table are borne by institutions (consent extensions, data-sharing infrastructure). Declaration makes those costs visible to the institutions that will pay them, and allows negotiation about who pays and when. Two-axis costing is asymmetric: openness gains often accrue to the network; governance costs often accrue to specific institutions. Declaration exposes this asymmetry so the network can see who is being asked to bear what. Coordination with design-state lineage: cycle and event declarations are candidate entries in ukrns/design-state-lineage. The declaration mechanic feeds the versioning mechanic. Mechanic, in short: Mechanic: how the current openness/governance composition is declared and contestable. Serves: open-the-triangle's invariant. Axis: cycle-level ↔ event-level declaration. Without this pattern: the axis exists in the paper but not in operations. - At each cycle boundary, publish the current composition (low-governance loop / governance-first / subset pilot) and the reasoning - For each event within the cycle, cost it on the two axes and note whether it is consistent with the cycle declaration - Provide a contestation channel: institutions can flag events they think violate the declared position - Cross-reference with ukrns/design-state-lineage (cycle declarations are versioned design-state changes)

title: Treat Design as a Function of Evidence
text: Treat Design as a Function of Evidence A learning system should change because evidence says it should, not because habit, enthusiasm, or fashion pushes it around. But it should not change so often that the institutions inside it cannot plan against a stable offer. The current paper turns that tension into an operating discipline: quarterly checks, annual indicators, stakeholder walks, and a Year-2 commitment decision in which continue, vary, and stand down are all genuinely live. A design change should be traceable to evidence; the absence of a design change should also be defensible. The current working paper no longer frames this mainly as a model-update problem. It frames it as an operational commitment. Year 1 is a real launch, not a symbolic pilot. The service runs seven quarterly yes/no checks on itself, performs three annual stakeholder walks to see whether the operation can actually be used without the writing team in the room, and then makes a Year-2 decision on the basis of what was learned. The point of the pattern is to make sure evidence terminates in consequences rather than accumulating harmlessly at the edge of the system. The pattern operates on the axis: responsiveness ↔ stability. Irreducible: a service cannot be maximally responsive to each new signal and maximally stable for the institutions trying to use it. Every operating model chooses a position on that axis. Real costs: responsiveness catches problems early and can improve fit quickly, but too much of it turns the service into a moving target. Stability makes planning easier, but too much of it leaves a weak design in place after evidence has already shown the weakness. Neither end is free. Active dynamic: the right balance changes over time. Early in a new service, the case for adjustment is stronger because many uncertainties are still open. Later, once the operating rhythm and evidence chain are established, stability deserves more weight. - Evidence-without-change: checks and evaluation happen, but nothing downstream ever moves - Change-without-evidence: the service changes shape, scope, or emphasis without a clear evidential basis - Permanent-pilot: Year 1 produces learning but no real commitment decision ever arrives - Hidden variation: operational changes are made informally and never surfaced as explicit choices - No-stand-down option: continuation is assumed, so verification has no real teeth - Quarterly thrash: every small signal produces operational rework before anyone can tell whether it matters Choose an explicit position on the axis and make the consequences visible. (1) Quarterly adjustment inside an annual frame: run regular checks and allow limited in-year variation, but reserve the largest commitments for the annual decision point. This is the position closest to the current paper. It gives up perfect immediacy in exchange for manageability. (2) Annual-batch revision: hold the design largely stable through the year and revise mainly at year-end. Gives up speed of correction. (3) Continuous operational revision: treat each new signal as a potential live change to the service. Gives up predictability and makes governance harder. These compositions are not ranked in the abstract. The point is that the service should be able to say which one it is using and why. Engaged when: each material operational change can be tied back to evidence; the seven quarterly checks are actually run; the annual stakeholder walks expose whether the service is usable by the actors who must carry it; the Year-2 decision can continue, vary, or stop. Failing when: learning is gathered but has no consequences; the operation changes for reasons no one can inspect; stand-down is named but never really available. Evidence only matters if it changes consequences: The paper's live claim is not just that evaluation should happen, but that it should terminate in decisions. Otherwise the design is not a learning system; it is a reporting system. Year-1 launch makes the discipline operational: The quarterly checks, the annual indicators, and the stakeholder walks are the mechanism by which evidence enters the design. They are not side documentation. They are the operating discipline that prevents both complacency and panic. Stand-down is part of the pattern: A Year-2 choice between continue and vary is not enough if stopping was never a real option. The stand-down path is what makes the verification posture credible. If the service cannot fail in principle, it cannot learn honestly in practice. Relationship to participation and visible impact: This pattern still answers the same structural concern as the older library language: if people contribute evidence or downstream experience, that contribution should matter. The service demonstrates that it matters by letting the evidence chain end in visible operational consequence rather than in a dead archive. Mechanic, in short: Derived from the paper's Year-1 launch discipline: quarterly checks, annual stakeholder walks, and an explicit Year-2 commitment decision. Answers the general problem of evidence that never changes the system it describes. Mapped to the learning loop at the update step: after diagnosis, provisioning, delivery, and evaluation, something must be allowed to change. Coordination requirement: High. The service, institutions, and partners all need to know what can change when, and on what basis. - Publish the seven quarterly checks as part of the operating model, not as an internal afterthought - Record any material in-year variation in the service and the evidence that prompted it - Use the three annual stakeholder walks as decision tests rather than as presentational exercises - Keep continue, vary, and stand down genuinely live at the Year-2 decision point - Use this pattern downstream of measurement and cross-institutional comparison, where evidence is mature enough to justify operational consequence

title: Design-State Lineage — Versioned Service-Design Changes (Implementation Pattern)
text: Design-State Lineage — Versioned Service-Design Changes (Implementation Pattern) A service that claims design updates as a function of evidence must be able to show, for any point in time, (a) the design state that was active then, (b) the evidence that produced it, and (c) the update-policy clause that authorised the update. The service states which composition it is running on the axis between fine-grained versioning (every change versioned) and coarse-grained versioning (changes batched into versioned releases). Every design-state change is versioned and traces to (evidence update identifier, policy clause). The composition on the versioning axis is declared. Past design states are reconstructible. This implementation pattern specifies the versioning mechanic behind ukrns/design-as-function-of-evidence. The pattern's invariant-statement requires every service change to trace to an evidence update and policy clause; without a lineage mechanism, that requirement is unverifiable. Design-state lineage is what makes the main pattern's traceability claim operational. The pattern operates on the axis: fine-grained versioning (every change versioned separately, full evidence-trace per change) ↔ coarse-grained versioning (changes batched into periodic releases). Irreducible: a single versioning strategy cannot simultaneously maximise per-change traceability and minimise release noise. Real costs: fine-grained costs overhead — more version tags, more release noise; coarse-grained costs traceability — readers cannot see individual changes within a release. Active dynamic: early in a programme, changes are few and coarse-grained suffices; as update cadence rises (under a continuous or threshold policy from ukrns/design-as-function-of-evidence), fine-grained becomes more informative. - Untraced change: design state updates without a recorded reason - Policy-clause-missing: change traces to evidence but not to the policy clause that authorised it - Reconstruction-impossible: past design states cannot be recovered from the lineage - Fine-grained-overload: every recompute gets a version; release noise overwhelms readers - Coarse-grained-opaque: cycle-release rolls up so many changes that nothing specific is traceable - Ad hoc versioning: version numbers exist but carry no consistent meaning Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Per-change versioning: every update gets its own version tag and evidence-trace. Gives up version-count simplicity; highest traceability. (2) Per-cycle versioning: quarterly or per-T1-wave releases batch internal changes into a single version tag; internal changes logged separately but not versioned. Gives up per-change traceability. (3) Dual-track: canonical versions (per-cycle, citable) + internal log (per-change, for reconstruction). Gives up simplicity; both audiences served. The paper currently operates informally through git history; operational use at UKRN-S requires a declared composition. Engaged when: the design state at any past date is reconstructible; every change traces to an evidence update identifier and an update-policy clause; the chosen composition (fine / coarse / dual) is declared. Failing when: past design states cannot be reconstructed; changes trace to "updated 2026-05" with no evidence identifier; the policy clause that authorised each change is not recorded. Traceability is the main pattern's invariant: ukrns/design-as-function-of-evidence requires every service change to trace to evidence + policy clause. Lineage makes this trace constructible for any historical moment, not only the present. Lineage vs log: a log records changes; a lineage preserves the ability to reconstruct the state at any past point. Institutions that planned around the design state at time T need to be able to retrieve that state, not just read the change log. Cross-pattern coordination: this pattern operates downstream of ukrns/assumptions-commons (evidence provenance) and ukrns/model-recompute-schedule (rerun events); it operates upstream of ukrns/publication-cadence (which versions get canonicalised). A coherent lineage mechanism is the backbone of the implementation-pattern stack. Commons accountability: institutions contributing evidence should be able to see their observation's effect on the design state. Without lineage, the contribution-pathway (equity/contribution-pathways) terminates in opacity. Mechanic, in short: Mechanic: how design-state changes are versioned and traced. Serves: design-as-function-of-evidence's traceability invariant. Axis: fine-grained ↔ coarse-grained. Without this pattern: the main pattern's invariant cannot be checked. - Declare the current composition in project documentation - Make each design-state change carry: version identifier, evidence revision, policy clause, date - Expose the lineage as a queryable history (even a simple chronological log is better than none) - Cross-reference with ukrns/assumptions-commons (evidence provenance) and ukrns/publication-cadence (which versions are canonical) - Provide a reconstruction example: "here is how to retrieve the design state as of 2026-Q1"

title: Diagnose Before Prescribing
text: Diagnose Before Prescribing A training service should diagnose the main constraint before choosing its response. In the current paper's terms, the important distinction is whether an institution is mainly constrained by delivery, by institutional architecture, by both, or by a substrate problem the service cannot lift within scope. A single offer for everyone is easy to run and easy to explain, but it misfits a visible part of the network. A diagnosed offer states what seems to be binding, says what that implies for the service response, and leaves room for revision when later evidence shows the diagnosis was wrong or incomplete. The current working paper separates two main dimensions of the problem. Delivery asks whether training is actually reaching people and being taken up. Institutional architecture asks whether the setting around the training can hold and use what is being delivered. The design also distinguishes what it can affect directly, what it can affect only indirectly, and what sits outside its scope. Verification then shows that institutions do not all sit in the same place: some are mainly delivery-constrained, some mainly architecture-constrained, some constrained on both, and some blocked by wider substrate conditions that the service alone cannot shift. The pattern operates on the axis: universal offer ↔ diagnosed offer. Irreducible: a service cannot maximise both uniformity and fit at the same time. The more the offer is standardised, the easier it is to communicate and run. The more it is diagnosed, the more it can respond to real differences across the network. Real costs: a universal offer is cheaper, simpler, and easier to explain; a diagnosed offer is harder to run, harder to justify quickly, and more exposed to disagreement about the diagnosis itself. Both ends of the axis carry real cost. Active dynamic: the right position can change over time. Early in a service cycle, diagnosis may be rough and the case for a common baseline may be stronger. Later, once evaluation and comparison are in place, the service has more reason to differentiate. - One-offer-for-all: every institution receives the same response regardless of what is actually blocking progress - Variance-as-effort: uneven outcomes are explained as trainer quality or local enthusiasm rather than as differences in constraint structure - Boundary-blindness: the service keeps promising lift where the blocking condition is outside its scope - Scope-denial: a substrate problem is treated as if a training-service adjustment can solve it - Frozen diagnosis: the initial judgement is never revised after new evaluation evidence arrives - Hidden diagnosis: the service acts on a diagnosis internally but never states it to the institutions affected by it Operate an explicit move on the named axis; make the diagnosis inspectable; revise it when evidence warrants. (1) Diagnostic-first: use the early wave of delivery and evaluation to establish what is mainly constraining each institution or cluster before differentiating the response. Gives up speed at the start. (2) Universal baseline plus selective escalation: begin with a common offer, then add differentiated support where evidence shows a stronger delivery or architecture constraint. Gives up simplicity of message. (3) Mostly universal offer: keep the service largely standardised and accept that some institutions will be served imperfectly. Gives up fit for reach and ease. These compositions are not ranked. The point of the pattern is to make the trade visible and to stop the service pretending that one common offer is automatically the right answer everywhere. Engaged when: the service can say, for any institution or cluster, what seems to be binding and what evidence supports that judgement; the response follows from that judgement; later evidence can revise it. Failing when: every institution gets the same answer by default; differences in outcome are explained away as effort or enthusiasm; no one can say what the service thinks is actually in the way. Central finding of the paper: The paper's headline claim is that the institutional setting matters at least as much as the training content itself. That is exactly why diagnosis matters. If the main problem is not the same everywhere, the same response will not work everywhere. Evidence from the model and verification: The design and verification work distinguish boundary cases, floor cases, and higher-throughput cases rather than treating the whole network as flat. That difference is what a diagnosed service is trying to respect. The point is not to claim certainty; it is to stop making undifferentiated promises where the evidence already shows meaningful differences. Relationship to direct, indirect, and out-of-scope levers: Diagnosis also disciplines ambition. If the problem looks directly serviceable, the service can act. If the problem can only be shifted indirectly, the service should say so. If the main blockage is outside scope, the honest response is not to overclaim. Governance value: A stated diagnosis can be challenged. An unstated diagnosis cannot. By naming what it thinks is binding, the service gives institutions something they can contest, refine, or confirm with better evidence. Mechanic, in short: Derived from the paper's distinction between delivery and institutional architecture, the verification work's separation of different institution types, and the later distinction between direct, indirect, and out-of-scope effects. Answers equity/confident-adaptation at service scale: just as trainers need to know what is fixed around them, the service needs to know what is actually blocking progress before prescribing a response. Mapped to the learning loop at the diagnose step: upstream of capability placement, evidence gathering, and operational differentiation. Coordination requirement: Moderate. The service can make an initial diagnosis centrally, but it needs institutions to contest and refine it. - State, for each participating institution or cluster, whether the main current constraint appears to be delivery, institutional architecture, both, or something outside scope - Tie service choices back to that diagnosis rather than treating them as free-standing preferences - Let institutions challenge the diagnosis with their own evidence - Re-run the diagnosis after the first evaluation wave and again at the Year-2 commitment point - Use this pattern upstream of capability placement and evidence-prioritisation decisions

title: Distinguish Delivery from Practice Change (Sketch)
text: Distinguish Delivery from Practice Change (Sketch) Attendance proves reach into rooms; it does not prove changed research practice afterwards. A training system that reports delivery as if it were impact will systematically overstate what it knows. The current paper's training track already makes this distinction explicit: 2,816 trainees can establish network-scale delivery, but not whether those researchers subsequently changed how they work. The pattern operates on the axis: delivery evidence ↔ outcome evidence. Real costs: delivery is visible sooner and more cheaply than practice change, so programmes are persistently tempted to let the first stand in for the second. Use delivery counts to claim delivery, and reserve impact claims for downstream evidence that actually tracks changed practice.

title: Distributed Coverage — Coverage as a Network Property, Not an Individual Requirement (Sixth Main Pattern)
text: Distributed Coverage — Coverage as a Network Property, Not an Individual Requirement (Sixth Main Pattern) The breadth of open-research topics exceeds what any single trainer can confidently cover. A programme that requires uniform coverage from every trainer produces breadth overload, impostor syndrome, and absorbed-mode delivery. A programme that treats coverage as a network property — each trainer declaring the modules they will own, each institution committing an explicit coverage profile, the programme maintaining an aggregate view — converts the same breadth from an individual burden into a distributed responsibility. The service states which composition it is running on the axis between uniform-coverage-per-trainer and distributed-coverage-across-the-network. Each trainer has a declared module subset. Each participating institution has a committed coverage profile. The programme maintains a current network-level coverage map. Coverage gaps are visible; institutional commitments are contestable. This pattern addresses the hole (H5) that the five main design patterns left open: protected-interaction (breadth overload) is only partially answered by network-scale provisioning of coordination support (ukrns/provision-at-network-scale). Network-scale coordination helps trainers find each other but does not itself distribute the coverage burden. The equity-domain protected-interaction pattern diagnoses the institutional failure (trainers silently absorb a coordination problem that extends beyond their remit); this design pattern specifies a service-level response that makes coverage distribution explicit. The paper-v2.3 resolution for protected-interaction — declared delivery profiles, institutional coverage commitments, coverage as network property — is formalised here as its own design pattern. The pattern operates on the axis: uniform coverage per trainer (every trainer expected to cover all topics) ↔ distributed coverage across the network (each trainer owns a subset, the network guarantees totality). Irreducible: coverage cannot be simultaneously uniform-per-trainer and distributed-across-network. The same module either is expected of every trainer or is owned by a declared subset. Real costs: uniform is communicatively simple ('all our trainers deliver the full open-research curriculum') and requires no coordination infrastructure; distributed requires declaration, aggregation, institutional commitment, and active maintenance of the coverage map. Both carry real costs. Active dynamic: the right position shifts with the territory. A narrow curriculum favours uniform; the wide, evolving territory of open-research favours distributed. As the territory grows (AI for research, new replication methods, new data-governance requirements), the case for distributed strengthens. - Breadth overload: trainers silently cover topics outside their primary expertise without team support - Impostor-driven delivery: session held while trainer under-prepared because declaration infrastructure was absent - Un-profiled institution: institution participates without naming what it covers or what it resources - Uniform-communication with distributed-reality: programme is described as if coverage is uniform but actually absorbed by a subset of trainers - Coverage-map drift: declared profiles exist but the aggregate map is stale - Institutional-refusal unacknowledged: some institutions cannot commit but Composition (3)'s honesty is not declared; gaps are hidden - Absorbed-mode as individual failure: breadth overload read as trainer motivation problem rather than architectural absence Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Declared delivery profiles: each trainer declares the modules they will own; each participating institution commits an explicit coverage profile with resourcing; the programme maintains an aggregate coverage view. Coverage is a network property; gaps are visible. Gives up communicative simplicity; demands declaration infrastructure. (2) Uniform expectation: every trainer expected to cover the full curriculum; breadth overload and impostor syndrome become individual problems; absorbed-mode delivery is the predictable outcome. Gives up the distributed trainer experience; easy to describe to funders. (3) Curriculum triage per institution: each institution picks which subset to deliver based on its profile; coverage gaps are flagged rather than hidden; the programme does not guarantee totality at the network level. Gives up network-level totality; gains institution-level honesty about what is delivered. These compositions are not ranked; the paper-v2.3 (companion journal article) resolution for protected-interaction favours Composition (1) with institutional coverage commitments. Composition (3) is a realistic fallback when institutional capacity is uneven. Engaged when: every trainer can point to their declared module subset; each participating institution has a committed coverage profile; the programme maintains a current aggregate coverage map; coverage gaps (modules not owned by anyone at sufficient depth) are visible. Failing when: individual trainers silently absorb breadth overload; no institutional coverage commitment exists; coverage is described uniformly ('our trainers deliver the full curriculum') without distribution evidence; impostor syndrome is widespread and its structural cause is not named. Breadth-vs-depth tension (equity/protected-interaction link): the equity-domain pattern names the tension at institutional scale: the territory is wider than any single trainer's expertise, so uniform expectation produces either superficial coverage or impostor-mode delivery. Distributed coverage resolves the tension structurally rather than by asking individuals to work harder. Network-property framing: coverage as a network property is the move that reframes the problem. Under uniform expectation, a gap in a trainer's competence is a trainer problem. Under distributed coverage, the same gap is a network problem ('this module is owned by trainers X, Y, Z; the network needs to ensure their resourcing') — which locates the problem where the resources exist to resolve it. Absorbed-mode signature: absorbed input (companion paper) is the implementation mode where individuals carry what the architecture should distribute. Breadth overload is a specific absorbed-mode signature; distributed coverage is the architectural response. Profile-contingency: institutions differ in what they can resource. Composition (1) presumes institutional commitment; Composition (3) acknowledges that some institutions cannot commit to full modules. The choice is itself a profile-contingent decision (linked: ukrns/diagnose-before-prescribing). Cross-pattern: the coverage map is a specific instance of ukrns/scale-register — coverage is a capability whose scale is 'distributed across declared trainers/institutions'. Maintaining the map is an operational act governed by the scale-register mechanics. Observation (2026-04, UKRN Services recruitment): UKRN Services issued a call for expressions of interest seeking trainers to deliver 'open research and related topics to the wider sector and beyond'. Despite addressing a population of recently-trained, motivated open-research trainers (the ORP Training Community of Practice, ~200-strong), the response rate was disappointingly low. UKRN-S itself has acknowledged the finding and wants to understand why the transition from 'trainer on open research within your institution' to 'providing training to others via UKRN Services' has not happened at the rate they hoped. Reading through the pattern: the call asks candidates to volunteer for delivery of an unspecified subset of a wide territory, without a scaffold for what the service will deliver (confident-adaptation, at UKRN-S scale) and without a mechanism for declaring which modules a trainer will own (distributed-coverage, at trainer scale). The pattern predicts that breadth-overload and impostor effects — already documented at ORP delivery stage — will recur at the recruitment stage. Observed low response is consistent with this prediction. Implication for operational use: adoption of the pattern's discipline — declared delivery profiles, institutional (or trainer-level) coverage commitments, a network-level coverage map, and an explicit expectation scaffold for UKRN-S delivery — would be expected to reduce this transition friction. The argument generalises the paper's ORP-era findings into UKRN-S's own recruitment experience; the same architectural gap produces the same absorbed-mode signature at a different point in the pipeline. Mechanic, in short: Derived from paper-v2.3 protected-interaction resolution (declared delivery profiles, institutional coverage as network property) and from the hole (H5) in the original five-pattern set where ukrns/provision-at-network-scale answered equity/protected-interaction only partially. Answers equity/protected-interaction fully at service scale: network provisioning of coordination (ukrns/provision-at-network-scale) + distributed coverage (this pattern) + declared delivery profiles (trainer-level declaration). Mapped to the learning loop: this pattern operates alongside provision-at-network-scale during the 'provision' step. Once diagnosis (ukrns/diagnose-before-prescribing) has named a profile, both scale choice (ukrns/provision-at-network-scale) and coverage distribution (this pattern) are chosen. Axis framing follows the paper-draft-16-april Tension / Composition / Check structure. Coordination requirement: Medium (trainer + institution + programme) to High (network-scale coverage map maintenance). Sixth main pattern: the original five covered the openness, diagnostic, scale, measurement, and update disciplines; this sixth pattern covers the coverage-distribution discipline that completes the response to equity/protected-interaction. - Ask each participating trainer to declare the modules they will own - Ask each participating institution to commit an explicit coverage profile with resourcing - Maintain an aggregate network-level coverage map (linked: ukrns/scale-register) - Audit the map for gaps (modules without owners or with only under-resourced owners) - Where Composition (3) applies: flag coverage gaps as institutional honesty rather than hiding them - Use this pattern alongside ukrns/diagnose-before-prescribing (which profile can commit to which composition?) and ukrns/provision-at-network-scale (what coordination does distributed coverage require?)

title: Exercise Response Capture — What Happens When Readers Pick Positions (Implementation Pattern)
text: Exercise Response Capture — What Happens When Readers Pick Positions (Implementation Pattern) A paper that invites readers to pick positions on axes has a choice about what to do when they do. The service states which composition it is running on the axis between passive exercises (reader picks privately, no capture) and captured responses (positions logged, with consent, and aggregated). Capture without consent is a privacy failure; capture followed by silence is a trust failure. The current composition on the capture axis is declared. If responses are captured, consent is explicit and feedback is provided. Reader privacy is preserved under the declared composition. This implementation pattern specifies the response mechanic behind ukrns/reader-as-participant. The meta-pattern invites readers into the diagnosis; this pattern addresses the practical question of what happens after they accept the invitation. Without a declared response-capture policy, exercises are either purely rhetorical (reader picks privately) or covertly data-producing (captured without visible consent). The pattern operates on the axis: passive exercises (reader picks privately; no capture mechanism) ↔ captured responses (positions logged with consent; distribution aggregated and fed back). Irreducible: an exercise cannot be both maximally frictionless and maximally data-producing. Real costs: passive costs the aggregate signal readers' responses could produce — the service never learns what distribution of positions its readers hold; captured costs reader friction, privacy risk, and the overhead of maintaining the capture infrastructure. Active dynamic: early in a paper's life, passive suffices; as the exercise set matures, captured responses become informative (and as operational UKRN-S moves from paper to service, capture becomes a natural fit). - Covert capture: responses captured without visible consent - Capture without feedback: responses logged but never surfaced; readers contribute to a black box - Passive exercises framed as captured: the paper implies responses matter operationally but has no channel for them to land - Over-engineered capture: interactive infrastructure built but exercises do not produce responses worth capturing - Consent-creep: initial consent is narrow but response use expands silently Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Passive-only: exercises invite but no response mechanism exists; reader picks privately. Paper's current state. Gives up aggregate signal. (2) Opt-in capture: invitation to submit responses via a declared channel (form, email, repo issue); responses aggregated and distribution published; consent explicit at point of response. Gives up universal participation. (3) Embedded capture: interactive notebook (or live HTML with JavaScript) where positions are captured by default; consent must be architected into the interface, not assumed. Gives up low-tech accessibility; requires privacy infrastructure. The paper currently operates at (1). Composition (3) is a future state requiring specific infrastructure. Engaged when: the composition is declared; if responses are captured, consent is explicit and responses are fed back in some form; if passive, the exercises make clear that no capture is occurring. Failing when: responses are captured without visible consent; captured responses are never surfaced back; the paper invites participation but there is no channel for responses to land anywhere. Consent-first discipline: capture without visible consent is coercive — readers who thought their responses were private discover they have been counted. Any composition above (1) requires explicit consent architecture, and the consent must be present at the point the response is given. Feedback-or-don't: capturing responses and never surfacing them back to readers is a trust failure. If the service asks readers to respond, the minimal contract is that the service reports what the responses were. Composition (2) requires aggregated feedback; composition (3) benefits from live visibility. Pedagogical vs diagnostic purpose: the exercises serve two purposes in ukrns/reader-as-participant: they teach pattern-reading (pedagogical) and they invite the reader's position (diagnostic). The pedagogical purpose is served by passive exercises; the diagnostic purpose requires some form of capture. The composition choice names which purpose is being served. Commons-adjacent: if responses are captured, the aggregate distribution is itself a commons artefact. Governance of that data (who can see it, how it is curated, how long it is retained) mirrors ukrns/assumptions-commons' concerns. Mechanic, in short: Mechanic: what happens to reader positions on exercise axes. Serves: reader-as-participant's invitation claim. Axis: passive ↔ captured responses. Without this pattern: invitations are rhetorical, and any capture risks coercion. - Declare the current composition in the paper or project documentation - If (2) or (3): write a consent statement; declare retention policy; set up a feedback mechanism for aggregates - If (1): make it explicit that exercises are for the reader alone - Cross-reference with ukrns/assumptions-commons if responses feed into evidence

title: Join Up Training, Indicators, and Sector Positioning (Sketch)
text: Join Up Training, Indicators, and Sector Positioning (Sketch) Training without indicators cannot show what changed. Indicators without sector positioning do not reach the bodies that could act on them. Sector positioning without a live training offer is positioning without product. The three lines only pay fully when they are joined up. The current paper's background section identifies these three lines of evidence separately, then concludes that their parallel treatment is one of the main current failure modes. The pattern operates on the axis: parallel evidence lines ↔ operationally joined evidence lines. Real costs: joining the lines up requires more coordination and more role clarity than running each stream on its own. Design the exchanges so training generates indicators-relevant evidence, indicators feed sector translation, and sector signals feed the next training and evaluation wave.

title: Measure Where Uncertainty Is Highest
text: Measure Where Uncertainty Is Highest A service with limited evaluation capacity should measure where the next observation is most likely to matter. Sometimes that means measuring where the evidence gap is biggest. Sometimes it means measuring where board attention, funder attention, or sector attention is already concentrated. The key discipline is to choose deliberately and to say which principle is selecting the next wave of work. Measurement should not drift toward whatever is easiest, most flattering, or most familiar. The current paper makes two things clear. First, some open-research indicators can already be measured reasonably well, while others still cannot. Second, the wider sector conversation and funder cycle do not attend evenly to every topic, institution type, or signal. Because evaluation capacity is bounded, UKRN Services cannot treat every possible question as equally urgent. It needs a rule for deciding where the next piece of measurement effort goes. The pattern operates on the axis: uncertainty reduction ↔ stakeholder attention. Irreducible: the place where the service is least sure is not always the place where outside attention is already waiting. A single wave of evaluation often has to choose which question it is trying to answer first. Real costs: measuring where uncertainty is highest sharpens the design fastest, but it may miss the places where visible accountability is most needed. Measuring where attention already sits may help with governance, legitimacy, and partnership, but it may tell the service little that it does not broadly know already. Active dynamic: both maps move. Uncertainty should shrink if the service is learning. Attention should shift as sector priorities, funder cycles, and public pressures change. So the selection rule cannot be fixed once and forgotten. - Convenience drift: the same easy-to-reach settings are measured repeatedly because they are easy - Reassurance drift: measurement is aimed mainly at places most likely to produce good news - Uncertainty neglect: the service keeps talking confidently about areas it still has weak evidence on - Attention neglect: the service learns things internally but cannot answer the questions external stakeholders actually ask - Hidden mix: a wave is really selected on mixed grounds, but only one reason is published - Measure-everything fiction: a bounded service pretends it can observe everything at once and ends up observing none of it well Choose the selection principle for each wave before the work starts, and publish it. (1) Uncertainty-first: use the wave mainly to tighten the weakest parts of the evidence base. Gives up some immediate external legibility. (2) Attention-first: use the wave mainly to answer the question that funders, partners, or member institutions are already pressing on. Gives up some learning efficiency. (3) Split wave: reserve part of the budget for the biggest evidence gaps and part for the most watched questions. Gives up some reach in order to do both honestly. These compositions are not ranked in the abstract. The current paper leans toward uncertainty-first when the aim is to improve the design, but it also makes clear that attention cannot simply be ignored. Engaged when: each evaluation wave has a stated reason for selection; the service can say which open question or implementation decision the wave is meant to inform; the next wave reflects what the last one learned. Failing when: measurement choices are made post hoc; the same terrain is measured repeatedly for convenience; or no one can explain why this wave happened here rather than somewhere else. Indicator capacity is uneven: The paper is explicit that some indicators are already tractable and some are not. That means measurement discipline is not a luxury. It is how the service avoids promising to demonstrate things it still cannot actually demonstrate. Learning depends on selective observation: If evidence is supposed to shape design, then the service has to decide where an additional observation will change its judgement most. Otherwise evaluation becomes diffuse activity rather than decision support. External attention is real: Member institutions, funders, and partners do not care about all questions equally. A service that never measures where scrutiny already sits may become internally coherent but externally unpersuasive. Governance benefit: Stating the selection principle before fieldwork makes the service's reasoning inspectable. It allows institutions and partners to challenge not only the findings, but the choice of what was measured in the first place. Mechanic, in short: Derived from the paper's distinction between what can currently be measured, where uncertainty still lives, and where sector attention already sits. Answers the service-level version of the visible-impact problem: not just whether evidence exists, but where the service chooses to look next. Mapped to the learning loop at the measure step: after diagnosis and provisioning, bounded evaluation effort is placed where it will matter most. Coordination requirement: Medium, rising when a wave depends on distributed data collection across institutions. - Publish, for each evaluation wave, whether it is mainly uncertainty-reducing, attention-facing, or a stated mix - Tie each wave explicitly to one of the paper's open questions or implementation decisions - Reassess the selection rule after each wave rather than repeating the same pattern by habit - Keep a visible list of questions the service still cannot yet measure well, so silence is not mistaken for closure - Use this pattern upstream of design revision, where evidence is meant to produce operational consequence

title: Model Recompute Schedule — When Computation Runs Operationally (Implementation Pattern)
text: Model Recompute Schedule — When Computation Runs Operationally (Implementation Pattern) A notebook that loads evidence and recomputes the model is inert until someone triggers a rerun. The service states when and why the model recomputes — on evidence arrival (event-driven), on a calendar (cadence-driven), or in a declared hybrid — and which recomputes produce published design-state changes. Every rerun output carries a timestamp and an evidence-revision identifier; no output circulates without those. The current recompute composition is declared. Every output carries a timestamp and evidence-revision identifier. A recompute log is maintained. This implementation pattern specifies the operational mechanics behind ukrns/self-application (the paper is a re-runnable notebook) and ukrns/design-as-function-of-evidence (updates trace to evidence). Without a declared recompute schedule, self-application is a property of the artefact that nobody exercises, and design-state updates happen silently. The pattern operates on the axis: event-driven recompute (triggered by evidence arrival or assumptions change) ↔ cadence-driven recompute (triggered on a published calendar). Irreducible: a single policy cannot be both maximally event-responsive and maximally predictable-by-calendar. Real costs: event-driven costs predictability — readers do not know when a change will happen; cadence-driven costs latency — evidence sits unprocessed until the next scheduled rerun.
