Concentrating on the linking loop lets partners judge whether collective sense-making improves. next[Pick 1–2 partners and co-design a lightweight pilot plan documenting observations.] next[Define a decision threshold (e.g., pilots report new shared insights) that gates broader feature build-out.]

title: Non-Destructive Relational Layers
text: Non-Destructive Relational Layers Add relational layers that connect stories without rewriting the originals. You are extending a story corpus into a shared world while preserving narrative sovereignty. This does not apply when stories are intentionally merged into a single authored narrative. Contributors need to propose links, arcs, or interpretations across stories without altering the canonical texts. Forcing links into canonical layers violates sovereignty and can create incoherence or conflict. Introduce opt-in relational layers (e.g., overlays, adjacency maps, interpretive bridges) that sit beside canonical stories and can be accepted, revised, or retired without changing originals. Non-destructive layers allow shared meaning to emerge while protecting ownership and provenance. next[Define a lightweight relational proposal schema (links, arcs, bridges) and a review workflow.] next[Prototype an opt-in overlay view that preserves original stories.] next[Sketch an “emporium” adjacency map for three stories and define a minimal adjacency link type.] next[Record one case where the layer prevented a canonical conflict and one case where it added noise.]

title: Offer Ladder
text: Offer Ladder Define a simple offer ladder (intro workshop → multi-session pilot → annual programme) where each rung has a clear scope, price band, and expected outcome. You are translating 'story manifold' capabilities into a small set of concrete (purchasable) offerings that institutions can understand, budget for, and adopt. This does not apply when procurement requires a single bundled offer. A story platform with rich theory but no articulated “offers” risks being seen as a research toy rather than a service. Communities, NGOs, and universities buy concrete packages—workshops, courses, facilitation, reporting—rather than abstract infrastructures. Define a simple offer ladder (intro workshop → multi-session pilot → annual programme) where each rung has a clear scope, price band, and expected outcome. A visible ladder of offers turns VSATLAS from an idea into a portfolio of bookable engagements that can recover costs and demonstrate real-world demand. next[Draft the three-rung ladder with scope, price band, and outcomes.] next[Test the ladder with one partner and refine based on feedback.] next[Define adoption signals (e.g., partner picks a rung without extra explanation) and revise if absent.] next[Define where interpretation sessions sit in the ladder (e.g., a mid-tier offer).]

title: Open Ecosystem Mandate
text: Open Ecosystem Mandate Publish core components under open licences, cultivate a distributed developer community, and document governance primitives. You are considering whether there is a strategic requirement that the platform’s foundations remain open, forkable, and governable to support long-term collective authorship. This does not apply to short-lived prototypes where governance is not yet in scope. Centralised proprietary systems limit trust, adoption, and collaboration. Multi-author worlds require transparent, forkable, and collectively governed foundations. Publish core components under open licences, cultivate a distributed developer community, and document governance primitives. Only an open ecosystem can support pluriversality, collective authorship, and long-term resilience. next[Draft an open-ecosystem charter and list the non-negotiables.] next[Identify the first two governance primitives to document publicly.] next[Define evidence signals (e.g., external contributors, forks, governance participation) and a failure case (e.g., no uptake despite openness).]

text: Peeragogical Infrastructures Embed scaffolds for co-authorship, negotiation of meaning, stewardship, and joint decision-making inside the manifold. Peeragogical competence is required to maintain shared worlds and enable social imagination. next[Add one explicit co-authorship ritual to the onboarding flow.] next[Define a stewardship checkpoint that requires shared decision-making.] next[Define success signals (e.g., shared decisions recorded) and a failure signal (e.g., coordination breakdown persists).]

title: Turn Pilot Results into Offers
text: Turn Pilot Results into Offers Translate successful pilots into a few clearly named offerings that organisations can adopt and fund. Pilots show that linked stories help cohorts see shared situations. Leaving results as “internal improvements” obscures what partners are buying. title: Pluriversal Infrastructure
text: Pluriversal Infrastructure Build infrastructure for, and with, thriving pluriverses. Communities facing structural inequities produce fragmented testimony that outsiders often reframe for spectators. External framing erases agency and reinforces dependency. Provide infrastructure where communities author, connect, and interpret their own stories across the manifold. Pluriversal design ensures “nothing about us without us” and turns distributed knowledge into collective power. + next[Draft a community-authored charter that defines story ownership and interpretation rights.] + next[Prototype a consent workflow for linking stories across communities.] + next[Define evidence signals (e.g., community-led interpretation sessions) and a falsifier (e.g., community rejects the linking process).]

title: Precise Concept to Test
text: Precise Concept to Test Define the VSAT proof-of-concept as testing whether a minimal story-linking capability helps groups understand their shared situation better. You are defining proof-of-concept to be a single testable claim (in this case, whether minimal story linking helps groups gain shared insight). This does not apply once the linking claim is already validated for the target cohort. Individual stories already shine; the missing capability is “story links → group insight”. Without a crisp test concept, funding can drift into general improvements. State that the POC will test whether a basic link/propose/confirm/view loop yields new insight for cohorts. title: Proof Through Pilots
text: Proof Through Pilots Structure development around a small constellation of pilots, each framed as a question (“What can a connected story-world do for X?”) and each yielding stories, participant feedback, and a short interpretive report. Pilots can be a primary vehicle for evidence, and can structure development around real, concrete, questions, rather than a finished system. Small grants and limited runway cannot support a full build-out of the three-layer manifold. Attempting to “finish” the system in one go produces brittle code, shallow uptake, and no reusable evidence of value. Structure development around a small constellation of pilots, each framed as a question (“What can a connected story-world do for X?”) and each yielding stories, participant feedback, and a short interpretive report. Proof through pilots turns the business plan into a sequence of situated experiments whose successes—and failures—offer persuasive material for future commissions and follow-on funding. next[Define the first pilot question and the evidence you will capture.] next[Draft a template for the interpretive report delivered after each pilot.] next[Define what counts as proof (e.g., measurable changes in shared insight or coordination) and a falsifier.]

text: Reasons-to-Causes Gear Train Use cross-story arcs to convert individual testimony into distributed reasons and, ultimately, coordinated causes. title: Shared Stewardship Compact
text: Shared Stewardship Compact Articulate a shared stewardship compact that clarifies which parts of VSATLAS are commons (open protocols, core code), which are services (facilitation, training, customisation), and how partners can participate in governance over time. You are defining how ownership, responsibility, and governance are shared so partners can commit to a shared effort, without relying on a single founder or lab. This does not apply to short-lived experiments with no governance commitments. Early-stage platforms often rely on one or two overburdened founders who are expected to be visionaries, engineers, salespeople, and custodians. Concentrating all ownership and responsibility undermines resilience and makes partners wary of long-term dependence on a single individual or lab. Articulate a shared stewardship compact that clarifies which parts of VSATLAS are commons (open protocols, core code), which are services (facilitation, training, customisation), and how partners can participate in governance over time. A clear compact reassures institutions, invites co-ownership, and aligns the business model with the manifold’s deeper claim: that worlds worth living in are co-created and co-stewarded. next[Draft the compact as a one-page charter and circulate to anchor partners.] next[Define a first governance checkpoint and the decision rights it covers.] next[Define evidence signals (e.g., signed charter, shared decision logs) and a failure case (e.g., partners decline co-ownership).]

title: Story Emporium
text: Story Emporium Model the manifold as an emporium—an interior space where sovereign stories gain new meaning through adjacency and optional relations. You are framing the 'story manifold' as a shared interior where stories remain sovereign, but gain meaning through proximity and (optional) relationships. Vibrant ecosystems emerge when independent narrative units coexist in proximity. Model the manifold as an emporium—an interior space where sovereign stories gain new meaning through adjacency and optional relations. title: Sustainable Trajectory
text: Sustainable Trajectory Define PoC success as evidence that the system can move from cost → partial cost recovery → stable participation → self-sustaining adoption, documenting each step with narrative + financial proof. Small proof-of-concept grants (<£25k) rarely fund a fully operational system and success gets measured by total revenue beating total cost. Early-stage platforms need to show direction of travel, not immediate surplus; the key indicator is whether early deployments generate recoverable value and attract repeat participation. Define PoC success as evidence that the system can move from cost → partial cost recovery → stable participation → self-sustaining adoption, documenting each step with narrative + financial proof. title: Anthology as Constellation Filter
text: Anthology as Constellation Filter Use pilot-defined story subsets as anthology filters that reshape the constellation to a focused sub-world, preserving all spatial and relational affordances. You are curating viewing experiences for different audiences or sessions from the same corpus. This does not apply when all stories are always relevant to all viewers. A facilitator, exhibition, or course module needs a focused subset of the full story world. Showing everything overwhelms; building separate installations duplicates effort. Reuse the pilot (anthology) model to filter stories at query time (?pilot=N). The dome re-projects around fewer clusters, vertical spread is clamped for small collections, and all navigation (planetarium, geomview, VR) works on the filtered set. Filtering is cheaper than forking. The same relational infrastructure serves multiple curatorial frames without duplicating data or code. next[Test whether small anthologies (2–4 stories) feel spatially coherent or sparse.] next[Explore nested anthologies (pilot within pilot) for multi-session programmes.] next[Add anthology selection to the VR interface (controller menu or gaze-based selector).]

title: Arc as Typed Relation
text: Arc as Typed Relation Render inter-story links as coloured, curved arcs with type, status, and rationale so relational meaning is visible geometry, not hidden metadata. You are making the interpretive layer legible as spatial form. This does not apply when link volume is so high that arcs would become visual noise. Viewers need to see why stories are connected — not just that they are. Undifferentiated lines flatten thematic, causal, adjacency, and contrast links into a single "related" signal. Colour arcs by link type, modulate opacity by status (accepted bright, proposed mid, retired faint), and bow arcs inward (planetarium) or outward (geomview) so they read as spatial bridges rather than flat edges. Provide legend toggles to show/hide types independently. Typed arcs externalise the interpretive grammar that VSATLAS contributors use when proposing connections, making review and discussion concrete rather than abstract. next[Add arc hover interaction showing link rationale text in-scene.] next[Measure whether typed arcs improve participants' ability to articulate connection reasons.] next[Define a visual-noise threshold (arc count) where filtering or aggregation becomes necessary.]

title: Cached Layout Computation
text: Cached Layout Computation Cache the O(N²) force-directed layout across requests so the planetarium loads instantly when story data has not changed. You are serving a 3D visualisation from SSR where layout computation is the bottleneck. This does not apply to client-side-only visualisations where the cost is borne by the browser. The force-directed simulation (spring forces, repulsion, centering) runs on every request, consuming CPU proportional to scene count squared. Story data changes rarely — most requests see the same constellation. Fingerprint the inputs (story IDs, scene counts, link IDs, view mode, pilot filter) and cache the computed layout in a globalThis-backed in-memory store. Invalidate automatically when the fingerprint changes. First-load computes; subsequent loads return instantly. This turned a 200% CPU incident on a 2-CPU host into sub-millisecond cache hits. next[Add cache-hit/miss logging to measure real-world hit rate.] next[Consider persisting the cache to disk for cold-start performance after server restart.]

title: Cluster as Story, Node as Scene
text: Cluster as Story, Node as Scene Represent each story as a spatial cluster of scene nodes so internal narrative structure is visible alongside inter-story connections. You are designing a visualisation that must convey both within-story structure and between-story relationships at a glance. This does not apply to single-story views where internal navigation is sufficient. Viewers need to grasp both the shape of individual stories and how they relate to one another. Collapsing stories to single points hides internal richness; flattening all scenes to one level hides story boundaries. Use a two-level layout: stories are clusters positioned on the dome via golden-spiral distribution, and scenes within each cluster are arranged by force-directed simulation around the cluster centre. Narrative arcs (within) and interpretive links (between) are drawn as distinct arc types. Two-level clustering preserves the part-whole relationship that makes a story more than a bag of scenes, while still exposing the relational fabric that VSATLAS adds across stories. next[Test legibility with 50+ stories to find the threshold where clusters overlap.] next[Experiment with alternative intra-cluster layouts (radial, timeline) for stories with strong sequence.]

title: Dome Projection as Reading Frame
text: Dome Projection as Reading Frame Project story constellations onto a dome surface so the viewer occupies a privileged interior position — reading outward rather than inspecting from above. You are choosing a spatial metaphor for browsing a connected story world. This does not apply when the corpus is small enough that a flat list suffices. A collection of linked stories needs a spatial reading frame that communicates immersion and equal proximity. Flat graphs or tree views impose implicit hierarchies and lose the sense of being surrounded by a world. Map story clusters onto the inner surface of a sphere (planetarium model) so the viewer looks outward at the constellation from its centre, with drag-to-rotate giving access to the full sky. The dome equalises distance — every story is the same radius away, and orientation replaces ranking as the primary navigation axis. next[Measure whether dome vs flat-list affects exploration breadth (stories visited per session).] next[Test with screen-reader users to define a non-visual equivalent of dome orientation.]

title: Embodied Browsing (VR as First-Class Navigation)
text: Embodied Browsing (VR as First-Class Navigation) Treat VR headset navigation as a first-class mode where the viewer's body (head orientation, hand pointing, controller buttons) replaces mouse and scroll as the primary interface to the constellation. You are designing for immersive hardware (Quest 2/3, future AR) where the viewer is physically inside the dome. This does not apply to desktop-only deployments. The planetarium metaphor maps naturally to VR — the viewer is literally inside a sphere of stories. Porting mouse interactions to VR produces clumsy, imprecise pointing at small targets with no tactile feedback. Add generous invisible hit volumes around nodes and labels, use controller buttons for structural navigation (B = back to planetarium), and keep the viewer inside the scene rather than navigating away (overlay architecture for story reading). Embodied interfaces reward spatial memory — viewers remember where a story is in the dome and reach for it, building familiarity through physical gesture rather than text search. next[Prototype the overlay architecture so story-reading stays inside the planetarium scene.] next[Test with AR passthrough to see if the dome works as a mixed-reality installation.] next[Measure whether VR visitors explore more stories than desktop visitors (spatial memory effect).]

title: Sky-Disk Continuum (Immersion ↔ Overview)
text: Sky-Disk Continuum (Immersion ↔ Overview) Allow continuous zoom from immersive dome interior to external sky-disk overview so viewers can shift between situated reading and structural comprehension without changing mode. You are designing navigation that spans close-reading and bird's-eye analysis within a single interaction. This does not apply when the corpus has no spatial projection (e.g., pure list views). Viewers need to alternate between exploring a neighbourhood of stories and surveying the whole constellation. Discrete mode switches (planetarium button vs geomview button) break flow and lose spatial orientation. Let scroll-back move the camera past the dome origin so the surrounding sphere contracts into a visible disk. As the camera retreats, dome-projected arcs smoothly straighten to their natural bezier paths via debounced redraw at blended dome radius. Continuous zoom preserves the viewer's mental model of where they are in the constellation. The transition from "inside looking out" to "outside looking in" is a zoom, not a teleport. next[Animate node positions to match arc straightening (currently nodes stay dome-projected).] next[Test whether the sky-disk view is useful for facilitators projecting to a group.] next[Explore whether the continuum works in VR (headset zoom via thumbstick push/pull).]

title: Vapor as Affective Dimension
text: Vapor as Affective Dimension Use a continuous "vapor" slider to control atmospheric intensity — bloom, glow, particles, colour shift — so viewers can modulate the affective register of the constellation without changing its structure. You are designing an interface where emotional tone is a parameter alongside structural navigation. This does not apply to purely analytic views where atmosphere would be misleading. The same constellation serves both analytical review and evocative exhibition contexts. A fixed aesthetic either feels too clinical for exhibition or too decorative for analysis. Provide a single slider that continuously blends from minimal (dark, precise, subtle arcs) to maximal (pink glow, bloom on arcs, particle dust, background colour shift, hover halos). The underlying data stays identical. Separating affect from structure lets the same tool serve a facilitator's workshop (vapor low) and a gallery wall (vapor high) without rebuilding the view. next[Test whether high-vapor mode influences which stories viewers explore first (affect-driven navigation).] next[Consider per-cluster vapor levels to highlight focal stories in a facilitated session.]

title: Dome Projection as Reading Frame
text: Dome Projection as Reading Frame Cache the O(N²) force-directed layout across requests so the planetarium loads instantly when data has not changed. You are choosing a spatial metaphor for browsing a connected story world. This does not apply when the corpus is small enough that a flat list suffices. You are designing a visualisation that must convey both within-story structure and between-story relationships at a glance. You are making the interpretive layer legible as spatial form. You are curating viewing experiences for different audiences or sessions from the same corpus. You are designing navigation that spans close-reading and bird's-eye analysis within a single interaction. You are designing for immersive hardware where the viewer is physically inside the dome. You are designing an interface where emotional tone is a parameter alongside structural navigation. You are serving a 3D visualisation from SSR where layout is the bottleneck. A collection of linked stories needs a spatial reading frame that communicates immersion and equal proximity. Viewers need to grasp both the shape of individual stories and how they relate to one another. Viewers need to see why stories are connected — not just that they are. A facilitator, exhibition, or course module needs a focused subset of the full story world. Viewers need to alternate between exploring a neighbourhood and surveying the whole constellation. The planetarium metaphor maps naturally to VR — the viewer is literally inside a sphere of stories. The same constellation serves both analytical review and evocative exhibition. The force-directed simulation runs on every request, consuming CPU proportional to scene count squared. Flat graphs or tree views impose implicit hierarchies and lose the sense of being surrounded by a world. Collapsing stories to single points hides internal richness; flattening all scenes to one level hides story boundaries. Undifferentiated lines flatten thematic, causal, adjacency, and contrast links into a single "related" signal. Showing everything overwhelms; building separate installations duplicates effort. Discrete mode switches break flow and lose spatial orientation. Porting mouse interactions to VR produces clumsy, imprecise pointing. A fixed aesthetic either feels too clinical for exhibition or too decorative for analysis. Story data changes rarely — most requests see the same constellation. Map story clusters onto the inner surface of a sphere (planetarium model) so the viewer looks outward at the constellation from its centre. Use a two-level layout: stories are clusters positioned on the dome via golden-spiral distribution, and scenes within each cluster are arranged by force-directed simulation. Colour arcs by link type, modulate opacity by status, bow arcs to read as spatial bridges. Provide legend toggles to show/hide types independently. Reuse the pilot model to filter stories at query time. The dome re-projects around fewer clusters with clamped vertical spread. Let scroll-back move the camera past the dome origin so the surrounding sphere contracts into a visible disk, with arcs smoothly straightening. Add generous hit volumes, controller buttons for structural navigation, and keep the viewer inside the scene via overlay architecture. Provide a single slider that blends from minimal (dark, precise) to maximal (glow, bloom, particles). The data stays identical. Fingerprint inputs and cache the layout in a globalThis-backed store. Invalidate when the fingerprint changes. The dome equalises distance — every story is the same radius away, and orientation replaces ranking as the primary navigation axis. Two-level clustering preserves the part-whole relationship that makes a story more than a bag of scenes. Typed arcs externalise the interpretive grammar that contributors use when proposing connections. Filtering is cheaper than forking. The same infrastructure serves multiple curatorial frames. Continuous zoom preserves the viewer's mental model. The transition from "inside looking out" to "outside looking in" is a zoom, not a teleport. Embodied interfaces reward spatial memory — viewers remember where a story is and reach for it. Separating affect from structure lets the same tool serve a workshop and a gallery wall. First-load computes; subsequent loads return instantly.

title: Advanceability — An Open Mission Is an Autonomous Target Only If It Has a Concrete Next Hole
text: Advanceability — An Open Mission Is an Autonomous Target Only If It Has a Concrete Next Hole An open mission is an admissible autonomous WM target only if it has at least one open hole — a concrete next increment. A hole-less open mission (its gap not yet articulated) is NOT auto-actionable: surface it (NAG), do not pick it. Among admissible missions, prefer the single-cycle leaf (exactly one open hole). The WM ranks open missions to advance. Missions sit at varying lifecycle phases (IDENTIFY..INSTANTIATE); some carry articulated open work (counted holes), others — early or stub — carry none. Your autonomous loop selects "advance mission M" actions over a landscape of missions at different maturities. A mission with zero open holes has nothing concrete to advance THIS cycle — either its gap is not yet articulated (an un-agreed IDENTIFY) or it is effectively done. Picking it means the agent "engages" but has no bounded next step, so it flails or fake-finishes. And — the subtle failure — a body-size score that rewards smallness will PERVERSELY prefer the 0-hole mission (nothing-to-do scores best) over a 1-hole single-cycle leaf (one real cycle of work). Gate `:open-mission` actions with `open-mission-with-holes?` (`open?` AND `open-hole-count ≥ 1`). A 0-hole open mission is inadmissible for autonomous advancement → NAG: *"nothing concrete to advance here; articulate the next hole / agree the gap, or it's not ready."* Among admissible (≥1-hole) missions, prefer the **single-cycle leaf** — exactly one open hole = exactly one bounded cycle. Advance one hole per cycle (don't flood). The WM advances work, and "advance" requires a concrete increment — a hole. The hole-count is the advanceability proxy. Without the ≥1-hole gate the agent picks vacuous targets; with a naive small-is-good body term it actively prefers them. Both are real, observed failure modes (below). The gate also carries the hole-budget discipline (one hole/cycle, the E-cheesemonger bound) — bounded, earned, no fake-finish. - The gate lives in `autonomous-admissible?` (`futon3c/wm/guardrails.clj` → `open-mission-with-holes?` / `positive-open-hole-count?`). - Pairs with pattern-warranted-choice-point: the 0-hole NAG carries the advanceability warrant (here is why, here is the gap = articulate the hole). - Hardening (separate): the EFE body-size term should prefer EXACTLY one hole (a "distance-from-1-hole" shape), not merely reward fewer holes — so a 0-hole mission never out-scores a single-cycle leaf even if the admissibility filter is bypassed (defense-in-depth). - evidence: 0-hole picks rejected per run; single-cycle-leaf pick rate; fake-finish (claimed-discharge, field-didn't-move) rate. - evidence-shape: {:zero-hole-rejected :int, :single-cycle-leaf-picks :int, :multi-hole-picks :int, :fake-finishes :int} Selection surfaces where every candidate is guaranteed to carry articulated work (no hole-less items can appear). Non-mission action classes (advanceability is mission-specific). - Terminal-C3 (M-capability-star-map, 2026-06-07): the RAW candidate run top-ranked `M-arxana-roundtrip` (0 holes, `:identify`) purely because body=0 scored best; the PRODUCTION `open-mission-with-holes?` gate excluded it, and EFE then top-ranked the 1-hole single-cycle leaf `M-essay-corpus-substrate` — C3 PASS. The gate is the difference between a vacuous pick and a real one.

title: Ambient Pattern Retrieval
text: Ambient Pattern Retrieval A library of reusable strategies that is searched automatically on every conversation turn functions as ambient intelligence - the system's background awareness of what it knows, surfaced without being asked. futon3a's pattern library is searched via MiniLM embeddings on every A->B turn in the REPL, and the results appear as desktop notifications with evidence certificates. The operator does not request the search; it happens as a side-effect of working. Over time, the activation pattern across the library reveals which strategies are repeatedly relevant and which are never activated. The system can search a large pattern library automatically on each work turn and surface the results ambiently rather than as an interruption. A large knowledge base is only useful when the right pieces surface at the right time. Retrieval quality depends on embedding quality and library coverage, and notification fatigue will turn ambient retrieval into noise if low-relevance patterns keep firing. Search the library on every turn as a background process. Display results as ambient notifications, log the activation history as evidence, and use the resulting hot-zone / cold-zone pattern to tune retrieval and train later pre-hoc prediction. Expert practitioners develop intuitions that surface relevant knowledge without deliberate recall. Ambient retrieval externalises that intuition: the system maintains a background awareness of its own knowledge and surfaces relevant pieces as the situation evolves. next[Use the activation history to tune retrieval quality and distinguish genuine hot zones from cold library regions that never become relevant.]

title: Coordination Bottleneck
text: Coordination Bottleneck Multi-agent coordination fails at infrastructure seams, not at intelligence boundaries: the bottleneck is merge permissions, liveness signals, and orchestration state, not agent capability. The Tickle Experiment ran a multi-agent CT review pipeline with rising approval quality, but much of the rework came from merge gaps, a stateless orchestrator, and silent failures. The agents were competent; the plumbing leaked. Multiple agents are working across a shared pipeline and the same coordination failures recur across otherwise capable agents. A system can work at the agent level while still failing at the infrastructure level. Some failures are still agent-level, and infrastructure investment eventually hits diminishing returns, but repeated cross-agent failure is a systems signal first. Invest first in liveness heartbeats, stateful orchestration, and merge automation before trying to solve the problem with more capable agents or larger prompts. Coordination is a system property, not an agent property. Improving the parts while ignoring the relations between them produces more capable agents that still cannot coordinate. next[Instrument liveness, stateful assignment tracking, and merge automation before scheduling another capability-only improvement pass.]

title: Dynamic Over Static
text: Dynamic Over Static A dynamic display that animates state changes over time reveals patterns that a static snapshot hides - trends, rhythms, decay, and momentum become visible as motion. The futon2 ant war visualiser makes colony momentum obvious within seconds, whereas a single screenshot only shows positions. The same applies to strategic state: a static report can show counts but not whether those counts are growing, shrinking, or stalled. The operator needs to distinguish growth from decay, acceleration from stagnation, or winning motion from a dead-even snapshot. Static reports show position but not momentum. Animation also adds complexity and can be distracting if motion overwhelms semantically important but quieter regions. Animate the strategic state over time, with replay controls and a spatial layout that makes both position and trajectory visible at once, while keeping the table as a drill-down renderer for exact values. Temporal patterns are perceptible in animation but invisible in snapshots. For strategic awareness, the trajectory matters more than the position; you need the movie, not just the frame. next[Replay recent strategic history as a controllable animation and check whether the motion reveals distinctions the static report concealed.]

title: Half-Blind Observation
text: Half-Blind Observation An observation surface that covers half the system produces worse decisions than no observation surface at all, because it creates false confidence in completeness. The evidence store initially scanned only part of the repo set, yet still produced plausible coverage statistics. Review exposed that missing channels and missing repos were being treated as invisible rather than as first-class uncertainty. The system is building an observation surface to drive recommendations, summaries, or prioritisation. Partial coverage is inevitable, but unacknowledged partial coverage is dangerous. A half-blind observer overweights what it can see and confidently ignores what it cannot. Make every observation channel report both its findings and its coverage, and surface missing data as prominently as positive findings. An observer that knows it is blind can at least flag uncertainty. An observer that believes it sees everything makes confident wrong recommendations. next[Add explicit coverage reporting to every observation channel and refuse aggregate confidence claims that hide missing surfaces.]

title: Ideal Actual Gap
text: Ideal Actual Gap A self-representing system needs two images - what it aspires to be and what it actually is - plus a computable comparison between them. The stack already maintains ideal self-images in devmaps and actual state in evidence and code, but the comparison between them is still manual. Joe reads both and synthesises the discrepancy in his head. The system maintains both aspirational specifications and evidence about its current implementation and coverage. Self-representation without self-comparison turns into portraiture rather than correction. Some ideals remain only partly measurable, but the raw discrepancy still needs to be machine-detectable. Compute the ideal/actual gap: compare devmap components against mission inventory, compare sorry topology against implementation state, and surface the discrepancy as a first-class report. The war machine operates in smooth space but periodically needs a computable comparison against its striated self-image to detect drift at scale. next[Build a discrepancy report that pairs each ideal component with current evidence and flags the gaps that still require human judgment.]

title: Inhabitation Threshold
text: Inhabitation Threshold Infrastructure that is 90% built and 0% inhabited produces zero value; the last 10% that reduces entry friction is what creates the value because it crosses the inhabitation threshold. The evidence pipeline, pattern retrieval, browser surfaces, and HUD were all built before the session that finally fixed the entry ceremony. Once the friction bugs were removed, the already-built infrastructure became inhabited immediately. A stack surface is largely built but still too awkward, brittle, or ritual-heavy to enter during ordinary work. Prerequisite build-out is real, and inhabitation alone can also become a trap if it never deposits externally. The failure mode here is not building, but infrastructure that exists without being used. Treat entry friction as severity-critical. Measure inhabitation as a first-class metric and prioritise the fixes that let ordinary work actually pass through the surface. The war machine exists only when it is inhabited. No new capability was required once the entry bugs were fixed; the same infrastructure started producing evidence as soon as the threshold was crossed. next[Audit every major surface for the exact bug or ritual that still blocks ordinary entry, and fix those before adding new capability.]

title: Operational Not Decorative
text: Operational Not Decorative Infrastructure that validates is operational; infrastructure that only documents is decorative. The test is whether the artifact changes behaviour when it fails. Wiring diagrams were assumed decorative until they began catching structural errors at scale. Once a wrong arrow produced a detectable failure, the diagram stopped being mere documentation. The system is relying on a document, diagram, or status surface to steer or validate work. Decorative infrastructure can still aid comprehension, and some sketches are intentionally aspirational. The failure comes when decorative artifacts are trusted as if they were operational. Make the artifact testable: derive status from evidence, validate diagrams, and wire failures so they force correction instead of silently going stale. Operational infrastructure is defined by observable failure. A README can drift forever; a validator, gate, or checked diagram changes behaviour when reality diverges. next[For each strategic artifact, name the failure condition that would force correction; if none exists, treat it as decorative until one is built.]

title: Spatial Over Tabular
text: Spatial Over Tabular A spatial display that shows state as shape and colour earns inhabitation; a tabular display that encodes state as numbers in rows becomes wallpaper. The ant war visualiser is watched at a glance, while markdown tables require deliberate reading and synthesis. The same information becomes obvious when presented spatially and becomes homework when presented only as rows. Strategic state needs to be grasped quickly and revisited often rather than read line by line on demand. Tables are still better for precise lookup, and spatial layouts can mislead if they are visually active but semantically arbitrary. Render the same state spatially - active regions glow, neglected regions dim, imbalances show as asymmetric shape - while keeping the table as a precise drill-down fallback. Human vision processes colour, size, position, and motion pre-attentively. Strategic overviews need repeated comprehension at low cost, and spatial layout lowers that cost every time. next[Prefer semantically grounded spatial layouts for strategic overviews, then keep exact counts and dates available as tabular drill-down.]

title: State Capture
text: State Capture A nomadic practice is captured when it begins reproducing itself rather than following external flows; the test is whether today's work closes an external sorry or only improves the infrastructure for closing sorrys. Joe HUD signals showed stack work dominating consulting and portfolio work. The system was becoming better at maintaining itself while external sorrys remained the ground truth that justified the stack in the first place. Infrastructure maintenance begins to dominate the work mix and stack activity starts serving more stack activity than external deposition. Some self-maintenance is necessary, and there is a live philosophical question about which side is the nomad and which is the State. The pattern matters when self-maintenance dominates instead of supporting grounded obligations. Use pocketwatch-style constraints and explicit external-sorry checks: every stack work item must answer which outside obligation it closes, and stack hours must stay bounded relative to portfolio and consulting hours. The war machine can be captured by the institution it created. Without an explicit test, the stack quietly redirects nomadic practice toward self-reproduction. next[Require each stack task to name the external sorry it closes, and treat tasks with no such answer as capture until proven otherwise.]

title: Close Then Reframe Focus
text: Close Then Reframe Focus Close the current focus deliberately, then explicitly choose the next focus, so agenda pressure does not silently turn into priority drift. next[Define what counts as "done enough" for the current FOCUS, list overrun items with a one-line statement of leverage, and choose the next FOCUS explicitly rather than by drift.]

title: Single-Focus Amidst Agenda Saturation
text: Single-Focus Amidst Agenda Saturation Close Then Reframe Focus The week agenda contains many TODO, NEXT, WAIT, and SHIP items across ORPM and AOB, but only one item is explicitly marked FOCUS. The current agenda has one explicit FOCUS item alongside many scheduled tasks that have accumulated partial progress or overrun status. There is exactly one FOCUS item while multiple other tasks remain scheduled, recurring, or deadline-bearing. A FOCUS item is sufficiently bounded that it can be brought to a defensible stopping point. Several non-FOCUS items still demand attention due to deadlines, dependencies, or institutional expectations. Multiple overrun items compete as plausible successors and risk pulling attention prematurely. Treat the FOCUS item as the sole candidate for discretionary depth, and constrain all other items to execution at their minimal viable level unless they directly unblock or materially enrich the FOCUS. Complete the current FOCUS to a clear "finished enough" artifact, then deliberately select the next FOCUS from the overrun set based on leverage rather than urgency. A single declared focus only functions as such if it is protected from dilution by equally attention-hungry tasks. Focus only compounds value when it reaches closure, producing a reference point that informs the next prioritization rather than fragmenting effort. next[Check whether any non-FOCUS items causally unblock or substantially reshape the FOCUS; if so, either promote them or explicitly time-box them to prevent silent priority creep.]

title: Sign-Off Affordance for Deep Work
text: Sign-Off Affordance for Deep Work Sign-Off Affordance for Deep Work You are working in a high-agency, high-immersion environment (Emacs, Codex, ChatGPT, long arcs) where attention is valuable and interruptions are minimal by design. Deep work environments are successful at holding attention and reducing friction. They systematically erase natural stopping cues, making it easy to overshoot physical, cognitive, or temporal limits without noticing until damage has already accumulated. Persistence requires an explicit sign-off affordance at the FUTON-0 level: a mechanism that helps you recognize when continuation has stopped being beneficial before exhaustion, distortion, or resentment appear. Long-arc work fails not when people start poorly, but when they lack reliable ways to stop without loss of identity, momentum, or meaning. next[Treat signing off as a first-class state transition, not an absence of work.] next[Identify concrete signals already present (time of day, bodily cues, repetition, diminishing returns) that could be surfaced rather than inferred.] next[Prototype something minimal and reversible (a prompt, a timer with semantic meaning, a closing ritual, a FUTON-0 log entry) and observe whether it preserves desire to return.]

title: External Project Index as System of Record
text: External Project Index as System of Record External Project Index as System of Record The ChatGPT web sidebar is a slow, weak global navigator, and you are aiming to reduce dependence on the web UI. An external index can treat projects as contexts you can enter via stable pointers, while your own system becomes the canonical registry. You can identify a stable entry URL per project (for example, one canonical chat inside each project) and store it in a fast local registry. Some projects will not have a single obvious entry point, and links can become stale if you reorganize, rename, or delete chats. Maintain a minimal registry that maps project-id or name to entry URL + short intent + last-touched date, and add a periodic link-audit micro-loop that refreshes broken pointers and promotes better entry chats when needed. A small, explicit registry decouples navigation from a slow UI surface and makes "where do I go next?" an inspectable, improvable artifact rather than an interaction with a sidebar. next[Pick 10 high-use projects, create (or designate) one entry chat each, capture their URLs into a single file (or FUTON1 node set), and do a weekly audit for one month measuring time-to-open and percentage of stale links.]

title: Five Spheres Equilibrium
text: Five Spheres Equilibrium preserve equilibrium across five spheres: Institutional, Consulting, Technical, Reflective, Infrastructure Work naturally clusters into five spheres with different rhythms and demands; imbalance in any sphere propagates stress to the others. one sphere dominates attention for multiple weeks while others go untouched without periodic review, sphere drift is invisible until a neglected area creates urgent demand during weekly review, check that each sphere received some attention (even minimal); flag spheres with no recent activity each sphere has at least one touched item (commit, session, or note) in the past 14 days equilibrium across spheres prevents crisis-driven context switching and keeps all commitments viable track each sphere via tags or labels on org entries, git commits, or session notes. A sphere is "touched" if at least one tagged artifact exists within the window. Private time-management sources may be used as internal signal sources, but publish only the aggregate count of touched spheres. next[Use this pattern to frame the monthly review as a sphere-balance checkpoint.] next[Add tags or labels so sphere touches can be counted without manual review.]

title: Weekly Rhythm Check
text: Weekly Rhythm Check verify that AOB check-in and Ambitions sync occurred within the past 7 days Epistemic rhythm depends on regular review cycles; skipped weeks accumulate drift and allow salients to decay unnoticed. more than 7 days have passed since the last AOB or Ambitions sync event without automated detection, missed weeks go unnoticed until cognitive load spikes or commitments slip flag the gap in Stack HUD; prompt review before new work starts timestamp of last sync event in futon1 or Tatami logs < 7 days ago weekly rhythm prevents unbounded WIP, keeps salients fresh, and makes life feel lighter and more tractable record a weekly sync marker in one of: (a) aob.org/org logs with a timestamped "AOB check-in" / "Ambitions sync" entry, (b) futon1 or Tatami logs with a dedicated event tag, or (c) a git commit note that references the sync event. Use the most recent marker as the check timestamp. next[Add a lightweight sync marker (org log entry, tag, or commit note) so the weekly cadence check has a reliable timestamp.] next[Use this pattern to anchor the regular backup routine as a weekly cadence check.]

title: WIP Cap Enforcement
text: WIP Cap Enforcement regularly review WIP balance; more than 3 active focus areas requires pausing one before starting new work Cognitive load grows nonlinearly with active threads; beyond a threshold, progress on all threads degrades. more than 3 focus areas are marked active simultaneously new work feels urgent and pausing feels like loss, so WIP creeps upward without deliberate enforcement block new work initiation until one active thread is paused or completed; surface the constraint in Stack HUD count of items with status=active in futon1 or Org <= 3 bounded WIP protects depth of focus and prevents the affect collapse that accompanies overload define "active" as any item marked FOCUS or SHIP in org exports, or any futon1 status=active entry. Capture a weekly count from the org columnview table or futon1 status report and store it as a scan note.

title: Lead With the Real Claim; Strawmen Appear Only If a Reader Would
text: Lead With the Real Claim; Strawmen Appear Only If a Reader Would The construction "not X, but also not Y; rather Z" frequently hides the fact that Z is doing all the argumentative work while X and Y are strawmen no reader would actually have proposed. The balanced pair lends Z the appearance of hard-won middle ground. Lead with Z; introduce X and Y only when a reader plausibly would have raised them. AI prose loves the balanced pair. The construction is rhetorically soothing — it signals consideration, nuance, dialectical thinking — even when the X and Y positions exist only in the paragraph that rejects them. When Z stands up on its own, the pair is padding. When Z would be misread without the pair, the pair is earning its keep. The pattern operates on the axis: rhetorical setup ↔ argumentative economy. Irreducible: the same construction cannot simultaneously be (a) necessary dialectical framing and (b) padding. It is one or the other for any given use. Real costs: a genuine dialectical move clarifies what a position is by showing what it rejects. A synthetic dialectical move gives the position unearned weight by inventing rejections. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every claim the writer is not sure will land on its own. - Strawman X: the rejected position is one the paper's own argument makes implausible. - Abstracted poles: X and Y are maximally abstract opposites ("not purely technical, not purely social") framing a Z that could be stated directly. - Triangulated comfort: the balanced pair appears in every paragraph, regardless of whether Z needs dialectical setup. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Lead with Z: state the claim directly. If the reader accepts it without confusion, X and Y were unnecessary. (2) Reintroduce the pair only for a live misreading: if a reader plausibly would have taken Z to mean X or Y, introduce X or Y as the specific misreading being ruled out, not as generic alternatives. (3) Cut Z: occasionally the discovery is that Z is itself unclear. The balanced pair was doing work Z should be doing. Rewrite Z. Engaged when: every "not X, but Y" construction in the draft survives the question "would a reader actually have proposed X?" Failing when: X is a position no competent reader of the paper would have held.

title: Cash the Citation on Load-Bearing Claims
text: Cash the Citation on Load-Bearing Claims A load-bearing claim — one the rest of an argument rests on — must exhibit enough on-page evidence for a reader to judge whether it holds. When a thesis, central finding, or bolded sentence rests on a thin citation (a phrase gesturing at a study, framework, or interview without naming what specifically was found, on what data, with what comparison), the reader is being asked to take the load-bearing move on trust. Typographic emphasis and structural role expose the claim to challenge; the on-page citation must scale with the exposure. Cash the citation, soften the claim, or reposition the load — but do not run a bolded comparative claim on a sixteen-word reference. Working papers often inherit findings from companion or upstream work and treat them as established by reference. This is appropriate when the finding is well-known to the audience, when the reference is short and the claim is incidental, or when the working paper is one of several that compose into a single body of evidence. It fails when the claim is bolded or otherwise typographically marked as load-bearing; the claim makes a comparative or causal assertion ("X matters more than Y", "X drives Z") that requires both sides measured to support directionally; the reference is one phrase rather than a citation with specifics; the companion work's details aren't reproducible from the reference alone. In these cases, the typographic emphasis or the comparative structure promises more than the citation delivers. The reader is left with two unattractive options: take the claim on faith (which subverts the paper's argumentative discipline) or chase down the reference (which a working paper should not require for its central claims). The pattern operates on the axis: claim exposure ↔ citation density. Irreducible: a claim's typographic emphasis and structural role expose it to challenge; the on-page citation must give the reader something to judge against, OR the claim must shrink to match what the citation delivers, OR the load must move to a sibling claim that does have on-page support. Real costs: shoring up a citation means adding sentences that may feel pedagogical, redundant with a companion paper, or off the working paper's central concern. Softening the claim means giving up directional or comparative strength that the analysis genuinely produced. Repositioning the load may demote a finding the writer wants to keep prominent. Each composition gives something up; the pattern's discipline is to choose explicitly rather than to leave the mismatch implicit and hope the reader is generous. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a working paper inherits findings from upstream work. The inheritance pattern wants to be referential ("see X for details") but the load-bearing claim wants the details on-page. Bolding amplifies the mismatch: bold tells the reader "this is what I'm asking you to act on," which raises the citation bar. - Bolded-claim-thin-cite: the claim is typographically marked as load-bearing but the citation is one short phrase. The bold makes a promise the citation does not keep. - Comparative-without-comparison: "X matters more than Y" without exhibiting both X-side and Y-side measured. Comparative direction can only be inferred from one side if the comparison frame itself is well-established in the field, which is rarely the case for novel claims. - Framework-as-citation: the claim cites a methodological framework (NPT, AIF, etc.) instead of a finding from analysis using that framework. Naming the framework does not name the finding. - Reference-only inheritance: the load-bearing claim is established in a companion paper, but the working paper relies on the reader knowing that and chasing it. Acceptable for incidental claims; not for the paper's thesis. - Hedge-instead-of-cite: instead of shoring up the citation, the writer softens with "with reasonable confidence" or similar — preserving the claim's emphasis while gesturing at uncertainty. The hedge is doing the work the citation should do. Match citation density to claim exposure. Pick one explicit composition. (1) Shore up the citation in-line. Augmentation schema: {:claim-form :preserved :evidence-summary <what specifically was found> :method-detail <how it was inferred> :finding-direction <if directional>} Entity types produced: :evidence-summary, :method-detail, :finding-direction-justification Effect: the claim retains its emphasis; the citation grows on-page to support it. Most appropriate when the directional or comparative content is genuinely supported and the paper has room. (2) Soften the claim to match the citation. Augmentation schema: {:claim-direction-fate :dropped-or-preserved :emphasis-form <foregrounding | named-finding | conditional>} Entity types produced: :foregrounded-claim (replaces comparative with "foregrounded as more consequential"), :named-finding-claim (replaces directional with "the analysis named X as the load-bearing factor"), :conditional-claim (replaces unconditional with "under the conditions analysed, X"). Effect: the claim's emphasis shrinks to fit the citation's specificity. Most appropriate when the directional content cannot be honestly supported on one-sided data, or when the comparative is rhetorical rather than substantive. (3) Move the load-bearing weight elsewhere. Augmentation schema: {:load-shift-target <section-id> :replacement-role <subsidiary | supporting | contextual>} Entity types produced: :reference-to-load-bearing-section (the now-secondary claim cites its sibling that does the load-bearing). Effect: a stronger sibling claim — one with denser on-page support — carries the argumentative weight, and the original load-bearing claim becomes supporting rather than central. Appropriate when a different finding in the same paper actually deserves the emphasis. Engaged when every load-bearing claim either (i) exhibits enough on-page citation for evaluation, (ii) is softened to match the citation's specificity, or (iii) is repositioned so a stronger sibling claim carries the load. A skeptical reader, finding a bolded or thesis-level claim, can identify the specific evidence on-page that supports its directional or causal content. Failing when a bolded comparative claim rests on a single-phrase citation and the writer relies on the reader to chase the reference.

title: Use One Canonical Wording for the Same Claim
text: Use One Canonical Wording for the Same Claim When the same factual claim is made in two sections of a paper using different wording, the reader cannot tell whether the difference is a refinement, a qualification, or an inconsistency. Reviewers default to inconsistency. A load-bearing factual claim should have one canonical wording, used verbatim wherever the claim is invoked, with deliberate variation only when the variation is itself doing argumentative work. Section-level rewrites — done at different times, often in response to different reviewer comments — produce drift that the writer doesn't notice because each section locally reads well. Methods says "X for purposes A, B, C"; Limitations says "X for purposes A, B"; Discussion says "X for purpose A". Each is plausible in isolation; together they read as the writer not having decided what the claim is. Distinct from `paraphrase-drift` (intra-paragraph elegant restatement that fails to advance): operates at the section level and concerns *factual* alignment, not rhetorical advancement. The pattern operates on the axis: local fluency in each section ↔ factual coherence across the paper. Irreducible: a load-bearing factual claim either has a canonical formulation in the paper or it does not. Drift cannot simultaneously be (a) inadvertent paraphrase and (b) deliberate argumentative variation. Real costs: a single canonical wording lets the reader recognise repeat invocation as repeat invocation. Variation forces the reader to reconcile the variants and decide which is authoritative. Active dynamic: the pull recurs in any paper rewritten in passes, especially when different reviewers prompt edits in different sections. - Inadvertent narrowing: Limitations restates the claim with one element dropped, suggesting (without intending to) that the dropped element doesn't apply there. - Inadvertent widening: Discussion restates the claim with one element added, suggesting a stronger claim than the paper supports. - Stylistic paraphrase: the writer rephrases for variety, treating the claim as prose rather than as a fixed proposition. - Vocabulary drift across sections: the same entity is named differently in different sections ("training input", "the training course", "the T3 programme"), so the reader cannot tell whether they are the same. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Establish the canonical wording: in the section where the claim does its primary work, settle on one phrasing. Treat that phrasing as the load-bearing version. (2) Quote-and-reuse elsewhere: when the same claim is invoked in another section, use the canonical wording verbatim, or refer back to its first statement. (3) Mark deliberate variation: where a section needs to *qualify* the canonical claim ("subject to X", "in the limit of Y"), make the qualification explicit; do not let the variation read as paraphrase. (4) Audit during integration: when finalising a draft, list every load-bearing claim and the sections where it appears; check that each appearance uses the canonical wording or marks its variation. Engaged when: every restatement of a load-bearing claim either uses the canonical wording verbatim or visibly marks its variation as deliberate. Failing when: the same claim appears in three sections with three subtly different formulations and no signal that any variation is intentional.

title: Discharge the Term at First Mention
text: Discharge the Term at First Mention A domain-specific named entity — an acronym, a programme name, a role title, a coined term — must be introduced at its first mention, even when a fuller treatment is reserved for a later section. When the term first appears unintroduced, the reader carries an unresolved name across paragraphs and sections, hoping that the deferred definition will eventually arrive. This is not the same as preserving suspense; it is forcing the reader to read in low resolution while the writer waits for the right moment to switch on the lights. Acronyms (ORP, ORCA, T3), programme names (the Open Research Programme), role titles ("stewards", "evaluators"), and coined terms ("receiving structure", "logic-model gates") all tend to leak into the introduction or background sections of a paper before they have been introduced. The writer knows what they mean; the reader does not. Distinct from `floating-formalism` (typed vocabulary without grounded named instances) and from `plain-language-thesis` (jargon-reliance at thesis position): here the term *will* be defined later, but the cost is paid now. The pattern operates on the axis: local economy of prose ↔ continuous reader comprehension. Irreducible: the reader either knows what the term means at the point of first use, or does not. No amount of later discharge retroactively closes the comprehension gap during the intervening pages. Real costs: deferring a definition is sometimes the correct choice — when the term is used only ornamentally at first mention and a full definition would derail the paragraph. But ornamental use is rare; load-bearing use is common, and load-bearing terms must be introduced when first invoked. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever the writer is deep enough in the material to forget that the reader is meeting the term for the first time. - Acronym leak: the acronym appears in the introduction; the expansion is parked in the methods section. - Cast member implied: a role ("stewards", "ORCAs") is invoked as if the reader already knows who fills it. - Programme-as-given: a programme or initiative is named without a one-phrase gloss of what it consists of. - Coined-term seeding: a coined term is dropped into the prose with the implicit promise that it will be explained later — and the explanation, when it arrives, no longer fits the contexts in which the term has already done work. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Discharge in plain language: introduce the entity in one phrase at first mention, even if a fuller treatment lives later. "the UKRN Open Research Programme — a distributed five-work-package programme operating across 24 UK higher-education institutions". (2) Demote to ornamental: if first mention is genuinely ornamental, rephrase to avoid invoking the named entity at all, and reserve the term for the section where it earns introduction. (3) Promote the definition: move the full definition to the location of first mention. Subsequent sections then become second-mentions, not first-mentions, and read accordingly. Engaged when: at every named-entity first mention, the reader can state what the entity is from the text adjacent to that first mention. Failing when: the reader has to scan ahead, look up an acronym table, or carry an unresolved name through subsequent paragraphs.

title: Ground the Formalism in Named Instances
text: Ground the Formalism in Named Instances A formalism — a typed vocabulary, a category system, a quadrant diagram, a symbolic notation — earns its place in an argument by compressing content the writer has. A formalism that is invented to *replace* content the writer lacks is free-floating: it looks rigorous without doing the work rigour does. Free-floating formalism is diagnostic of a reality deficit. When you reach for a typed flow, a capitalised-term taxonomy, or a new symbolic schema, check first: can you name a real instance for each element of the formalism? If not, what the argument needs is not more formalism but more reality. No formal element is kept in the argument unless at least one named instance from the actual domain populates it. Formalism that cannot be grounded is either cut or marked as provisional with a note of what grounding would look like. AI-assisted drafting reaches for formalism reliably. A paragraph describing "cross-mode evidence flows" feels stronger than a paragraph naming actual flows between specific places. A table of four quadrants feels stronger than a list of named cases occupying two of them. The feeling tracks the writer's uncertainty: where reality is thin, the formalism compensates. But the reader — especially a reader whose domain is the one the formalism invents for — sees the compensation. Domain experts recognise their own world stripped of its proper nouns and typed into anonymous categories; the formalism reads as signal that the writer did not know the instances. The pattern operates on the axis: formal compression ↔ instance grounding. Irreducible: the same formal vocabulary cannot simultaneously be (a) load-bearing compression over existing reality and (b) substitute for reality the writer does not have. At use time it is doing one or the other. Real costs: a genuine formalism compresses. "Voltage drop across this resistor" is shorter than and equivalent to a paragraph describing the specific physical situation the resistor is in. The formalism earns its compression because the instances are available when needed. An ungrounded formalism extracts the compression without paying for it: the categories exist only in the paper's own text and the instances are never supplied. Active dynamic: the pull recurs every time a writer is describing a domain they know less deeply than the reader — which for AI is most domains that have specific named inhabitants. - Typed flows without named instances: arrows labelled "degradation signal", "diagnostic field report", "repair pattern" between boxes labelled "Multiplied", "Absorbed", "Mismatch" — with no named flow of actual information between two actual places. - Empty quadrants: 2×2 diagrams where three of four quadrants are labelled but only one is populated. - Capitalised-term taxonomy: Capitalized Terms of Art appear only in the paper's own text and carry no external referent. - Symbolic notation without reduction: a new notation is introduced but the argument could be stated without it at comparable length. - Over-typed tables: column headers use formal categories (Valence, Modality, Grain) that the body cells then populate with prose — the formalism adds columns but no compression. - Diagrams as decoration: box-and-arrow figures where the boxes are noun phrases from the surrounding paragraph rather than named entities. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Replace formalism with named instances: if "cross-mode evidence flows" is in the draft, name specific flows between specific places — "external training provided by the Digital Research Academy and the Centre for Open Science", "peer-interview protocols between institutions A and B". Named instances carry the structural point AND ground it. (2) Cash each type with at least one instance: if the formalism is load-bearing and must stay, for every type / category / quadrant, name at least one real instance that occupies it. Empty types are the failure mode; every type populated is the pattern engaged. (3) Drop the formalism: if no instances are available now, the argument does not need the formalism now. State what you can say without it. The formalism can be introduced later, in a draft that has the reality to ground it. Engaged when: every formal element (type, category, quadrant, symbol, capitalised term) can be paired with a named real-world instance drawn from the paper's domain. Failing when: (a) the formalism has types that are never populated with instances; (b) the "instances" supplied are themselves further formal categories; (c) a domain expert reading the passage could name three real things that belong in the formalism but the paper names none. **Reality-deficit test:** list the formal elements. For each, write out the first real instance you can think of from the actual domain. If you stall on more than a third, the formalism is floating.

title: Commit, Defer Properly, or Cut
text: Commit, Defer Properly, or Cut A strong sentence immediately softened by a disclaimer — "though beyond the scope of this paper", "though further work is needed", "though we do not defend this claim here" — asks the reader to both accept the lift and exempt the writer from defending it. The hedge does rhetorical work the argument has not done. Either commit and defend, or defer properly with a forward pointer the reader can chase, or cut. Hedging is useful. A hedge that names a precise scope limit is a service to the reader. A hedge that gestures vaguely at limits ("though beyond the scope", "more research is needed", "though nuance exists") is authorial risk management masquerading as scholarly care. The same sentence cannot both lift and retreat. The pattern operates on the axis: claim strength ↔ authorial safety. Irreducible: a sentence cannot maximise both strength and safety; the hedge is the visible negotiation. Real costs: every claim exposes the writer to challenge; the stronger the claim, the larger the exposure. Hedges reduce exposure but also reduce what the reader can take away. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every strong-claim sentence, particularly in conclusion paragraphs and abstracts. - Beyond-the-scope: "important, though beyond the scope of this paper". - Future-work as escape: "we leave a full treatment to future work" with no indication of what the treatment would involve. - Complexity plea: "the situation is of course more complex than this". - Obligatory nuance: "while acknowledging important nuances..." followed by none. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Commit and defend: keep the strong sentence; use the next sentence to give the reader the argument or evidence behind it. Pay what the lift promised. (2) Defer properly: keep the strong sentence; replace the vague hedge with a forward pointer the reader can follow — "(see §5 for the structural argument)", "(this is the subject of a forthcoming paper, Corneli in preparation)". The deferral is now a service, not an escape. (3) Cut: if the claim cannot be defended now and cannot be properly deferred, it does not belong in the text. Remove the sentence. Engaged when: every strong claim in the draft is either followed by a defence, accompanied by a precise forward pointer, or removed. Failing when: strong claims are followed by vague acknowledgements of limits ("though this is complex", "though nuance exists") that neither defend nor defer.

title: Meet the Reader Where They Are
text: Meet the Reader Where They Are A document grounded in one register (strategic, theoretical, architectural) often has a reader grounded in another (operational, calendar-based, decision-driven). When the registers do not meet, the document looks evasive even when it is principled. The remedy is not to rewrite in the reader's register, which sacrifices the rigour the abstraction was protecting; nor to leave the document unanchored, which forces the reader to translate every passage. The remedy is to insert minimal anchors — calendar tags, cost bands, decision dates, applicability flags — that let the operational reader land without disturbing the document's stance. The move is additive: anchors are parenthetical, italicised, and elidable; the original disclaimer that protects the abstraction's openness must be restated nearby, in the same eyeshot as the anchors. Common in interdisciplinary writing where one document serves planning audiences and theoretical ones at once. Strategic frameworks are deliberately abstract because they hold open future-decision space; operational readers experience that abstraction as refusal. The diagnostic shows up when an operational reviewer reports that the document "doesn't tell me what to do" while a theoretical reviewer reports that the same document is "appropriately principled". Distinct from `meta-lede` (about opening sentences, not register-mismatch across the document), `floating-formalism` (about an unanchored formalism, not an unanchored reader), and `plain-language-thesis` (about thesis legibility, not register accommodation). The pattern operates on the axis: principled abstraction ↔ reader's operational frame. Irreducible: rewriting the document into the operational register sacrifices the rigour the abstraction was protecting; leaving the document fully abstract sacrifices the operational reader. Real costs: an unanchored strategic document forces the operational reader to translate every passage and creates the impression of evasion; an over-anchored document loses the future-space the abstraction was holding and starts to read like a project plan. Active dynamic: the temptation to "soften" the abstraction grows whenever the operational reader pushes back; the temptation to "purify" the abstraction grows whenever a theoretical reader objects to clutter. The pattern recurs at every interface between strategic and operational registers in the document. - Capitulation: rewrite in the operational register and lose the rigour. The strategic frame becomes a project plan. - Refusal: leave the document unanchored and let the reader translate. The operational reader concludes the document is evasive. - Over-anchoring: insert so many anchors that the abstraction's openness collapses. The reader can no longer tell which positions the document is holding open. - Disclaimer drift: anchors are inserted without a nearby restatement of the abstraction's openness; the anchors get read as commitments. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Insert minimal italicised anchors at the points of register interface: `*(≤3 mo)*`, `*(governance-gated)*`, `*[ORP-only]*`, `*(decision binds at Stage 1)*`. Anchors must be parenthetical and visually distinct from the running argument. (2) Restate disclaimers verbatim within the same paragraph or the immediately following one: "These brackets reflect a plausible quickstart calendar; the disclaimer about effort ranges still holds." The anchor and the disclaimer must be in the same eyeshot. (3) Direct the operational reader to a companion document: "the operational addendum names the actions, time horizons, and resource bands required for the framework to become operative." This preserves the main document's register while serving the operational frame elsewhere. (4) Audit by elision: re-read the section without the anchors. The argument should still hold and the disclaimer should still protect openness. If removing the anchors changes the argument, the pattern has been over-applied. Engaged when anchors are present, parenthetical, and elidable; the original disclaimer is restated in the same eyeshot; and the argument runs the same with or without the anchors. Failing when anchors carry argumentative weight (the reader cannot elide them), or no nearby disclaimer protects the abstraction's openness, or the document has been rewritten in the operational register entirely.

title: Open on the Argument, Not on Its Shape
text: Open on the Argument, Not on Its Shape A paragraph's first sentence should perform the argument, not describe the shape of the argument it is about to make. Announcing the shape — "these two things differ in important ways, and those differences have consequences" — tells the reader a paragraph is coming rather than starting it. The concrete contrast itself, stated directly, is both more informative and more economical; the shape becomes visible from the content without being named. AI prose reliably opens paragraphs with a meta-description of the paragraph's own structure: "Both X and Y share Z, but they differ in W, and that difference matters for..." The sentence reads as considered and schematic, but it adds no claim the reader could disagree with. A direct opener spends the same number of words making the actual argument, and the reader hits the claim in the first sentence rather than the second or third. The pattern operates on the axis: argument announcement ↔ argument performance. Irreducible: the same sentence cannot simultaneously describe the shape of a claim and make the claim. Real costs: an announcement flags the paragraph's structure for a skimming reader; a performance commits the writer to content from the first sentence. Both have a place — announcements work for section summaries, chapter heads, abstracts — but inside a working paragraph the performance does more. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every paragraph start, because the meta-sentence is easier to write than the direct one. - Shape-announcement: "X and Y both do Z, but they differ in ways that matter for W." - Topical preamble: "There are several things to say about X, the most important of which is..." - Relevance claim: "This distinction is important, and understanding it requires..." - Apparatus-description: "In what follows, we examine how X relates to Y, and what this implies for Z." Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Cut the meta: delete the announcement sentence entirely. The paragraph's second sentence becomes its first; the shape of the argument emerges from the content. (2) Move the meta up: if the announcement genuinely frames a multi-paragraph section, lift it to a section heading or section-opening sentence where it does structural work, and let the paragraph itself open on the argument. (3) Rewrite as entry: fuse the announcement and the direct claim into one sentence — the "X differs from Y in Z" form where Z is the content, not the claim that content exists. Engaged when: the first sentence of the paragraph states a claim a reader could disagree with, and which carries argumentative weight independently of the rest of the paragraph. Failing when: the first sentence announces that a claim, contrast, or distinction is coming — without making it.

title: Title the Section by What It Says, Not What It Discusses
text: Title the Section by What It Says, Not What It Discusses A title — section, sub-section, working-paper, or document — should answer the question "what is this saying" in itself, not invite the reader to ask. Where a paragraph opening can describe shape without disqualifying itself (the failure named by `meta-lede`), a title that describes shape — "What endorsement commits", "Three concrete commitments", "On the question of X" — fails more sharply, because the reader hits the title and is left needing to read on simply to discover what claim the section makes. The discipline is therefore sharper for titles than for paragraph leads: a meta paragraph opener is suboptimal; a meta title is broken.
