The remedy is to replace the label with the section's actual claim, in plain language, ideally drawn from the section's own load-bearing sentence. AI prose and human first-drafts often title sections with descriptions of what the section will do ("What X means", "On Y", "About Z", "Three observations") rather than statements of what the section says. The reader hits a meta title and is forced to ask "what does X mean? what about Y?" — questions the title itself was supposed to close. Distinct from `meta-lede` (paragraph-level shape-vs-content failure that the paragraph itself can recover from in subsequent sentences) and from `subheading-without-paragraph` (the paragraph fails to discharge what the subheading promised; meta-title is a related but inverse failure where the heading does not even commit to a claim the paragraph could discharge). Closely related to `plain-language-thesis`: titles, like top-level claims, must be readable standalone, by a reader who has not read the section yet. The pattern operates on the axis: title as label-for-topic ↔ title as claim-about-content. Irreducible: a title that names the shape of an argument and a title that performs the argument cannot be the same title. Real costs: a label-style title ("Methods", "Limitations", "Discussion") works in conventional scholarly contexts where the reader knows what each section will contain. A claim-style title does more work in essays, working papers, and any section that is making an argument. The right form depends on genre. Mistaking a working-paper section for a methods section is one source of meta titles; the genre should be diagnosed before the title is set. Active dynamic: meta titles are easier to write because the writer can pull a phrase out of the section's purpose and use it as a label without committing to what the section actually claims. The pull recurs at every section break, especially when the section is being drafted before its claim has stabilised. - Topic label: "On X" / "About Y" / "What X commits" — titles that name a topic without making a claim. Reader is left asking what about X. - Question title: "What does X mean?" — invites the reader to read on for an answer the title should already have provided. - Count-announcement: "Three commitments" / "Four claims" — names a count without naming the content. Reader is left asking what the three or four are. - Shape-announcement: "Argument structure" / "How the model works" — describes the shape of what is to come rather than what is being said. - Genre-confusion: a working paper section uses scholarly conventional labels ("Methodology", "Background") where a claim-style title would do more work for the reader. Replace the label with the section's actual claim; use the section's own load-bearing sentence as candidate; audit by question-test. (1) Replace label with claim: "What endorsement commits" → "Reproducible research applied to learning system design" (the section's own concluding sentence; performs what the section says). "Three commitments" → "Three concrete commitments follow from endorsement" (still light, but at least makes the claim). (2) Use the section's load-bearing sentence: if a single sentence in the section captures what the section says, that sentence (or a compressed form of it) is a candidate title. Often the section's *own concluding line* is the cleanest title for the section. (3) Audit by question-test: read the title; ask "what does the reader still want to know after reading just this title?" If the answer is "what claim the section actually makes", the title is meta. If the answer is "the details that support the claim the title made", the title is fine. (4) Diagnose the genre: if the document is a working paper or argumentative essay, prefer claim-style titles. If it is conventional scholarly prose with established section labels, label-style titles are acceptable and do not need to be replaced. Engaged when reading the title alone tells the reader what the section claims, in plain language, without further reading. Failing when the title describes the section's topic, announces a count without naming what is counted, asks a question the section will answer, or labels the section by its conventional role rather than its content. - In any working paper or argumentative section, audit every subsection heading against this pattern; replace meta titles with their load-bearing claims, often drawn from the section's own concluding line. - Where genre conventions favour label-style titles (Methods, Limitations, References), flag the genre choice as deliberate rather than default. The pattern is then engaged because the writer has named the choice.

title: Name the Mechanism That Makes the Contrast Bite
text: Name the Mechanism That Makes the Contrast Bite A contrast stated without its mechanism is a fact. A contrast stated with its mechanism is generative — it produces consequences the reader can follow to new claims. A paragraph that names a difference but never names what the difference does leaves the reader holding a distinction with nothing to do with it. The mechanism is the hinge between "what the contrast is" and "what the contrast implies"; the visible hinge is often a single sentence of the form "this divides X at the point of Y" or "the consequence is that Z". AI prose is strong at naming contrasts and weak at cashing them. A paragraph will set up "A differs from B because A does X while B does Y" and then close without saying what follows. The reader absorbs the contrast as decorative. A paragraph that names the mechanism — "this divides their working methods at the point of revision" — opens a door to consequences the contrast then pays out: opposite risks, opposite failure modes, opposite affordances. Without the mechanism, the paragraph is complete as description but exhausted as argument. The pattern operates on the axis: contrast as fact ↔ contrast as generator. Irreducible: the same paragraph cannot simultaneously leave the contrast at rest and develop it. To develop, the writer must commit to what the contrast does. Real costs: a well-stated contrast can stand on its own as observation; the writer is not obliged to extract consequences. But a paragraph whose purpose is argument needs its contrasts to generate. A contrast without mechanism closes down; a contrast with mechanism opens up. Active dynamic: the pull recurs every time a writer states a contrast they find satisfying and is tempted to move on. - Decorative contrast: "X does it one way; Y does it another" stated and immediately restated, with no consequence. - Asserted significance: "and that difference decides almost everything" — the significance is claimed but not discharged. - Mechanism in metaphor only: the mechanism is implied by a vivid image but never stated in terms the argument can use. - Consequence-free closing: the paragraph closes on a meta-reframe of the contrast rather than on what the contrast implies. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Name the mechanism explicitly: add a hinge sentence of the form "this divides X at the point of Y" or "the consequence is that Z", then cash the consequences in the sentences that follow. (2) Implicit mechanism + immediate consequence: skip the hinge but immediately state a consequence that reveals the mechanism by inference — "Van Gogh risks the image never arriving..." does this for the revision mechanism. (3) Retire the contrast: if no mechanism is available, the contrast may not belong in an argumentative paragraph. Keep it as description elsewhere (a portrait, a sidebar) or cut. Engaged when: every contrast stated in an argumentative paragraph has, by the end of the paragraph, either an explicit mechanism sentence or an immediate consequence sentence that reveals one. Failing when: the paragraph states a contrast and paraphrases it without ever saying what the contrast produces.

title: Name What You Drop, Not Only What You Inherit
text: Name What You Drop, Not Only What You Inherit When a section describes what a successor project inherits from a predecessor, listing only the inheritance leaves readers to infer the full extent of the inheritance — which they will do generously. The remedy is to name, alongside what is taken, what is deliberately dropped. The drop list is short, explicit, and located in the same eyeshot as the inheritance list; without it, scope is implicit-by-omission and readers will silently over-attribute. The discipline applies symmetrically: when naming what one is doing with a predecessor's work, name what one is leaving behind. Common in working papers, successor proposals, derived programmes, replication studies — anywhere a new effort is positioned relative to a prior effort. The writer knows what they are carrying forward AND what they are letting go; the reader sees only the carrying forward. This produces the silent failure mode where readers assume continuity in scope decisions where the writer has actually re-decided. Distinct from `scope-mush` (about hedged enumeration pretending to scope without specifying it): here the failure is the *absence* of the negative list, not the hedging of a list that exists. The pattern operates on the axis: positive scope visible to reader ↔ scope decisions visible to reader. Irreducible: the reader either has the drop list, or fills it in by default with the predecessor's full scope. Default-fill is generous — the reader assumes inheritance unless told otherwise. Real costs: the drop list looks negative, and the writer often resists writing it for that reason; producing it forces the writer to re-articulate why each dropped item is dropped, which exposes whether the drop is principled or accidental. Active dynamic: the temptation to omit grows whenever the writer believes the drops are obvious; they rarely are, and obvious-to-the-writer is not obvious-to-the-reader. - Silent inheritance: list of inheritances published; list of drops withheld; reader infers full scope continuity. - Hidden drop justifications: drop is mentioned somewhere in the document but not co-located with the inheritance, so the reader does not see it as part of the same scope decision. - Apologetic drop: drops are mentioned but qualified ("we cannot do X for resource reasons"), making them feel temporary even when the decision is principled and permanent. - Drop-as-limitation: drops are placed in a Limitations section, where they read as caveats rather than as architectural decisions. Add an explicit drop list adjacent to the inheritance list; treat each drop as a positive scope decision with its own brief justification. (1) Co-locate the drop list: place "what we drop" / "what is out of scope" / "what we leave behind" immediately after or beside the inheritance list. Eyeshot proximity matters: if the lists are in different sections, the reader will not pair them. (2) Justify the drop, not just name it: each item in the drop list gets a one-clause justification explaining why it is dropped. "Trainer cascade obligations as a contractual structure: UKRN-S trainers deliver, they do not also recruit and train next-tier trainers." The justification turns the drop into a scope decision rather than a deficit. (3) Use a positive frame: "what we drop" or "what we leave behind" frames the list as decision; "what we cannot do" or "limitations" frames it as deficit. Choose decision framing unless deficit is the actual content. (4) Audit by symmetry: read the section listing inheritances; ask "would a reader who saw this list assume we inherit X?" for each candidate drop. If yes for any, the drop list needs to include X. Engaged when the section that lists inheritances is paired with a drop list of comparable visibility, each drop carries its own justification, and the framing presents drops as decisions rather than deficits. Failing when inheritances are listed without their corresponding drops, or when drops are scattered into footnotes or limitations sections rather than co-located with inheritances.

title: One Paragraph Per Typed Claim
text: One Paragraph Per Typed Claim When a paragraph carries multiple structurally distinct claims — two scenarios, three cases, several findings — each fused together by em-dashes and semicolons doing the structural-separation work that paragraph breaks should do, the reader has to recover the claim-count from punctuation rather than from layout. This is most visible when the prose is meant to correspond to an external visual (a figure with N panels, a table with N rows): if the figure shows four panels but the prose collapses two of them into one paragraph, the prose-figure correspondence breaks at exactly the point a reader scanning between them would expect to find alignment. The fix is structurally honest: one paragraph per typed claim, or one bullet per claim, or move to a list/table form when the claim-count gets large. Prose paragraphs are typed by their structural role — an evidence-presentation paragraph, a synthesis paragraph, a scenario-description paragraph, a counter-claim paragraph. When a single paragraph carries two scenarios, two findings, or two arguments, it's doing the work of two paragraphs in one — and signalling this only with internal punctuation (em-dashes, semicolons, "and" coordinators). Readers who skim by paragraph count miss the implicit structure entirely. Readers cross-referencing to a figure see N panels and N-1 paragraphs and have to figure out where the missing-paragraph's content went. The fix is to split. The pattern operates on the axis: paragraph-as-structural-unit ↔ paragraph-as-prose-rhythm. Irreducible: either the paragraph count matches the typed-claim count, or the typed-claim count is hidden inside punctuation. Real costs: splitting a fused paragraph into two paragraphs can lose narrative flow (sometimes the em-dash and semicolon were doing genuine connective work). Short paragraphs can read as choppy. And not every multi-claim paragraph is best split — sometimes the claims are genuinely subordinate (a main claim with a parenthetical caveat), and splitting promotes the caveat above its rank. Active dynamic: the pull toward fusion is strongest in synthesis or summary paragraphs (where multiple findings are being assembled), in scenario-bounding paragraphs (where the writer is naming "two scenarios that bracket the envelope" and treating them as a pair), and in evidence-presentation paragraphs (where a primary claim and its supporting detail get rolled together). - Em-dash structural work: the em-dash is carrying paragraph-break weight (separating two scenarios, two findings, two cases) where a paragraph break is the appropriate structural marker. - Semicolon-stack: three or more semicolons in a paragraph that's actually three or more claims stitched together. - Prose-figure misalignment: a figure has N panels (or a table has N rows); the corresponding prose has fewer paragraphs, with some panels' content fused into others. - "Two scenarios" sentence followed by one paragraph: the writer explicitly says "two scenarios" but writes only one paragraph to cover both — the announce-vs-deliver mismatch. - List collapsed into prose: what should have been a 3-item list ("first, ...; second, ...; third, ...") gets written as one prose paragraph; the reader has to count manually. Match paragraph structure to typed-claim structure. Pick one composition. (1) Split into one paragraph per claim. Augmentation schema: {:claim-count <n> :paragraph-titles <optional, one per claim>} Entity types produced: :split-paragraph (one per claim) Effect: paragraph count now matches claim count; figure-correspondence (if applicable) becomes legible. (2) Convert to a list or table. Augmentation schema: {:list-or-table :list | :table :columns <if table>} Entity types produced: :structured-list, :typed-row Effect: most appropriate when the claims are short, parallel, and would be served by visual alignment (a 4-row table is more legible than 4 short paragraphs). (3) Subordinate the secondary claim. Augmentation schema: {:primary-claim <id> :subordinate-claim <id> :subordination-form :parenthetical | :footnote | :inline-clause} Entity types produced: :subordinated-claim Effect: when the two claims aren't actually structurally equal (one is the main scenario, one is a caveat), explicitly mark the subordinate as parenthetical rather than fusing as if both were primary. Engaged when paragraph count matches typed-claim count (for paragraphs carrying scenarios, findings, or cases) and any prose-figure correspondence is exhibitable by 1:1 alignment. A skeptical reader can count claims by counting paragraphs. Failing when a sentence announcing "N scenarios" is followed by fewer than N paragraphs, or when an em-dash inside a paragraph is doing paragraph-break work.

title: Every Sentence Must Advance
text: Every Sentence Must Advance Each sentence in a paragraph must add something the preceding sentences did not. A sentence that re-expresses a prior claim in prettier language — however elegant the rephrasing — is drift, not development. The paragraph ends in roughly the same place it started, and the reader has absorbed two or three beautiful versions of a single idea rather than one idea plus two or three consequences of it. Paraphrase drift is the most literate failure mode in AI-assisted prose. It reads as sophisticated because each restatement reaches for a new metaphor — "the surface is a transcript", "evidence of a nervous system", "a rendering medium" — and the cumulative effect is of depth. But a reader who tracks what the paragraph claims, sentence by sentence, finds the sentences say the same thing. A good paragraph states the claim once and then spends its remaining sentences on what follows from it: a mechanism, a consequence, a contrast, a complication. The pattern operates on the axis: restatement ↔ development. Irreducible: a single sentence cannot simultaneously restate the prior sentence and advance beyond it. The choice is local and binary. Real costs: restatement is easier, prettier, and feels safer — each new phrasing reduces the risk that one phrasing lands badly. Development is harder because it commits to a next claim that must itself be defended. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every sentence boundary, especially after a sentence the writer is pleased with. - Metaphor stack: "the surface is a transcript; paint as evidence of a nervous system; a record of its own making" — three images, one claim. - Semicolon-pair chains: the same contrast re-rendered as "X does A; Y does B" three times with different As and Bs that mean the same thing. - Elegant-close drift: the paragraph's last sentence is its most beautiful restatement rather than its strongest consequence. - Synonymous parallelism: "Not only X, but also Y" where X and Y are the same observation in different words. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Develop: replace a restatement sentence with a sentence that names the mechanism, consequence, or condition that follows from the prior claim. The paragraph now advances. (2) Cut: delete the restatement entirely. If the prior sentence was well-made, the paragraph does not lose argument by losing the paraphrase. (3) Promote one phrasing, cut the others: if multiple paraphrases exist across consecutive sentences, keep the strongest and cut the rest. A single well-chosen metaphor beats three stacked. Engaged when: every sentence in a paragraph adds a claim, mechanism, consequence, or precondition not present in the preceding sentences. Failing when: consecutive sentences map, under paraphrase, to the same underlying assertion.

title: State Top-Level Claims in Plain Language
text: State Top-Level Claims in Plain Language A top-level claim — the paper's thesis, a section's "lemma"-style opening assertion, an exec-summary proposition — must be readable standalone, by a reader who has not read the rest of the work. This means: no load-bearing jargon (terms that require prior definition from the paper to resolve), and no syntactic contortion (subjects buried behind referring expressions the reader has to unpack). Body paragraphs can lean on technical vocabulary the paper earns as it goes; top-level claims cannot, because they are the first thing the reader meets and the last thing the reader remembers. AI-assisted drafting routinely produces top-level claims that sound precise to the writer — who has the whole paper loaded — but require the paper-internal context to parse. "UKRN-S's core function is to hold the evidence apex" reads cleanly if §1 is in head; reads as an impenetrable noun phrase otherwise. Similarly "the service bearing it accepts five design disciplines" forces the reader to reconstruct what "the service bearing it" refers to, which introduces a small but repeating friction with every re-read. The claim may be correct; it is not *landing* as a claim. The pattern operates on the axis: precision ↔ standalone readability. Irreducible: the same sentence cannot simultaneously be maximally precise (using the paper's earned terms) and maximally standalone (using terms any reader already carries). At thesis position, standalone wins; at body position, precision can win. Real costs: technical vocabulary earns compression. The same sentence with jargon can encode more than its plain-language sibling. But at the thesis position, the compression is paid by readers who don't have the prior context — which, for a thesis, is every reader on first encounter and every skimming reader on every encounter. Active dynamic: the pull recurs every time the writer states a claim at the paper or section top — because the writer has the context and the reader, at that position, provably does not. - Jargon-reliance: "UKRN-S's core function is to hold the evidence apex that the ORP could not" — "evidence apex" requires §1; "ORP" requires prior-knowledge acronym expansion. - Syntactic displacement: "the service bearing it accepts five design disciplines" — "it" resolves to something the sentence does not carry; "the service bearing it" puts the real subject three words in. - Shibboleth: "We operationalise five coherence patterns under NPT sub-construct ratings in a prior-predictive framework" — parses only for readers inside the paper's community. - Nested-clause thesis: "The claim, which rests on the observation that X, when Y, is Z" — correct but unparseable cold. - Capitalised-concept overload: "The Sustainability Tetrahedron's Evidence Apex coordinates the Three Mode-Sub-Tetrahedra" — internal capitalisation does not compensate for missing definitions. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Strip the jargon: name the referent directly using a term the reader already carries. "Evidence apex" → "the kind of cross-institutional evidence that makes local success conditions legible to others". Longer, but readable cold. (2) Unbury the subject: the sentence's actor and verb should be first-hit parseable. "The service bearing it accepts five disciplines" has subject "the service bearing it" — a three-word referring expression before the main verb. "A centrally-administered training programme becomes a learning system when..." leads with a concrete subject. (3) Define-and-use in the same sentence: if a technical term is genuinely load-bearing and cannot be unstripped, define it in the sentence before invoking it — "UKRN-S's core function is to hold the evidence apex — the shareable, translatable evidence of what works locally". Rare; costs length; paid only when the term earns it. (4) Two-sentence decompression: one sentence states the claim in plain language; the next promotes the technical term. "UKRN-S becomes a learning system when it inhabits the design tensions the programme has named. In the paper's geometric terms, UKRN-S holds the evidence apex relative to three mode-tetrahedra." The plain version is the thesis; the technical version is the operational sharpening. Engaged when: the top-level claim is comprehensible to a reader who has not read the paper, with no forward-reference to section content, and parses on first read without mental contortion. Failing when: (a) a term in the claim requires prior paper content to resolve (jargon-reliance), or (b) the subject-verb-object structure requires the reader to re-parse to locate what acts on what (syntactic displacement), or (c) the claim reads as signal of membership in the paper's argument community rather than as a claim (shibboleth). **Standalone-reader test:** paste the sentence alone into a message to someone unfamiliar with the work. Can they tell what is being claimed, even roughly? If not, the pattern is not engaged.

title: Show the Recursion at at Least One Scale, or Drop It
text: Show the Recursion at at Least One Scale, or Drop It A sentence claiming that an argument applies at multiple scales — "the same argument applies within X as across X", "the structure is recursive: the same pattern holds at each level" — writes a cheque that must be cashed. Either the paper demonstrates the claim at at least one scale, or it does not belong. Recursion, fractality, and self-similarity are analytical devices only when they produce a result the flat view does not. Recursion claims are attractive because they sound elegant and ambitious. They promise that one argument covers multiple phenomena. They are dangerous because the elegance is free — the writer pays nothing to claim recursion, and the reader has no way to check unless the paper exhibits it. AI prose tips toward making recursion claims that the paper has set up but not demonstrated. The pattern operates on the axis: generalisation claim ↔ demonstration capacity. Irreducible: a claim cannot simultaneously generalise across scales and decline to show any scale beyond the original. Real costs: recursion, when genuine, is a powerful compression. Recursion, when asserted without demonstration, is mere rhetoric. The paper cannot have the compression without paying for it. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a paper's main argument feels "big enough" to generalise but has only been shown in one form. - Undemonstrated within-X: "the same logic that holds across institutions holds within them" with no within-institution case. - Asserted fractality: "the structure is recursive / fractal / self-similar" as a closing gesture. - Free elegance: recursion claim appears only in the conclusion, not in the body. - Circular defence: when questioned, the writer points to the main argument as evidence the recursion holds — but the main argument is at the primary scale only. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Cash at one scale: keep the recursion claim; add one concrete instance at a second scale. Show the argument biting at the smaller or larger scale the claim names. The recursion is now earned by exhibition. (2) Cash at both scales: if the recursion is structurally central (not decorative), demonstrate it at both. This is the highest-commitment path and is appropriate when the recursion IS the result. (3) Drop the claim: if no scale-shifted demonstration is available, remove the recursion sentence. The paper still has everything it had before; what it loses is a claim it could not back. Engaged when: every recursion or multi-scale claim in the paper is accompanied by at least one concrete demonstration beyond the primary scale. Failing when: "the same argument applies at scale Y" appears without a demonstration at scale Y.

title: Name the Real Reasons Individually, or Not at All
text: Name the Real Reasons Individually, or Not at All Constructions like "this matters for a variety of reasons, including..." or "among other things, X, Y, and Z..." typically contain either one real reason padded with filler, or several reasons of unequal weight that would each deserve a sentence. The mush signals coverage without paying its cost. Name the reasons individually and defend each, or state a single reason cleanly, or drop the list. Scope mush is a form of enumeration that has lost faith in its own items. The "variety" hedges the quantity; the "including" hedges the selection; the "among other things" hedges both. AI prose reaches for the mush when the writer has not sorted which reasons are load-bearing. Readers sense the lack of commitment and discount the whole sentence. The pattern operates on the axis: coverage ↔ specificity. Irreducible: a sentence cannot simultaneously claim broad coverage and commit to specific items. Either the scope is wide and the items are examples, or the scope is narrow and the items are the argument. Real costs: a genuinely multi-reason claim deserves enumeration with defences per item. A single-reason claim deserves one sentence that states the reason cleanly. Mush optimises for neither. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a writer has more than one candidate reason but has not ranked or differentiated them. - Variety hedge: "for a variety of reasons, including..." with one real reason and filler. - Among-other-things: "among other things, X, Y, and Z" where the "other things" never surface. - Uneven weight: a three-item list where item 1 carries the claim and items 2–3 are illustrations promoted to parallel status. - Open-ended enumeration: "such as A, B, C, ..." where the trailing "..." exempts the writer from completeness. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Name one and defend it: if one reason is load-bearing, cut the list and state that reason with its defence. "This matters because X" beats "this matters for a variety of reasons". (2) Split into sentences: if several reasons carry distinct weight, give each its own sentence with its own defence. The enumeration is now an argument, not a gesture. (3) Drop the list: if the claim stands alone without a reason catalogue, remove the list entirely. Readers are not well-served by the variety-claim if the items are not going to work. Engaged when: every "variety of reasons" / "among other things" / "including" list in the draft has been rewritten as either a single committed reason or as per-sentence enumerated reasons. Failing when: lists appear where the items are not individually defended and are not clearly illustrative of a single committed claim.

title: Bridge the Section Boundary
text: Bridge the Section Boundary A section boundary is the place where the reader most needs help: the closing paragraph must name what has been established, and the next opening paragraph must name what is now to be addressed. When the closing sentence reads as a finding rather than a positioning move, and the next section begins cold, the reader cannot tell whether the closing claim was the section's conclusion or its setup. The section-to-section connective tissue has been silently elided, and the argument's spine goes invisible at exactly the joints. AI drafts and condensed academic prose both tend to drop the bridge. Each paragraph stands locally well, and each section opens with a competent topic sentence; but the relationship between them has been left to the reader to reconstruct from the section titles alone. Reviewers experience this as "the argument jumps" even when no individual paragraph is weak. Distinct from `throat-clearing-close` (which is about ending on attitude rather than claim) and from `meta-lede` (which is about opening on shape rather than content): here the diagnostic is the *transition*, not either sentence in isolation. The pattern operates on the axis: local paragraph competence ↔ argumentative continuity across sections. Irreducible: the bridge cannot be supplied by section titles alone — titles signal topic, but the reader needs the argumentative move from one to the next. Real costs: a strong closing paragraph orients the reader to what has just been established; a strong opening paragraph names what is now at stake. Without both, the section boundary asserts a structural break the argument never repairs. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every section break, and is strongest where the writer has been deep inside one section and forgets that the reader is about to leave it. - Cold open: the next section begins with a topic sentence that ignores the closing claim of the previous section. - Finding-as-close: the closing sentence asserts a result without orienting the reader to what is next. - Title-as-bridge: the writer relies on the section title to do the connective work, leaving the reader to infer the argumentative move. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Close on positioning: rewrite the closing sentence so it names what the section established AND points at what remains open. "Frameworks for collective stewardship therefore direct attention away from individual motivation and toward whether the institutional conditions are in place." (2) Open on connection: add a connective sentence at the start of the next section that names the move being made. "A complementary perspective comes from implementation science, which distinguishes adoption from implementation from sustainability." (3) Audit at every break: read the last sentence of section N immediately followed by the first sentence of section N+1, with nothing else. If the move from one to the other is not legible from those two sentences, the bridge is missing. Engaged when: the last sentence of each section reads as a positioning move AND the first sentence of the next section names what is now being addressed. Failing when: either the close reads as a finding without forward orientation, or the open begins cold without acknowledging what the previous section established.

title: Audit the Downstream After Restructure
text: Audit the Downstream After Restructure When a paper undergoes a structural change — a section removed, a step renumbered, a definition revised, a term renamed — every downstream reference to the changed element becomes a candidate for staleness. The drift is referential, not stylistic: the wording is unchanged, but what the wording points at no longer exists or no longer means what it did. Local re-reading does not catch it because each section reads correctly in isolation. The remedy is an audit pass at the moment of restructure that lists each affected element and its referents, then updates each referent to reflect the new structure or flags it for deletion. Common during late-stage paper revision when the author is making one structural change at a time and not running a full re-read. Especially common when a section is moved, a numbered step is dropped, or a worked example is replaced. Distinct from `cross-section-claim-drift` (about wording variation across sections sharing a claim) and from `paraphrase-drift` (about local sentence-level restatement): here the wording is consistent and the semantics has shifted underneath it. The diagnostic is "the sentence is fine, but its referent is gone." The pattern operates on the axis: local section coherence ↔ post-restructure global coherence. Irreducible: a reference either points at something the document still contains, or it does not. Local rewording does not change which. Real costs: a full audit after every micro-edit is expensive and slows iteration; deferring the audit to a final pass risks accumulating drift that becomes hard to untangle. Active dynamic: the temptation to skip the audit grows with the size of the document and the smallness of the edit, even though the failure mode does not depend on edit size — a single removed bullet can leave stale references in three later sections. - Numbered-step drift: "Step 4" referenced in a downstream pattern composition after Step 4 has been removed from the bootstrap sequence. - Renamed-term shadow: a term renamed in the methods is still referred to by its old name in the discussion. - Cross-reference to vanished section: "see §3.2" remains in the text after §3.2 has been merged into §3.1. - Deleted-figure reference: "as Figure 4 shows" persists after Figure 4 was cut. - Worked-example drift: a worked example revised in §3 is still cited in §5 with the old numbers. Audit at the moment of restructure; update or delete every downstream reference; verify by grep. (1) Audit at the moment of restructure: when removing or renaming an element, immediately grep the document for every reference to the element and decide for each whether to update, delete, or flag. This is cheaper than deferring. (2) Maintain a restructure log: keep a running list of structural changes during a revision pass; before declaring the pass complete, audit every reference against the log. (3) Use unique tokens for high-risk elements: when a structural element is likely to be referenced (numbered steps, named patterns, figure numbers), keep the token as distinctive as possible so an audit grep is reliable. (4) Audit by elision-test: re-read each section that references an element after the element has been changed; the section should still hold without the reference. If removing the reference breaks the section, the reference is load-bearing and must be updated, not merely removed. Engaged when no downstream reference points at an element that has been removed, renamed, or moved without being updated. Failing when grepping for a removed element returns hits in sections other than the one where the removal happened. - Validate the system-level analogue when a documented use-case becomes available. The principle plausibly extends from documents to systems: when a system is restructured (a service decommissioned, an interface renamed, a role redistributed), every downstream dependency becomes a candidate for staleness, and the same audit discipline applies. Confirming the analogue requires concrete cases of system restructure and dependency-staleness; without those, the analogue is conjectural and should not be promoted to `system-coherence` on speculation (per `system-coherence/argue-empirically-not-persuasively`: a pattern must follow from a use-case, not be speculated forward). - If the system-level analogue is later validated, draft `system-coherence/audit-downstream-dependencies-after-restructure` with concrete failure-modes drawn from the validating cases.

title: Normalise Heading Conventions Across Logical Depths
text: Normalise Heading Conventions Across Logical Depths Headings, sub-headings, and run-in bold labels carry the document's hierarchy. When their format drifts within the document — level-3 hashes in one section, run-in bold in another, sentence case here, title case there, terminating period sometimes and not others — the reader scanning the table of contents or skim-reading cannot infer which subheadings carry equal weight. The hierarchy that the writer has in mind is not the hierarchy the reader can see. Distinct from `subheading-without-paragraph` (about whether the body discharges the subheading's promise): here the body is fine but the *form* of the subheading drifts. Documents written in passes, or assembled from multiple authors' contributions, accumulate heading-style inconsistency the way they accumulate citation-style inconsistency — locally invisible, globally distracting. Run-in bold for some level-3s and hashes for others; sentence case here and title case there; sometimes "Methods.", sometimes "Methods", sometimes "Methods:". Reviewers read the inconsistency as a sign that the document has not been edited as a whole. The pattern operates on the axis: local readability of each section ↔ document-level legibility of the hierarchy. Irreducible: a heading at logical depth N either follows the same format as other headings at depth N, or it doesn't. The reader has no other channel for inferring depth. Real costs: the convention chosen at each logical depth is a small thing. Choosing inconsistently is also a small thing per-occurrence. Across a 30-page document, the cumulative effect is that no reader can use the heading hierarchy as a navigation aid. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever the document grows, and especially when content is moved between sections without re-styling its headings. - Mixed levels: some level-3s use hashes, others use run-in bold; the table of contents gives the reader a misleading skeleton. - Capitalisation drift: title case ("Logic Model Composition") and sentence case ("Logic model composition") both appear at the same depth. - Punctuation drift: some headings end with a period, some with a colon, some with neither. - Inherited formatting: a section copied from another document carries that document's heading style and was never normalised. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Choose one convention per depth: at each logical depth, pick a single format (hash level, capitalisation, terminating punctuation, bold/italic) and apply it everywhere at that depth. (2) Audit top-to-bottom: in one pass, read the document looking only at headings — ignore body text — and normalise to the chosen conventions. (3) Demote run-in bold to bold paragraph leads only where they are doing genuinely different work from a subheading: a run-in bold "Logic model composition." that introduces a multi-paragraph subsection should be promoted to a subheading; a run-in bold that introduces a single-sentence note should be left as run-in bold. (4) Decide the punctuation rule once: terminating period or no, colon or no, sentence or title case — and apply it. Engaged when: a reader scrolling the document or scanning the table of contents can correctly infer logical depth from formatting alone. Failing when: two headings at the same logical depth are formatted differently, or two headings at different logical depths look the same.

title: Discharge the Subheading's Claim
text: Discharge the Subheading's Claim A subheading is a promise that the following paragraph will make a specific claim. When the paragraph names the concept but does not discharge the promise — two or three sentences that gesture at the label without stating what the label actually asserts — the subheading is a label looking for a paragraph, and the document's structural skeleton goes soft at that point. AI drafts frequently produce subheadings that sound structural ("Ontogenetic accretion", "Architectural sustainability", "The recursive scaffold") but whose paragraphs merely restate the concept's existence. The subheading commits to more than the text pays. The pattern operates on the axis: structural promise ↔ content capacity. Irreducible: a subheading cannot both promise a claim and merely name a concept. Real costs: a strong subheading carves the argument into inspectable units; an under-discharged subheading creates the appearance of structure without the argumentative weight. Readers track subheadings as a proxy for what the paper claims. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a writer has a strong concept name but hasn't yet written the paragraph that earns it. - Concept-drop: the subheading names a concept; the paragraph says the concept is important. - Two-sentence stub: a paragraph of two sentences under a subheading, neither of which states a claim. - Restatement: the paragraph restates the subheading in a full sentence and stops. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Expand: discharge the promise. Write the paragraph that makes the claim the subheading asserted. If the concept is "ontogenetic accretion", walk the reader through what accretes, at which stage, from which prior deposit. (2) Fold: drop the subheading and merge the existing content into an adjacent section as a closing remark or bridge sentence. Concept survives; structural promise retracts. (3) Rename: replace the ambitious subheading with one that matches the claim actually present. If the paragraph says "each stage depends on prior stages", the subheading should say that, not "ontogenetic accretion". Engaged when: reader can state the subheading's claim in one sentence, independent of the subheading, drawn from the paragraph body. Failing when: the only sentence that makes the claim is the subheading itself.

title: End on the Claim, Not the Attitude
text: End on the Claim, Not the Attitude A paragraph — especially an executive-summary or section-closing paragraph — earns its ending by leaving the reader with a claim. When the last sentence instead expresses an aim, hope, or authorial posture toward the work, it tells the reader what the writer feels rather than what they argue, and the paragraph loses its structural payload. AI-assisted prose tends to close warm: "the overall aim is to help X inhabit this space", "we hope this will serve as a starting point", "this paper aims to contribute to...". These closers function as rhetorical exhale after the real argument. They are not wrong — they are under-committed. The pattern operates on the axis: warmth / attitude ↔ claim / proposition. Irreducible: a single sentence cannot be simultaneously maximally warm and maximally propositional; the two pull in opposite directions. Real costs: warmth signals intellectual humility and softens the ask; a claim commits, which is riskier and harder to retract. Both have costs. Active dynamic: the pull recurs at every paragraph close — warmth wants the last word because it is easier to write. - Aim-as-close: "the aim is to help X inhabit / learn / grow / develop". - Hope-as-close: "we hope this contributes to / opens a conversation about". - Meta-as-close: "this paper attempts to set out a framework for...". - Self-congratulation: "this approach represents a promising direction". Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Commit: replace the softener with the strongest claim the paragraph supports. "This paper argues X" lands harder than "this paper aims to help with X". (2) Relocate warmth: move the attitudinal sentence upstream (into the paragraph's opening or the section intro) so it frames rather than closes, and end on the claim. (3) Cut: delete the softener entirely. Readers rarely miss it; they were already weighing the claim. Engaged when: the last sentence of the paragraph states a proposition a careful reader could disagree with. Failing when: the last sentence expresses an aim, a hope, a promise of help, or a meta-reflection about what the paper is doing.

title: Make the Third Item Earn Its Place
text: Make the Third Item Earn Its Place Three parallel items where two would do — because three sounds structural — leaves the third item carrying no weight the first two do not. The triad inflates the appearance of a considered enumeration. The third term earns its place only when it carries a distinct claim the reader could lose by dropping it. The rule of three has genuine force: it signals completeness, rhythm, balance. It also has genuine cost: a triad invites the writer to round out a pair with a filler term that is a hyponym, synonym, or restatement. AI prose does this often — "conceptually, structurally, and operationally" — where the three adverbs overlap substantially in meaning. The pattern operates on the axis: parallelism as polish ↔ argumentative weight. Irreducible: a list cannot simultaneously optimise rhythm and carry distinct weight per item; one must give. Real costs: symmetric lists feel complete and read well. Asymmetric lists feel unfinished even when they are accurate. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a pair would read as incomplete. - Adverb stack: "conceptually, structurally, and operationally" where the three overlap. - Synonym triad: "robust, durable, and resilient" — three words for one property. - Instance promoted to parallel: "physics, chemistry, and the hard sciences generally" — category error disguised as triad. - Rhetorical rhythm: the triad appears because two-item lists felt incomplete, not because the third term earned its place. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Drop the third: if the third item does not carry distinct weight, cut it. Pairs are not weaker than triads; they are more honest. (2) Replace the third with a specific instance: convert the third abstract term into a concrete example that exemplifies both of the first two. The triad now carries different work per slot. (3) Keep all three and declare what each does: if the triad is load-bearing, make the per-slot distinction visible in the surrounding sentences, so the reader can see why three and not two. Engaged when: removing the third item changes what the reader would conclude. Failing when: the third item is a hyponym of, synonym for, or restatement of the first or second.

title: Replace the Rhetorical Collapse With the Structural Reason
text: Replace the Rhetorical Collapse With the Structural Reason Words like "essentially", "fundamentally", "simply", "basically", "just" ask the reader to accept that the current sentence is the collapsed form of a deeper argument. They do rhetorical work the paper has not done. Either the actual structural reason belongs in the sentence — at which point the adverb is redundant — or no collapse has been earned — at which point the adverb lies. These adverbs are one of the clearest AI-prose signatures. They compress without doing the work of compression. Used well, "essentially" signals that a careful argument has been made earlier and is now being invoked; used badly, it signals that the writer wishes the argument had been made. The pattern operates on the axis: rhetorical force ↔ argumentative warrant. Irreducible: the same adverb cannot simultaneously earn its collapse (reader has the derivation) and substitute for the derivation (reader does not). Real costs: a genuine "essentially" is efficient — it lets a reader skip the full derivation when they already have it. A counterfeit "essentially" extracts the efficiency without paying for it. Active dynamic: the pull recurs whenever a claim needs to sound harder-earned than the paper has actually earned. - Essentially as warrant: "the relationship is essentially X" where X is the actual structural claim being made for the first time. - Simply as softener: "the argument is simply that..." where the argument is, in fact, not simple. - Fundamentally as gravitas: "fundamentally, this is about..." where the adverb adds weight but no information. - Just as scope control: "we just need to show that..." where the claim being shown is actually substantial. Operate an explicit move on the named axis (see substructure below); steward the pattern against the declared discipline. (1) Replace with the structural reason: if the adverb is load-bearing, state the reason it compresses. "Essentially multiplicative" becomes "multiplicative because D and A combine as a product, so either dimension alone can bound the whole" — and the adverb is redundant. (2) Cut the adverb: if the reader already has the derivation from earlier in the paper, the collapse is earned and the adverb is decorative. Remove it. (3) Earn the collapse: if the adverb is load-bearing and the derivation has not appeared, write the derivation (possibly in a prior paragraph or footnote) before invoking the collapse. Engaged when: every instance of "essentially / fundamentally / simply / basically / just" in the draft either has a prior derivation the reader can point to, or is explicitly replaced by the structural reason, or is cut. Failing when: the adverb is the strongest warrant the claim has.

title: Live Recording Bridge
text: Live Recording Bridge Capture live performances as artifacts so divergent aspirations can align. A collaborative music project contains divergent but compatible aspirations about presence and durable artifacts. A collaborator seeks to play gigs as a primary mode of engagement. Another collaborator is motivated by the creation of recorded albums rather than by live performance as an end in itself. The artifact-oriented collaborator can support live performances by equipping themselves to capture those performances as live recordings. This reframes gigs as opportunities for artifact production, allowing both aspirations to be met without forcing alignment on performance-first or studio-first priorities. - Attend to whether the capture setup remains proportionate to the artifact goal. - Watch for pressures that attempt to reclassify it as general-purpose live-sound infrastructure.
